article_title: Dewey's Theory of Inquiry and Reflective Administration.
citation: Willower, Donald J. (1992). Dewey's Theory of Inquiry and Reflective Administration. Paper presented at the annual convention of the University Council for Educational Administration, Minneapolis. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED355669
title: Institutionalize reflective methods in organizational norms, symbols, and procedures so critical appraisal becomes routine
description: The paper argues that individual reflective administrators need organizational support, since reflective methods threaten fixed and favorite beliefs and will not take hold without widespread openness to communication and critical assessment of ideas. Institutionalization means embedding reflective methods in the norms, values, symbols, shared meanings, values structures and procedures of the organization, so that critical appraisal becomes routine, part and parcel of everyday organizational life. The paper reports that institutionalized reflective methods should lead to better and more ethical organizational decisions and that decisions subject to reflective assessment are usually easy to defend.
requirements: Organizational arrangements, beliefs, and practices geared toward reflective methods
Widespread openness to communication and to the critical assessment of ideas
constraints: The paper warns reflective methods are not a technology to be imposed, not a panacea nor even a sure thing, and that honest and critical discussions of problems are anything but typical of organizations
examples: The paper lists sample organizational comments such as 'We're not afraid to criticize ideas' and devices for formal groups including a devil's advocate and 'What can go wrong?' sessions
key_sources: Willower, Donald J. (1992). Dewey's Theory of Inquiry and Reflective Administration. Paper presented at the annual convention of the University Council for Educational Administration, Minneapolis. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED355669

article_title: Connect: UNESCO-UNEP Environmental Education Newsletter, 1993.
citation: United Nations Educational, Scientific, and Cultural Organization, Paris (France). Environmental Education Section. (1993). Connect: UNESCO-UNEP Environmental Education Newsletter, 1993. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED368567
title: Infuse global change instruction into existing curricula while ensuring in-depth issue knowledge, investigation skills, citizenship skills and an internal locus of control
description: Because global change instruction is interdisciplinary, the article argues the most effective way to deliver it in schools is to incorporate it into existing curricula rather than teach it as a separate subject. It specifies broad principles the infused curriculum must provide: "An in-depthknowledgeof issues", teaching skills of issue analysis and investigation, teaching citizenship skills for issue remediation, and "An attempt to develop aninternal locus of control". In secondary schools, contents and skills can be integrated into courses such as agriculture, home economics, health, science, social studies or language arts without jeopardising the courses themselves.
requirements: Cooperation from all teachers responsible for the infused programmes, whose willingness to build and carry out an infusion plan the article calls a key component of effectiveness
target_learners: secondary school teachers infusing EE into subject courses
examples: The article states that courses in agriculture, home economics, health, science, social studies or language arts could lend themselves to infusion of global change contents and skills
key_sources: United Nations Educational, Scientific, and Cultural Organization, Paris (France). Environmental Education Section. (1993). Connect: UNESCO-UNEP Environmental Education Newsletter, 1993. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED368567

article_title: Deep Learning as an Individual, Conditional, and Contextual Influence on First-Year Student Outcomes
citation: Reason, R. D., Cox, B. E., McIntosh, K., & Terenzini, P. T. (2010). Deep learning as an individual, conditional, and contextual influence on first-year student outcomes. Paper presented at the Annual Forum of the Association for Institutional Research, Chicago, IL.
title: Do not expect environmental interventions alone to produce deep-learning benefits; students must personally engage in deep learning activities
description: Based on the finding that institutional aggregate DEEP scores predicted no outcomes while individual DEEP scores did, the authors conclude that "simply being a part of an environment in which deep learning is emphasized does not benefit students." Administrators designing environments to encourage deep processing should not expect a panacea effect, particularly for objective measures of learning; benefits require students' own effortful engagement in deep learning activities.
requirements: Students must personally put forth effort to engage in deep learning activities for benefits to accrue
constraints: The authors state the assumption that engagement is the mechanism through which deep processing affects learning needs further study
examples: The study found no significant relationship between institutions' average DEEP Learning scores and any of the four outcomes, while individual DEEP scores predicted all three self-reported gain scales
key_sources: Reason, R. D., Cox, B. E., McIntosh, K., & Terenzini, P. T. (2010). Deep learning as an individual, conditional, and contextual influence on first-year student outcomes. Paper presented at the Annual Forum of the Association for Institutional Research, Chicago, IL. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED520486

article_title: A Call to Action: Towards an Ecological-Dynamics Theory of Mathematics Learning, Teaching, and Design
citation: Dor Abrahamson & Raúl Sánchez–García. (2015). A Call to Action: Towards an Ecological-Dynamics Theory of Mathematics Learning, Teaching, and Design. Proceedings of the 37th annual meeting of the North American Chapter of the International Group for the Psychology of Mathematics Education. http://www.tinyurl.com/FreeMITP
title: Treat all forms of instructional intervention — physical guidance, metaphoric framing, overlays — as productive constraints channeling the self-organizing learner–environment system
description: Drawing on ecological dynamics, the article proposes that instructors shape learning by channeling the self-organizing behavior of goal-oriented dynamical systems. It states that 'ecological dynamics regards all forms of intervention, such as physical guidance or metaphoric framing, as productive constraints on the solution of motor-action problems', with Newell's three constraint sources — organism, environment, and task — affecting behavior on short and long time scales. This gives STEM educational research interpretive schemes for modeling instructors' multimodal utterance and actions.
requirements: A goal-oriented motor-action problem whose solution space can be narrowed by manipulating organism, environment, or task constraints
constraints: The framework is offered for motor-action inquiry problems; the article notes institutional adoption would require rethinking teachers' professional practice from epistemology through assessment
target_learning_goals: construction of mathematically oriented operatory schemes
examples: The MIT-P facilitator's incremental overlay of cursors, grid, and numerals as environmental constraints on action
key_sources: Dor Abrahamson & Raúl Sánchez–García. (2015). A Call to Action: Towards an Ecological-Dynamics Theory of Mathematics Learning, Teaching, and Design. Proceedings of the 37th annual meeting of the North American Chapter of the International Group for the Psychology of Mathematics Education. http://www.tinyurl.com/FreeMITP

article_title: Spaceflight human optimization and performance: positioning astronauts in an operational framework to promote health, fitness, and mission readiness.
citation: Dickerson Broderick L., Gonzalez Drew E., Comfort Paul, Hardy John G., Hines Kelly E., Anderson Danielle N., Macaulay Timothy R., Stankovic Aleksandra, Twine Corey A. (2026). Spaceflight human optimization and performance: positioning astronauts in an operational framework to promote health, fitness, and mission readiness. Frontiers in Physiology. https://doi.org/10.3389/fphys.2026.1950155
title: Integrate cognitive, physiological, behavioral, and operational metrics into mission-readiness monitoring
description: The review argues that no single monitoring stream captures mission readiness, so future monitoring systems should combine measurement streams. It states that "monitoring systems implemented in future LDS missions should integrate cognitive examinations with physiological, behavioral, and operational metrics to provide a comprehensive state of mission readiness". This includes wearable devices monitoring physiological stress responses, sleep, workload, and physical activity as adjunctive information, designed and ethically implemented to be operationally actionable.
requirements: Wearable and monitoring technologies must adhere to mission constraints and produce operationally actionable information
constraints: The review notes behavioral health monitoring is operationally difficult because interpersonal dynamics, stress, and mood are hard to quantify objectively, and astronauts may be reluctant to disclose stressors
target_learners: astronaut crews and mission-support teams across all mission phases
target_learning_goals: data-driven decision-making on physical and behavioral readiness
examples: The review describes wearable technology capable of monitoring heart rate variability, electrodermal activity, sleep patterns, workload, and physical activity
key_sources: Dickerson Broderick L., Gonzalez Drew E., Comfort Paul, Hardy John G., Hines Kelly E., Anderson Danielle N., Macaulay Timothy R., Stankovic Aleksandra, Twine Corey A. (2026). Spaceflight human optimization and performance: positioning astronauts in an operational framework to promote health, fitness, and mission readiness. Frontiers in Physiology. https://doi.org/10.3389/fphys.2026.1950155

article_title: Social Skills Training (Early Childhood, Children with Disabilities)
citation: Social Skills Training. (2013). What Works Clearinghouse Intervention Report: Early Childhood Education Interventions for Children with Disabilities. U.S. Department of Education. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc
title: Behavioral social skills lesson pattern: instruct, model, practice, reinforce
description: The reviewed interventions share a recurring lesson structure: children are instructed on target behaviors, instructors model the behavior, children practice it with peers, and appropriate behavior is reinforced. In Guglielmo and Tryon (2001), "Instructors modeled the activities for the children using puppets and a short skit. Following this activity, children practiced the sharing skills with their peers," with reinforcement including continuous verbal acknowledgment and tangible rewards. LeBlanc and Matson (1995) similarly modeled with a puppet, had children model with a puppet and then with another child, and reinforced during a play phase.
requirements: Target behaviors must be specified (e.g., sharing, being in a group, greeting, initiating play)
Reinforcement of targeted behaviors during and after practice
constraints: In LeBlanc and Matson (1995), children engaging in inappropriate behavior were prompted toward an opposite positive behavior, with a one-minute time-out if they refused
target_learners: preschool children with disabilities or developmental delays
target_learning_goals: age-appropriate social skills such as sharing, joining a group, greeting, and initiating play
examples: Guglielmo and Tryon (2001) taught children to establish eye contact, tap children on the shoulder to gain attention, and ask to play with others
LeBlanc and Matson (1995) split each session into an approximately 15-minute instruction and modeling phase and an approximately 45-minute reinforced play phase
key_sources: Social Skills Training. (2013). What Works Clearinghouse Intervention Report: Early Childhood Education Interventions for Children with Disabilities. U.S. Department of Education. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/InterventionReport/578

article_title: GO Tutor Corps High-Impact Math Tutoring
citation: GO Tutor Corps (Evidence Rating: Promising). (2024). GO Tutor Corps evidence summary. https://www.evidenceforessl.org/
title: Supplement classroom instruction with consistent in-school tutoring sessions that use student performance data to guide instruction
description: The article describes a tutoring model in which sessions occur during the school day, are consistent across the year, and use "student performance data to guide instruction." Tutoring is intended to supplement, not replace, regular classroom instruction, with progress monitoring tracking student progress over the school year.
requirements: A designated non-teaching staff member to manage tutors on-site during serving hours.
constraints: The evidence base is a single quasi-experimental study rated Promising, with a small +0.10 effect size.
target_learners: Students identified as needing additional help in mathematics
target_learning_goals: Improving mathematics achievement over the school year
examples: GO Tutor Corps delivered individualized or small-group math tutoring during the school day in participating schools, with progress monitoring across the year.
key_sources: GO Tutor Corps (Evidence Rating: Promising). (2024). GO Tutor Corps evidence summary. https://www.evidenceforessl.org/

article_title: Teacher and Teaching Effects on Students' Academic Behaviors and Mindsets
citation: David Blazar, Matthew A. Kraft. (2015). Teacher and Teaching Effects on Students' Academic Behaviors and Mindsets. Working Paper 41. Cambridge, MA: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/teacher-and-teaching-effects-on-students-academic-behaviors-and-mindsets
title: Use measures of academic behaviors and mindsets, alongside test scores, to inform teacher development and evaluation policy
description: The paper positions its findings as directly usable for policy: because teachers affect behaviors and mindsets substantially and differently from test scores, "Findings can inform policy around teacher development and evaluation." The principle is that teacher development and evaluation systems should attend to non-tested outcomes and the practices that develop them, not only test scores. It rests on the paper's findings about teacher effects and their dissociation from test-score effectiveness.
requirements: Measures of students' academic behaviors and mindsets must be collected for the teachers being developed or evaluated.
constraints: The evidence base is upper-elementary teachers and math outcomes, as reported in the paper's summary.
examples: The paper reports that teachers effective at improving behaviors and mindsets often are not the same as those who raise math test scores, motivating evaluation systems that capture both.
key_sources: David Blazar, Matthew A. Kraft. (2015). Teacher and Teaching Effects on Students' Academic Behaviors and Mindsets. Working Paper 41. Cambridge, MA: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/teacher-and-teaching-effects-on-students-academic-behaviors-and-mindsets

article_title: Sensitivity of Teacher Value-Added Estimates to Student and Peer Control Variables (Journal Article)
citation: Matthew T. Johnson, Stephen Lipscomb, Brian Gill. (2015). Sensitivity of Teacher Value-Added Estimates to Student and Peer Control Variables. Journal of Research on Educational Effectiveness, vol. 8, issue 1. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/sensitivity-of-teacher-value-added-estimates-to-student-and-peer-control-variables
title: When constructing teacher value-added models, include student and peer background characteristics, especially for districts with many disadvantaged students
description: The article recommends attention to control-variable choice because specification differences have direct implications for which teacher estimates change. It reports that "teachers in a district with a large fraction of disadvantaged students receive lower ratings when background characteristics are omitted," so omitting background controls disadvantages such teachers. The principle applies to policymakers and analysts constructing VAMs.
requirements: Value-added models must isolate teachers' contributions to student achievement to be valid, which requires decisions about student and peer control variables and lagged achievement scores.
constraints: The article notes other modeling choices have smaller practical consequences, and none are as important as selecting which assessment to use as the outcome measure.
target_learners: K-12 students in districts evaluated via teacher value-added models
target_learning_goals: Valid measurement of teachers' contributions to student achievement
examples: The study compared VAM specifications with and without student and peer background characteristics and a double-lagged achievement score using data from a northern state.
key_sources: Matthew T. Johnson, Stephen Lipscomb, Brian Gill. (2015). Sensitivity of Teacher Value-Added Estimates to Student and Peer Control Variables. Journal of Research on Educational Effectiveness, vol. 8, issue 1. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/journal-article-sensitivity-of-teacher-valueadded-estimates-to-student-and-peer-control-variables

article_title: Expanding Beyond Academics: Who Benefits and How?
citation: John Deke, Joshua Haimson. (2006). Expanding Beyond Academics: Who Benefits and How? Trends in Education Research, Issue Brief #2. Princeton, NJ: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org
title: Individualize competency development rather than applying a one-size-fits-all approach
description: Because students differ in which competencies predict their later success, the brief suggests education should be individualized rather than uniform. It concludes that "not all students would benefit from improving the same competencies," so schools should tailor which competencies they help each student develop.
requirements: Schools must be able to identify which competencies matter for individual students' later success.
constraints: The brief frames this as a suggestion based on predictive associations, not a tested intervention.
examples: The brief analyzed how high school competencies including academic achievement, leadership skills, sports-related skills, work habits, prosocial behavior, and locus of control relate to later attainment and earnings.
key_sources: John Deke, Joshua Haimson. (2006). Expanding Beyond Academics: Who Benefits and How? Trends in Education Research, Issue Brief #2. Princeton, NJ: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/expanding-beyond-academics-who-benefits-and-how

article_title: Impacts of a Summer Learning Program: A Random Assignment Study of Building Educated Leaders for Life BELL
citation: Duncan Chaplin, Jeffrey Capizzano. (2006). Impacts of a Summer Learning Program: A Random Assignment Study of Building Educated Leaders for Life BELL. Washington, DC: Urban Institute. https://www.urban.org/
title: Invest in out-of-school-time summer programming for low-income children
description: The article recommends continued investment in summer out-of-school-time programming for low-income children, because its random assignment study found a well-implemented summer program "can improve reading test scores" and increase parents' encouragement of reading. It names current funding streams such as the 21st Century Community Learning Centers program and Title I Supplemental Services as examples of such investment.
requirements: The program must be well-implemented, as the finding is qualified by implementation quality.
constraints: Support is stated as "some support" for investments, not definitive proof of scale-up.
examples: The study evaluated the BELL (Building Educated Leaders for Life) summer learning program using random assignment.
key_sources: Duncan Chaplin, Jeffrey Capizzano. (2006). Impacts of a Summer Learning Program: A Random Assignment Study of Building Educated Leaders for Life BELL. Washington, DC: Urban Institute. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/impacts-of-a-summer-learning-program-a-random-assignment-study-of-building-educated-leaders-for-life-bell

article_title: The BASIE (BAyeSian Interpretation of Estimates) Framework for Interpreting Findings from Impact Evaluations: A Practical Guide for Education Researchers
citation: John Deke, Mariel Finucane, Dan Thal. (2022). The BASIE (BAyeSian Interpretation of Estimates) Framework for Interpreting Findings from Impact Evaluations: A Practical Guide for Education Researchers. Washington, DC: U.S. Department of Education, Institute of Education Sciences, National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/pubs/2022005/
title: Interpret impact estimates with explicit prior evidence rather than defaulting to null hypothesis significance testing
description: The guide's core recommendation for research practice: when reading evaluation results, education researchers should interpret impact estimates within the BASIE framework, which brings selected prior evidence to bear, rather than relying on null hypothesis significance testing. The guide serves both researchers, through practical steps, and "evaluation methodologists", through "conceptual and technical details".
requirements: Researchers must select appropriate prior evidence to combine with new estimates
constraints: The recommendation is scoped to interpreting findings from impact evaluations
examples: The guide provides both practical walkthrough steps for researchers and technical detail for methodologists
key_sources: John Deke, Mariel Finucane, Dan Thal. (2022). The BASIE (BAyeSian Interpretation of Estimates) Framework for Interpreting Findings from Impact Evaluations: A Practical Guide for Education Researchers. Washington, DC: U.S. Department of Education, Institute of Education Sciences, National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/pubs/2022005/

article_title: Training and Retaining Effective School Leaders
citation: Rivkin, S.G., Sartain, L., & Schiman, J.C. (2023). Training and retaining effective school leaders: Results from efforts to improve principal effectiveness in Chicago Public Schools. Chicago, IL: University of Chicago Consortium on School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/
title: Invest in principal training and support, but design policies to avoid shifting effort away from noncognitive skill development
description: The brief's forward-looking recommendation is that because principals have lasting impacts on students, "investments in principal training and support are likely well spent." At the same time, it cautions that accountability policies focused primarily on test scores may shift effort away from noncognitive skills, which principals can influence and which recent research shows is much more valuable for young adults' long-term success. Districts should therefore pair principal-effectiveness investments with policy designs that do not crowd out noncognitive skill development.
requirements: District capacity to fund and sustain principal training and support programs over multiple years
constraints: Accountability policies focused primarily on student test scores may shift efforts away from developing students' noncognitive skills
target_learners: K-12 students in urban public school districts
target_learning_goals: Cognitive and noncognitive skill development shaped by school leadership
examples: CPS partnered with local universities on the Chicago Leadership Collaborative residency program and introduced merit bonuses of up to $20,000 for principals of schools with the highest achievement growth
key_sources: Rivkin, S.G., Sartain, L., & Schiman, J.C. (2023). Training and retaining effective school leaders: Results from efforts to improve principal effectiveness in Chicago Public Schools. Chicago, IL: University of Chicago Consortium on School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/training-retaining-effective-school-leaders

article_title: Reaching for Improvement
citation: Shyjka, A. (2022). Reaching for improvement: Teacher evaluation and its role in instructional improvement. Chicago, IL: University of Chicago Consortium on School Research. https://www.cps.edu/about/departments/talent/
title: Integrate elements of the teacher evaluation system into the school's Instructional Improvement Support System for coaching purposes
description: The article recommends that if REACH-related coaching is to be feasible for schools, it would likely be both most efficient and effective to integrate relevant elements of the REACH evaluation system into the IISS of a school. As the article states, "If REACH-related coaching is to be feasible for schools, it would likely be both most efficient and effective to integrate relevant elements of the REACH evaluation system into the IISS of a school." This means using the Framework for Teaching as a shared vision language and connecting evaluation feedback to ongoing collaborative improvement work.
requirements: Schools must have existing collaborative structures and instructional leadership capacity to absorb integration demands
Coaching systems or willingness to build them must be present
constraints: Coaching toward improvement may place additional demands on schools' already strained capacities if coaching systems are not already present
target_learners: K-12 teachers in public schools undergoing teacher evaluation
target_learning_goals: Instructional improvement driven by evaluation feedback and coaching
examples: Docherty High School integrated the FFT as a shared vision of instructional quality, connected improvement initiatives to FFT practice change goals, and offered optional weekly REACH domain-focused professional development
key_sources: Shyjka, A. (2022). Reaching for improvement: Teacher evaluation and its role in instructional improvement. Chicago, IL: University of Chicago Consortium on School Research. https://www.cps.edu/about/departments/talent/

article_title: Arts Education and Social-Emotional Learning Outcomes Among K-12 Students
citation: Camille A. Farrington, Joseph Maurer, Meredith R. Aska McBride, Jenny Nagaoka, J. S. Puller, Steve Shewfelt, Elizabeth M. Weiss, and Lindsay Wright. (2018). Arts Education and Social-Emotional Learning Outcomes Among K–12 Students: Developing a Theory of Action. University of Chicago Consortium on School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/arts-education-and-social-emotional-learning-outcomes-among-k–12-students
title: Be intentional about the social-emotional contexts arts lessons create, because effects occur regardless of instructor intent and can be negative
description: The report's central practical implication is that arts education produces social-emotional effects whether or not instructors plan for them. As the executive summary states, "arts education has social-emotional effects regardless of instructor intent—and these effects can be either positive or negative." Students may feel deeply exposed or ashamed, or conclude they lack artistic talent, and avoid arts thereafter. Educators should therefore consciously design lessons so students take advantage of social-emotional components and are guided toward improved competencies.
requirements: Deliberate planning and awareness by a skilled instructor to shape lessons into spaces for social-emotional development
constraints: The report cautions instructors should not shy away from uncomfortable or challenging content, since challenge in a safe space is one of the catalytic opportunities in arts education
target_learners: K–12 students in arts education settings
target_learning_goals: Positive social-emotional competency development and avoidance of negative social-emotional effects
examples: The report notes that even where evidence showed significant effects, there was much variation in outcomes among participants and across settings, motivating the call for intentional design
key_sources: Camille A. Farrington, Joseph Maurer, Meredith R. Aska McBride, Jenny Nagaoka, J. S. Puller, Steve Shewfelt, Elizabeth M. Weiss, and Lindsay Wright. (2018). Arts Education and Social-Emotional Learning Outcomes Among K–12 Students: Developing a Theory of Action. University of Chicago Consortium on School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/arts-education-and-social-emotional-learning-outcomes

article_title: Why Do Students Get Good Grades, or Bad Ones? The Influence of the Teacher, Class, School, and Student
citation: Elaine M. Allensworth and Stuart Luppescu. (2016). Why do students get good grades, or bad ones? The influence of the teacher, class, school, and student. University of Chicago Consortium on School Research working paper. https://consortium.uchicago.edu
title: Interpret course grades in light of observable context—attendance, course conditions and class composition—rather than treating them as incomparable across teachers and schools
description: The article argues that because most grade variation is explained by observable factors, practitioners can use contextual information when interpreting grades. It finds "there are observable factors that systematically explain most of the differences in the grades that students receive in different types of schools, and with different teachers." Grades remain useful for early warning and readiness indicators, but a low grade may reflect course conditions, schedule demands, or attendance patterns rather than idiosyncratic grading.
requirements: Knowledge of the course conditions (subject, level, peer achievement, period, term, class size) and the student's attendance in the course
constraints: Attendance and test scores are incomplete measures of effort and skills, so the study likely underestimates how much grades reflect real differences in effort and skills
target_learning_goals: Accurate interpretation of course grades and GPAs as indicators of academic readiness in educational decision-making
examples: The study used the universe of core-course grades from 118 Chicago public high schools to quantify how much teacher, school and course-condition variation remains after accounting for attendance and test scores
key_sources: Elaine M. Allensworth and Stuart Luppescu. (2016). Why do students get good grades, or bad ones? The influence of the teacher, class, school, and student. University of Chicago Consortium on School Research working paper. https://consortium.uchicago.edu

article_title: How Do Secondary Principals Influence Teaching and Learning?
citation: Sebastian, J., & Allensworth, E. (2013). How Do Secondary Principals Influence Teaching and Learning? Principal's Research Review, 8(4). https://www.nassp.org/prr
title: Secondary principals should act as instructional leaders who organize the school for instruction, not as instructional coaches
description: The article cautions against confusing instructional leadership with instructional coaching. As instructional leaders, principals set the stage for good instruction by organizing the school to support teachers—with a safe, orderly, academically focused climate, high-quality professional development, and collaboration among teachers and with parents. Direct involvement with instruction showed "no benefits and even some detriments" for instruction quality, so the article suggests caution to leaders considering reducing organization-building time to spend more time as instructional coaches.
requirements: Principals must still support individual teacher improvement through sustained quality professional development and coherent instructional programming across departments
constraints: At the high school level, principals' direct interaction with classroom instruction may be perceived as unhelpful by teachers
target_learning_goals: classroom instructional quality and student achievement
examples: The review describes principals setting the stage for instruction by ensuring an academically focused climate, professional development opportunities, and teacher and parent collaboration, rather than coaching instruction directly.
key_sources: Sebastian, J., & Allensworth, E. (2013). How Do Secondary Principals Influence Teaching and Learning? Principal's Research Review, 8(4). https://www.nassp.org/prr

article_title: The Forgotten 20 Percent: Achievement and Growth in Rural Schools Across the Nation
citation: Angela Johnson, Megan Kuhfeld, James Soland. (2021). The forgotten 20 percent: Achievement and growth in rural schools across the nation. AERA Open. https://aeraopen.org
title: Interpret rural school performance using seasonal learning patterns, not just year-end scores
description: The article argues that achievement comparisons across school settings should account for when learning happens — during school years versus summers. Because "The divergence is driven by larger summer losses for rural students," the authors state that "These findings highlight the importance of seasonal learning patterns in interpreting rural school performance." Year-end snapshots alone can misattribute rural–nonrural differences to school quality when they arise over summers.
requirements: Achievement data from both fall and spring administrations to distinguish school-year growth from summer loss
target_learners: Kindergarten through eighth-grade students in rural and nonrural public schools
target_learning_goals: Accurate interpretation of achievement gaps and school performance for rural students
examples: The study decomposed rural–nonrural achievement trajectories into school-year growth and summer loss components across grades K–8.
key_sources: Angela Johnson, Megan Kuhfeld, James Soland. (2021). The forgotten 20 percent: Achievement and growth in rural schools across the nation. AERA Open. https://www.nwea.org/research/publication/the-forgotten-20-percent-achievement-and-growth-in-rural-schools-across-the-nation/

article_title: Practitioner's Guide to Integrating Literacy and Science
citation: Practitioner's guide to integrating literacy and science. (2025). HMH Education Company / NWEA. https://www.nwea.org
title: Introduce science vocabulary as the need for words arises, rather than without need or context
description: The guide recommends introducing and defining science vocabulary during discourse when students allude to technical ideas, for example when a student mentions light "bouncing off objects," so words like absorb and reflect are learned in context. It states plainly: "It's important to introduce words as the need arises, rather than introducing words without need or context." This connects vocabulary work to the rich-vocabulary component and to students' own models and questions.
requirements: A classroom discussion context in which students raise ideas that allude to technical terms
target_learning_goals: Science vocabulary development supporting comprehension across subjects
examples: In Lesson 3, students learn definitions of absorb and reflect as they suggest revisions to the classroom model.
key_sources: Practitioner's guide to integrating literacy and science. (2025). HMH Education Company / NWEA. https://www.nwea.org/research/publication/practitioners-guide-to-integrating-literacy-and-science/

article_title: A method for identifying partial test-taking engagement
citation: Steven Wise, Megan Kuhfeld. (2021). A method for identifying partial test-taking engagement. Applied Measurement in Education, 34(2), 150-161. https://www.nwea.org/research/publication/a-method-for-identifying-partial-test-taking-engagement/
title: Interpret effort-moderated scores cautiously when test events indicate partial engagement
description: This principle states the article's recommended practice for score interpretation: effort-moderated (E-M) scores estimate what a disengaged test taker would have scored when fully engaged, but retained responses can still "be distorted by disengagement" when engagement is partial. The article directs that when test events indicate partial engagement, such scores should be read as tentative rather than taken at face value. It serves measurement professionals interpreting E-M adjusted results.
requirements: Test events must be available that can indicate the presence of partial engagement, so that the identification method can flag affected scores before interpretation.
constraints: The article states the caution applies when test events indicate the presence of partial engagement; it does not claim E-M scores are generally untrustworthy.
target_learners: K-12 students taking computer-based achievement tests
target_learning_goals: Accurate interpretation of achievement test scores adjusted for test-taking disengagement
examples: The article recommends that when test events indicate the presence of partial engagement, effort-moderated scores should be interpreted cautiously.
key_sources: Steven Wise, Megan Kuhfeld. (2021). A method for identifying partial test-taking engagement. Applied Measurement in Education, 34(2), 150-161. https://www.nwea.org/research/publication/a-method-for-identifying-partial-test-taking-engagement/

article_title: User guide for interpreting the NWEA state dashboard: Exploring the educational impacts of COVID-19
citation: User guide for interpreting the NWEA state dashboard: Exploring the educational impacts of COVID-19. (2021). NWEA Center for School and Student Progress. https://www.nwea.org
title: Interpret cross-sectional COVID-era achievement differences alongside shifts in the number and composition of students tested
description: The guide advises dashboard users to consider testing-pattern changes when reading term-over-term results. It states that "testing patterns across the country have varied significantly this year within and between schools and observed student attrition is not random," so users must understand shifts in numbers of students tested before interpreting cross-sectional differences in outcomes across terms.
requirements: Access to the dashboard's information on how the number of students tested has potentially changed between terms for the groups and schools of interest
constraints: Cross-sectional samples may include schools that tested in one term but not the other, so samples can differ between terms
target_learners: kindergarten to eighth grade public school students in selected states
target_learning_goals: accurate interpretation of COVID-era achievement and growth trends in reading and math
examples: The guide quotes the NWEA attrition study finding larger fractions of attriters were minoritized students and students with lower fall 2019 achievement
key_sources: User guide for interpreting the NWEA state dashboard: Exploring the educational impacts of COVID-19. (2021). NWEA Center for School and Student Progress. https://www.nwea.org/research/publication/user-guide-for-interpreting-the-nwea-state-dashboard-exploring-the-educational-impacts-of-covid-19/

article_title: NWEA 2020 MAP Growth Achievement Status and Growth Norms for Students and Schools
citation: Thum, Y. M., & Kuhfeld, M. (2020). NWEA 2020 MAP Growth Achievement Status and Growth Norms for Students and Schools. NWEA Research Report. Portland, OR: NWEA. https://www.nwea.org
title: Use school instructional calendars to reflect each student's instructional exposure when norming
description: This principle holds that norms should be calibrated to the amount of instruction a student actually received before testing, using school-specific calendars rather than a uniform assumption. The report states: "we continued to reﬁne the use of sch ool calendars to better reﬂect the level of instructional exposure available to the student when she/h e/they test." Instructional days are computed by accounting for non-instructional days within each school's calendar, and growth is modeled against instructional exposure.
requirements: Accurate instructional calendar information for each school, including non-instructional days
target_learners: K-12 students in U.S. public schools
target_learning_goals: fair comparison of achievement and growth across students with differing instructional time
examples: The report includes a chapter on instructional exposure with instructional calendars, non-instructional days, and calculation of instructional days, illustrated by an instructional calendar example figure
key_sources: Thum, Y. M., & Kuhfeld, M. (2020). NWEA 2020 MAP Growth Achievement Status and Growth Norms for Students and Schools. NWEA Research Report. Portland, OR: NWEA. https://www.nwea.org/research/publication/nwea-2020-map-growth-achievement-status-and-growth-norms-for-students-and-schools/

article_title: Instructors’ technology experience and iPad delivered intervention implementation: A mixed methods replication study
citation: Lina Shanley, Mari Strand Cary, Ben Clarke, Meg Guerreiro, Michael Thier. (2017). Instructors’ technology experience and iPad delivered intervention implementation: A mixed methods replication study. Educational Technology Research and Development 65, 815–830.
title: Plan for instructor facilitation and professional development when implementing technology-based interventions in authentic school settings
description: The article positions instructor facilitation as central to whether technology-based interventions are implemented successfully in real classrooms: "Instructor facilitation is an essential element in the successful implementation of technology-based interventions in authentic school settings." Because instructors' varying technology experience and reported barriers corresponded with variable student use, the authors draw implications for technology-based intervention implementation and professional development.
requirements: Instructors with sufficient technology experience and support, since instructor-reported experience and barriers corresponded with student use patterns
constraints: Instructors with moderate iPad experience and/or no reported barriers to technology integration demonstrated the least desirable student use patterns, so experience and barrier profiles alone do not guarantee desirable implementation
target_learners: kindergarten teachers and other instructors implementing technology-based interventions
target_learning_goals: successful implementation of technology-based interventions as measured by student use
examples: The two KinderTEK development studies related instructor-reported iPad experience and technology-integration barriers to student use of the iPad-delivered intervention
key_sources: Lina Shanley, Mari Strand Cary, Ben Clarke, Meg Guerreiro, Michael Thier. (2017). Instructors’ technology experience and iPad delivered intervention implementation: A mixed methods replication study. Educational Technology Research and Development 65, 815–830. https://www.nwea.org/research/publication/instructors-technology-experience-and-ipad-delivered-intervention-implementation-a-mixed-methods-replication-study/

article_title: The changing landscape of assessment and accommodation policies
citation: Elizabeth Barker. (2019). The changing landscape of assessment and accommodation policies. Accessibility, Compliance, & Equity, 72-77. https://www.nwea.org
title: Include accommodations in educational assessments in pursuit of accessibility for all
description: The article's opening design recommendation is that "Educational assessments must include accommodations in the pursuit of accessibility for all." It treats accommodations as a necessary component of accessible assessment design, while cautioning that their role is unsettled and evolving. The article uses this principle to motivate its review of the accommodations landscape across past, present, and future policy developments.
requirements: Assessment developers must treat accommodations as part of assessment design rather than an afterthought, per the article's statement that assessments "must include accommodations."
constraints: The article notes accommodations, once adopted, "feel transitional" and rarely seem like an organic and fully equal part of an assessment.
target_learners: All students taking educational assessments, including students requiring accommodations
target_learning_goals: Accessible and equitable measurement of student achievement
examples: The article frames its review of the accommodations landscape as motivated by this accessibility requirement.
key_sources: Elizabeth Barker. (2019). The changing landscape of assessment and accommodation policies. Accessibility, Compliance, & Equity, 72-77. https://www.nwea.org/research/publication/the-changing-landscape-of-assessment-and-accommodation-policies/

article_title: Computational Thinking for an Inclusive World: A Resource for Educators to Learn and Lead, Quick Start and Discussion Guide
citation: Mills, K., Coenraad, M., Ruiz, P., Burke, Q., & Weisgrau J. (2021, December). Computational thinking for an inclusive world: A resource for educators to learn and lead, Quick start and discussion guide. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/140
title: Inclusive computational thinking pedagogies in three categories: accessible instruction, connecting to homes and communities, and combating inequity
description: The guide organizes inclusive computing pedagogies into three categories emphasizing different approaches to inclusivity. Designing Accessible Instruction engages all learners; Connecting to Students' Interests, Homes, and Communities draws on student experiences to highlight computing's relevance; and Acknowledging and Combating Inequity supports students to recognize and take a stand against oppression of marginalized groups. The guide states these pedagogies are "divided into three categories to emphasize different pedagogical approaches to inclusivity."
requirements: Inclusive learning experiences must intentionally integrate connections to students' interests, homes and communities and acknowledge and challenge inequity at the outset of the learning rather than as an afterthought
target_learners: All K-12 learners, including Black, Native American, and Latinx students; students with disabilities; girls and non-binary students
target_learning_goals: Equitable participation in computational thinking and computing
examples: Example practices include using Universal Design for Learning principles, pair programming and POGIL, translanguaging and translated Scratch blocks, recruiting excluded students to CS classes, and teaching about biases in algorithms and artificial intelligence
key_sources: Mills, K., Coenraad, M., Ruiz, P., Burke, Q., & Weisgrau J. (2021, December). Computational thinking for an inclusive world: A resource for educators to learn and lead, Quick start and discussion guide. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/140

article_title: Artificial Intelligence and the Future of Teaching and Learning
citation: Judi Fusco, Pati Ruiz, Jeremy Roschelle. (2023). Artificial Intelligence and the Future of Teaching and Learning. Digital Promise presentation. https://tech.ed.gov/ai/
title: Design educational AI as intelligence augmentation that centers educators' professional judgment and learners' voice
description: The article recommends a focus on Intelligence Augmentation rather than artificial intelligence in education. In its 2021 blog post it states: we recommend a focus on Intelligence Augmentation in education that would put educators' professional judgement and learners' voice at the center of innovative designs and features. This positions AI as supporting, not replacing, human decision-making in teaching and learning.
requirements: AI designs must keep educators' professional judgement and learners' voice at the center
target_learning_goals: safe, equitable, and meaningful use of AI in teaching and learning
examples: Digital Promise's 2020 recommendations include developing AI systems that assist teachers and improve teaching, and accelerating development of human-centered or responsible AI
key_sources: Judi Fusco, Pati Ruiz, Jeremy Roschelle. (2023). Artificial Intelligence and the Future of Teaching and Learning. Digital Promise presentation. https://tech.ed.gov/ai/

article_title: Realizing District-Community Driven Outcomes Through Inclusive Innovation
citation: White, L. P. and Merritt Johnson, A. (2024, May). Realizing District-Community Driven Outcomes Through Inclusive Innovation. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/214
title: Four conditions Core Teams identified as supporting solution success: the Inclusive Innovation model structure, student voice, safe spaces, and flexible implementation
description: Across the pilot districts, Core Team members identified four conditions that enabled their co-created solutions to achieve intended outcomes. The report states that "these four themes—Inclusive Innovation, student voice, the creation of safe spaces, and flexible implementation—were instrumental in creating the conditions that enabled the solution to achieve its intended outcomes." Student voice meant students were involved from design through implementation and decision-making; safe spaces encouraged open participation, particularly for students of color; flexibility allowed adjustments based on classroom or community needs, emphasizing teacher and student choice.
requirements: Students involved from the beginning of solution development, not only implementation
Environments where students can share perspectives among adults who traditionally hold power
constraints: Conditions were identified retrospectively by participants in four pilot districts, not experimentally tested
target_learners: district and community Core Team participants
target_learning_goals: co-designing equity-centered solutions to locally identified educational challenges
examples: In Pilot District 3, teachers adapted the Compact Writing Assignments to fit classroom dynamics, which a student said made them "work better for the classes now"
key_sources: White, L. P. and Merritt Johnson, A. (2024, May). Realizing District-Community Driven Outcomes Through Inclusive Innovation. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/214

article_title: Rapid Cycle Pilots: Using Edtech to Support English Learners
citation: Luke, Christina C.; Gibson, Sierra; Francisco, Aubrey T. (2017). Rapid Cycle Pilots: Using Edtech to Support English Learners. Digital Promise. https://www.digitalpromise.org
title: Include comparison groups in edtech pilots whenever possible to generate interpretable efficacy results
description: This principle holds that pilot studies of edtech products should include a comparison group of students not using the tool so that outcome differences can be attributed to the tool. The article's two pilots illustrate the contrast: Cajon Valley's comparison-group design supported a significant finding, while Vista's single-group design left results uninterpretable. As the report states, districts' results "demonstrate the necessity to include comparison groups when possible in pilots in order to generate powerful results."
requirements: A pool of comparable students not using the tool, matched or at least comparable to pilot students, available for the same pre- and post-assessments
constraints: The article notes Cajon Valley's comparison group was constrained to fifth grade, limiting the analysis to that grade level
target_learners: K-12 English Learners in district edtech pilots
target_learning_goals: Evaluating whether an edtech tool improves English language development and reading outcomes
examples: Cajon Valley included a comparison group and could attribute Lexile differences to Achieve3000; Vista had no comparison group, so the authors state it is possible non-users grew substantially or declined, and no conclusions could be drawn
key_sources: Luke, Christina C.; Gibson, Sierra; Francisco, Aubrey T. (2017). Rapid Cycle Pilots: Using Edtech to Support English Learners. Digital Promise. https://digitalpromise.dspacedirect.org/items/383e02ba-587a-4192-be68-175543798661

article_title: Research and the Promise of Personalized Learning
citation: Research and the Promise of Personalized Learning. (2015). Digital Promise Global, Making Learning Personal for All series. https://global.digitalpromise.org
title: Inclusive design and assistive technologies benefit all learners (curb-cut effect)
description: Drawing on inclusive design and Universal Design for Learning research, the article states that "most assistive technologies and inclusive design approaches also help all learners learn more effectively." Jutta Treviranus is quoted asserting that designing for accessibility is just better design, illustrated by the curb-cut effect: sidewalk curb cuts designed for wheelchairs ended up benefiting people pushing strollers and riding bikes. Products designed for learners with impairments affecting vision, speech, or writing can also help learners struggling with literacy or numeracy more broadly.
requirements: Design should explicitly account for learner variability, including specialized needs
constraints: The article presents this via cited research and expert assertion, not as a tested result of its own
target_learners: All learners, including those with physical or developmental impairments
target_learning_goals: Effective literacy and numeracy learning supported by accessible product design
examples: Assistive products for vision, speech, or writing impairments that also help other learners with literacy or numeracy struggles; the curb-cut analogy from sidewalk design
key_sources: Research and the Promise of Personalized Learning. (2015). Digital Promise Global, Making Learning Personal for All series. https://global.digitalpromise.org

article_title: Tough As Nails and Drawing on Kinship: Rigorous and inclusive educational research in Kentucky Appalachia
citation: Emi Iwatani. (2023). Tough as Nails & Drawing on Kinship: Rigorous and inclusive educational research in Kentucky Appalachia [Invited speaker session]. American Educational Research Association Annual Meeting, Chicago, IL. https://bit.ly/TANrefs
title: Include community members in designing futures they will inhabit, since people do not want to design a future they are not in
description: The presentation's second civic imagination rationale is that design processes must include the people whose future is at stake: "People don't want to design a future that they aren't in." It illustrates this with a teacher's reflection after local industry presenters (Appalachian Wireless) connected to students: the presenters conveyed that "the skills they use/need are the exact skills I see in my students", producing what the teacher called a big "A-ha" moment.
requirements: Local industry and community voices must be present in curriculum design and professional learning
constraints: Grounded in Appalachian community contexts where outside-designed futures are distrusted
target_learners: Teachers and district leaders designing K-8 instruction
target_learning_goals: Connecting student skills to authentic local career applications
examples: Appalachian Wireless employees presented at a summer institute, prompting teachers to see student skills mirrored in local tech careers
key_sources: Emi Iwatani. (2023). Tough as Nails & Drawing on Kinship: Rigorous and inclusive educational research in Kentucky Appalachia [Invited speaker session]. American Educational Research Association Annual Meeting, Chicago, IL. https://bit.ly/TANrefs

article_title: Designing for the future of research: Putting equity-relevant research into practice with scenarios and personas
citation: Pakhira, D., & Fusco, J. (2022, October). Designing for the future of research: Putting equity-relevant research into practice with scenarios and personas. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/163
title: Include researchers from diverse backgrounds and communities most targeted by intersectional structural inequality to guide equity-relevant research
description: The article's first recommendation is that equity-relevant research teams must include researchers from diverse backgrounds and diverse research methods. It argues that "these lived experiences give insights about issues of equity that those without the experiences cannot easily see or always keep at the forefront of their thinking," and that without intentional inclusion it is too easy to only include dominant perspectives. Diversity is needed both in the people on the team and in the development process.
requirements: Intentional inclusion of diverse perspectives, since without it dominant ones dominate
Research enabling active, equitable, and real participation of historically excluded groups
target_learning_goals: envisioning pathways that make learning accessible for all groups of students
examples: The SEERNet personas were created to provoke thinking about what different researchers bring to their work and make apparent new features or capabilities that might be needed
key_sources: Pakhira, D., & Fusco, J. (2022, October). Designing for the future of research: Putting equity-relevant research into practice with scenarios and personas. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/163

article_title: Shifting Education with Learning Pathways: Becoming Your Portrait of a Graduate
citation: Mills, K., Weisgrau, J., Burke, Q., Lee, K., Solorzano, T. and Coenraad, M. (2024, March). Shifting Education with Learning Pathways: Becoming Your Portrait of a Graduate. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/205
title: Integrated Learning Pathways defined by four principles: competency-based, complementary, cumulative, and consistent
description: Learning pathways are system-wide learning progressions that "function according to four principles: They are competency-based, complementary to disciplinary learning, consistent across classrooms, and cumulative from year to year." Competency-based means Portrait Skill Sets are broken into actionable Practices learners demonstrate; complementary means pathways supplement rather than replace existing structures; cumulative means developmentally appropriate progressions articulated as "I can" statements across grade bands; and consistent means practice opportunities are designed into every classroom so attributes are "realistically attainable by each of their students." The design process is intended to be adapted to each district's Portrait.
requirements: Teachers, leaders, and experts work together to identify and map integration opportunities; a designated team of district, school, and teacher leaders guides development
constraints: Each competency-based Practice should not be integrated universally or indiscriminately across grade bands and disciplines; consistency does not mean pathways are blind to context
target_learners: K-12 students across all classrooms and grade bands
target_learning_goals: Portrait Skill Sets and Practices developed dispositionally across disciplines and grades
key_sources: Mills, K., Weisgrau, J., Burke, Q., Lee, K., Solorzano, T. and Coenraad, M. (2024, March). Shifting Education with Learning Pathways: Becoming Your Portrait of a Graduate. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/205

article_title: Learning by Design: How Design Tech High School Uses Research
citation: Digital Promise. (2017). Learning by Design: How Design Tech High School Uses Research. Digital Promise. https://www.digitalpromise.org
title: Integrate the learning sciences into a school's existing culture and practices so it becomes an ongoing practice
description: The report recommends that schools fold learning sciences principles, like retrieval practice and interleaving, into the decision-making processes, professional development, and program design structures they already use; this allowed d.tech to maintain it as an ongoing practice rather than a one-time initiative. Schools are advised to analyze their own mission and structures to find the easiest integration points.
requirements: An analysis of the institution's mission and structures to determine the easiest ways to integrate the science of learning
constraints: The account is drawn from a single charter school's experience
target_learning_goals: Sustained school-wide adoption of evidence-based learning strategies
examples: d.tech folded learning sciences principles into its existing design thinking processes and made follow-on professional development throughout the year so it was not one-and-done.
key_sources: Digital Promise. (2017). Learning by Design: How Design Tech High School Uses Research. Digital Promise. https://digitalpromise.dspacedirect.org/items/93bddee8-5856-4faf-8758-71aae4ce8716

article_title: Technology and Family Literacy Case Study: Briya Public Charter School, Washington, D.C.
citation: Technology and Family Literacy Case Study: Briya. (2016). Digital Promise. https://www.digitalpromise.org
title: Integrate English language learning with digital literacy instruction in one curriculum for immigrant adult learners
description: Briya combines English learning and digital skills in a single curriculum: "All of their devices, software, and online programs use English, so their learners are integrating their English language learning (ELL) with their digital literacy work." Teachers also use traditional ELL strategies in digital literacy classes, such as having students read aloud website names, URLs, and email addresses to practice pronunciation. The case study's key takeaways state these "can be effectively combined in one curriculum, increasing practice with English while also learning digital skills."
requirements: Devices, software, and online programs that operate in English so learners practice the target language while building digital skills
examples: Teachers have students read aloud website names, URLs, and email addresses so they hear and practice English pronunciations
key_sources: Technology and Family Literacy Case Study: Briya. (2016). Digital Promise. https://www.digitalpromise.org

article_title: Scaling Career Pathways Statewide: A Blueprint for Creating K-12 + Postsecondary + Industry Pathways
citation: Scaling career pathways statewide: A blueprint for creating K-12 + postsecondary + industry pathways. (2026). Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/287
title: Include historically excluded students and families at the pathways research and design table
description: The blueprint holds that equitable pathways require the direct beneficiaries to participate in designing them. It states that "students and families who have historically been unable to fully access, participate, and benefit are at the research and design table," and that engaging them alongside state, regional, and community leaders and funders ensures policies and practices reflect and address needs that are often missed. The article's stakeholder table distinguishes lead organizations, stakeholder organizations, direct beneficiaries, and key investors.
requirements: Engaging students and families alongside key state, regional, and community leaders and funders
target_learners: students and families historically unable to fully access, participate in, and benefit from pathways
target_learning_goals: pathways policies and practices that reflect and address learner needs
examples: The stakeholder table assigns direct beneficiaries—current and prospective pathways learners, parents and families, and community-based organizations—the role of contributing to pathways research and design to meet student needs
key_sources: Scaling career pathways statewide: A blueprint for creating K-12 + postsecondary + industry pathways. (2026). Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/287

article_title: Designing a Process for Inclusive Innovation: A Radical Commitment to Equity
citation: Angevine, C., Cator, K., Liberman, B., Smith, K., & Young, V. (2019). Designing a Process for Inclusive Innovation: A Radical Commitment to Equity. Digital Promise. https://digitalpromise.org
title: Five-stage iterative Inclusive Innovation process with community as the central strand
description: The Inclusive Innovation process moves iteratively across five stages: Connect & Commit, Inquire & Investigate, Design & Develop, Implement & Iterate, and Sustain & Scale. Each stage has its own goals, practices, tools for data collection and analysis, protocols, and guidance on roles. The graphic shows community as the central strand on which development and research work is anchored, with researcher, developer, and community paths intertwining and merging for equity and mutuality checks between stages.
requirements: Each stage includes equity and mutuality checks before moving into the next stage
Protocols and tools for data collection and analysis embedded within each phase
constraints: The stages are not linear or unidirectional and the boundaries between them are porous
target_learners: Education practitioners, researchers, developers, and community members addressing challenges affecting marginalized students
target_learning_goals: Co-designed and co-owned solutions for broader and persistent impact
examples: Appendix A illustrates the process applied to literacy in the primary grades, from building trust via listening tours to agreeing on target outcomes such as reading on grade level by third grade
key_sources: Angevine, C., Cator, K., Liberman, B., Smith, K., & Young, V. (2019). Designing a Process for Inclusive Innovation: A Radical Commitment to Equity. Digital Promise. https://digitalpromise.dspacedirect.org/items/d6db3e76-2dc9-4ea6-ae68-49814c88e6b6

article_title: Defining Computational Thinking for a District: Inclusive Computing Pathways in Indian Prairie School District
citation: Digital Promise. (2021). Defining computational thinking for a district: Inclusive computing pathways in Indian Prairie School District. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/131
title: Include building leaders and teachers in CT initiative learning from the beginning, and bring wider stakeholder experts into early planning
description: In reflection, IPSD states that starting with the District Curriculum and Instruction team meant the team learned on its own before expanding to teachers and building leaders; including building leaders and teachers in the learning from the beginning "would have considerably helped to push the pathway forward." The district also would have brought wider stakeholder experts, such as business leaders, into year-one definition and planning.
requirements: District willingness to broaden the initial learning group beyond the central curriculum team
target_learners: Building leaders, teachers, and district stakeholders in K-12 districts
target_learning_goals: Building shared capacity and momentum for a K-12 computing pathway
examples: IPSD's leadership team took considerable time to learn on their own before expanding to teachers and building leaders
key_sources: Digital Promise. (2021). Defining computational thinking for a district: Inclusive computing pathways in Indian Prairie School District. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/131

article_title: Classroom-Based Experimentation in a Digital Learning Platform
citation: Murphy, A. (2026, July). Classroom-Based experimentation in a digital learning platform. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/306
title: Build measurement into learning by using intrinsic platform data as outcome measures
description: The report's second insight is to measure outcomes during the learning activity itself rather than only through external assessments. In MATHia, transactions such as "problem attempts, hint requests, steps towards skill mastery" create rich behavioral data tracing the learning process in real time. Built-in measures like skill mastery, hint-seeking behavior, and error rates can serve as meaningful outcome measures, and platforms must be intentionally designed with fine-grained, structured data logging for research access.
requirements: The digital learning platform must be well-instrumented to collect, store, and export data, logging fine-grained student transactions with contextual information in structured formats.
constraints: Built-in measures reflect competencies the system is explicitly designed to track, which vary with the platform's goals.
target_learners: K-12 students using digital learning platforms
target_learning_goals: Observing how learning progresses during interventions, not just whether students learned
examples: MATHia's skill mastery adaptation, hint-seeking behavior, and error rates are cited as inherent measures usable as outcomes.
key_sources: Murphy, A. (2026, July). Classroom-Based experimentation in a digital learning platform. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/306

article_title: Effective Literacy and English Language Instruction for English Learners in the Elementary Grades
citation: Gersten, R., Baker, S.K., Shanahan, T., Linan-Thompson, S., Collins, P., & Scarcella, R. (2007). Effective Literacy and English Language Instruction for English Learners in the Elementary Grades: A Practice Guide (NCEE 2007-4011). Washington, DC: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. http://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/publications/practiceguides
title: Provide focused, intensive small-group reading interventions including the five core reading elements, delivered mainly through explicit, direct instruction
description: The guide recommends intensive small-group interventions for English learners determined to be at risk for reading problems, with time and intensity matched to degree of risk. Interventions "should include the five core reading elements (phonological awareness, phonics, reading fluency, vocabulary, and comprehension)", with "Explicit, direct instruction should be the primary means of instructional delivery." Implementation should be daily for at least 30 minutes in homogeneous groups of three to six students, with training and ongoing support for teachers and interventionists.
requirements: Implemented daily for at least 30 minutes in small, homogeneous groups of three to six students
Training and ongoing support for the teachers and interventionists who provide the small-group instruction
constraints: Amount of time and intensity should reflect the degree of risk determined by reading assessment data and other indicators
target_learners: English learners in the elementary grades at risk for reading problems
target_learning_goals: Foundational reading skills: phonological awareness, phonics, fluency, vocabulary, and comprehension
examples: Use an intervention program with students who enter the first grade with weak reading and prereading skills, or with older elementary students with reading problems.
key_sources: Gersten, R., Baker, S.K., Shanahan, T., Linan-Thompson, S., Collins, P., & Scarcella, R. (2007). Effective Literacy and English Language Instruction for English Learners in the Elementary Grades: A Practice Guide (NCEE 2007-4011). Washington, DC: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/PracticeGuide/6

article_title: Improving Adolescent Literacy: Effective Classroom and Intervention Practices
citation: Kamil, M. L., Borman, G. D., Dole, J., Kral, C. C., Salinger, T., and Torgesen, J. (2008). Improving adolescent literacy: Effective classroom and intervention practices: A Practice Guide (NCEE #2008-4027). Washington, DC: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. http://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc
title: Make available intensive and individualized interventions for struggling readers provided by trained specialists
description: The guide's fifth recommendation addresses students who score well below peers and cannot improve under normal classroom conditions. If struggling readers are identified and "their weaknesses in reading are carefully assessed by trained specialists using measures that detect strengths and weaknesses, and this assessment is followed by intensive interventions that are focused on their particular needs, they will have more opportunities to improve their literacy skills substantially." Intervention intensity should match instructional need, varying with group size and instructional time.
requirements: Use reliable screening assessments to identify students with reading difficulties, followed by formal and informal assessments to pinpoint instructional needs
Select an intervention that provides an explicit instructional focus to meet each student's identified learning needs
Match intervention intensity to student need, relating group size and amount of instructional time to the level of need
constraints: The fifth recommendation refers to reading interventions that in many cases must be provided by reading specialists or specially trained teachers, not ordinary classroom teachers
target_learners: Adolescent struggling readers whose poor literacy skills weaken their ability to make sense of written material
target_learning_goals: Accelerated reading growth toward grade-level literacy standards
examples: The panel rates the evidence strong and warns that schools housing such programs within special education serve only a small proportion of the students who could benefit.
key_sources: Kamil, M. L., Borman, G. D., Dole, J., Kral, C. C., Salinger, T., and Torgesen, J. (2008). Improving adolescent literacy: Effective classroom and intervention practices: A Practice Guide (NCEE #2008-4027). Washington, DC: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/PracticeGuide/8

article_title: Designing an App to Support Families’ Joint Engagement with Media: Design Principles and Lessons from Research
citation: Digital Promise, The Jim Henson Company, Concord Evaluation Group, & Curious Media. (2021). Designing an app to support families' joint engagement with media: Design principles and lessons from research. [White Paper]. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/121
title: Include conversation starters to help families discuss key ideas while watching and reflect after viewing
description: This principle recommends embedding conversation starters in family media apps to encourage discussion of key science ideas during viewing and reflection afterward. Findings from Phases 3 and 4 showed families "accessed and used all different sets of conversation starters to engage in science talk," and parents reported feeling more confident engaging in science talk after using the app.
requirements: Prompts designed for before, during, and after viewing scenarios
Prompts aligned to families' typical co-viewing interaction patterns
constraints: Families did not necessarily use the starters as initially designed; some used before and during prompts after viewing because they did not want to interrupt children
Before prompts were most challenging because families did not have context for the episode
target_learners: Parents and caregivers of young children
target_learning_goals: Facilitating rich science conversations between parents and children

Repeated opportunities for children to practice what they are learning

The guide is direct about the mechanism: "Children learn more from conversing with the teacher than from listening to teachers talk for extended periods." Developmentally appropriate instruction for ages 3-5 uses hands-on activities, short verbal instructions, and no expectation that children sit still more than 10-15 minutes or complete worksheets.

Hands-on instructional activities with short verbal instructions

description: This pattern embeds academic learning content inside career and technical education classes rather than teaching academics separately. The brief examines efforts "infusing more math into CTE curricula," presenting academic-CTE integration as a curriculum development endeavor. It reports that such integration is challenging, benefits from detailed CTE teacher feedback, and demands substantial time, effort, and other resources from educators and curriculum developers.

article_title: CASEL SEL Framework
citation: Collaborative for Academic, Social, and Emotional Learning (CASEL). (2020). What Is SEL? https://casel.org/fundamentals-of-sel/
title: Weave SEL into all students' educational experiences across classrooms, schools, homes, and communities
description: The page's implementation guidance holds that SEL is most effective when integrated across key settings rather than delivered as isolated lessons. It states, "SEL is most effective when it's woven into all students' educational experiences," and that SEL is "integrated across key settings where students live and learn: classrooms, schools, homes, and communities." This principle guides systemwide SEL implementation.

constraints: SEL efforts both contribute to and depend upon a school climate where all students and adults feel respected, supported, and engaged

article_title: Beable One
citation: Beable. (2024). Beable evidence rating: Promising. https://www.beable.com
title: Blended implementation combining independent student practice with teacher-led full-class and small-group instruction
description: The Beable implementation model combines digital independent practice with teacher instruction: it "supports independent student practice with feedback, complemented by teacher-led instruction for both full class and small group settings." Teacher-led and independent learning supplemental materials are aligned with effective instruction, progression of skills, progress monitoring, and measures of success.
