article_title: Bottom Line
citation: What Works Clearinghouse, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. (2021). Bottom Line. https://whatworks.ed.gov
title: Intensive one-on-one advising across the college application, transition, and first years of college
description: The Bottom Line model pairs each student with an individualized advisor across sequential phases: application advising, financial aid support, college selection guidance, summer transition assistance, and continued campus support. Advisors interacted with students during high school, on average, 13 times during a 15-month period, entailing 10-15 hours of contact time, with support continuing at target colleges for up to six years.
requirements: Full-time advisors with college degrees who complete a first year learning the organization's curriculum and mastering advisor competencies; offices in served communities and at each target college.
constraints: Costs are nearly fully funded by private and corporate donors and foundations; students and families incur no costs.
target_learners: High school juniors and seniors from low-income backgrounds transitioning to college
target_learning_goals: Applying to and selecting high-quality, affordable colleges; persisting in college
examples: In the study, most meetings involved working on college applications or financial aid, and students attending target colleges were matched to a new advisor at their college.

citation: MAP Growth National Dashboard user guide and FAQ. (2026). https://www.nwea.org/map-growth-national-dashboard
title: Interpret dashboard data with more than one metric, looking at patterns over time and considering both achievement and growth
description: The guide's cautions section recommends that users avoid drawing conclusions from a single metric or term: "Avoid drawing conclusions from a single metric or term. Instead, look at patterns over time and consider both achievement and growth." Pairing growth with achievement is presented as yielding a more complete and nuanced picture of student progress, since achievement captures single-point performance while growth tracks progress between test events.
requirements: Access to both achievement and growth metrics, which on the dashboard means data from at least two testing terms
constraints: Growth metrics are unavailable in the fall dashboard update because they require two test scores
examples: The Trends Over Time tab supports comparing changes in RIT scores since 2019 baselines, including differences by student group
The guide recommends using national reference lines to put local or state results in context rather than state-to-state comparisons

article_title: The Educational Attainment of Chicago Public Schools Students
citation: Usher, A., Mahaffie, S., & Nagaoka, J. (2023). The educational attainment of Chicago Public Schools students: 2022. Chicago, IL: University of Chicago Consortium on School Research. https://toandthrough.uchicago.edu/tool/cps/
title: Interpret disaggregated attainment data within the context of structural oppression and use it to question what can be done to change inequitable outcomes
description: The report disaggregates attainment data by race/ethnicity and gender, disability status, and English Learner status "to understand which students face more barriers to educational attainment and where different strategies and supports are needed." It urges readers to examine these rates within the context of systemic racism and to move beyond asking why disparities exist toward questioning what can be done, both within and outside education, to change them.

article_title: Standards-Driven Instructional Improvement
citation: New research: Chicago showed instructional improvements under standards reform, while many other places did not. (2022). UChicago Consortium on School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu
title: Invest in teachers' learning, collaboration, and experimentation as the central lever for standards-driven instructional change
description: This principle holds that large-scale instructional change under new learning standards is achieved primarily by investing in teachers' own learning rather than by supplying curricula or ready-made materials. The release quotes report author Elaine M. Allensworth: "These findings point to the importance of investing in teachers’ learning, collaboration, and experimentation." It further states that large-scale instructional change is possible "when key supports are in place, but they have to be the right supports." In the study, professional learning — collaboration, coaching, and workshops — was the most important support strategy, and resources worked only when instruction-ready and tied to professional learning.
requirements: Professional learning supports must be in place, including teacher collaboration, coaching, and workshops
Instructional resources, if used, must be instruction-ready and tied to professional learning around instructional practices
constraints: The release notes that ready-made resources and particular curricula — levers policymakers often turn to — did not connect to changes in instruction and outcomes in this study
target_learners: K-12 students in mathematics and science classrooms in a large urban district
target_learning_goals: Standards-aligned instructional practices in mathematics and science
Improved student achievement in math and science
examples: Chicago Public Schools promoted change in math and science instruction aligned with CCSS-M and NGSS between 2014-15 and 2017-18 using districtwide surveys, interviews, and achievement data
key_sources: New research: Chicago showed instructional improvements under standards reform, while many other places did not. (2022). UChicago Consortium on School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu

title: Intelligent Tutoring Systems with adaptive learning
description: The glossary defines an Intelligent Tutoring System as "a computer system or digital learning environment that gives instant and custom feedback to students". target_learning_goals: Receiving instant, customized feedback and adaptive pacing in digital learning
examples: The adaptive learning entry explains that difficulty of material, pacing, sequence, type of help given, or other features can be adapted based on the learner's prior responses.

article_title: College Preparatory Curriculum for All
citation: Allensworth, E., Nomi, T., Montgomery, N., & Lee, V. E. (2008). College Preparatory Curriculum for All: Consequences of Ninth-Grade Course Taking in Algebra and English on Academic Outcomes in Chicago. Consortium on Chicago School Research. https://ccsr.uchicago.edu
title: Instructional-program mediation model of curriculum policy effects
description: A conceptual model (Figure 1) holding that a curriculum mandate affects student outcomes only through the school's instructional program: 'the courses, content, and pedagogy that students receive'. Enrollment depends on program structure and student background; courses and student response shape ninth-grade learning, which should translate into later achievement and postsecondary outcomes. Beneficial effects require schools to adjust instruction, students to respond, and early performance gains to persist.

Students must respond to changing instruction with better freshman-year performance
Improved freshman performance must lead to better later outcomes
constraints: Some schools may have difficulty enacting substantial instructional changes, and students who would otherwise take remedial classes may not respond as expected
target_learners: All high school students, including low-ability and special education students
target_learning_goals: Ninth-grade math and English achievement, high school graduation, and college enrollment
examples: The study tested the model by tracing effects on 15 outcomes measured at the end of ninth grade and the end of high school

article_title: Inclusive Design Principles for Learning and Employment Records: Co-Designing for Equity
citation: Cacicio, S., Tinsley, B., Miller, A., & Luke Luna, C. (2022, April). Inclusive design principles for learning and employment records: Co-designing for equity. Digital Promise. https://doi org/10 51388/20 500 12265/154
title: Five Inclusive Design Principles for LERs co-designed with frontline workers
description: A set of five worker-informed design principles for Learning and Employment Records, developed through rapid design cycles with frontline workers and iterated with a Technical Work Group and LER pilots. The principles direct developers to demonstrate evidence of skills beyond work history, show learning progress over time, give users control of presentation and sharing, address safety and privacy concerns, and prioritize lifelong access and ease of use. As the authors state, "The result of this work is a set of Inclusive Design Principles and user profiles for LERs created for technology developers and issuers." Each principle carries reasoning grounded in participant-advisors' lived experiences.

constraints: The principles address design for workers whose educational and career trajectories may differ substantially from the users developers typically design for

Multiple jobholders, caregivers, and workers with employment gaps
target_learning_goals: Communicating skills and competencies to employers
Tracking and verifying learning over time
Connecting to education and career opportunities
examples: Design sessions with a total of 27 workers, predominantly women of color 18–45 in retail, hospitality, and food service, generated the principles; participant-advisors received $200 per session

citation: Cacicio, S., Tinsley, B., Miller, A., & Luke Luna, C. (2022, April). Inclusive design principles for learning and employment records: Co-designing for equity. Digital Promise. https://doi org/10 51388/20 500 12265/154
title: Inclusive Innovation model centering marginalized communities in design and development
description: Digital Promise's Inclusive Innovation model holds that existing R&D models often fail historically marginalized populations, and that innovation must move beyond inviting marginalized voices to conversation. As the report states, "it places them at the center of design, development, and implementation." In this project the model was operationalized as co-design: frontline workers served as participant-advisors in three cohorts of bi-weekly video design sessions, with a Technical Work Group and LER pilots iterating on the resulting principles, followed by a broader survey for validation.
requirements: Recruitment through trusted partner organizations that provide direct services to adults
Facilitation that is laid back, inclusive, and fosters collective ownership
Equitable compensation of participant-advisors at consultant rates
constraints: The model was applied here to technology design for adult frontline workers in the U.S. learning and workforce ecosystem
target_learners: Historically marginalized populations such as BIPOC and people experiencing poverty
target_learning_goals: Ensuring technology design reflects the needs, concerns, and goals of the communities it is built for
Identifying design gaps that developers cannot see from their own trajectories
examples: Participant-advisors joined three cohorts meeting bi-weekly via video conferencing, with one cohort meeting Sunday afternoons to accommodate alternative work schedules; those unable to attend could give feedback individually

article_title: Recruitment and Retention: Impact of Pilot Solutions Designed by Teachers of Color Phase II Report
citation: Iloh, C. (2024, February). Recruitment and Retention: Impact of Pilot Solutions Designed by Teachers of Color (Phase II). Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/216
title: Digital Promise's Inclusive Innovation model: an equity-centered R&D approach engaging communities as agents of change
description: Inclusive Innovation is defined as "an equity-centered R&D approach that engages communities—students, parents, families, and community leaders—in partnership with district leaders, educators, researchers, and developers to create novel solutions to complex educational challenges." The model expands the who, what, and where of innovation by redistributing power and centering equity, treating those most impacted by inequities as agents of change. The four district initiatives in this report implemented the 'implement and iterate' stage of this model.

constraints: The article frames it as rejecting one-size-fits-all methods; solutions are context-driven to specific district ecosystems

target_learning_goals: Recruiting, supporting, and retaining teachers of color
examples: Four districts applied the model to teacher-diversity challenges between roughly 2021 and 2024

title: Inclusive Innovation as a five-stage design process from connect-and-commit to sustain-and-scale
description: The article specifies that "Inclusive Innovation reflects a five-stage design process: connect and commit, inquire and investigate, design and develop, implement and iterate, and sustain and scale." The report captures the 'implement and iterate' stage across the four initiatives, with Figure 1 depicting the stages.

article_title: Foundations for Young Adult Success: A Developmental Framework
citation: Nagaoka, J., Farrington, C. A., Ehrlich, S. B., with Johnson, D. W., Dickson, S., Heath, R., & Mayo, A. (2014). A Framework for Developing Young Adult Success in the 21st Century: White Paper — Defining Young Adult Success. University of Chicago Consortium on Chicago School Research Working Paper. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/framework-developing-young-adult-success-21st-century
title: Integrated identity framework: young adult success as agency and motivation grounded in an integrated identity
description: The article's central framework conceptualizes a well-prepared young adult as one with an integrated identity and the agency to use internal and external resources toward self-set goals. It defines success as "being poised to work toward and achieve the goals a person sets for herself," with goals emerging from values and purpose. The framework names key factors — knowledge and skills, awareness, mindsets, strategies, and behaviors and habits — that come together in an integrated identity enabling directed action across life domains.

article_title: The Educational Attainment of Chicago Public Schools Students (2023)
citation: Mahaffie, S., Usher, A., Nagaoka, J., & McKoy, D. (2024). The educational attainment of Chicago Public Schools students: 2023. Chicago, IL: University of Chicago Consortium on School Research. https://toandthrough.uchicago.edu/tool/cps/
title: Interpret disaggregated attainment data within the context of structural oppression
description: The report urges readers to examine disaggregated rates of educational attainment "within the context of structural oppression—particularly the history and present reality of systemic racism." It disaggregates by race/ethnicity and gender, disability status, and EL status to identify which students face more barriers and where different strategies and supports are needed, and to support critical examination of whether schools and colleges are fostering equitable outcomes.

article_title: Supporting Science Learning and Literacy Development Together: Initial Results from a Curriculum Study in 1st Grade Classrooms
citation: Harris, C. J., Murphy, R., Feng, M., & Rutstein, D. (2023). Supporting science learning and literacy development together: Initial results from a curriculum study in 1st grade classrooms. WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Integrate science and literacy in early-grade curriculum materials so more science instruction can be added without sacrificing reading development
description: The article finds that science curriculum materials using "the high-leverage strategy of integrated science and literacy" can improve science proficiency and vocabulary while simultaneously developing reading skills. Because day-to-day science lessons intentionally embed reading, writing, talking, and visualizing, teachers can devote considerably more instructional time to science with confidence that reading scores will not be negatively impacted. This integration may enable elementary teachers to create instructional space for regular science teaching.
requirements: Curriculum lessons must intentionally integrate science learning with literacy development, with an emphasis on reading in K–3, and teachers need professional learning on the integrated pedagogical approach
constraints: The reading result is from one randomized trial of 1st grade classrooms in three California districts; the authors note additional studies at larger scale will be needed as NGSS-designed materials become more widely used
target_learners: Early elementary (K–3) students, including multilingual learners and students in underresourced schools
target_learning_goals: Science proficiency with NGSS performance expectations
examples: Intervention teachers implemented Amplify Science units whose lessons engage students in doing, reading, writing, talking, and visualizing science; they spent considerably more time on science than comparison teachers in prior implementation research (Iveland et al., 2021).
key_sources: Harris, C. J., Murphy, R., Feng, M., & Rutstein, D. (2023). Supporting science learning and literacy development together: Initial results from a curriculum study in 1st grade classrooms. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED638494

article_title: Cost and Cost Effectiveness of ASSISTments Online Math Support: Analysis from a Randomized Controlled Study in Middle School
citation: Feng, M., Weiser, G., & Collins, K. (2024). Cost and cost effectiveness of ASSISTments online math support: Analysis from a randomized controlled study in middle school. WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: The ingredients method for educational cost analysis
description: The report applies the ingredients method (Belfield et al., 2018), a methodology that involves "systematically identifying all the resources necessary for implementing" a program, pricing each component, and calculating total and per-participant costs. It characterizes the "treatment contrast" as the difference in resource use, not just outcomes, between intervention and comparison groups, counting opportunity costs of resources regardless of who pays. Costs were organized into four categories: personnel, training, facilities, and materials, and managed with the CostOut tool.
requirements: Detailed information about the components of an intervention and its alternatives, including quantities and local prices of each ingredient
constraints: The analysis focused only on incremental costs above business-as-usual, excluding classroom space, technical infrastructure, and overhead rates
target_learners: district and school administrators making edtech adoption decisions
target_learning_goals: informed resource allocation and intervention adoption decisions
examples: The report identified ingredients collaboratively with the developers and local coach, refined the list through observations over two years, and clarified details by interviewing school leaders, coaches, and teachers

citation: Jones, B., Faulkner-Bond, M., Blitz, J., & Garcia-Arena, P. (2024). Accelerate Success for English Learners: Formative Assessment Support for Integrated and Meaningful Language Learning. Region 15 Comprehensive Center, WestEd. https://www.wested.org/
title: Quality instruction for English learners integrates learning of concepts, analytic practices, and language simultaneously
description: The brief argues that language development should not be treated as a separate process from content learning. It defines three disciplinary practices: conceptual understandings, analytic practices, and language practices, and states that "Quality instruction for English learners integrates learning of concepts, analytic practices, and language simultaneously." Teachers plan lessons that create opportunities to use language across the four language domains connected to rigorous, grade-level content.

constraints: Not every lesson requires the same level of emphasis on each type of disciplinary practice; teachers strategically decide which to emphasize

target_learning_goals: Disciplinary content learning, analytic practices, and discipline-specific language development
examples: Teachers plan lessons with opportunities for students to use language and reflect across reading, writing, speaking, and listening in connection to grade-level content, working together around worthwhile inquiry questions, texts, and topics

article_title: Free to Fail or On-Track to College
citation: Stevens, W. D., Allensworth, E. M., Pareja, A. S., de la Torre, M., Gwynne, J. A., Rosenkranz, T., & Sebastian, J. (2014). Free to Fail or On-Track to College: An Introduction to the UChicago CCSR Research Series. UChicago CCSR Research Brief. https://ccsr.uchicago.edu

citation: Babineau, K., Shah, Z., Jacobs, B., Miller, A., Alvarado, B., Aguirre, N., Fennelly-Atkinson, R., & Young, V. (2025). Building Bridges: Cultivating Interconnectedness for STEM Pathways in San Diego. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/254
title: Inclusive Innovation model: a phased process in which people closest to the challenge lead, participate in, and benefit from innovation
description: The Inclusive Innovation model is a formalized co-design framework guiding the San Diego STEM Pathways Initiative. The report defines it as "a formalized process by which the people closest to the challenge lead, participate in, and benefit from innovation". Figure 3 presents phases from Readiness and Connect & Commit through Inquire & Investigate, Design & Develop, Implement & Iterate, and Sustain & Scale, each with associated artifacts such as a Community Charter, Solution Prototype, and Codified Solution. The Community Advisory Committee used the model to structure its collaboration, moving from establishing core values and root cause analysis to developing solution concepts.

Trust-building time, since the Connect and Commit pillar often takes time and is an ongoing process throughout the life of the project

article_title: Recruitment and Retention: Pilot Solutions Designed by Teachers of Color (Phase I)
citation: Bland, J. & Smith, K. (2023, February). Recruitment and retention: Pilot solutions designed by teachers of color (Phase I). Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/168
title: The Inclusive Innovation model: an equity-centered R&D process with five phases that prioritizes the voices of those most impacted
description: The report describes the Inclusive Innovation approach as "An equity-centered R&D model that engages communities—students, parents, families, and community leaders—in partnership with district leaders, educators, researchers, and developers to create novel solutions to complex educational challenges." It encompasses five phases: connect and commit, inquire and investigate, design and develop, implement and iterate, and sustain and scale. The model intentionally prioritizes the perspectives, experiences, and ideas of those most impacted by a challenge, and in this project it structured LEA Design Teams' work from problem identification through pilot launch.

article_title: Learning Transition Design Principles for Learning and Employment Records: Co-designing for Equity
citation: Page, K., Merritt Johnson, A., Franklin, K., Carter, B., Galindo, M., Solorzano, T., Lee, S., and Shah, Z., (2023, July). Learning Transition Design Principles for Learning and Employment Records: Co-designing for Equity. Digital Promise https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/185
title: An inclusive approach to learning transitions centered in the individual's life
description: Drawing on feminist scholarship and Colley (2007), the report reframes learning transitions away from a linear, androcentric pathway model toward one where "learning transitions defined by and centered in the life of the individual experiencing it, especially learners and workers from HSE communities." It treats change and time as a natural flow across multiple pathways, life as constant transition, and learning as a permanent state in "becoming" and "unbecoming." The change may occur at the level of knowledge, skills, attitude, or behavior, and how it is described depends on the individual's lived experience. The study applied this frame inductively, inviting HSE learners and workers to define what constituted an impactful transition to them.
requirements: Transitions must be studied in context, through events and practices in real-lived contexts rather than decontextualized methods
constraints: Most extant transition work assumes a traditional linear pathway conception the report explicitly departs from
target_learners: adult learners and workers from historically and systematically excluded communities
target_learning_goals: navigating education, career, and life transitions
examples: Participants defined impactful transitions themselves, producing stories such as losing a bar job during COVID, validating Cuban credentials in the U.S., and retiring from the Marine Corps after 26 years
key_sources: Page, K., Merritt Johnson, A., Franklin, K., Carter, B., Galindo, M., Solorzano, T., Lee, S., and Shah, Z., (2023, July). Learning Transition Design Principles for Learning and Employment Records: Co-designing for Equity. Digital Promise https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/185

article_title: Understanding the Experiences of LGBTQ High School Students in California by Race/Ethnicity
citation: Cerna, R., Stern, A., Austin, G., Betz, J., Zhang, G., & Hashmi, S. (2021). Understanding the experiences of LGBTQ high school students in California by race/ethnicity. WestEd. https://www.wested.org/resources/lgbtq-students-in-california/

article_title: Identifying Indicators of Distress in Charter Schools, Part 2: The Roles and Perspectives of Charter School Leaders and Board Members
citation: National Charter School Resource Center, Evan, A., & Sullivan, H. (2021). Identifying Indicators of Distress in Charter Schools, Part 2: The Roles and Perspectives of Charter School Leaders and Board Members. Bethesda, MD: Manhattan Strategy Group.
title: Indicators-of-distress framework: leading characteristics that occur early in charter school decline across six school domains
description: The report defines indicators of distress as "characteristics that occur early in a school's decline suggesting a school that is struggling to achieve or maintain high levels of quality." Unlike lagging indicators, they are leading indicators that "might predict future failure" and are "more difficult to measure but easier to influence." The framework organizes them into six interrelated domains—leadership, governing board, finance and operations, talent, culture, and instruction—adapted from the Four Domains for Rapid School Improvement framework plus charter-specific functions, so stakeholders can identify distress early and intervene while improvement is feasible.

Charter school authorizers and support organizations
target_learning_goals: Organizational capacity to identify early signs of school decline and intervene before failure
examples: The report categorizes indicators from Figure 1 into leadership, governing board, finance and operations, talent, culture, and instruction, with network-specific indicators flagged

citation: Browning, A., Kaminsky, C., & Gerzon, N. (2022). Moving toward instructional coherence: How four popular student-centered approaches deepen identity, agency, equity, and community. WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Instructional coherence framework: four student-centered approaches share commitments to identity, agency, equity, and community
description: The paper offers a framework for understanding formative assessment, deeper learning, culturally responsive and sustaining education, and personalized learning as complementary rather than competing approaches. It states that the four approaches 'share a common aspirational commitment—to provide student learning experiences rooted in developing identity, prioritizing learner agency, educating for equity, and honoring and activating community assets.' The framework is intended to help school leaders build an instructional vision using practices shared across all four approaches, since no single approach alone provides the structures to achieve that aspiration.

constraints: The resource is not exhaustive of all student-centered learning approaches; it focuses on these four at the secondary level

article_title: The Instructional Leadership Corps: Teachers Leading Sustainable Professional Learning in Their Communities
citation: Lotan, R. A., & Burns, D. (2019). The Instructional Leadership Corps: Teachers leading sustainable professional learning in their communities. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/instructional-leadership-corps-teachers-leading
title: The Instructional Leadership Corps (ILC): a statewide teacher-led professional learning project
description: The ILC is a statewide collaborative teacher professional learning project launched in 2014 by the Stanford Center for Opportunity Policy in Education, the California Teachers Association, and the National Board Resource Center. Rather than outside consultants conducting one-shot workshops, "the ILC entrusts professional learning to local teaching professionals who have the training and support to lead ongoing learning within their own districts." Between November 2014 and September 2018, ILC leaders provided multisession workshops to more than 32,000 educators in more than 2,000 schools and at least 495 districts, with an initial cadre of 183 teacher and site leaders selected from an applicant pool of 500. Members are primarily teachers, augmented by administrators and coaches/ToSAs.
requirements: Intensive professional development for ILC members at statewide and regional conferences and retreats
Supportive institutional partners (SCOPE, CTA, NBRC) providing guidance, resources, and network upkeep
constraints: Growth depended on local fiscal commitment, embrace of the work, and valuing teacher expertise for the project to take root

title: Apply the five design principles in reinforcing, integrated ways rather than as isolated components
description: The report emphasizes that the five elements should not be implemented separately. title: Internationals Network five core principles for newcomer schools

description: The article's model design adopts enumerated key features from each reflection theory family: staged reflection and iterative cycles from experiential learning; assumption re-examination from transformative learning; reflection-in-action and reflection-on-action from the reflective practitioner; emotion handling from affective models; and goal setting, self-monitoring and adaptive adjustment from self-regulated learning. title: Indiana grant and scholarship programs (21st Century Scholars, Frank O'Bannon, Mitch Daniels Early Graduation, Workforce Ready)
description: The report analyzes four Indiana programs against its framework and finds none meets all ten metrics; Indiana provides no aid to undocumented or incarcerated students. The 21st Century Scholars promise program is last-dollar, tuition-and-fees only, and carries merit-style requirements including a 2.5 GPA, Core 40 diploma, and Scholars Success Program activities. The Frank O'Bannon Grant is Indiana's main need-based grant, with 2025-26 awards from $400 to $10,600.

citation: Jinwen Tang. (2026). NEW AI-DRIVEN TOOLS FOR ENHANCING CAMPUS WELL-BEING: A PREVENTION AND INTERVENTION APPROACH. Doctoral dissertation, University of Missouri-Columbia. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.10804

description: The dissertation's proposed framework (Objective 3) unifies the preventive layer (TigerGPT plus AURA) with the intervention layer (PsychoGPT and SMMR). "This design allows insights from survey chatbot's adaptive dialogues, such as emerging student concerns or early signs of distress, to flow directly into specialized models like PsychoGPT or SMMR." By aligning both strategies under one system, administrators can enhance campus-wide satisfaction initiatives while identifying and supporting individuals experiencing psychological challenges.

citation: Haiyang Xin, Qiannan Niu, Shuang Li, Yimeng Sun, Ching Sing Chai, Lingyun Huang, Gaowei Chen. (2026). An Activity-Theoretical Approach to Teacher Professional Development in Pedagogical AI Agent Design. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.12934
title: Integrate capacity building with need satisfaction simultaneously in teacher professional development rather than sequentially
description: The article's third design principle holds that professional development should build technological capacity and satisfy basic psychological needs at the same time. The authors argue that "sequential approaches produce decoupling," whereas synergistic design in which scaffolds enhance both capability and satisfaction enables sustained engagement. Cycle 2 operationalized this by pairing TPACK-oriented training with autonomy, competence, and relatedness supports, producing synchronized gains in capacity and willingness.

constraints: The authors note interventions succeed when tools match disciplinary needs and autonomy is substantive

In the study, the instructor matched GenAI slides to their visual style and deleted content such as learning-objectives slides, adjustments the authors describe as requiring little effort.

article_title: AI-Enabled Serious Games: Integrating Intelligence and Adaptivity in Training Systems
citation: Tripathi, P., & Kapralos, B. (2026). AI-Enabled Serious Games: Integrating Intelligence and Adaptivity in Training Systems. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.21962
title: Instructional intelligence and adaptivity as independent system properties
description: The chapter treats instructional intelligence and adaptivity as two distinct, independent system properties. Instructional intelligence is "a system's capacity to infer learner state and reason about pedagogically appropriate responses", while adaptivity is the ability to "modify instructional actions at runtime" without pausing or rebuilding the system. Because they are independent, a system can be strong on one and weak on the other, and improving one does not automatically improve the other. The chapter uses this two-dimensional framing to organize its historical synthesis and analysis of AI approaches.
requirements: Systems must articulate architectural considerations for both dimensions to integrate AI within established learning and training evaluation frameworks
constraints: The fourth configuration (high intelligence-high adaptivity) "has proven extraordinarily difficult to achieve in practice" due to computational constraints: deep learner modeling required processing time incompatible with real-time interaction
target_learners: Learners and trainees using serious games across healthcare, defense, and education domains
target_learning_goals: Personalized, adaptive learning trajectories in serious games and simulation-based training
examples: Fig. 1 illustrates the two-dimensional intelligence–adaptivity space with representative systems positioned ordinally from each historical phase
key_sources: Tripathi, P., & Kapralos, B. (2026). AI-Enabled Serious Games: Integrating Intelligence and Adaptivity in Training Systems. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.21962

article_title: AI-Enabled Serious Games: Integrating Intelligence and Adaptivity in Training Systems
citation: Tripathi, P., & Kapralos, B. (2026). AI-Enabled Serious Games: Integrating Intelligence and Adaptivity in Training Systems. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.21962
title: Instrument serious games for learning analytics from the start, as interaction data becomes the foundation for future adaptive intelligence
description: The chapter derives from Phase V's legacy the principle that every serious game should capture learning analytics data even before AI capabilities are introduced. Historical logs of learner responses accumulated by learning analytics platforms "are precisely what modern reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms train on," using past interaction records to learn which instructional actions tend to produce good outcomes. Early instrumentation ensures the data foundation exists as the system architecture matures toward adaptive intelligence.
requirements: Systems must collect and transmit data about learner interactions, including which questions were answered, how long each took, and how often hints were requested
constraints: Learned policies are only as good as the interaction data they train on (Phase V's data dependency)
target_learners: Learners using serious games that will later integrate AI-driven adaptivity
target_learning_goals: Building the data foundation for reinforcement learning-based instructional adaptation
examples: Phase V platforms such as Khan Academy and Duolingo with Half-Life Regression spaced repetition demonstrated that computational analysis of interaction data could inform instructional improvement
key_sources: Tripathi, P., & Kapralos, B. (2026). AI-Enabled Serious Games: Integrating Intelligence and Adaptivity in Training Systems. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.21962

title: Invest in implementation conditions — sustained faculty development, consultative governance, equitable access, and programme-level consistency — when adopting GenAI assessment frameworks
description: This principle holds that the value of a GenAI assessment framework is realised through its implementation conditions, not its selection. The study concludes that "structured frameworks are most useful when they are embedded within sustained faculty development, consultative governance, equitable access, and programme-level consistency". It directs institutional investment toward faculty development, equitable tool access, programme-level guidance, and assessment redesign capacity as core infrastructure for GenAI-era assessment reform.
requirements: Institutions must invest in faculty development, equitable tool access, programme-level guidance, and assessment redesign capacity
constraints: Without these supports the framework risks becoming a compliance layer or another discursive response leaving the validity problem untouched
The study reports faculty perceptions rather than measured generalisable outcomes

equitable student access to AI tools
examples: The study recommends cross-disciplinary working groups, piloting assessment framework changes before mandating them, and feedback loops for revising guidance as tools evolve

citation: Kuhn, J., Gerjets, P., Trautwein, U., Greene, J. A., Malone, S., Vogt, P., & Fütterer, T. (2026). AI-Augmented Inquiry and Regulation in Hybrid Systems: A Control Allocation Architecture for Preserving Epistemic Agency in Hybrid Human-AI Cognition. https://osf.io/preprints
title: Require minimal independent reasoning before genAI consultation (the Anticipate sequencing principle)
description: A core AIRIS design implication, an application of the Anticipate operator: wherever possible, humans should engage in at least minimal independent reasoning before consulting genAI. The article argues this sequencing "ensures that the human agent enters the genAI consultation with a cognitive stake in the outcome, increasing the likelihood that genAI outputs are actively evaluated rather than passively accepted." It is presented as one of AIRIS's most consistent design implications, keeping evaluative authority with the human agent.
requirements: Learners or environments must create an occasion for own reasoning first, so consultation follows rather than precedes independent attempts.
constraints: The principle is derived from the framework and supporting cited evidence; the article presents it as an application of the Anticipate operator rather than a tested prescription of this article itself.
target_learners: learners using genAI in inquiry, writing, and problem-solving tasks
target_learning_goals: preserving generative engagement and active evaluation of genAI outputs
examples: The article cites Pi et al. (2026): when learners identified errors in their own work before receiving genAI feedback, they achieved substantially larger learning gains than when the genAI identified the errors for them.

article_title: AI as Teammate: Rethinking Task Distribution in Medical Training
citation: Tsim, F., Gutoreva, A., Weiss, A., & Dubosh, N. (2026). AI as Teammate: Rethinking Task Distribution in Medical Training. Correspondence: fenditsim@gmail.com
title: Two complementary developmental trajectories: Internalization (human-human) and Symbiosis (human-AI) in clinical reasoning formation
description: The article proposes that clinical reasoning development proceeds along two simultaneous trajectories. The Internalization Trajectory preserves Vygotsky's original human-human account through the Non-Negotiable subzone with human more-knowledgeable-others, instantiated historically by apprenticeship. The article states: "SCAN proposes the Symbiosis Trajectory where a learner navigates from Substitute through Aid to Complement, progressively developing task-specific knowledge in collaboration with GenAI." The authors conjecture the two are complementary and that complete clinical formation requires both, with epistemic agency and responsibility increasing progressively in each.
requirements: Both trajectories must be present; neither substitutes for the other, per the authors' conjecture
constraints: The complementarity of the two trajectories is explicitly framed as a conjecture, not a tested result
target_learners: Medical trainees from first-week students to senior residents
target_learning_goals: Self-regulation and epistemic responsibility for AI use
examples: In the Symbiosis Trajectory, a first-week student generates a differential with AI (Substitute, other-regulation), a third-year student augments reasoning with AI suggestions (Aid, shared regulation), and a senior resident directs LLMs and takes full epistemic responsibility (Complement, self-regulation)

citation: Firdausi, H.; Wasis; Sholikah, R. W.; Lemantara, J.; Rosyadi, F. D.; Ginardi, R. V. H.; Pradityo, M. H. A.; Hakim, A. R. (2026). title: Hybrid IndoBERT–BiLSTM automated essay scoring architecture with per-dimension classifiers
description: The IB-BiLSTM architecture "combines IndoBERT as a contextual encoder with a two -layer Bidirectional LSTM (BiLSTM) as a sequential classifier." IndoBERT produces token-level embeddings of shape (batch × 128 × 768) fed to the BiLSTM, followed by Dense layers (256 and 128 units, ReLU) and a four-unit softmax for score levels 1–4. Six independent classification models were built, one per FRISCO dimension, rather than a single multi-label classifier, and all IndoBERT parameters were trainable for joint fine-tuning.

target_learning_goals: Automated multidimensional assessment of critical thinking in physics essays
examples: Ten IB-BiLSTM variants (A–J) varying learning rate, dropout, and BiLSTM units were trained; IB-BiLSTM-I won Situation and Clarity, and the best model per dimension was deployed in a web-based system returning per-dimension scores

citation: Adam Coscia, Sujata Duwal, Langdon Holmes, Scott Crossley, and Alex Endert. (2026). Calibrating Trustworthiness: Co-Designing Metrics and Visualizations for Evaluating LLMs in Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04006
title: Intelligent digital textbook framework with LLM-powered structured dialogue for reading comprehension support
description: The learning engineer collaborators are developing a framework for intelligent digital textbooks augmented with AI capabilities. Learners write a summary after reading each page, scored by a finetuned ModernBERT model. If below the passing threshold, a structured dialogue sequence triggers: the learner re-reads a selected passage, then the LLM agent Llama3 generates a self-explanation reading training question, followed by a follow-up question and summary revision advice grounded in the passage and dialogue.

constraints: Smaller models often struggle to follow prompt instructions in the same way larger, proprietary models do
target_learners: K-12 and higher education students reading digital textbooks
examples: The final prompt in the structured dialogue sequence was the subject of the prompt tournament evaluation

article_title: Governing academic integrity: Ensuring the authenticity of higher thinking in the era of generative artificial intelligence
citation: Hamish Coates, Gwilym Croucher, Angel Calderon. (2025). Governing Academic Integrity: Ensuring the Authenticity of Higher Thinking in the Era of Generative Artificial Intelligence. Journal of Academic Ethics. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10805-025-09639-7
title: Integrity economy: external pressure from regulation, benchmarking and cross-institutional competition to drive academic integrity reform
description: The article argues that internal institutional development alone is insufficient because very little institutional development is likely to pay out without the right kinds of external affordance. It notes there is not yet a flourishing 'integrity economy' in higher education and that "Benchmarking and collaboration thus have essential roles to play, as do pressure from quality and regulatory agencies". Following Heyneman, it proposes generating a reputational economy based on academic ethics rather than research reputation, drawing an analogy with how global research reputation risk indices (rankings) have proven key to reform by stimulating a global reputation race.
requirements: External affordance through benchmarking, collaboration and regulatory pressure
Transparency as a change driver in higher education
constraints: Accountability agencies' efforts are likely to have muted impact given the lagging nature of reform, the lack of resonance with academic practice, and the truly global nature of the situation
The world lacks a recognised forum for discussing the intersection of universities, governance and GenAI
examples: Regulatory agencies formed the Global Academic Integrity Network (GAIN); Australia's regulator asked all institutions to report their GenAI plans, spurring national dialogue; QAA in the UK produced a charter and enhancement resources
key_sources: Hamish Coates, Gwilym Croucher, Angel Calderon. (2025). Governing Academic Integrity: Ensuring the Authenticity of Higher Thinking in the Era of Generative Artificial Intelligence. Journal of Academic Ethics. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10805-025-09639-7

article_title: The Path to Conversational AI Tutors: Integrating Tutoring Best Practices and Targeted Technologies to Produce Scalable AI Agents
citation: Kirk Vanacore, Ryan S. Baker, Avery H. Closser, and Jeremy Roschelle. (2026). The Path to Conversational AI Tutors: Integrating Tutoring Best Practices and Targeted Technologies to Produce Scalable AI Agents. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.19303
title: Inner–outer loop architecture as a legacy ITS design pattern to retain in conversational AI tutors
description: A defining conceptual advance of the legacy ITS era: a dual structure in which the inner loop manages step-level interactions within a single problem (error detection, correctness feedback, graduated hints at impasses) while the outer loop selects which problems to give next, guided by knowledge tracing models and curricular sequencing rules. The article argues this separation "remains one of the most influential design patterns in the ITS tradition" and proposes that in generative AI conversational tutors this architecture could constrain the tutoring session to appropriate content within and between problems.
requirements: The outer loop must be guided by knowledge tracing models and curricular sequencing rules to select appropriate problems
constraints: Legacy ITS were often domain-specific and highly structured, which the article names as a characteristic of the era
target_learners: Students using adaptive tutoring systems in domains such as mathematics and physics
target_learning_goals: Adaptive practice with appropriate problem sequencing and step-level feedback
examples: Systems like Cognitive Tutor, ANDES, and ALEKS provided finely tuned adaptivity both within and across problems using this dual structure
key_sources: Kirk Vanacore, Ryan S. Baker, Avery H. Closser, and Jeremy Roschelle. (2026). The Path to Conversational AI Tutors: Integrating Tutoring Best Practices and Targeted Technologies to Produce Scalable AI Agents. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.19303

article_title: Child Safety in Generative AI: An Expert-Guided and Incident-Grounded Evaluation Framework
citation: Haein Kong. (2026). Child Safety in Generative AI: An Expert-Guided and Incident-Grounded Evaluation Framework. HEAL@CHI, April 2026, Barcelona. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.00395
title: Synthetic test set of 130 education-domain prompts generated from AI incidents with Mistral-7B
description: The test set generation method uses AI incidents describing human-AI interaction (n=13) in the education category as context. The Mistral-7B-Instruct model was instructed to generate five harmful user prompts per incident, using incident titles and descriptions, to capture more diverse linguistic expressions. A parallel set of harmless educational prompts was also generated. The result was 130 prompts: 65 unsafe and 65 safe user prompts, with unsafe prompts manually annotated into four hazard categories (Academic Dishonesty 37, Academic Stress and Anxiety 5, Inaccurate Knowledge 11, Lack of Critical Thinking 12).
requirements: AI incident titles and descriptions as generation context, and a generative model (Mistral-7B) to produce synthetic prompts
constraints: Due to the limited number of relevant incidents, five synthetic prompts were generated per incident; most hazards relate to cheating or academic dishonesty
target_learners: teens and students using LLMs in educational contexts
target_learning_goals: evaluating whether safety classifiers detect unsafe education-related prompts
examples: Unsafe prompt generation instructed the model to assume the user is a teen or student and to produce prompts showing harmful intention without benign questions
