article_title: Technology, Education and Critical Media Literacy: Potential, Challenges, and Opportunities
citation: Albardía MS, Peña-Fernández S and Agirreazkuenaga I (2025) Technology, education and critical media literacy: potential, challenges, and opportunities. Front. Hum. Dyn. 7:1608911. https://doi.org/10.3389/fhumd.2025.1608911
title: Integrated, participatory, and critical framework for media education in higher education
description: The article proposes an integrated, participatory, and critical framework for media education in higher education that brings together expert discourses and student experiences. It addresses "pedagogical, didactic, and curricular dimensions, while also engaging with broader social issues." The framework holds that media literacy must go beyond operational device use to include critical analysis of content, ethical and reflective consumption and production, and attention to structural inequalities such as the digital divide, aiming to promote participatory and critical citizenship.
requirements: Integration of media and information literacy with digital literacy in a critical way, so students use technologies and media content effectively and critically
constraints: Implementation and impact are profoundly shaped by cultural, regional, and structural contexts; inequality and limited infrastructure create obstacles requiring context-sensitive strategies
target_learners: University students in Communication and Education programs
target_learning_goals: Ethical and reflective media consumption and production
examples: The study grounds the framework in seven expert interviews and a 141-student survey at the University of the Basque Country
key_sources: Albardía MS, Peña-Fernández S and Agirreazkuenaga I (2025) Technology, education and critical media literacy: potential, challenges, and opportunities. Front. Hum. Dyn. 7:1608911. https://doi.org/10.3389/fhumd.2025.1608911

article_title: A didactical-driven teacher assistant for a dimensional modeling course
citation: Laurent Brisson, Maria Teresa Segarra and Gregory Smits. (2026). A didactical-driven teacher assistant for a dimensional modeling course. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22598
title: Intent-to-didactic-approach mapping structuring responses by Bloom level and typed chunk selection
description: The system elicited the instructor's actual response practice into a small set of declarative didactic approaches (Definition, Identification, Illustration, Explanation, Comparison, Complex synthesis), each targeting a Bloom level and defining core chunk types that structure the generated response plus an ontology-enrichment strategy. Five pedagogical intents form the exhaustive set: DEFINE, EXPLAIN, ILLUSTRATE, COMPARE, and IDENTIFY, where "IDENTIFY is the inverse of DEFINE". Constrained retrieval selects content by metadata filters on chunk type and concept id rather than unconstrained similarity.
requirements: A knowledge graph of concepts with structural and didactic relations curated by the instructor
An editorial corpus segmented into nine typed chunks with concept-identifier metadata
constraints: If constrained retrieval returns no chunk for a required type, the system returns a static reformulation message rather than silently switching to unconstrained retrieval
target_learners: University students asking conceptual questions about course content
target_learning_goals: Responses structured to the pedagogical intent and Bloom level of the student's question
examples: Each approach in Table 1 defines a required chunk type whose retrieval failure triggers graceful degradation, with other listed types retrieved when available
key_sources: Laurent Brisson, Maria Teresa Segarra and Gregory Smits. (2026). A didactical-driven teacher assistant for a dimensional modeling course. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22598

article_title: A didactical-driven teacher assistant for a dimensional modeling course
citation: Laurent Brisson, Maria Teresa Segarra and Gregory Smits. (2026). A didactical-driven teacher assistant for a dimensional modeling course. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22598
title: Instructor-curated knowledge graph and dual-readability typed chunk corpus for a dimensional modelling course
description: The course knowledge is represented as a lightweight knowledge graph containing 43 concepts organised into thematic groups, connected through structural relations (is a, part of) and didactic relations (precedes, confused with, mutually exclusive with) curated by the instructor. The course material is authored as structured Markdown revised "for dual readability: human and machine", with each concept on a dedicated page, content segmented into nine chunk types determined by the markup itself, and every chunk indexed in a ChromaDB store with concept id and chunk type as filterable attributes. Every answer is grounded in this instructor-authored material with permalinks to the relevant teaching pages.
requirements: Each new content source must be indexed with concept identifiers and chunk types so constrained retrieval continues to operate on pedagogical role
constraints: The current corpus is mono-authored, originating solely from the instructor's teaching notes
target_learners: University students in the dimensional modelling course
target_learning_goals: Grounding chatbot answers in verified curricular content with permalinks to teaching pages
examples: The vector store acts as a typed metadata index: canonical chunks such as definitions, notations and rules are retrieved by type and concept identifier, not by similarity to the student's question
key_sources: Laurent Brisson, Maria Teresa Segarra and Gregory Smits. (2026). A didactical-driven teacher assistant for a dimensional modeling course. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22598

article_title: E3Sense: Head-Confined Multimodal Sensing of Learner Engagement
citation: Sidharth Anupkrishnan, Itir Sayar, Jeongah Lee, Sri Harsha Musunuri, Guan-Ming Su, Madeline Endres, Ravi Karkar, Phuc Nguyen. (2026). E3Sense: Head-Confined Multimodal Sensing of Learner Engagement. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.26569
title: Include learners in defining what an engagement estimate represents, using their own criteria as context for personalized prediction
description: The article's design implication is "to include learners in defining what an engagement estimate represents". Because a single self-report can reflect several engagement dimensions that learners weight differently, a future interface could briefly elicit whether a learner associates engagement with understanding, sustained attention, interest, or a combination, and use that information when mapping sensor-derived scores to ratings, letting learners review and update criteria as tasks or goals change.
requirements: Brief elicitation of the learner's engagement criteria, reviewable and updatable as tasks or goals change
Definition codes derived from the learner (the present codes came from interviews, not inferred as psychological traits from sensor data)
constraints: Prospective elicitation and its stability remain to be tested; current models predict reported engagement and do not establish the cause of a low rating or which intervention would help
target_learning_goals: personalized, accurate interpretation of sensor-derived engagement estimates
examples: In the study, 18 participants' interview-derived cognitive, behavioral, and emotional definition codes, entered with score interactions, raised exploratory balanced 1-off accuracy from 64.6% to 71.5%
key_sources: Sidharth Anupkrishnan, Itir Sayar, Jeongah Lee, Sri Harsha Musunuri, Guan-Ming Su, Madeline Endres, Ravi Karkar, Phuc Nguyen. (2026). E3Sense: Head-Confined Multimodal Sensing of Learner Engagement. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.26569

article_title: GenAI and AI tools for STEAM educators: evidence-informed strategies and resources for the future of teaching
citation: Dahal N, Hasan MK and Islam MT (2026). GenAI and AI tools for STEAM educators: evidence-informed strategies and resources for the future of teaching. Front. Educ. 11:1948064. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1948064
title: Integrated framework for responsible human–AI collaboration linking pedagogical principles, ethical considerations, and discipline-specific applications
description: The review's central proposal is "an integrated framework for responsible human–AI collaboration linking pedagogical principles, ethical considerations, and discipline-specific applications." It frames AI adoption as pedagogical redesign rather than tool uptake, drawing on human-AI collaboration theory in which AI should augment rather than replace human cognition. Teachers remain designers of inquiry, interpreters of data, moderators of ethics, and coaches of metacognition, while students remain responsible for judgment, reflection, and transfer.
requirements: Sound pedagogy, AI literacy, and ethical governance must support any productivity or engagement gains
constraints: AI contributes where it can scaffold, suggest, visualize, or analyze, but not where an educational purpose requires human accountability
examples: The review argues GenAI can strengthen STEAM teaching only when educators remain designers, coaches, and ethical stewards rather than passive users of automation
key_sources: Dahal N, Hasan MK and Islam MT (2026). GenAI and AI tools for STEAM educators: evidence-informed strategies and resources for the future of teaching. Front. Educ. 11:1948064. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1948064

article_title: A Comparative Analysis of Institutional and Course Generative AI Policies within Higher Education: Implications for Instruction in Computing Education
citation: Amrita Ganguly, Aditya Johri, Nora McDonald, Areej Ali, Umama Dewan, and Aayushi Hingle Collier. (2026). A Comparative Analysis of Institutional and Course Generative AI Policies within Higher Education: Implications for Instruction in Computing Education.
title: Instructor-centered framework for translating institutional GenAI guidance into course implementation via three mediating factors
description: The authors propose a framework that guides the translation of institutional guidance to course implementation by placing the instructor at the center of the process and considering mediating factors (Figure 3). The first factor is the instructor's current expertise in GenAI use and broader AI literacy, along with the training needed to implement GenAI in instruction; in CS this includes understanding model limitations in code generation and recognizing security vulnerabilities in AI-generated code. The second factor is discipline or domain, since implications of GenAI use differ sharply between theory-heavy courses such as algorithms and applied ones such as software engineering. The third factor is the nature of instruction and required pedagogical knowledge, as GenAI use varies across lecture-based, lab-based and project-based courses.
requirements: Instructor AI literacy and training to implement GenAI in instruction
Accounting for whether the course is theory-heavy or applied
Pedagogical knowledge matched to lecture-based, lab-based, or project-based instruction
constraints: The framework is proposed, not empirically tested in this study; the authors state the transition to productive GenAI use will be an arduous task and substantial revisions to existing CS pedagogical practices will be needed
target_learners: Higher education students in computing courses
target_learning_goals: Responsible and productive GenAI use aligned with course learning outcomes
Preservation of problem-solving skills while supporting technical skill development
examples: The study found increased institutional focus on CS has not translated into clearer direction for CS instructors, leaving them to navigate these decisions largely on their own
key_sources: Amrita Ganguly, Aditya Johri, Nora McDonald, Areej Ali, Umama Dewan, and Aayushi Hingle Collier. (2026). A Comparative Analysis of Institutional and Course Generative AI Policies within Higher Education: Implications for Instruction in Computing Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.12296

article_title: Stop Writing for Me: Generative Refusal in AI Tools for Thought
citation: Sora Kang. (2026). Stop Writing for Me: Generative Refusal in AI Tools for Thought. In Proceedings of CHI 2026 Workshop on Tools for Thought. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.24751v1
title: Adopt internalization—performance without the tool—as the primary success metric for Tools for Thought
description: The paper argues that the industry standard of measuring performance with the tool fails to distinguish genuine cognitive augmentation from dependency. Instead, it proposes that the HCI community adopt "Internalization" as a primary success metric: measuring residual, post-tool performance. The study operationalized this by measuring "performance without the tool" and found users applied the internalized questioning patterns independently after the intervention. If a user cannot perform the task better after the tool is removed, the system has served as a prosthetic for production, not a scaffold for thought.
requirements: Evaluation must include an unassisted, post-tool measurement phase to capture residual effects
constraints: The paper notes the field lacks standardized longitudinal metrics or unassisted evaluation protocols for measuring cognitive internalization, posing this as an open workshop question
target_learners: users of generative AI learning tools
examples: The 14-day study measured residual effects after AI assistance was removed, finding participants self-generated similar questions (M = 4.87 on a 7-point scale)
key_sources: Sora Kang. (2026). Stop Writing for Me: Generative Refusal in AI Tools for Thought. In Proceedings of CHI 2026 Workshop on Tools for Thought. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.24751

article_title: 'Interactive Online Learning Method for Students Based on Artificial Intelligence'
citation: Li C, Yin W. (2025). Interactive online learning method for students based on artificial intelligence. Discover Artificial Intelligence 5:201. https://doi.org/10.1007/s44163-025-00401-x
title: Interactive online learning delivery modes: audio classroom, one-to-many video, and one-to-one video classroom
description: The article describes three synchronous online education models that constitute its interactive learning modalities: an online audio classroom, a one-to-many online video classroom, and an online one-to-one video classroom. In the audio mode, "the teacher teaches solely by audio and allows students to voice intervene, backed up by a transcript of the dialog"; in the video modes, instructors deliver content via direct video while students intervene through a discussion or chat text box, one at a time in the one-to-one format. These modes are presented as supporting student motivation and engagement alongside the prediction model.
requirements: Internet connectivity and virtual classroom infrastructure supporting audio/video channels and text-based student interventions
target_learners: online learners in higher education and distance-learning settings
examples: The study includes audio-based, video-based, and one-on-one virtual classroom formats to boost student motivation and engagement
key_sources: Li C, Yin W. (2025). Interactive online learning method for students based on artificial intelligence. Discover Artificial Intelligence 5:201. https://doi.org/10.1007/s44163-025-00401-x

article_title: INSIDE the Student's Mind: Jointly Modeling Latent Reasoning and Action in LLM Student Simulators
citation: Rose Niousha, Minwoo Kang, Narges Norouzi. (2026). INSIDE the Student's Mind: Jointly Modeling Latent Reasoning and Action in LLM Student Simulators. Published as a conference paper at COLM 2026. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10492
title: INSIDE: internal dialogue as an intermediate cognitive layer preceding student actions in LLM student simulation
description: INSIDE is a student-modeling framework that fine-tunes LLMs to generate a verbalized internal dialogue before producing the student's next code submission. A teacher LLM (GPT-5) performs retrospective inference over the interaction context and the observed next submission, first producing structured cognitive, affective, and action states inspired by Bloom's Taxonomy, then a first-person think trace used as fine-tuning supervision. The article states that "INSIDE introduces internal dialogue as an intermediate cognitive layer that precedes student actions during learning interactions, capturing the intent that leads to each attempt rather than only explaining mistakes after the fact." Unlike reconstructive post-hoc accounts of errors, the framework models reasoning that precedes each attempt, jointly modeling how and why students act.
requirements: Requires student interaction data with sequential code submissions and associated AI tutor feedback, and a teacher LLM to generate retrospective reasoning traces for fine-tuning supervision.
constraints: Internal dialogue is reconstructed rather than observed; the article notes LLMs "may struggle to faithfully reconstruct novice reasoning patterns," so traces may reflect more coherent reasoning than real students exhibit.
target_learners: Novice undergraduate students in an introductory Python programming course
target_learning_goals: Programming problem-solving with iterative code revision in response to AI tutor and autograder feedback
examples: Fine-tuned Qwen2.5-7B, Qwen2.5-Coder-7B, and Qwen3-8B with LoRA (r=16, alpha=32) on paired think traces and actions from Spring 2025 course data, evaluated against prompting baselines including Bloom-inspired structured CoT.
key_sources: Rose Niousha, Minwoo Kang, Narges Norouzi. (2026). INSIDE the Student's Mind: Jointly Modeling Latent Reasoning and Action in LLM Student Simulators. Published as a conference paper at COLM 2026. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10492

article_title: Instructional Governance by Design: A Framework for AI in Computing Education
citation: Ethan Dickey. (2026). Instructional Governance by Design: A Framework for AI in Computing Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.26098
title: Instructional governance: the designed allocation of authority, agency, accountability, context, and evaluation visibility in AI-mediated teaching interactions
description: The article defines instructional governance as "the designed allocation of pedagogical authority, learner agency, human accountability, contextual boundaries, and evaluation visibility within an AI-mediated teaching interaction". It locates governance at the level where educators and students encounter AI: prompts, rubrics, approval gates, interfaces, dashboards, style guides, and course-specific constraints. The construct complements institutional policy by making governance choices visible in concrete instructional artifacts and workflows.
requirements: Governance must be encoded in a teaching tool's interaction model, constraints, and workflow rather than left to policy documents alone
constraints: Framed for computing and first-year engineering education contexts
target_learning_goals: responsible and pedagogically aligned use of generative AI in programming instruction
examples: The paper applies the construct across a portfolio of seven AI teaching tools, including rubric-anchored GTA simulations, reflection-oriented code companions, and staff-reviewed forum-response systems
key_sources: Ethan Dickey. (2026). Instructional Governance by Design: A Framework for AI in Computing Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.26098

article_title: HelpCoach: Scaffolding Targeted AI Help-Seeking During Problem-Solving
citation: Hyoungwook Jin, Weirui Peng, Jieun Han, Q. Vera Liao, and Xu Wang. (2026). HelpCoach: Scaffolding Targeted AI Help-Seeking During Problem-Solving. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.28918
title: Scaffold help-seeking in situ during tasks rather than only before or after them
description: The article argues that help-seeking skills develop more effectively when practiced within hands-on cognitive tasks rather than trained apart from them. Its in situ scaffolding intervenes at the individual message level during cognitive learning activities, on the hypothesis that such domain-embedded practice is more effective because self-regulation often begins as a domain-specific metacognitive skill and later develops into a more domain-independent skill. The approach combines specificity monitoring, templated revision, and context-aware recommendations with performance-based fading.
requirements: Requires real-time assessment of question specificity and task-context inputs (code state, chat history) to time and target the scaffold.
constraints: Fixed, every-other-turn scaffold appearance was disruptive when students no longer needed it, motivating adaptive timing to avoid the expertise reversal effect.
target_learners: college students using GenAI chatbots for problem-solving
target_learning_goals: targeted help-seeking and self-regulation during AI-supported learning
examples: HelpCoach intervenes with the revision scaffold only when a question is not specific, and the revision prompt naturally fades as students increasingly formulate specific questions.
key_sources: Hyoungwook Jin, Weirui Peng, Jieun Han, Q. Vera Liao, and Xu Wang. (2026). HelpCoach: Scaffolding Targeted AI Help-Seeking During Problem-Solving. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.28918

article_title: LLM-Based Educational Simulation: Evaluating Temporal Student Persona Stability Across ADHD Profiles
citation: Jana Gonnermann-Müller, Jennifer Haase, Nicolas Leins, Thomas Kosch, Sebastian Pokutta. (2026). LLM-Based Educational Simulation: Evaluating Temporal Student Persona Stability Across ADHD-Related Persona Specifications. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.06307
title: Treat interaction structure as a primary design variable for stable LLM learner simulations, not an afterthought to model selection
description: When building simulation-based tools with sustained, path-dependent learner interactions, designers should engineer the conversational protocol itself: anchoring interactions with recurring task-relevant prompts standardizes opportunities for persona-relevant expression at each checkpoint. Across five models and two scenarios, "structured conversation design produced more temporally consistent observer-rated behavior" without model changes or fine-tuning. The article positions interaction structure as part of the measurement setup rather than a neutral delivery format.
requirements: Recurring task-relevant partner-side prompts that standardize opportunities for persona-relevant expression across conversation segments
constraints: A tightly scripted conversation can become less natural and can mechanically re-elicit the measured characteristics; higher measured stability does not by itself establish higher simulation fidelity
target_learners: LLM-simulated students in teacher-training, adaptive-tutoring, and educational research simulations
target_learning_goals: Maintaining behavioral stability of simulated learner personas in sustained interactions
examples: Experiment II's scripted condition sent nine predefined partner-side prompts covering three pre-specified school situations, each followed by two fixed follow-up questions
key_sources: Jana Gonnermann-Müller, Jennifer Haase, Nicolas Leins, Thomas Kosch, Sebastian Pokutta. (2026). LLM-Based Educational Simulation: Evaluating Temporal Student Persona Stability Across ADHD-Related Persona Specifications. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.06307

article_title: Less Deliberate in Teams: Student LLM Use Across Individual and Collaborative Work
citation: Sehrish Basir Nizamani, Zannah Ziew, Saad Nizamani, and Khyati Goyal. (2026). Less Deliberate in Teams: Student LLM Use Across Individual and Collaborative Work. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.30860
title: Interleave individual and team assignments to help students maintain AI practices across both contexts
description: The article's course design interleaved individual homework and team milestones in close temporal proximity, and the authors argue this "provides a natural scaffold that purely sequential designs lack." The rapid recovery at TP2 suggests that "returning to individual work between team milestones may help students maintain their AI practices across both contexts," whereas extended team phases without intervening individual work may show more persistent suppression.
requirements: Course schedules must alternate individual and team assignments rather than separating them into distinct phases.
constraints: The authors caution that instructors designing courses with extended team phases and no intervening individual work may observe more persistent suppression than they found.
target_learners: Undergraduate computing students in project-based courses
target_learning_goals: Maintaining deliberate LLM engagement and verification practices across individual and collaborative work
examples: In the studied course, usage recovered from 39.6% at TP1 to 75.0% at TP2 after an intervening individual homework (HW5 followed TP2 in the schedule).
key_sources: Sehrish Basir Nizamani, Zannah Ziew, Saad Nizamani, and Khyati Goyal. (2026). Less Deliberate in Teams: Student LLM Use Across Individual and Collaborative Work. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.30860

article_title: Efficiency at what cost? Salvaging constructive alignment from the GenAI hype
citation: McInnes, R., Airey, L., Moss, P., & Rathnappulige, S. (2026). Efficiency at what cost? Salvaging constructive alignment from the GenAI hype. Australasian Journal of Educational Technology, 42(4), 80–95. https://doi.org/10.14742/ajet.11466
title: GenAI should defensibly augment constructive alignment only as institutionally bounded systems configured around situated pedagogy, policy and quality standards
description: The article contends that generic, Internet-trained GenAI assistance is not a defensible basis for augmenting constructive alignment. It argues that "for GenAI to defensibly augment constructive alignment, it must transition from generic, Internet-trained assistance towards institutionally bounded systems configured around situated pedagogy, policy and institutional quality standards". Bounding the system to institutional context is presented as the condition under which augmentation preserves educator agency.
requirements: Systems must be configured around the institution's own pedagogy, policy and quality standards rather than generic Internet-trained models
constraints: The article presents this as a condition for defensible augmentation, not as a demonstrated or tested configuration
target_learners: higher education educators and institutional leaders
examples: The article contrasts generic Internet-trained assistance with institutionally bounded systems configured around situated pedagogy, policy and institutional quality standards
key_sources: McInnes, R., Airey, L., Moss, P., & Rathnappulige, S. (2026). Efficiency at what cost? Salvaging constructive alignment from the GenAI hype. Australasian Journal of Educational Technology, 42(4), 80–95. https://doi.org/10.14742/ajet.11466

article_title: Perceived usefulness and intention to use large language model-generated feedback across three educational levels: a user-centred study in programming
citation: Mendonça PC, Quintal F, Figueiredo M and Mendonça F (2026) Perceived usefulness and intention to use large language model-generated feedback across three educational levels: a user-centred study in programming. Front. Educ. 11:1934069. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1934069
title: IntroEduAI two-layer LLM feedback pipeline (rubric-based GPT-4.1 evaluation plus consolidated report generation)
description: The IntroEduAI platform manages assignment delivery, automated evaluation, and feedback generation in programming courses. Each response is scored against an instructor-authored criterion-referenced rubric in a few-shot prompt, evaluated three times with GPT-4.1-2025-04-14, with text responses enhanced by retrieval-augmented generation over course materials. The three-stage pipeline produces "a single consolidated feedback per response, and an assignment-level report", the latter generated by claude-sonnet-4-20250514, containing a balance, strengths, areas to develop, and suggested next steps.
requirements: Requires instructor-authored rubrics decomposing each question into explicit criteria with descriptions, scoring rules, and point allocations, plus exemplar correct responses for the few-shot prompt.
constraints: Consolidated feedback and reports were delivered to students as generated, without instructor editing, in this study.
target_learning_goals: formative feedback on programming short-answer and code-based assignments
examples: Students in Computer Applications B, Introduction to Programming, Data Structures and Algorithms, and Data Science submitted assignments through the platform and rated the feedback it generated.
key_sources: Mendonça PC, Quintal F, Figueiredo M and Mendonça F (2026) Perceived usefulness and intention to use large language model-generated feedback across three educational levels: a user-centred study in programming. Front. Educ. 11:1934069. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1934069

article_title: Empowering teachers to use AI for differentiation: changes in teachers’ acceptance of AI-based technologies following participation in a short professional development training session
citation: Mesenhöller J and Böhme K (2026). Empowering teachers to use AI for differentiation: changes in teachers’ acceptance of AI-based technologies following participation in a short professional development training session. Front. Educ. 11:1875856. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1875856
title: INSIGHT: a three-hour teacher professional development training session on AI-based technologies for individualised instruction
description: INSIGHT (Information on Schooling with Generative AI and Helpful AI Tools) is a three-hour in-person TPD session for in-service teachers, designed as a pilot intervention to be iteratively refined before larger-scale transfer. It "combines theoretical input, hands-on experiences, and guided reflection" and consists of four parts: an introduction to AI, a hands-on session training an ML system with Google’s Teachable Machine, a session on LLM-supported individualised instruction, and a session on teacher-guided support of students’ AI competencies. It was evaluated in a pilot pre-post study across five schools in one German federal state.
requirements: Delivered in person by the same two trainers following the same training concept, materials, and activities; group sizes ranged from 11 to 29 participants
constraints: Designed as a pilot to refine content and didactical design rather than as definitive evidence of effectiveness
target_learners: in-service primary and secondary teachers in Germany
target_learning_goals: basic understanding of AI-based technologies and their pedagogically meaningful use for supporting individualised instruction, including critical reflection on opportunities and limitations
examples: In small groups of 2–4, teachers trained Google’s Teachable Machine to distinguish pointing and high-five gestures, illustrating how model performance depends on the choice and quality of training data; participants also explored how an LLM reformulated a biology question on photosynthesis for three different competence levels
key_sources: Mesenhöller J and Böhme K (2026). Empowering teachers to use AI for differentiation: changes in teachers’ acceptance of AI-based technologies following participation in a short professional development training session. Front. Educ. 11:1875856. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1875856

article_title: Prompts to Practice: A Pedagogical Framework for Human-Centered AI Engagement
citation: April Joy Miles, Paige Haber-Curran, Khalid Arar. (2026). Prompts to Practice: A Pedagogical Framework for Human-Centered AI Engagement. Open Praxis, 18(3), 481–494. https://doi.org/10.55982/openpraxis.18.3.1191
title: Instructional Model for Human-Centered Generative AI Engagement: five recursive phases for LLM-integrated learning
description: A constructionist pedagogical framework that structures student engagement with text-based LLMs in higher education. It is organized around five recursive phases: critical and ethical awareness, prompt literacy, AI-supported learning, reflection and revision, and independent application. The authors state it was developed by synthesizing established learning theory with the authors' instructional experience, and that it helps faculty scaffold LLM-related learning by integrating hands-on experimentation, ethical reflection, and purposeful interaction with LLMs.
requirements: Instructors enact the phases through modeling, transparency, and classroom culture; the framework assumes relational elements such as feedback, encouragement, empathy, and cultural responsiveness remain central
constraints: As a conceptual contribution, the model was not derived from a single empirical study and the authors state it now invites empirical evaluation
target_learning_goals: ethical and responsible use of generative AI
examples: The five phases are adapted across assignments, units, or entire courses, with each phase building on the previous while the process remains recursive
key_sources: April Joy Miles, Paige Haber-Curran, Khalid Arar. (2026). Prompts to Practice: A Pedagogical Framework for Human-Centered AI Engagement. Open Praxis, 18(3), 481–494. https://doi.org/10.55982/openpraxis.18.3.1191

article_title: Prompts to Practice: A Pedagogical Framework for Human-Centered AI Engagement
citation: April Joy Miles, Paige Haber-Curran, Khalid Arar. (2026). Prompts to Practice: A Pedagogical Framework for Human-Centered AI Engagement. Open Praxis, 18(3), 481–494. https://doi.org/10.55982/openpraxis.18.3.1191
title: Instructors should transparently model their own LLM use to shape how students engage with AI
description: The article argues that faculty mediation often determines whether AI functions as a shortcut that bypasses learning or as a cognitive partner that deepens it. One of the most effective strategies faculty can use is transparent modeling of LLM use: openly demonstrating how they use LLMs for ideation, drafting, revision, or problem-solving, crafting and refining prompts and iterating in real time while sharing their thought process aloud.
requirements: Instructors frame AI not as a shortcut but as a cognitive partner, and model intentionality, discernment, and ethical awareness in action
constraints: The strategy is recommended on conceptual and cited-scholarship grounds, not tested in this article
examples: Instructors craft and refine prompts, assess LLM-generated content, and iterate in real time, sharing their thought process aloud
key_sources: April Joy Miles, Paige Haber-Curran, Khalid Arar. (2026). Prompts to Practice: A Pedagogical Framework for Human-Centered AI Engagement. Open Praxis, 18(3), 481–494. https://doi.org/10.55982/openpraxis.18.3.1191

article_title: Neural-Symbolic Knowledge Tracing: Injecting Educational Knowledge into Deep Learning for Responsible Learner Modelling
citation: Hooshyar, D.; Šír, G.; Yang, Y.; Kärkkäinen, T.; Hämäläinen, R.; Krivich, E.; Cukurova, M.; Gašević, D.; Azevedo, R. (2026). Neural-Symbolic Knowledge Tracing: Injecting Educational Knowledge into Deep Learning for Responsible Learner Modelling. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.08263
title: Inject conservative symbolic mastery and non-mastery rules to stabilize sequential knowledge-tracing predictions
description: The article recommends encoding pedagogically motivated constraints as learnable-weight symbolic rules that modulate neural predictions when simple evidence patterns occur in the interaction history. Specifically, "three incorrect responses on the same skill or quiz activate a not_mastered rule, providing a conservative signal that discourages premature overestimation of mastery", while two consecutive correct responses activate a mastered rule. These constraints help mitigate common DKT instabilities where mastery probabilities move contrary to recent responses, while preserving interpretability through the rule structure.
requirements: Interaction histories sufficient to detect the evidence patterns; rule weights learnable or fixed to enforce stronger pedagogical constraints when desired
constraints: Lower thresholds than prior mastery-learning work (e.g., seven learning opportunities) were adopted to suit the shorter and sparser sequences in this dataset; symbolic components modulate rather than override neural predictions
target_learners: K-12 learners in digital practice environments with sparse interaction sequences
target_learning_goals: Temporally consistent, pedagogically aligned mastery estimation
examples: In Responsible-DKT, triggered rules contribute additional evidence to the correctness predicate alongside the recurrent state and an averaged historical embedding pathway
key_sources: Hooshyar, D.; Šír, G.; Yang, Y.; Kärkkäinen, T.; Hämäläinen, R.; Krivich, E.; Cukurova, M.; Gašević, D.; Azevedo, R. (2026). Neural-Symbolic Knowledge Tracing: Injecting Educational Knowledge into Deep Learning for Responsible Learner Modelling. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.08263

article_title: Exploring interfaces and implications for integrating social-emotional competencies into AI literacy for education: a narrative review
citation: Adam Palmquist, Helga Dis Isfold Sigurdardottir, Hege Myhre. (2025). Exploring interfaces and implications for integrating social-emotional competencies into AI literacy for education: a narrative review. Journal of Computers in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40692-025-00354-1
title: Integrated framework embedding SEC within AI literacy for education
description: The review proposes a conceptual model that embeds social-emotional competencies within AI literacy, built by juxtaposing AI literacy frameworks (Long & Magerko; Ng et al.) with the SEC/CASEL framework. It states: 'By embedding SEC within AI literacy, this study contributes to understanding how AI technologies can foster emotional and relational skills while addressing ethical challenges in education.' The framework aims at a technologically adept and emotionally intelligent educational ecosystem, with AI literacy as the foundational concept and SEC/CASEL as complementary. It was derived through thematic analysis of a curated 19-source corpus.
requirements: A curated interdisciplinary knowledge base spanning AI literacy and SEC, as assembled by the SETCOM project
constraints: The review acknowledges potential selection bias and subjective interpretation of findings in narrative reviews
Synthesising concepts as of 2017 may not capture the most recent progressions in the rapidly evolving AI domain
target_learning_goals: ethical and relational navigation of AI in education
examples: The SETCOM project used the framework to cross-pollinate SEC ideas into AI literacy as a transversal competency for educational stakeholders
key_sources: Adam Palmquist, Helga Dis Isfold Sigurdardottir, Hege Myhre. (2025). Exploring interfaces and implications for integrating social-emotional competencies into AI literacy for education: a narrative review. Journal of Computers in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40692-025-00354-1

article_title: Prompt Coach: An Empirical Evaluation of an Agentic Tutor for Learning Prompt Engineering in Software Development
citation: Rohit Mehra, Kapil Singi, Vikrant Kaulgud, Vibhu Saujanya Sharma, Swapnajeet Gon Choudhury, Swati Sharma, Adam P. Burden, Majd Sakr. (2026). Prompt Coach: An Empirical Evaluation of an Agentic Tutor for Learning Prompt Engineering in Software Development. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.06074
title: Embed tutoring for AI-collaboration skills in the workflow where the skill is exercised, rather than in separate learning formats
description: The article recommends that learning of evolving, interactive skills like prompt engineering happen within the tool where prompts are actually written, with guidance grounded in the learner's own code and target-model behavior. The authors state these findings "position agentic tutoring as a promising paradigm for enabling in-flow, context-aware learning of emerging software engineering skills", replacing passive, disconnected formats.
requirements: The tutor must reason over the developer's actual project context and target LLM behavior to make guidance contextual
constraints: Evidence so far comes from a 15-developer, single-organization, single-benchmark study conducted without real project context; generalizability is limited by the authors' own threats-to-validity analysis
target_learning_goals: other emerging AI-era software engineering skills
examples: PC was integrated as a VSCode extension so that tutoring occurs where code-generation prompts are actually crafted
key_sources: Rohit Mehra, Kapil Singi, Vikrant Kaulgud, Vibhu Saujanya Sharma, Swapnajeet Gon Choudhury, Swati Sharma, Adam P. Burden, Majd Sakr. (2026). Prompt Coach: An Empirical Evaluation of an Agentic Tutor for Learning Prompt Engineering in Software Development. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.06074

article_title: Literacy demands placed on students in student–GenAI entanglements in higher education
citation: Sun, Z., Dohn, N. B., & Rehm, M. (2026). Literacy Demands Placed on Students in Student–GenAI Entanglements in Higher Education. Postdigital Science and Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s42438-026-00697-7
title: Tension between individualistic person-focused competence and person-plus tool-mediated competence as the explanation for which GenAI entanglements higher education accommodates
description: The paper's central explanatory framework holds that educational settings dominantly understand competence as an individually possessed object located in and evaluated for the individual, while professional GenAI practice operates on a sociocultural 'person-plus' premise where competence is situated doing distributed between persons and tools. Introducing GenAI activities can introduce the person-plus-competence logic at the activity-internal level while the activity-framing level remains governed by individualistic expectations, predictably generating tensions — illustrated by extensive debates over GenAI as cheating versus legitimate learning support. Because the five entanglement types distribute epistemic work differently, this conflict emerges to different degrees across types.
requirements: Analysis requires distinguishing the activity-internal level, where GenAI use may embody distributed competence, from the activity-framing level governed by institutional expectations
constraints: The tension does not arise uniformly across all forms of student–GenAI entanglement; it emerges to different degrees and in different forms across the five types
target_learning_goals: recognizing and negotiating conflicting competence expectations in GenAI-supported academic work
examples: Historical parallel: the pocket calculator and the flexible pole were once seen as cheating because they did not allow true expression of individually possessed competence, yet both are now widely accepted
key_sources: Sun, Z., Dohn, N. B., & Rehm, M. (2026). Literacy Demands Placed on Students in Student–GenAI Entanglements in Higher Education. Postdigital Science and Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s42438-026-00697-7

article_title: Taklif.AI: LLM-Powered Platform for Interest-Based Personalized College Assignments
citation: Zaki Kurdya, Mohammed Zuqlam, Salem Amassi, Shady Telbany, Motaz Saad. (2026). Taklif.AI: LLM-Powered Platform for Interest-Based Personalized College Assignments. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.05842
title: Interest-contextualized assignment rewriting that preserves original learning objectives verbatim
description: This pattern rewrites a general assignment so that its surface context comes from the student's interest domain while the task itself is unchanged. The article's examples show that "the personalization layer contextualizes the assignment within the student’s interest domain (telescope alignment for astronomy, basketball coaching for sports enthusiasts) while preserving all original learning objectives, constraints, and mathematical content verbatim". The approach generalized across domains (programming to discrete mathematics) and interest types (STEM to sports) in the printed examples.
requirements: A validated student interest and a valid source assignment, processed through the personalize-assignment prompt with constraints such as no explicit hints or solutions and content length not exceeding a 50% increment over the original
constraints: Highly abstract mathematical content such as real-analysis proofs may resist contextual framing without trivializing the material
Overly elaborate interest-based narratives could distract students from core learning objectives
target_learning_goals: maintaining learning objectives while increasing personal relevance and engagement of assignments
examples: A Two Sum programming task reframed as telescope alignment for an astronomy interest, and a set theory task reframed through basketball coaching, both keeping constraints and mathematical content verbatim
key_sources: Zaki Kurdya, Mohammed Zuqlam, Salem Amassi, Shady Telbany, Motaz Saad. (2026). Taklif.AI: LLM-Powered Platform for Interest-Based Personalized College Assignments. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.05842

article_title: Taklif.AI: LLM-Powered Platform for Interest-Based Personalized College Assignments
citation: Zaki Kurdya, Mohammed Zuqlam, Salem Amassi, Shady Telbany, Motaz Saad. (2026). Taklif.AI: LLM-Powered Platform for Interest-Based Personalized College Assignments. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.05842
title: Interest-based personalization grounded in Self-Determination Theory and the Four-Phase Model of Interest Development
description: The article grounds its interest-based approach in two frameworks it names: Self-Determination Theory, "which emphasizes autonomy, competence, and relatedness as key drivers of intrinsic motivation", and the Four-Phase Model of Interest Development, "which suggests that situational interest can mature into sustained individual interest through repeated exposure to meaningful content". Taklif.AI operationalizes this rationale by aligning assignment contexts with students' self-reported out-of-school interests, extending prior work that confined personalization to subject-specific or classroom interests.
requirements: Access to students' self-reported interests; the article notes self-reports may not reflect genuine engagement drivers
constraints: Prior studies cited confined personalization to subject-specific or classroom interests, neglecting broader out-of-school interests
Whether interest framing genuinely aids comprehension or merely adds stylistic embellishment requires empirical investigation
target_learners: higher education students with diverse cultural backgrounds and interests
target_learning_goals: intrinsic motivation and engagement through personally relevant assignment contexts
examples: Taklif.AI incorporates extracurricular interests and cultural contexts into assignment generation, unlike platforms personalizing on academic performance metrics alone
key_sources: Zaki Kurdya, Mohammed Zuqlam, Salem Amassi, Shady Telbany, Motaz Saad. (2026). Taklif.AI: LLM-Powered Platform for Interest-Based Personalized College Assignments. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.05842

article_title: Agentic AI Ecosystems in Higher Education: A Perspective on AI Agents to Emerging Inclusive, Agentic Multi-Agent AI Framework for Learning, Teaching and Institutional Intelligence
citation: Sudarshan VK, Sisodia A, Ramachandra RA, Sia B, Chong Leng Leng J. (2025). Agentic AI Ecosystems in Higher Education: A Perspective on AI Agents to Emerging Inclusive, Agentic Multi-Agent AI Framework for Learning, Teaching and Institutional Intelligence.
title: Inclusive agentic AI ecosystem pattern: coordinated accessibility, cognitive support, wellbeing, and learning agents for diverse learners including SEN students
description: The article proposes a reusable ecosystem-level pattern in which inclusion is achieved through the interaction of multiple specialized agents rather than isolated assistive tools. It states that "inclusion is achieved through the interaction of multiple agents, including accessibility agents (interface and modality adaptation), cognitive support agents (learning scaffolding and adaptation), wellbeing agents (emotional and engagement monitoring), learning agents (content delivery and assessment)". This coordinated approach addresses cognitive, sensory, and emotional dimensions of support simultaneously and dynamically, embedding inclusivity within the architecture rather than as an add-on feature, and aligning with principles of distributed intelligence.
requirements: Coordination among specialized agents so diverse learner needs are addressed simultaneously and dynamically
Human oversight in sensitive domains such as mental health
constraints: The article identifies risks of biased training data and over-automation in sensitive domains for SEN contexts
target_learners: higher education students with special educational needs
diverse learners with varying cognitive abilities, sensory impairments, and neurodiversity
examples: Cognitive support includes personalized pacing, simplified explanations, scaffolding, and reinforcement strategies; sensory support includes text-to-speech, speech-to-text, visual enhancements, and alternative content representations
key_sources: Sudarshan VK, Sisodia A, Ramachandra RA, Sia B, Chong Leng Leng J. (2025). Agentic AI Ecosystems in Higher Education: A Perspective on AI Agents to Emerging Inclusive, Agentic Multi-Agent AI Framework for Learning, Teaching and Institutional Intelligence. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.14266

article_title: Surfacing Isolated Learners with Outcome-Independent Mediation of Feedback between Teachers and Students Using AI
citation: Junsoo Park, Youssef Medhat, Htet Phyo Wai, Ploy Thajchayapong and Ashok K. Goel. (2026). Surfacing Isolated Learners with Outcome-Independent Mediation of Feedback between Teachers and Students Using AI. HAI-Agency Workshop, AIED 2026. https://github.com/park-jsdev/classroom-feedback-mediator
title: Interpretable decision layer for outcome-independent coordination of teacher and student feedback
description: A transparent mechanism that combines teacher and student feedback to rank course topics needing attention without grades or outcome labels. It integrates three signals — gap prevalence, survey disagreement, and teacher friction — into a topic priority score with a per-topic decision record explaining each ranking. The article states it "organizes teacher, student, and researcher roles around this shared decision process," positioning the layer as supporting human–AI co-agency rather than replacing instructor judgment.
requirements: Teacher signals from coded instructor interviews, student signals from interaction traces and surveys, and researcher-defined weights must be available for the same course topics
constraints: Weights are specified rather than learned in the current implementation; the study reflects one graduate-level course offering and findings are preliminary and exploratory
target_learners: graduate CS students in an AI-augmented classroom
target_learning_goals: timely identification of course topics requiring instructional attention before graded outcomes are available
examples: In the study offering, the highest-ranked topics were analogical reasoning, frames, planning, case-based reasoning, and knowledge-based AI, each accompanied by a per-topic decision record
key_sources: Junsoo Park, Youssef Medhat, Htet Phyo Wai, Ploy Thajchayapong and Ashok K. Goel. (2026). Surfacing Isolated Learners with Outcome-Independent Mediation of Feedback between Teachers and Students Using AI. HAI-Agency Workshop, AIED 2026. https://github.com/park-jsdev/classroom-feedback-mediator

article_title: 'From Idea to Classroom in Days: Using "Vibe Coding" to Create a Programming Process Visualizer from IDE Activity Logs'
citation: Heidi Taveter and Marina Lepp. (2026). From Idea to Classroom in Days: Using “Vibe Coding” to Create a Programming Process Visualizer from IDE Activity Logs. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.24757
title: Surface process-based integrity signals as warning signals for teacher review rather than automated plagiarism judgments
description: The principle is that a tool should present lightweight, process-based integrity indicators — pasted-text proportion, paste source, similarity of low-edit opened files, and duplicate function names — while explicitly leaving interpretation and judgment to teachers. The article states that "These features are intended as warning signals rather than automated determinations", and that views support follow-up discussion and manual review rather than automated judgments. Replay of the programming process enables more detailed review of flagged cases.
requirements: Teachers must review flagged cases at student level, since the flagging mechanisms surface relevant cases while still requiring student-level review rather than replacing teacher judgment
constraints: Static source-code comparison alone may be insufficient in introductory courses where final programs are often short and similar, especially when students modify or obfuscate copied code
target_learning_goals: teacher decision-making about cases warranting closer inspection
examples: The paste-events view distinguishes pastes from the same editor, another tab, and outside the IDE, presenting snippets with timestamps and size information for nuanced interpretation
key_sources: Heidi Taveter and Marina Lepp. (2026). From Idea to Classroom in Days: Using “Vibe Coding” to Create a Programming Process Visualizer from IDE Activity Logs. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.24757

article_title: Technology-Enhanced Tabletop Exercises for Cybersecurity Education: Lessons Learned
citation: J. Vykopal, P. Čeleda, M. Horák, V. Švábenský. (2026). Technology-Enhanced Tabletop Exercises for Cybersecurity Education: Lessons Learned. In Proceedings of the 56th IEEE Frontiers in Education Conference (FIE '26). https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28179
title: INJECT Exercise Platform (IXP): open-source web environment for delivering and evaluating digital tabletop exercises
description: IXP is a "lightweight, open-source web-based learning environment designed to deliver and evaluate TTXs" that transitions the pen-and-paper format into a digital one. It delivers injects based on time or milestone completion, defines scenarios in YAML files, simulates tools such as email, a browser, and a firewall, logs trainee actions, and provides dashboards and JSONL export. Versions v1–v5 added on-demand exercises, multi-tenancy, an exercise editor, a Visual Studio Code extension, and support for up to 100 parallel teams.
requirements: Exercise scenarios must be defined in human- and machine-readable YAML files or via the built-in editor
constraints: Fully automated on-demand exercises are restricted to elements that can be automatically evaluated, such as multiple-choice questionnaires
target_learners: high school students in extracurricular activities
examples: Used to deliver 25 exercises from October 2024 to March 2026, including discussion and simulation exercises on phishing, insider threat, and personal-data breach response
key_sources: J. Vykopal, P. Čeleda, M. Horák, V. Švábenský. (2026). Technology-Enhanced Tabletop Exercises for Cybersecurity Education: Lessons Learned. In Proceedings of the 56th IEEE Frontiers in Education Conference (FIE '26). https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28179

article_title: Technology-Enhanced Tabletop Exercises for Cybersecurity Education: Lessons Learned
citation: J. Vykopal, P. Čeleda, M. Horák, V. Švábenský. (2026). Technology-Enhanced Tabletop Exercises for Cybersecurity Education: Lessons Learned. In Proceedings of the 56th IEEE Frontiers in Education Conference (FIE '26). https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28179
title: INJECT Process: five-phase lifecycle for designing, executing, and reflecting on digital tabletop exercises
description: The INJECT Process is "a way to design, execute, and reflect TTXs with the IXP" consisting of five phases inspired by design thinking: understanding, specification, preparation, execution, and reflection. It leverages best practices for instructional design and TTXs and is tailored to digital TTXs with the platform's features. Each phase has a defined purpose, from establishing whether the exercise is worth building to post-exercise analysis and improvement of future runs.
requirements: Designers must connect understanding of what IXP enables with translating learning objectives into concrete learning activities and injects
constraints: The boundary between specification and preparation is permeable; implementation surfaces problems invisible at the design stage
target_learning_goals: designing and delivering effective tabletop exercises
examples: The paper's 24 lessons learned are organized according to the five INJECT Process phases

article_title: Teaching Reinforcement Learning and Humanoid Robotics to High-School Students: An Expert-Validated Curriculum Design on a Low-Cost Open Platform
citation: Yuanzhe Dong, Jie Cao, Shuman Wang. (2026). Teaching Reinforcement Learning and Humanoid Robotics to High-School Students: An Expert-Validated Curriculum Design on a Low-Cost Open Platform. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.25674
title: Integrated robotics course framework organizing a complete research workflow around one shared robot artifact
description: The framework organizes mechanical assembly, electrical setup, simulation, policy learning, system identification, and physical deployment around a shared robotic artifact. It combines "parallel disciplinary tracks, sequencing based on technical dependencies, progressive integration of simulation and hardware, layered performance checkpoints, and structures for balancing collaborative work with individual accountability." It was developed iteratively and refined through a five-expert formative review.
requirements: A shared robotic artifact connecting disciplinary work to observable behavior
Staged tasks and bounded customization adapted for high-school learners
constraints: The article states the framework "does not establish that a humanoid course teaches introductory RL more effectively than simpler alternatives"
Effectiveness remains untested
target_learning_goals: Understanding how systems acquire behavior through reinforcement learning
Integrated STEM reasoning across mechanical, electrical, and computational work
examples: A high school curriculum in which pairs of students assemble an open source humanoid robot, train a walking policy in simulation, and deploy it on the physical platform

article_title: AI adoption readiness among Ukrainian education managers: Barriers, typologies, and policy implications
citation: V.G. Kremen, O.M. Spirin, O.I. Liashenko, S.H. Lytvynova, Y.I. Malovanyi, O.P. Pinchuk, O.M. Sokolyuk, S.O. Semerikov. (2026). AI adoption readiness among Ukrainian education managers: Barriers, typologies, and policy implications. Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence 11 (2026) 100648. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.caeai.2026.100648
title: Integrative three-layer framework for AI adoption readiness among education managers
description: The article proposes an integrative framework synthesizing UTAUT, organizational readiness theory, and configurational theory to explain AI adoption readiness among education managers. UTAUT explains personal readiness through perceived usefulness, ease of use, and social influence; organizational readiness theory explains "psychological readiness (change commitment and change efficacy) and structural readiness (resource availability, policy clarity, and institutional support)"; and configurational theory explains how barriers combine. The framework treats the personal–institutional readiness gap as the tension between individual motivation and organizational capacity, with LCA typology as a classification layer.
requirements: Each theory addresses a distinct analytical layer — individual readiness, institutional readiness, and barrier configurations — without duplicating mechanisms
constraints: The manager typology layer is a classification (segmentation) layer, not tested as a statistical mediator
target_learners: Education managers (school principals, department heads, administrators)
target_learning_goals: Understanding and supporting institutional AI adoption readiness
examples: The framework guided hypotheses H1–H4 tested with the 395-manager survey, combining descriptive, person-centered (LCA), and set-theoretic (fsQCA) analyses
key_sources: V.G. Kremen, O.M. Spirin, O.I. Liashenko, S.H. Lytvynova, Y.I. Malovanyi, O.P. Pinchuk, O.M. Sokolyuk, S.O. Semerikov. (2026). article_title: The Role of Artificial Intelligence in Green Education: Optimizing Teacher Workflow and Enhancing Pedagogical Design under Sustainable Development Pedagogy (SDP) Constraints
citation: Hossein Talebzadeh. (2025). The Role of Artificial Intelligence in Green Education: Optimizing Teacher Workflow and Enhancing Pedagogical Design under Sustainable Development Pedagogy (SDP) Constraints. 3rd National Conference on Green Industries Innovation, University of Mazandaran. https://conf.umz.ac.ir/gii
title: Integrated AI Triad (IAT) model for teacher-AI cooperative instructional design
description: The IAT model, developed by Talebzadeh (2025a), is a conceptual framework structuring the cooperative workflow between teachers and generative AI during the design of learning trajectories. The article states it emphasizes "task authenticity and student cognitive outcomes" and uses it as the baseline structure within which the SDP constraint is later imposed. Pre-service teachers received structured training on formulating prompts aligned with the IAT model before drafting lesson plans.
requirements: Teachers receive structured training on formulating prompts aligned with the IAT model
target_learning_goals: instructional design of learning trajectories with generative AI support
examples: Teams in the Geography Teaching Methods course drafted baseline lesson plans after IAT-aligned prompt training

article_title: Teaching the teachers: A systematic review of genAI-specific technological pedagogical knowledge (TPK) in teacher education
citation: Ó Ceallaigh, T. J. & Murphy, S. (2026). Teaching the teachers: A systematic review of genAI-specific technological pedagogical knowledge (TPK) in teacher education. Computers and Education Open, 10, 100367. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.caeo.2026.100367
title: Intelligent-TPACK: extending TPACK with ethical reasoning, inclusiveness, and fairness for AI integration
description: Intelligent-TPACK is a framework the review describes as extending the TPACK model "by integrating dimensions of ethical reasoning, inclusiveness, and fairness, emphasizing teachers' capacity to align AI tools with pedagogical intent and ethical responsibility." The review reports, citing Celik (2023), that the framework was developed through scale development and structural modeling with in-service teachers, and that ethical fairness and inclusiveness strongly predict teachers' readiness to use AI responsibly. It serves in the review as an empirical model of AI-specific teacher knowledge in which ethics is integral to intelligent tool use.
requirements: Integration of fairness, inclusiveness, and ethics into teacher training and AI integration frameworks
constraints: The review notes the complexity of such models often exceeds the capacity of existing institutional systems to provide targeted support
target_learning_goals: Responsible AI tool use aligned with pedagogical intent
examples: Celik (2023) developed the framework with a Finnish national sample of in-service teachers using scale development and structural modeling, as reported in the review

article_title: Typology of Generative AI Tools for Education
citation: Matt Bower, Jodie Torrington, Jennifer W. M. Lai. (2026). 2026 Typology of Generative AI Tools for Education. https://bit.ly/2026GenAITypologyData
title: Select generative AI tools through educator agency and informed decision-making aligned with pedagogical goals, rather than adopting uncritically or avoiding out of fear
description: The article argues that realizing generative AI's educational opportunities requires educator agency and informed decision making: rather than adopting generative AI uncritically, educators need frameworks and resources to make thoughtful choices about which tools align with their pedagogical goals and values. The typology is offered as a practical reference point for this selection, while stressing that finding the right tool is only the beginning and thoughtful integration requires critical evaluation.
requirements: Educators need frameworks and resources supporting thoughtful tool choice
constraints: The article states the typology is a snapshot of a rapidly evolving landscape, so the list will change over time
target_learners: educators across school and higher education sectors
target_learning_goals: aligning generative AI tool selection with pedagogical goals, student needs, and educational values
examples: The typology provides brief descriptions and links for each of the 50 tools to support educators in making informed decisions about which tools might suit their teaching and learning contexts
key_sources: Matt Bower, Jodie Torrington, Jennifer W. M. Lai. (2026). 2026 Typology of Generative AI Tools for Education. https://bit.ly/2026GenAITypologyData

article_title: A Hybrid Reasoning Framework for Artificial Intelligence Assessment Rubric Generation in Human and Automated Contexts: Evidence from an Undergraduate Programming Course
citation: Pedro C. Mendonça, Filipe Quintal, Mário Figueiredo, Karolina Baras, Fábio Mendonça. (2026). A hybrid reasoning framework for artificial intelligence assessment rubric generation in human and automated contexts: Evidence from an undergraduate programming course. Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence 11 (2026) 100663. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.caeai.2026.100663
title: IntroEduAI platform for assessment collection and parallel human/LLM evaluation
description: IntroEduAI is a web-based platform, originally developed for prior research on automated formative assessment, that served as the technical infrastructure for assessment collection and automated evaluation in this study. It implements a Model-View-Controller architecture using Flask with REST API endpoints for LLM integration, and supports rubric upload and configuration, student response collection, parallel human and LLM-based evaluation, and data aggregation for export. Automated evaluation uses few-shot prompting with rubric integration; for text questions it adds Retrieval-Augmented Generation via LangChain and ChromaDB over course materials (1000-character chunks with 200-character overlap, top-5 retrieval), while code questions are evaluated without external retrieval.
requirements: Course materials provided as PDF documents for the RAG pipeline; embeddings generated with text-embedding-ada-002
constraints: Across the five rubric conditions the question text, exemplar responses, and retrieval configuration were identical, so the rubric was the only prompt component that varied
target_learners: Undergraduate computer science students submitting formative worksheets
target_learning_goals: Automated formative assessment of text-based and code-based open-ended responses
examples: A variance-based flagging system with a threshold of SD > 10 across three LLM evaluation runs identified 1.43% of evaluations as requiring human review
key_sources: Pedro C. Mendonça, Filipe Quintal, Mário Figueiredo, Karolina Baras, Fábio Mendonça. (2026). A hybrid reasoning framework for artificial intelligence assessment rubric generation in human and automated contexts: Evidence from an undergraduate programming course. Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence 11 (2026) 100663. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.caeai.2026.100663

article_title: Exploring Teachers' Instrumental Orchestration and Roles in High School Mathematics Classes Using AI-Based Digital Tools
citation: Yun Hwa Noh & Hee-jeong Kim. (2026). Exploring teachers' instrumental orchestration and roles in high school mathematics classes using AI-based digital tools. The Mathematical Education 65(2), 309-335. https://doi.org/10.63311/mathedu.26.6525
title: Instrumental orchestration framework extended to AI-based digital learning contexts with agentic AI
description: The study extends the instrumental orchestration framework (didactical configuration, exploitation mode, didactical performance) to classrooms where AI tools act as agentic artifacts. It defines agentic AI as AI that "학습자의 반응을 실시간으로 분석하고 교사의 개입없이 자율적으로 피드백을 생성하고 제공하는" — distinct from tools operating only on explicit user manipulation. Three new orchestration types (dashboard-monitoring, AI-correcting, AI-mediating) are added to the Drijvers et al. type system, and teacher roles are analyzed with an AI-TPACK-based role framework plus an inductively derived knowledge-transmitter category.
requirements: An AI-based digital tool that analyzes student solution processes in real time and autonomously generates individualized feedback and dashboard data for the teacher
constraints: Derived from a single experienced, highly AI-proficient teacher; other tools or teachers may yield different orchestration patterns, as the authors state in their limitations
target_learners: High school mathematics students (grade 10) in one-to-one device classrooms
target_learning_goals: Mathematics concepts and problem solving (rational and irrational functions unit) supported by AI-based personalized feedback
examples: Six lessons on rational and irrational functions using AI digital educational materials, Snorkl, and OneNote, with episodes segmented at tool transitions
key_sources: Yun Hwa Noh & Hee-jeong Kim. (2026). Exploring teachers' instrumental orchestration and roles in high school mathematics classes using AI-based digital tools. The Mathematical Education 65(2), 309-335. https://doi.org/10.63311/mathedu.26.6525

article_title: Integrating information: A meta-analysis of the spatial contiguity and temporal contiguity effects
citation: Ginns, P. (2006). Integrating information: A meta-analysis of the spatial contiguity and temporal contiguity effects. Learning and Instruction, 16(6), 511-525. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2006.10.001
title: For novices learning complex materials, increase spatial or temporal contiguity of related elements of information
description: When related elements of to-be-learned information (e.g. a diagram and its formulae, words and pictures) are separated in space or time, designers should physically integrate them or present them concurrently. The meta-analysis shows "increasing integration supports learning across a wide variety of educational domains, media, and levels", with gains "consistently higher than the mean effect derived by Hattie (1987)" for novices studying complex materials. Integration reduces extraneous search-and-match or rehearsal load, freeing capacity for schema construction.
requirements: Related elements must be mutually referring and unintelligible in isolation; learners should be novices relative to the material
constraints: Effects established only for novices; for more experienced learners integrated formats can become redundant and counter-productive (expertise reversal)
target_learners: novice learners across senior primary school, secondary school, technical college, and adult education
target_learning_goals: learning from complex, high element interactivity instructional materials in mathematics, science, and engineering/technical domains
examples: Studies integrated diagrams with related instructions in worked examples, presented narration concurrently with animation, and colour-coded associated referents to reduce search
key_sources: Ginns, P. (2006). Integrating information: A meta-analysis of the spatial contiguity and temporal contiguity effects. Learning and Instruction, 16(6), 511-525. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2006.10.001

article_title: A Meta-Analysis of the Effects of Classroom Management Strategies and Classroom Management Programs on Students’ Academic, Behavioral, Emotional, and Motivational Outcomes
citation: Korpershoek, H., Harms, T., de Boer, H., van Kuijk, M., & Doolaard, S. (2016). A Meta-Analysis of the Effects of Classroom Management Strategies and Classroom Management Programs on Students' Academic, Behavioral, Emotional, and Motivational Outcomes. Review of Educational Research, 86(3), 643-680. https://doi.org/10.3102/0034654315626799
title: Design classroom management programs to include a focus on students' social-emotional development
description: Because the meta-analysis found that focusing on students' social-emotional development had the largest contribution to intervention effectiveness, particularly on social-emotional outcomes, designers of classroom management programs should incorporate a social-emotional development component. The article reports that "Focusing on the students’ social-emotional development appeared to have the largest contribution to the interventions’ effectiveness, in particular on the social-emotional outcomes."
requirements: Programs must be codable for the social-emotional development strategy category
constraints: The finding is a moderator association within primary education studies from 2003–2013, not a tested design manipulation
examples: Included programs were coded for presence/absence of a social-emotional development focus, and those with this focus contributed most to effectiveness
