article_title: INPUT, INTERACTION, AND SECOND LANGUAGE DEVELOPMENT
citation: Alison Mackey. (1999). INPUT, INTERACTION, AND SECOND LANGUAGE DEVELOPMENT: An Empirical Study of Question Formation in ESL. Studies in Second Language Acquisition, 21(4). https://doi.org/10.1017/S0272263199004027
title: Long's (1996) updated interactionist hypothesis: implicit negative feedback obtained through negotiated interaction facilitates SLA
description: The study is framed by Long's (1996) updated version of the interactionist hypothesis, which "claims thatimplicit negative feedback, which can be obtained through negotiated interaction, facilitatesSLA." Similar claims are attributed to Pica (1994) and Gass (1997). The article tests this framework empirically by manipulating learners' participation in task-based conversational interaction and measuring grammatical development. It positions the hypothesis against prior partial support from studies of production, lexical acquisition, pushed output, and recasts.
requirements: Conversational interaction must provide opportunities for negotiated interaction through which implicit negative feedback can be obtained
constraints: Prior studies cited in the article, such as Loschky (1994), did not find effects for interaction on grammatical development
target_learners: adult ESL learners of varying L1 backgrounds
target_learning_goals: second language grammatical development, specifically question formation
examples: The study assigned 34 adult ESL learners to four experimental groups and one control group for task-based interaction in a pretest-posttest design
key_sources: Alison Mackey. (1999). INPUT, INTERACTION, AND SECOND LANGUAGE DEVELOPMENT: An Empirical Study of Question Formation in ESL. Studies in Second Language Acquisition, 21(4). https://doi.org/10.1017/S0272263199004027

article_title: Modeling Individualization in a Bayesian Networks Implementation of Knowledge Tracing
citation: Pardos, Z.A., Heffernan, N.T. (2010). Modeling Individualization in a Bayesian Networks Implementation of Knowledge Tracing. UMAP 2010, Lecture Notes in Computer Science, vol 6075. Springer. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-642-13470-8_24
title: Individualized Bayesian knowledge tracing framework
description: The article introduces a reformulation of the knowledge tracing model within a Bayesian networks framework so that individual student parameters can be estimated. It formulates "the individualization problem entirely within a Bayesian networks framework that fits individualized as well as skill specific parameters simultaneously, in a single step." This extends the Corbett and Anderson knowledge tracing approach, which the field had used for over a decade without allowing individual learning rates or individualized initial knowledge estimates.
requirements: A Bayesian networks implementation of knowledge tracing that can fit individual student parameters alongside skill-specific parameters in a single step
target_learning_goals: Accurate estimation of student knowledge and skill mastery
examples: The authors applied the framework to real-world data from 42 problem sets in an intelligent tutoring system
key_sources: Pardos, Z.A., Heffernan, N.T. (2010). Modeling Individualization in a Bayesian Networks Implementation of Knowledge Tracing. UMAP 2010, Lecture Notes in Computer Science, vol 6075. Springer. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-642-13470-8_24

article_title: Using adaptive learning technologies to personalize instruction to student interests
citation: Walkington, C. A. (2013). Using adaptive learning technologies to personalize instruction to student interests: The impact of relevant contexts on performance and learning outcomes. Journal of Educational Data Mining, 5(1). https://jedm.educationaldatamining.org/index.php/JEDM
title: Interest-based framework for context personalization: individual, situational, and topic interest in adaptive learning
description: The article frames context personalization within Hidi and Renninger's interest framework, defining interest as "the psychological state of engaging or the predisposition to re-engage with particular classes of objects, events, or ideas over time." It distinguishes individual interest (stable preferences with stored value and knowledge), situational interest (attention-focusing reaction to environmental stimuli), and topic interest (interest triggered by a specific topic). Personalization is positioned as both an environmental modification to trigger and maintain situational interest and a way of leveraging individual interests in out-of-school topics. The framework connects interest activation to improved situation-model construction in mathematical word problem solving.
requirements: Instructional contexts must be matched to learners' actual interests via an assessment such as an interests survey
Interest-based triggers must be tied explicitly to the content to be learned rather than being decorative or incidental
constraints: Personalization effects are moderated by learner ability level, with strongest effects for struggling students
Effects are moderated by task difficulty, with the largest impacts on hard knowledge components
target_learning_goals: writing symbolic equations from story scenarios
examples: Students rated interest in 9 topic areas on a 4-point survey, and the tutor selected the highest-rated interest variation of each story problem
key_sources: Walkington, C. A. (2013). Using adaptive learning technologies to personalize instruction to student interests: The impact of relevant contexts on performance and learning outcomes. Journal of Educational Data Mining, 5(1). https://jedm.educationaldatamining.org/index.php/JEDM

article_title: Why interleaving enhances inductive learning: The roles of discrimination and retrieval
citation: Monica S. Birnbaum, Nate Kornell, Elizabeth Ligon Bjork, & Robert A. Bjork. (2013). Why interleaving enhances inductive learning: The roles of discrimination and retrieval. Memory & Cognition, 41, 392–402. https://doi.org/10.3758/s13421-012-0272-7
title: Interleave exemplars of different categories for inductive learning, and achieve spacing by increasing lag rather than inserting gaps
description: The article's foremost practical implication is "that successful inductive learning entails the juxtaposing of exemplars from different categories so as to promote discriminative contrast". Because inserted filler tasks can interrupt discrimination processing, the authors advise that "Increasing the lag between interleaved items may be wiser than inserting gaps between inductive-learning trials". Spacing remains valuable when it does not interfere with discriminative contrast.
requirements: Learning goal must be inductive category learning in which learners must classify new exemplars
constraints: Spacing that interrupts juxtaposition of interleaved categories impaired learning in Experiment 1; the authors acknowledge a possible untested upper limit to how much spacing can occur before performance suffers
target_learners: classroom learners studying naturalistic categories, including mathematics problem types
target_learning_goals: discriminating between confusable categories of problems or exemplars
examples: Taylor and Rohrer's mathematics study found interleaving enhanced delayed-test problem solving even with spacing held constant, which the authors cite as extending the implication beyond visual categories
key_sources: Monica S. Birnbaum, Nate Kornell, Elizabeth Ligon Bjork, & Robert A. Bjork. (2013). Why interleaving enhances inductive learning: The roles of discrimination and retrieval. Memory & Cognition, 41, 392–402. https://doi.org/10.3758/s13421-012-0272-7

article_title: Kindergarten Entrance Age and Children’s Achievement
citation: Todd E. Elder and Darren H. Lubotsky. (2009). Kindergarten Entrance Age and Children’s Achievement: Impacts of State Policies, Family Background, and Peers. Journal of Human Resources. https://doi.org/10.3368/jhr.44.3.641
title: Interpret kindergarten entrance-age achievement gaps as evidence of prior skill accumulation, not of older children learning more in school
description: The article’s evidence supports reading entrance-age achievement differences as reflecting skills children bring to school rather than differences in capacity to learn once there. The authors “present evidence that the positive relationship between kindergarten entrance age and school achievement primarily reflects skill accumulation prior to kindergarten.” The timing pattern — the gap “appears during the first months of kindergarten” and “declines sharply in subsequent years” — is the basis for this interpretation, along with its concentration among upper-income children.
requirements: Achievement data spanning the first months of kindergarten and subsequent years are needed to distinguish pre-entry skill accumulation from in-school learning differences.
constraints: The interpretation rests on the article’s stated pattern that the association declines sharply after the first months of kindergarten; the full supporting analyses were not available in the supplied text.
target_learning_goals: achievement test performance in early elementary school
examples: The article contrasts the interpretation that older entrants learn more in school with its finding that the gap appears immediately at kindergarten entry and fades in later years.
key_sources: Todd E. Elder and Darren H. Lubotsky. (2009). Kindergarten Entrance Age and Children’s Achievement: Impacts of State Policies, Family Background, and Peers. Journal of Human Resources. https://doi.org/10.3368/jhr.44.3.641

article_title: Interlanguage Variability in Narrative Discourse: Style Shifting in the Use of the Past Tense
citation: Rod Ellis. (1987). Interlanguage Variability in Narrative Discourse: Style Shifting in the Use of the Past Tense. Studies in Second Language Acquisition, Volume 9, Issue 1. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0272263100006483
title: Style shifting in interlanguage varies by linguistic feature within a single discourse mode
description: The study frames interlanguage variability as style shifting that can be observed within one discourse mode by manipulating planning time, rather than by comparing different tasks or discourse types as previous studies did. It examines three past tense morphemes—regular past, irregular past, and past copula—among 17 intermediate L2 learners, and finds that "Different patterns of style shifting were observed for three morphemes, suggesting that the nature of the linguistic feature under investigation is a determining factor."
requirements: Data collection under at least two conditions differing in planning time within the same discourse mode
constraints: Findings concern intermediate L2 learners of English and the three past tense morphemes studied
target_learning_goals: accurate use of past tense morphemes in narrative discourse
examples: Data were collected under planned writing, planned speech, and unplanned speech conditions in narrative discourse
key_sources: Rod Ellis. (1987). Interlanguage Variability in Narrative Discourse: Style Shifting in the Use of the Past Tense. Studies in Second Language Acquisition, Volume 9, Issue 1. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0272263100006483

article_title: Changing Provider Behavior
citation: Jeremy M. Grimshaw, Liz Shirran, Ruth Thomas, Graham Mowatt, Cynthia Fraser, Lisa Bero, Roberto Grilli, Emma Harvey, Andy Oxman, Mary Ann O'Brien. (2001). Changing Provider Behavior: An Overview of Systematic Reviews of Interventions. Medical Care 39(8). https://doi.org/10.1097/00005650-200108002-00004
title: Quality improvement and educational activities should be informed by the findings of systematic reviews of behavior change interventions
description: The article recommends that those planning professional education or quality improvement draw on the existing systematic review evidence rather than intuition or passive habit. It concludes that "Future quality improvement or educational activities should be informed by the findings of systematic reviews of professional behavior change interventions," because the evidence, though incomplete, "provides valuable insights into the likely effectiveness of different interventions."
requirements: Access to systematic reviews of professional behavior change interventions relevant to the planned activity
constraints: The article notes the current evidence base is incomplete, so reviews inform likely effectiveness rather than guarantee it
target_learners: Professionals targeted by quality improvement or educational activities, and the policy makers and professionals designing them
target_learning_goals: Effective selection of dissemination and implementation strategies to change professional practice
examples: The overview itself was conducted to make the growing body of evidence about the effectiveness of different strategies accessible to policy makers and professionals.

Changing Provider Behavior: An Overview of Systematic Reviews of Interventions. Medical Care 39(8). https://doi.org/10.1097/00005650-200108002-00002

article_title: Comprehensible Input and Second Language Acquisition
citation: Lester Loschky. (1994). Comprehensible Input and Second Language Acquisition: What is the Relationship? Studies in Second Language Acquisition, Volume 16, Issue 3, pp. 303-323. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0272263100013103
title: Input hypothesis and its interactionist modification as competing accounts of the comprehension-acquisition relationship
description: The study is framed as an empirical test of Krashen's input hypothesis and Long's modification of it, which hold that second language acquisition is driven by comprehensible input, with negotiated interaction serving as a route to comprehension. The article experimentally operationalizes this by contrasting "unmodified input with no interaction," "premodified input with no interaction," and "unmodified input with the chance for negotiated interaction," and by measuring both comprehension and subsequent acquisition. Its findings complicate the hypothesis: interaction aided moment-to-moment comprehension but comprehension differences did not predict acquisition gains.
requirements: Testing the hypothesis requires experimentally differentiating input and interaction conditions and measuring both moment-to-moment comprehension and subsequent acquisition outcomes
constraints: The study used Japanese as the target language and two Japanese locative structures plus vocabulary as acquisition measures
target_learning_goals: acquisition of Japanese locative grammatical structures
examples: The article states: "This study attempts to test aspects of the input hypothesis (Krashen, 1980, 1983, 1985) and Long's modification of it (Long, 1980, 1983a, 1985)."
key_sources: Lester Loschky. (1994). Comprehensible Input and Second Language Acquisition: What is the Relationship? Studies in Second Language Acquisition, Volume 16, Issue 3, pp. 303-323. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0272263100013103

article_title: Vocabulary enhancement activities and reading for meaning in second language vocabulary acquisition
citation: T. Sima Paribakht and Marjorie Wesche. (1996). Vocabulary enhancement activities and reading for meaning in second language vocabulary acquisition. Second Language Vocabulary Acquisition: A Rationale for Pedagogy, Cambridge University Press. https://doi.org/10.1017/CBO9781139524643.013
title: Instructional intervention can support incidental L2 vocabulary acquisition through reading by making the process more directed and efficient
description: The chapter proposes that while incidental vocabulary acquisition through reading is slow and unpredictable, instructional intervention can support the process and make it more directed and efficient. It does so by using procedures that "increase the salience and cognitive processing of targeted words" encountered by L2 students in reading texts, combining reading for meaning with vocabulary enhancement activities rather than relying on reading alone or decontextualized exercises.
requirements: Targeted words must be encountered by learners in meaningful reading texts, with enhancement procedures layered onto the reading
constraints: Incidental acquisition through reading alone is slow and unpredictable, which is the problem the intervention addresses
target_learning_goals: Acquisition of targeted second language vocabulary through reading for meaning
examples: The chapter's classroom experiments used instructional procedures designed to increase the salience and cognitive processing of targeted words in reading texts, tracking acquisition with the Vocabulary Knowledge Scale.
key_sources: T. Sima Paribakht and Marjorie Wesche. (1996). Vocabulary enhancement activities and reading for meaning in second language vocabulary acquisition. Second Language Vocabulary Acquisition: A Rationale for Pedagogy, Cambridge University Press. https://doi.org/10.1017/CBO9781139524643.013

article_title: BEYOND STUDENT PERCEPTIONS: ISSUES OF INTERACTION, PRESENCE, AND PERFORMANCE IN AN ONLINE COURSE
citation: Picciano, A. G. (2002). Beyond Student Perceptions: Issues of Interaction, Presence, and Performance in an Online Course. Online Learning, 6(1). https://doi.org/10.24059/olj.v6i1.1870
title: Interaction and sense of presence as paired constructs for understanding online course success
description: The article organizes its inquiry around two constructs: interaction and the student's sense of presence in an online course. It treats both as measurable independent variables whose relationship to performance can be analyzed, framing interaction as central to a successful course and presence as a distinct sense students have in the course environment. The study design pairs these constructs with performance measures, reflecting the article's view that both interaction and presence matter for online learning effectiveness.
requirements: Both interaction and presence must be operationalized as measurable variables so their relationship to performance can be analyzed.
target_learners: students in Web-based asynchronous online courses
target_learning_goals: learning effectiveness in online and computer-mediated courses
examples: The study collected measures of interaction and of students' sense of presence in the course as independent variables alongside performance measures.
key_sources: Picciano, A. G. (2002). Beyond Student Perceptions: Issues of Interaction, Presence, and Performance in an Online Course. Online Learning, 6(1). https://doi.org/10.24059/olj.v6i1.1870

article_title: Explicit Instruction and Input Processing
citation: Bill VanPatten and Teresa Cadierno. (1993). Explicit Instruction and Input Processing. Studies in Second Language Acquisition, Volume 15, Issue 2. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0272263100011979
title: Input processing: learner strategies in processing input as the basis for determining explicit instruction
description: Input processing is the framework the article uses to link second language acquisition to how learners process input data. It holds that "learner strategies in input processing" should serve as "the starting point for determining what explicit instruction should look like." Processing instruction operationalizes this by having learners practice processing input rather than producing output after grammar explanation.
requirements: Instruction must be designed around identified learner strategies in input processing.
target_learners: second language learners in classroom instruction
target_learning_goals: grammatical interpretation and production of the targeted linguistic form
examples: The experiment's processing instruction treatment involved "explanation and practice/experience processing input data."
key_sources: Bill VanPatten and Teresa Cadierno. (1993). Explicit Instruction and Input Processing. Studies in Second Language Acquisition, Volume 15, Issue 2. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0272263100011979

article_title: Using Spacing to Enhance Diverse Forms of Learning: Review of Recent Research and Implications for Instruction
citation: Carpenter, S.K., Cepeda, N.J., Rohrer, D., Kang, S.H.K., & Pashler, H. (2012). Using Spacing to Enhance Diverse Forms of Learning: Review of Recent Research and Implications for Instruction. Educational Psychology Review, 24, 369–378. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-012-9205-z
title: Incorporate spacing into everyday instruction by separating study sessions over time rather than massing them
description: The article closes by offering guidance on applying spacing research to teaching: it "conclude[s] with a list of recommendations on how spacing might be incorporated into everyday instruction". The principle is that instructors should schedule multiple study or review opportunities separated in time rather than in immediate succession, because spaced sessions improve final-test performance. The specific recommendations are listed in the article body, which is not available in the preview text.
requirements: Instruction must include multiple study opportunities that can be distributed across time rather than delivered in one massed session.
target_learning_goals: durable memory retention of studied material
examples: The authors state the article concludes with a list of recommendations on how spacing might be incorporated into everyday instruction.
key_sources: Carpenter, S.K., Cepeda, N.J., Rohrer, D., Kang, S.H.K., & Pashler, H. (2012). Using Spacing to Enhance Diverse Forms of Learning: Review of Recent Research and Implications for Instruction. Educational Psychology Review, 24, 369–378. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-012-9205-z

article_title: A Meta‐Analysis and Meta‐Regression of Incidental Second Language Word Learning from Spoken Input
citation: de Vos, J. F., Schriefers, H., Nivard, M. G., & Lemhöfer, K. (2018). A Meta-Analysis and Meta-Regression of Incidental Second Language Word Learning from Spoken Input. Language Learning. https://doi.org/10.1111/lang.12296
title: Involvement Load Hypothesis as a mechanism account of incidental word learning
description: The article presents the Involvement Load Hypothesis (Laufer & Hulstijn, 2001) as one mechanism explaining why incidental exposure can produce learning. It holds that "Involvement is seen as consisting of three dimensions: need, search, and evaluation", and that "activities that require a higher involvement from the learner are expected to lead to more learning". The article cites a prior meta-analysis finding support for it, and uses such mechanism accounts to motivate why meaning-focused activities differ in effectiveness.
requirements: Learning activities must differ in the motivational (need) and cognitive (search, evaluation) demands they place on learners for the hypothesis to predict differential learning.
constraints: The article reports the hypothesis as tested on output-versus-reading comparisons in prior work, not directly tested in its own meta-regression.
target_learning_goals: incidental L2 vocabulary learning from meaning-focused activities
examples: The article cites Huang, Willson, and Eslami (2012) finding that participants who completed an output task acquired more vocabulary than those who only read a text.
key_sources: de Vos, J. F., Schriefers, H., Nivard, M. G., & Lemhöfer, K. (2018). A Meta-Analysis and Meta-Regression of Incidental Second Language Word Learning from Spoken Input. Language Learning. https://doi.org/10.1111/lang.12296

article_title: Fostering self-monitoring of university students by means of a standardized learning journal—a longitudinal study with process analyses
citation: Fabriz, S., Dignath-van Ewijk, C., Poarch, G., Büttner, G. (2014). Fostering self-monitoring of university students by means of a standardized learning journal—a longitudinal study with process analyses. Eur J Psychol Educ, 29, 239–255. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10212-013-0196-z
title: Inform students on the benefits of self-monitoring when assigning structured learning diaries, to sustain their motivation
description: The article concludes that structured learning diaries should not be assigned as a bare self-monitoring tool: students need to be informed why self-monitoring helps. It states that "in order for students to profit in keeping a structured learning diary, they should be informed on the benefits of self-monitoring to increase their motivation." This pairs the diary with instruction on self-regulated learning rather than diary-keeping alone.
requirements: Students keep a structured learning diary over an extended period
Students receive information on the benefits of self-monitoring and self-regulated learning alongside the diary
constraints: Diary-keeping alone decreased motivation and did not improve self-regulation
No academic performance improvements were found even with the combined intervention
examples: In two of four courses students kept a structured learning diary and/or received a weekly course intervention on self-regulated learning, while other courses received no treatment
key_sources: Fabriz, S., Dignath-van Ewijk, C., Poarch, G., Büttner, G. (2014). Fostering self-monitoring of university students by means of a standardized learning journal—a longitudinal study with process analyses. Eur J Psychol Educ, 29, 239–255. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10212-013-0196-z

article_title: Outsourcing Memory to External Tools: A Review of ‘Intention Offloading’
citation: Gilbert, S. J., Boldt, A., Sachdeva, C., Scarampi, C., & Tsai, P.-C. (2023). Outsourcing Memory to External Tools: A Review of 'Intention Offloading'. Psychonomic Bulletin & Review. https://doi.org/10.3758/s13423-022-02139-4
title: Intention offloading framework: storing intentions in extended environments alongside brain-based memory
description: Intention offloading is defined as 'the process of creating a cue in the external environment to trigger a delayed intention', a specific case of cognitive offloading. The review argues intentions are stored in 'our extended physical and social environments, not just in our brains', and that the phenomenon provides a testbed for interrelations between memory, planning, metacognitive monitoring and control, and decision making. It organises research on measurement, triggers (metacognition, effort avoidance, strategy perseveration), lifespan change, and neural mechanisms.
requirements: Individuals must have a free choice between internal memory and external reminder-setting for the paradigm to measure offloading strategy
constraints: Laboratory tasks reviewed use short retention intervals of seconds to minutes, and the authors note most studies used 'rather artificial experimental tasks'
examples: The Gilbert (2015a) web-based paradigm where participants drag numbered circles and can set reminders by placing target circles next to their instructed location
key_sources: Gilbert, S. J., Boldt, A., Sachdeva, C., Scarampi, C., & Tsai, P.-C. (2023). Outsourcing Memory to External Tools: A Review of 'Intention Offloading'. Psychonomic Bulletin & Review. https://doi.org/10.3758/s13423-022-02139-4

article_title: AI literacy and its implications for prompt engineering strategies
citation: Knoth, N., Tolzin, A., Janson, A., & Leimeister, J. M. (2024). AI literacy and its implications for prompt engineering strategies. Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.caeai.2024.100225
title: Integrate AI educational content into current curricula to enable effective student use of generative AI tools
description: The article argues that because prompt engineering skill quality predicts LLM output quality and AI literacy aspects play a role in prompting, education should embed AI content in existing curricula. The authors "argue for the integration of AI educational content into current curricula to enable a hybrid intelligent society in which students can effectively use generative AI tools such as ChatGPT". This is a curricular design recommendation grounded in the study's findings on students' prompting behavior.
requirements: Curricula must have room to add AI educational content alongside existing subjects
constraints: The recommendation is framed for higher education contexts and LLM-based tools such as ChatGPT
target_learning_goals: effective use of generative AI tools such as ChatGPT
examples: The study provides qualitative insights into students' intuitive behaviors towards LLM-based AI systems in a higher education context
key_sources: Knoth, N., Tolzin, A., Janson, A., & Leimeister, J. M. (2024). AI literacy and its implications for prompt engineering strategies. Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.caeai.2024.100225

article_title: Reducing implicit racial preferences: I. A comparative investigation of 17 interventions.
citation: C. K. Lai; M. Marini; S. A. Lehr; C. Cerruti; J. L. Shin; J. A. Joy Gaba; A. K. Ho; B. A. Teachman; S. P. Wojcik; S. P. Koleva; R. S. Frazier; L. Heiphetz; E. Chen; R. N. Turner; J. Haidt; S. Kesebir; C. B. Hawkins; H. S. Schaefer; Sandro Rubichi; G. Sartori; C. M. Dial; N. Sriram; M. R. Banaji; B. A. Nosek (2014). Reducing implicit racial preferences: I. A comparative investigation of 17 interventions. JOURNAL OF EXPERIMENTAL PSYCHOLOGY. GENERAL. https://dx.doi.org/10.1037/a0036260
title: Research contest method for experimentally comparing interventions with revision rules between studies
description: A crowdsourced research contest in which teams submitted candidate interventions that were then experimentally compared head-to-head. Teams "submitted 17 interventions that were tested an average of 3.70 times each in 4 studies (total N ! 17,021), with rules for revising interventions between studies." The method enables relative-effectiveness comparisons among many interventions under a common protocol, addressing the gap that "little is known about their relative effectiveness."
requirements: Multiple independent teams submitting candidate interventions
A common experimental outcome measure across studies
Rules governing revision of interventions between studies
target_learners: Adult research participants in implicit-preference studies
examples: The contest compared 17 interventions across 4 studies with a total sample of 17,021, allowing identification of eight effective and nine ineffective intervention types.
