article_title: Promoting Self-Determination in Early Elementary School
citation: Palmer, S.B., & Wehmeyer, M.L. (2003). Promoting self-determination in early elementary school: Teaching self-regulated problem-solving and goal-setting skills. Remedial and Special Education, 24, 115-126. http://dx.doi.org/10.1177/07419325030240020601
title: Infuse self-determination instruction into existing early elementary curricula rather than adding separate programming
description: The article proposes that teachers can infuse self-determination activities — problem solving and goal setting — into existing curricula and programs in early elementary grades, rather than treating them as a separate add-on. The model was validated as usable "in a variety of subjects and settings with students having diverse learning needs," supporting integration across the school day.
requirements: Teachers must be able to implement the instructional model within their existing curricula and programs.
target_learners: Early elementary students ages 5-6 and up
examples: Teachers used the model to support investigation of student interests, facilitation of choices, and goal setting and attainment of young children.
key_sources: Palmer, S.B., & Wehmeyer, M.L. (2003). Promoting self-determination in early elementary school: Teaching self-regulated problem-solving and goal-setting skills. Remedial and Special Education, 24, 115-126. http://dx.doi.org/10.1177/07419325030240020601

article_title: Enhancing academic writing skills and motivation: assessing the efficacy of ChatGPT in AI-assisted language learning for EFL students
citation: Song, C., and Song, Y. (2023). Enhancing academic writing skills and motivation: assessing the efficacy of ChatGPT in AI-assisted language learning for EFL students. Frontiers in Psychology. https://www.frontiersin.org
title: Integrate AI chatbots into writing courses to supplement instruction while safeguarding learners' independent writing development
description: This principle holds that automated AI feedback should complement, not replace, instruction in L2 writing courses. The article's evidence that ChatGPT-integrated instruction produced significantly higher writing motivation than conventional instruction supports integration, while its caution that over-reliance on AI-generated feedback may hinder independent writing skills requires instructors to frame the tool's role and teach critical evaluation of its output.
requirements: Instructors must frame the AI's role and teach students to evaluate and act on the feedback it gives
constraints: Over-reliance on AI-generated feedback may hinder the development of learners' independent writing skills, per the article's stated concern
examples: The study paired conventional writing instruction with ChatGPT access in the experimental group and compared motivation outcomes against a control group receiving instruction without the tool
key_sources: Song, C., and Song, Y. (2023). Enhancing academic writing skills and motivation: assessing the efficacy of ChatGPT in AI-assisted language learning for EFL students. Frontiers in Psychology. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2023.1260843

article_title: Element Interactivity and Intrinsic, Extraneous, and Germane Cognitive Load
citation: Sweller, J. (2010). Element Interactivity and Intrinsic, Extraneous, and Germane Cognitive Load. Educational Psychology Review, 22, 123–138. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-010-9128-5
title: Judge instructional procedures by whether the element interactivity they impose is essential to the task
description: Because the article grounds both intrinsic and extraneous load in element interactivity, instructional design should ask whether the interactivity a task imposes is "essential to the task at hand" or merely "a function of instructional procedures". Interactivity essential to the task reflects intrinsic load, while interactivity introduced by the way material is presented reflects extraneous load and is a target for design reduction.
requirements: Designers must be able to identify the interacting elements of the material and of the instructional presentation separately
constraints: The article presents this distinction as a theoretical relation; the supplied text does not report empirical tests of design recommendations based on it
target_learning_goals: reducing extraneous processing during schema acquisition
key_sources: Sweller, J. (2010). Element Interactivity and Intrinsic, Extraneous, and Germane Cognitive Load. Educational Psychology Review, 22, 123–138. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-010-9128-5

article_title: Exploring the impact of using Chat-GPT on student learning outcomes in technology learning: The comprehensive experiment
citation: Hakiki, M., Fadli, R., Samala, A. D., Fricticarani, A., Dayurni, P., Rahmadani, K., Astiti, A. D., & Sabir, A. (2023). Exploring the impact of using Chat-GPT on student learning outcomes in technology learning: The comprehensive experiment. Advances in Mobile Learning Educational Research, 3(2), 859-872. https://doi.org/10.25082/AMLER.2023.02.013
title: Integrate ChatGPT into technology learning as a tool to improve student learning outcomes and overall learning experience quality
description: Based on their experimental finding of significantly higher post-test scores in the ChatGPT class, the authors recommend institutional adoption: "It is recommended that educational institutions and educators consider integrating Chat GPT as a tool to improve student learning outcomes and enhance the overall quality of the technology learning experience." The principle treats ChatGPT's interactive, personalized feedback as a support for participation and engagement in technology courses.
requirements: Educators and institutions integrate ChatGPT within technology learning activities so students can interact with it during the learning process.
constraints: The recommendation rests on one quasi-experimental study at a single university; the authors note further research should explore long-term effects and applications in other educational contexts.
target_learning_goals: Improved learning outcomes and engagement in technology learning
examples: In the study, the experimental class used ChatGPT during learning and outscored the conventionally taught control class (81.81 vs 70.45) on the final test.
key_sources: Hakiki, M., Fadli, R., Samala, A. D., Fricticarani, A., Dayurni, P., Rahmadani, K., Astiti, A. D., & Sabir, A. (2023). Exploring the impact of using Chat-GPT on student learning outcomes in technology learning: The comprehensive experiment. Advances in Mobile Learning Educational Research, 3(2), 859-872. https://doi.org/10.25082/AMLER.2023.02.013

article_title: From Gatekeeping to Engagement: A Multicontextual, Mixed Method Study of Student Academic Engagement in Introductory STEM Courses
citation: Gasiewski, J. A., Eagan, M. K., Garcia, G. A., Hurtado, S., & Chang, M. J. (2012). From Gatekeeping to Engagement: A Multicontextual, Mixed Method Study of Student Academic Engagement in Introductory STEM Courses. Research in Higher Education, 53, 229–261. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11162-011-9247-y
title: In introductory STEM courses, signal openness to student questions and take responsibility for student success to support engagement
description: Because behavioral engagement depends on the classroom context instructors create, instructors should consistently signal accessibility cues: welcoming even elementary questions, acknowledging their role in helping students succeed, and making time for individualized attention. The HLM showed "Faculty agreement: In my classroom, there is no such thing as a question that is too elementary" positively predicted engagement, while agreeing that success is primarily up to students or that there is not enough time for individualized attention negatively predicted it. Reducing lecture time in favor of discussion and group work complements this climate work.
requirements: Faculty must convey genuine accessibility cues rather than simply stating policies; students' felt comfort asking questions is the proximate predictor
constraints: Course-level climate variables account for a marginal share of engagement variance (3.1% across classrooms), so instructor climate alone will not transform student engagement
target_learners: Undergraduates in large introductory STEM gatekeeper courses
target_learning_goals: Behavioral academic engagement, including question-asking, help-seeking, and collaboration
examples: Faculty survey items measured instructor agreement with statements about classroom climate, and the authors discuss instructional implications of signaling openness to questions and a role in student success
key_sources: Gasiewski, J. A., Eagan, M. K., Garcia, G. A., Hurtado, S., & Chang, M. J. (2012). From Gatekeeping to Engagement: A Multicontextual, Mixed Method Study of Student Academic Engagement in Introductory STEM Courses. Research in Higher Education, 53, 229–261. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11162-011-9247-y

article_title: Race and gender differences in how sense of belonging influences decisions to major in STEM
citation: Katherine Rainey, Melissa Dancy, Roslyn Mickelson, Elizabeth Stearns and Stephanie Moller. (2018). Race and gender differences in how sense of belonging influences decisions to major in STEM. International Journal of STEM Education 5:10. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40594-018-0115-6
title: An intersectional account of STEM sense of belonging structured by four contributing factors
description: The article organizes students' belonging reports through an intersectional lens: identity axes of race and gender "are not unitary and mutually exclusive, but instead interact to construct one's identity." Within this framework, belonging is explained by four coded factors—interpersonal relationships, science identity, personal interest, and competence—defined for both having and lacking each reason (Table 1). The framework also links belonging to representation: demographic similarity to others in a field is described as positively impacting belonging. It is used descriptively to interpret who persists in and leaves STEM majors.
requirements: Data must capture students' self-reported belonging and permit disaggregation by race and gender intersections, which the article's interview protocol and coding scheme were designed to do
constraints: The study recorded only two axes of identity, race and gender, a limitation the authors acknowledge
Findings come from a self-selected purposive sample of North Carolina college seniors, which the authors say restricts generalizability beyond the sample
target_learners: women and students of color in STEM
target_learning_goals: persistence and retention in STEM majors
sense of belonging in STEM fields
examples: Interview codes applied to responses about belonging, e.g., a white female biology major coded as having interpersonal relationships said, 'Most of my friends are biology majors. I feel like it's where I belong.'
key_sources: Katherine Rainey, Melissa Dancy, Roslyn Mickelson, Elizabeth Stearns and Stephanie Moller. (2018). Race and gender differences in how sense of belonging influences decisions to major in STEM. International Journal of STEM Education 5:10. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40594-018-0115-6

article_title: Inhibitory control and counterintuitive science and maths reasoning in adolescence
citation: Brookman-Byrne A, Mareschal D, Tolmie AK, Dumontheil I (2018) Inhibitory control and counterintuitive science and maths reasoning in adolescence. PLoS ONE 13(6): e0198973. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0198973
title: Inhibitory control account of counterintuitive reasoning: naïve theories and misleading cues persist and must be suppressed
description: The article endorses the account that learning counterintuitive science and maths concepts does not replace prior concepts: "prior beliefs remain in the face of new evidence" and misconceptions persist into adulthood. Inhibitory control, "the ability to suppress a prepotent response or irrelevant information", is thought to allow suppression of naïve theories, incorrect strategies, or misleading perceptual cues during counterintuitive reasoning. The study's findings that semantic inhibition related to accuracy and response inhibition to reaction times are offered as further support for this hypothesis in adolescence.
requirements: Reasoning about concepts where a misconception may be held, so that an intuitive response competes with the correct counterintuitive answer
constraints: The article states the association between inhibitory control and counterintuitive reasoning is correlational; intervention studies would be needed to establish causality, which the current paper could not address directly
target_learners: Adolescents aged 11–15 years in secondary school science and maths
target_learning_goals: Counterintuitive science and maths reasoning aligned with the Key Stage 3 curriculum
examples: The study measured response inhibition with simple and complex Go/No-Go tasks and semantic inhibition with a numerical Stroop task, alongside a novel 48-problem-set science and maths misconceptions task
key_sources: Brookman-Byrne A, Mareschal D, Tolmie AK, Dumontheil I (2018) Inhibitory control and counterintuitive science and maths reasoning in adolescence. PLoS ONE 13(6): e0198973. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0198973

article_title: A meta-analytic investigation of the role of reward on inhibitory control
citation: Burton, S., Knibb, G., & Jones, A. (2021). A meta-analytic investigation of the role of reward on inhibitory control. Quarterly Journal of Experimental Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1177/17470218211008895
title: Inhibitory control as a transient, motivation-sensitive state rather than a stable trait
description: The article frames inhibitory control not as a fixed trait but as a state that fluctuates with motivational context, drawing on value-based models in which "IC is a value-based process and represents a trade-off between short- and long-term rewards". Reward prospect raises the momentary value (gain) of inhibition relative to its costs, so expression of IC depends on internal and external factors. The meta-analytic reward effect is presented as support for this account.
requirements: Requires tasks in which reward for successful inhibition is manipulated against a no-reward control condition
constraints: The article could not examine reactive versus proactive control due to lack of data, so conclusions cannot be drawn about which mechanism reward affects
target_learners: Clinical populations including ADHD and substance use disorder
target_learning_goals: Improving inhibitory control and self-regulation through motivational context
examples: The meta-analysis pooled rewarded versus non-rewarded inhibition trials across stop signal, go/no-go, Flanker, Simon, Stroop, and Anti-saccade tasks
key_sources: Burton, S., Knibb, G., & Jones, A. (2021). A meta-analytic investigation of the role of reward on inhibitory control. Quarterly Journal of Experimental Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1177/17470218211008895

article_title: States of curiosity and interest enhance memory differently in adolescents and in children
citation: Fandakova Yana, Gruber Matthias J. (2021). States of curiosity and interest enhance memory differently in adolescents and in children. Developmental Science, 24(1), e13005. https://doi.org/10.1111/desc.13005
title: Information prediction errors (IPEs) as a driver of memory, in line with reward prediction errors and the information gap theory
description: The article frames IPEs as "the discrepancy between post-information interest and pre-information curiosity", proposed as an important driver of memory (Marvin & Shohamy, 2016). IPEs are presented as a critical aspect of information gap theory, which postulates that predicting whether expected information will resolve uncertainty is critical for curiosity, and as parallel to reward prediction errors, which are "a key driver of learning in various contexts". The study computes an IPE score per trial as the difference between initial curiosity rating and post-answer interest rating and uses it to predict recall.
requirements: Requires participants to rate pre-information curiosity and post-information interest so the discrepancy can be computed per trial
constraints: The article notes the neural mechanisms of IPEs in a trivia paradigm have not been directly investigated, and how IPEs map onto reward prediction errors neurally is not known
target_learning_goals: episodic memory for newly learned factual information (trivia answers)
examples: In the study, an IPE score was computed for each trial as the difference between the initial curiosity rating and the post-answer interest rating, following Marvin & Shohamy (2016)
key_sources: Fandakova Yana, Gruber Matthias J. (2021). States of curiosity and interest enhance memory differently in adolescents and in children. Developmental Science, 24(1), e13005. https://doi.org/10.1111/desc.13005

article_title: Examining the relationship of empathy, social support, and prosocial behavior of adolescents in China: a structural equation modeling approach
citation: Fu W, Wang C, Chai H, Xue R. (2022). Examining the relationship of empathy, social support, and prosocial behavior of adolescents in China: a structural equation modeling approach. Humanities and Social Sciences Communications. https://doi.org/10.1057/s41599-022-01296-0
title: Interpersonal-emotion account of prosocial behavior: internal empathy and external social support jointly shape prosociality
description: The article frames prosocial behavior development as depending on internal factors (empathy) and external factors (social support), explored "from the perspective of interpersonal emotion" based on the biological emotion theory of prosocial behavior. High-empathy individuals more actively perceive care and support from others, building relationships that yield more support, which in turn fosters prosocial behavior; the buffer effect hypothesis is invoked for how perceived support underpins prosociality.
requirements: Measurement of both internal (empathy) and external (social support) factors to capture the mechanism
constraints: Tested in a Chinese adolescent sample; the authors note prosocial behavior is affected by the social and cultural environment
examples: The structural equation model tested empathy, social support, and prosocial behavior as three linked variables with social support as mediator
key_sources: Fu W, Wang C, Chai H, Xue R. (2022). Examining the relationship of empathy, social support, and prosocial behavior of adolescents in China: a structural equation modeling approach. Humanities and Social Sciences Communications. https://doi.org/10.1057/s41599-022-01296-0

article_title: Individual Differences in Inhibitory Control, Not Non-Verbal Number Acuity, Correlate with Mathematics Achievement
citation: Gilmore C, Attridge N, Clayton S, Cragg L, Johnson S, Marlow N, Simms V, Inglis M. (2013). Individual Differences in Inhibitory Control, Not Non-Verbal Number Acuity, Correlate with Mathematics Achievement. PLoS ONE 8(6): e67374. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0067374
title: Inhibition-based account of dot comparison task performance
description: The article proposes that a dot comparison trial can be solved in two ways: by responding to salient visual characteristics such as dot size or area, or by inhibiting that response and answering on the basis of approximate number representations. Because congruent trials reward the visual-cue route while incongruent trials punish it, "an individuals' score on a dot comparison task will reflect not only the precision of their nonsymbolic representations, but also their inhibition skills". The account explains why dot comparison performance correlates with mathematics achievement: the inhibition component, not representational precision, drives the correlation.
requirements: Task formats must include incongruent trials in which visual characteristics conflict with number for the inhibition component to be engaged
constraints: The authors state it remains to be established whether and how the ANS is involved in early symbolic number learning
target_learners: school-aged children from diverse socio-economic backgrounds
target_learning_goals: understanding the cognitive underpinnings of mathematics achievement
examples: Experiment 1 used Pica-style congruent and incongruent dot arrays; Experiment 2 used Gebuis and Reynvoet stimuli with a NEPSY-II inhibition subtest separating inhibition from naming speed.
key_sources: Gilmore C, Attridge N, Clayton S, Cragg L, Johnson S, Marlow N, Simms V, Inglis M. (2013). Individual Differences in Inhibitory Control, Not Non-Verbal Number Acuity, Correlate with Mathematics Achievement. PLoS ONE 8(6): e67374. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0067374

article_title: Training Inhibition and Social Cognition in the Classrooms
citation: Honoré N, Houssa M, Volckaert A, Noël M-P and Nader-Grosbois N (2020) Training Inhibition and Social Cognition in the Classrooms. Front. Psychol. 11:1974. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2020.01974
title: Combined inhibition and social cognition classroom training program (18 weekly sessions with metacognitive characters)
description: A manualized classroom program of "eighteen 45-min sessions implemented in the classroom in the presence of the teacher", delivered once a week over 6 months by a trained psychologist. It trains four inhibition components (predominant response, interruption of an ongoing response, external distractors, impulsivity control) through three metacognitive characters — Mr. Stop, the Detective and the Statue — plus ToM and SIP activities of increasing difficulty, with weekly teacher follow-up activities and record books.
requirements: Sessions delivered in the classroom by a trained psychologist in the presence of the teacher
Teachers asked to use the concepts and materials during the rest of the week and keep a weekly record book
constraints: Designed for typically developing 5- and 6-year-olds; children with language disorders or intellectual disabilities were excluded
Activities presented in order of increasing difficulty according to the zone of proximal development
target_learners: Children in the last year of kindergarten (K3) and first year of primary school (P1)
examples: 85% of experimental-group participants attended 16 or more of the 18 sessions; mean teacher involvement was 3.31 ± 1.40 on the 5-point scale
key_sources: Honoré N, Houssa M, Volckaert A, Noël M-P and Nader-Grosbois N (2020) Training Inhibition and Social Cognition in the Classrooms. Front. Psychol. 11:1974. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2020.01974

article_title: Intelligence and Verbal Short-Term Memory/Working Memory: Their Interrelationships from Childhood to Young Adulthood and Their Impact on Academic Achievement
citation: Schneider Wolfgang, Niklas Frank. (2017). Intelligence and Verbal Short-Term Memory/Working Memory: Their Interrelationships from Childhood to Young Adulthood and Their Impact on Academic Achievement. Journal of Intelligence. https://doi.org/10.3390/jintelligence5020026
title: Studies of cognitive predictors of achievement should include domain-knowledge indicators at every measurement point
description: The article concludes that IQ and WM may matter mainly in early schooling when domain knowledge is not yet developed, and that their impact fades once prior domain knowledge is estimated. It therefore recommends that "future research on the topic should be based on longitudinal designs" that "include relevant indicators of domain knowledge at each time point in order to estimate the size of specific IQ and WM effects and their changes over time." This is a methodological design principle for research on cognitive predictors of learning.
requirements: Longitudinal designs with several representative measures of IQ and WM during early and later assessment periods, plus relevant indicators of domain knowledge at each time point
constraints: The article notes its own memory measures seem to tap STM more than WM, and different measures had to be used across time points, limiting comparability
target_learners: children and adolescents in school, ages 6 to 23
target_learning_goals: reading comprehension, spelling, and mathematics achievement
examples: The LOGIC reanalysis entered preceding academic achievement as precursors before IQ and WMC in regression and SEM models, which eliminated most cognitive-predictor effects at later waves
key_sources: Schneider Wolfgang, Niklas Frank. (2017). Intelligence and Verbal Short-Term Memory/Working Memory: Their Interrelationships from Childhood to Young Adulthood and Their Impact on Academic Achievement. Journal of Intelligence. https://doi.org/10.3390/jintelligence5020026

article_title: Reward improves cancellation and restraint inhibition across childhood and adolescence.
citation: Sinopoli, K.J., Schachar, R., & Dennis, M. (2011). Reward Improves Cancellation and Restraint Inhibition Across Childhood and Adolescence. Developmental Psychology, 47(5), 1479-89. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0024440
title: Incentive salience account of reward effects on inhibitory control
description: The article offers an incentive salience account (drawing on Berridge) for why reward speeds inhibition: rewards "tag" conditioned stimuli that predict reward value, increasing the incentive salience ("wanting") of the stop signal. Because the stop signal is linked to points leading to a prize while the go response is not rewarded, the net effect is facilitation of SSRT but not response execution. The authors hypothesize the mesocorticolimbic dopamine system adds incentive salience to the stop signal, possibly via IFG-mediated salience-detection pathways or striatal gating.
requirements: Rewards must be contingent on successful inhibitory control trials, so the stop signal becomes linked to a positive outcome
constraints: The authors state it is not possible to elucidate how rewards affected IC in the current study; the account is offered as hypotheses
Participants did not anecdotally report increased pleasure during reward trials, which the authors note weighs against a hedonia account
target_learning_goals: regulation of thought and action (inhibitory control)
examples: Rewards were earned only for successful inhibition trials, with points displayed on a visual analog scale and a $10 gift certificate prize for reaching 400 points
key_sources: Sinopoli, K.J., Schachar, R., & Dennis, M. (2011). Reward Improves Cancellation and Restraint Inhibition Across Childhood and Adolescence. Developmental Psychology, 47(5), 1479-89. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0024440

article_title: Game-based learning: A design-based theory of teaching–learning–assessment systems
citation: Sireci, S. G., Tucker, E. M., & Gordon, E. W. (Eds.). (2025). Handbook for Assessment in the Service of Learning, Volume II: Reconceptualizing Assessment to Improve Learning. University of Massachusetts Amherst Libraries. https://openpublishing.library.umass.edu/
title: Intellective competence as the holistic aim of assessment in the service of learning
description: Intellective competence is Gordon's term for the broader goal that reconceived assessment should foster and capture. He defines it: "Intellective competence, a term I coined, denotes the ability and disposition to use one's knowledge, strategies, and values to solve problems and to continue learning." It is a holistic notion going beyond memorization of facts or routine skills, encompassing critical thinking, adaptability, creativity, and the capacity to learn how to learn. Assessing for it means posing authentic, complex challenges and analyzing how students approach them, including ingenuity, learning from failure, and trying alternative strategies.
requirements: Assessments that pose authentic, complex challenges and gather evidence of process, not only correctness
target_learning_goals: Critical thinking, adaptability, creativity, learning how to learn
examples: Gordon proposes analyzing whether students showed ingenuity in finding a solution and learned from initial failures
key_sources: Sireci, S. G., Tucker, E. M., & Gordon, E. W. (Eds.). (2025). Handbook for Assessment in the Service of Learning, Volume II: Reconceptualizing Assessment to Improve Learning. University of Massachusetts Amherst Libraries. https://openpublishing.library.umass.edu/

article_title: An inventory of peer assessment diversity
citation: Gielen, S., Dochy, F., & Onghena, P. (2011). An inventory of peer assessment diversity. Assessment & Evaluation in Higher Education, 36(2), 137–155. https://doi.org/10.1080/02602930903221444
title: Inventory of peer assessment diversity: 20 variables grouped into five clusters
description: The article develops a classification framework for describing peer assessment practices, replacing Topping's discrete-variable typology because 'the range of variation appeared to no longer be a list of separate values but rather a continuum, or sometimes even a multi-dimensional space'. Eight new variables were added and another eight extended with extra sub-dimensions, five original variables were absorbed into larger entities, and the 20 resulting variables were grouped into five clusters: decisions concerning use, links to the learning environment, interaction between peers, composition of assessment groups, and management of the assessment procedure.
requirements: Each peer assessment design should be described on all 20 variables for studies to be comparable and synthesizable
constraints: The authors note 'a list of distinguishing features will never be exhaustive'
target_learners: learners in formal and non-formal education participating in peer assessment
target_learning_goals: designing, describing and comparing peer assessment practices
examples: Table 4 of the article prints the full summary of the 20 variables and their dimensions, from Setting and Object through Format, Requirement, Reward, Training/guidance and Quality control
key_sources: Gielen, S., Dochy, F., & Onghena, P. (2011). An inventory of peer assessment diversity. Assessment & Evaluation in Higher Education, 36(2), 137–155. https://doi.org/10.1080/02602930903221444

article_title: Assessment of Teams in a Digital Game Environment
citation: Mayer, I. (2018). Assessment of Teams in a Digital Game Environment. Simulation & Gaming, 49(6), 602-619. https://doi.org/10.1177/1046878118770831
title: Internal validity as precondition for game-based team assessment
description: The article frames validation research as preceding intervention research: before asking whether games train teams effectively, one must establish whether in-game measures relate to in-game team quality. "Internal validity implies that teams with better in-game performance also have better team quality, and vice versa. In-game team performance scores by themselves have very little external value." In-game performance serves as a proxy for team quality demonstrated during play, and unobtrusively logged game analytics (stealth assessment) are the key advantage of digital serious games for training and assessment.
requirements: Triangulation of self-reporting, personal observation and digital observation data
In-game team quality factors that are relatively stable and transferrable to the outside world
constraints: Internal validity is a precondition but not a guarantee for external validity
External validity of TEAMUP was not an objective of this study and remains undetermined
target_learners: professional and student teams in organisational training contexts
target_learning_goals: valid assessment of team quality and team performance through game play
examples: The study tested internal validity by correlating logged in-game indicators with psychometric team quality constructs from pre- and post-game questionnaires
key_sources: Mayer, I. (2018). Assessment of Teams in a Digital Game Environment. Simulation & Gaming, 49(6), 602-619. https://doi.org/10.1177/1046878118770831

article_title: Expert blind spot: When content knowledge eclipses pedagogical content knowledge
citation: Nathan, M. J., Koedinger, K. R., & Alibali, M. W. (2001). Expert Blind Spot: When Content Knowledge Eclipses Pedagogical Content Knowledge. Proceeding of the Third International Conference on Cognitive Science. https://www.google.com/search?q=%22Expert+Blind+Spot%22+Nathan+Koedinger+Alibali
title: Teachers should integrate assessment practices that challenge their assumptions about students' mathematical development
description: Because advanced content knowledge can produce expert-based views of curricula at odds with the learning process, the article argues teachers should "integrate assessment practices in their classroom curricula that have the potential to challenge their assumptions about mathematical development in their students." This grounds instruction in students' actual performance rather than in the teacher's own expert intuitions, and underscores the need for empirically based theories of instruction.
requirements: Assessment practices embedded in classroom curricula that reveal students' actual performance and developmental propensities
constraints: The article develops this recommendation specifically for mathematics and language arts instruction
target_learners: middle school, high school and college students
target_learning_goals: aligning instruction with students' actual developmental processes in mathematics and language arts
examples: Nathan & Koedinger (2000b) compared teachers' difficulty rankings against ninth graders' actual problem-solving performance, revealing high school teachers' rankings were unrelated to student performance
key_sources: Nathan, M. J., Koedinger, K. R., & Alibali, M. W. (2001). Expert Blind Spot: When Content Knowledge Eclipses Pedagogical Content Knowledge. Proceeding of the Third International Conference on Cognitive Science. https://www.google.com/search?q=%22Expert+Blind+Spot%22+Nathan+Koedinger+Alibali

article_title: An Examination of the Effects of ADHD Coaching on University Students' Executive Functioning
citation: Parker, D. R., Field Hoffman, S., Sawilowsky, S., & Rolands, L. (2010). An Examination of the Effects of ADHD Coaching on University Students' Executive Functioning. Journal of Postsecondary Education and Disability, 24(2), 115-132. https://www.edgefoundation.org
title: Inquiry model of ADHD coaching
description: The article describes ADHD coaching as an "inquiry" model that contrasts with didactic academic services such as tutoring or strategy instruction. Rather than telling students what to do, "coaches use speciﬁc types of questions to model effective executive functioning and to elicit students' own ideas as they increase their capacity to clarify, plan, and take action on goals." Coaches' questions promote reflection and more accurate self-awareness, after which coaches hold clients accountable for acting on their plans, so students learn what supports or restricts their goal attainment.
requirements: Coaches with specialized training and experience coaching students with ADHD
Regular accountability check-ins between sessions
constraints: Developed as a private practice model; distinct from therapy, tutoring, and strategy instruction
examples: Coaches asked questions such as "What's important for you to remember as you go through your week?" instead of telling students how to organize a calendar system
key_sources: Parker, D. R., Field Hoffman, S., Sawilowsky, S., & Rolands, L. (2010). An Examination of the Effects of ADHD Coaching on University Students' Executive Functioning. Journal of Postsecondary Education and Disability, 24(2), 115-132. https://www.edgefoundation.org

article_title: A meta-analytic examination of the instructional effectiveness of computer-based simulation games
citation: Traci Sitzmann. (2011). A Meta-Analytic Examination of the Instructional Effectiveness of Computer-Based Simulation Games. Personnel Psychology, 64, 489-528. https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/journal/17446570
title: Interactive cognitive complexity theory: simulation games engage affective and cognitive processes simultaneously
description: Interactive cognitive complexity is an integrative information processing model the article uses as its central theoretical framework for simulation game effectiveness. It "proposes learning is the result of an interaction between variables internal and external to the cognitive systems of trainees": trainees' affective structures (motivation, attitudes) and cognitive structures (memory, knowledge base, executive control) interact with each other and with sensory information from the simulation game in an iterative process that stores new information. Because both affective and cognitive structures are essential, the theory predicts simulation games should outperform other methods because they target both structures. The meta-analytic results are interpreted against this framework.
requirements: Learning must be the primary goal of the simulation game for it to fall under this framework
constraints: The theory applies to instruction delivered via personal computer immersing trainees in a decision-making exercise in an artificial environment
target_learners: adult trainees in work-related training programs
target_learning_goals: work-related knowledge and skills, including declarative knowledge, procedural knowledge, and retention
examples: The meta-analysis tested the theory's prediction that simulation games engage both affective and cognitive processes, finding higher self-efficacy and learning relative to comparison groups.
key_sources: Traci Sitzmann. (2011). A Meta-Analytic Examination of the Instructional Effectiveness of Computer-Based Simulation Games. Personnel Psychology, 64, 489-528. https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/journal/17446570

article_title: A systematic review of game-based assessment in education in the past decade
citation: Su, F., & Zou, D. (2024). A systematic review of game-based assessment in education in the past decade. Knowledge Management & E-Learning, 16(3), 451–476. https://doi.org/10.34105/j.kmel.2024.16.021
title: In-game assessment designs are associated with game features, differing systematically across simulation, immersive, video, gamification, puzzle, and board game types
description: The review details how in-game assessment is implemented differently per game genre. Simulation GBA "progressively assessed learners' curriculum knowledge" with performance reflecting real-life actions; immersive GBA "yields rich data on learners' learning experiences" as students complete tasks at different paces; video GBA involves "students using dynamic game elements to address problems, offering open-ended solutions without fixed answers"; gamification-based assessment awards points for predetermined questions; puzzle and board games assess spatial reasoning and quiz performance respectively.
requirements: Games must provide explicit game features and embedded assessment details for in-game assessment to be designed and analyzed
constraints: Assessment approaches differ even for the same game across studies, e.g., Scientopolis used multiple-choice questions in one study and interaction-frequency data in another
target_learners: School and university students across disciplines
target_learning_goals: Assessing subject knowledge, reasoning, inquiry, and problem-solving skills during gameplay
examples: Physics Playground recorded correct/incorrect attempts, time spent, restarts, and objects used in log files to deduce qualitative-physics understanding; Semideus awarded 100-500 coins based on estimation correctness and reduced energy by 15% for inaccurate estimation
key_sources: Su, F., & Zou, D. (2024). A systematic review of game-based assessment in education in the past decade. Knowledge Management & E-Learning, 16(3), 451–476. https://doi.org/10.34105/j.kmel.2024.16.021

article_title: The effectiveness of self-regulated learning scaffolds on academic performance in computer-based learning environments: a meta-analysis
citation: Lanqin Zheng. (2016). The effectiveness of self-regulated learning scaffolds on academic performance in computer-based learning environments: a meta-analysis. Asia Pacific Education Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s12564-016-9426-9
title: Design SRL scaffolds to support the whole self-regulation process using integrated, multiple, and combined domain-general and domain-specific scaffolds
description: The article recommends that scaffolds in computer-based environments support the entire SRL cycle rather than a single phase, and that designers combine scaffold types. It states scaffolds "should support the whole process of SRL, ranging from setting goals, making plans, and enacting strategies, to adapting metacognition", and that "integrated SRL tools with multiple functions and multiple kinds of scaffolds should be considered as the optimal way to promote academic performance". Scaffold design should also consider contextual factors of learners, environment, and their interactions.
requirements: Scaffolds must address the full SRL cycle: goal setting, planning, strategy enactment, monitoring, self-evaluation, and metacognitive adaptation
constraints: The article notes few adaptive scaffolds were used in the reviewed studies, and suggests adaptive scaffolding may be more beneficial since it adjusts to students' learning needs
examples: The meta-analysis found integrated SRL tools with multiple functions had the highest effect size among scaffold mechanisms (ES = 0.947), and studies using both scaffold modes had the highest effect (ES = 1.699)
key_sources: Lanqin Zheng. (2016). The effectiveness of self-regulated learning scaffolds on academic performance in computer-based learning environments: a meta-analysis. Asia Pacific Education Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s12564-016-9426-9

article_title: Early predictors of middle school fraction knowledge
citation: Bailey Drew H., Siegler Robert S., Geary David C. (2014). Early Predictors of Middle School Fraction Knowledge. Developmental Science. https://doi.org/10.1111/desc.12155
title: Integrated theory of numerical development
description: The article invokes Siegler, Thompson, and Schneider's (2011) integrated theory of numerical development, which "proposes that fractions play a key role in learning the properties that are and are not invariant for real numbers, and thus that learning fractions plays a crucial role in acquiring a mature concept of number". It assumes understanding of fractions is continuous with understanding of whole numbers, so individual differences in the two should be related independent of domain-general abilities. The study's longitudinal findings are presented as consistent with this assumption.
requirements: Understanding that the one property uniting whole numbers and fractions is that they represent magnitudes orderable on a number line
constraints: The theory provided no obvious reason to expect early whole number knowledge to predict later reading achievement, and the reading null was consistent with this
target_learners: children in elementary and middle school learning whole numbers and fractions
target_learning_goals: acquiring a mature concept of number
distinguishing properties invariant for whole numbers versus all real numbers
examples: The study tested the theory's assumption by predicting middle school fraction knowledge from first-grade whole number knowledge while controlling for IQ, executive functioning, and demographics
key_sources: Bailey Drew H., Siegler Robert S., Geary David C. (2014). Early Predictors of Middle School Fraction Knowledge. Developmental Science. https://doi.org/10.1111/desc.12155

article_title: Working memory, inhibitory control, and reading disability
citation: Chiappe, P., Hasher, L., & Siegel, L. S. (2000). Working memory, inhibitory control, and reading disability. Memory & Cognition, 28(1), 8-17. https://www.psychonomic.org
title: Inhibitory control hypothesis: three functions (access, deletion, restraint) govern working memory contents
description: The article tests the Hasher and colleagues account in which inhibition controls the contents of working memory through three functions. As the article states, "These functions are access, deletion, and restraint": access prevents goal-irrelevant information from entering working memory, deletion suppresses information that has become irrelevant (whose failure yields proactive interference), and restraint prevents strong responses from seizing control so other responses can be considered. The study uses intrusion error types and a mixed span format to index these functions in relation to age and reading skill.
requirements: Assessment requires error analysis of span-task recall, classifying intrusions as current nonfinal, previous, or extraneous
constraints: The article reports the error analyses provided only mixed support for the hypothesis as applied to aging, with no age effects for previous or extraneous intrusions
target_learners: individuals aged 6-49, including those with reading disabilities
target_learning_goals: working memory capacity for storage during processing
examples: Experiment 1 used the blocked listening span format and Experiment 2 a mixed format to test whether reducing proactive interference would diminish age and reading-skill differences
key_sources: Chiappe, P., Hasher, L., & Siegel, L. S. (2000). Working memory, inhibitory control, and reading disability. Memory & Cognition, 28(1), 8-17. https://doi.org/10.3758/bf03211570

article_title: Ethnic Stigma, Academic Anxiety, and Intrinsic Motivation in Middle Childhood
citation: Gillen-O’Neel, C., Ruble, D. N., & Fuligni, A. J. (2011). Ethnic Stigma, Academic Anxiety, and Intrinsic Motivation in Middle Childhood. Child Development. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-8624.2011.01621.x
title: Consider interventions aimed at increasing perception of group status as a promising area for future academic anxiety research
description: The article reports that perception of status was associated with 31–51% of the higher levels of academic anxiety reported by African-American, Chinese, and Dominican children as compared to their European-American peers. Although the findings are not causal, the authors state that interventions aimed at increasing perception of group status (e.g., community role models) could be a promising area for future academic anxiety research.
requirements: Future research should employ longitudinal or experimental designs to determine whether perceived group status directly affects academic anxiety
constraints: The data were measured concurrently, so the causality in the relationship between perception of group status and academic anxiety has yet to be determined
target_learning_goals: reducing academic anxiety associated with stigma awareness
examples: The study found group status mediated the ethnic differences in academic anxiety for African-American, Chinese, and Dominican children but not Russians
key_sources: Gillen-O’Neel, C., Ruble, D. N., & Fuligni, A. J. (2011). Ethnic Stigma, Academic Anxiety, and Intrinsic Motivation in Middle Childhood. Child Development. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-8624.2011.01621.x

article_title: Parent praise to toddlers predicts fourth grade academic achievement via children’s incremental mindsets.
citation: Gunderson, E. A., Sorhagen, N. S., Gripshover, S. J., Dweck, C. S., Goldin-Meadow, S., & Levine, S. C. (2018). Parent Praise to Toddlers Predicts Fourth Grade Academic Achievement via Children's Incremental Mindsets. Developmental Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/dev0000444
title: Incremental versus fixed motivational frameworks as a developmental pathway from praise to achievement
description: The article organizes its findings around motivational frameworks: coherent systems of beliefs, attributions, and attitudes toward challenge that follow from children's mindsets about intelligence. Children with an incremental mindset "tend to focus on learning, believe in the efficacy of effort" and show resilience, whereas a fixed mindset leads children to avoid challenges that might reveal low ability. The framework serves as the hypothesized mediator between early process praise and later achievement, and is measured as a composite of trait beliefs, learning goals, and attributions.
requirements: Assessment requires children old enough to report beliefs about trait stability, learning goals, and attributions (here ages 7–8)
constraints: Framework effects are expected mainly when students face challenge or failure; less impact under low challenge
target_learning_goals: academic achievement in mathematics and reading comprehension
adaptive beliefs about intelligence and effort
examples: The study measured frameworks at ages 7–8 with a composite (α = .70) spanning intelligence and sociomoral trait beliefs, learning goals, and attributions
key_sources: Gunderson, E. A., Sorhagen, N. S., Gripshover, S. J., Dweck, C. S., Goldin-Meadow, S., & Levine, S. C. (2018). Parent Praise to Toddlers Predicts Fourth Grade Academic Achievement via Children's Incremental Mindsets. Developmental Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/dev0000444

article_title: Domain-general mediators of the relation between kindergarten number sense and first-grade mathematics achievement
citation: Hassinger-Das, B., Jordan, N. C., Glutting, J., Irwin, C., & Dyson, N. (2013). Domain General Mediators of the Relation between Kindergarten Number Sense and First-Grade Mathematics Achievement. Journal of Experimental Child Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jecp.2013.09.008
title: Interventions for kindergartners with low number sense should target executive functioning and attention problems in addition to number skills instruction
description: The article recommends that early mathematics interventions for children with low number sense address domain-general skills alongside number competencies. It states: "we provide empirical support for the development of interventions that target these skills, either through specific executive functioning interventions (e.g., Diamond & Lee, 2011) or interventions incorporated into components of mathematics instruction". The recommendation rests on the study's regression and mediation findings.
requirements: Children identified as having low number sense in kindergarten (e.g., screening with a number sense measure such as the NSB)
constraints: The evidence base is limited to high-risk children showing low number sense performance in kindergarten; causal relationships among executive functioning, attention problems, and mathematics outcomes remain to be tested
target_learners: kindergartners with low initial number sense at risk for mathematics difficulties
target_learning_goals: early number sense and first-grade mathematics achievement (calculation and applied problems)
examples: The authors cite their earlier randomized small-group number sense intervention for kindergartners not progressing in mathematics, which produced lasting improvements with moderate to large effect sizes, as context for extending intervention targets to executive functioning and attention.
key_sources: Hassinger-Das, B., Jordan, N. C., Glutting, J., Irwin, C., & Dyson, N. (2013). Domain General Mediators of the Relation between Kindergarten Number Sense and First-Grade Mathematics Achievement. Journal of Experimental Child Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jecp.2013.09.008

article_title: Reporting and Interpreting Working Memory Performance in n-back Tasks
citation: Meule A (2017). Reporting and Interpreting Working Memory Performance in n-back Tasks. Front. Psychol. 8:352. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2017.00352
title: Report and interpret reaction times and accuracy separately, choosing the measure with more meaningful variability
description: The article argues that reaction times and accuracy in n-back tasks "should not be interpreted interchangeably," because studies reaching similar conclusions from different dependent variables may not be comparable. Researchers should interpret the measure showing meaningful variation for the task at hand, as Hur et al. did by focusing on reaction times in a perception task and accuracy in a working memory task.
requirements: Researchers must report which dependent variable conclusions rest on and consider ceiling effects and variability in each measure.
constraints: The recommendation concerns n-back task performance indices specifically.
target_learners: researchers using n-back tasks to assess working memory
target_learning_goals: accurate measurement and interpretation of working memory performance
examples: Hur et al. focused on reaction times in a 0-back perception task where accuracy showed a ceiling effect, and on accuracy in a 2-back working memory task.
key_sources: Meule A (2017). Reporting and Interpreting Working Memory Performance in n-back Tasks. Front. Psychol. 8:352. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2017.00352

article_title: The increasing role of metacognitive skills in math: a cross-sectional study from a developmental perspective
citation: Van der Stel, M., Veenman, M. V. J., Deelen, K., & Haenen, J. (2010). The increasing role of metacognitive skills in math: a cross-sectional study from a developmental perspective. ZDM Mathematics Education, 42, 219–229. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11858-009-0224-2
title: Three models of the relation between intellectual ability and metacognitive skillfulness as predictors of learning performance
description: The article describes three mutually exclusive models, attributed to Veenman and colleagues, concerning how intellectual ability and metacognitive skillfulness relate as predictors of learning performance. The intelligence model "regards metacognitive skillfulness as an integral part of intellectual ability", so metacognition has no predictive value independent of intelligence; the independency model treats the two as entirely independent predictors; and the mixed model holds that the two are correlated to a certain extent while metacognition keeps its own unique contribution on top of intellectual ability. The study's results support the mixed model for metacognitive quality.
requirements: Assessment of both intellectual ability and metacognitive skillfulness together with learning performance in the same participants
constraints: The article notes many prior studies are hard to compare due to differences in assessment method (thinking-aloud vs. questionnaires), participants, tasks and domains
key_sources: Van der Stel, M., Veenman, M. V. J., Deelen, K., & Haenen, J. (2010). The increasing role of metacognitive skills in math: a cross-sectional study from a developmental perspective. ZDM Mathematics Education, 42, 219–229. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11858-009-0224-2

article_title: Literacy, Cognitive Function, and Health: Results of the LitCog Study
citation: Wolf, M.S., Curtis, L.M., Wilson, E.A.H., et al. (2012). Literacy, Cognitive Function, and Health: Results of the LitCog Study. J GEN INTERN MED. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11606-012-2079-4
title: Interventions should respond to all cognitive demands patients face in managing health, beyond reading and numeracy
description: The article recommends that future health interventions look beyond reading and numeracy skills and address the full range of cognitive abilities patients rely on to manage their health. It states: "Future interventions should respond to all of the cognitive demands patients face in managing health, beyond reading and numeracy." This follows from the finding that cognitive abilities substantially account for the health literacy–task performance association.
requirements: Interventions must be designed around the fluid and crystallized cognitive demands of self-care tasks, not only literacy and numeracy content.
constraints: Evidence base is cross-sectional and limited to English-speaking older adults ages 55 to 74.
target_learners: older adults (ages 55 to 74) managing their own health
target_learning_goals: capacity to engage in self-care and achieve desirable health outcomes
examples: The LitCog study assessed performance on healthcare tasks including comprehending print information, recalling spoken and multimedia information, dosing and organizing medication, and healthcare problem-solving.
key_sources: Wolf, M.S., Curtis, L.M., Wilson, E.A.H., et al. (2012). Literacy, Cognitive Function, and Health: Results of the LitCog Study. J GEN INTERN MED. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11606-012-2079-4

article_title: Creative Thinking in Adolescents with Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD)
citation: Abraham, Anna; Windmann, Sabine; Siefen, Rainer; Daum, Irene; Güntürkün, Onur. (2006). Creative thinking in adolescents with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). Child Neuropsychology, 12(2), 111-123. https://doi.org/10.1080/09297040500320691
title: Inhibitory control mechanisms and contextual modulation of creative cognition account for ADHD creativity findings
description: The article offers an explanatory account in which creative cognition is shaped by inhibitory control mechanisms and by the contextual modulation of information processing. Within this account, a widened attentional focus associated with ADHD can help overcome the constraining influence of examples, while weaker inhibitory control can impair tasks requiring a functional invention. The authors use it to interpret the selective advantages and disadvantages their ADHD group showed across creativity measures.
requirements: Applicable to interpreting creativity task performance in populations differing in attentional focus and inhibitory control.
constraints: The article presents this as an interpretation of its findings, not as a directly tested mechanism.
key_sources: Abraham, Anna; Windmann, Sabine; Siefen, Rainer; Daum, Irene; Güntürkün, Onur. (2006). Creative thinking in adolescents with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). Child Neuropsychology, 12(2), 111-123. https://doi.org/10.1080/09297040500320691

article_title: The Relationship between Executive Functions, Working Memory, and Intelligence in Kindergarten Children
citation: Ger Ebru, Roebers Claudia M. (2023). The Relationship between Executive Functions, Working Memory, and Intelligence in Kindergarten Children. Journal of Intelligence. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC10143737/
title: Inhibition rather than monitoring and cognitive control underlies EF–WM–intelligence associations at kindergarten age
description: The article proposes that at kindergarten age, the shared variance between executive functions, working memory, and intelligence is carried primarily by inhibition rather than by metacognitive monitoring and cognitive control (indexed by post-error slowing). The authors conclude: "EF, WM, and intelligence might be linked through inhibition rather than monitoring and cognitive control, at least at kindergarten ages." This framework draws on Miyake et al.'s three-component model of EF and the developmental observation that inhibition is the earliest-developing EF component.
requirements: Assessment of EF components with separate tasks (inhibition, shifting, WM) plus a fluid intelligence measure, as the framework depends on distinguishing component-specific contributions.
constraints: The framework applies to kindergarten ages (5.5–7.5 years); monitoring and cognitive control may explain shared variance only once they reach a substantial level of development, potentially at school age.
target_learning_goals: Understanding cognitive development of executive functions, working memory, and intelligence
examples: The study operationalized monitoring and cognitive control via post-error slowing in the Hearts and Flowers task and found it unrelated to intelligence or WM, while inhibition accuracy showed the expected associations.
key_sources: Ger Ebru, Roebers Claudia M. (2023). The Relationship between Executive Functions, Working Memory, and Intelligence in Kindergarten Children. Journal of Intelligence. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC10143737/

article_title: Children’s scientific curiosity: In search of an operational definition of an elusive concept
citation: Jirout, J. & Klahr, D. (2011). Children's scientific curiosity: In search of an operational definition of an elusive concept. Developmental Review (in press, draft). https://www.sciencedirect.com/journal/developmental-review
title: Loewenstein's information-gap theory of curiosity as a framework for measuring children's exploratory curiosity
description: The information-gap theory holds that curiosity arises from feelings of deprivation that are aversive and motivate information-seeking to reduce them. The review adopts it as the conceptual framework for evaluating procedures for measuring children's exploratory curiosity, defining curiosity as "the threshold of desired uncertainty in the environment that leads to exploratory behavior." The authors extend it to young children as a stable uncertainty preference.
requirements: Curiosity is operationalized through behavioral measures of exploration under varying uncertainty, since the theory concerns deprivation-motivated information seeking
constraints: The theory does not consider non-aversive information-seeking, such as externally rewarded or general-interest seeking, to be curiosity
examples: The authors adapted a preference-for-the-unknown task into a new measure of children's exploratory preference under different levels of uncertainty
key_sources: Jirout, J. & Klahr, D. (2011). Children's scientific curiosity: In search of an operational definition of an elusive concept. Developmental Review (in press, draft). https://www.sciencedirect.com/journal/developmental-review

article_title: Affect Recognition in Adults With ADHD
citation: Miller, M., Hanford, R. B., Fassbender, C., Duke, M., & Schweitzer, J. B. (2011). Affect Recognition in Adults with Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder. Journal of Attention Disorders. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3950374/
title: Inattention-specific account of affect recognition deficits in adult ADHD
description: The article advances an explanatory account in which affect recognition difficulties in adult ADHD are tied specifically to inattentive symptoms rather than to hyperactive-impulsive symptoms or to ADHD diagnosis as a category. The authors state that "the ANOVA and regression results link inattentive symptoms with affect decoding deficits and provide some evidence of linking ADHD with deficits in fearful affect recognition specifically." They propose that adults with more severe inattentive symptoms may fail to attend to social cues, have less social interaction experience, and be more passive in social situations, producing decoding errors. The account also entertains whether deficits reflect an attention problem rather than impaired emotional processing per se.
requirements: Replication in larger, more heterogeneous samples to confirm the inattention-specific pattern
constraints: The authors state the finding is in need of replication and that the study sample was small and highly intelligent, limiting generalizability
target_learning_goals: accurate interpretation of nonverbal social and emotional cues in social interactions
examples: The authors suggest individuals with more severe inattentive symptoms are not attending properly to take in appropriate social cues when in social situations
key_sources: Miller, M., Hanford, R. B., Fassbender, C., Duke, M., & Schweitzer, J. B. (2011). Affect Recognition in Adults with Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder. Journal of Attention Disorders. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3950374/

article_title: Cognitive flexibility-related prefrontal activation in preschoolers: A biological approach to temperamental effortful control
citation: Quiñones-Camacho Laura E., Fishburn Frank A., Camacho M. Catalina, Wakschlag Lauren S., Perlman Susan B. (2019). Cognitive flexibility-related prefrontal activation in preschoolers: A biological approach to temperamental effortful control. Developmental Cognitive Neuroscience. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC6969345/
title: Integrative model of temperament, behavior, and brain activation for cognitive flexibility
description: The article tests and supports an integrative individual-differences model in which "individual differences in behavioral responses are supported by differential recruitment of key neural regions and networks." Specifically, parent-reported temperamental effortful control (a latent factor of attentional focusing, inhibitory control, perceptual sensitivity, and low intensity pleasure) is linked to both cognitive flexibility task behavior and DLPFC activation measured with fNIRS during a child-friendly Stroop task in preschoolers. The model proposes that children with greater effortful control recruit the DLPFC more efficiently, requiring less activation for similar performance.
requirements: Parent-report measure of temperamental effortful control (CBQ short form)
A cognitive flexibility task appropriate for the age group
Neuroimaging capable of measuring prefrontal activation in young children
constraints: Cross-sectional design; no longitudinal data, limiting interpretation of how associations change across early childhood
Task also likely required inhibitory control and working memory, complicating dimension-specific interpretation
Only one form of cognitive flexibility was measured; other aspects might show different patterns
Focused on PFC only; the model could apply to other neural networks
target_learning_goals: understanding individual differences in cognitive flexibility and effortful control
examples: SEM analysis in 123 preschoolers linked parent-reported effortful control to both Stroop accuracy and DLPFC activation during the Pet Store Stroop task
key_sources: Quiñones-Camacho Laura E., Fishburn Frank A., Camacho M. Catalina, Wakschlag Lauren S., Perlman Susan B. (2019). Cognitive flexibility-related prefrontal activation in preschoolers: A biological approach to temperamental effortful control. Developmental Cognitive Neuroscience. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC6969345/

article_title: Being right is its own reward: Load and performance related ventral striatum activation to correct responses during a working memory task in youth
citation: Satterthwaite Theodore D. M.D., M.A.; Ruparel Kosha M.S.; Loughead James Ph.D; Elliott Mark A. Ph.D.; Gerraty Raphael T. B.A.; Calkins Monica E. Ph.D.; Hakonarson Hakon M.D. Ph.D.; Gur Ruben C. Ph.D.; Gur Raquel E. M.D., Ph.D.; Wolf Daniel H. M.D., Ph.D. (2012). Being Right Is Its Own Reward: Load and Performance Related Ventral Striatum Activation to Correct Responses During a Working Memory Task in Youth. Neuroimage. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3358426/
title: Intrinsic reinforcement signals in the ventral striatum during standard cognitive tasks
description: The article proposes that ventral striatum responses to correct responses during ordinary cognitive tasks, without external feedback or rewards, represent "intrinsic reinforcement signals". The account draws on the reward prediction error framework: correct responses are less expected at higher task difficulty, so they provoke larger reinforcement responses, analogous to unexpected rewards. The authors suggest this provides "a plausible neural correlate for the prior observation and common experience that accurate performance is reinforcing in proportion to the difficulty of the task".
requirements: A cognitive task that parametrically varies difficulty, such as the n-back task, so that correct responses vary in how expected they are
constraints: The design does not directly link VS response to subject-level motivation; the authors note future studies should vary reward contingencies and obtain subjective measures of response confidence, reward sensitivity, and intrinsic motivation
Robust VS activation to correct responses without feedback may only occur in tasks more difficult than those commonly used in many fMRI studies
target_learning_goals: intrinsic motivation during cognitive task performance
examples: Participants performed 0-back, 1-back, and 2-back conditions with fractal stimuli and received no performance feedback at any point

article_title: Interventions Shown to Aid Executive Function Development in Children 4 to 12 Years Old
citation: Diamond Adele, Lee Kathleen. (2011). Interventions shown to Aid Executive Function Development in Children 4–12 Years Old. Science. https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1204529
title: Children with initially poorest EFs gain the most from EF interventions, making early EF training a candidate for reducing achievement gaps
description: The review states that lower-income, lower working-memory span, and ADHD children, and in one study boys, generally show the most EF improvement from any program. Because EFs predict later academic performance, early EF training is an excellent candidate for leveling the playing field and reducing the achievement gap between more- and less-advantaged children.
requirements: Programs must be accessible early enough to get children on a positive trajectory; public school curricula hold the greatest promise for accessibility to all
constraints: Since computer training and after-school activities cost money, they are not possible for all families
target_learners: children 4–12 years old, especially lower-income children and those with initially poor EFs
target_learning_goals: executive functions supporting school readiness and academic achievement
examples: Children with initially poor EFs after mindfulness training improved overall and in shifting and monitoring, bringing their scores up to average
key_sources: Diamond Adele, Lee Kathleen. (2011). Interventions shown to Aid Executive Function Development in Children 4–12 Years Old. Science. https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1204529

article_title: Supporting Student Self-Regulated Learning in Problem- and Project-Based Learning
citation: Mary C. English, Anastasia Kitsantas. (2013). Supporting Self-Regulated Learning in Problem- and Project-Based Learning. Interdisciplinary Journal of Problem-based Learning. https://doi.org/10.7771/1541-5015.1339
title: Design PBL learning environments and teaching practices with intention to support students' self-regulated learning
description: Because SRL processes do not arise spontaneously for many students, the article argues that PBL environments and teaching practices "must be designed with intention to support students' self-regulated learning (SRL)." The principle directs educators to plan environment features and teaching moves deliberately around SRL, rather than assuming responsibility for learning will emerge on its own from the PBL format.
requirements: Educators must deliberately plan learning environment features and teaching practices rather than relying on the PBL format alone
target_learners: students in problem- or project-based learning settings
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning and student responsibility for learning
examples: The paper describes specific learning environment features and teaching practices shown to foster student responsibility for learning in each phase of PBL.
key_sources: Mary C. English, Anastasia Kitsantas. (2013). Supporting Self-Regulated Learning in Problem- and Project-Based Learning. Interdisciplinary Journal of Problem-based Learning. https://doi.org/10.7771/1541-5015.1339

article_title: Math Circles: A Tool for Promoting Engagement Among Middle School Minority Males
citation: Eugene Kennedy & Lawrence Smolinsky (2016). Math Circles: A Tool for Promoting Engagement among Middle School Minority Males. Eurasia Journal of Mathematics, Science & Technology Education, 12(4), 717-732. https://doi.org/10.12973/eurasia.2016.1223a
title: Six major design components of an inclusive math circle for low-income minority middle school students
description: The authors concluded the circle's effectiveness rested on a set of design components conceptualized as part of an enculturation process into the culture of mathematics: control of the physical environment (meeting in the mathematics department lounge), the circle leader being a professional mathematician, labels and normative expectations from selection, creation of a safe mathematical community, natural peer groupings, games and competition, and conveying the value of mathematics. They state: "We concluded that there were 6 major components of the design that were most effective." The components were identified interpretively from the case, not experimentally manipulated.
requirements: A professional mathematician as circle leader and access to a university mathematics department space
constraints: The article states only one circle was examined and none of the factors considered impactful were systematically manipulated
target_learning_goals: enculturation into the community of mathematics
examples: Students met weekly for 90 minutes over 9 months in the mathematics department lounge, played Atari Go with mini-tournaments, and heard discussions of the value of mathematics and the heroes of mathematics
key_sources: Eugene Kennedy & Lawrence Smolinsky (2016). Math Circles: A Tool for Promoting Engagement among Middle School Minority Males. Eurasia Journal of Mathematics, Science & Technology Education, 12(4), 717-732. https://doi.org/10.12973/eurasia.2016.1223a

article_title: Fostering Critical Thinking Skills in Preschool Education: Designing, Implementing and Assessing a Multiliteracies-Oriented Program Based on Intercultural Tales
citation: Papadopoulos, I., & Bisiri, E. (2020). Fostering Critical Thinking Skills in Preschool Education: Designing, Implementing and Assessing a Multiliteracies-Oriented Program Based on Intercultural Tales. Multilingual Academic Journal of Education and Social Sciences, 8(1), 87–105. https://doi.org/10.46886/MAJESS/v8-i1/7263
title: Intercultural folk-tale multiliteracies program for preschool critical thinking
description: A seven-month pedagogical program implemented in a preschool in Larissa, Central Greece, during the school year 2018-2019 with 25 five-year-old children (48% boys, 52% girls). A mini syllabus was "centered around intercultural folk-tales, incorporating multiple creative activities that fostered a more critical stance and behavior of the children." Seven folk-tales from Greece, Albania, Cyprus, Serbia, Bulgaria, Romania, North Macedonia and Croatia each formed a thematic unit lasting 2 to 3 weeks, with expected outcomes in critical thinking, social skills and multicultural sensitivity.
requirements: Folk-tales unfamiliar to the children were deliberately chosen, on the researchers' view that children develop more critical tendencies when coming into contact with something not known to them
constraints: Applied to a single class of 25 Greek-origin preschoolers in one school; evaluation relied on qualitative journal and portfolio data
examples: Tasks included predicting story content from pictures, categorizing heroes and villains with justification, sequencing story scenes, and retelling stories with drawings
key_sources: Papadopoulos, I., & Bisiri, E. (2020). Fostering Critical Thinking Skills in Preschool Education: Designing, Implementing and Assessing a Multiliteracies-Oriented Program Based on Intercultural Tales. Multilingual Academic Journal of Education and Social Sciences, 8(1), 87–105. https://doi.org/10.46886/MAJESS/v8-i1/7263

article_title: Sixth-grade students’ reasoning on the order relation of integers as influenced by prior experience: an inferentialist analysis
citation: Maike Schindler, Stephan Hußmann, Per Nilsson, Arthur Bakker. (2017). Sixth-grade students' reasoning on the order relation of integers as influenced by prior experience: an inferentialist analysis. Math Ed Res J 29:471–492. https://doi.org/10.1007/s13394-017-0202-x
title: Inferentialist epistemology for analyzing students' mathematical reasoning
description: The article develops an epistemological framework based on Brandom's inferentialism for studying students' reasoning on the order relation of integers. It treats reasoning as social, situated in the 'game of giving and asking for reasons' (GoGAR), implicitly normative, and holistic, with concepts interconnected in students' claims. It asks for the inferences students draw from out-of-school life, the mathematics classroom, contexts, and external representations such as the number line, prioritizing the reasoning itself over internal mental models.
requirements: Empirical settings must explicitly encourage students to make their reasons, inferences, and the origins of their inferences explicit
constraints: The framework does not aim to isolate individual knowledge or abstract mental models from students' utterances
target_learning_goals: reasoning on the order relation of integers
examples: Semi-structured, task-oriented clinical interviews in which the interviewer asked 'Why's that?' and 'Where do you know this from?' before and after a lesson series
key_sources: Maike Schindler, Stephan Hußmann, Per Nilsson, Arthur Bakker. (2017). Sixth-grade students' reasoning on the order relation of integers as influenced by prior experience: an inferentialist analysis. Math Ed Res J 29:471–492. https://doi.org/10.1007/s13394-017-0202-x

article_title: Enriching Mathematics Education with Visual Arts: Effects on Elementary School Students’ Ability in Geometry and Visual Arts
citation: Eveline M. Schoevers & Paul P. M. Leseman & Evelyn H. Kroesbergen. (2019). Enriching Mathematics Education with Visual Arts: Effects on Elementary School Students' Ability in Geometry and Visual Arts. International Journal of Science and Mathematics Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10763-019-10018-z
title: Use integrated visual arts and geometry lessons instead of regular geometry lessons to teach the geometry curriculum and visual arts perception
description: The article recommends that teachers replace regular textbook geometry lessons with the integrated MACE lesson series, because students reached the same level of geometrical understanding through open, creative lessons while additionally improving in perceiving geometrical aspects of visual artworks. As the authors state, "teachers could use the integrated MACE lesson series instead of regular geometry lessons, in order to teach the geometry curriculum and visual arts perception", which may save time for teachers under curriculum time pressure.
requirements: Teachers use the MACE lesson series and its pedagogy (artwork discussion, open activities, reflection, peer communication, facilitator role)
constraints: The advantage over regular lessons held for visual arts perception and daily geometrical words, not for geometrical understanding, creativity, or academic vocabulary; the authors note more research is needed, e.g. applying the approach across more mathematics lessons
examples: In the quasi-experiment, MACE students received nine 60-90 minute integrated lessons while comparison students received seven 30-40 minute textbook-based geometry lessons of the same geometrical content
key_sources: Eveline M. Schoevers & Paul P. M. Leseman & Evelyn H. Kroesbergen. (2019). Enriching Mathematics Education with Visual Arts: Effects on Elementary School Students' Ability in Geometry and Visual Arts.
