International Journal of Science and Mathematics Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10763-019-10018-z

article_title: Planning prompts increase and forecast course completion in massive open online courses
citation: Yeomans, Michael and Reich, Justin. 2017. "Planning Prompts Increase and Forecast Course Completion in Massive Open Online Courses." Association for Computing Machinery (ACM). https://doi.org/10.1145/3027385.3027416
title: The intention-action gap in MOOC learning and plan-making as a cheap, effective nudge
description: The article frames MOOC non-completion as an instance of the intention-action gap: "Among all of the learners in Massive Open Online Courses (MOOCs) who intend to complete a course, the majority fail to do so." Drawing on research in similar goal-pursuit domains, it positions plan-making as "a cheap and effective nudge to encourage follow-through", operationalized as open-ended planning prompts delivered at the beginning of a course. The framework treats prompts as helping learners adopt productive frames of mind at the outset of a learning goal, which both encourages and forecasts success.
requirements: Learners must already intend to complete the course; the gap the framework addresses exists among intenders, since the majority of intending learners fail to complete.
target_learners: MOOC learners who intend to complete a course
target_learning_goals: Course completion and follow-through on learning intentions
examples: In three HarvardX courses, some students received open-ended planning prompts at the beginning of a course, raising completion by 29% and certificate payment by 40%.
key_sources: Yeomans, Michael and Reich, Justin. 2017. "Planning Prompts Increase and Forecast Course Completion in Massive Open Online Courses." Association for Computing Machinery (ACM). https://doi.org/10.1145/3027385.3027416

article_title: Learning Words from Context
citation: Nagy, William E.; Herman, Patricia A.; Anderson, Richard C.; Pearson, P. David. (1984). Learning Words from Context. Center for the Study of Reading, Technical Report No. 319, University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED248470
title: Incremental word learning: word meanings are acquired in small partial increments across repeated encounters, requiring measures sensitive to partial knowledge
description: The article's explanatory framework holds that "incidental learning from context proceeds in terms of small increments, so that any one encounter with a word in text will be likely to produce only a partial increase in knowledge of that word." A single encounter can still yield substantial, incomplete knowledge (fast mapping), while full mastery extends over years of repeated encounters. The framework explains why prior studies failed to detect context learning: they tested for full word knowledge, which underestimates incremental gains. The study therefore used interviews and multiple-choice items designed to tap partial knowledge at three levels of difficulty.
requirements: Assessment measures must be sensitive to partial word knowledge rather than requiring full, adult-like knowledge of meanings for a correct answer
constraints: Complete learning of a word's meaning is a gradual process, probably extending over years of repeated encounters
target_learners: middle-grade (junior high) students of average and above-average reading ability
target_learning_goals: vocabulary acquisition — partial and full knowledge of word meanings from reading
examples: The study scored interviews on a four-point scale from no correct knowledge to a totally correct answer, and built multiple-choice items at three levels of distractor similarity, to detect small increments of word knowledge
key_sources: Nagy, William E.; Herman, Patricia A.; Anderson, Richard C.; Pearson, P. David. (1984). Learning Words from Context. Center for the Study of Reading, Technical Report No. 319, University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED248470

article_title: Conceptualizing the intersubjective group
citation: Gerry Stahl. (2015). Conceptualizing the intersubjective group. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn 10:209–217. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-015-9220-4
title: Intersubjectivity as the defining characteristic of CSCL, built and repaired through interaction
description: The article defines intersubjectivity as shared understanding achieved not by individuals holding similar views but by "participating productively in a joint meaning-making discourse within a communal world." A group has intersubjectivity when members "interact well enough to pursue the group's aims." It must be "built up gradually through interaction and repaired frequently." CSCL pedagogies promote it and CSCL technologies support it through communication media and scaffolds for meaning making.
requirements: Groups must interact over time so shared understanding can be built up and repaired through discourse
target_learners: collaborative learning groups in CSCL settings
target_learning_goals: joint meaning making and shared understanding
key_sources: Gerry Stahl. (2015). Conceptualizing the intersubjective group. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn 10:209–217. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-015-9220-4

article_title: Cognizing mediating: Unpacking the entanglement of artifacts with collective minds
citation: Gerry Stahl. (2012). Cognizing mediating: Unpacking the entanglement of artifacts with collective minds. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning 7:187–191. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-012-9148-x
title: Instrumental genesis as the theory of artifact-agent connection best suited to CSCL's small-group level
description: Instrumental genesis, developed in France by Pierre Rabardel and colleagues, describes how the agent-artifact connection evolves over time through usage and re-design. The editorial argues it can more naturally be applied to the small-group collective level central to CSCL than affordances theory (individual-focused) or structuration (societal-level), introducing it to the CSCL community at methodological, technological, and theoretical levels.
requirements: Analysis of how groups enact features of computer-support systems through use
constraints: The editorial notes the theory's application so far rests on high-level descriptions of data rather than detailed empirical analysis
target_learners: small groups of students in CSCL settings
target_learning_goals: enacting and appropriating technological artifacts for collaborative learning
examples: The first article in the issue discusses how triads of students enacted a feature of an argumentation-support software system
key_sources: Gerry Stahl. (2012). Cognizing mediating: Unpacking the entanglement of artifacts with collective minds. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning 7:187–191. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-012-9148-x

article_title: Learning across levels
citation: Gerry Stahl. (2013). Learning across levels. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 8, 1–12. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-013-9169-0
title: Lifecycle of interactional resources: reification, sedimentation, institutionalization and personalization
description: The article describes a developmental trajectory for interactional resources. Through repetition in group discussion a term or object becomes a reified resource with ephemeral-emergent existence; continued usage yields a sedimented resource retaining meaning across group interactions; sedimented resources may be institutionalized by a larger community or personalized into individual understanding, corresponding to Vygotskian micro-genesis of internalization. The article notes these seminal processes' 'empirical investigation remains as a major challenge for future CSCL research.'
requirements: Repeated use within group discussion for a resource to take on settled significance
constraints: Vygotsky's personalization processes are described as lengthy, complex, non-transparent and little understood
target_learners: small-group and community learners in CSCL
target_learning_goals: shared meaning making and individual internalization of group practices
examples: Husserl's account of geometers' ideas becoming sedimented in geometry's cultural heritage, and Livingston's contrast of discovering versus presenting a proof
key_sources: Gerry Stahl. (2013). Learning across levels. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 8, 1–12. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-013-9169-0

article_title: Transactive discourse in CSCL
citation: Gerry Stahl. (2013). Transactive discourse in CSCL. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning 8:145–147. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-013-9171-6
title: Design shared-computer collaboration with different but interdependent roles to foster transactive building
description: The editorial reports that in keeping with transactivity theory, kindergarten triads were given "different but interdependent roles or tasks" on a single computer with three mice and distinct screen areas. Interacting on one computer is argued to increase shared attention and hence the tendency to build transactively, developing social skills while pursuing a common goal.
requirements: A teacher must mediate when learners are inexperienced, analogous to scripted prompts for college students
constraints: Reported for young kindergarten children on a single shared computer; effectiveness attributed to combining individual roles with group interaction
target_learning_goals: social skills and collaborative achievement of a common goal
examples: Triads worked on one computer with three mice and three distinct screen areas, engaging in group processes toward a common goal
key_sources: Gerry Stahl. (2013). Transactive discourse in CSCL. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning 8:145–147. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-013-9171-6

article_title: Different leaders: Emergent organizational and intellectual leadership in children’s collaborative learning groups
citation: E. M. Mercier, S. E. Higgins, Laura da Costa. (2014). Different leaders: Emergent organizational and intellectual leadership in children's collaborative learning groups. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-014-9201-z
title: Two-type taxonomy of emergent leadership: intellectual and organizational leadership moves
description: The article adapts the Li et al. (2007) coding scheme to distinguish two types of emergent leadership in collaborative groups. Intellectual leadership comprises Topic Control and Idea Management and Development, moves that address "the intellectual aspects of the activity, such as idea management and development." Organizational leadership comprises Planning and Organizing, Turn Management and Acknowledgment, moves that support "the group's interaction process, helping monitor and influence turn taking and participation." Leadership is defined as emerging only when leadership bids are accepted by the group; ignored bids are failed bids, and the bid-maker cannot be defined as a leader.
requirements: Leadership moves must be accepted by other group members to count as leadership; a bid ignored by the group is a failed bid and does not make the bidder a leader.
constraints: The taxonomy was developed and applied with children in year six collaborative mystery tasks in England; the article notes the role of group spokesperson appears different from the leadership described and was beyond its scope.
target_learners: primary school students (year six, mean age about 10.6 years)
target_learning_goals: participating effectively in collaborative learning groups
managing group participation and intellectual progress during collaborative tasks
examples: In the opening vignette, Amy organized the group and managed turn-taking while Georgia pushed the ideas forward intellectually, illustrating the two leadership types in one group.
key_sources: E. M. Mercier, S. E. Higgins, Laura da Costa. (2014). Different leaders: Emergent organizational and intellectual leadership in children's collaborative learning groups. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-014-9201-z

article_title: Experiences, appearances, and interprofessional training: The instructional use of video in post-simulation debriefings
citation: Elin Johansson, Oskar Lindwall, Hans Rystedt. (2017). Experiences, appearances, and interprofessional training: The instructional use of video in post-simulation debriefings. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-017-9252-z
title: Guide video-supported reflection with instructional questions that focus attention, but expect appearance-experience contrasts to require negotiation
description: The article argues video use requires guidance: participants given insufficient pointers "may find it hard to concentrate on important, substantive aspects". In the analyzed debriefings, facilitators' instructional questions focused attention on intended aspects and projected positive assessments. However, students' prior experiences remain a background against which appearances are interpreted, and disagreement about how visible performances should be assessed persists even with agreement on what is shown.
requirements: Facilitator questions designed in terms of what students see
Framing statements establishing the pedagogical rationale for the clip
constraints: Video invitations may be rejected: a student countered a positive reading by claiming the clip does not show everything
Reflection is not done by isolated individuals but through the instructional and collaborative organization of the debriefing
target_learners: health care students practising interprofessional teamwork
target_learning_goals: reconceptualising one's own collaborative performance; distinguishing characteristics of well-functioning teamwork
examples: Asking 'Do you see something that works well here?' after showing a clip, and asking students to return to previously reported feelings and contrast them with the video
key_sources: Elin Johansson, Oskar Lindwall, Hans Rystedt. (2017). Experiences, appearances, and interprofessional training: The instructional use of video in post-simulation debriefings. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-017-9252-z

article_title: Future direction for the CSCL field: Methodologies and eight controversies
citation: Ludvigsen, S., Cress, U., Law, N., Stahl, G., & Rosé, C. P. (2017). Future direction for the CSCL field: Methodologies and eight controversies. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 12, 337–341. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-017-9268-4
title: Interaction geography: an analytical approach connecting physical movement and talk in museum settings
description: Interaction geography is an analytical approach introduced by Shapiro, Hall, and Owens that connects "novel forms of analyses" to constitute "the key elements of the analytical approach." It extends interaction analysis by including physical movements: through movement analysis researchers "can explore how the syntax of space creates an 'interaction geography' from which visitors' gestures and activities can be analyzed."
requirements: Data on participants' movements and talk across forms of representation such as photographs, videos, descriptions, and online conversations.
constraints: The study is "the first step in exploring the use of interaction geography"; further studies "in a variety of settings would be necessary to explore the potential contribution."
target_learners: Museum visitors, including groups with diverse professional backgrounds
target_learning_goals: Meaning-making through movement, gestures, and talk across representations
examples: The study was performed in a cultural heritage museum with data collected from 22 groups, some of whose members were music professionals.
key_sources: Ludvigsen, S., Cress, U., Law, N., Stahl, G., & Rosé, C. P. (2017). Future direction for the CSCL field: Methodologies and eight controversies. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 12, 337–341. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-017-9268-4

article_title: Conceptualizing the designs of authentic computer-supported collaborative learning environments in schools
citation: Yotam Hod, Ornit Sagy. (2019). Conceptualizing the Designs of Authentic Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning Environments in Schools. http://link.springer.com/article/10.1007%2Fs11412-019-09300-7 https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-019-09300-7
title: Designers should make the intended culture explicit, with the teacher acting as a legitimate gatekeeper of values and practices
description: Because authentic designs involve a designer's vision of the authentic culture — a figured world — the review argues the intended culture "must be a vital part of any conceptualization." Without it, people may be misled into thinking authentic designs aim to duplicate professional practice; to the contrary, "in authentic designs there is a legitimate role for a teacher to be a gatekeeper of values and practices, as well as to create developmentally appropriate tasks."
requirements: The intended culture should be defined and communicated as part of any design for authenticity
constraints: The teacher need not be a member of the authentic culture; practitioners are sometimes bad teachers, and the review does not rank the two situations
target_learners: students in classrooms designed for authenticity
target_learning_goals: enculturation of intended (filtered, developmentally appropriate) versions of expert practices
examples: The review's three-culture framework and figured-worlds analysis instantiate this principle across the 28 cases
key_sources: Yotam Hod, Ornit Sagy. (2019). Conceptualizing the Designs of Authentic Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning Environments in Schools. http://link.springer.com/article/10.1007%2Fs11412-019-09300-7 https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-019-09300-7

article_title: Building community together: towards equitable CSCL practices and processes
citation: Carolyn P. Rosé & Sanna Järvelä. (2020). Building community together: towards equitable CSCL practices and processes. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-020-09329-z
title: Interactional Ethnography and dialogic intervisualizing as an analytical lens for multimodal collaborative conversation
description: The editorial describes Bridges et al.'s methodological lens, Interactional Ethnography (IE), as "a logic-of-inquiry that can be used to examine collaborative processes" as undergraduate students and their facilitator work with multimodal text. Its companion conceptualization, dialogic intervisualizing, is designed to capture "the interplay between the conversation, the broader collaborative problem solving processes, and the evolving artifacts produced during the interaction", drawing on Silverstein's concept of indexical order for how conceptual objects are decontextualized and recontextualized across modalities.
requirements: Extensive analysis of video data expanding on earlier sociocultural analyses
application in a facilitated collaborative setting such as Problem Based Learning
constraints: The editorial locates this lens specifically in a medical school Problem Based Learning context with undergraduate students and a facilitator
target_learning_goals: Multimodal inquiry and collaborative problem solving in problem-based learning
examples: The editorial situates IE as expanding on earlier sociocultural analyses of video data (Bezemer 2017; Danish 2018; Kershner et al. 2010; Koschmann 1999; Steier et al. 2019) and draws on Silverstein's (2003) indexical order for recontextualizing conceptual objects between modalities.
key_sources: Carolyn P. Rosé & Sanna Järvelä. (2020). Building community together: towards equitable CSCL practices and processes. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-020-09329-z

article_title: Integrating collaboration scripts, group awareness, and self-regulation in computer-supported collaborative learning
citation: Lenka Schnaubert · Freydis Vogel. (2022). Integrating collaboration scripts, group awareness, and self-regulation in computer-supported collaborative learning. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn (2022) 17:1–10. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-022-09367-9
title: Balance script-imposed self-regulation demands by integrating regulation activities into collaboration script scaffolds
description: The editorial draws a design principle from the special-issue studies: "the demands for self-regulation when learning with CSCL scripts can be balanced by integrating self-regulation activities in script scaffolds." Scripts can take over parts of regulatory processes, for example by distributing roles and assigning specific activities to each role, or explicitly scaffold regulation activities such as planning, execution and reflection support. This may then lead to better regulation during learning and eventually improved learning outcomes.
requirements: Careful choices when designing scripts; scripts must either take over parts of the regulatory processes (e.g., via role distribution) or explicitly scaffold regulation activities
constraints: Less structured CSCL scripts leaving learners degrees of freedom and adaptation possibilities demand more self-regulation skills from the learner
target_learners: collaborative learners in CSCL settings, from elementary school to university
target_learning_goals: effective regulation of collaborative learning and improved collaborative learning outcomes
examples: Zimmerman and Land's script distributed roles and assigned activities to each role; Kielstra et al.'s script explicitly scaffolded regulation activities for planning, execution and reflection
key_sources: Lenka Schnaubert · Freydis Vogel. (2022). Integrating collaboration scripts, group awareness, and self-regulation in computer-supported collaborative learning. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn (2022) 17:1–10. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-022-09367-9

article_title: Highlighting tools and technologies for collaborative learning
citation: Carolyn P. Rosé, Nancy Law, Ulrike Cress, Sten Ludvigsen. (2019). Highlighting tools and technologies for collaborative learning. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. (2019) 14:1–6. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-019-09297-z
title: Instrumental Genesis as a framework for how collaborators enact design practices
description: Instrumental Genesis (IG), grounded in Activity Theory, models the joint evolution of artifacts with their uses within specific collaborative environments, treating technology in collaboration as a first-class contribution. A central concept is how artifacts mediate joint activity, with the editorial highlighting four forms of mediation: Epistemic, Pragmatic, Reflexive, and Inter-personal. The framework was applied to what is termed the preparation phase in CSCL, involving students, instructors, and design researchers.
requirements: Analysis attends to how artifacts mediate joint activity within specific collaborative environments
constraints: The article specifically focuses on the preparation phase in CSCL
target_learning_goals: collaborative design practices in design studios
examples: Carvalho, Martinez-Maldonado, and Goodyear's two in-depth qualitative studies of teams engaged in course redesign activities
key_sources: Carolyn P. Rosé, Nancy Law, Ulrike Cress, Sten Ludvigsen. (2019). Highlighting tools and technologies for collaborative learning. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. (2019) 14:1–6. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-019-09297-z

article_title: Accomplishing collaboration at scale: How professionals jointly frame problems on Stack Overflow
citation: Alena Seredko. (2025). Accomplishing collaboration at scale: How professionals jointly frame problems on Stack Overflow. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-025-09451-w
title: Intelligibility as practical accomplishment via shared methods in mass collaboration
description: Adopting a practice-based, ethnomethodological perspective, the article treats collaboration as continuously accomplished in participants' 'doings and sayings'. Shared understanding is framed as "intelligibility, i.e., a practical accomplishment through which actions and utterances are produced to be recognized and understood within interaction so that work can go on". The methods sustaining it are "taken-for-granted interactional techniques that produce and sustain intelligibility in joint activities", observed in the sequential organization of platform traces. Shared goals are products of continuous interaction rather than pre-existing.
requirements: Sequential trace data in which each turn's uptake by participants is observable, so repeated patterns across threads can be inferred as collectively relied-upon methods
constraints: The article notes intelligibility remains underexplored on large-scale platforms; group boundaries are difficult or impossible to specify under fluid participation
target_learning_goals: sustaining mutual intelligibility in asynchronous joint work
examples: Thread analyses trace request–response sequences, compliance, negotiation, repair and edit reporting as methods of intelligibility
key_sources: Alena Seredko. (2025). Accomplishing collaboration at scale: How professionals jointly frame problems on Stack Overflow. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-025-09451-w

article_title: Signaling cues and focused prompts for professional vision support: The interplay of instructional design and situational interest in preservice teachers’ video analysis
citation: Meg Farrell, Monika Martin, Ricardo Böheim, Alexander Renkl, Werner Rieß, Karen D. Könings, Jeroen J. G. van Merriënboer, Tina Seidel. (2024). Signaling cues and focused prompts for professional vision support: The interplay of instructional design and situational interest in preservice teachers' video analysis. Instructional Science (2024) 52:879–917. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-024-09662-y
title: Integrated signaling keyword cues delivered within video viewing
description: In the cues condition, videos displayed keyword cues tied to tutoring strategies from the pre-training text. "Before an event began, the video paused for one second, displaying the tutoring strategy that would take place (Fig. 1a). Then the video resumed and the keyword cue remained in the top right corner of the video for the event's duration". Cues were shown for seven events in the elicitation-phase video and five events in the learning-phase video, chosen by research-group consensus so salient PPK and PCK events were equally represented.
requirements: keywords integrated into the video to avoid the split-attention the article attributes to Moreno's (2007) list-format cues
constraints: cues targeted only the tutoring strategies planned into the scripts and the introductory texts
target_learners: preservice teachers who are novices at video analysis
target_learning_goals: attention guidance toward theoretically relevant tutoring events during video viewing
examples: The condition was randomly assigned: 63 received cues and 67 viewed plain versions of the same videos.
key_sources: Meg Farrell, Monika Martin, Ricardo Böheim, Alexander Renkl, Werner Rieß, Karen D. Könings, Jeroen J. G. van Merriënboer, Tina Seidel. (2024). Signaling cues and focused prompts for professional vision support: The interplay of instructional design and situational interest in preservice teachers' video analysis. Instructional Science (2024) 52:879–917. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-024-09662-y

article_title: Learning from interactive video: the influence of self-explanations, navigation, and cognitive load
citation: Beege, M., & Ploetzner, R. (2025). Learning from interactive video: the influence of self-explanations, navigation, and cognitive load. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-024-09693-5
title: Do not assume interactive video features are generally beneficial: check learner use, response quality, and time-on-task boundaries
description: The article concludes that enriching instructional videos so learning shifts from receptive to active and constructive modes "is not generally beneficial", and that "the quality of the self-explanations and the control of the learning time seem to play an important role". Designers and researchers should therefore treat interactivity additions as conditional: low-quality self-explanations or unused navigation yield no gains beyond restudying. The article recommends considering moderator variables and boundary conditions rather than assuming generalizability of prior positive effects.
requirements: Interactive features must actually be used effectively by learners and elicit adequate-quality self-explanations for benefits to appear
constraints: Positive effects summarized in prior meta-analytic research may not generalize when learning time is controlled and responses are poor to moderate in quality
target_learners: university students learning from instructional video
target_learning_goals: retention and comprehension of conceptual science content such as thunderstorm formation
examples: In the experiment, navigation and prompts were each provided with strategic instructions, yet neither improved retention or comprehension with learning time fixed at 12 minutes
key_sources: Beege, M., & Ploetzner, R. (2025). Learning from interactive video: the influence of self-explanations, navigation, and cognitive load. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-024-09693-5

article_title: Dynamics of university students’ epistemic emotions during game-based learning in an international relations course
citation: Ketonen, E. E., Kruskopf, M., Lonka, K., & Mattlin, M. (2026). Dynamics of university students' epistemic emotions during game-based learning in an international relations course. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09771-2
title: Use process-oriented intra-individual (time-series) analysis to capture emotion dynamics that group-level findings conceal
description: The study advocates measuring emotions repeatedly after every session and analysing them with dynamic structural equation modelling, a process-oriented, intra-individual approach "only recently applied in educational research". This distinguishes within-person processes, between-person differences and learning context. The unique individual emotional trajectories showed that group-level conclusions about emotion trends were not applicable to all individuals, since individuals with decreasing emotions learned better.
requirements: Intensive session-to-session self-report data (212 situational questionnaires across 22 students)
Bayesian estimation because of the small number of clusters
constraints: Performed at only the within level because of the small number of clusters at the between level; models assumed data missing at random
target_learners: University students in course-long intensive follow-up designs
target_learning_goals: Understanding and supporting emotional dynamics of learning over time
examples: Emotions were measured with single-item EES measures after each of 13 and 11 sessions across two course implementations, capturing situational fluctuation.
key_sources: Ketonen, E. E., Kruskopf, M., Lonka, K., & Mattlin, M. (2026). Dynamics of university students' epistemic emotions during game-based learning in an international relations course. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09771-2

article_title: Examining secondary school students’ views of model evaluation through an integrated framework of personal epistemology
citation: Lee, S. W.-Y., Wu, H., & Chang, H. (2021). Examining secondary school students' views of model evaluation through an integrated framework of personal epistemology. Instructional Science, 49, 223–248. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-021-09534-9
title: Integrated framework of personal epistemology for model evaluation: Kuhn's three developmental stages crossed with Kitchener's three epistemic-cognition dimensions
description: The framework interlaces Kuhn's developmental levels (absolutist, multiplist, evaluatist) with Kitchener's dimensions of epistemic cognition (limits of knowing, certainty of knowing, criteria of knowing) to form a matrix for analyzing students' epistemic views of model evaluation. As the article states, "the three epistemic levels describing the absolutist, multiplist, and evaluatist... and the three epistemic dimensions describing limits of knowing, certainty of knowing, and criteria of knowing (Kitchener 1983) are interlaced to form a new framework for analyzing students' epistemic views of model evaluation." It was operationalized in coding themes and used to interpret students' justifications.
requirements: Written justifications and forced-choice assumption responses so that epistemic levels and dimensions can be coded and triangulated
constraints: The article notes relatively fewer students referred to the limits of knowing, and the framework was applied to two non-textbook science contexts with high uncertainty
target_learning_goals: epistemic understanding of scientific model evaluation
examples: Students' justifications were coded into themes mapped onto the framework's dimensions and levels, and each student's assumption choice was compared with the coded written response to confirm their epistemic level
key_sources: Lee, S. W.-Y., Wu, H., & Chang, H. (2021). Examining secondary school students' views of model evaluation through an integrated framework of personal epistemology. Instructional Science, 49, 223–248. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-021-09534-9

article_title: Inclusive pedagogy in practice within the multi-tiered systems of support framework: a design-based research in a Chinese EFL classroom
citation: Lin, T., Mullick, J., & Campbell, M. (2026). Inclusive pedagogy in practice within the multi-tiered systems of support framework: a design-based research in a Chinese EFL classroom. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09754-3
title: Design principles for inclusive pedagogy within MTSS derived from DBR iterations
description: From three iterations of planning, action, development, and reflection, the study distilled principles that "were emerged as actionable guidelines to implement inclusive pedagogy in similar contexts". The first printed principle is "Differentiation and flexibility: Instruction was tailored to meet the diverse needs of students, including those with neurodiverse conditions", operationalised through tiered tasks, random lottery participation with discreetly tailored questions, and individualised assessment alongside unified exams.
requirements: Iterative DBR cycles of planning, action, development, and reflection, refined against student performance data, teacher observations, and parent feedback
constraints: The design principles section is presented for similar contexts; the study itself was a single class in one rural boarding school
target_learners: diverse elementary EFL learners including students with neurodiverse conditions and SEN
target_learning_goals: equitable access to English language learning
engagement and belonging for all performance levels
examples: Higher-performing students received more challenging tasks while lower-performing students received simpler ones, and a lottery bucket gave all students equal participation chances
key_sources: Lin, T., Mullick, J., & Campbell, M. (2026). Inclusive pedagogy in practice within the multi-tiered systems of support framework: a design-based research in a Chinese EFL classroom. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09754-3

article_title: Localizing, describing, interpreting: effects of different audio text structures on attributing meaning to digital pictures
citation: Manuela Glaser, Manuel Knoos, Stephan Schwan. (2022). Localizing, describing, interpreting: effects of different audio text structures on attributing meaning to digital pictures. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-022-09593-6
title: Design audio explanations of complex pictures with an integrated LDI structure, presenting each element's localization, description, and interpretation in immediate succession
description: The article recommends that audio explanations of pictures localize, describe, and interpret each picture element in immediate succession rather than separating all descriptions from all interpretations. Integrated structures establish local coherence and keep visual attention on the relevant element during interpretation, enabling dual coding. The authors state that "audio explanations with LDI integrated structure as often used for audio guides (Popp, 2013) seem to be more appropriate than LDI separated structures" for educational videos, website audio texts, and museum audio guides.
requirements: Audio explanations must include localization information that directs viewers' attention to the respective picture elements before describing and interpreting them.
constraints: Evidence comes from a laboratory study with a rather homogeneous group of 55 participants; the authors call for replication in the field, e.g. with educational videos on YouTube or museum websites.
Participants with high prior knowledge (art, art history, history) were excluded, so effects for knowledgeable learners are untested.
target_learners: adult learners without domain-specific prior knowledge in art or history
viewers of educational videos, museum audio guides, and website audio explanations
target_learning_goals: linking verbal interpretations to visual picture elements
examples: Participants viewed history paintings with audio explanations in which each picture detail's description was immediately followed by its interpretation (LDI integrated) or with descriptions and interpretations in separate blocks (LDI separated).
key_sources: Manuela Glaser, Manuel Knoos, Stephan Schwan. (2022). Localizing, describing, interpreting: effects of different audio text structures on attributing meaning to digital pictures. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-022-09593-6

article_title: Discovery learning: zombie, phoenix, or elephant?
citation: Arthur Bakker. (2018). Discovery learning: zombie, phoenix, or elephant? Instructional Science, 46, 169–183. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-018-9450-8
title: Inferentialism: concepts as norms governing use, with understanding as practical mastery of inferences
description: The article describes inferentialism (Brandom) as "a holistic, pragmatist, expressivist, and rationalist theory of meaning" in which a concept is not a representation of a class of referents but "the norm governing the use of the concept." Understanding a concept means having practical mastery over the inferences it is involved in, so understanding is always a matter of degree and concepts come in packages. The author applies this to argue that direct instruction cannot fully explain concepts, and that students discovering their own knowledge is equally untenable because the teacher represents disciplinary norms.
requirements: Understanding this theory takes some investment, and studying teacher-student interaction as a game of giving and asking for reasons with scorekeeping.
constraints: The article notes the inferences that can be made with concepts are boundless, so no explanation can be complete.
target_learners: Students learning disciplinary concepts such as standard deviation in statistics education
target_learning_goals: Conceptual understanding as practical mastery of inferential relations between concepts
examples: The author's own hours-long struggle to construct a distribution with a given mean, SD, and minimum illustrates exploring the inferential terrain of the standard deviation concept with a tool and a colleague.
key_sources: Arthur Bakker. (2018). Discovery learning: zombie, phoenix, or elephant? Instructional Science, 46, 169–183. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-018-9450-8

article_title: Fostering pre-service teachers’ theoretical knowledge application: studying with and without text-based cases
citation: Baier, F., Maurer, C., Dignath, C., & Kunter, M. (2021). Fostering pre-service teachers' theoretical knowledge application: studying with and without text-based cases. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-021-09560-7
title: Inert knowledge and situated cognition account of the theory-practice gap in teacher education
description: The article frames pre-service teachers' failure to apply scientific theory as the inert knowledge problem: knowledge learned at university remains purely declarative and is not used in real teaching. It draws on two explanatory families: deficits in the knowledge itself, such as insufficient conceptual knowledge and knowledge compartmentalization, and situated cognition models. As the authors put it, "situated cognition models consider inert knowledge to be a consequence of missing congruence between the context in which classroom management is studied (e.g. in university lectures) and in which it has to be applied (e.g. in the school classroom)". Case-based learning is proposed as a method to establish this congruence and thereby prevent inert knowledge.
requirements: The framework presupposes that learners study scientific theories that are meant to be applied later in real teaching situations.
constraints: The article notes that inert knowledge may also arise from deficits in the knowledge itself, such as insufficient conceptual knowledge or knowledge compartmentalization, not only from missing context congruence.
target_learners: pre-service teachers in university teacher education
target_learning_goals: application of scientific theories on classroom management to authentic teaching situations
examples: The study operationalized the framework by comparing application of the same theory to real-world text-based cases versus to abstract theoretical models in an online learning environment.
key_sources: Baier, F., Maurer, C., Dignath, C., & Kunter, M. (2021). Fostering pre-service teachers' theoretical knowledge application: studying with and without text-based cases. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-021-09560-7

article_title: Effectiveness of invention tasks and explicit instruction in preparing intellectually gifted adolescents for learning
citation: Lim, S., Jung, J. Y., & Kalyuga, S. (2023). Effectiveness of invention tasks and explicit instruction in preparing intellectually gifted adolescents for learning. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-023-09616-w
title: Invention-first instruction (Invention as Preparation for Future Learning / productive failure)
description: Invention-first instruction is an instructional sequence in which learners first attempt to solve or invent solutions to a novel problem and only then receive explicit instruction on the canonical solution. The article describes it as "hallmarked by two essential components—first, the solving of problems, followed by explicit instruction", and notes it is also called productive failure. Proposed mechanisms include increased awareness of knowledge gaps, heightened epistemic curiosity, and recognition of deep structure via contrast between cases. The study operationalises it against example-first instruction with gifted and non-gifted adolescents.
requirements: Learners attempt an invention or problem-solving activity prior to receiving explicit instruction on the canonical solution
Instruction follows the invention stage so the preparatory effect can operate
constraints: The article notes the specific mechanisms are not fully clarified and only a handful of studies have investigated them
target_learners: secondary school students, especially gifted adolescents in grades 6 and above
target_learning_goals: preparation for learning new conceptual content
examples: In this study, invention-first participants spent 15 min generating a crowdedness index for clown bus companies before receiving an instructional booklet, while example-first participants studied a worked example of the same task.
key_sources: Lim, S., Jung, J. Y., & Kalyuga, S. (2023). Effectiveness of invention tasks and explicit instruction in preparing intellectually gifted adolescents for learning. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-023-09616-w

article_title: Effectiveness of invention tasks and explicit instruction in preparing intellectually gifted adolescents for learning
citation: Lim, S., Jung, J. Y., & Kalyuga, S. (2023). Effectiveness of invention tasks and explicit instruction in preparing intellectually gifted adolescents for learning. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-023-09616-w
title: Balanced invention-first vs example-first design with a shared additional practice stage
description: The study's instructional design gives all conditions identical stages except the first: pre-instruction (invention or worked example), problem-solving/worked example practice, recall, consolidation, and post-test. Unlike prior designs, "an additional practice stage of a problem-solving task and a worked example ... was included for all conditions prior to final consolidation", so both a problem-solving task and a worked example were given to every condition in the same order. This holds practice constant across conditions and isolates the effect of the initial activity, while responding to findings that additional problem-solving practice may increase the benefits of invention-first instruction.
requirements: All conditions must receive the same practice activities in the same order after the differing first stage
The initial stage (invention vs worked example) uses the same task materials
constraints: The article notes the low contrast conditions may not have given invention-first participants all information needed to solve the task, so high vs low contrast is a comparison of materials rather than of cases
target_learners: seventh-grade students in selective and non-selective classes
examples: Four conditions were used: invention-first high contrast, example-first high contrast, invention-first low contrast, and example-first low contrast, each with the same five sequential stages.
key_sources: Lim, S., Jung, J. Y., & Kalyuga, S. (2023). Effectiveness of invention tasks and explicit instruction in preparing intellectually gifted adolescents for learning. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-023-09616-w

article_title: Effectiveness of invention tasks and explicit instruction in preparing intellectually gifted adolescents for learning
citation: Lim, S., Jung, J. Y., & Kalyuga, S. (2023). Effectiveness of invention tasks and explicit instruction in preparing intellectually gifted adolescents for learning. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-023-09616-w
title: Invention-first instruction is a candidate strategy for gifted secondary students, pending confirmation
description: Based on the significant giftedness-by-instruction interaction and the theoretical fit between gifted learners' profiles and problem-solving, the article proposes invention-first instruction as a promising alternative to the conventional explicit-instruction modality in gifted education. It explicitly "puts forward the possibility of the invention-first strategy as an effective instructional strategy for gifted students". The framing is tentative: results are described with may, and the authors note prior evidence that older and higher-ability students appear more responsive to invention-first methods.
requirements: Students at secondary level (grade 6 and above), where invention-first benefits have been reported
Tasks that offer appropriate challenge and opportunities for problem-solving and creativity
constraints: Contrast materials were not found to affect performance in this study
Gifted classification relied on self-identification plus psychologist or school identification
target_learners: intellectually gifted and academically talented adolescents
examples: The study administered a crowdedness-index invention task adapted from Schwartz et al. (2011) to gifted and non-gifted seventh graders before explicit instruction.
key_sources: Lim, S., Jung, J. Y., & Kalyuga, S. (2023). Effectiveness of invention tasks and explicit instruction in preparing intellectually gifted adolescents for learning. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-023-09616-w

article_title: Development of legal expertise
citation: Glöckner, A., Towfigh, E., & Traxler, C. (2013). Development of legal expertise. Instructional Science, 41, 989–1007. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-013-9266-5
title: Students with good initial performance should focus on area-specific practice exams while students with poor initial performance should prioritize general exam practice
description: The authors recommend that "students with good initial performance should focus more on area-of-law speciﬁc practice exams whereas students with poor initial performance seem to proﬁt more from general exam practice in all areas of law." This differential recommendation follows from the significant interaction effects between initial performance and both general and area-specific practice experience.
requirements: Students must have taken enough early exams to assess their initial performance level
constraints: Recommendation is derived from interaction effects estimated for advanced law students in a mock exam preparation course
target_learners: advanced law students preparing for state exams
target_learning_goals: optimizing practice allocation for case-solving skill development
examples: The authors advise students to use their performance in early exams to predict their potential for improvements and plan their time accordingly
key_sources: Glöckner, A., Towfigh, E., & Traxler, C. (2013). Development of legal expertise. Instructional Science, 41, 989–1007. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-013-9266-5

article_title: Bridging domains: examining the effects of relevance instructions and guiding questions on pre-service teachers’ first- and second-order knowledge integration
citation: Lehmann, T. (2024). Bridging domains: examining the effects of relevance instructions and guiding questions on pre-service teachers' first- and second-order knowledge integration. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-023-09655-3
title: Integrated knowledge application test: justified evaluation and improvement of a tabular lesson plan
description: The study's measure of second-order KI asks participants to evaluate how a planned third-grade spelling lesson is or is not appropriate for promoting spelling skills. Participants list positive features and suggest improvements, each with a justification, in a pre-structured template. Responses are coded for whether they apply CK, PK, PCK, prior knowledge, or incorrect knowledge, and rationales drawing on more domains score more points, yielding an overall second-order KI index. Interrater reliability was excellent (ICCs between 0.82 and 0.94).
requirements: A lesson plan containing both strengths and weaknesses identifiable from the three domain-specific text sources
Raters blind to condition and trained on the coding scheme
constraints: The scoring deducts one point per incorrect knowledge application, so the index penalizes misconceptions as well as rewarding integration
target_learning_goals: integrated simultaneous application of CK, PK, and PCK in a lesson-planning evaluation task
examples: Sample coded response: a PK application justifying more group work phases because "the cognitive activation of the pupils could probably be increased"
key_sources: Lehmann, T. (2024). Bridging domains: examining the effects of relevance instructions and guiding questions on pre-service teachers' first- and second-order knowledge integration. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-023-09655-3

article_title: Modelling evidence-based practice in initial teacher training: effects on teachers’ skills, knowledge and self-efficacy
citation: Sam Sims, Harry Fletcher-Wood, Thomas Godfrey-Faussett, Peps Mccrea, Stefanie Meliss. (2026). Modelling evidence-based practice in initial teacher training: effects on teachers’ skills, knowledge and self-efficacy. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09779-2
title: Incorporate observable video models when training early-career teachers in evidence-based teaching practices
description: Because models give trainees an observable example of the focal practice, teacher educators should build video models into initial training on evidence-based techniques rather than relying on written evidence summaries alone. The experiment found models roughly doubled simulator skill scores while restudy produced no measurable gain. The authors conclude: “Findings support the theory that incorporating models in initial teacher training can help new teachers make use of evidence-based teaching practices.”
requirements: The model should demonstrate the same evidence-based principles contained in the written guidance trainees receive
constraints: Lab simulator setting with reduced ecological validity; the skill measure has not been previously validated; benefits shown for explicit models following a written summary, not implicit models
target_learning_goals: classroom skill in using evidence-based teaching techniques
examples: Participants watched a 4.5-minute video of a real primary teacher demonstrating all five evidence-based principles of questioning for retrieval before a second simulator attempt
key_sources: Sam Sims, Harry Fletcher-Wood, Thomas Godfrey-Faussett, Peps Mccrea, Stefanie Meliss. (2026). Modelling evidence-based practice in initial teacher training: effects on teachers’ skills, knowledge and self-efficacy. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09779-2

article_title: How to assist the students while learning from text? Effects of inserting adjunct questions on text processing
citation: Alba Rubio, Eduardo Vidal-Abarca, Marian Serrano-Mendizábal. (2022). How to assist the students while learning from text? Effects of inserting adjunct questions on text processing. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-022-09592-7
title: Insert adjunct questions immediately after the question-relevant text segments when students study challenging texts with the text available
description: This principle holds that questions used as learning activities should be placed in the text right after the information needed to answer them, rather than massed after the whole text, when students study challenging, interconnected texts with the text available. The article argues that "inserting the questions would assist readers while text processing compared to post-reading questions", because the short delay keeps relevant information active and supports inference making. It is grounded in the study's finding that inserted questions produced better delayed transfer learning and more efficient processing.
requirements: Texts challenging enough that understanding sections is interconnected
Questions placed immediately after all question-relevant information has been read
Text available to students while answering the questions
constraints: Benefits may not generalize to less challenging texts or texts with relatively disconnected sections
The study cannot confirm which condition is better for retention of non-question information
No control group without questions, so comparison to just reading the text is not possible
Evidence limited to college freshmen; younger students may not benefit
target_learners: first-year college students studying challenging science texts
target_learning_goals: deep comprehension and delayed transfer of challenging conceptual text ideas
examples: In the experiment, questions were inserted immediately after reading all the information needed to answer them, and students answered with the text available on a single screen
key_sources: Alba Rubio, Eduardo Vidal-Abarca, Marian Serrano-Mendizábal. (2022). How to assist the students while learning from text? Effects of inserting adjunct questions on text processing. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-022-09592-7

article_title: Two comparative studies of computer simulations and experiments as learning tools in school and out-of-school education
citation: Krüger, J. T., Höffler, T. N., Wahl, M., Knickmeier, K., & Parchmann, I. (2022). Two comparative studies of computer simulations and experiments as learning tools in school and out-of-school education. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-021-09566-1
title: Support simulation-based learning with guiding scripts and supervisor help to prevent disorientation and cognitive overload
description: In both studies the simulations were used with structured instructional support: paper or digital scripts with guiding questions that students answered while working, plus supervisors for technical and content questions. The article states this was done "To avoid disorientation and cognitive overload especially by working on the simulation", and the introduction notes that simulations without support tend to cause disorientation and extraneous load.
requirements: Scripts with the same guiding questions for both methods
A supervisor available for technical and content-related questions
constraints: The studies did not distinguish intrinsic from extraneous load, using a short two-item overall load measure
target_learning_goals: content knowledge of complex socioscientific issues
managing cognitive load during simulation-based learning
examples: In Study II the simulation script was digital and embedded in the simulation website with operation instructions and parameter information, while experiment scripts were paper-based with per-station instructions
key_sources: Krüger, J. T., Höffler, T. N., Wahl, M., Knickmeier, K., & Parchmann, I. (2022). Two comparative studies of computer simulations and experiments as learning tools in school and out-of-school education. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-021-09566-1

article_title: How vocal and silent forms of participation in combination relate to student achievement
citation: Sedova, K., & Sedlacek, M. (2023). How vocal and silent forms of participation in combination relate to student achievement. Instructional Science, 51, 343–361. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-022-09609-1
title: Teachers should invite all students to participate in classroom conversation rather than assuming silent, engaged students benefit equally
description: The article derives a practical implication from its profile findings: because inequalities in student talk create uneven learning opportunities, "Teachers should invite all students to participate in classroom conversations". Teachers should not assume that silent but attentive and engaged students benefit from classroom discourse in the same way as vocal peers; the internally engaged but silent diligent students are identified as at risk, and the authors argue teachers should help such students raise their voices.
requirements: Applicable in classroom settings where whole-class discussion occurs and talk time can be distributed across students
constraints: Findings come from Czech language and language arts lessons in traditionally taught, non-dialogue-rich Czech classrooms; the article notes similar results might not be found in non-linguistic subjects
Participation was operationalized as talk quantity only, not quality
target_learners: lower secondary school students (ninth grade, ages 14–15)
examples: In the study, teachers taught two observed Czech language and language arts lessons as they normally would; talk time per student averaged approximately 12 s per lesson, and 46 students spoke for 0 s
key_sources: Sedova, K., & Sedlacek, M. (2023). How vocal and silent forms of participation in combination relate to student achievement. Instructional Science, 51, 343–361. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-022-09609-1

article_title: Comparison of more effective and typical teachers’ instructional quality and implementation of engaged reader processes
citation: Fatima Zehra Allahverdi, Lynn Gelzheiser. (2025). Comparison of more effective and typical teachers' instructional quality and implementation of engaged reader processes. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09725-8
title: Instructional Quality and Implementation Coding system combining Wood's contingent teaching with Meichenbaum and Biemiller's self-direction dimension
description: A coding system the authors developed to measure explicit instruction and scaffolding of purpose setting at fine grain. It draws on Vygotsky's ZPD and the GRR model "while also incorporating research on scaffolding", operationalizing the GRR through Wood's (2003) contingent teaching (domain and instructional contingencies) and Meichenbaum and Biemiller's (1998) self-direction dimension moving students from other-directed to self-directed. Coding covers actor, content, quality of scaffold, and communication mode within instructional cycles, and uniquely includes student application, which Wood's theory does not address.
requirements: Transcribed audio/video sessions segmented into instructional cycles beginning with a purpose set for reading
Coders trained to reliability; the study reported agreement of 100% for the author, 91.4% for content, 84% for quality, and 97% for instruction communication
constraints: Applied in this study only to acquisition and early consolidation lessons related to purpose setting; no validity coefficient is available
target_learners: third- and fourth-grade students with limited reading comprehension
target_learning_goals: reading comprehension through engaged reader processes such as purpose setting
examples: Five sessions per teacher were transcribed and coded for two case-study teachers, producing Tables 9 and 10 patterns in teacher instruction and student purpose setting
key_sources: Fatima Zehra Allahverdi, Lynn Gelzheiser. (2025). Comparison of more effective and typical teachers' instructional quality and implementation of engaged reader processes. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09725-8

article_title: Designing a self-improving tutor: PROTO-TEG
citation: Dillenbourg, P. (1989). The design of a self-improving tutor: PROTO-TEG. Instructional Science, 18(3), 193–216. https://doi.org/10.1007/BF00053359
title: Design tutors so they can induce their own strategy-selection criteria from recorded tutoring episodes
description: The article proposes that a tutor's strategy-selection knowledge need not be fully pre-specified: the system can discover "criteria useful for selecting the didactic strategies it has at its disposal" by learning concepts from examples drawn from its own recorded episodes. This shifts part of the design burden from hand-coding selection rules to recording student model states and applying machine learning over them.
requirements: Recording of student model states during tutoring episodes
Labels distinguishing episodes where a strategy was effective from those where it was not
Machine learning methods for learning concepts from examples
constraints: In this implementation the acquired criteria did not improve student performance, and conditions were found for only five of nine strategies
examples: PROTO-TEG compared student model states from effective and ineffective uses of the same didactic strategy to induce selection conditions
key_sources: Dillenbourg, P. (1989). The design of a self-improving tutor: PROTO-TEG. Instructional Science, 18(3), 193–216. https://doi.org/10.1007/BF00053359

article_title: Exploring the association of student perceptions of science instruction and emotional engagement: The variance between grade level
citation: Xin Xia, Robert Tai. (2026). Exploring the association of student perceptions of science instruction and emotional engagement: The variance between grade level. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09800-8
title: Design science instruction that students perceive as interesting and understandable to foster positive emotional experiences, especially in transition grades
description: The article's findings support teachers preparing science lessons that students experience as interesting and as clear and understandable, because both perceptions are positively associated with emotional engagement. The authors state this "emphasizes the importance of advocating for teachers to prepare science classes in an interesting, organized, easy-to-understand way to foster positive emotional experiences in science classrooms." Because the grade-6 transition year shows the strongest sensitivity to perceived interestingness, targeted attention to instruction during transition grades is recommended. Understandable instruction means scaffolding complexity, not simplifying content.
requirements: Teachers' pedagogical training and practice in designing engaging, comprehensible science lessons
constraints: The study did not examine which specific instructional methods or components produce these perceptions; understandable does not imply reducing conceptual difficulty
target_learners: Students in grades 3–12, particularly students in transition grades such as grade 6
target_learning_goals: Sustaining emotional engagement and positive affect in science learning
examples: The multilevel analysis of 6,465 students found each unit increase in perceived interesting instruction associated with a 0.32 increase in emotional engagement, and the grade-6 interaction was the steepest among significant interactions
key_sources: Xin Xia, Robert Tai. (2026). Exploring the association of student perceptions of science instruction and emotional engagement: The variance between grade level. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09800-8

article_title: Besides knowledge: a cross-sectional study on the relations between epistemic beliefs, achievement goals, self-beliefs, and achievement in science
citation: Mason, L., Boscolo, P., Tornatora, M. C., & Ronconi, L. (2012). Besides knowledge: a cross-sectional study on the relations between epistemic beliefs, achievement goals, self-beliefs, and achievement in science. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-012-9210-0
title: A conceptual model integrating epistemic beliefs, achievement goals, self-beliefs, domain knowledge, and achievement in science
description: The article proposes and tests a path model in which domain-specific epistemic beliefs (development and justification of scientific knowledge) relate to achievement goals (mastery, performance-approach, performance-avoidance), which relate to self-efficacy and self-concept, which together with domain knowledge predict science achievement. The model was tested via SEM at three grade levels and showed good fit at all levels, though not all hypothesized paths were significant. The authors state that 'no causal relationships are established, which would require longitudinal or experimental designs.'
requirements: Domain-specific measurement of epistemic beliefs, achievement goals, and self-beliefs within the same academic domain
constraints: Cross-sectional design establishes no causal relationships
Not all hypothesized paths were statistically significant at any grade level
examples: Tested with 696 Italian students across grades 5, 8, and 11 using questionnaires and domain knowledge tests
key_sources: Mason, L., Boscolo, P., Tornatora, M. C., & Ronconi, L. (2012). Besides knowledge: a cross-sectional study on the relations between epistemic beliefs, achievement goals, self-beliefs, and achievement in science. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-012-9210-0

article_title: Learner control in animated multimedia instructions
citation: Huib K. Tabbers, Bastiaan de Koeijer. (2010). Learner control in animated multimedia instructions. Instructional Science, 38, 441–453. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-009-9119-4
title: The interactivity principle: people learn better from multimedia instruction when they control both order and pace of the presentation
description: The interactivity principle, introduced by Mayer et al. (2003) within Mayer's theory of multimedia learning and cognitive load theory, states that "people learn better from a multimedia instruction when they are able to control both order and pace of the presentation". Its rationale is that segment-by-segment control reduces cognitive load and permits progressive mental model building, freeing resources for deeper understanding measured by transfer. This study tested the principle in its fullest form and replicated the transfer benefit, while questioning the load-reduction explanation.
requirements: Learners must be able to control both the order and the pace of the multimedia presentation, as in the Mayer et al. (2003) interactive versions.
constraints: The article argues the cognitive-load-reduction rationale is not sufficiently supported: Mayer and Chandler (2001) found no mental effort difference and system-controlled mental effort scores of 2.59 on a 1-7 scale indicated no overload.
The benefit may be confounded with increased time-on-task, which prior studies did not report.
target_learners: University students studying animated multimedia instructions
target_learning_goals: Deeper understanding (transfer) of causal-process explanations such as lightning formation
examples: The experiment gave learners stop/play buttons, a 'what happens here' narration button, and a navigation menu over 16 slides of a lightning-formation lesson.
key_sources: Huib K. Tabbers, Bastiaan de Koeijer. (2010). Learner control in animated multimedia instructions. Instructional Science, 38, 441–453. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-009-9119-4

article_title: CID: a framework for the cognitive analysis of composite instructional designs
citation: Katharina Loibl · Timo Leuders · Inga Glogger-Frey · Nikol Rummel. (2025). CID: a framework for the cognitive analysis of composite instructional designs. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-024-09665-9
title: Typology of intermediate-knowledge types and their interplay with second-phase learning processes
description: The article distinguishes types of intermediate knowledge (K1) generated in the first phase: partial or erroneous knowledge serving integration in the second phase (partial knowledge integrated into target knowledge, erroneous knowledge contributing via refutation, specific negative knowledge focusing on relevant aspects), and instrumental knowledge that supports rather than becomes target knowledge (situational knowledge as a concrete anchor, unspecific negative knowledge as global awareness of knowledge gaps generating motivation, and supportive knowledge such as strategies or fluency freeing cognitive capacity). As illustrated in Fig. 5, these types "contribute differently to the learning processes (L2) initiated by the instructional design of the second phase".
requirements: Manipulating and/or measuring the different types of intermediate knowledge separately, wherever possible, to understand composite-design mechanisms
constraints: The framework analysis focuses primarily on cognitive dimensions; affective-motivational states are treated only in parallel
target_learning_goals: Explaining how first-phase outcomes prepare learning from subsequent instruction
examples: Used to explain the contradictory Glogger-Frey et al. (2015 vs. 2017) findings via differences in the quality of intermediate knowledge
key_sources: Katharina Loibl · Timo Leuders · Inga Glogger-Frey · Nikol Rummel. (2025). CID: a framework for the cognitive analysis of composite instructional designs. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-024-09665-9

article_title: Connecting teachers’ classroom instructions with children’s metacognition and learning in elementary school
citation: Mariëtte H. van Loon, et al. (2021). Connecting teachers' classroom instructions with children's metacognition and learning in elementary school. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-020-09248-2
title: Support children's metacognition through the way instructions are given, not only their content
description: The study's central design implication is that how teachers deliver instructions matters for children's procedural metacognition. Child-centered practices that give children autonomy to regulate their own learning predicted more effective restudy and more accurate self-monitoring, whereas teacher-directed delivery predicted less accurate monitoring. As the authors put it, "not only the content of the instructions itself, but particularly the way these are given, affects children's metacognition." Teachers should therefore pair strategy content with opportunities for children to practice self-regulated strategy use.
requirements: Teachers must provide opportunities for children to practice strategies during self-regulated learning activities, not only describe strategies.
constraints: Evidence comes from one standardized 30-minute secret-code lesson in second and fourth grade classrooms; relations are correlational, and the restudy benefit of child-centered instruction appeared for second graders in this sample.
target_learners: Elementary school children (second and fourth grade)
target_learning_goals: Effective restudy selection and regulation of study
examples: Teachers taught the same secret-code task in their own way for 30 minutes; classrooms varying in child-centered instruction were compared on children's restudy selections and confidence judgments.
key_sources: Mariëtte H. van Loon, et al. (2021). Connecting teachers' classroom instructions with children's metacognition and learning in elementary school. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-020-09248-2

article_title: Longitudinal associations between executive functions and metacognitive monitoring in 5- to 8-year-olds
citation: Sonja Kälin, Claudia M. Roebers. (2022). Longitudinal associations between executive functions and metacognitive monitoring in 5- to 8-year-olds. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-022-09306-x
title: Inhibition-as-prerequisite account: inhibition enables children to hesitate and take time when monitoring, producing less overconfident judgments
description: The article proposes a mechanism account in which metacognitive monitoring requires time to accumulate evidence, and inhibition skills allow children to suppress impulsive confidence judgments and hesitate. Better inhibition is assumed to down-regulate anterior cingulate cortex activation, enabling slower, more thorough reflection on mental processes and thus more accurate, less overconfident monitoring. The account explains why inhibition, but not working memory or shifting, predicted later monitoring in this study.
requirements: Children must have sufficient inhibition skills to override the impulse to give a rushed confidence judgment so that evidence can be accumulated over time
constraints: The article states it cannot rule out an alternative direct effect in which inhibition suppresses the default of indicating high confidence independent of judgment time
The account is offered as an interpretation; the study measured associations, not the mediating process
target_learners: Children aged 5 to 8 years transitioning from kindergarten to elementary school
target_learning_goals: Accurate metacognitive monitoring of one's own performance (realistic confidence judgments)
examples: The authors draw on Espinet et al. (2013), linking reflection, slower responding and down-regulation of ACC activation to better EF skills, and on Pleskac & Busemeyer (2010) on evidence accumulation for confidence judgments
key_sources: Sonja Kälin, Claudia M. Roebers. (2022). Longitudinal associations between executive functions and metacognitive monitoring in 5- to 8-year-olds. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-022-09306-x

article_title: The effect of writing script on efficiency and metacognitive monitoring in inferential word learning
citation: Polyanskaya, L., El-Dakhs, D. A. S., Tao, M., Chu, F., & Ordin, M. (2024). The effect of writing script on efficiency and metacognitive monitoring in inferential word learning. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-024-09380-3
title: Inferential word-learning task with retrospective confidence ratings and hierarchical Bayesian meta-d' estimation
description: A cross-modal experimental instrument in which participants learn 20 pseudoword–referent pairings through disambiguation of semantically ambiguous scenes (e.g. selecting a table with a "dax"), then select referents while rating confidence on a 4-point scale. Metacognition is quantified as meta-d' via "the signal detection theory framework", estimated with Fleming's hierarchical Bayesian HMeta-d code; metacognitive efficiency is the ratio of meta-d' to d'. The article used it to compare word-learning accuracy and metacognitive monitoring across Arabic, Chinese and Portuguese speakers in visual and auditory modalities.
requirements: Pseudowords tailored to each language's phonotactics (UniPseudo for Portuguese and Saudi Arabic; MELD-SCH non-existent characters for Chinese) and counterbalancing of modality order and referents across participants and genders
constraints: The study was not preregistered; metacognition is measured only via retrospective confidence ratings, which the authors admit cannot separate confidence judgments guided with versus without conscious awareness
target_learners: University students aged 18-30, native speakers of Arabic, Mandarin Chinese or Portuguese, with intermediate formal English knowledge
target_learning_goals: Inferential word learning from contextual cues and metacognitive monitoring of vocabulary learning success
examples: In the visual modality participants read sentences instructing them to select one of two images differing by a minor detail, learning referents implicitly across trials; in the auditory modality the same procedure used heard pseudowords and sentences
key_sources: Polyanskaya, L., El-Dakhs, D. A. S., Tao, M., Chu, F., & Ordin, M. (2024). The effect of writing script on efficiency and metacognitive monitoring in inferential word learning. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-024-09380-3

article_title: Integrating self-regulated learning and individual differences in the prediction of university academic achievement across a three-year-long degree
citation: Juan-Carlos Pérez-González, Gemma Filella, Anna Soldevila, Yasmine Faiad, Maria-Jose Sanchez-Ruiz. (2022). Integrating self-regulated learning and individual differences in the prediction of university academic achievement across a three-year-long degree. Metacognition and Learning (2022) 17:1141–1165. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-022-09315-w
title: Integrative framework combining the SRL and individual-differences approaches to predictors of academic performance
description: The article proposes a parsimonious framework (Table 1) that organizes predictors of academic performance by crossing two research traditions: "individual differences and SRL".
