It maps cognitive factors (cognitive abilities, cognitive and metacognitive learning strategies) and non-cognitive factors (personality, motivation, affect, behavior, context regulation) onto Pintrich's five self-regulatory learning areas and Hilgard's three areas of psychological functioning. It is offered as a starting point for future integrative models and was partially tested via the study's regressions and SEMs.
requirements: Measured variables spanning both cognitive and non-cognitive domains, operationalized as in Table 1
constraints: The authors state there is no consensus on how to reconcile the different classifications of variables, and present the framework as tentative and parsimonious rather than established
target_learning_goals: identification of non-cognitive factors supporting self-regulated learning
examples: The framework guided selection of predictors for the three-year hierarchical regressions and the two structural equation models
key_sources: Juan-Carlos Pérez-González, Gemma Filella, Anna Soldevila, Yasmine Faiad, Maria-Jose Sanchez-Ruiz. (2022). Integrating self-regulated learning and individual differences in the prediction of university academic achievement across a three-year-long degree. Metacognition and Learning (2022) 17:1141–1165. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-022-09315-w

article_title: Linking teachers’ and students’ motivation for self-regulated learning: is there a signal and how is it transmitted?
citation: Johannes Jud, Yves Karlen, Carmen Nadja Hirt. (2024). Linking teachers' and students' motivation for self-regulated learning: is there a signal and how is it transmitted? Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-024-09393-y
title: Include student reports of instructional practices alongside teacher self-reports when studying links between teacher and student motivation
description: When investigating whether teacher motivation transmits to student motivation, researchers and evaluators should capture students' perceptions of the instructional practice, not only teachers' self-reports. In this study, models using only teacher-reported SRL promotion found no indirect links, whereas "including student reports of SRL promotion is especially crucial to finding indirect links". Teachers tend to overestimate their instruction, and student reports are stronger predictors of student outcomes.
requirements: Both teacher- and student-reported measures of the instructional practice must be collected
Rater-specific effects must be accounted for in the analysis
constraints: Evidence comes from a cross-sectional correlational design in Swiss lower-secondary classes; the authors call for longitudinal designs before causal conclusions
target_learning_goals: Understanding and fostering students' motivation for self-regulated learning and strategy use
examples: The authors calculated partial-perspective models with either teacher- or student-reported SRL promotion and systematically compared which perspective yielded indirect teacher-to-student motivation links
key_sources: Johannes Jud, Yves Karlen, Carmen Nadja Hirt. (2024). Linking teachers' and students' motivation for self-regulated learning: is there a signal and how is it transmitted? Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-024-09393-y

article_title: Promoting explicit instruction of strategies for self-regulated learning: evaluating a teacher professional development program in primary education
citation: Patrick Sins, Renske de Leeuw, Jaap de Brouwer, Emmy Vrieling-Teunter. (2024). Promoting explicit instruction of strategies for self-regulated learning: evaluating a teacher professional development program in primary education. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-023-09368-5
title: Instruct SRL strategies explicitly and integrated within subject-matter teaching rather than in decontextualized study lessons
description: The article recommends an integrated approach in which "the instruction of SRL strategies ... takes place during the teaching of subjects since the use of these strategies is domain specific", so students directly apply strategies within a curricular context. Explicit instruction means teachers clearly explain how strategies are applied, when they are most effective and what their benefits are, for example by modelling strategies through thinking out loud. iSELF trains teachers in both didactics.
requirements: teachers select SRL strategies matched to the lesson's subject domain and learning goals, e.g. via the iSELF flowchart
constraints: the article notes integration of SRL instruction does not seem to receive priority in primary education, and students first need explicit training to benefit from implicit instruction
target_learning_goals: acquiring SRL strategies within subject-matter contexts
examples: the article cites SRSD for writing, in which teachers model planning with the POW mnemonic, as an example of an integrated explicit approach
key_sources: Patrick Sins, Renske de Leeuw, Jaap de Brouwer, Emmy Vrieling-Teunter. (2024). Promoting explicit instruction of strategies for self-regulated learning: evaluating a teacher professional development program in primary education. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-023-09368-5

article_title: Technology-Supported Interventions and Learners’ Metacognition: A Three-Level Meta-Analysis
citation: Yijia Yuan & Yiran Du. (2026). Technology-Supported Interventions and Learners' Metacognition: A Three-Level Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10227-3
title: Interpret claims of metacognitive improvement in light of the regulatory process targeted and the measurement format used
description: Because metacognition is a multicomponent construct measured in different ways, the article recommends that conclusions about metacognitive improvement take account of both the metacognitive domain assessed and the measurement format. Self-reported awareness or strategy use is conceptually different from demonstrated monitoring or control during performance. The meta-analysis itself illustrates this: 95.7% of effect sizes relied on self-report, so the pooled association primarily reflects self-reported metacognitive regulation.
requirements: Studies should report which metacognitive domain (knowledge, regulation, composite) and which measurement format (self-report, performance/calibration, trace/log, researcher-rated) underlies each effect
constraints: The article states the validity of process-oriented indicators depends on whether observed behaviour can be linked convincingly to the regulatory construct of interest
target_learning_goals: Accurate interpretation of metacognitive outcome evidence in technology-supported learning research
examples: The meta-analysis used measurement format as a descriptive construct-validity audit rather than as an additional moderator, because non-self-report formats were sparse
key_sources: Yijia Yuan & Yiran Du. (2026). Technology-Supported Interventions and Learners' Metacognition: A Three-Level Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10227-3

article_title: Children’s Theory of Mind and Academic Achievement: a Meta-analysis on Reading Comprehension and Math Skills
citation: Lecce, S., Stagnitto, S. M., Mascheretti, S., Lampis, V., & Devine, R. T. (2026). Children's Theory of Mind and Academic Achievement: a Meta-analysis on Reading Comprehension and Math Skills. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10185-w
title: Individual-differences account of theory of mind as a cognitive resource for academic learning
description: The article adopts an individual-differences account of ToM, contrasting with earlier views of ToM as an innate, modular capacity. On this view, "there is an important variation in the children’s ability to put standard ToM concepts into use", these differences "reflect a stable trait rather than measurement error", and ToM may serve "as a cognitive resource that supports children’s learning and school achievement". The meta-analysis tests this account by estimating the ToM–achievement association and its independence from covariates.
requirements: Studies must measure ToM with behavioral tasks and correlate performance with academic achievement measures
constraints: The account concerns variability in using standard ToM concepts among school-aged children and adolescents, not the presence or absence of ToM itself
target_learners: children and adolescents aged approximately 2.5 to 17 years in formal schooling
examples: The meta-analysis operationalizes the account by pooling zero-order and partial correlations between behavioral ToM tasks and reading, math, and general achievement measures across 53 studies
key_sources: Lecce, S., Stagnitto, S. M., Mascheretti, S., Lampis, V., & Devine, R. T. (2026). Children's Theory of Mind and Academic Achievement: a Meta-analysis on Reading Comprehension and Math Skills. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10185-w

article_title: Bridging Reasoning in Mathematics and Science: a Document Analysis of Applying and Reasoning in the TIMSS Assessment Framework and the Case for Utilization of Resources
citation: Kyong Mi Choi, Jin Mun, Brian Hand. (2026). Bridging Reasoning in Mathematics and Science: a Document Analysis of Applying and Reasoning in the TIMSS Assessment Framework and the Case for Utilization of Resources. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10115-2
title: Integrated list of TIMSS applying and reasoning components across four assessment cycles (2011–2023)
description: The authors constructed an integrated list of cognitive components from the MR, MA, SR, and SA domains across the 2011, 2015, 2019, and 2023 TIMSS cycles, presented in Tables 2 and 3. The integration documented three revision types: new additions (e.g., Evaluate added to MR in 2015), component combinations (e.g., Represent and Model combined as Represent–Model), and name changes with unchanged descriptions (e.g., Select renamed Determine, later Formulate; Use Models changed to Interpret Models). This list served as the data corpus for identifying commonality and subset relationships between components.
requirements: Components were consolidated across cycles only when semantic meaning remained consistent despite nominal changes
constraints: The knowing domains were excluded from the integrated analysis
target_learners: K-12 mathematics and science students assessed in TIMSS
target_learning_goals: Characterizing applying and reasoning cognitive demands in international assessment
examples: The Mathematics Applying component Select in the 2011 framework was renamed Determine in later cycles with no changes to its description
key_sources: Kyong Mi Choi, Jin Mun, Brian Hand. (2026). Bridging Reasoning in Mathematics and Science: a Document Analysis of Applying and Reasoning in the TIMSS Assessment Framework and the Case for Utilization of Resources. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10115-2

article_title: Editor’s Note: Introducing Intervention Studies as a New Article Category
citation: Daniel H. Robinson. (2012). Editor's Note: Introducing Intervention Studies as a New Article Category. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-012-9209-8
title: Demonstrate the stability of potentially useful interventions through independent replication before trusting them
description: The editor argues, quoting Wainer, that replicability is the principal epistemological tenet of modern science: small initial studies tolerate false positives, and other investigators should rush to replicate so anomalous results are brushed aside. He suggests educational psychology should "demonstrate the stability of potentially useful interventions through independent replication" and states that EDPR encourages such replications.
requirements: Independent investigators replicating others' intervention studies rather than only producing novel studies
constraints: In educational psychology, the field generally does not attempt to replicate others' work, so it is unknown whether its literature is littered with anomalous findings
target_learning_goals: Establishing which interventions have stable, replicable effects
examples: EDPR retains its replication article category despite receiving few replication studies, in the hope that replications will be valued in the field
key_sources: Daniel H. Robinson. (2012). Editor's Note: Introducing Intervention Studies as a New Article Category. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-012-9209-8

article_title: Instructional Implications of Evolutionary Perspective on Human Cognitive Architecture as an Intelligent Natural Information Processing System
citation: Kalyuga, S. (2026). Instructional Implications of Evolutionary Perspective on Human Cognitive Architecture as an Intelligent Natural Information Processing System. Educational Psychology Review, 38, 33. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10135-6
title: Human cognition as an intelligent natural information processing system integrating primary and secondary processes
description: The article characterizes human cognitive architecture as a higher-level natural information processing system that, unlike other such systems, integrates evolved implicit (biologically primary) abilities with controlled explicit (biologically secondary) processes. It builds on five principles of natural information processing systems and a provisionally added explicit intention to learn principle. The article states that intelligent systems "are capable to intentionally, willingly switch to the controlled, explicit mode of operation" and generate biologically secondary knowledge in novel situations.
requirements: The framework presupposes the five established principles of natural information processing systems (information store, borrowing and reorganizing, randomness as genesis, narrow limits of change, environmental organizing and linking) as its base.
constraints: The article notes the explicit intention to learn principle "remains in need of direct empirical testing before it becomes a settled principle."
target_learning_goals: generating and learning biologically secondary knowledge
key_sources: Kalyuga, S. (2026). Instructional Implications of Evolutionary Perspective on Human Cognitive Architecture as an Intelligent Natural Information Processing System. Educational Psychology Review, 38, 33. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10135-6

article_title: Further Redefining Motivation with Situated Cognition, Power, and Belonging
citation: Daniel T. Hickey, Charmian Lam. (2026). Further Redefining Motivation with Situated Cognition, Power, and Belonging. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10219-3
title: Introduce accountability gradually along an inside-out continuum from self to recognized authorities
description: The article describes an "inside-out" approach to accountability, drawing on Lampert's continuum of justification, as essential to motivating productive disciplinary engagement. "Learners begin by explaining why their ideas make sense to themselves, then share their reasoning with trusted peers, proceed to peers who offer greater intellectual challenge, and eventually present their ideas to recognized authorities within and beyond the immediate learning community." At each stage students strengthen and refine their thinking while maintaining ownership of their ideas.
requirements: The progression must be carefully timed so learners can compare their ideas with authoritative perspectives and revise
constraints: Accountability should be introduced gradually rather than imposed at full rigor from the start
target_learning_goals: Maintaining ownership of ideas while refining thinking against disciplinary standards
examples: The article's progressive accountability structure: self, then safe peers, then challenging peers, then recognized authorities across contexts
key_sources: Daniel T. Hickey, Charmian Lam. (2026). Further Redefining Motivation with Situated Cognition, Power, and Belonging. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10219-3

article_title: School Belonging: Evidence, Experts, and Everyday Gaps
citation: Kelly-Ann Allen. (2025). School Belonging: Evidence, Experts, and Everyday Gaps. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10055-x
title: Integrative Framework of Belonging, extended for school contexts
description: The Integrative Framework of Belonging (Allen et al., 2021) organizes belonging around "four primary antecedents—perceptions, competencies, motivations, and opportunities—shaped by both systemic features and individual experiences". It was designed as a practical, non-prescriptive guide to address the how of fostering belonging for leaders, psychologists, and educators. This study extends it by showing school belonging is an ongoing, negotiated process also shaped by social hierarchies, variation in the need to belong, intersecting identities, and interpersonal, instructional, and institutional opportunities.
requirements: Requires synthesis of empirical, conceptual, and theoretical work on belonging within a unified structure, with flexibility to evolve as new knowledge emerges
constraints: The framework was never intended to be a prescriptive model; interviewees noted it gives limited attention to cultural and political contexts, historically colonized settings, structural and compositional aspects of schools, and social networks
target_learners: school students across primary, secondary, and higher education
target_learning_goals: fostering students' sense of school belonging to support motivation, wellbeing, and persistence
examples: Semi-structured interviews with ten internationally recognized scholars were organized around the framework's four antecedents and contextual, temporal, structural, and individual factors
key_sources: Kelly-Ann Allen. (2025). School Belonging: Evidence, Experts, and Everyday Gaps. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10055-x

article_title: Commentary: How can We Come to Terms when Discussing the Role of Effort from the Perspective of Cognitive Load Theory and Theories of Self-regulated Learning?
citation: Katharina Scheiter. (2025). Commentary: How can We Come to Terms when Discussing the Role of Effort from the Perspective of Cognitive Load Theory and Theories of Self-regulated Learning? Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10037-z
title: Move beyond fragmented mapping toward integrated theories of cognition and motivation linking CLT and SRL
description: The commentary argues that borrowing isolated assumptions, constructs, and measures across CLT and SRL — as the EMR framework research has done — has been empirically productive but has not produced a coherent theoretical integration. It recommends that "there is a necessity to formulate integrated theories of cognition and motivation by defining intertheoretical connections between existing theories and evaluating their congruence," either via a rigorous structuralist mapping or by inserting each account's missing assumptions into the other (e.g., a central executive in CLT; information-processing detail in SRL).
requirements: Identifying matches, contradictions, and non-correspondences between the two theories' assumption networks, ensuring no contradictions between networks
constraints: The structuralist integration approach is described as very rigorous but also very demanding; De Bruin and van Merriënboer (2017) estimated at least 25 years to develop a combined approach
target_learners: learners in complex, longer-duration self-regulated learning scenarios
target_learning_goals: comprehensive explanation of how effort is monitored and regulated at the meta-level and implemented at the object level of information processing
examples: The commentary notes van Merriënboer and Sluijsmans (2009) used CLT to derive instructional support recommendations for SRL without unifying the theories
key_sources: Katharina Scheiter. (2025). Commentary: How can We Come to Terms when Discussing the Role of Effort from the Perspective of Cognitive Load Theory and Theories of Self-regulated Learning? Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10037-z

article_title: Concreteness and Abstraction in Mathematics Education: A Taxonomy of the Semantic Landscape
citation: Julia Chatain, Charlotte Müller, Keny Chatain, Leon Calabrese, Manu Kapur. (2025). Concreteness and Abstraction in Mathematics Education: A Taxonomy of the Semantic Landscape. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10073-9
title: Interaction-level axes of concreteness are subjective, depending on the learner's perception of the representation
description: The taxonomy distinguishes five interaction-level axes relating to how the learner perceives the representation: familiarity, interest, simplicity, relevance, and sensoriality. The article states that "all axes at the interaction level depend on the representation and on the learners and are therefore related to the subjective experience of the learners." Designing along these axes requires knowing the targeted learners, and only actual measurement with target learners can ensure the desired effect occurred.
requirements: Designing according to these axes requires knowing who the targeted learners are
Only actual measurement with target learners can ensure that the desired effect indeed happened
constraints: Whether a designed effect occurs depends on learners' sensory abilities and on how and whether they choose to engage with the representation
target_learners: Mathematics learners in high school and higher education
target_learning_goals: Selecting representations whose perceived familiarity, interest, simplicity, relevance and sensoriality support learning
examples: A designer might create a physical and interactive object to increase engagement, but whether it increases interest depends on the learner
key_sources: Julia Chatain, Charlotte Müller, Keny Chatain, Leon Calabrese, Manu Kapur. (2025). Concreteness and Abstraction in Mathematics Education: A Taxonomy of the Semantic Landscape. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10073-9

article_title: How Rigorous is Active Learning Research in STEM Education? An Examination of Key Internal Validity Controls in Intervention Studies
citation: Amedee Marchand Martella, Ronald C. Martella, Jane K. Yatcilla, Alexandra Newson, Eric N. Shannon, Charissa Voorhis. (2023). How Rigorous is Active Learning Research in STEM Education? An Examination of Key Internal Validity Controls in Intervention Studies. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09826-1
title: Active learning intervention studies should incorporate internal validity controls such as randomization, group equivalence checks, matched instructors, dosage matching, and implementation fidelity assessment
description: The review recommends that active learning researchers apply a set of internal validity controls—randomized designs, group equivalence measures, attrition equivalency, matched sample size and instructor, operational definitions, dosage matching, matched time frame and content, equal dependent measures, and implementation fidelity—so that cause-and-effect claims about active learning interventions are warranted. It coded studies against these 12 controls and found "high percentages of articles that did not meet each internal validity control."
requirements: Studies must report group equivalence measures, operational definitions of both conditions, dosage, and implementation fidelity for the controls to be evaluable
constraints: The review examined undergraduate STEM/STEMM face-to-face courses comparing active learning with lecture or other active learning, so its recommendations are scoped to that literature
examples: The authors coded 176 Freeman et al. (2014) articles and a random sample of 84 post-2015 articles against the 12 controls and found no article met all of them
key_sources: Amedee Marchand Martella, Ronald C. Martella, Jane K. Yatcilla, Alexandra Newson, Eric N. Shannon, Charissa Voorhis. (2023). How Rigorous is Active Learning Research in STEM Education? An Examination of Key Internal Validity Controls in Intervention Studies. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09826-1

article_title: Educational Responses Toward Community Violence: A Critical Analysis of Perspectives on Causes and Solutions
citation: van Dijk, A, de Haan, M & de Winter, M 2026, 'Educational Responses Toward Community Violence : A Critical Analysis of Perspectives on Causes and Solutions', Review of Educational Research, vol. 96, no. 3, pp. 829-869. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543251324491
title: Integrative review of theory and research on educational interventions to counter community violence
description: The article itself is an integrative review: it states "This paper presents an integrative review of theory and research on the broad range of educational interventions to counter community violence." Motivated by "alarming rates of community violence and the detrimental impact on youth and communities", the review spans multiple disciplines, critically analyzes distinctions in perspectives, objectives, and strategies, and yields the multidisciplinary taxonomy and the coherent overview of current educational responses that structure the paper's contributions.
requirements: Requires theory and research on the broad range of educational interventions to counter community violence
constraints: The review notes strategies for transformation of social systems are underrepresented in the literature it covers
examples: The review establishes a multidisciplinary taxonomy of distinguishable approaches based on critical analysis of perspectives, objectives, and strategies
key_sources: van Dijk, A, de Haan, M & de Winter, M 2026, 'Educational Responses Toward Community Violence : A Critical Analysis of Perspectives on Causes and Solutions', Review of Educational Research, vol. 96, no. 3, pp. 829-869. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543251324491

article_title: Impact of In-Service Professional Development Programs for Early Childhood Teachers on Quality Ratings and Child Outcomes: A Meta-Analysis
citation: F. Egert, R.G. Fukkink, A.G. Eckhardt. (2018). Impact of In-Service Professional Development Programs for Early Childhood Teachers on Quality Ratings and Child Outcomes: A Meta-Analysis. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/0034654317751918
title: Invest in in-service professional development for ECEC professionals as a lever for raising process quality and child outcomes
description: The article supports investing in in-service training for early childhood professionals because its synthesis shows such training reliably raises externally rated process quality and, through quality improvement, child development. It concludes that "quality improvement is a key mechanism to accelerate the development of young children," with a medium teacher-level effect (ES = 0.68) and a small but significant child-level effect (ES = 0.14).
requirements: Training should target improvements in pedagogical process quality as rated by external observers
Programs should be evaluated with (quasi)-experimental designs to verify quality and child outcomes
constraints: Child-level effects are small and depend on the training also improving quality ratings
target_learners: in-service early childhood education and care professionals and the young children they teach
target_learning_goals: improving pedagogical process quality and accelerating young children's development
examples: The meta-analysis aggregated 36 studies with 2,891 teachers on quality ratings and nine studies with 4,504 children on child development
key_sources: F. Egert, R.G. Fukkink, A.G. Eckhardt. (2018). Impact of In-Service Professional Development Programs for Early Childhood Teachers on Quality Ratings and Child Outcomes: A Meta-Analysis. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/0034654317751918

article_title: What kind of individual support activities in interventions foster pre-service and beginning teachers’ self-efficacy? A meta-analysis
citation: Mok, S. Y., Rupp, D., & Holzberger, D. (2022). What kind of individual support activities in interventions foster pre-service and beginning teachers' self-efficacy? A meta-analysis. Preprint submitted for peer-review.
title: Individual support activities taxonomy linking mentoring activities to Bandura's sources of self-efficacy
description: The article organizes mentoring-type interventions around individual support activities provided by support persons (mentors, cooperating teachers, supervisors): "modeling of lesson planning and teaching practices, giving feedback on a lesson plan, giving feedback on observed lessons, providing opportunities to observe teaching practices enacted by a support person, and guiding reflection processes". These activities are mapped onto Bandura's sources of self-efficacy: modeling activates vicarious experiences, feedback serves as verbal persuasion, and guided reflection relates to verbal persuasion and psychological and affective cues, with mastery experiences in authentic teaching situations as the most impactful source.
requirements: A support person (mentor, cooperating teacher, instructor, or supervisor) collaborating with the pre-service or beginning teacher
constraints: The article focuses on mastery experiences within a teaching practicum or field experience that closely resembles authentic teaching situations in schools
target_learners: Beginning teachers in their first year of teaching
examples: The meta-analysis dummy-coded each activity (code 1 if it occurred in a study, code 0 if not) and tested them as moderators of intervention effects on teacher self-efficacy
key_sources: Mok, S. Y., Rupp, D., & Holzberger, D. (2022). What kind of individual support activities in interventions foster pre-service and beginning teachers' self-efficacy? A meta-analysis. Preprint submitted for peer-review. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2023.100552

article_title: What kind of individual support activities in interventions foster pre-service and beginning teachers’ self-efficacy? A meta-analysis
citation: Mok, S. Y., Rupp, D., & Holzberger, D. (2022). What kind of individual support activities in interventions foster pre-service and beginning teachers' self-efficacy? A meta-analysis. Preprint submitted for peer-review.
title: Include feedback on lesson plans in interventions for early career teachers to foster teacher self-efficacy
description: The article recommends that interventions for pre-service and beginning teachers include feedback on lesson plans, because this activity "has the potential to increase teacher self-efficacy above and beyond the averaged intervention effect". Support persons providing feedback on lesson plans before the lesson is taught serves as verbal persuasion and helps early career teachers imagine how they can be successful. The article discusses implications for future interventions regarding teacher self-efficacy for early career teachers based on this moderator finding.
requirements: A support person with appropriate expertise who reviews and discusses the pre-service or beginning teacher's lesson plans before teaching
constraints: The moderator effect slightly missed the .05 significance level in both meta-regression models and was no longer significant in the Wald contrast after methodological controls; the article calls for more intervention studies to provide a solid base
target_learners: Beginning teachers in their first year of teaching
examples: In the meta-analysis, feedback on lesson plans was coded in j = 5 studies and k = 7 effects, and showed a large moderator effect (g = 1.033, p = .056) in model 1
key_sources: Mok, S. Y., Rupp, D., & Holzberger, D. (2022). What kind of individual support activities in interventions foster pre-service and beginning teachers' self-efficacy? A meta-analysis. Preprint submitted for peer-review. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2023.100552

article_title: Why do we know so little about the factors associated with gifted underachievement? A systematic literature review
citation: White, Sonia, Graham, Linda, & Blaas, Sabrina (2018). Why do we know so little about the factors associated with gifted underachievement? A systematic literature review. Educational Research Review, 24, pp. 55-66. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2018.03.001
title: Use individually referenced benchmarks, not researcher-determined cut-offs, when identifying gifted underachievement
description: This principle holds that identification of gifted underachievement should compare a student's achievement to their own expected achievement based on cognitive ability, rather than to an arbitrary group cut-off set by researchers. The review argues researcher-determined benchmarks are "conceptually inconsistent with the discrepancy model" and can misclassify capable students. It recommends designs aligned with the discrepancy model that underpins the definition of gifted underachievement.
requirements: Studies must report both a cognitive ability measure and an achievement measure so an individual discrepancy can be computed
constraints: The review notes only three of nine reviewed studies used individually referenced benchmarks; the approach assumes gifted students' characteristics can vary across domains
target_learners: intellectually gifted elementary and secondary school students
target_learning_goals: accurate identification of gifted underachievement for research and support
examples: Dixon et al. (2006), Obergriesser and Stoeger (2015) and Stoeger et al. (2008) identified underachievers whose achievement was more than one standard deviation below their own expected achievement based on cognitive ability score
key_sources: White, Sonia, Graham, Linda, & Blaas, Sabrina (2018). Why do we know so little about the factors associated with gifted underachievement? A systematic literature review. Educational Research Review, 24, pp. 55-66. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2018.03.001

article_title: Beyond inquiry or direct instruction: Pressing issues for designing impactful science learning opportunities
citation: Ton de Jong, Ard W. Lazonder, Clark A. Chinn, Frank Fischer, Janice Gobert, Cindy E. Hmelo-Silver, Ken R. Koedinger, Joseph S. Krajcik, Eleni A. Kyza, Marcia C. Linn, Margus Pedaste, Katharina Scheiter, Zacharias C. Zacharia. (2024). Beyond inquiry or direct instruction: Pressing issues for designing impactful science learning opportunities. Educational Research Review, 44. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2024.100623
title: Inquiry-based learning is grounded in both cognitive (knowledge-integration, generative learning) and sociocultural theories
description: The article argues inquiry-based instruction is not theory-free: cognitive theories explain its success through "the active integration of knowledge," generative learning activities, and schema (re)construction, while sociocultural theory treats learning as "changes in patterns of participation in social activity" supported by scaffolds, tools, and collaborative engagement with meaningful tasks. Together these accounts explain why guided inquiry fosters deep conceptual knowledge and motivation, and they guide the design of instructional interventions.
requirements: Cognitive effort must stay within learners' cognitive capacities, supported by scaffolds and guidance.
target_learning_goals: Deep conceptual knowledge in science domains
examples: The article cites Eysink et al. (2009) as a cognitive explanation and traces the sociocultural line to Rousseau, Dewey, and Vygotsky.
key_sources: Ton de Jong, Ard W. Lazonder, Clark A. Chinn, Frank Fischer, Janice Gobert, Cindy E. Hmelo-Silver, Ken R. Koedinger, Joseph S. Krajcik, Eleni A. Kyza, Marcia C. Linn, Margus Pedaste, Katharina Scheiter, Zacharias C. Zacharia. (2024). Beyond inquiry or direct instruction: Pressing issues for designing impactful science learning opportunities. Educational Research Review, 44. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2024.100623

article_title: Theoretical foundations and approaches in research on educational escape rooms: A systematic review
citation: Vorderobermeier, A., Abel, J., & Sailer, M. (2024). Theoretical foundations and approaches in research on educational escape rooms: A systematic review. Educational Research Review, 44, 100625. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2024.100625
title: Interweave theory, didactic instruction, and practice in future EER research and development
description: The review's central recommendation is that future EER research move beyond superficial name-dropping toward genuine interweaving of theoretical foundations with didactic decisions and practical implementation, because "the theoretical foundation in current research on EERs is weak". Studies like Veldkamp et al. (2022) and Hamilton et al. (2021), which empirically investigated whether and how a named theory (e.g., collaborative learning) is promoted in an EER, "can be particularly valuable for instructional decisions" and reveal mechanisms behind successful learning environments.
requirements: Research designs must connect a named theory to specific didactic decisions and measure the outcome empirically
constraints: The recommendation rests on only a few included studies reaching the empirical-validation pattern
target_learning_goals: understanding mechanisms behind successful learning environments with EERs
examples: Veldkamp et al. (2022) studied collaborative learning in an EER through pre/post-test, experience questionnaire, interviews, and classroom observation
Hamilton et al. (2021) formulated research hypotheses comparing linear and open path escape room settings
key_sources: Vorderobermeier, A., Abel, J., & Sailer, M. (2024). Theoretical foundations and approaches in research on educational escape rooms: A systematic review. Educational Research Review, 44, 100625. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2024.100625

article_title: Interactivity in Video-based Models
citation: Wouters, P., Tabbers, H. K., & Paas, F. (2007). Interactivity in Video-based Models. Educational Psychology Review, 19, 327–342. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-007-9045-4
title: Guidelines for interactivity in video-based modeling mapped to cognitive processes and skill-acquisition stages
description: The review identifies a set of guidelines for implementing interactivity in video-based models, classified by required prior knowledge, behavioral component, cognitive processes supported, and stage of the social cognitive model. As the abstract states, "Pacing, cues, control over appearance, prediction, working in dyads, personalized task selection, and reflection prompts are identified as guidelines that might support learners to interactively construct schemas." Each guideline specifies who implements control (learner or system), which processes (elaboration, induction, compilation, strengthening) it mediates, and the stage where it applies.
requirements: Implementation must match the learner's level of prior knowledge, since a guideline effective for low-experience learners may be ineffective for high-experience learners
constraints: The guidelines are presented in isolation and it is not clear how they are related or whether an ideal sequence exists; hardly any research has investigated interactivity in cognitive modeling directly
target_learners: novices through experienced learners of complex motor and cognitive skills
target_learning_goals: schema construction and schema automation during observation and practice of modeled skills
examples: Table 1 classifies each guideline; e.g., dissolving cues for low prior knowledge in the observation stage, personalized task selection for high prior knowledge in the self-control and self-regulation stages, and personalized task selection with part-task practice for compilation and strengthening
key_sources: Wouters, P., Tabbers, H. K., & Paas, F. (2007). Interactivity in Video-based Models. Educational Psychology Review, 19, 327–342. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-007-9045-4

article_title: Integrating Fractions into Physical Education classes can improve Mathematical Performance in 11–13-Year-Olds - The Basketball Mathematics project
citation: Jensen, O. E., Damsgaard, L., Rohde, R. A., Nielsen, G., Fosnaes, O., Hauge, J., Wienecke, J. (2026). Integrating Fractions into Physical Education classes can improve Mathematical Performance in 11–13-Year-Olds - The Basketball Mathematics project. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10175-y
title: Integrate subject-specific academic content into existing PE lessons to strengthen learning without adding instructional hours
description: The article advocates targeted integration of academic content into physical education as an add-in to the regular timetable. It reports that "the structure of the school timetable can be rethought without necessarily adding more hours" and that "with a small change physical education-classes can contribute meaningfully to learning and academic performance." The BM program replaced one weekly PE lesson, keeping total instructional hours constant while adding mathematics practice.
requirements: Integration must be thoughtfully designed and targeted rather than merging all subjects; mathematical content was tailored to each class's proficiency level with input from the mathematics teacher.
constraints: Teachers were instructed not to conduct similar mixed exercises between pre- and post-testing; the authors note alignment between gym and classroom content could have been stronger.
examples: One weekly 60-minute BM session replaced regular PE for 8 weeks; each session had an introduction, warm-up, two-three integrated exercises, and a concluding summary, with mathematical themes integrated into basketball drills.
key_sources: Jensen, O. E., Damsgaard, L., Rohde, R. A., Nielsen, G., Fosnaes, O., Hauge, J., Wienecke, J. (2026). Integrating Fractions into Physical Education classes can improve Mathematical Performance in 11–13-Year-Olds - The Basketball Mathematics project. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10175-y

article_title: Interventions as Probes of Cognitive Architecture: Commentary on Zhang et al. (2026)
citation: David Moreau, Kristina Wiebels. (2026). Interventions as Probes of Cognitive Architecture: Commentary on Zhang et al. (2026). Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10150-7
title: Design interventions to maximize theoretical insight, not only efficacy
description: The article proposes that when interventions are leveraged as probes of cognitive architecture, their design should prioritize interpretability alongside feasibility. It enumerates principles: "First, temporal specificity is critical." — aligning assessment timing with the perturbation's time course; treating content alignment between intervention context and measurement as a design variable; combining broad perturbations with specific measurement; and anticipating null effects in the inferential framework. Dissociations across aligned and non-aligned measures provide direct evidence about contextual recruitment of cognitive processes.
requirements: Cognitive assessment must be aligned with the expected time course of the perturbation, and measures must be sufficiently challenging to engage the processes of interest
constraints: When task demands are too low, even well-aligned measures may fail to reveal modulation
target_learners: school-aged learners in authentic classroom settings
target_learning_goals: mapping which cognitive processes are modifiable, under what conditions, and at what timescales
examples: Brief exercise embedded into classroom routines without altering instructional content, paired with measures differing in instructional alignment, as in Zhang et al. (2026).
key_sources: David Moreau, Kristina Wiebels. (2026). Interventions as Probes of Cognitive Architecture: Commentary on Zhang et al. (2026). Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10150-7

article_title: How to Optimize Self-Assessment Accuracy in Cognitive Skill Acquisition When Learning from Worked Examples
citation: Waldeyer, J., Endres, T., Roelle, J., Baars, M., & Renkl, A. (2024). How to Optimize Self-Assessment Accuracy in Cognitive Skill Acquisition When Learning from Worked Examples. Educational Psychology Review, 36, 103. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09944-4
title: Inform learners about the to-be-monitored self-assessment cue before, not after, the problem-solving phase
description: When learners must self-assess their understanding at the end of an initial problem-solving phase, tell them at the start of that phase which cue they should monitor for their self-assessment. In Experiment 1, learners "informed about the to-be-monitored cue already before the problem-solving phase showed better self-assessment accuracy" than learners informed only afterwards, apparently because attending to the cue during problem-solving is less error-prone than reconstructing it afterwards. The authors found no evidence that this advance information overloaded learners or compromised problem-solving.
requirements: Learners must be told the specific cue (e.g., problem-solving performance or ability to explain) they will later use for their self-assessment.
constraints: The benefit was shown when mental effort was relatively low (M = 5.37 on a 9-point scale); the article notes high cognitive load could in principle compromise performance or lead learners to disengage from monitoring.
target_learners: university students in self-regulated example-based learning
target_learning_goals: accurate self-assessment of understanding after initial problem-solving
examples: In Experiment 1, learners in the before conditions received instructions such as "please pay attention to how well you can solve the problems" at the start of the problem-solving phase, with the note "You will need this information afterwards."
key_sources: Waldeyer, J., Endres, T., Roelle, J., Baars, M., & Renkl, A. (2024). How to Optimize Self-Assessment Accuracy in Cognitive Skill Acquisition When Learning from Worked Examples. Educational Psychology Review, 36, 103. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09944-4

article_title: Special Issue on Cognitive Load Theory: Editorial
citation: Paul Ginns & Jimmie Leppink. (2019). Special Issue on Cognitive Load Theory: Editorial. Educational Psychology Review, 31, 255–259. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-019-09474-4
title: Integrated working memory model with a common finite attentional resource across modalities
description: Sepp et al. (2019) propose a new integrated working memory model to help understand how the human motor system may influence learning and cognition. Its central tenet is "a common and finite attentional resource that can be distributed across multiple modalities." The model may help researchers understand effects of gestures and other movements on cognitive load, and the authors call for increased use of eye tracking and motion tracking technology in future experiments.
requirements: Future experiments using eye tracking and motion tracking technology, which may also capture fine hand and finger movements relevant to tracing effects
target_learners: learners in multimedia and movement-rich learning environments
target_learning_goals: understanding effects of gestures and movement on cognitive load
examples: Motion tracking may measure full body movement and fine hand and finger movements, shedding light on effects of tracing on cognitive load
key_sources: Paul Ginns & Jimmie Leppink. (2019). Special Issue on Cognitive Load Theory: Editorial. Educational Psychology Review, 31, 255–259. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-019-09474-4

article_title: An Interactive Layers Model of Self-Regulated Learning and Cognitive Load
citation: Joachim Wirth, Ferdinand Stebner, Melanie Trypke, Corinna Schuster, & Detlev Leutner. (2020). An Interactive Layers Model of Self-Regulated Learning and Cognitive Load. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09568-4
title: Interactive layers model of self-regulated learning and cognitive load
description: The article proposes a model that represents self-regulated learning across three layers — a content layer, a learning strategy layer, and a metacognitive layer — each spanning sensory memory, working memory, and long-term memory. It distinguishes conscious self-regulation in working memory, which induces cognitive load, from unconscious self-regulation initiated by resonant states in sensory memory, which does not. Layers interact through monitoring and control processes, both consciously in working memory and automatically in sensory memory.
requirements: The model assumes the three structural memory components proposed by Atkinson and Shiffrin (1968): sensory memory, working memory, and long-term memory
constraints: The model is proposed as a theoretical framework substantiated by a narrative review; the authors state it must be tested empirically in future research
target_learners: learners across educational levels engaged in self-regulated learning
examples: The authors use the model to re-interpret inconsistent findings on self-regulation correlations, questionnaire validity, the underconfidence-with-practice effect, and the expertise reversal effect
key_sources: Joachim Wirth, Ferdinand Stebner, Melanie Trypke, Corinna Schuster, & Detlev Leutner. (2020). An Interactive Layers Model of Self-Regulated Learning and Cognitive Load. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09568-4

article_title: How Representation Matters: Conceptualizing Systemic Racism to Develop Diversity Research Agendas for Undergraduate STEM Education
citation: Sedlacek, Q., Villa, A. M., III, Friend, M., Pérez, G., Dozier, S., Haeger, H., Lomelí, K., & Mejia, J. A. (2025). How Representation Matters: Conceptualizing Systemic Racism to Develop Diversity Research Agendas for Undergraduate STEM Education. Educational Psychology Review, 37:49. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10021-7
title: Intersectionality as a framework for analyzing interlocking oppressions in STEM education research
description: The review presents intersectionality theory as a framework holding that multiple systems of oppression must be analyzed together rather than in isolation. It states that "Intersectionality theory suggests that since multiple systems of oppression shape our world simultaneously with each other, these systems of oppression cannot necessarily be understood in isolation from each other," forming a matrix of domination. In diversity research, it pushes researchers to center multiply marginalized persons, such as Black women and LGBTQ+ people of color, to avoid unidimensional analyses focused only on racism.
requirements: Researchers must theorize racialized and gendered oppression together rather than isolating effects of racism from sexism or cisheterosexism
constraints: The review notes intersectionality is not an Oppression Olympics ranking identities by oppression, nor a tool to explore infinite combinations of difference
target_learning_goals: avoiding overlooking the needs and experiences of multiply marginalized populations in STEM diversity research
examples: The review cites Rodriguez and Blaney (2021)'s qualitative study in which Latina students reported belonging experiences distinct from their male Latino peers
key_sources: Sedlacek, Q., Villa, A. M., III, Friend, M., Pérez, G., Dozier, S., Haeger, H., Lomelí, K., & Mejia, J. A. (2025). How Representation Matters: Conceptualizing Systemic Racism to Develop Diversity Research Agendas for Undergraduate STEM Education. Educational Psychology Review, 37:49. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10021-7

article_title: How Do We Deal with Uncertain Information? Effects of Verbal and Visual Expressions of Uncertainty on Learning
citation: Glaser, M., Lengyel, D., Toulouse, C., & Schwan, S. (2022). How Do We Deal with Uncertain Information? Effects of Verbal and Visual Expressions of Uncertainty on Learning. Educational Psychology Review (2022) 34:1097–1131. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-022-09659-4
title: Integrated model of processing evidence and its uncertainty values in multimedia learning
description: The article proposes an integrated theoretical approach combining the knowledge generation model for visual analytics (Sacha et al.), the cognitive theory of multimedia learning, and the multimedia principle to explain how learners process content marked with uncertainty. The model "describes how knowledge is built based on the awareness of uncertainty markers and trust building cues" and identifies "an exploration loop, a verification loop, and a knowledge generation loop" of cognitive processing. It predicts that certain content is processed with higher priority and that the multimedia effect extends to metainformation such as uncertainty values.
requirements: Learners must become aware of uncertainty information and hold it in working memory for it to influence processing
constraints: Presented as a first step in validating the integrated model, applied to archeological reconstructions with deficient/epistemic uncertainty
target_learners: Students and laypersons learning scientific content with uncertain information
target_learning_goals: Learning scientific content while understanding the epistemic uncertainty of that content
examples: The study operationalized the model with temple reconstructions whose elements carried lexical hedges and visual uncertainty markers in a 4×3 design
key_sources: Glaser, M., Lengyel, D., Toulouse, C., & Schwan, S. (2022). How Do We Deal with Uncertain Information? Effects of Verbal and Visual Expressions of Uncertainty on Learning. Educational Psychology Review (2022) 34:1097–1131. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-022-09659-4

article_title: Culture, Motivation, Self-Regulation, and the Impactful Work of Dennis M. McInerney
citation: Bembenutty, H., Liem, G.A.D., Allen, K.A., King, R.B., Martin, A.J., Marsh, H.W., Craven, R.G., Kaplan, A., Schunk, D.H., DiBenedetto, M.K., & Datu, J.A.D. (2023). Culture, Motivation, Self-Regulation, and the Impactful Work of Dennis M. McInerney. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09743-3
title: Conduct Indigenous educational research to test the cross-cultural applicability of motivation theories
description: This principle, drawn from McInerney's agenda as described in the tribute, holds that motivation research should include Indigenous educational research so that mainstream theories are examined "to understand the extent to which mainstream motivation theories apply to culturally diverse groups". It directs researchers to subject established motivation theories to cross-cultural testing rather than assuming universality.
requirements: Motivation theories must be tested against data from culturally diverse groups, including Indigenous students, rather than only mainstream samples.
constraints: The tribute presents this as McInerney's belief and research agenda, not as a validated recommendation with evidence in the accessible text.
examples: The tribute notes McInerney dedicated a significant part of his career to researching problems associated with studying culture in motivation research.
key_sources: Bembenutty, H., Liem, G.A.D., Allen, K.A., King, R.B., Martin, A.J., Marsh, H.W., Craven, R.G., Kaplan, A., Schunk, D.H., DiBenedetto, M.K., & Datu, J.A.D. (2023). Culture, Motivation, Self-Regulation, and the Impactful Work of Dennis M. McInerney. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09743-3

article_title: Culture, Motivation, Self-Regulation, and the Impactful Work of Dennis M. McInerney
citation: Bembenutty, H., Liem, G.A.D., Allen, K.A., King, R.B., Martin, A.J., Marsh, H.W., Craven, R.G., Kaplan, A., Schunk, D.H., DiBenedetto, M.K., & Datu, J.A.D. (2023). Culture, Motivation, Self-Regulation, and the Impactful Work of Dennis M. McInerney. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09743-3
title: Inventory of School Motivation as a cross-culturally validated motivation measure
description: The Inventory of School Motivation (ISM) is a motivation instrument McInerney developed and validated across cultural groups; the tribute's reference list cites work on its "Cross cultural model testing: Inventory of School Motivation" and its cross-cultural validation with Navajo and Anglo students, as well as measurement-invariance testing across Chinese and US college students. It served as a key measurement tool in his cross-cultural motivation research program.
requirements: The instrument requires cross-cultural validation and invariance testing before use with new cultural groups.
constraints: The accessible text describes the ISM only through reference-list titles; no psychometric details are printed.
examples: The reference list cites McInerney and Sinclair's cross-cultural model testing of the Inventory of School Motivation and its validation with Navajo and Anglo students.

article_title: Teacher Expectations and Self-Determination Theory: Considering Convergence and Divergence of Theories
citation: Lisette Hornstra, Kim Stroet, Christine Rubie-Davies, Annaline Flint. (2023). Teacher Expectations and Self-Determination Theory: Considering Convergence and Divergence of Theories. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09788-4
title: Integrated HET–SDT model with need satisfaction mediating between teaching practices and student outcomes
description: The article proposes an integrative model (Fig. 1) combining high expectation theory and self-determination theory. It maps HET's three principles and SDT's need-supportive teaching dimensions as convergent teaching practices, with teacher beliefs and contextual conditions shaping whether teachers enact them. The model's central mechanism is that "need satisfaction" mediates between teaching practices and student outcomes: practices may be effective "because they help to satisfy students' needs and help stu dents to feel autonomous, competent, and related to others." The mediational pathways are offered as hypotheses for future empirical work.
requirements: Empirical work is needed to test the hypothesized mediational pathways from teaching practices through need satisfaction to student outcomes
constraints: Some relations in the model (dashed arrows) are stated to be beyond the scope of the present paper
target_learners: school students in primary and secondary classrooms
examples: The model positions mixed ability grouping (HET) as expected to satisfy students' need for competence (SDT), a pathway the authors propose for empirical investigation
key_sources: Lisette Hornstra, Kim Stroet, Christine Rubie-Davies, Annaline Flint. (2023). Teacher Expectations and Self-Determination Theory: Considering Convergence and Divergence of Theories. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09788-4

article_title: A Framework for Motivating Teacher-Student Relationships
citation: Robinson, C. D. (2022). A Framework for Motivating Teacher-Student Relationships. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-022-09706-0
title: Design TSR interventions to target teachers' motivational beliefs, not just behaviors
description: The article recommends that interventions to improve teacher-student relationships be grounded in the Motivating TSRs framework by addressing teachers' role beliefs, values, and relational self-efficacy rather than only delivering relationship-building techniques. It hypothesizes that past interventions had "mixed success in improving TSRs" partly because they "do not adequately address teachers' underlying beliefs about TSRs." Interventions aligned with teachers' ideal roles and values should be more successful at changing behavior.
requirements: Intervention designers must diagnose which of the three beliefs (role, value, self-efficacy) is limiting a teacher's motivation
Belief-targeting components should draw on the four sources of self-efficacy, such as mastery and vicarious experiences
constraints: The evidence base for TSR interventions is small and correlational research cannot confirm that improving TSRs causes improved outcomes
target_learners: Teacher educators and professional development designers
target_learning_goals: Improving the quality of teacher-student relationships
Sustaining teachers' motivation to invest in relationship-building
examples: The article proposes that interventions leveraging mastery experiences, vicarious models, verbal persuasion, and positive affective states could raise teachers' relational self-efficacy and thereby their relationship-building efforts
key_sources: Robinson, C. D. (2022). A Framework for Motivating Teacher-Student Relationships. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-022-09706-0

article_title: Learning to Read in Chinese: A Meta-analytic Structural Equation Modeling Analysis of Cognitive-Linguistic Skills in Chinese Word Reading
citation: Learning to read in Chinese: A Meta-analytic Structural Equation Modeling analysis of cognitive-linguistic skills in Chinese word reading. (2025). https://osf.io/s7tjp/?view_only=4865c0558529407aa0a9e35777761117
title: Choose early literacy instruction methods in awareness of their trade-off between phonological and morphological reliance in Chinese word reading
description: The article's moderator results show that how children are taught to read reshapes which skills carry word reading: phonetic coding systems (Pinyin, Zhuyin Fuhao) strengthen reliance on PA while reducing reliance on MA, whereas look-and-say instruction leaves greater weight on MA. The article reports that phonological instruction via Pinyin and Bopomofo "has been found to promote children's sub-syllabic awareness, such as rime/onset awareness and phonemic awareness." Educators should therefore expect instructional method, not just script, to shape the skill profile children draw on.
requirements: Requires knowing which instructional method (phonetic coding system vs. look-and-say) a child population receives when interpreting or planning assessment of cognitive-linguistic skills
constraints: Instructional method was coded from study site (mainland China/Taiwan vs. Hong Kong), so script and instructional differences were confounded in the coding; the article cautions that interpretations of site differences need caution
target_learners: Children learning to read Chinese in kindergarten and elementary school
target_learning_goals: Word reading in Chinese; phonological and morphological awareness
examples: The MASEM compared Hong Kong look-and-say children with mainland China and Taiwan children taught via Pinyin or Zhuyin Fuhao, finding Δβ = .071 for PA and Δβ = -.093 for MA
key_sources: Learning to read in Chinese: A Meta-analytic Structural Equation Modeling analysis of cognitive-linguistic skills in Chinese word reading. (2025). https://osf.io/s7tjp/?view_only=4865c0558529407aa0a9e35777761117

article_title: Does Individual Performance Feedback Increase the Use of Retrieval Practice?
citation: Luotong Hui, Anique B. H. de Bruin, Jeroen Donkers, & Jeroen J. G. van Merriënboer. (2021). Does Individual Performance Feedback Increase the Use of Retrieval Practice? Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09604-x
title: Show learners their own performance feedback comparing strategies so they experience a strategy's benefits before expecting them to adopt it
description: This principle holds that learners adopt an effective learning strategy more readily when shown their own actual learning outcomes under that strategy versus an alternative, rather than only receiving general instruction about the strategy's benefits. The article found that "individual feedback led to enhanced use in the long term by those who had actually experienced its benefits". General instruction alone did not sustain long-term use.
requirements: Learners must actually experience the strategy's benefit (obtain a higher score under it) for the feedback to change their strategy choices
Feedback must compare the learner's own outcomes across strategies rather than only presenting class averages or general claims
constraints: Only about half of students benefited from retrieval practice in these experiments, so many learners will not experience the benefit
Individual feedback showed no impact when students who benefited from restudy or had equal scores were included
The general-feedback group came to consider retrieval practice less useful after trying it, so instruction without personal outcome information may backfire in the long term
target_learners: university students studying new factual material
target_learning_goals: adoption of effective learning strategies such as retrieval practice
examples: In Experiment 2, students on day 8 received either individual feedback showing their own 7-day delayed test scores after each strategy, or general feedback presenting the average rate at which retrieval practice was found superior to restudy from prior studies
key_sources: Luotong Hui, Anique B. H. de Bruin, Jeroen Donkers, & Jeroen J. G. van Merriënboer. (2021). Does Individual Performance Feedback Increase the Use of Retrieval Practice? Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09604-x

article_title: Making the Executive ‘Function’ for the Foundations of Mathematics: the Need for Explicit Theories of Change for Early Interventions
citation: Scerif, G., Blakey, E., Gattas, S., Hawes, Z., Howard, S., Merkley, R., O'Connor, R., & Simms, V. (2023). Making the Executive 'Function' for the Foundations of Mathematics: the Need for Explicit Theories of Change for Early Interventions. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09824-3
title: Developmental cognitive neuroscience account: interactive specialisation explains why isolated EF training transfers poorly in children
description: The review argues that adult models of EF transfer — training frontoparietal control networks to better gate expert systems — apply poorly to developing brains. Because "control networks (involved in EFs) and expert systems (involved in mathematical expertise) are not yet as efficient and specialised as in their adult counterparts", training them in isolation is inefficient; instead they should co-ordinate so they specialise via interactive specialisation processes. The account also notes that session number does not moderate computerised training gains, suggesting such training improves task-specific strategies rather than underlying systems, and that optimal arousal levels support frontoparietal engagement.
requirements: Interventions should co-ordinate developing control and expert systems rather than training control networks in isolation
constraints: The account is framed for developing (child) brains; the review notes EFs remain relevant to adult mathematics, especially for novel and challenging content
target_learning_goals: Understanding mechanisms of transfer from EF training to mathematics
examples: The review cites child–adult differences in frontoparietal recruitment during mathematics, and adults showing child-like recruitment for novel tasks such as negative numbers
key_sources: Scerif, G., Blakey, E., Gattas, S., Hawes, Z., Howard, S., Merkley, R., O'Connor, R., & Simms, V. (2023). Making the Executive 'Function' for the Foundations of Mathematics: the Need for Explicit Theories of Change for Early Interventions. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09824-3

article_title: Self-Regulated Learning Interventions for Pre-service Teachers: a Systematic Review
citation: Alazne Fernández Ortube, Ernesto Panadero, Charlotte Dignath. (2024). Self-Regulated Learning Interventions for Pre-service Teachers: a Systematic Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09919-5
title: SRL interventions for pre-service teachers rely mainly on indirect instruction within constructivist environments, with a guiding trainer
description: The review classifies pedagogical characteristics into direct promotion of SRL (direct instruction of strategies, work on beliefs, specific methodologies) and indirect activation of SRL (constructivist environments where learners drive their own regulated learning). Among the coded interventions, 34 promoted constructivist environments, pre-service teachers were given opportunities to "actively explore, reflect, and seek for learning" in 62 interventions, and the trainer acted as a guide in 50. Direct instruction most often took the form of metacognitive training.
requirements: A learning environment offering meaningful activities and cooperation with peers and instructors so learners can practise self-regulation and take responsibility for their learning
constraints: Only five interventions targeted pre-service teachers' beliefs towards SRL and learning
target_learners: pre-service teachers in initial teacher education
examples: Interventions used cooperative learning environments and problem-based learning as indirect instruction; direct instruction used metacognitive training, concept maps and rubrics
key_sources: Alazne Fernández Ortube, Ernesto Panadero, Charlotte Dignath. (2024). Self-Regulated Learning Interventions for Pre-service Teachers: a Systematic Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09919-5

article_title: Integration in the Achievement Motivation Literature and the Hierarchical Model of Achievement Motivation
citation: Andrew J. Elliot · Nicolas Sommet. (2023). Integration in the Achievement Motivation Literature and the Hierarchical Model of Achievement Motivation. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09785-7
title: Prioritize integrative research over siloed, competitive study of motivational constructs
description: The article argues that because the primary explanatory constructs in achievement motivation have been identified and sufficiently understood, research should now integrate them rather than study them in isolation or cast them as competitors. The authors contend that 'the major advances of the next decade (and, likely, beyond) within the achievement motivation literature will be integrative in nature,' and that failing to move from isolation to integration risks stagnation and incompleteness.
requirements: Clear, precise construct definition and conceptualization must come first, since without such clarity jingle and jangle fallacies abound
constraints: Initial independent study of constituent constructs is described as necessary and beneficial before integration
target_learners: researchers and theorists studying learner motivation
target_learning_goals: a comprehensive account of achievement motivation in educational settings
examples: The hierarchical model's two-step process—first separating and defining energization and direction, then joining them—is offered as a template for how existing frameworks emphasizing one component can be brought together in a single model
key_sources: Andrew J. Elliot · Nicolas Sommet. (2023). Integration in the Achievement Motivation Literature and the Hierarchical Model of Achievement Motivation. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09785-7

article_title: Hybridizing Motivational Strains: How Integrative Models Are Crucial for Advancing Motivation Science
citation: Ronnel B. King, Luke K. Fryer. (2024). Hybridizing Motivational Strains: How Integrative Models Are Crucial for Advancing Motivation Science. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09850-9
title: Integrate theories with care for meta-theoretical assumptions and boundary conditions, not for integration's sake
description: The essay cautions that integration must not be done haphazardly: 'Careful attention to meta-theoretical assumptions and boundary conditions must be made.' Quoting Ryan (2024), it warns that good theories 'can often collapse under the weight of swallowing too much'. It also notes, citing Pekrun (2024), that integration is only one strategy among others including differentiating, revising, generating, and discarding theories, and that the ultimate goal is promoting learning and academic development for all students.
requirements: Researchers must reconcile the meta-theoretical, ontological, and epistemological bases of the theories they integrate
constraints: Integration may be unhelpful in some situations; it should be pursued independently or alongside other theory-improvement strategies depending on the phenomenon
target_learning_goals: producing integrative theoretical models that genuinely improve understanding of student motivation
examples: Commenter Alexander urged authors to evaluate integration efforts by their prospective value to learning and academic development for all students
key_sources: Ronnel B. King, Luke K. Fryer. (2024). Hybridizing Motivational Strains: How Integrative Models Are Crucial for Advancing Motivation Science. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09850-9

article_title: Synthesizing Cognitive Load and Self-regulation Theory: a Theoretical Framework and Research Agenda
citation: de Bruin, A. B. H., Roelle, J., Carpenter, S. K., & Baars, M. (2020). Synthesizing Cognitive Load and Self-regulation Theory: a Theoretical Framework and Research Agenda. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09576-4
title: The interactive layers model describes self-regulated learning as occurring in three layers, consciously or unconsciously
description: The special-issue paper by Wirth, Stebner, Trypke, Schuster, and Leutner introduces what the editorial calls "a novel, interactive layers model of self-regulated learning and cognitive load". It describes how self-regulated learning can be unconscious, not loading onto working memory but relying on resonant states in sensory memory, or conscious and related to schema construction in working memory. Both conscious and unconscious self-regulation is described to take place in three layers: a content layer, a learning strategy layer, and a metacognitive layer. The model is then applied to explain existing inconsistent empirical findings in the literature.
requirements: The model is applied to explain existing inconsistent empirical findings, requiring empirical phenomena to interpret
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning and management of cognitive load
examples: The editorial illustrates unconscious self-regulation with an experienced highway driver responding effectively to traffic without remembering it seconds later
key_sources: de Bruin, A. B. H., Roelle, J., Carpenter, S. K., & Baars, M. (2020). Synthesizing Cognitive Load and Self-regulation Theory: a Theoretical Framework and Research Agenda. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09576-4

article_title: Agency in Educational Technology: Interdisciplinary Perspectives and Implications for Learning Design
citation: Garvin Brod, Natalia Kucirkova, Joshua Shepherd, Dietsje Jolles, Inge Molenaar. (2023). Agency in Educational Technology: Interdisciplinary Perspectives and Implications for Learning Design. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09749-x
title: Interdisciplinary taxonomy of agency: types, levels, and developmental prerequisites across philosophy, education, and psychology
description: The review organizes agency along two philosophical axes: types of agency defined by the normative structures they are sensitive to, and levels or degrees of agency varying in sophistication of capacities. Types include epistemic agency, which "is the kind of agency that is sensitive to epistemic norms (e.g., norms regarding when a belief or action is justified)", plus skilled, aesthetic, moral, practical, and group agency. The educational perspective highlights child-adult-technology interactions, and the psychological perspective treats agency beliefs and perceived control as mechanisms whose effective exercise depends on prior knowledge, executive functions, and metacognition that develop across childhood.
requirements: Distinguishing which dimension of agency a design decision targets, since agency is multi-dimensional and EdTech choices impact multiple facets at once
constraints: The article notes philosophy has little advanced understanding of children's agency, and the conceptualization excludes anthropology, sociology, and neuroscience
target_learning_goals: fostering learners' agency in technology-supported learning
examples: EdTech prompts that let learners explore the epistemic space, gaining familiarity with evidence assessment, propaganda detection, and decisions to change one's mind
key_sources: Garvin Brod, Natalia Kucirkova, Joshua Shepherd, Dietsje Jolles, Inge Molenaar. (2023). Agency in Educational Technology: Interdisciplinary Perspectives and Implications for Learning Design. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09749-x

article_title: Associations Between Teacher-Student Relationship Quality and Middle and Secondary School Teachers’ Wellbeing: A Systematic Review
citation: Rhoda Lai, Jennifer Southam, Luella Mageean, Sue Roffey, Kelly-Ann Allen. (2026). Associations Between Teacher-Student Relationship Quality and Middle and Secondary School Teachers' Wellbeing: A Systematic Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10107-2
title: Internal working models of teacher-student relationships (Spilt et al., 2011) as a framework for teacher wellbeing
description: The review adopts Spilt and colleagues' (2011) model, in which teachers form internal working models of their relationships with students that shape interpretations of student behaviour and emotional responses. The article states "the internal working models that teachers form of these relationships are important for them as they relate to their sense of meaning and perceptions of their professional identities". Teachers hold general models of students as well as individual models per student, and bring biases and efficacy beliefs to these representations. Relationship quality is treated as a subjectively perceived phenomenon.
requirements: Relationship quality must be measured as subjective personal perceptions of teachers or students, not third-party observations of behaviours.
constraints: Attachment theory does not explain why teachers would require fleeting attachment bonds with students or why such relationships matter for teacher wellbeing relative to colleague relationships; limited contact time leads students to use teachers as 'ad hoc' attachments.
target_learning_goals: understanding how relationship perceptions shape teacher emotional responses and wellbeing
examples: A negative internalised relationship model leads a teacher to interpret challenging behaviour as threatening, whereas a positive model supports interpreting it as situational.
key_sources: Rhoda Lai, Jennifer Southam, Luella Mageean, Sue Roffey, Kelly-Ann Allen. (2026).
