Associations Between Teacher-Student Relationship Quality and Middle and Secondary School Teachers' Wellbeing: A Systematic Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10107-2

article_title: Commentary on Highly Successful Female Educational Psychologists: Equity and Intersectionality in Success Definitions
citation: Kucirkova, N. (2023). Commentary on Highly Successful Female Educational Psychologists: Equity and Intersectionality in Success Definitions. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09727-3
title: Intersectionality framework for interpreting academic success narratives
description: The commentary applies intersectionality, "an interdisciplinary critical framework that refers to the connections and dependencies between various identity types", coined by Kimberlé Crenshaw in 1989 and rooted in Black feminism and Critical Race Theory. It is used as both method and epistemology to interrogate how power and intersecting identities are embedded in social relations, highlighting "accumulated advantages for dominant social groups". The author uses it to show that factors like research specialisation and placements at top universities exemplify cumulative benefits that intersect with inequalities.
requirements: Analysis must attend to power dynamics and the mutual influence of social positionings rather than treating identity categories separately
constraints: The commentary notes prior studies showed the relationship between gender and ethnicity, rather than each as separate categories, affected female academics' experiences
target_learners: academic women and minority scholars in higher education
target_learning_goals: understanding systemic barriers to academic career progression and equitable definitions of scholarly success
examples: The commentary reinterprets Prinz et al.'s (2021) and Kiewra et al.'s (2021) success trajectories of interviewees as exemplifying cumulative benefits that intersect with inequalities
key_sources: Kucirkova, N. (2023). Commentary on Highly Successful Female Educational Psychologists: Equity and Intersectionality in Success Definitions. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09727-3

article_title: Reporting of Methodological Rigor in Empirical Mixed Methods Research in Educational Psychology
citation: Matthew T. McCrudden · Macy Bowman · Gala Sofia Campos Oaxaca. (2025). Reporting of Methodological Rigor in Empirical Mixed Methods Research in Educational Psychology. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10090-8
title: Three integration strategies in mixed methods research: connecting, building, and merging (with meta-inferences)
description: A framework describing how researchers link quantitative and qualitative strands. Integration is "the linking of qualitative and quantitative approaches and dimensions together to create a new whole or a more holistic understanding than achieved by either alone". Connecting uses results from one strand to inform participant selection for the other; building uses one strand's data collection and analysis to inform the other's; merging brings findings together for comparison and to generate meta-inferences — insights not possible from either strand alone. The review used these strategies as criteria for evaluating reporting of integration.
requirements: Integration must be planned at the start of a study (how and why strands will be integrated) and communicated transparently to readers
constraints: Reporting integration within journal word-count limits is a stated barrier; meta-inference types relate to the design rationale
target_learning_goals: achieving and reporting integration of quantitative and qualitative strands
examples: McCrudden et al. (2016) used connecting (purposeful sampling from experiment results), building (quantitative findings informed the interview protocol), and merging (qualitative findings explained quantitative findings)
key_sources: Matthew T. McCrudden · Macy Bowman · Gala Sofia Campos Oaxaca. (2025). Reporting of Methodological Rigor in Empirical Mixed Methods Research in Educational Psychology. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10090-8

article_title: Enhancing School Students’ Self-Regulated Learning through Generative AI Support: A Randomized Controlled Trial
citation: Tim Fütterer, Lisa Bardach, Jochen Kuhn, Stefan Daniel Keller, Peter Gerjets. (2026). Enhancing School Students’ Self-Regulated Learning through Generative AI Support: A Randomized Controlled Trial. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10133-8
title: Integrative framework of self-regulation in education (Wortha et al.) with four interacting components
description: The study draws on an integrative model situating SRL within a broader account of self-regulation in education. "This model distinguishes four key components that interact to shape learning outcomes: personal dispositions (e.g., personality traits such as conscientiousness), driving forces (e.g., current motivation), limited resources (e.g., cognitive capacity, executive functions), and learning activities (e.g., cognitive learning strategies)". The components are assumed to interact in complex, partially compensatory ways, and the framework is grounded in a person–situation interaction view. The study targeted driving forces and learning activities because these can be directly affected by short-term interventions.
requirements: Interventions should target components amenable to change, such as driving forces and learning activities, rather than stable dispositions
constraints: Personal dispositions and limited cognitive resources are described as less likely to be changed by short-term instructional support
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning, including motivation and cognitive learning strategies
examples: The RCT operationalized the framework by contrasting a utility value (driving forces) intervention with a cognitive learning strategy (learning activities) intervention
key_sources: Tim Fütterer, Lisa Bardach, Jochen Kuhn, Stefan Daniel Keller, Peter Gerjets. (2026). Enhancing School Students’ Self-Regulated Learning through Generative AI Support: A Randomized Controlled Trial. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10133-8

article_title: Patterns in Student Learning: Relationships Between Learning Strategies, Conceptions of Learning, and Learning Orientations
citation: Vermunt, J. D. & Vermetten, Y. J. (2004). Patterns in Student Learning: Relationships Between Learning Strategies, Conceptions of Learning, and Learning Orientations. Educational Psychology Review. https://dspacelibrary.uu.nl/handle/1874/11958
title: Integrative theory of student learning uniting cognitive, regulative, metacognitive, and motivational components and the interplay of self- and external regulation
description: The article presents an integrative learning theory in which student learning comprises cognitive processing activities, affective activities, and regulation activities that steer the other two, plus conceptions of learning and learning orientations. It focusses on "the interplay between self-regulation and external regulation of learning processes as a theoretical framework," and the ILS instrument was built from it. The theory also distinguishes teaching/learning functions and predicts congruence or friction (constructive and destructive) between teaching and learning strategies.
requirements: Measurement of processing, regulation, conceptions, and orientations together, as operationalized in the ILS
constraints: Developed and validated mainly with students in the beginning years of higher education; structures deviate in other populations and contexts
target_learning_goals: quality of learning strategies and conceptions
examples: Vermunt (1996, 1998) discerned three processing strategies (deep, stepwise, concrete) and three regulation strategies (self-regulated, externally regulated, lack of regulation) in empirical studies
key_sources: Vermunt, J. D. & Vermetten, Y. J. (2004). Patterns in Student Learning: Relationships Between Learning Strategies, Conceptions of Learning, and Learning Orientations. Educational Psychology Review. https://dspacelibrary.uu.nl/handle/1874/11958

article_title: The Relation Between Teacher-Student Eye Contact and Teachers’ Interpersonal Behavior During Group Work: a Multiple-Person Gaze-Tracking Case Study in Secondary Mathematics Education
citation: Haataja, E., Salonen, V., Laine, A., Toivanen, M., & Hannula, M. S. (2021). The Relation Between Teacher-Student Eye Contact and Teachers' Interpersonal Behavior During Group Work: a Multiple-Person Gaze-Tracking Case Study in Secondary Mathematics Education. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09538-w
title: Interpersonal theory's agency-communion cycle extended to micro-level reciprocal teacher-student gaze interaction
description: The article applies interpersonal theory, in which "human interaction is conceptualized as a continuous cycle of initiatives and responses between people", conceptualized "with two dimensions: agency and communion". It extends this framework from whole-class interaction to reciprocal communication between the teacher and individual students, arguing that interpersonal adaptation in the classroom is visible at the level of gaze behavior and that both teachers and students can use gaze to take initiative. The authors conclude that such individualization of micro-level interactions should be included in further developments of interpersonal theory.
requirements: Momentary, continuous coding of teacher interpersonal behavior (e.g., the computer-joystick method) synchronized with gaze data is needed to link micro-level gaze to communion and agency.
constraints: The article states its results are not necessarily generalizable to other contexts, and the effect sizes of the statistical results were relatively low throughout the research.
target_learners: Secondary school students (15-16-year-old ninth-grade mathematics students)
target_learning_goals: Teacher-student interaction and classroom communication during collaborative mathematical problem solving
examples: The study coded three teachers' interpersonal behavior continuously with the computer-joystick method and synchronized it with ELAN-coded gaze dwells during 16-18-minute collaborative problem-solving phases.
key_sources: Haataja, E., Salonen, V., Laine, A., Toivanen, M., & Hannula, M. S. (2021). The Relation Between Teacher-Student Eye Contact and Teachers' Interpersonal Behavior During Group Work: a Multiple-Person Gaze-Tracking Case Study in Secondary Mathematics Education. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09538-w

article_title: Motivation and Personality: Current Integrative Perspectives and the Way Ahead
citation: Lisa Bardach, Luise von Keyserlingk, Jacque S. Eccles. (2026). Motivation and Personality: Current Integrative Perspectives and the Way Ahead. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10147-2
title: Intellectual investment trait theory: reciprocal enrichment and success pathways
description: Intellectual Investment Trait Theory is a family of theories linking investment traits (e.g., intellectual curiosity, interests, typical intellectual engagement, need for cognition) with cognitive abilities. Building on Cattell's idea that crystallized intelligence develops through investment of fluid intelligence, Ackerman (1996) proposed that certain personality traits and motivations contribute to crystallized intelligence beyond fluid intelligence. The article highlights "the environmental enrichment hypothesis" (investment traits lead individuals to seek learning opportunities that foster cognitive development) and "the environmental success hypothesis" (higher cognitive abilities enable more effective engagement in enriching experiences that shape investment traits), assuming a reciprocal relationship, and extends the reasoning to Big Five traits and educational motivation such as expectancies and task values.
requirements: The theory assumes a reciprocal relationship between investment traits and cognitive abilities rather than mutually exclusive directional hypotheses
constraints: Recent extensions reformulate the two key hypotheses as situation exploration and situation exploitation hypotheses to reflect reciprocal state-level interplay
target_learners: students and learners across domains and professions
target_learning_goals: knowledge acquisition, information-seeking behaviors, and cognitive development
examples: A highly conscientious person seeks a well-structured environment, does well there, which contributes to expectancies of success and domain value, reinforcing conscientiousness
key_sources: Lisa Bardach, Luise von Keyserlingk, Jacque S. Eccles. (2026). Motivation and Personality: Current Integrative Perspectives and the Way Ahead. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10147-2

article_title: Self-Regulation Competence as a Superpower: An Integrated Framework for K-12
citation: Ulrich Trautwein, Janina Eberhart, Charlotte Dignath, Cavan V. Bonner, Brent W. Roberts. (2026). Self-Regulation Competence as a Superpower: An Integrated Framework for K-12. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10190-z
title: Integrated multicomponent model of self-regulation competence unifying SRL, executive functions, and conscientiousness
description: The article proposes an integrated multicomponent model that treats self-regulation competence as a broad, integrative capacity encompassing cognitive, motivational, affective, and behavioral components, uniting the SRL, EF, and conscientiousness research traditions. It rests on three propositions: the construct predicts broad outcomes, the three traditions share a core of "goal-directedness, monitoring, and control", and the construct is malleable through instruction. The model frames self-regulation competence as a developmental "superpower" that schools can deliberately cultivate.
requirements: Integration requires sufficient conceptual and empirical overlap among SRL, EFs, and conscientiousness to warrant grouping them under one construct
Evidence must show the construct predicts a broad range of educational and developmental outcomes
constraints: The authors acknowledge parts of the multicomponent-promotion argument are somewhat more speculative and essentially a task for the future
EF components, particularly working memory beyond early childhood, are seen as difficult to train
target_learning_goals: Self-regulation competence: monitoring and controlling cognition, emotion, and behavior adaptively to achieve personal goals
examples: The article reviews three research traditions—SRL in educational psychology, EFs in developmental psychology, and conscientiousness in personality psychology—and reports its own 313-student canonical correlation study of their overlap.
key_sources: Ulrich Trautwein, Janina Eberhart, Charlotte Dignath, Cavan V. Bonner, Brent W. Roberts. (2026). Self-Regulation Competence as a Superpower: An Integrated Framework for K-12. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10190-z

article_title: Coaching for the PISA test
citation: Brunner, M.; Artelt, C.; Krauss, Stefan; Baumert, J. (2007). Coaching for the PISA test. Learning and Instruction 17 (2), S. 111-122. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2007.01.002
title: Interpret low-stakes large-scale assessment scores with caution because coaching plus pretesting can raise performance
description: Because this study found that "only the combined effects of pretesting and coaching have substantial positive effects on student performance" on the low-stakes PISA assessments, score gains in large-scale assessments may partly reflect coaching and pretesting rather than pure achievement. The article draws implications for the interpretation of large-scale assessment programs from this finding.
requirements: Applies to low-stakes tests, which the article defines as tests with no personal relevance for the students taking them
constraints: The substantial positive effect required the combination of pretesting and coaching, not either alone
target_learners: Students taking large-scale assessments such as PISA
target_learning_goals: Valid interpretation of reading and mathematics achievement scores from large-scale assessment programs
examples: A pre-/posttest quasi-experimental study in German Hauptschule and Gymnasium schools examined coaching and pretest effects on PISA reading and mathematics performance separately by content domain
key_sources: Brunner, M.; Artelt, C.; Krauss, Stefan; Baumert, J. (2007). Coaching for the PISA test. Learning and Instruction 17 (2), S. 111-122. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2007.01.002

article_title: Variation in situation-specific engagement among lower secondary school students
citation: Pöysä, S., Vasalampi, K., Muotka, J., Lerkkanen, M.-K., Poikkeus, A.-M., & Nurmi, J.-E. (2018). Variation in situation-specific engagement among lower secondary school students. Learning and Instruction, 53, 64-73. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2017.07.007
title: InSitu mobile-based instrument for lesson-to-lesson ratings of situation-specific engagement
description: The InSitu (InSituations) instrument is a mobile application pre-programmed into smart phones with which students rate their situation-specific engagement at the end of lessons; "InSitu consists of 17 items (Table 1) rated on a 5-point scale (1 = not at all; 5 = very much)." Confirmatory factor analysis established a five-factor structure (behavioral/cognitive engagement, emotional engagement, disaffection, competence experiences, help-seeking) with acceptable fit (CFI = .932; RMSEA = .058; SRMR = .051). The present study used the first three latent factors.
requirements: Ratings are collected at the end of each lesson with phones handed out simultaneously and collected a few minutes later, requiring device logistics per lesson
constraints: The instrument has not yet been widely used in previous research
It did not distinguish between cognitive and behavioral engagement
target_learning_goals: situational behavioral/cognitive engagement, emotional engagement, and disaffection in lessons
examples: In the study, 57 students produced 1,328 time-stamped ratings with a total response rate of 81.8% during a one-week intensive follow-up
key_sources: Pöysä, S., Vasalampi, K., Muotka, J., Lerkkanen, M.-K., Poikkeus, A.-M., & Nurmi, J.-E. (2018). Variation in situation-specific engagement among lower secondary school students. Learning and Instruction, 53, 64-73. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2017.07.007

article_title: Training for fostering knowledge co-construction from collaborative inference-drawing
citation: Deiglmayr, A., & Spada, H. (2011). Training for fostering knowledge co-construction from collaborative inference-drawing. Learning and Instruction, 21(3), 441-451. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2010.06.004
title: A priori taxonomy of three inference types defined by how interdependent information is distributed between collaborators
description: The article distinguishes three types of solution-relevant inferences, defined a priori by the experimental distribution of two interdependent pieces of information in a dyad: "Collaborative inferences" result from unshared, distributed information and "can only be drawn collaboratively"; individual inferences result from unshared information located with the same person; shared inferences result from information known to both partners. The taxonomy allows systematic comparison of inference difficulty, since the distribution is manipulated experimentally.
requirements: Information distribution between group members must be experimentally controlled so that each inference type can be identified a priori
constraints: Defined and tested in dyads working on hidden-profile-style tasks in which complementary pieces of information yield solution-relevant inferences
target_learning_goals: drawing solution-relevant inferences from distributed information during collaborative problem solving
examples: Murder-mystery testing case in which 12 solution-relevant inferences (four of each type) were distributed across counterbalanced text versions
key_sources: Deiglmayr, A., & Spada, H. (2011). Training for fostering knowledge co-construction from collaborative inference-drawing. Learning and Instruction, 21(3), 441-451. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2010.06.004

article_title: Training for fostering knowledge co-construction from collaborative inference-drawing
citation: Deiglmayr, A., & Spada, H. (2011). Training for fostering knowledge co-construction from collaborative inference-drawing. Learning and Instruction, 21(3), 441-451. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2010.06.004
title: Semi-computerized inference tutoring tool providing adaptive feedback and prompts during collaborative training
description: A semi-computerized tutoring tool developed for the training phase, controlled by a human observer who monitored the discussion and sent four types of messages based on an observation matrix: new information feedback announcing when "a piece of case information was mentioned for the first time", complete inference feedback on drawn inferences, missing information reminders, and missing information hints. It provided "just-in-time feedback on their performance, pointed out relevant cues... and prompted strategy application".
requirements: A human observer able to identify solution-relevant information mentions and inferences in real time and fill in the observation matrix
constraints: Guidance was provided during the training phase only, and not available during the unscaffolded testing phase
target_learners: university students in dyads collaborating via audio connection and shared word processor
target_learning_goals: applying information connection, pooling, and take-up strategies during collaboration
examples: Tutored training dyads received tutor messages displayed in both participants' rooms while collaborating on the medical-diagnosis case; 7 of 9 tutored dyads solved the training case correctly
key_sources: Deiglmayr, A., & Spada, H. (2011). Training for fostering knowledge co-construction from collaborative inference-drawing. Learning and Instruction, 21(3), 441-451. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2010.06.004

article_title: Spelling predictors; investigating the role of phonological ability and rapid naming in a large cross-sectional British study
citation: Niolaki, G., Vousden, J., Terzopoulos, A., Shepherd, D.-L., Debney, L., & Masterson, J. (2022). Spelling predictors; investigating the role of phonological ability and rapid naming in a large cross-sectional British study. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2022.101635
title: Interpretive Spelling Test (IST)
description: The Interpretive Spelling Test is a spelling-to-dictation assessment distinguishing three letter string types: irregular words, regular words and pseudowords. The article states "The IST comprises three sections: 36 irregular words, 36 regular words and 34 pseudowords", matched on psycholinguistic variables such as zipf frequency, letters, phonemes and syllables. It was designed because standardised spelling tests do not distinguish letter string types, allowing separate analysis of lexical and sublexical spelling processes across year groups.
requirements: Administered as spelling to dictation with target word, embedded sentence, and repetition; pseudoword items repeated three times
constraints: Regularity defined parsimoniously by the most frequent context-insensitive phoneme-grapheme correspondence, which the authors note is somewhat subjective
target_learners: Primary school children aged 4–12 (Yr R to Yr 6)
target_learning_goals: Single-word spelling of regular words, irregular words and pseudowords
examples: Children in all year groups spelled all 106 IST items, scored one point per correct regular or irregular word and against a bank of phonologically acceptable pseudoword responses
key_sources: Niolaki, G., Vousden, J., Terzopoulos, A., Shepherd, D.-L., Debney, L., & Masterson, J. (2022). Spelling predictors; investigating the role of phonological ability and rapid naming in a large cross-sectional British study. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2022.101635

article_title: Learning by explaining orally or in written form? Text complexity matters
citation: Jacob, L., Lachner, A., & Scheiter, K. (2019). Learning by Explaining Orally or In Written Form? Text Difficulty Matters. https://aspredicted.org/sv3zv.pdf
title: Indirect social presence account of the explaining modality effect
description: The article advances an account in which the learning benefit of oral over written explaining arises because oral explaining raises awareness of social presence, which in turn triggers more generative processing. The authors state their "findings rather support the indirect social presence hypothesis, as we only obtained a significant serial mediation effect of the explaining modality on students' learning via social presence and comprehensiveness of explanations but not a direct effect solely via social presence." Social presence is operationalized as the number of personal references in explanations, and generative processing as comprehensiveness (number of concepts).
requirements: Explanations must be coded for personal references and concepts to trace the indirect pathway
constraints: Supported only for high-difficult text material and inference-based questions in this laboratory study
Based on explanation products rather than online process measures
target_learners: university students from non-biology study programs
examples: In the experiment, oral explanations contained more personal references (d = 0.50) and more concepts (d = 0.83) than written explanations, and the serial mediation via references → concepts was significant
key_sources: Jacob, L., Lachner, A., & Scheiter, K. (2019). Learning by Explaining Orally or In Written Form? Text Difficulty Matters. https://aspredicted.org/sv3zv.pdf

article_title: Methodological issues in developing a multi-dimensional coding procedure for small-group chat communication
citation: Jan Willem Strijbos, Gerry Stahl. (2007). Methodological issues in developing a multi-dimensional coding procedure for small group chat communication. Learning and Instruction. https://hal.science/hal-00703042
title: When coding small group chat communication, incorporate threading between analysis units to handle fragmentation and support reliability
description: A design principle for chat communication analysis methodology: coding procedures for small group chat should build in threading, i.e. "connections between analysis units", because the article found threading "proved essential to handle unit fragmentation, to reconstruct the response structure and for reliability of coding". Without threading, unit fragmentation and an unreconstructable response structure undermine both the analysis and the trustworthiness of reliability figures.
requirements: Coding must operate on defined analysis units; threading connections between those units must be reconstructed as part of the procedure.
constraints: Established for small group chat communication in CSCL; the article also warns of "a risk for reliability overestimation", so reliability determination must be designed to avoid overestimation.
target_learners: researchers and analysts coding small group chat collaboration in CSCL
target_learning_goals: valid, reliable analysis of collaborative learning processes in chat communication
examples: The article's multi-dimensional coding procedure for small group chat communication was developed around threading to handle unit fragmentation, reconstruct the response structure, and support reliability of coding.
key_sources: Jan Willem Strijbos, Gerry Stahl. (2007). Methodological issues in developing a multi-dimensional coding procedure for small group chat communication. Learning and Instruction. https://hal.science/hal-00703042

article_title: Change and transmission of students' and teachers’ lesson-specific emotions
citation: Sorkkila, M., Malmberg, L.-E., Pöysä, S., Kiuru, N., Lerkkanen, M.-K., & Pakarinen, E. (2026). Change and transmission of students' and teachers' lesson-specific emotions. Learning and Instruction, 102, Article 102298. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102298
title: InSitu and InSituT mobile-based lesson-specific emotion instruments
description: The InSituations (InSitu) student instrument and its teacher version (InSituT) are mobile-based questionnaires administered towards the end of each lesson to capture lesson-specific emotions in real time. The student version contributed three emotional-engagement items (positive emotions) and two disaffection items (negative emotions) on a 5-point Likert scale; the teacher version contributed three items each. The article states the instruments "allowed us to collect multi-informant 'real--time' data and observe both change and spill-over of emotions" and reports good reliability and validity among Finnish adolescents and teachers.
requirements: Research assistants provide mobile phones and administer the questionnaire towards the end of each lesson; short questionnaires are needed to keep response rates high in real-time data collection
constraints: In this study the reliability of teachers' negative emotions was relatively low (α = .58; ω = 0.64), and the reader is advised to be careful in interpreting results for this scale
target_learning_goals: Measuring momentary emotional engagement and disaffection during lessons
examples: In this study 672 student lesson-reports nested in 61 lessons and 61 teacher lesson-reports nested in 20 teachers were collected on one school day
key_sources: Sorkkila, M., Malmberg, L.-E., Pöysä, S., Kiuru, N., Lerkkanen, M.-K., & Pakarinen, E. (2026). Change and transmission of students' and teachers' lesson-specific emotions. Learning and Instruction, 102, Article 102298. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102298

article_title: Bridging the gap: Fraction understanding is central to mathematics achievement in students from three different continents
citation: Torbeyns, J., Schneider, M., Xin, Z., & Siegler, R. S. (2015). Bridging the Gap: Fraction Understanding is Central to Mathematics Achievement in Students from Three Different Continents. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2014.03.002
title: Integrated theory of numerical development
description: Siegler, Thompson, and Schneider's (2011) integrated theory of numerical development unites whole number and fraction learning in a single framework, in contrast to conceptual change theories that posit a gap between them. It holds that numerical development is a "steadily expanding understanding of the connection between numbers and their magnitudes", involving both expansion of the range of whole numbers whose magnitudes are understood and a conceptual change toward understanding rational numbers via their single defining feature, their magnitudes. The theory views interference from whole number knowledge as only one of several sources of difficulty in learning fractions, and recognizes the positive role of whole number magnitude knowledge in learning fractions. This study tested its major assumption cross-culturally.
requirements: Fraction magnitude understanding must be assessable, e.g., via number line estimation and magnitude comparison tasks, for the theory's central relation to be tested.
constraints: The theory's applicability to irrational numbers had not been tested empirically, according to the article.
target_learners: Elementary and middle school students (6th and 8th graders)
examples: The study tested the theory's assumption that fraction magnitude understanding is crucial to overall mathematics learning in Belgium (Flanders), China, and the U.S., countries differing in teachers' knowledge, instructional practices, and student performance.
key_sources: Torbeyns, J., Schneider, M., Xin, Z., & Siegler, R. S. (2015). Bridging the Gap: Fraction Understanding is Central to Mathematics Achievement in Students from Three Different Continents. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2014.03.002

article_title: Feedback processing and emotion regulation in nursing students during internship
citation: Feedback processing and emotion regulation in nursing students during internship. (2022). https://eric.ed.gov/?q=feedback+processing+and+emotion+regulation+in+nursing+students+during+internship
title: Integrated model of internship feedback processing in nursing students
description: A four-phase, circular model of how nursing students process internship feedback, integrating emotional processing with prior findings on self-esteem and learning behavior. Phase one activates determinants (personal dispositions, task perception, context); phase two interprets feedback content and form through cognitive and emotional processes; phase three concerns deciding about feedback; phase four concerns consequences for motivational beliefs and behaviors oriented toward self-protection or learning regulation. The article states "this model operates in a circular dynamic," with consequences feeding back into dispositions and perceptions of the next task. Emotions and their regulation are central and appear in bold in the model.
requirements: Feedback situations recur over time so that consequences of one episode can influence dispositions and perceptions in the next
constraints: Developed in the context of nursing internships in French-speaking Belgium
Emotion regulation strategies were often unconscious and could not always be identified as such from T1 interview data
target_learners: nursing students on internship (higher education, vocational bachelor's)
target_learning_goals: constructive processing and use of clinical feedback
examples: The model was built by integrating this study's findings on emotions and regulation with the authors' previous publications on self-esteem and feedback interpretation
key_sources: Feedback processing and emotion regulation in nursing students during internship. (2022). https://eric.ed.gov/?q=feedback+processing+and+emotion+regulation+in+nursing+students+during+internship

article_title: The Effect of Rate of Silent Reading on Ability to Recall.
citation: Gilliland, A. R. (1922). The effect of rate of silent reading on ability to recall. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://psycnet.apa.org/record/1922-02093-001
title: Teachers should insist upon accurate, rapid silent reading to save preparation time and increase efficiency
description: The article recommends that reading instruction push pupils toward faster silent reading, because recall did not drop when reading rate increased while time saved was substantial. As the author puts it, "the teacher of reading by insistence upon accurate, rapid, silent reading would be able to reduce not only the time required by pupils in the schools in the preparation of their lessons but also and more important still greatly increase their efficiency in life."
requirements: Reading material of the ordinary kind used in the study; the author concedes there are limits in speed beyond which one should not go.
constraints: The recommendation is grounded in short, relatively easy paragraphs with immediate recall; the author flags longer, vaguer selections and delayed recall as untested.
target_learning_goals: efficient silent reading with retained comprehension
examples: In the supporting experiment each subject read two paragraphs at each of three rates and immediately wrote down everything remembered, with comprehension roughly constant across rates.
key_sources: Gilliland, A. R. (1922). The effect of rate of silent reading on ability to recall. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://psycnet.apa.org/record/1922-02093-001

article_title: Pitfalls in Rating Schemes.
citation: Knight, F. B., & Franzen, R. H. (1921). Pitfalls in rating schemes. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://psycnet.apa.org
title: Interpret ratings as behavior rather than as truthful accounts of the rated person
description: The article argues that a rating's value lies in what it reveals about the rater's judgments and point of view, not in its accuracy as a report of fact. As the authors put it, "ratings are of value only when these are interpreted as behavior and not as truthful accounts." A self-report that a person thinks something is important data regardless of whether the person really thinks it. The article demonstrates this by reading self-versus-peer rating discrepancies as evidence of self-defense mechanisms rather than as measurement error alone.
requirements: Ratings must be interpreted with awareness of tendencies such as self-overrating and the spread of a general impression across traits
constraints: The article states the fluctuations of the self-overrating tendency are unknown, and whether it extends to rating liked or disliked others is unknown
target_learners: users of rating schemes in educational and psychological assessment
target_learning_goals: accurate interpretation of self-ratings and peer ratings of traits and interests
examples: The 110-junior study read the +0.13 introspective-objective correlation as difference in the rater's point of view rather than difference in facts
key_sources: Knight, F. B., & Franzen, R. H. (1921). Pitfalls in rating schemes. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0073817

article_title: Language error tests.
citation: Wilson, G. M. (1921). Language Error Tests. The Journal of Educational Psychology.
title: Use parallel-equated language error tests interchangeably to diagnose class weaknesses
description: Because the three forms were shown to be of practically equal value, the author recommends that superintendents and measurement experts use them interchangeably and send summaries of returns to the writer. Working directly with the tests, he argues, reveals "the language ability of school children and the points on which a particular class is weak", giving the tests diagnostic as well as measurement value.
requirements: Forms administered as printed, with the teacher-read game directions and rights-based scoring
constraints: Equating evidence rests on administrations in Sioux City and Duluth and one small city system; the author planned a separate article on diagnostic use and scoring
target_learners: School pupils in grades III to XII
target_learning_goals: Diagnosing language ability and identifying specific language errors weak in a particular class
examples: The author invites superintendents and measurement experts throughout the country to make use of the tests and send summaries of the returns
key_sources: Wilson, G. M. (1921). Language Error Tests. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0064444

article_title: The Relation between Mental and Physical Growth.
citation: Bird T. Baldwin. (1922). The Relation Between Mental and Physical Growth. The Journal of Educational Psychology, Vol. XIII, No. 1. https://psycnet.apa.org/journals/edu/13/1/193
title: Individual longitudinal growth-curve method for studying mental and physical development
description: Baldwin advocates the individualizing method: following the same children consecutively over years with both physical and mental measurements, rather than cross-sectional snapshots. He argues that "The day for the study of physical growth processes by single measurements is over" and that prediction of later status requires identifying a child's growth-curve type, chronological and physiological age. The method underpins all the paper's prediction analyses and his call for intensive consecutive studies of the same individuals across a series of years.
requirements: Consecutive measurements on the same individuals over several years under standardized conditions with uniform methods and scales
constraints: The author notes no complete longitudinal mental-development data comparable to the physical data yet existed, and that exact prediction error for various examination intervals could not be determined from his data
target_learners: children from early childhood through adolescence in longitudinal growth studies
target_learning_goals: understanding and prediction of individual mental and physical growth trajectories
examples: The Iowa series of approximately 2500 individuals measured for 30 physical traits over 18 to 24 semi-annual intervals, and 143 children given repeated Stanford-Binet examinations beginning in 1917
key_sources: Bird T. Baldwin. (1922). The Relation Between Mental and Physical Growth. The Journal of Educational Psychology, Vol. XIII, No. 1. https://psycnet.apa.org/journals/edu/13/1/193

article_title: Predicting age of becoming a cardinal principle knower.
citation: Geary David C., vanMarle Kristy, Chu Felicia W., Hoard Mary K., Nugent Lara. (2019). Predicting Age of Becoming a Cardinal Principle Knower. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000277
title: Interventions for delayed CPKs should combine domain-specific instruction with supports for domain-general deficits
description: The article argues that interventions focused only on preschoolers' quantitative deficits "will not be sufficient, if they do not also include features that address these children's difficulties with attentional and inhibitory control." Following Fuchs et al. (2016), well-designed interventions can compensate for domain-general weaknesses by integrating domain-specific instruction with compensatory supports. Explicit, teacher-directed instruction may help compensate for domain-general deficits, and instruction pace may need to be slower for children with below-average FSIQ.
requirements: Interventions must address executive function deficits alongside quantitative content
Domain-specific content should include the count list and enumeration
constraints: Interventions of this type remain to be developed; the recommendation is based on correlational data
target_learners: preschool children with delayed cardinal principle knower status
examples: The article suggests instructional components that explicitly link number words to enumerated objects, and numeral learning and discrimination components with explicit focus on cardinal value for children with visual symbol learning deficits
key_sources: Geary David C., vanMarle Kristy, Chu Felicia W., Hoard Mary K., Nugent Lara. (2019). Predicting Age of Becoming a Cardinal Principle Knower. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000277

article_title: Fluctuations in elementary school children’s working memory performance in the school context.
citation: Dirk, Judith; Schmiedek, Florian. (2016). Fluctuations in elementary school children's working memory performance in the school context. The journal of educational psychology 108 (2016) 5, S. 722-739. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000076
title: Educational practice should account for substantial WM fluctuations at all timescales and adopt interventions that increase children's attentional focus and self-regulation
description: The article recommends that practice respond to the demonstrated instability of children's working memory. It states that "Educational practice may be informed by the substantial WM fluctuations at all timescales and adopt interventions that increase children's attentional focus and self-regulation." The recommendation rests on the ambulatory assessment findings that daily WM performance fluctuates substantially within person across days, occasions, and moments.
requirements: Practitioners need awareness that a child's WM performance varies substantially from day to day, occasion to occasion, and moment to moment
constraints: The article presents this as a possibility informed by the findings, not as an intervention tested in the study
target_learners: elementary school students in Grades 3 and 4 (8 to 11 years old)
examples: Grade 3 and 4 students completed WM tasks on smartphones 3 times a day in school and at home for 4 weeks, revealing substantial within-person fluctuations
key_sources: Dirk, Judith; Schmiedek, Florian. (2016). Fluctuations in elementary school children's working memory performance in the school context. The journal of educational psychology 108 (2016) 5, S. 722-739. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000076

article_title: Intelligence and its measurement: A symposium--I.
citation: E. L. Thorndike and L. M. Terman. (1921). Intelligence and Its Measurement. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://archive.org/search?query=Journal+of+Educational+Psychology+1921
title: Thorndike's definition of intellect as the power of good responses with respect to truth or fact, specialized by data and operation
description: Thorndike defines intellect pragmatically as "the power of good responses from the point of view of truth or fact", and separates varieties by whether the situation is taken grossly or abstractly and whether it is experienced directly or thought of. The abstract, idea-directed variety is called "the more intellectual variety of intellect". Each variety is further specialized by the data operated on and the form of the operation, so goodness of response varies with the particular task. The framework underlies his argument that no single test score captures a general power determining every intellectual task.
requirements: Definitions and distinctions are treated as pragmatic rather than absolute, accepting that behavior shows intermediate forms between directly sensed and planned, concrete and abstract responses
constraints: Thorndike warns against trying to separate responses to directly sensed situations from those concerned with planning, or concrete from abstract responses, as behavior shows all sorts of intermediate forms
target_learners: children and adults whose intellectual status is being measured
target_learning_goals: general intellectual performance across varied tasks and data
examples: Thorndike illustrates specialization by noting the child best at mental multiplication of two-place numbers will not be best at thinking out verbal puzzles
key_sources: E. L. Thorndike and L. M. Terman. (1921). Intelligence and Its Measurement. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://archive.org/search?query=Journal+of+Educational+Psychology+1921

article_title: The use of tests in the evaluation of methods of instruction.
citation: Buford Johnson. (1918). The Use of Tests in the Evaluation of Methods of Instruction. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://www.google.com/search?q=The+Use+of+Tests+in+the+Evaluation+of+Methods+of+Instruction+Johnson+1918
title: Instruction should be devised from elaborated testing built on analysis of individual performance
description: The article argues that the most effective use of educational measurements is determining methods of instruction, meaning an elasticity of program adjusting drill, assignments, recitation forms and groupings to individual needs. It holds that "Only by an elaboration of testing, the scheme of which is built upon the analysis of the individual performance, can the instruction be devised that makes for conservation of energy and interest." The most significant result of testing is described as a reconstruction in method on the basis of the facts obtained.
requirements: Standardized tests administered under supervision, plus records of age and deficiencies, and teacher judgment ratings as a basis for determining methodology of instruction
constraints: Under the routine adopted, even in the summer session, the necessary stimulation for correction of the trouble will not be given
target_learners: Pupils in grades 4-8 who failed of promotion because of deficiency in fundamental subjects
target_learning_goals: Remediation of specific deficiencies in arithmetic and English (reading, spelling, composition, grammar)
examples: Standard tests were given to pupils by students in the university course of experimental education under direct supervision of the instructor, and each teacher rated her pupils on a judgment scale
key_sources: Buford Johnson. (1918). The Use of Tests in the Evaluation of Methods of Instruction. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://www.google.com/search?q=The+Use+of+Tests+in+the+Evaluation+of+Methods+of+Instruction+Johnson+1918

article_title: The Psychopathology of Every-day Life.
citation: Mayer, H. (1911). The Psychopathology of Everyday Life. American Journal of Psychology, 22, 477-527. https://www.jstor.org/stable/1412853
title: An introductory textbook should be judged chiefly by whether it induces pupils to think, with class exercises that stimulate introspection
description: In a companion book notice, the reviewer states that "Probably the chief function of an introductory textbook is to induce the pupils to think," and praises the reviewed text for accomplishing this through a terse, vigorous style and short, easily grasped sentences. The chapter-end class exercises are singled out as "admirably chosen to stimulate introspection," making introspective exercises a design feature of an introductory psychology text.
requirements: Exercises placed at the end of each chapter, chosen to prompt pupils' introspection
constraints: Stated for introductory psychology textbooks
target_learners: pupils in an introductory psychology course
target_learning_goals: stimulating thinking and introspection about mental facts
examples: The reviewed textbook's class exercises follow each chapter and are described as admirably chosen to stimulate introspection.
key_sources: Mayer, H. (1911). The Psychopathology of Everyday Life. American Journal of Psychology, 22, 477-527. https://www.jstor.org/stable/1412853

article_title: Teacher coaching in upper secondary school: Examining the effects on teacher–student interaction and student engagement.
citation: Ertesvåg, S. K., Vaaland, G. S., Tvedt, M. S., Virtanen, T. E., Idsoe, T., Panayiotou, M., Lerang, M. S., Sølvik, R. M., & Lerkkanen, M.-K. (2026). Teacher coaching in upper secondary school: Examining the effects on teacher–student interaction and student engagement. Journal of Educational Psychology, 118(1), 118-137. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000986
title: INTERACT video-based, web-mediated teacher coaching intervention
description: INTERACT is a structured, personalized, and interactive coaching process built on "coaching dialogues based on authentic video-recorded classroom practice from the teacher's classroom." Delivery involves three components: seven coaching cycles of six steps each using the IRIS Connect recording system, implementation support (webinars, workshops, video library, podcasts, articles), and data- and knowledge-driven decision making guided by TTI and the CLASS-S. Ten trained coaches each worked with assigned teachers across the 2022–2023 school year.
requirements: Teachers record lessons approximately every third week using the IRIS Connect system
Coaches complete 5-day coach training plus 2-day CLASS-S observer training with certification
constraints: Evaluated in Norwegian upper secondary schools; no prior studies of teacher coaching on TSI and engagement had been conducted outside the United States at this level
target_learning_goals: improve teacher–student interaction quality and student engagement
examples: Teachers in the intervention group were assigned to a coach (10 coaches in total) and participated in seven coaching cycles throughout the 2022–2023 school year
key_sources: Ertesvåg, S. K., Vaaland, G. S., Tvedt, M. S., Virtanen, T. E., Idsoe, T., Panayiotou, M., Lerang, M. S., Sølvik, R. M., & Lerkkanen, M.-K. (2026). Teacher coaching in upper secondary school: Examining the effects on teacher–student interaction and student engagement. Journal of Educational Psychology, 118(1), 118-137. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000986

article_title: Preliminary study of the relative efficiency of inductive and deductive teaching of logical reasoning.
citation: Felix Sachs. (1913). Preliminary Study of the Relative Efficiency of Inductive and Deductive Teaching of Logical Reasoning. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://www.jstor.org/journal/jeducpsyc
title: Teach forms of fallacious reasoning inductively through drill on concrete everyday examples rather than by deductive presentation of rules
description: The article recommends replacing deductive logic teaching, accompanied as it too often is by sheer memorizing of logical figures and rules, with painstaking drill in analyzing concrete examples of argumentation taken from various phases of everyday life. Instruction proceeded by having observers understand each fallacy from a typical example, then labelling it, then drilling with valid and fallacious examples until each could state validity, reasons, and fallacy name.
requirements: Requires a collection of suitable concrete, non-technical examples of each fallacy type, which the author reports was no easy task to assemble
constraints: The author concedes the experiment does not prove the conviction incontestably and calls it a preliminary study; the comparison confounded inductive with deductive and individual with classroom instruction
examples: About 20 hours of tutoring in which examples such as a strike argument were varied premise by premise until observers themselves identified which inferences were wrong, after which the fallacy names Denying the Antecedent and Affirming the Consequent were given
key_sources: Felix Sachs. (1913). Preliminary Study of the Relative Efficiency of Inductive and Deductive Teaching of Logical Reasoning. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://www.jstor.org/journal/jeducpsyc

article_title: Adolescent well-being and school engagement as a function of teacher and peer relatedness: The more (relatedness) is not always the merrier.
citation: Núñez-Regueiro, F., & Wang, M.-T. (2024). Adolescent Well-Being and School Engagement as a Function of Teacher and Peer Relatedness: The More (Relatedness) Is Not Always the Merrier. Journal of Educational Psychology, 117(3), 466-484. https://hal.science/hal-04920252v1
title: Design interventions and theories around peer and teacher relatedness as interdependent, rather than independent, factors of adolescent development
description: The article's implications state that "peer and teacher relatedness appear to be interdependent factors of positive development", which "changes the way psychological needs for relatedness are conceived in educational theories". Interventions should therefore foster healthy socialization processes with both peers and teachers together, since benefits of one source depend on the other. The principle rests on the two-study cubic RSA evidence that single-source relatedness was often not adaptive.
requirements: Interventions must assess and address both peer and teacher relatedness rather than a single source
constraints: Peer relatedness did not contribute to well-being in the absence of teacher relatedness, and teacher relatedness alone did not contribute to well-being
examples: The Educational Impact and Implications Statement reports that the findings open new avenues for interventions aiming to foster healthy socialization processes at school.
key_sources: Núñez-Regueiro, F., & Wang, M.-T. (2024). Adolescent Well-Being and School Engagement as a Function of Teacher and Peer Relatedness: The More (Relatedness) Is Not Always the Merrier. Journal of Educational Psychology, 117(3), 466-484. https://hal.science/hal-04920252v1

article_title: Practice and transference in normal and feeble-minded children.
citation: Woodrow, H. (1915). Practice and transference in normal and feeble-minded children. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=%22Practice+and+Transference+in+Normal+and+Feeble-Minded+Children%22
title: Incapacity for mental development reflects inability to grow rather than inability to learn
description: The author proposes that the capacity to gain from practice (learning) is separable from the capacity for mental development (growth). The practice data showing equal improvement in feeble-minded and normal children of the same mental age suggest that "it is not inability to learn which characterizes incapacity for mental development, but inability to grow, and that the two are quite distinguishable." The author argues that prejudice against admitting equal practice effects stems from wrongly identifying mental development capacity with ability to learn.
requirements: Requires comparing feeble-minded children with normal children of the same mental age and initial ability, not the same chronological age
constraints: The author notes the conclusion is based on one type of work and small groups, and that the matter of the spread of training remains to be considered in a subsequent paper
target_learners: normal children of the same mental age
target_learning_goals: practice effects on perceptual-motor sorting tasks
examples: The four-group experiment compared practice curves and found equal improvement, leading the author to distinguish learning from growth as separate capacities
key_sources: Woodrow, H. (1915). Practice and transference in normal and feeble-minded children. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=%22Practice+and+Transference+in+Normal+and+Feeble-Minded+Children%22

article_title: An outline for institutional education and treatment of young offenders.
citation: William Healy and Augusta F. Bronner. (1916). An Outline for Institutional Education and Treatment of Young Offenders. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://psycnet.apa.org
title: Institutional life should be wholly educational and highly individualized to fit delinquents for outside environment
description: The authors state that "the entire institutional life should be adjusted with the idea that it is treatment, that it is educational," aimed at fitting the delinquent for an outside environment. This requires high individualization: both education and work must be adapted to individual needs, and the method should be elastic in all ways, particularly in institutions for girls.
requirements: Staff must avoid deceit, pedantry, and any demonstration of irrationality, modeling rationality and honesty by example
constraints: Modification cannot always be thought of in terms of building up; some offenders have self-will too strong or physical vigor too redundant, and harmful modifications can come from throwing delinquents together
target_learners: young offenders in training or industrial schools
target_learning_goals: coping with all phases of an ordinary social environment
examples: The outline allows for outbreaks and explosions of pent-up emotions and energies in institutions for girls, and for physical fluctuations
key_sources: William Healy and Augusta F. Bronner. (1916). An Outline for Institutional Education and Treatment of Young Offenders. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0071384

article_title: A study of initial spurt in the case of addition.
citation: Chapman, J. C. (1914). A Study of Initial Spurt in the Case of Addition. The Journal of Educational Psychology.
title: Initial spurt doctrine: maximum efficiency at the very commencement of mental work
description: The article names and states the doctrine of initial spurt as a candidate general characteristic of mental work: "At the very commencement of work, other things being equal, the individual tends to exhibit his maximum efficiency." The proposed explanation is that the individual "commences work with a too exacting standard" and is soon compelled to relax it. The article treats the doctrine as attractive but previously unsupported, and sets out to test it with short time periods and many subjects.
requirements: Testing the doctrine requires measuring continuous work divided into periods short enough to capture the spurt, with a sufficient number of subjects
constraints: The article notes the subject is usually so mixed up with accidental variations that selection can make them look like a general law
target_learning_goals: efficiency of sustained mental work over time
examples: The author tested the doctrine with 46 college students adding columns of numbers, scoring five successive two-minute periods within each ten-minute test
key_sources: Chapman, J. C. (1914). A Study of Initial Spurt in the Case of Addition. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0070019

article_title: Multiple pathways to success: An examination of integrative motivational profiles among upper elementary and college students.
citation: Linnenbrink-Garcia, L., Wormington, S. V., Snyder, K. E., Riggsbee, J., Perez, T., Ben-Eliyahu, A., & Hill, N. E. (2018). Multiple Pathways to Success: An Examination of Integrative Motivational Profiles Among Upper Elementary and College Students. Journal of Educational Psychology, 110(7), 1026-1048. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000245
title: Integrative motivational profile framework combining Expectancy-Value Theory and Achievement Goal Theory
description: This framework integrates constructs from Expectancy-Value Theory and Achievement Goal Theory to describe how students' motivational beliefs cohere into profiles. As the authors state, "we aimed to identify integrative motivational profiles consisting of competence beliefs (representing expectancies from Expectancy-Value Theory), task value, and three types of achievement goal orientations (mastery, performance-approach, performance-avoidance)". Competence beliefs address whether students believe they can succeed, while task value and goals address why they engage. The framework underpins the person-oriented analyses in both studies.
requirements: Measures of perceived competence, task value, mastery goals, performance-approach goals, and performance-avoidance goals on comparable scales, combined via latent profile analysis.
constraints: Profiles identified are by design unique to each sample, raising generalizability concerns the authors note from prior person-oriented research.
examples: In Study 1, fifth graders' domain-general schooling motivation was profiled into four groups; in Study 2, college students' science motivation was profiled in a gateway chemistry context.
key_sources: Linnenbrink-Garcia, L., Wormington, S. V., Snyder, K. E., Riggsbee, J., Perez, T., Ben-Eliyahu, A., & Hill, N. E. (2018). Multiple Pathways to Success: An Examination of Integrative Motivational Profiles Among Upper Elementary and College Students. Journal of Educational Psychology, 110(7), 1026-1048. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000245

article_title: Response to instruction in preschool: Results of two randomized studies with children at significant risk of reading difficulties.
citation: Lonigan, C. J., & Phillips, B. M. (2016). Response to Instruction in Preschool: Results of Two Randomized Studies with Children At Significant Risk of Reading Difficulties. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000054
title: Intensified Tier II design: narrowed content targets, smaller groups, separated strands, and progress-monitoring-based pacing
description: This design pattern describes how the authors revised their Tier II preschool intervention between studies. They narrowed content within each strand "to allow more time on topic across fewer distinct content targets", reduced the maximum small-group size from 6 to 4 children, separated phonological awareness and print knowledge into distinct strands, and added regular progress-monitoring assessments that determined whether groups advanced or repeated lessons. Lesson plans also explicitly included upward and downward scaffolding instructions so within-group instruction could be differentiated.
requirements: Detailed written lesson plans describing daily activities, duration, and scripts; interventionists trained (approximately 20 hours in Study 2) with audio-recorded sessions reviewed for fidelity and weekly feedback
constraints: Evaluated with 11-week small-group supplemental instruction for preschoolers already failing to progress under an evidence-based Tier I curriculum in Title I preschools
target_learners: preschool children at significant risk of reading difficulties identified via RTI screening
target_learning_goals: phonological awareness, print knowledge (letter names and sounds), and oral language/vocabulary
examples: In Study 2, letter instruction covered only letters in each child's name plus 11 target letters with cumulative weekly review, and PA focused only on compound words, two-syllable words, and onset-rime
key_sources: Lonigan, C. J., & Phillips, B. M. (2016). Response to Instruction in Preschool: Results of Two Randomized Studies with Children At Significant Risk of Reading Difficulties. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000054

article_title: Graded mental tests. Part I. Attention, perception, comprehension and memory.
citation: Squire, C. R. (1912). Graded Mental Tests. Part I. Attention, Perception, Comprehension and Memory. The Journal of Educational Psychology, III(7). https://www.jstor.org/journal/jeducpsych
title: Individual administration of mental tests is essential to reliability when working with children
description: The article recommends giving mental tests to children individually rather than in groups, because individual testing "gives every individual an equal opportunity". The experimenter and child come into close rapport, questions can be adapted to the individual child's comprehension, and the exercise can feel like a pleasant game rather than a test, which is requisite to a good working mood in a child. All of this, the author argues, is impossible in group testing.
requirements: Standard conditions maintained throughout the series, with tests adapted to each age and individual
constraints: Individual testing consumes more time than group testing
target_learners: elementary school children aged six to thirteen
target_learning_goals: accurate measurement of mental capacity for diagnosis and grading
examples: All tests in the series were given individually; with the six-year-old group responses were oral and recorded by the examiner, while older children wrote their own responses where time was not the determinant
key_sources: Squire, C. R. (1912). Graded Mental Tests. Part I. Attention, Perception, Comprehension and Memory. The Journal of Educational Psychology, III(7). https://www.jstor.org/journal/jeducpsych

article_title: Autonomy and task performance: Explaining the impact of grades on intrinsic motivation.
citation: Pulfrey, C., Darnon, C., & Butera, F. (2013). Autonomy and task performance: Explaining the impact of grades on intrinsic motivation. Journal of Educational Psychology, 105(1), 39–57. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0029376
title: Integrative model differentiating the mediational roles of task performance and task autonomy in the grading–intrinsic motivation link
description: The article proposes an integrative model that treats posttask intrinsic motivation as two distinct but related constructs — self-report task interest and continuing motivation for the task — and tests two mediators simultaneously. It holds that both perceived task autonomy and reward-contingent task performance mediate the link between grading context and task interest, whereas task autonomy, and not task performance, mediates the link between grading context and continuing motivation. The model was tested in a school context using two contrasts against a standard-grade reference condition. As the authors state, the model tests "the mediational role of task performance and of perceived task autonomy on the relationship between grading and both self-report task interest and continuing motivation for the task."
requirements: Two experimental contrasts against a standard-grade reference condition: a reward contrast (high grade vs. standard grade) and an autonomy contrast (no grade vs. standard grade)
Simultaneous measurement of task performance and perceived task autonomy as mediators, with task autonomy measured before the main task to preserve chronological order
constraints: Tested in the ecologically valid context of Swiss secondary school classrooms with anagram tasks
Grounded in the SDT versus GIT debate over performance-contingent rewards
target_learners: Secondary school pupils in academic tracks (Grades 7–9)
target_learning_goals: Intrinsic motivation for academic tasks, measured as task interest and continuing motivation for the task
examples: Experiment 1 with 89 lowest-track pupils and Experiment 2 with 122 seventh graders across three tracks used anagram exercises under no-grade, high-grade, and standard-grade conditions
key_sources: Pulfrey, C., Darnon, C., & Butera, F. (2013). Autonomy and task performance: Explaining the impact of grades on intrinsic motivation. Journal of Educational Psychology, 105(1), 39–57. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0029376

article_title: Are we afraid of competition?
citation: Are We Afraid of Competition? The Function of Examinations. (1910). The Journal of Educational Psychology, 1. https://psycnet.apa.org/journal/edu
title: Introduce a larger amount of competition and scholastic rewards into the American school system
description: This principle is the editorial's own recommendation: American schools should make freer use of competition, on the model of English school systems whose monthly announcements of scholarships, fellowships, prizes and exhibitions the author finds nothing short of astounding to an American reader. It rests on the editorial's judgment that competition is particularly valuable in developing the capacities of pupils of more than average ability.
requirements: A school system prepared to make free use of competition, with a visible apparatus of scholastic rewards such as the English model the editorial describes
constraints: The editorial itself records the counter-arguments that competition arouses jealousy and bitterness and may lead pupils of poor vitality to bankrupt their health
target_learners: school pupils, especially pupils of more than average ability
target_learning_goals: identification and advancement of promising pupils
examples: The editorial cites The Educational Times of London's monthly announcements of scholarships, fellowships, prizes and exhibitions under the caption The Educational Ladder as the competitive apparatus inspiring the recommendation
key_sources: Are We Afraid of Competition? The Function of Examinations. (1910). The Journal of Educational Psychology, 1. https://psycnet.apa.org/journal/edu

article_title: Immersive auditory-cognitive training improves speech-in-noise perception in older adults with varying hearing and working memory
citation: Vanessa Frei & Nathalie Giroud. (2025). Immersive auditory-cognitive training improves speech-in-noise perception in older adults with varying hearing and working memory. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00306-5
title: Integrated perceptual-cognitive system theory (Schneider and Pichora-Fuller) as the article's resource-allocation account of speech comprehension
description: The article adopts this theory as its explanatory framework for why combined sensory and cognitive training should work: speech comprehension succeeds through a direct link between sensory and cognitive processing that draws on shared resources. As the article states, "The theory assumes a direct link between sensory and cognitive processing, based on a shared pool of processing resources." Efficient allocation of these resources toward the sensory and cognitive demands of speech enables comprehension, whereas increased load or reduced individual capacities limit success. The authors use it to interpret why the immersive environment's extra sensory information intensified training, particularly for listeners with limited hearing or auditory working memory.
requirements: A training situation that imposes both sensory and cognitive demand so that allocation of shared processing resources must be managed
constraints: The article notes that in very favorable listening situations additional visual speech cues have been proposed to act as increased sensory load rather than support, per cited empirical works
target_learners: older adults with varying hearing acuity and cognitive capacities
target_learning_goals: efficient allocation of processing resources between sensory and cognitive demand
examples: The authors interpret the immersive session's extra redundant sensory information as provoking resource allocation between sensory information and varying memory load, potentially producing the stronger training effect
key_sources: Vanessa Frei & Nathalie Giroud. (2025). Immersive auditory-cognitive training improves speech-in-noise perception in older adults with varying hearing and working memory. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00306-5

article_title: Socioeconomic and genomic roots of verbal ability from current evidence
citation: Guang Guo, Meng-Jung Lin and Kathleen Mullan Harris. (2022). Socioeconomic and genomic roots of verbal ability from current evidence. npj Science of Learning 7:22. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-022-00137-8
title: Include both SES and offspring genome in the same model, and routinely collect DNA in large social-science studies, to obtain more accurate estimates of SES effects
description: The article argues that the decades-long practice of including SES in a model and interpreting its coefficients as purely environmental effects needs amendment, because about 20–30% of conventionally estimated SES coefficients are parentally genomic. It states: "A straightforward and ready solution is to include both SES and offspring genome in the same model," which corrects roughly 50% of the upward bias in SES effects and makes genetic effects more truly a reflection of children's own genomes. It further recommends routinely collecting DNA data in large social-science studies granted their primary purpose is understanding social and environmental influences.
requirements: DNA measures (polygenic scores) and rich longitudinal SES measures collected on the same individuals
constraints: Published GWAS are mostly based on individuals of European descent, so the approach does not apply as well to racial minorities; the analysis excludes African Americans, Asian Americans, Native Americans and Hispanic African Americans
target_learners: Youth aged 12–18 in longitudinal social-science studies
examples: The Add Health analysis of 7194 individuals shows the education PGS effect reduced by more than 20% and SES effects by about 10–15% when both are modeled jointly
key_sources: Guang Guo, Meng-Jung Lin and Kathleen Mullan Harris. (2022). Socioeconomic and genomic roots of verbal ability from current evidence. npj Science of Learning 7:22. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-022-00137-8

article_title: Applying, not ignoring: how feedback uptake and neural synchrony drive creativity
citation: Junting Yin, Zheyu Jin, Yuxuan Zhang, Xuening Li, Yangzhuo Li, Guoping Zhang & Junlong Luo. (2025). Applying, not ignoring: how feedback uptake and neural synchrony drive creativity. npj Science of Learning 10:61. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00351-0
title: Design feedback dialogues that let receivers actively respond, and include why/how content alongside emotional feedback
description: The article recommends interactive feedback environments, "such as dialogic exchanges between teachers and students or struc- tured peer collaboration", to promote cognitive alignment and divergent thinking. It further advocates that feedback should "actively guide learners in integrating and applying new input" and that providers include "why" or "how-to" feedback alongside emotional feedback, because comments and scaffolding were more likely applied and application tracked creativity gains.
requirements: Feedback must allow receivers to respond and articulate understanding, as in the IF condition's 30-second response turns
constraints: Benefits were assessed within a single session with a short interval; the article calls for testing persistence over longer periods
The AUT measure primarily reflects divergent thinking and does not capture the full range of creativity
The majority of participants were female; the article calls for more gender-diverse samples
target_learners: adult learners in workplace performance-review settings
target_learning_goals: divergent thinking and creativity acquisition and transfer
effective uptake and application of feedback
examples: In the experiment, IF dyads exchanged 30-second feedback and response turns, while OF receivers rested without responding; only IF improved both acquisition and transfer
key_sources: Junting Yin, Zheyu Jin, Yuxuan Zhang, Xuening Li, Yangzhuo Li, Guoping Zhang & Junlong Luo. (2025). Applying, not ignoring: how feedback uptake and neural synchrony drive creativity. npj Science of Learning 10:61. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00351-0

article_title: Differential effects of changes in cardiorespiratory fitness on worst- and best- school subjects
citation: Toru Ishihara, Noriteru Morita, Toshihiro Nakajima, Koji Yamatsu, Koichi Okita, Masato Sagawa and Keita Kamijo. (2021). Differential effects of changes in cardiorespiratory fitness on worst- and best- school subjects. npj Science of Learning 6:8. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00086-8
title: Intra-individual variability in grade points as a moderator of the physical fitness–academic performance association
description: The article proposes that the association between physical fitness and academic performance is moderated by intra-individual variability in grade points: improvements in fitness benefit a student's worst subjects selectively rather than raising all subjects uniformly. The authors state that "the longitudinal association between improvements in physical ﬁtness and academic performance is moderated by intra- individual variability in academic grades," and suggest this moderator might explain why some large-scale cluster RCTs found no overall effect of physical activity interventions on academic performance. It reframes baseline-performance moderation from an inter-individual to an intra-individual level.
requirements: Requires measuring each student's lowest and highest subject grade points separately over time, rather than only aggregate or overall academic scores
constraints: Derived from an observational two-year study in Japanese junior high schools using teacher-assessed grade points; the authors note the GP system varies among countries and that catch-up growth cannot be ruled out
target_learners: junior high school students (12–13 years old at baseline)
target_learning_goals: academic performance across five curriculum subjects (Japanese, mathematics, social studies, science, English)
examples: The study analyzed 469 students' lowest and highest GPs at the end of seventh and ninth grades, controlling for household income, maternal education, sex, change in BMI, and change in learning time
