key_sources: Toru Ishihara, Noriteru Morita, Toshihiro Nakajima, Koji Yamatsu, Koichi Okita, Masato Sagawa and Keita Kamijo. (2021). Differential effects of changes in cardiorespiratory fitness on worst- and best- school subjects. npj Science of Learning 6:8. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00086-8

article_title: Interleaved practice enhances memory and problem-solving ability in undergraduate physics
citation: Joshua Samani and Steven C. Pan. (2021). Interleaved practice enhances memory and problem-solving ability in undergraduate physics. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00110-x
title: Replace conventionally blocked homework with interleaved homework when assignments contain multiple isomorphic problems per topic
description: The article recommends that instructors convert blocked homework assignments, in which one topic is practiced at a time, into interleaved assignments that switch between topics, because this simple rearrangement of the same problems fostered longer-lasting and more generalizable learning in undergraduate physics. As the authors put it, "Simply interleaving those assignments in a similar fashion may greatly enhance their effectiveness." The intervention is described as a relatively low-cost learning intervention in terms of time and equipment.
requirements: Assignments should contain multiple isomorphic or nearly isomorphic problems for each topic, as in the present study
constraints: The article cautions it is unclear whether interleaving benefits will be apparent on high-stakes exams after extensive cramming, and implementation issues such as the relative predictability of interleaving schedules and the point during learning when interleaving is introduced remain to be resolved
target_learners: students in courses where multiple topics are learned using blocked homework assignments
target_learning_goals: problem-solving with novel, more challenging problems
examples: In the study, only the arrangement of homework problems during normal instruction was manipulated: blocked assignments had three successive isomorphic problems per topic, whereas interleaved assignments had one problem per topic, with all students completing the same 84 total problems
key_sources: Joshua Samani and Steven C. Pan. (2021). Interleaved practice enhances memory and problem-solving ability in undergraduate physics. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00110-x

article_title: Regulation competencies and social well-being in at-risk adolescents: a systematic review of behavioral and neurophysiological research
citation: Jamaludin, A., Samyuktha, S. & Tan, A. L. (2026). Regulation competencies and social well-being in at-risk adolescents: a systematic review of behavioral and neurophysiological research. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00435-5
title: Integrative framework of regulation competencies as a multi-level, context-sensitive developmental capability linking adversity to social well-being
description: The review articulates an integrative conceptualization (Figure 3) in which structural and relational risks such as socioeconomic disadvantage and trauma exposure exert influence through regulation competencies spanning emotional (ER), metacognitive (MR), and social (SR) domains. Regulation competencies "function as proximal mechanisms that translate contextual adversity into social well-being outcomes, including empathy, belonging, distress regulation, and prosocial engagement". The framework reframes regulation from an individual-level attribute to a context-sensitive developmental capacity, with neurophysiological measures anchoring regulatory capacities in observable neural and autonomic processes.
requirements: Testing the framework as a whole requires designs that assess regulation competencies, biological processes, and social well-being outcomes within the same adolescents
constraints: The review notes the literature has largely examined individual components of this framework in isolation rather than testing the framework as a whole
target_learners: at-risk adolescents aged 10 to 18 facing socioeconomic disadvantage, trauma exposure, marginalized status, or clinical vulnerability
target_learning_goals: emotional, metacognitive, and social regulation supporting empathy, belonging, resilience, and prosocial engagement
examples: The review consolidates 45 studies into tabular matrices mapping regulation domains, designs, outcomes, and risk profiles (Supplementary Table S2)
key_sources: Jamaludin, A., Samyuktha, S. & Tan, A. L. (2026). Regulation competencies and social well-being in at-risk adolescents: a systematic review of behavioral and neurophysiological research. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00435-5

article_title: Comparing models of learning and relearning in large-scale cognitive training data sets
citation: Aakriti Kumar, Aaron S. Benjamin, Andrew Heathcote and Mark Steyvers. (2022). Comparing models of learning and relearning in large-scale cognitive training data sets. npj Science of Learning 7:24. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-022-00142-x
title: Interactive two-timescale model of naturalistic learning (M4): permanent skill plus labile task-set preparedness that is lost with delay and rapidly regained with practice
description: M4 models performance as the sum of a slow learning process indexing permanent skill, based on total games played, and a fast process representing task-set preparedness whose weight depends on a context-loss function of elapsed time between sessions. The article states that "task-set preparedness is lost between sessions but is also more rapidly regained with each additional practice session", and that skill, like riding a bike, "is maintained permanently, without loss". The context loss function L(t) = 1 - e^(-γt) captures varied temporal patterns; for the fitted data, 50% of context is lost after about 450 days and close to 80% after 800 days.
requirements: Practice data spanning multiple sessions with varied between-session delays, so that context loss and relearning can be estimated
constraints: The forgetting rate parameter γ is assumed to be shared across participants because not all participants have enough data for a stable individual estimate
target_learners: adult self-directed learners on online cognitive training platforms
target_learning_goals: long-term skill acquisition and retention of cognitive tasks such as selective attention and task switching
examples: The model was fit to individual users' gameplay histories from two Lumosity games, Lost in Migration (a flanker task) and Ebb and Flow (a task switching game), and its relearning predictions plotted against empirical curves in Figs. 5 and 6
key_sources: Aakriti Kumar, Aaron S. Benjamin, Andrew Heathcote and Mark Steyvers. (2022). Comparing models of learning and relearning in large-scale cognitive training data sets. npj Science of Learning 7:24. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-022-00142-x

article_title: Anterograde interference in multitask perceptual learning
citation: Jia Yang, Fang-Fang Yan, Tingting Wang, Zile Wang, Qingshang Ma, Jinmei Xiao, Xianyuan Yang, Zhong-Lin Lu & Chang-Bing Huang. (2025). Anterograde interference in multitask perceptual learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00312-7
title: Integrated reweighting account with shared and protected weight structures for multitask learning
description: The article extends the Integration Reweighting Theory to sequential multitask learning: "The Integration Reweighting Theory and related reweighting models propose thatl e a r n i n gi n v o l v es optimizing connection weights between stable stimulus representation and task decisions." The authors propose that perceptual learning engages distinct plastic sites with compatible or incompatible overlapping weight structures, and that a network preserving learned-task weights while adjusting non-overlapping nodes can yield the observed asymmetric anterograde interference. This supports a meta-plasticity strategy of reducing plasticity in previously engaged regions to protect established learning.
requirements: Models of perceptual learning would need to incorporate shared and independent hidden layers that preserve weight structures from learned tasks
constraints: The theory and models have primarily been applied to investigate perceptual learning and transfer in single tasks; extension to sequential multitask learning is the article's proposal
target_learners: adults learning multiple perceptual tasks sequentially
target_learning_goals: acquisition of multiple perceptual skills with preserved prior learning
examples: A schematic neural network in which learning task A first protects task-A weights, so task B learned via non-overlapping nodes is unaffected by sequence position, while learning task B first prevents the optimal decision boundary for task A
key_sources: Jia Yang, Fang-Fang Yan, Tingting Wang, Zile Wang, Qingshang Ma, Jinmei Xiao, Xianyuan Yang, Zhong-Lin Lu & Chang-Bing Huang. (2025). Anterograde interference in multitask perceptual learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00312-7

article_title: Interpersonal neural synchronization underlies interactive concept learning in older adults
citation: Zi-Wei Liang, Zhi-Jun Zhan, Ying-Chen Liu, Hong-Zhou Xu & Jing Yu. (2025). Interpersonal neural synchronization underlies interactive concept learning in older adults. npj Science of Learning 10:75. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00368-5
title: Interpersonal neural synchronization as a dyadic neural mechanism of interactive learning, examined via fNIRS hyperscanning, INS, and IS-RSA
description: The article frames interactive learning as a joint action whose effectiveness is underwritten by "interpersonal neural synchronization (INS), the coupling of neural processes across brains", which "supports dyadic interaction through shared attention, mutual prediction, and co-regulation". It operationalizes this with fNIRS hyperscanning (wavelet transform coherence between instructor and learner HbO signals), permutation tests against pseudo dyads, Granger causality for directional coupling, and IS-RSA to link inter-individual performance similarity with neural similarity, focusing on the prefrontal cortex.
requirements: Simultaneous dual-brain recording (fNIRS hyperscanning) of both instructor and learner during real interaction
constraints: The fNIRS setup captured only frontal cortical activity, leaving other cortical and subcortical regions unexplored
The one-to-one laboratory setting does not fully reflect real-world lifelong learning contexts where group instruction and peer interactions are common
target_learners: Older adults (55+) in lifelong-learning settings, with younger-adult comparison groups
target_learning_goals: Concept learning (social psychology concepts) in interactive instructor-led settings
examples: Study 1 and Study 2 recorded dyads with a Shimadzu FORE3000 fNIRS system over the PFC, computing instructor-learner INS via wavelet transform coherence and validating against 1000 pseudo dyads
key_sources: Zi-Wei Liang, Zhi-Jun Zhan, Ying-Chen Liu, Hong-Zhou Xu & Jing Yu. (2025). Interpersonal neural synchronization underlies interactive concept learning in older adults. npj Science of Learning 10:75. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00368-5

article_title: Spatiotemporal predictions guide attention throughout the adult lifespan
citation: Nir Shalev, Sage Boettcher & Anna C. Nobre. (2024). Spatiotemporal predictions guide attention throughout the adult lifespan. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00281-3
title: Integrate spatiotemporal regularities into dynamic, realistic search scenes to enhance ecological validity
description: The authors recommend extending dynamic search paradigms beyond well-controlled artificial environments by embedding spatiotemporal regularities in realistic scenes. They note that in real life some regularities are stored in long-term memory, such as expectations about traffic lights, and that such designs "would not only enhance ecological validity but also enable exploration of whether spatiotemporal regularities guide attention across adulthood based on long-term expectations."
requirements: Prior experience with realistic stimuli as a meaningful source of attentional guidance
constraints: The influence of prior experience with spatiotemporal regularities has not been tested with dynamic objects and scenes, per the authors
target_learners: Adults across the adult lifespan, including older adults
target_learning_goals: Proactive attentional guidance using learned temporal and spatial regularities
examples: The current study used a controlled artificial display with fixed quadrant-onset pairings to maximize trial-by-trial learning; the authors propose realistic scenes as the next step.
key_sources: Nir Shalev, Sage Boettcher & Anna C. Nobre. (2024). Spatiotemporal predictions guide attention throughout the adult lifespan. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00281-3

article_title: Growth mindset and academic outcomes: a comparison of US and Chinese students
citation: Xin Sun, Shaylene Nancekivell, Susan A. Gelman and Priti Shah. (2021). Growth mindset and academic outcomes: a comparison of US and Chinese students. npj Science of Learning 6:21. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00100-z
title: Mindset interventions can target the malleability of school performance and effort attribution rather than the malleability of intelligence
description: The article proposes an alternative route to motivation intervention: rather than increasing beliefs about the malleability of intelligence, interventions "can focus on the malleability of mastering school subjects and directly promoting a more effort-oriented attribution to school performance." This rests on the finding that students in both cultures view effort as more important than ability for school-level achievement, so students can be motivated to invest effort even without a growth view of intelligence. A related suggested message is that school success is only modestly related to intelligence per se.
requirements: Students must already view effort as more important than ability for school-level achievement, as both samples in the article did
constraints: The classic mindset intervention paradigm was reported as not effective on a sample of N = 624 Chinese students, cited as consistent with the current investigation
The article notes this alternative is a theoretical proposal ('in theory, could be more impactful'), not a tested intervention
target_learners: Middle-school and college students in US and Chinese educational contexts
target_learning_goals: Academic motivation and effort investment in school mathematics achievement
examples: Study 2 measured effort-ability attributions for school-level achievements such as achieving an A in a middle-school algebra course, where both samples rated effort above ability
key_sources: Xin Sun, Shaylene Nancekivell, Susan A. Gelman and Priti Shah. (2021). Growth mindset and academic outcomes: a comparison of US and Chinese students. npj Science of Learning 6:21. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00100-z

article_title: The inherence bias in preschoolers’ explanations for achievement differences: replication and extension
citation: Renoux, M., Goudeau, S., Alexopoulos, T., Bouquet, C. A. & Cimpian, A. (2024). The inherence bias in preschoolers' explanations for achievement differences: replication and extension. npj Science of Learning 9:10. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00218-w
title: The inherence bias: a cognitive account of why explanations overweight inherent factors and underweight extrinsic ones
description: The inherence bias is the tendency to explain observations by appealing to factors inherent to the entities involved (e.g., intelligence, personality) rather than extrinsic contextual factors. The article presents it as "a general version of the so-called correspondence bias" and links it to psychological essentialism. It arises from attentional spotlight effects, memory accessibility differences, and working-memory limitations, with cultural context amplifying or attenuating these factors. The studies here test its operation in preschoolers' explanations of achievement differences.
requirements: Explanations must be elicited about observations with both inherent and extrinsic candidate causes available
constraints: The article states the degree of deviation from a perfectly rational thinker "will vary from case to case depending on the reasoner, the context, and the observation being explained"; it is not an inescapable deterministic pattern
target_learning_goals: children's explanations and perceptions of academic achievement differences among peers
examples: Study 1 vignettes about a peer called on more often or talking longer in class discussions; Study 2 scenarios in which the child does better or worse than a peer on a math exercise
key_sources: Renoux, M., Goudeau, S., Alexopoulos, T., Bouquet, C. A. & Cimpian, A. (2024). The inherence bias in preschoolers' explanations for achievement differences: replication and extension. npj Science of Learning 9:10. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00218-w

article_title: Trends in testing effect research: from lab to classroom, but not yet for all learners
citation: Wilschut, T., Sense, F. & van Rijn, H. (2026). Trends in testing effect research: from lab to classroom, but not yet for all learners. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00400-2
title: Design retrieval practice environments inclusively by reducing decoding and orthographic demands, e.g., spoken prompts, verbal responses, and auditory feedback
description: The article recommends adapting computerized retrieval practice applications to the needs of learners with SLDs. It states that "adjustments—such as providing spoken prompts, accepting verbal responses, or integrating audi-313 tory feedback—can help reduce demands from decoding and orthographic processing and better314 support neurodiverse learners." Further suggested customizations include balancing verbs and nouns in study sets, pacing/pausing options, scaffolding, and adapting repetition schedules, with systematic analysis of each feature's effects on learners' motivational, affective, cognitive, and perceptual needs.
requirements: Learning environments whose input format, difficulty, and pacing can be adjusted to individual learners' needs
constraints: The article presents these as design recommendations grounded in limited evidence; the underlying empirical base for SLD learners is very small
target_learners: Learners with specific learning disabilities, including dyslexia and DLD
Neurodiverse learners in educational and digital learning contexts
target_learning_goals: Long-term retention of learned material via retrieval practice
examples: Wilschut et al.'s adaptive retrieval practice paradigm compared typing-based and speech-based response modes in dyslexic and typically developing learners
Balancing the proportion of verbs and nouns in a study set to manage task difficulty for learners with DLD
key_sources: Wilschut, T., Sense, F. & van Rijn, H. (2026). Trends in testing effect research: from lab to classroom, but not yet for all learners. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00400-2

article_title: Quantifying two-dimensional and three-dimensional stereoscopic learning in anatomy using electroencephalography
citation: Anderson, S. J., Jamniczky, H. A., Krigolson, O. E., Coderre, S. P. & Hecker, K. G. (2019). Quantifying two-dimensional and three-dimensional stereoscopic learning in anatomy using electroencephalography. npj Science of Learning 4:10. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-019-0050-4
title: Teach with both 2D and 3D models interleaved rather than 3D models exclusively, to promote generalization between dimensions
description: Based on the neural findings, the authors recommend that stereoscopic 3D models aid visual recognition but should not be used alone: "exclusive use of 3D models should be avoided. Instead, teaching that includes both 2D and 3D models is likely the most advantageous, as it promotes generalization of knowledge by forcing students to practice moving ﬂuidly between dimensions." The interleaved 2D/3D group's decreased reward positivity during retention and transfer supports this recommendation.
requirements: Access to both 2D and stereoscopic 3D representations of the same anatomical content, presented in an interleaved fashion
constraints: The authors caution educators should be conscious of overall cognitive load when designing curricula, since stereopsis adds complexity and real educational settings may add further load
target_learning_goals: spatial understanding of anatomical structures; retention and transfer of anatomical knowledge
examples: Participants in the combined group viewed models randomly as 2D or 3D on a trial-by-trial basis, each 50% of the time, during the first module
key_sources: Anderson, S. J., Jamniczky, H. A., Krigolson, O. E., Coderre, S. P. & Hecker, K. G. (2019). Quantifying two-dimensional and three-dimensional stereoscopic learning in anatomy using electroencephalography. npj Science of Learning 4:10. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-019-0050-4

article_title: Mechanisms of interactive specialization and emergence of functional brain circuits supporting cognitive development in children
citation: Christian Battista, Tanya M. Evans, Tricia J. Ngoon, Tianwen Chen, Lang Chen, John Kochalka and Vinod Menon. (2018). Mechanisms of interactive specialization and emergence of functional brain circuits supporting cognitive development in children. npj Science of Learning 3:1. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-017-0017-2
title: Interactive specialization model of functional brain circuit development, refined by longitudinal evidence
description: The interactive specialization (IS) model posits that cognitive development depends on selective strengthening of inter-regional connections over time, giving rise to specialized functional systems. This study tests and refines IS at the level of functional brain circuits, summarizing four features: "selective strengthening of some functional brain circuits, and corresponding weakening of others"; increased local intra- and inter-hemispheric connectivity in posterior task-relevant regions; strengthening of dorsal–ventral stream interactions (IPS–VTOC); and decreasing engagement of fronto–parietal circuits over childhood. The authors argue regional specializations emerge from dynamic changes in inter-regional connectivity rather than domain-specific regional specialization alone.
requirements: Longitudinal task-based fMRI with behavioral and cognitive data at multiple time points in the same children
constraints: The article states a strong IS interpretation predicting matching activation changes was not supported; how circuit changes contribute to regional specialization remains a significant challenge for future studies.
target_learners: Children and adolescents ages 7–14 developing arithmetic skills
target_learning_goals: Numerical problem solving and arithmetic skill acquisition
examples: In the study, left IPS connectivity with right IPS, SPL and FG increased with age while connectivity with dlPFC, vlPFC and insula decreased, in a 30-child longitudinal cohort over 6 years.
key_sources: Christian Battista, Tanya M. Evans, Tricia J. Ngoon, Tianwen Chen, Lang Chen, John Kochalka and Vinod Menon. (2018). Mechanisms of interactive specialization and emergence of functional brain circuits supporting cognitive development in children. npj Science of Learning 3:1. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-017-0017-2

article_title: What data and analytics can and do say about effective learning
citation: Jason M. Lodge and Linda Corrin. (2017). What data and analytics can and do say about effective learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-017-0006-5
title: Interpret learning analytics data with reference to the learning design of the activities that produced it
description: The commentary argues that meaning-making from data in real educational settings requires reference to how learning activities are designed: just as experimental design licenses inference in the lab, learning design gives meaning to classroom behavioural data. Examining behaviour "with reference to a particular learning design helps teachers to see if students engaged with activities in the way they expected", and mismatches signal that the design may need review. This positions analytics as a bridge between laboratory and classroom.
requirements: Teachers or designers must know the pedagogical intent of the learning activities against which behaviour patterns are interpreted
constraints: Data without reference to learning design cannot support inferences about learning, as the article states the conditions give meaning to the data
target_learners: higher education students learning in online and blended environments
target_learning_goals: understanding and improving how students engage with designed learning activities
examples: The article describes teachers checking whether student behaviour patterns match the pedagogical reasons an activity should lead to learning, and reviewing the design if they do not
key_sources: Jason M. Lodge and Linda Corrin. (2017). What data and analytics can and do say about effective learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-017-0006-5

article_title: Deliberately making miskates: Behavioural consistency under win maximization and loss maximization conditions
citation: Yajing Zhang, Thi Kim Truc Huynh and Benjamin James Dyson. (2023). Deliberately making miskates: Behavioural consistency under win maximization and loss maximization conditions. npj Science of Learning 8:55. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00206-6
title: Feedback valence should be interpreted relative to the learner's goal rather than assumed universally negative for losses
description: This principle holds that putatively positive ('win') and negative ('lose') feedback are malleable in interpretation, and disruption arises from mismatch with the learner's goal, not from valence itself. The authors state that "our data show that people are ﬂexible in de ﬁning ‘success’ speciﬁcally via the malleable interpretation of putatively positive ( win) and negative (lose) forms of feedback". Designers and educators should therefore consider what goal a learner holds when predicting reactions to success and failure feedback.
requirements: The learner's goal state must be known or set so feedback congruency can be established.
constraints: Evidence comes from abstracted points-based games with university samples; the authors caution about generalization to tangible rewards and punishments.
The article notes the historical emphasis on win-stay/lose-shift and loss-related disruption reflects "our implicit focus on win maximization" in the behavioural sciences.
target_learners: Adult learners in game-based or competitive learning settings
target_learning_goals: Interpretation of performance feedback; emotion and motivation following success and failure
examples: The article links the flexibility to deliberately seek loss to the principle of 'fun failure' in games and to acts of intentional self-sabotage demonstrating cognitive proficiency.
key_sources: Yajing Zhang, Thi Kim Truc Huynh and Benjamin James Dyson. (2023). Deliberately making miskates: Behavioural consistency under win maximization and loss maximization conditions. npj Science of Learning 8:55. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00206-6

article_title: Inter-brain coupling reflects disciplinary differences in real-world classroom learning
citation: Jingjing Chen, Penghao Qian, Xinqiao Gao, Baosong Li, Yu Zhang and Dan Zhang. (2023). Inter-brain coupling reflects disciplinary differences in real-world classroom learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00162-1
title: Inter-brain coupling framework distinguishing student-class coupling (hard disciplines) from student-top coupling (soft disciplines)
description: A framework in which individual students' inter-brain coupling to others during real classroom learning indexes the learning process without needing parametric task designs. Student-class coupling (to all other classmates) is proposed to reflect engagement with course content, whereas student-top coupling (to top-performing peers) captures alignment with exemplars of personal construction. The article argues the two serve as "potential neural correlates for successful learning in hard and soft disciplines correspondingly", with distinct dominant frequency bands (theta vs alpha) for the two disciplines.
requirements: Wearable EEG recording from an entire class during regular lessons across a semester
Final exam scores as outcome measures and both Pearson and permutation tests for significance
constraints: Findings rest on uncorrected p values for two disciplines in one class; effect sizes were relatively small (r2 = 0.187 for Chinese, r2 = 0.115 for Math) and the hard-soft dimension itself is described as contentious
target_learning_goals: successful classroom learning in hard disciplines (Math) and soft disciplines (Chinese)
examples: Thirty-four grade-10 students wore two-electrode headband EEG devices during 18 Chinese and 20 Math sessions over 4 months, with total interdependence (TI) used to compute pairwise inter-brain couplings
key_sources: Jingjing Chen, Penghao Qian, Xinqiao Gao, Baosong Li, Yu Zhang and Dan Zhang. (2023). Inter-brain coupling reflects disciplinary differences in real-world classroom learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00162-1

article_title: Brain dynamics of (a)typical reading development—a review of longitudinal studies
citation: Chyl, K., Fraga-González, G., Brem, S. & Jednoróg, K. (2021). Brain dynamics of (a)typical reading development—a review of longitudinal studies. npj Science of Learning 6:4. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-020-00081-5
title: Interactive account of ventral occipito-temporal function in reading development
description: The review presents the interactive account of vOT function as an explanatory framework for the inverted U-shaped development of visual specialization to print. It "emphasizes the dynamic contribution of top-down predictions from other language areas (involved in phonology and semantics) across reading development". According to the review, "vOT activation is the highest during learning, when the stimulus is recognized as potentially meaningful, but with a high prediction error", and the prediction error decreases with expertise, leading to a decline in vOT activation with higher reading skill.
requirements: Longitudinal sensitivity data across reading stages to observe the rise and decline of vOT activation
constraints: The account is motivated by ERP evidence of inverted U-shape development; the review notes testing similar inverted U-shapes in language-network regions beyond second/third grade would require further studies
target_learning_goals: development of visual word recognition and reading fluency
examples: The review uses the account to interpret longitudinal N1 print-sensitivity data that emerge at reading onset and level off with practice
key_sources: Chyl, K., Fraga-González, G., Brem, S. & Jednoróg, K. (2021). Brain dynamics of (a)typical reading development—a review of longitudinal studies. npj Science of Learning 6:4. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-020-00081-5

article_title: Student teacher inter brain coupling forecast cross semester academic fluctuation in real world classrooms
citation: Xiaomeng Xu, Dan Zhang & Yu Zhang. (2026). Student teacher inter brain coupling forecast cross semester academic fluctuation in real world classrooms. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00421-x
title: Inter-brain coupling as a process-level signature of interpersonal alignment during classroom instruction
description: The article advances an account in which inter-brain coupling, quantified as total interdependence (TI) of student-teacher EEG coherence, is "a process-level signature of interpersonal alignment during communication, reflecting coordinated attention, shared task engagement, and mutual adaptation in moment-to-moment information processing." It further proposes that high-beta coupling indexes deeper, effortful, top-down engagement while theta synchrony reflects moment-to-moment responsiveness to instruction. The account underpins the paper's use of coupling dynamics as a longitudinal marker of effective pedagogy in ecologically valid classrooms.
requirements: Requires wearable dual-channel EEG (Fp1/Fp2) recorded simultaneously from teachers and students during regular lessons, with TI computed per frequency band and averaged within waves
constraints: The authors state the contribution is primarily empirical and that the precise theoretical meaning and underlying mechanisms of inter-brain coupling remain to be specified and tested in future work
target_learners: junior and senior secondary school students (aged 12-15)
target_learning_goals: academic achievement in Chinese and math
examples: The study measured TI across broadband, delta, theta, alpha, low-beta and high-beta bands in 393 regular classes over three semesters
key_sources: Xiaomeng Xu, Dan Zhang & Yu Zhang. (2026). Student teacher inter brain coupling forecast cross semester academic fluctuation in real world classrooms. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00421-x

article_title: Intelligent Tutoring Systems by and for the Developing World: A Review of Trends and Approaches for Educational Technology in a Global Context
citation: Benjamin D. Nye. (2015). Intelligent Tutoring Systems by and for the Developing World: A Review of Trends and Approaches for Educational Technology in a Global Context. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-014-0028-6
title: Inner-loop/outer-loop adaptivity criterion defining intelligent tutoring systems
description: The article defines ITS via VanLehn's (2006) two types of adaptivity: an outer loop that determines the next learning task, typically keeping tasks within the learner's zone of proximal development, and an inner loop that helps the learner while working on a given task. The inner loop provides step-specific scaffolding such as hint sequences, error-correction feedback, and cues toward important parts of the problem state. The article uses this inner-loop criterion as its inclusion test for the mapping study, with an 'adaptive learning systems' category for outer-loop-only fringe systems.
requirements: Inclusion requires step-based tutoring, i.e., adaptive support while working on a task, providing hints and/or feedback intelligently
constraints: The article notes the search was not designed to comprehensively cover adaptive learning systems, which were analyzed only to consider the fringe of inclusion criteria
target_learning_goals: step-specific scaffolding, hints, and error-correction feedback during problem solving
examples: The review cites a meta-analysis (VanLehn 2011) finding that systems with step-based adaptivity produced higher learning gains than those with only an outer loop
key_sources: Benjamin D. Nye. (2015). Intelligent Tutoring Systems by and for the Developing World: A Review of Trends and Approaches for Educational Technology in a Global Context. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-014-0028-6

article_title: How to Improve the Explanatory Power of an Intelligent Textbook: a Case Study in Legal Writing
citation: Sovrano Francesco, Ashley Kevin, Brusilovsky Peter Leonid, Vitali Fabio. (2024). How to Improve the Explanatory Power of an Intelligent Textbook: a Case Study in Legal Writing. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-024-00399-w
title: Intelligent Explanation Generator: an algorithm selecting questions best answered by the whole text collection
description: The Intelligent Explanation Generator is the component of YAI4Edu responsible for selecting pedagogically useful implicit questions. It computes the Degree of Explainability (DoX) of text snippets about an explanandum, takes the top k snippets, extracts archetypal questions from them with a fine-tuned T5 model, and filters pertinent answers through sub-steps that remove over-long questions, correct grammar via Gramformer, drop overly similar questions, and keep the top q questions sorted by answer pertinence. It operationalizes Hypothesis 1: the most useful implicit questions are those best answered by the collection as a whole, neither too detailed nor too general.
requirements: A fine-tuned T5 question-extraction model and a pre-trained answer-retrieval language model
Hyper-parameters: pertinence threshold p, question length threshold L, similarity threshold s, and caps q and a
constraints: Questions extracted by the T5 model can be imperfect, containing errors that could propagate to the Intelligent Explanation Generator
target_learning_goals: Retrieving helpful explanations efficiently from large text collections
examples: In the case study it was configured with k=10, p=.57, L=50, s=.95, answer lengths 150–1000, q=4 questions and a=2 answers per overview question
key_sources: Sovrano Francesco, Ashley Kevin, Brusilovsky Peter Leonid, Vitali Fabio. (2024). How to Improve the Explanatory Power of an Intelligent Textbook: a Case Study in Legal Writing. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-024-00399-w

article_title: Debiasing Education Algorithms
citation: Jamiu Adekunle Idowu. (2024). Debiasing Education Algorithms. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00389-4
title: Two-category taxonomy of algorithmic fairness: individual fairness and group fairness
description: The review organizes algorithmic fairness into two broad categories. Individual fairness holds that "similar individuals should receive similar outcomes", with measures including fairness through awareness, fairness through unawareness, and counterfactual fairness. Group fairness "focuses on ensuring equal statistical outcomes across distinct groups partitioned by protected attributes", with measures such as equal opportunity, demographic parity, and equalized odds. The review uses this taxonomy to frame which metrics education studies adopt.
requirements: Choosing a fairness definition requires contextualizing it to the application, as the review notes definitions may not align with real-world applications
constraints: The review notes that pursuing demographic parity will harm equalized odds, so multiple fairness measures cannot be satisfied simultaneously
target_learners: students affected by predictive models in educational settings
target_learning_goals: equitable treatment of students by educational prediction and recommendation algorithms
key_sources: Jamiu Adekunle Idowu. (2024). Debiasing Education Algorithms. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00389-4

article_title: Autograding Mathematical Induction Proofs with Natural Language Processing
citation: Zhao, C., Silva, M., & Poulsen, S. (2025). Autograding Mathematical Induction Proofs with Natural Language Processing. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 35, 3202–3232. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-025-00498-2
title: Labeled corpus of student induction proofs graded against a 7-point rubric
description: A dataset of student-written induction proofs collected from pretests and posttests, graded by a research team against a 7-point rubric covering base cases, the inductive hypothesis, and the inductive step. Grades were collapsed from a 0/1/2 scale to a binary correct/incorrect label per rubric point for training autograding models.
requirements: Proofs must be graded against a consistent rubric by multiple raters to provide usable training labels
constraints: Grades were collapsed to binary per rubric point, limiting the granularity of feedback compared to a multi-level scale
target_learning_goals: Identifying and correcting common misconceptions in proof by induction
examples: Proofs from four distinct induction problems were labeled and used to train and evaluate the autograding models
key_sources: Zhao, C., Silva, M., & Poulsen, S. (2025). Autograding Mathematical Induction Proofs with Natural Language Processing. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 35, 3202–3232. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-025-00498-2

article_title: Ensemble Learning for Estimating Individualized Treatment Effects in Student Success Studies
citation: Beemer, J., Spoon, K., He, L., Fan, J., & Levine, R.A. (2018). Ensemble Learning for Estimating Individualized Treatment Effects in Student Success Studies. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 28, 315–335. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-017-0148-x
title: Individualized treatment effects (ITE) as a framework for student success analytics
description: Individualized treatment effects, borrowed from the personalized medicine literature, quantify for each student the predicted difference in an outcome between experiencing an intervention and not, even though each student experiences only one modality. The article computes ITE by training separate ensemble learners on treatment and control groups and using each to predict the counterfactual outcome for the other group. It states the ensemble learner serves "as a best guess of the outcome for the treatment (control) group students if they had experienced the control (treatment)". ITE then support evaluating interventions, characterizing benefiting subgroups, and advising individual students.
requirements: Data on students who did and did not experience the intervention, with covariates available in student information system or learning management system databases
A trained predictive ensemble learner for each group to estimate the counterfactual outcome
constraints: Randomized experiments or crossover designs are typically not an option in education settings, so non-randomized assignment may leave unobserved confounders unadjusted; the method was illustrated without direct measures of attitudes, behavior, or motivation
target_learners: higher education students in large enrollment bottleneck courses
at-risk student subgroups such as URM, EOP, and first-generation students
target_learning_goals: evaluating the impact of instructional interventions on course success, retention, and graduation outcomes
examples: Applied to a supplemental instruction section in STAT 119 at SDSU, producing average ITE of 9.3 exam points and 0.45 grade points and example-student profiles of predicted grade-letter improvements
key_sources: Beemer, J., Spoon, K., He, L., Fan, J., & Levine, R.A. (2018). Ensemble Learning for Estimating Individualized Treatment Effects in Student Success Studies. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 28, 315–335. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-017-0148-x

article_title: ELM-ART – An Interactive and Intelligent Web-Based Electronic Textbook
citation: Gerhard Weber & Peter Brusilovsky. (2016). ELM-ART – An Interactive and Intelligent Web-Based Electronic Textbook. Int J Artif Intell Educ 26. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0066-8
title: The interactive and intelligent textbook paradigm combining intelligent tutoring and adaptive hypermedia
description: ELM-ART introduced a paradigm in which a Web-based textbook looks like a traditional programming textbook with sections of text, program examples and problems, but all content is interactive and the book is intelligent, using AI technologies such as intelligent program analysis, concept-based hyperspace organization, intelligent links between examples and problems, and adaptive navigation support. The article calls it "a winning approach to combine intelligent tutoring and adaptive hypermedia technologies into a consistent design that matches the hypertext nature of the Web". This paradigm served as a blueprint for later systems and authoring tools.
requirements: Learning content organized as concept-based hypertext pages with exercises whose solutions can be diagnosed by the system
A student model updated from interactions with text questions and problem solving to drive adaptation
constraints: The original implementation applied the full diagnosis machinery only to early lessons of functional programming in LISP
target_learners: university students in introductory programming courses
target_learning_goals: programming concepts and recursive programming in LISP
examples: ELM-ART's first three lessons used adaptive navigation support and curriculum sequencing with a traffic light metaphor; lessons four to six provided example-based problem solving with ELM cognitive diagnosis and detailed feedback
key_sources: Gerhard Weber & Peter Brusilovsky. (2016). ELM-ART – An Interactive and Intelligent Web-Based Electronic Textbook. Int J Artif Intell Educ 26. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0066-8

article_title: Intelligent Textbooks
citation: Sergey Sosnovsky, Peter Brusilovsky, Andrew Lan. (2025). Intelligent Textbooks. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-024-00451-9
title: Five-generation taxonomy of intelligent textbook research: engineered, integrated, extracted, datamined, and generated intelligence
description: The article organizes the history of intelligent textbook research into five generations defined by their source of intelligence. Generation 1 relied on human domain experts to engineer domain models for closed-corpus adaptive systems; Generation 2 used open architectures and Semantic Web ontologies to integrate external resources; Generation 3 applied ML and NLP to extract knowledge from textbook content; Generation 4 data-mined student interaction logs; and Generation 5 incorporates large language models. The article states that "the first and second generations were driven by classical AI approaches for symbolic knowledge representation and logic-based knowledge inference, the third generation employed Machine Learning (ML) and Natural Language Processing (NLP) methods focusing on knowledge extraction."
requirements: Digital textbook content whose structure and text can be processed by the generation's chosen AI methods
constraints: First-generation systems were closed-corpus environments with limited collections of instructional texts
Second-generation closed-box systems were impossible to extend, modify, and scale once designed
target_learners: students reading digital textbooks across subject domains
target_learning_goals: improved access to, interaction with, and mastery of textbook content
examples: Figures 1–5 illustrate each generation: engineered domain models, ontology-based integration, content analysis pipelines, interaction-data mining, and generative AI interfaces
key_sources: Sergey Sosnovsky, Peter Brusilovsky, Andrew Lan. (2025). Intelligent Textbooks. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-024-00451-9

article_title: The Intertwined Histories of Artificial Intelligence and Education
citation: Shayan Doroudi. (2022). The Intertwined Histories of Artificial Intelligence and Education. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-022-00313-2
title: Information-processing psychology (Newell and Simon's symbolic approach to cognition and learning)
description: Newell and Simon's information-processing psychology laid foundations for both cognitive psychology and symbolic AI, positing that problem solving uses processes resembling human ones, studied via think-aloud protocols. Learning is framed as "gradually accumulating the various production rules necessary to solve a problem," where each production has "a bipartite form, consisting of a condition and an action." Simon and Newell argued this theory of problem solving "gives us a new basis for attacking the psychology of education and the learning process," positioning it as the basic science education lacked.
requirements: Detailed models of the information and programs skilled performers possess, developed by studying human problem-solving data such as think-aloud protocols
constraints: Newell and Simon themselves judged that studying performance must take precedence over learning "in the present state of the art" of the 1970s
examples: The 1971 Simon and Newell paper included a section on The Practice of Education; the approach informed Carnegie Mellon tutoring systems and the ACT theory of skill acquisition
key_sources: Shayan Doroudi. (2022). The Intertwined Histories of Artificial Intelligence and Education. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-022-00313-2

article_title: Jim Greer’s and Mary Mark’s Reviews of Evaluation Methods for Adaptive Systems: a Brief Comment about New Goals
citation: du Boulay, B. (2021). Jim Greer's and Mary Mark's Reviews of Evaluation Methods for Adaptive Systems: a Brief Comment about New Goals. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 31, 622–635. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-020-00198-z
title: Treat interest and engagement as necessary but not sufficient for learning, preserving room for reflection
description: The article warns of "a tension between capturing interest and provoking engagement as against fostering effective learning, in that interest and engagement are (mostly) necessary but not sufficient conditions for learning." Learning other than rote needs a reflective component that can be drowned out if engagement and fun leave no room for it. Designs that capture interest should therefore protect space for reflection, since individual differences in self-regulation and cognitive load affect how much is learned in game-based environments.
requirements: Learning designs must include a reflective component alongside interest-capture and engagement mechanisms
constraints: In game-based learning, individual differences in self-regulation ability and cognitive load capacity affect how much is actually learned
target_learners: learners in game-based or highly engaging learning environments
examples: The article cites reviews of the positive and negative attributes of game-based learning and notes that many questions about games' effectiveness remain unresolved.
key_sources: du Boulay, B. (2021). Jim Greer's and Mary Mark's Reviews of Evaluation Methods for Adaptive Systems: a Brief Comment about New Goals. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 31, 622–635. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-020-00198-z

article_title: Teaching Responsible Data Science: Charting New Pedagogical Territory
citation: Lewis Armanda; Stoyanovich Julia. (2021). Teaching Responsible Data Science: Charting New Pedagogical Territory. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-021-00241-7
title: A table of nine pedagogical activities for teaching interpretability, each paired with an assessment method
description: Table 1 of the article lays out pedagogically-sound activities mapping learning-science best practices to RDS interpretability practice, including replicating an existing study, reverse engineering a platform, diagnostic learning logs, problem recognition tasks, process analysis, peer review, before-after iteration, design and deploy, and creating a nutritional label for a machine learning platform. "Table 1 showcases several pedagogically-sound activities that map to best practices in the learning sciences and to RDS interpretability practices." Each activity is paired with an assessment method such as metrics evaluation, open coding, cognitive walkthroughs, or A/B testing.
requirements: Activities should be offered through multiple presentation modes and levels of interactivity to maximize engagement and promote heuristics development.
constraints: The authors state that future iterations of the course will tie in further pedagogical principles.
target_learners: diverse groups of students with varying technical and theoretical prior knowledge, from varied disciplinary backgrounds, and with different learning goals
target_learning_goals: transitioning from novice to expert level knowledge
examples: In Table 1, replicating an existing study has students reconstruct a (portion of a) published study and highlight any replication issues, assessed via metrics evaluation and content analysis.
The RDS course incorporates some of these activities; its final project combines replication study, process analysis, design and deployment, and nutritional label design.
key_sources: Lewis Armanda; Stoyanovich Julia. (2021). Teaching Responsible Data Science: Charting New Pedagogical Territory. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-021-00241-7

article_title: Modelling Human Teaching Tactics and Strategies for Tutoring Systems: 14 Years On
citation: Benedict du Boulay & Rosemary Luckin. (2015). Modelling Human Teaching Tactics and Strategies for Tutoring Systems: 14 Years On. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0053-0
title: INSPIRE framework characterising expert one-to-one tutors
description: The INSPIRE framework (Intelligent, Nurturant, Socratic, Progressive, Indirect, Reflective, Encouraging) provides an empirically observed account of expert human teachers working one-to-one. The review reports that it characterises expert behaviour, compared to less expert teachers, along dimensions including "their use of questions rather than didactic statements", attention to motivating and encouraging students, and fostering learner reflection on process. The review uses it as a benchmark of expert teaching richness and as a design source for the GURU tutor.
requirements: Requires empirical observation of expert tutors working one-to-one to ground the framework's dimensions
constraints: The review notes both the meta-analysis and meta-review underplay the motivational aspects of expert teaching that INSPIRE emphasises
target_learning_goals: domain learning supported alongside student motivation
examples: GURU embodied the INSPIRE framework of Lepper and Woolverton (2002) alongside expert-teacher coding to provide conversational teaching in Biology
key_sources: Benedict du Boulay & Rosemary Luckin. (2015). Modelling Human Teaching Tactics and Strategies for Tutoring Systems: 14 Years On. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0053-0

article_title: Computer-Based Interaction Analysis with DEGREE Revisited
citation: B. Barros & M. F. Verdejo (2015). Computer-Based Interaction Analysis with DEGREE Revisited. Int J Artif Intell Educ (2016) 26:113–123. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0063-y
title: Three-stage evolution of computer-based interaction analysis: small groups, learning communities, and big-data learning analytics
description: The article organizes the evolution of computer-based interaction analysis into three stages shown in Fig. 3: 1995–2005 (small groups, one data source, purpose-built systems, logs and visualization/awareness tools), 2000–2010 (large groups and small learning communities, e-learning platforms as data sources, social network analysis, statistical and Bayesian methods, machine learning), and 2005–2015 (an explosion of data from social networks, MOOCs and open, non-structured text sources, with information retrieval, classification, visualization, and learning analytics). Each stage is characterized by size of groups, sources of data, techniques, and representative systems.
requirements: In the latest stage, interaction analysis requires searching for and pre-processing unstructured data
constraints: The authors state a comprehensive overview is beyond the scope of the article and the references should be taken as illustrative
target_learners: learners in small groups, virtual learning communities, and MOOCs
target_learning_goals: analysis of collaboration and interaction for learning
examples: The authors themselves chose to work at small scale, no more than ten groups of two to three students, during the period when other approaches moved to large-scale unstructured settings
key_sources: B. Barros & M. F. Verdejo (2015). Computer-Based Interaction Analysis with DEGREE Revisited. Int J Artif Intell Educ (2016) 26:113–123. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0063-y

article_title: Automated Test Assembly for Handling Learner Cold-Start in Large-Scale Assessments
citation: Jill-Jêenn Vie, Fabrice Popineau, Éric Bruillard, Yolaine Bourda. (2018). Automated Test Assembly for Handling Learner Cold-Start in Large-Scale Assessments. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-017-0163-y
title: InitialD: DPP-based diverse question sampling for cold-start assessment
description: InitialD (for Initial Determinant) is an automated test-assembly algorithm that "samples k questions from the item bank according to a determinantal point process, using the question feature vectors", so that the selected questions measure different knowledge components and minimize redundancy in learner answers. It selects the first bundle of questions before any adaptation is possible, supports feedback naming knowledge components needing further work, and randomizes across newcomers, which the authors note is "interesting for security purposes" and helps calibrate various items. Sampling 10 questions from a bank of 10,000 takes about 10 million operations after preprocessing.
requirements: Question feature vectors (e.g., discrimination vectors from a calibrated student model) from which pairwise similarities can be computed
A preprocessed kernel matrix over the item bank
constraints: Exact DPP sampling was tested here only on item banks of up to 23 questions; exact best-subset search is NP-hard and intractable at scale
Complexity is O(nk3) after a preprocessing step in O(n3)
target_learning_goals: rapid initial diagnosis of learner knowledge
examples: Applied to the TIMSS 2003 (757 learners, 23 questions) and Fraction subtraction (536 students, 20 questions) datasets in a stratified 80/20 cross-validation protocol
key_sources: Jill-Jêenn Vie, Fabrice Popineau, Éric Bruillard, Yolaine Bourda. (2018). Automated Test Assembly for Handling Learner Cold-Start in Large-Scale Assessments. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-017-0163-y

article_title: Navigating the Ethical Frontier: Graduate Students’ Experiences with Generative AI-Mediated Scholarship
citation: Soroush Sabbaghan, & Sarah Elaine Eaton. (2025). Navigating the Ethical Frontier: Graduate Students' Experiences with Generative AI-Mediated Scholarship. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-024-00454-6
title: Institutions should develop ethical frameworks and policies that prioritize human agency and critical engagement with AI-generated content
description: Based on their findings, the authors argue that institutions must reconceptualize traditional notions of agency, authorship, and originality in the context of AI-assisted research. They call for developing ethical frameworks and institutional policies that prioritize human agency and critical engagement with AI-generated content. The study highlights that "the findings suggest a need for reconceptualizing traditional notions of agency, authorship, and originality in the context of AI-assisted research."
requirements: Policies must account for the nuanced, evolving relationship between integrity and GenAI collaboration rather than treating it as a simple dichotomy.
constraints: The authors note the need for further research on the long-term impacts of generative AI on intellectual and scholarly ethics.
examples: Participants sought institutional guidance and transparency norms, with one asking supervisors to authorize particular uses of AI tools.
key_sources: Soroush Sabbaghan, & Sarah Elaine Eaton. (2025). Navigating the Ethical Frontier: Graduate Students' Experiences with Generative AI-Mediated Scholarship. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-024-00454-6

article_title: STyLE-OLM: Interactive Open Learner Modelling
citation: Vania Dimitrova. (2003). STyLE-OLM: Interactive Open Learner Modelling. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://telearn.hal.science/hal-00197312
title: Interactive open learner modelling (IOLM): diagnosis as an interactive process between system and learner
description: IOLM conceives diagnosis not as a one-shot system inference but as "an interactive process involving both a computer system and a learner that discuss and together construct the learner model". The article outlines the architecture of an IOLM system and illustrates the method in a terminological domain through the STyLE-OLM demonstrator.
requirements: A system implementing IOLM must support discussion between the system and the learner over the contents of the learner model
constraints: The method was illustrated in a terminological domain
target_learning_goals: accurate diagnosis of the learner's cognitive state
examples: The STyLE-OLM demonstrator implements the IOLM approach in a terminological domain
key_sources: Vania Dimitrova. (2003). STyLE-OLM: Interactive Open Learner Modelling. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://telearn.hal.science/hal-00197312

article_title: AI Adaptivity in a Mixed-Reality System Improves Learning
citation: Yannier, N., Hudson, S. E., Chang, H., & Koedinger, K. R. (2024). AI Adaptivity in a Mixed-Reality System Improves Learning. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 34, 1541–1558. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00388-5
title: Intelligent Science Stations (EarthShake): AI vision mixed-reality learning system
description: Intelligent Science Stations are "mixed-reality systems that bridge the physical and virtual worlds to improve children's inquiry-based STEM learning". A depth camera and computer vision algorithm using blob detection and moment-of-inertia calculations recognize towers and falling events, while a gorilla character guides a predict-observe-explain cycle with contrasting cases, self-explanation menus, and real-time interactive feedback.
requirements: Depth-sensing camera and specialized computer vision algorithm to detect tower placement and falls
target_learning_goals: scientific principles of balance and stability
inquiry skills of prediction, observation, and explanation
examples: Children place towers on a physical earthquake table and predict which will fall first when the table shakes
key_sources: Yannier, N., Hudson, S. E., Chang, H., & Koedinger, K. R. (2024). AI Adaptivity in a Mixed-Reality System Improves Learning. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 34, 1541–1558. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00388-5

article_title: How Should Intelligent Tutoring Systems Sequence Multiple Graphical Representations of Fractions? A Multi-Methods Study
citation: Rau, M. A., Aleven, V., Rummel, N., & Pardos, Z. (2014). How Should Intelligent Tutoring Systems Sequence Multiple Graphical Representations of Fractions? A Multi-Methods Study. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-013-0011-7
title: Instructional materials should provide interleaved practice with multiple graphical representations to promote robust learning, especially for conceptual knowledge.
description: The article concludes that "instructional materials should provide interleaved practice with multiple graphical representations in order to promote students' robust learning, in particular if the goal is to promote the acquisition of conceptual knowledge that transfers to novel tasks." This principle is grounded in the classroom experiment showing qualified support for interleaving over blocking. The benefit was most evident for conceptual transfer at the delayed posttest.
requirements: The learning materials must employ multiple graphical representations of the same content, such as circle diagrams, rectangles, and number lines.
constraints: The advantage of interleaving depends on students' prior knowledge and the type of target knowledge; blocked practice may be effective early in the learning sequence.
target_learning_goals: Conceptual knowledge of fractions that transfers to novel tasks
examples: The classroom experiment contrasted blocked, moderately interleaved, fully interleaved, and increasingly interleaved practice schedules using the Fractions Tutor.
key_sources: Rau, M. A., Aleven, V., Rummel, N., & Pardos, Z. (2014). How Should Intelligent Tutoring Systems Sequence Multiple Graphical Representations of Fractions? A Multi-Methods Study. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-013-0011-7

article_title: AI Curriculum for European High Schools: An Embedded Intelligence Approach
citation: Bellas, F., Guerreiro-Santalla, S., Naya, M., & Duro, R. J. (2023). AI Curriculum for European High Schools: An Embedded Intelligence Approach. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-022-00315-0
title: Intelligent Agent Framework for AI Curriculum Organization
description: The curriculum is organized around the concept of an intelligent agent situated in an environment, cycling through sensing and actuation stages. Five internal processes are identified: motivation, representation, learning, reasoning, and memory. The article states that 'the agent is continuously interacting with its environment in a cycle' and that 'the agent can learn from its experience in order to improve the action selection process.'
requirements: The framework requires that all five operational blocks be present in any intelligent agent implementation, though their complexity can vary
constraints: Memory is excluded as a dedicated topic because 'a proper implementation of a memory system is out of the scope of this education level'
target_learners: High school students aged 15-18 in scientific programmes
target_learning_goals: Understanding the fundamental components and processes of intelligent agents
examples: The framework is presented to students in the introductory teaching unit and structures all eight AI topics in the curriculum
key_sources: Bellas, F., Guerreiro-Santalla, S., Naya, M., & Duro, R. J. (2023). AI Curriculum for European High Schools: An Embedded Intelligence Approach. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-022-00315-0

article_title: Impact of an Artificial Intelligence Research Frame on the Perceived Credibility of Educational Research Evidence
citation: Mutlu Cukurova & Rosemary Luckin & Carmel Kent. (2020). Impact of an Artificial Intelligence Research Frame on the Perceived Credibility of Educational Research Evidence. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-019-00188-w
title: The in-credible AI effect: disciplinary framing as a peripheral cue in credibility judgements
description: The article proposes that perceived credibility of unfamiliar research evidence is processed via a peripheral route, where "the perceived credibility is shaped by peripheral cues or heuristic rules, the subject frame in which the evidence is presented, for example". Within this framework, the discipline framing of identical evidence acts as a heuristic that biases credibility judgements, producing what the authors name "the in-credible AI effect". The framework draws on the Heuristic Systematic Model and the elaboration likelihood model of persuasion, and explains why AI-framed evidence is judged less credible than neuroscience- or educational-psychology-framed evidence.
requirements: Unfamiliar research evidence that recipients process via peripheral cues rather than central scrutiny
constraints: The effect applies to perceived credibility, not to the veracity of the evidence, which is held constant across frames
target_learning_goals: critical evaluation of educational research evidence
understanding of framing effects in credibility judgements
examples: The experiment presented identical educational research evidence in AI, neuroscience, and educational psychology frames and measured five credibility dimensions
key_sources: Mutlu Cukurova & Rosemary Luckin & Carmel Kent. (2020). Impact of an Artificial Intelligence Research Frame on the Perceived Credibility of Educational Research Evidence. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-019-00188-w

article_title: Stupid Tutoring Systems, Intelligent Humans
citation: Ryan S. Baker. (2016). Stupid Tutoring Systems, Intelligent Humans. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0105-0
title: Intelligence amplification as an alternate paradigm for AIED
description: The article proposes reframing AIED around intelligence amplification rather than artificial intelligence: AI technology derives important information about an online learning system, but action is taken by a human, not the system. As the author puts it, "The learning system is not itself intelligent; the human intelligence that surrounds the system is supported and leveraged." Designers are informed to support redesign, and instructors are informed so they can support students right away. The author frames this as what leading systems at scale already do, distilling information with sophisticated algorithms while placing "the ultimate decisions in the hands of a human being."
requirements: Data mining and reporting methods to inform humans, since humans cannot sift through large amounts of information quickly
constraints: Human beings vary in quality, so not all human responses to reporting are equally effective
target_learners: online learners across K-12 and higher education
target_learning_goals: improving learning outcomes through informed human decision-making rather than automated personalization
examples: ASSISTments uses simple interactions with hints, scaffolds, and three-in-a-row mastery, with data from hundreds of A/B tests analyzed by humans; Course Signals predicts risk and provides information to instructors who decide on action.
key_sources: Ryan S. Baker. (2016). Stupid Tutoring Systems, Intelligent Humans. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0105-0

article_title: The Impacts of Domain-General vs. Domain-Specific Diagramming Tools on Writing
citation: Barstow, B., Fazio, L., Lippman, J., Falakmasir, M., Schunn, C. D., & Ashley, K. D. (2017). The Impacts of Domain-General vs. Domain-Specific Diagramming Tools on Writing. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 27, 671–693. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0130-z
title: Integrate argument diagramming into college-level science course curricula to improve students' research writing
description: The article recommends that argument diagramming be embedded in course assignments rather than treated as an add-on: "the results of this study indicate that diagramming is a useful practice to employ in college-level psychology courses to improve students ' writing, and should be integrated into curricula." In the study, diagramming was woven into existing lab assignments via training, diagram creation, blind peer review of diagrams, revision based on feedback, and use of the diagram in drafting, without adding total lab time. The recommendation rests on the observed gains in citation relevance and opposing-evidence inclusion.
requirements: Time for diagramming activities must be reallocated from other course activities, as the study did not increase total lab or paper-writing time
constraints: Effects were demonstrated in a naturalistic system where training, peer review, and feedback were inseparable from diagram creation, so which element drives gains is unknown
target_learners: undergraduate students in introductory science and research methods courses
target_learning_goals: writing research paper introductions with relevant citations and opposing evidence
examples: Students created argument diagrams for their hypotheses, peer reviewed three other diagrams in SWoRD, revised their diagrams from feedback, and used TF feedback to draft introductions
key_sources: Barstow, B., Fazio, L., Lippman, J., Falakmasir, M., Schunn, C. D., & Ashley, K. D. (2017). The Impacts of Domain-General vs. Domain-Specific Diagramming Tools on Writing. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 27, 671–693. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0130-z

article_title: An Educational System for Learning Search Algorithms and Automatically Assessing Student Performance
citation: Grivokostopoulou, F., Perikos, I., & Hatzilygeroudis, I. (2016). An Educational System for Learning Search Algorithms and Automatically Assessing Student Performance. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0116-x
title: Interactive Step-Based Algorithm Visualizations Following Active Learning Principles
description: Algorithm visualizations in AITS are developed according to the essence of student active learning. During an animation demonstrating an algorithm, the system can stop at a random step and ask the student to specify the next action or justify why an action was made, using multiple choice questions. The principles of active learning postulate that the more users directly manipulate and act upon the learning material, the higher the mental efforts and psychological involvement and therefore the better the learning outcome.
requirements: Visualizations must pause at steps and request student input
Multiple choice questions for interaction
Immediate corrective feedback on erroneous answers
constraints: Applied to algorithm operation demonstrations in search algorithm topics
target_learning_goals: Understanding how search algorithms operate step by step
examples: During a visualization the system can pause and ask the student to specify the next algorithm's step by selecting the proper answer of a multiple choice question
key_sources: Grivokostopoulou, F., Perikos, I., & Hatzilygeroudis, I. (2016). An Educational System for Learning Search Algorithms and Automatically Assessing Student Performance. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0116-x

article_title: Instructional design for tutoring on interactive platforms: creating educational interventions overcoming the digital gap
citation: Rodríguez Rincón, Y., Munárriz, A., Campión Arrastia, M. J., & Goicoechea López-Vailo, M. I. (2025). Instructional design for tutoring on interactive platforms: creating educational interventions overcoming the digital gap. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10516-8
title: Instructional model for interactive quantitative-reinforcement tutoring platforms
description: The article proposes an instructional model serving as "a basic structural unit for the creation of educational reinforcement platforms" for quantitative competences at university. It is structured in two stages: a diagnostic stage using multiple-choice questions with hint and NA options, and a reinforcement stage of sequenced exercises of increasing difficulty with immediate explanatory feedback. The model is designed to be replicable by instructors lacking programming skills on free platforms such as Genially.com or Canva.
requirements: Free interactive platform software such as Genially.com or Canva with conditional screen-jumping functionality
Instructor-authored content: diagnostic questions, theory explanations, exercise sequences, and feedback
constraints: Designed for mathematics and quantitative disciplines; in other disciplines the optimal reinforcement strategy may differ
Question type should be adapted depending on target students' needs (age, special educational needs, gifted students)
target_learners: new incoming university students with heterogeneous quantitative backgrounds
examples: A flow chart (Fig. 3) shows the diagnostic question branching to the next concept, the tutoring process, or a hint window followed by a second diagnostic question

article_title: Instructor presence in instructional videos in higher education: three field experiments in university courses
citation: Steffi Heidig, Maik Beege, Günter Daniel Rey, Sascha Schneider. (2024). Instructor presence in instructional videos in higher education: three field experiments in university courses. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-024-10391-9
title: Interference Hypothesis
description: The Interference Hypothesis proposes that presenting a visible instructor next to slides increases extraneous processing and may harm learning. The additional visual information from the instructor's video overloads the visual/spatial channel and causes split attention between slides and instructor, reducing resources available for generative processing. The article tests this hypothesis across three field studies.
requirements: The visible instructor must add visual information that competes for limited working memory capacity alongside the slide content.
constraints: The hypothesis was not supported: no effects on extraneous processing or learning outcomes were found across three field studies.

citation: Hrastinski, S. (2021). Informing designs for learning when shifting to digital. Education Tech Research Dev, 69, 285–288. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09894-y
title: Design for learning as an informed practice
description: The article proposes understanding design for learning as an informed practice: "Teachers could be informed by 'what is known', such as theories, research, evidence, best and good practices, and previous experiences". Being informed also involves "applying professional judgment to reflect and act on analyses and evaluations of teaching and learning". This extends Bennett et al.'s descriptive model of teachers' design work toward improvement.

constraints: The article notes teachers' design practice has been given limited attention regarding how it could be improved

article_title: Informing designs for learning when shifting to digital
citation: Hrastinski, S. (2021). Informing designs for learning when shifting to digital. Education Tech Research Dev, 69, 285–288. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09894-y
title: Encourage teachers to inform their designs for learning and iteratively improve them through reflection and evaluation
description: The article recommends that "teachers should be encouraged to inform their designs for learning and iteratively improve their designs based on reflection and evaluation". Teachers should look into what is known and deliberately learn through reflection and evaluation rather than relying solely on implicit assumptions. This is framed as especially important when rapidly shifting to digital.
