description: The article concludes that "instructor cues such as pointing gestures and gaze shifts may be particularly helpful when teaching complex relationships, abstract constructs, or procedural content." This principle directs educators to incorporate instructor signaling when content complexity is high, as the study found a significant three-way interaction showing instructor signaling improved knowledge acquisition as perceived difficulty increased.

title: Instructional theory as a prescriptive collection of methods that best fit a design situation
description: The article defines an instructional theory as a prescriptive collection of methods that best fit a design situation, drawing on Gibbons and Rogers' (2009) concept of method layers: content, strategy, message, control, representation, media-logic, and data management. It uses this lens to critique the Giannakas et al. (2018) review of mobile game-based learning.

article_title: In-between worlds: Chilean university lecturers’ experiences of teaching transition between face-to-face and virtual reality contexts during the COVID-19 pandemic
citation: Dai, K., Garcia, J., & Olave-Encina, K. (2023). In-between worlds: Chilean university lecturers' experiences of teaching transition between face-to-face and virtual reality contexts during the COVID-19 pandemic. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10217-0
title: In-betweenness: a theoretical lens for educators' transitions between face-to-face and virtual teaching contexts.
description: Drawing on Bhabha's (1994) 'in-between space' and social constructivism, the article proposes 'in-betweenness' as the status of continuously shifting between face-to-face and virtual online teaching environments. In this inter-space, lecturers' identity, agency, and digital competencies are reshaped through agentic responses as they move back and forth between contexts. The authors offer it as a unique theoretical lens for exploring instructors' transitions from traditional to technology-mediated settings.
requirements: Applicable when educators transition between two distinct teaching contexts, such as face-to-face and virtual-world-based settings.
constraints: Findings from the underlying qualitative study may not generalise to other cases, as stated by the authors.
target_learning_goals: Professional identity and agency development in technology-mediated teaching

citation: Twyford, L., abstractor. (1955). Audio-Visual Communication Review research abstracts: training device effectiveness studies. Audio-Visual Communication Review. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Audio-Visual+Communication+Review
title: Use inexpensive mockups in place of actual equipment when the training objective does not require actual participation
description: This principle holds that a low-cost mockup of an instrument panel and controls can substitute for the real machine when the objective is procedural or nomenclature learning. The tank hull trainer study found the mockup "a better training aid than the tank hull trainer" for starting and stopping, and equal to the hull trainer and tank for nomenclature, concluding that on cost grounds the mockup is preferable.

article_title: Supporting motivation, task performance and retention in video tutorials for software training
citation: Hans van der Meij, Jan van der Meij, Tessa Voerman, Evert Duipmans. (2018). Supporting motivation, task performance and retention in video tutorials for software training. Education Tech Research Dev 66, 597–614. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-017-9560-z
title: Interleave modeling and production by keeping videos accessible during practice
description: The article argues, citing Bandura, that "modeling and production should be interleaved": practice immediately after observing a model reveals where imitation fails and prompts learners to replay video segments, addressing retention gaps and solidifying acquired knowledge. In the study, video access was blocked once participants started practicing, which the authors identify as a situational variable that likely limited learning and consolidation compared to earlier studies with unlimited access.
requirements: Learners must be able to replay video segments when practice reveals gaps in understanding
constraints: In this study access was blocked during practice tasks, which the authors say limited participants' opportunity for learning
target_learners: novice software learners, including elementary students
target_learning_goals: retention and consolidation of demonstrated procedures
examples: Participants in this study could view videos until they felt sure of the task but could not look back during practice; earlier studies with unlimited access found higher post-test scores and a review advantage

article_title: How research informs educational technology decision-making in higher education: the role of external research versus internal research
citation: Hollands, F., & Escueta, M. (2020). How research informs educational technology decision-making in higher education: the role of external research versus internal research. Education Tech Research Dev, 68, 163–180. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-019-09678-z
title: Interrogate the theory of change for an educational technology tool or strategy before expending resources on high-quality implementation
description: Before investing in careful implementation of an educational technology, decision-makers should first examine whether there is a plausible mechanism by which the technology can produce the intended outcomes. The article recommends this because many interviewees assumed "educational technology will improve student outcomes if it is implemented correctly" and that repeated tinkering would eventually produce success — beliefs that "may preclude serious examination of the underlying mechanism by which technology use is expected to affect learning." After implementation, periodic reassessment of efficacy is warranted to check whether the theory of change holds up in practice.
requirements: A stated theory of change linking the technology's use to the intended learning outcomes
Periodic reassessment of efficacy once the tool or strategy is implemented
constraints: The article frames this as a recommendation arising from observed decision-maker beliefs, not a tested intervention
target_learners: Higher education students affected by educational technology acquisition decisions
target_learning_goals: Ensuring educational technology investments plausibly improve academic outcomes
examples: The article's Example 1 institution presumed its educational technology strategy could improve outcomes if implementation were perfected, an approach the authors say does not rigorously vet effectiveness before scale-up

article_title: How mindful and mindless online searching affects curiosity and information recall
citation: Ju Ae Kim, Jiwon Kim, Sung-il Kim, Mimi Bong. (2026). How mindful and mindless online searching affects curiosity and information recall. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10570-2
title: Information gap theory of curiosity as the mechanism linking answer generation to mindful search and better retention
description: The article anchors its intervention in Loewenstein's information gap theory: "Curiosity emerges when the focus shifts to a gap in one's knowledge, creating a sense of deprivation", motivating information-seeking to resolve the gap, with resolution serving as a reward in a cyclical process. Combined with transactive memory system theory—where the internet acts as a new transactive memory partner—the framework explains why generating answers first makes knowledge gaps salient, induces curiosity, and buffers the metacognitive costs of mindless searching. The authors use it to interpret their finding that pre-search curiosity was elevated only in the answer-first group.
requirements: Learners must recognize a gap between what they know and what they need to know before searching
constraints: The hypothesized mechanism linking answer generation to recall via curiosity was only partially supported, since post-search curiosity and metacognitive judgments did not differ between groups
examples: Participants in the thinking-before-googling condition spent three minutes generating or guessing answers to three broad brainstorming questions about modern pentathlon before searching

article_title: The added value of game elements: better training performance but comparable learning gains
citation: Manuel Ninaus, Rodolpho Cortez, Izabel Hazin, Kristian Kiili, Silke M. Wortha, Elise Klein, Elisabeth M. Weiss, Korbinian Moeller. (2023). The added value of game elements: better training performance but comparable learning gains. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10263-8
title: Intrinsic integration of learning content into game core mechanics
description: Intrinsic integration is a game design approach in which the game's core mechanics are directly tied to the learning content, so that players process essential learning content through game actions. The article states it "refers to the general idea that there must be an intrinsic association between the game's core mechanics and the learning content or learning mechanic". The study applied it by implementing number line estimation as the game's walkable platform, letting learners experience fraction magnitudes as walking distances.
requirements: An intrinsic association between the game's core mechanics and the learning content or learning mechanic
constraints: The article notes the concept of intrinsic integration has not been studied extensively yet, and that to what extent it interacts with essential processing needs well-controlled experimental manipulations
examples: The game-based training embedded number line estimation as a walkable path on Mount Olympos where the avatar Semideus recovered hidden gold coins marked by fractions

article_title: Exploring the impact of a CALL tool for emergent bilinguals
citation: Nicholas Feroce, Jenny Liu, Rajendra Chattergoon. (2025). Exploring the impact of a CALL tool for emergent bilinguals. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10462-5
title: Interaction-approach SLA design: scaffolded output, comprehensible input, and corrective feedback in a CALL program
description: The program's linguistic components were intentionally developed based on theories within the interaction approach to second language acquisition. Speaking activities are framed as scaffolded conversational interactions implementing the Output Hypothesis, while language frames serve as comprehensible input under the Input Hypothesis. Program characters first model the sentence, followed by joint repetition, then independent student production, supporting purposeful repetition for fluency and automaticity. A Speech Recognition Engine with instant corrective feedback is intended to trigger learners' metalinguistic awareness as they hypothesize utterance formulation and test out sentences.
requirements: Speaking activities must be framed as scaffolded conversational interactions with program characters
Corrective feedback must be provided so learners can test sentences and receive feedback on whether they were understood
constraints: The program is not intended to replace real-life conversational interactions; its affordances lie in complementing classroom instruction
target_learners: K-6 Emergent Bilinguals learning academic English
target_learning_goals: Production of complete sentences with target vocabulary and grammar
Fluency and automaticity in oral academic language
examples: Program characters model a sentence, the character and student repeat together, then the student produces it independently.

article_title: Inter-brain coupling analysis reveals learning-related attention of primary school students
citation: Jingjing Chen, Bing Xu & Dan Zhang. (2022). Inter-brain coupling analysis reveals learning-related attention of primary school students. bioRxiv. https://doi.org/10.1101/2022.06.08.495411
title: Inter-brain attention coupling framework: class-average attention dynamics represent learning-related attention
description: The framework holds that learning-related attention follows the structure of course contents, so attention dynamics shared across students reflect course-content-driven processing. It defines "the degree to which an individual student’s attention dynamics match the attention dynamics averaged across classmates" as inter-brain attention coupling, computed with Pearson correlation over 30-s epochs. Comparing a student to the class average is expected to "filter out idiosyncratic dynamics responsive to distractors", capturing attention intended by the course contents even when a student's raw attention level is high but off-task.
requirements: Students must be engaged in the same learning task or course content so a meaningful class-average attention dynamic exists; the article builds on the inter-subject correlation framework applied to students situated in the same learning task.
constraints: Validated only in a grade-3 classroom with a single-channel EEG device and one neuroscience lecture topic; the authors note further validation with larger samples, other educational stages, and more kinds of courses is needed.
target_learners: primary school students (grade 3, ages 8-9 in the study)
target_learning_goals: monitoring learning-related attention and the learning process during classroom instruction
examples: Students wore EEG headbands through five ~20-minute sessions alternating a 2-minute meditation task with teacher lectures on introduction to neuroscience; coupling was computed per 30-s epoch against the class-average (all other students).
key_sources: Jingjing Chen, Bing Xu & Dan Zhang. (2022). Inter-brain coupling analysis reveals learning-related attention of primary school students. bioRxiv. https://doi.org/10.1101/2022.06.08.495411

article_title: Temporary instructor presence in lecture slides does not enhance online learning
citation: Tim Kühl, Felicia Teske, Martin Merkt, Christina Sondermann. (2025). Temporary instructor presence in lecture slides does not enhance online learning. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-024-10435-0
title: Interference and social-cue hypotheses as competing accounts of instructor presence in online lecture slides
description: The article frames instructor presence in online lecture slides with two competing lines of reasoning, both empirically supported. The interference hypothesis holds that the instructor acts as a seductive detail and induces split attention, raising extraneous cognitive load; the social-cue hypothesis, traced to Social Agency Theory, holds that the instructor "elicits a social response in learners that in turn triggers them to process the content more deeply", raising germane load. The study tested whether temporary presence could keep the benefit while avoiding the cost.
requirements: Both lines of reasoning are assumed to operate simultaneously, so their drawbacks and advantages may cancel each other out
constraints: The empirical evidence on instructor presence is described as equivocal, with the latest meta-analysis showing a small retention effect but no transfer effect
target_learning_goals: transfer of lecture content to new problems
examples: The two experiments operationalized temporary presence as showing the instructor only on introductory and transitional slides with hardly any content, about 10 of 16 slides lasting about three minutes

article_title: The recording of audience reactions by infra-red photography
citation: Greenhill, L. P. (1955). The Recording of Audience Reactions by Infra-Red Photography. article_title: Online discussion compensates for suboptimal timing of supportive information presentation in a digitally supported learning environment
citation: Noroozi, O., Busstra, M. C., Mulder, M., Biemans, H. J. A., Tobi, H., Geelen, A., van't Veer, P., Chizari, M. (2012). article_title: Improving the transfer of inquiry strategies by using short instructional videos
citation: Ana Saavedra · Daniel L. Schwartz. (2026). Improving the transfer of inquiry strategies by using short instructional videos. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10648-5
title: Internal psychological cue account of inquiry-strategy transfer
description: The article proposes that transfer of effortful inquiry strategies requires not only recognizing external situational cues but also attending to internally generated psychological cues. Because students' natural default strategy (difference reduction) feels easy at the outset, alerting students to the feelings that draw them to it — cognitive ease and later frustration — can help them inhibit it and switch to the more demanding means-ends strategy. The article states: "If we can help alert students to the internal cues associated with this natural tendency, we may be able to help them inhibit the default strategy and switch to the more cognitively demanding base-unit strategy." It blends cognitive and behavior-change approaches to transfer.
requirements: Students must have a well-worn default strategy that feels natural and effortless, generating recognizable internal cues
constraints: Tested for one inquiry strategy (base-unit) in simulation-based inquiry; the authors note it is unknown whether increasing instruction dosage improves transfer
target_learning_goals: transfer of learning strategies to new science simulations
examples: The Expanded video told students the default strategy feels easiest but makes things more complicated, and that effort at the beginning pays off
key_sources: Ana Saavedra · Daniel L. Schwartz. (2026). Improving the transfer of inquiry strategies by using short instructional videos. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10648-5

article_title: Determining mobile learning acceptance outside the classroom: an integrated acceptance model
citation: Chenxi Liu, Ana-Paula Correia, Young Min Kim. (2025). Determining mobile learning acceptance outside the classroom: an integrated acceptance model. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10514-w
title: Integrated m-learning acceptance model combining TAM with the updated DeLone and McLean IS Success Model
description: The article proposes a novel acceptance model that imports the three quality dimensions of the updated DL&ML into the TAM belief-intention structure. As printed: "The proposed model includes seven quality-related constructs. Among them, content quality and content design quality correspond to the information quality dimension; mobility, compatibility, interface design, and interactivity correspond to the system quality dimension; and service quality corresponds to the service quality dimension." These seven exogenous quality constructs are hypothesized to influence perceived ease of use and perceived usefulness, which in turn drive behavioral intention. The model was tested with SEM and supported eight of thirteen hypotheses.
requirements: Quality constructs must have clearly defined components; the article notes prior studies left components underdefined and inconsistent
constraints: Attitude was excluded from the instrument based on prior studies; content quality and interface design constructs were removed from the final analysis for discriminant validity
target_learners: Adult learners in the U.S., both students and non-students, using m-learning apps outside the classroom
target_learning_goals: Understanding and predicting learners' acceptance of mobile learning applications
examples: Tested via a two-step SEM strategy (measurement model then structural model) on 639 valid MTurk survey responses; structural model fit: RMSEA = 0.06, SRMR = 0.06, CFI = 0.91, TLI = 0.90
key_sources: Chenxi Liu, Ana-Paula Correia, Young Min Kim. (2025). Determining mobile learning acceptance outside the classroom: an integrated acceptance model. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10514-w

article_title: A bibliography of production, utilization, and research on instructional films
citation: RESEARCH ABSTRACTS: FILMS. (1953). Research abstracts, p. 819. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Instructional+Film+Research+Program
title: Bibliography of Production, Utilization, and Research on Instructional Films (SDC technical report)
description: A technical report from the Instructional Film Research Program at Pennsylvania State University, published November 1953, that alphabetically lists approximately 1950 references on instructional film production, utilization, and research, including indirectly related areas such as radio, music, learning theory, and research methods. Its purpose is to serve "professional people in the mass communication field, to research workers, and to students." Copies could be purchased from the Office of Technical Services in Washington, D.C.
requirements: Intended users are mass communication professionals, research workers, and students
constraints: Its usefulness is somewhat limited by the alphabetical listing; the authors hoped to publish a subject-matter cross-reference list
target_learners: research workers and students in the mass communication and instructional film fields
target_learning_goals: locating research literature on instructional film production, utilization, and research
examples: The bibliography includes studies indirectly related to instructional films, such as radio, music, learning theory, and research methods
key_sources: RESEARCH ABSTRACTS: FILMS. (1953). Research abstracts, p. 819. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Instructional+Film+Research+Program

article_title: Assessing the impact of substituting interaction types: an empirical study of the interaction equivalency theory
citation: Hauert, S., Luo, T., & Yen, C.-J. (2026). Assessing the impact of substituting interaction types: an empirical study of the interaction equivalency theory. Education Tech Research Dev, 74, 1–27. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10563-1
title: Interaction equivalency theory (Anderson's substitutivity thesis)
description: Anderson's (2003a) interaction equivalency theory is this study's theoretical foundation. Its first thesis posits that "Deep and meaningful formal learning is supported as long as one of the three forms of interaction (student–teacher; student–student; student–content) is at a high level," with the other two offered at minimal levels or eliminated without degrading the educational experience. At its core, the theory argues a well-designed course can substitute one interaction type for another without significantly impacting performance. The study provides the first experimental test with random assignment of this substitutive prong, distinguishing it from the well-studied additive second thesis.
requirements: At least one of the three interaction forms must be at a high level for deep and meaningful formal learning to be supported
constraints: The theory's substitutive prong had not previously been tested; this study tested it only for learner–content substituting for learner–learner, with explicit declarative knowledge, in one week-long episode with adult undergraduates
target_learning_goals: knowledge acquisition of explicit, declarative content in formal distance education
examples: The study operationalized the theory by randomly assigning students to an interactive multimedia lecture with adjunct questions or to vignette-based peer discussion, then comparing summative assessment scores
key_sources: Hauert, S., Luo, T., & Yen, C.-J. (2026). Assessing the impact of substituting interaction types: an empirical study of the interaction equivalency theory. Education Tech Research Dev, 74, 1–27. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10563-1

article_title: The effect of competition on learning in games
citation: Nergiz Ercil Cagiltay, Erol Ozcelik, Nese Sahin Ozcelik. (2015). The effect of competition on learning in games. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2015.04.001
title: Serious game designers should incorporate competition to facilitate learning
description: The article concludes that adding competition as a game design element improves learning outcomes and motivation. Based on their experiment, the authors state that "game designers should incorporate the element 'competition' to the games they created to facilitate learning." The competition was implemented as a real-time panel showing other players' scores, ranking and nick names.
requirements: A competition environment among human players, with visible scores, ranking and nick names in real time
constraints: The authors note some studies show cooperation is more effective than competition, and results need validation in larger samples and other domains and age groups
target_learners: undergraduate students in computer-related engineering departments
target_learning_goals: conceptual database modeling with entity-relationship diagrams
examples: In the study, half of 142 randomly assigned participants played a game version showing all current players' scores, ranking and nick names in real time, while the control version left that list empty.
key_sources: Nergiz Ercil Cagiltay, Erol Ozcelik, Nese Sahin Ozcelik. (2015). The effect of competition on learning in games. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2015.04.001

article_title: Factors influencing students’ perceived impact of learning and satisfaction in Computer Supported Collaborative Learning
citation: Pablo-César Muñoz-Carril, Nuria Hernández-Sellés, Eduardo-José Fuentes-Abeledo, Mercedes González-Sanmamed. (2021). Factors influencing students' perceived impact of learning and satisfaction in Computer Supported Collaborative Learning. Computers & Education, 174. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2021.104310
title: Integrated TAM–ECM–Flow research model of satisfaction and perceived impact on learning in CSCL
description: The article develops a research model combining seven constructs from three theories: "the Expectation-Confirmation Model (ECM) (Bhattacherjee, 2001), the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) (Davis, 1989) and Flow Theory (Csikszentmihalyi, 1997)". It links confirmation, perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use, attitude, perceived enjoyment, and satisfaction to perceived impact on learning, tested via PLS-SEM. The model explained 84% of the variance of perceived impact on learning and 86.3% of satisfaction, and all 13 hypothesised paths were supported.
requirements: Questionnaire scales previously validated in prior studies, reviewed by a panel of 5 international experts and pre-tested with 30 students
constraints: The article states the research was carried out in a single University and focuses only on student perception in a CSCL context
target_learners: university master's students in virtual courses
target_learning_goals: perceived impact on learning in CSCL
examples: PLS-SEM with SmartPLS 3.2.7 on questionnaire data from 701 master's students; bootstrapping with 5000 subsamples; SRMR of 0.05
key_sources: Pablo-César Muñoz-Carril, Nuria Hernández-Sellés, Eduardo-José Fuentes-Abeledo, Mercedes González-Sanmamed. (2021). Factors influencing students' perceived impact of learning and satisfaction in Computer Supported Collaborative Learning. Computers & Education, 174. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2021.104310

article_title: Examining the use of instructional video clips for teaching macroeconomics
citation: Expósito, A., Sánchez-Rivas, J., Gómez-Calero, M. P., & Pablo-Romero, M. P. (2020). Examining the use of instructional video clips for teaching macroeconomics. Computers & Education, 143, 103705. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2019.103705
title: Use instructional videos as complementary materials in blended-learning environments
description: The article recommends producing instructional videos as complementary teaching materials integrated with face-to-face lectures in a blended-learning environment. The videos "are designed to serve as a complement to other materials (e.g., books and notes taken in face-to-face classes), thus being used in a blended-learning environment." Videos were indexed to the subject's syllabus and produced in the participants' native language.
requirements: Videos should be designed as complements to existing face-to-face materials, not replacements
examples: Five instructional videos were produced and indexed to the subject's syllabus as complementary multimedia material
key_sources: Expósito, A., Sánchez-Rivas, J., Gómez-Calero, M. P., & Pablo-Romero, M. P. (2020). Examining the use of instructional video clips for teaching macroeconomics. Computers & Education, 143, 103705. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2019.103709

article_title: Analysis and discovery of procrastination patterns in a language learning MOOC
citation: Vázquez Mendoza, J. A., Ferri Ramírez, C., & Monserrat Aranda, C. (2024). Analysis and discovery of procrastination patterns in a language learning MOOC. Computers & Education, 223, 105154. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2024.105154
title: A taxonomy of two forms of procrastination in online learning environments: intra-session and extra-session procrastination.
description: The article identifies two forms of procrastination in online learning environments. "Intra-session procrastination" is "Characterised by intervals of inactivity during learning that are not wide enough to be considered as a threshold of inactivity between different study sessions." "Extra-session procrastination" is "characterised by being an excessively wide interval of inactivity time between the end of one session and the beginning of another." Extra-session procrastination is further subdivided into expected rest (25 min to 48 h), ordinary procrastination (48 h to 10 weeks), and extraordinary procrastination (more than 10 weeks).
requirements: Event logs from a learning platform that allow the calculation of inactivity intervals between and within study sessions
constraints: The thresholds used (e.g., a 25-minute inactivity threshold for session boundaries) are specific to the analysed course's material durations.
target_learners: Learners in self-paced online courses such as MOOCs
target_learning_goals: Understanding and detecting procrastination behaviours that affect learning outcomes
examples: The study applies this taxonomy to the 'Basic Spanish 1' MOOC to classify user inactivity intervals.
key_sources: Vázquez Mendoza, J. A., Ferri Ramírez, C., & Monserrat Aranda, C. (2024). Analysis and discovery of procrastination patterns in a language learning MOOC. Computers & Education, 223, 105154. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2024.105154

article_title: Instructor presence effect: Liking does not always lead to learning
citation: Wilson, K. E., Martinez, M., Mills, C., D'Mello, S., Smilek, D., & Risko, E. F. (2018). Instructor presence effect: Liking does not always lead to learning. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2018.03.011
title: Instructor Presence Effect: instructor visuals in video lectures act as seductive details that impair learning while increasing enjoyment and perceived learning
description: The Instructor Presence Effect names the dissociation between objective learning (comprehension) and subjective evaluation (enjoyment, interest, perceived learning) when visuals of the instructor are added to online lectures. The authors propose a seductive details mechanism: attention captured by the instructor's visual features is devoted to irrelevant processing rather than lecture content, impairing comprehension without increasing mind wandering. The article states that "visuals of the instructor potentially impairs comprehension, but learners prefer and believe they learn most effectively with this format."
requirements: Requires a comprehensive assessment comparing attention (mind wandering), learning (comprehension), and subjective evaluations across matched lecture formats
constraints: Demonstrated in online learning environments with adult participants; the authors note that laboratory studies may yield different attentional patterns due to differing sources of distraction
target_learning_goals: instructional design for online video lectures
key_sources: Wilson, K. E., Martinez, M., Mills, C., D'Mello, S., Smilek, D., & Risko, E. F. (2018). Instructor presence effect: Liking does not always lead to learning. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2018.03.011

article_title: Effects of Integrated Literacy and Content-Area Instruction on Vocabulary and Comprehension in the Elementary Years: A Meta-Analysis
citation: HyeJin Hwang, Sonia Q. Cabell & Rachel E. Joyner (2021). Effects of Integrated Literacy and Content-area Instruction on Vocabulary and Comprehension in the Elementary Years: A Meta-analysis. Scientific Studies of Reading. https://doi.org/10.1080/10888438.2021.1954005
title: Integrated literacy and content-area instruction as mutually enhancing literacy-content teaching
description: The article defines integrated instruction between literacy and the content areas as "instruction in which literacy activities (reading and/or writing) serve as a tool to cultivate content knowledge (science and/ or social studies) while, at the same time, content teaching serves as a lever to facilitate literacy skills". It is operationalized through connected texts sequenced to reflect content connections, repeated encounters with content-related words taught in relation to content rather than in isolation, and motivating purposes for literacy activities. The meta-analysis tests whether this mutually enhancing design improves vocabulary, comprehension, and content knowledge in K-5.
requirements: The approach blends ideas and skills in different subjects with balanced attention to each subject, rather than focusing on one subject with the other only used as a tool
constraints: The literature contains varied definitions of integrated models of instruction without a clear consensus
target_learners: Students in kindergarten through fifth grade
target_learning_goals: Science and social studies content knowledge
examples: Included interventions sequenced multiple coherently connected texts around science or social studies content and had students encounter and use content-related words repeatedly while reading and writing to learn the content
key_sources: HyeJin Hwang, Sonia Q. Cabell & Rachel E. Joyner (2021). Effects of Integrated Literacy and Content-area Instruction on Vocabulary and Comprehension in the Elementary Years: A Meta-analysis. Scientific Studies of Reading. https://doi.org/10.1080/10888438.2021.1954005

article_title: The Effectiveness Level of Material Use in Classroom Instruction: A Meta-Analysis Study
citation: Zeynel KABLAN, Beyda TOPAN, Burak ERKAN. (2013). The Effectiveness Level of Material Use in Classroom Instruction: A Meta-analysis Study. Educational Sciences: Theory & Practice. https://doi.org/10.12738/estp.2013.3.1692
title: Typology of classroom instructional materials by material type
description: The article organizes the materials used in the reviewed studies into five types: "computer presentations, hands-on materials, cartoons, concept maps, and combination of different materials". Computer presentations were in PowerPoint or animation format; hands-on materials are "materials that can be touched and moved around easily by students"; cartoons reveal important information about specific content; concept maps are two-dimensional diagrams showing relationships among concepts; and a combination category was used when more than one material was used. The typology served as a coding variable in the meta-analysis.
requirements: Studies must be classifiable into one of the five material categories for moderator coding
constraints: Distance learning, computer-based learning, and worksheet studies were excluded from the analysis
examples: The 57 included studies were coded into these material categories, with computer presentations most frequent (29.8%) and hands-on materials least frequent (14%)
key_sources: Zeynel KABLAN, Beyda TOPAN, Burak ERKAN. (2013). The Effectiveness Level of Material Use in Classroom Instruction: A Meta-analysis Study. Educational Sciences: Theory & Practice. https://doi.org/10.12738/estp.2013.3.1692

article_title: The Effect of STEM Education Integrated into Teaching-Learning Approaches (SEITLA) on Learning Outcomes: A Meta-Analysis Study
citation: Mustafa Çevik, Büşra Bakioğlu. (2022). The Effect of STEM Education Integrated into Teaching-Learning Approaches (SEITLA) on Learning Outcomes: A Meta-Analysis Study. International Journal of Progressive Education, 18(2). https://doi.org/10.29329/ijpe.2022.431.8
title: Integrate STEM activities with teaching-learning approaches such as mastery learning, evidence-based learning and blended learning for greater effectiveness
description: The article recommends that educators deliberately pair STEM activities with teaching-learning approaches whose pooled effects were largest. It states that "A STEM activity integrated especially with teaching-learning approaches like mastery learning, evidence-based learning and blended learning can be more effective", and that selection should also consider curriculum, student readiness, school administration and parents' situations.
requirements: Educators need teaching knowledge and skills beyond subject matter knowledge to select and implement appropriate approaches.
constraints: In STEM activities with intensive technology use, teacher competencies and readiness of infrastructure are of great importance.
Findings are limited to 33 studies meeting the inclusion criterion, with self-reported measurement tools and no standard sought for study groups.
target_learners: K-12 and higher education students in STEM subjects
target_learning_goals: STEM learning outcomes and academic achievement
examples: The meta-analysis pooled 33 experimental studies (2015-2021, 3822 participants) comparing SEITLA experimental groups with control groups using traditional learning.
key_sources: Mustafa Çevik, Büşra Bakioğlu. (2022). The Effect of STEM Education Integrated into Teaching-Learning Approaches (SEITLA) on Learning Outcomes: A Meta-Analysis Study. International Journal of Progressive Education, 18(2). https://doi.org/10.29329/ijpe.2022.431.8

article_title: Does Context-Based Learning Increase Academic Achievement and Learning Retention?: A Review Based on Meta-Analysis
citation: Tutal, Ö (2023). Does Context-Based Learning Increase Academic Achievement and Learning Retention?: A Review based on Meta-Analysis. Journal of Practical Studies in Education, 4(5), 1-16. https://doi.org/10.46809/jpse.v4i5.71
title: Educators should consider incorporating context-based learning strategies into instructional practices to support achievement and retention
description: Based on its meta-analytic findings, the article recommends that educators adopt context-based learning, an approach that "establish[es] a meaningful connection between everyday experiences and educational content" and emphasizes "the use of context as a powerful tool for constructing and understanding concepts." The recommendation is grounded in the significant positive overall effects on achievement and retention relative to lecture-based instruction.
requirements: Content should be situated within the learner's horizon and connected to real-life experiences, social events, or scientifically valid situations
constraints: The recommendation rests on Turkish thesis studies with experimental or quasi-experimental designs; evidence on retention comes from only 10 studies
target_learners: Elementary, middle, high school and tertiary students
examples: The meta-analysis synthesized 42 achievement studies and 10 retention studies, most conducted in science courses, comparing CBL to teacher-led instruction with pretest-posttest control group designs
key_sources: Tutal, Ö (2023). Does Context-Based Learning Increase Academic Achievement and Learning Retention?: A Review based on Meta-Analysis. Journal of Practical Studies in Education, 4(5), 1-16. https://doi.org/10.46809/jpse.v4i5.71

article_title: Effectiveness of technology-enhanced learning in neuroanatomy education among health professionals - a systematic review.
citation: K Anniesmitha, Rao K G Mohandas, Aithal P Ashwini, Bandekar Nikita N., Mandal Tatiyana, George Bincy M. (2026). Effectiveness of technology-enhanced learning in neuroanatomy education among health professionals - a systematic review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09764-w
title: Integrate technology-enhanced learning with, rather than as a replacement for, traditional anatomy teaching
description: The review concludes that technology-enhanced learning works best as a complement to conventional neuroanatomy teaching rather than a substitute for it. It states that "technology-enhanced learning is most effective when integrated with, rather than used as a replacement for, traditional anatomy teaching approaches", grounding this in engagement gains alongside inconsistent objective knowledge outcomes.
requirements: Traditional neuroanatomy teaching environments (e.g., didactic lectures, cadaveric dissection) remain available as comparators or anchors alongside the technology-enhanced component.
constraints: The evidence base was restricted to randomised controlled trials and driven from undergraduate medical student populations, which the review states may limit generalisability.
Considerable heterogeneity in intervention types, pedagogical approaches and outcome measures limits the ability to draw generalised conclusions.
target_learning_goals: Neuroanatomical knowledge and spatial understanding of complex three-dimensional brain structures
examples: Across the nine included RCTs, control groups were generally exposed to traditional neuroanatomy educational environments while intervention groups used 3D visualisation, VR, stereoscopic lectures or AR tools.
key_sources: K Anniesmitha, Rao K G Mohandas, Aithal P Ashwini, Bandekar Nikita N., Mandal Tatiyana, George Bincy M. (2026). Effectiveness of technology-enhanced learning in neuroanatomy education among health professionals - a systematic review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09764-w

article_title: Metacognitive regulation in physical therapists' clinical reasoning: a scoping review.
citation: Perdrix Yannick, Nael Jérémy, Dionne Eric, Pinsault Nicolas. (2026). Metacognitive regulation in physical therapists’ clinical reasoning: a scoping review. International Journal of Medical Education. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC13563282/
title: Integrative model of metacognitive regulation in physical therapists' clinical reasoning structured around five key characteristics
description: The review creates an integrative model synthesizing the relationships between the characteristics of metacognitive regulation (MR) during physical therapy clinical reasoning. The article states: "We therefore structured the results of the nature of metacognitive regulation around five key characteristics: the types, the timing, the tasks, the focals and the interactions." Type covers self-observation, self-judgment and self-reaction; timing covers concurrent or retrospective and pre-, during- or post-task; task covers cognitive, psychomotor, emotional, communicational or global management; focal is "the analysis grid with which metacognitive regulation is achieved"; and interaction covers the persons in interaction during MR. The model is presented as a comprehensive lens for educational and clinical settings.
requirements: Applies to task-dependent metacognitive regulation in clinical reasoning contexts; only task-dependent activities were considered in the review
constraints: Developed from a qualitative synthesis of 36 studies; the authors state further empirical research is needed to test its applicability in educational and clinical settings
examples: The article's Example 2: a PT student one week after placement, in a professional-practices workshop with two other students, recalls gestures performed and asks whether he attended to the patient's reactions in order to adjust the intensity of his gestures
key_sources: Perdrix Yannick, Nael Jérémy, Dionne Eric, Pinsault Nicolas. (2026). Metacognitive regulation in physical therapists’ clinical reasoning: a scoping review. International Journal of Medical Education. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC13563282/

article_title: Bridging Pedagogy and Technology: A Systematic Literature Review on Inquiry-Collaborative Models Assisted with Virtual Laboratory in Physics Education.
citation: Yahya Fahmi, Rusijono Rusijono, Dewi Utari, Metafisika Kartika, Lestiani Winda, Hermansyah Hermansyah, Asbanu Dens E. S. I. (2026). Bridging Pedagogy and Technology: A Systematic Literature Review on Inquiry-Collaborative Models Assisted with Virtual Laboratory in Physics Education. F1000Research 15:1682. https://doi.org/10.12688/f1000research.191181.1
title: Inquiry-collaborative pedagogy as the joint framing framework for virtual-laboratory physics instruction
description: A review-level framework treating inquiry-based learning and collaborative learning as the joint pedagogical frame within which virtual laboratories are deployed, rather than analysing the three separately as prior reviews did. Inquiry is characterised through a five-phase cycle of "orientation, conceptualization, investigation, conclusion, and discussion", and collaboration through whether partners work on the problem together rather than in parallel. The synthesis shows inquiry is an explicit, measured framework in almost every report while collaboration is not, yielding an evidence base about inquiry with virtual labs that happen to be delivered in groups.
requirements: Studies must pair a digital experimental environment with an explicit inquiry and/or collaborative instructional model and report at least one learner outcome
constraints: Collaboration was explicitly designed in only 15.3% and measured in only 8.5% of the included reports, so the collaborative branch of the framework is under-evidenced
target_learners: Primary to higher-education physics learners, including prospective teachers
examples: The review synthesised 58 studies grouped by instructional design configuration rather than physics topic, using a six-phase thematic analysis coded towards the inquiry and collaboration frames
key_sources: Yahya Fahmi, Rusijono Rusijono, Dewi Utari, Metafisika Kartika, Lestiani Winda, Hermansyah Hermansyah, Asbanu Dens E. S. I. (2026). Bridging Pedagogy and Technology: A Systematic Literature Review on Inquiry-Collaborative Models Assisted with Virtual Laboratory in Physics Education. F1000Research 15:1682. https://doi.org/10.12688/f1000research.191181.1

article_title: Simulation-Based Training for Nursing Students to Improve Patient Safety: Systematic Review.
citation: González-Sanz A, López-García JC, Sutil-Rodríguez E, Juárez-Vela R, Santos-Sánchez JÁ, Navas-Echazarreta N, Martínez-Sabater A, Sancho-Sanchez C. (2026). Simulation-Based Training for Nursing Students to Improve Patient Safety: Systematic Review. JMIR Nursing. https://doi.org/10.2196/87898
title: Integrate structured simulation into nursing curricula to bridge the theory-practice gap
description: The review concludes simulation is an essential pedagogical strategy for preparing nursing students to deliver safe care and recommends that structured simulation be integrated into nursing curricula. It argues simulation provides controlled environments where students develop safety competencies and error-recognition skills before clinical practice, addressing the theory-practice gap. This aligns with an international coalition's call to integrate simulation-based learning into undergraduate and postgraduate curricula to foster a culture of safety.
requirements: Simulation should be structured and followed by debriefing, which the review says enables reflective analysis and identification of improvement strategies
constraints: Simulation must be designed so it does not compromise the psychological and physical integrity of participants
examples: The review's 20 included studies spanned single-session workshops (eg, 3.5 h) to multisession programs integrated into the curriculum
key_sources: González-Sanz A, López-García JC, Sutil-Rodríguez E, Juárez-Vela R, Santos-Sánchez JÁ, Navas-Echazarreta N, Martínez-Sabater A, Sancho-Sanchez C. (2026). Simulation-Based Training for Nursing Students to Improve Patient Safety: Systematic Review. JMIR Nursing. https://doi.org/10.2196/87898

article_title: A Scoping Review of the Conceptualization, Operationalization, and Institutional Recognition of the Scholarship of Teaching and Learning in Health Professions Education: Using Institutional Logics to Understand Inconsistencies.
citation: Varpio L, Jones F, Lege-Matsuura J, Schultz K, Amiel J, Dunleavy K, Jensen GM, Jeffries PR, Ellaway R. (2026). A Scoping Review of the Conceptualization, Operationalization, and Institutional Recognition of the Scholarship of Teaching and Learning in Health Professions Education: Using Institutional Logics to Understand Inconsistencies. Perspectives on Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.5334/pme.2740
title: Institutional Logics and Besharov & Smith's compatibility–centrality model explain variable SoTL recognition across HPE organizations
description: Institutional logics are "socially constructed and historically informed patterns of practices, assumptions, values, and rules" through which individuals produce meaning and justify actions. Besharov and Smith's model positions logics on two continuous dimensions—compatibility (consistency of rules for action) and centrality (equal validity to organizational functioning)—yielding four ideal types: contested, aligned, estranged, and dominant. The review applies this to argue that SoTL recognition varies with alignment between the logics of research and teaching: revised P&T guidelines suggest aligned organizations, while reliance on research metrics suggests estranged or contested ones.
requirements: Both the logics of research and SoTL must be articulated with clear prescriptions for action so their compatibility can be assessed
constraints: The review notes organizations can fall between ideal types because centrality and compatibility exist in degrees; some articles listed both supportive and obstructing factors
target_learning_goals: institutional recognition of educational scholarship in promotion and tenure decisions
examples: The review interprets P&T guideline revisions as high centrality plus high compatibility (aligned organizations), and committees applying research metrics to SoTL as low centrality and low compatibility (estranged) or high centrality with low compatibility (contested)
key_sources: Varpio L, Jones F, Lege-Matsuura J, Schultz K, Amiel J, Dunleavy K, Jensen GM, Jeffries PR, Ellaway R. (2026). A Scoping Review of the Conceptualization, Operationalization, and Institutional Recognition of the Scholarship of Teaching and Learning in Health Professions Education: Using Institutional Logics to Understand Inconsistencies. Perspectives on Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.5334/pme.2740

article_title: Nurses' Experiences and Perceptions of Evidence-Based Healthcare Competence: A Qualitative Systematic Review.
citation: Hietaniemi, A.‐M., Ylimäki, S., Härkönen, H., Hannila, H.‐M., Tuomikoski, A.‐M., Oikarinen, A., Jansson, M., Pölkki, T., Kanste, O. & Kääriäinen, M. (2026). Nurses' Experiences and Perceptions of Evidence‐Based Healthcare Competence: A Qualitative Systematic Review. Journal of Advanced Nursing. https://doi.org/10.1111/jan.70399
title: Integrate EBHC into education, mentoring and adequate resources to strengthen nurses' EBHC competence
description: The review's implication for the profession is that "Integration of EBHC into education, mentoring and adequate resources enhances nurses' competence, motivation and commitment to EBHC sub‐dimensions, while also strengthening their professional confidence and development". Synthesised findings support this: nurses described mentorship, supportive leadership, structured training programmes and practical workshops as enhancing evidence transfer and implementation. The principle directs nursing education and healthcare organisations to embed EBHC in curricula and provide mentoring and resources.
requirements: Adequate resources and organisational support for evidence‐based practice
Mentors and supportive leadership actively involved in implementing recommendations
constraints: The synthesised findings supporting this principle were graded low confidence with ConQual
examples: In Khoddam et al. (2023), the presence of a mentor and implementation of recommendations by the head nurse were reported as effective in an evidence‐based change in neonatal pain management
key_sources: Hietaniemi, A.‐M., Ylimäki, S., Härkönen, H., Hannila, H.‐M., Tuomikoski, A.‐M., Oikarinen, A., Jansson, M., Pölkki, T., Kanste, O. & Kääriäinen, M. (2026). Nurses' Experiences and Perceptions of Evidence‐Based Healthcare Competence: A Qualitative Systematic Review. Journal of Advanced Nursing. https://doi.org/10.1111/jan.70399

article_title: Fostering inclusion in healthcare: a systematic review of collaborative teaching with individuals with disorders of intellectual development.
citation: Felix Gorny, Anika Grohmann, Mareike Müller-Cleve, Daniela Bavaresco, Saskia Wirtz, Christan Brandt, Tanja Sappok. (2026). Fostering inclusion in healthcare: a systematic review of collaborative teaching with individuals with disorders of intellectual development. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09930-0
title: Recommended instructional strategies for inclusive co-teaching with co-teachers with Disorders of Intellectual Development
description: The review distills a set of instructional strategies and supports for inclusive co-teaching from the reviewed literature and best-practice guidelines. A guideline article "emphasized the importance of varied instructional strategies, including repetition and practice, use of visual support, establishment of routines, prioritization of group work, creation of worksheets over didactic instruction, use of clear and accessible language, flexibility, creativity, and fostering an enjoyable learning environment." The pattern also includes support persons for classroom management, collaborative planning with co-teachers, joint lectures, and involvement of co-teachers in roles beyond teaching.
requirements: Support persons for classroom management and reassurance
Collaborative planning and feedback with co-teachers
Adequate time and resources in the planning phase
constraints: Systemic barriers and insufficient structural support can limit effectiveness and sustainability
examples: Co-teachers collaborated with academic staff to deliver 12–16 two-hour lectures and participated in planning course modules, sometimes supported by assistants providing technical or general support
key_sources: Felix Gorny, Anika Grohmann, Mareike Müller-Cleve, Daniela Bavaresco, Saskia Wirtz, Christan Brandt, Tanja Sappok. (2026). Fostering inclusion in healthcare: a systematic review of collaborative teaching with individuals with disorders of intellectual development. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09930-0

article_title: Is ultrasound training sustainable? A systematic review of competency retention in healthcare trainees.
citation: Wang L‐W, Liu C‐H, Li W‐Y, Chiang W‐C, Chiu Y‐L, Ma M H‐M, Chen H‐L, Yang C‐W. (2025). Is ultrasound training sustainable? A systematic review of competency retention in healthcare trainees. Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1111/medu.15751
title: Design PoCUS curricula that integrate high-fidelity hands-on simulation and clinical context rather than relying on one-time short-course instruction
description: The review recommends "the implementation of integrated PoCUS curricula that incorporate multi‐modal educational strategies, supplemented by scheduled refresher training" with "supervised scanning sessions for image acquisition". It finds that "The integration of simulation‐based practice utilizing high‐fidelity simulators, coupled with authentic clinical scenarios, appears to optimize learner competency" across I-AIM domains, because short courses and interpretation-focused curricula leave skills prone to decay.
requirements: Extended durations (7 h to 3 months) and increased resources for clinical-context integration
Access to high-fidelity simulators, three-dimensional models, or cadaver-based practice
constraints: Comparative effectiveness studies between the 'bolus and drip' approach and traditional extended-duration training protocols warrant further investigation
target_learners: healthcare providers and trainees learning point-of-care ultrasound, particularly novice practitioners
target_learning_goals: long-term retention of PoCUS competency across all I-AIM domains
examples: The review recommends just-in-time refresher training for novice practitioners with abbreviated curricula (≤4 h) and a longitudinal 'bolus and drip' curriculum combining structured didactics with practical scanning sessions

article_title: Impact of early clinical exposure on medical students' competency development: a systematic review of evidence from Asian and African countries.
citation: Shaban Eman E., Elmelliti Hussam, Shaban Amira, Shaban Ahmed, Zaki Hany A. (2025). Impact of early clinical exposure on medical students’ competency development: a systematic review of evidence from Asian and African countries. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-08103-9
title: Integrate early clinical exposure into the pre-clinical undergraduate medical curriculum
description: The review concludes that "the overall evidence in this study supports the incorporation of ECE in undergraduate curricula to ensure that medical students are fully prepared to offer high-quality care to patients." ECE integrates early, often observational clinical experiences into pre-clinical years to contextualize theoretical knowledge. The authors recommend integration during early phases of medical training to enhance competency-based medical education.
requirements: ECE activities such as real patient contact, shadowing, case-based learning, or pre-clerkship education with supervision
constraints: Most outcomes relied on self-reported perceptions; implementation barriers include heavy workload, poor academic–health institution linkages, lack of orientation, and potential time consumption with large student groups
examples: Studies used real patient contact, case-based learning, shadowing, and pre-clerkship education as forms of ECE
key_sources: Shaban Eman E., Elmelliti Hussam, Shaban Amira, Shaban Ahmed, Zaki Hany A. (2025). Impact of early clinical exposure on medical students’ competency development: a systematic review of evidence from Asian and African countries. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-08103-9

article_title: Computer-based surgical skill training: a systematic review.
citation: Morsund Lars Andreas Lars, Singh Shraddha, Patel Agastya, Lancellotti Francesco, Satyadas Thomas. (2026). Computer-based surgical skill training: a systematic review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-08830-7
title: Integrate synchronous feedback during remote teaching with self-directed virtual teaching to optimize psychomotor learning
description: The review recommends combining the flexibility of self-directed virtual teaching with real-time instructor feedback during remote teaching. It concludes that "Integrating the flexibility of SDVT with synchronous feedback during RT can optimize psychomotor learning while maintaining instructional oversight." This design recommendation follows from findings that synchronous feedback was a key advantage of RT over purely self-directed formats.
requirements: Access to synchronous video-conferencing platforms and instructor availability for real-time feedback
constraints: The review notes CBL "cannot substitute for clinical experience" and that resource availability such as stable internet and devices can bar implementation
target_learning_goals: psychomotor surgical skills such as suturing, knot-tying and laparoscopic maneuvers
examples: Included studies used breakout rooms and audience-response platforms such as Mentimeter to increase engagement and interactivity of RT
key_sources: Morsund Lars Andreas Lars, Singh Shraddha, Patel Agastya, Lancellotti Francesco, Satyadas Thomas. (2026). Computer-based surgical skill training: a systematic review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-08830-7

article_title: Effectiveness of non-technical skills training for healthcare professionals in emergency departments: a systematic review.
citation: Zhang YuKun, Wang YuWei, Jiang ManYu, Sun XiHui, Tang LiYoong. (2026). Effectiveness of non-technical skills training for healthcare professionals in emergency departments: a systematic review. Scandinavian Journal of Trauma, Resuscitation and Emergency Medicine. https://doi.org/10.1186/s13049-026-01574-9
title: Invest in debriefing quality: train facilitators, use explicit behavioural anchors, and protect debriefing time.
description: The review's first actionable principle for ED leaders and educators is to "invest in debriefing quality", specifying that "facilitators require training, behavioural anchors should be explicit, and protected time should be standard". Aligning debriefing with validated domains improves measurement fidelity and rater calibration. This principle follows from the finding that programmes centred on CRM, high-fidelity simulation, and structured debriefing were consistently associated with improved team behaviours.
requirements: Facilitator training in debriefing
Explicit behavioural anchors
Protected time for debriefing
target_learners: Healthcare professionals working in emergency departments
target_learning_goals: Teamwork, communication, and leadership behaviours in emergency resuscitation teams
examples: The review cites RCT evidence using validated instruments such as TEAM and T-NOTECHS during video review with predefined anchors.

Effectiveness of non-technical skills training for healthcare professionals in emergency departments: a systematic review. Scandinavian Journal of Trauma, Resuscitation and Emergency Medicine. https://doi.org/10.1186/s13049-026-01574-9

article_title: Inclusive pedagogy in online simulation-based learning in undergraduate nursing education: A scoping review.
citation: Langan, L., Frazer, K., Darley, A., Goodman, L., Browne, F., Fulfilled, P., Halligan, P., & Redmond, C. (2025). Inclusive pedagogy in online simulation‐based learning in undergraduate nursing education: A scoping review. Journal of Advanced Nursing, 81, 591–606. https://doi.org/10.1111/jan.16284
title: Inclusive pedagogy is defined as an approach to teaching and learning that supports teachers to respond to individual differences between learners but avoids the marginalisation that can occur when some students are treated differently
description: The review adopts Florian and Spratt's (2013) definition of inclusive pedagogy as "an approach to teaching and learning that supports teachers to respond to individual differences between learners, but avoids the marginalisation that can occur when some students are treated differently". In adopting an inclusive pedagogical approach, educators not only encourage difference, they celebrate it, and see difference as a strength. This approach creates the optimal environment for the inclusion of all individuals through the intentional adoption of repeatable, flexible and individualized learning in an inclusive learning environment.
requirements: Educators need to have an in‐depth understanding of how and what students learn, and what students' individual needs are including disabilities.
target_learning_goals: responding to individual differences between learners
key_sources: Langan, L., Frazer, K., Darley, A., Goodman, L., Browne, F., Fulfilled, P., Halligan, P., & Redmond, C. (2025). Inclusive pedagogy in online simulation‐based learning in undergraduate nursing education: A scoping review. Journal of Advanced Nursing, 81, 591–606. https://doi.org/10.1111/jan.16284

article_title: Inclusive pedagogy in online simulation-based learning in undergraduate nursing education: A scoping review.
citation: Langan, L., Frazer, K., Darley, A., Goodman, L., Browne, F., Fulfilled, P., Halligan, P., & Redmond, C. (2025). Inclusive pedagogy in online simulation‐based learning in undergraduate nursing education: A scoping review. Journal of Advanced Nursing, 81, 591–606. https://doi.org/10.1111/jan.16284
title: INACSL Standards of Best Practice for healthcare simulation
description: The International Nursing Association for Clinical Simulation and Learning (INACSL) Standards of Best Practice were the most widely adopted standards in the reviewed studies. Studies that embedded these standards evidenced a responsive approach to the inclusion of students through acknowledging the diversity among learners, and the adoption of psychological safety, needs assessments and flexible and repeatable learning. The INACSL Best Practice Standards indicate that "simulations should be designed with experts and learners" and evaluated by participants, peer clinicians, educators, stakeholders and all involved in the simulation.
requirements: The standards require a more learner‐centred, facilitative approach to the planning of simulation design, including needs assessments and psychological safety protocols.
key_sources: Langan, L., Frazer, K., Darley, A., Goodman, L., Browne, F., Fulfilled, P., Halligan, P., & Redmond, C. (2025). Inclusive pedagogy in online simulation‐based learning in undergraduate nursing education: A scoping review. Journal of Advanced Nursing, 81, 591–606. https://doi.org/10.1111/jan.16284

article_title: Healthcare professionals' experiences of required competencies in mentoring of interprofessional students in clinical practice: A systematic review of qualitative studies.
citation: Juntunen, J., Tuomikoski, A.‐M., Pramila‐Savukoski, S., Kaarlela, V., Keinänen, A.‐L., Kääriäinen, M., & Mikkonen, K. (2025). Healthcare professionals' experiences of required competencies in mentoring of interprofessional students in clinical practice: A systematic review of qualitative studies. Journal of Advanced Nursing, 81, 701–729. https://doi.org/10.1111/jan.16347
title: Three-part competency framework for interprofessional mentoring in clinical practice
description: The review's organizing framework comprises three synthesized findings: "competencies related to (1) preparing for and developing interprofessional clinical practice, (2) supporting the learning process in interprofessional clinical practice and (3) creating an interprofessional mentor identity." Each synthesized finding is built from categories of extracted qualitative findings via JBI meta-aggregation. The framework maps the competencies healthcare professionals need when mentoring interprofessional student teams in clinical placements.
requirements: Mentors of interprofessional student teams in healthcare organizations
constraints: All three synthesized findings received a low ConQual score, downgraded for dependability issues and a mix of unequivocal/credible findings
target_learners: undergraduate healthcare, social care and medical students

article_title: Unveiling the ultimate advantage: a meta-analysis of 3D visualization and problem-based learning in orthopedic education.
citation: Li Ting, Hu Yidan, Song Ruohong, Liu Hangyu, Gao Xin, Wang Fei, Xiao Chengwei, Liu Xilin. (2025). Unveiling the ultimate advantage: a meta-analysis of 3D visualization and problem-based learning in orthopedic education. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-06654-5
title: Integrate 3D + PBL into orthopedic training programs by selecting appropriate 3D content, designing PBL scenarios, and integrating these elements into the curriculum
description: The article recommends that, given the unique demands of orthopedic education, programs should integrate 3D + PBL into existing orthopedic training. It states: "In the future, there should be an integration of 3D + PBL into existing orthopedic training programs, which includes selecting appropriate 3D content, designing PBL scenarios, and integrating these elements into the curriculum." This provides a comprehensive framework for implementing 3D + PBL in orthopedic education.
requirements: Selecting appropriate 3D content
Designing PBL scenarios
Integrating these elements into the curriculum
constraints: Implementing 3D + PBL teaching methods necessitates significant investment in resources such as advanced educational technology, software, and specialized training
The 3D + PBL approach demands considerable time and effort
target_learners: Medical students including trainee and resident doctors
examples: The meta-analysis included 18 RCTs comparing 3D + PBL teaching versus LBL teaching in orthopedic education
key_sources: Li Ting, Hu Yidan, Song Ruohong, Liu Hangyu, Gao Xin, Wang Fei, Xiao Chengwei, Liu Xilin. (2025). Unveiling the ultimate advantage: a meta-analysis of 3D visualization and problem-based learning in orthopedic education. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-06654-5

article_title: Self-directed learning versus traditional didactic learning in undergraduate medical education: a systemic review and meta-analysis.
citation: Aulakh Jasmine, Wahab Hana, Richards Christine, Bidaisee Satesh, Ramdass Prakash V. A. K. (2025). Self-directed learning versus traditional didactic learning in undergraduate medical education: a systemic review and meta-analysis. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-06449-0
title: SDL should be incorporated into undergraduate medical curricula as an effective learning strategy
description: The authors recommend that self-directed learning be deliberately incorporated into undergraduate medical curricula, on the grounds that their meta-analysis found a significant pooled advantage in exam scores over traditional didactic learning. They state that "when used appropriately and strategically as a learning strategy, SDL can be beneficial to medical education and should be incorporated into the curriculum." Educators are encouraged to tailor curricular components and explore pedagogical approaches that support SDL.
requirements: Educators should provide technology-enhanced learning tools, mentorship or guidance, and a supportive learning environment that promotes autonomy and self-regulation, as stated by the authors.
constraints: The authors caution that SDL "may not be as beneficial as traditional in-classroom didactic lectures for selected cognitive competencies or knowledge acquisition for certain subject areas."
The practical SDL subgroup did not reach statistical significance, so the recommendation is best supported for theoretical SDL.
target_learning_goals: Cognitive performance and knowledge application in medical curricula
examples: The review's meta-analysis of 14 studies found SDL favoured over TDL in 11 studies, with a pooled mean difference of 2.399.
key_sources: Aulakh Jasmine, Wahab Hana, Richards Christine, Bidaisee Satesh, Ramdass Prakash V. A. K. (2025). Self-directed learning versus traditional didactic learning in undergraduate medical education: a systemic review and meta-analysis. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-06449-0

article_title: Healthcare research and education: actively constructed research knowledge-a model for online systematic reviews and meta-analyses courses.
citation: El Ansari Walid, El-Ansari Kareem, Hany Mohamed. (2025). Healthcare research and education: actively constructed research knowledge–a model for online systematic reviews and meta-analyses courses. BMC Research Notes. https://doi.org/10.1186/s13104-025-07111-8
title: Provide individualized expert feedback on assignments in online research training
description: The article recommends that online SR/MA courses provide individualized constructive feedback from expert trainers on assignments, as this enhances learning, improves teaching planning, and promotes trainees' autonomous learning abilities. The article states that evaluation and feedback are crucial from both teachers' and learners' perspectives, and that only the proposed course among those compared delivers this feature.
requirements: Expert trainers with both discipline-specific knowledge and SR/MA skills
Sufficient resources including planning and time
constraints: Providing individualized feedback necessitates expert trainers and further resources
examples: The proposed course delivers one-on-one individualized feedback from expert trainers after each assignment.

article_title: Evaluating the outcomes of problem-based learning in postgraduate medical education: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
citation: Mensour Emma A, Tran Carolyn, Li Toni, Mallawaarachchi Indika, Shaw Jennifer M, Blissett Sarah. (2025). Evaluating the outcomes of problem-based learning in postgraduate medical education: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Canadian Medical Education Journal. https://doi.org/10.36834/cmej.77394
title: PGME programs should consider incorporating PBL into curricula for its satisfaction and behavioural benefits at no detriment to knowledge acquisition
description: The review concludes that PBL strengthens attitudes and behaviours of residents "at no detriment to their acquisition of medical knowledge," and recommends that "PGME programs should consider incorporating PBL into curricula." The recommendation rests on the review's synthesis showing similar learning outcomes but improved satisfaction and self-reported behaviours with PBL.
requirements: PBL requires small-group facilitation, dedicated self-study time, and a reconvened discussion session with a facilitator
constraints: PBL instructional formats require more time and potentially more facilitators; scheduling within busy PGME contexts with variable attendance is a challenge
examples: The review synthesized 21 studies in which PBL was embedded in existing programs (n=13) or delivered as additional sessions (n=8), mostly in person (n=19)

article_title: Effectiveness of multiple teaching methods in standardized training of internal medicine residents in China: a network meta-analysis.
citation: Guan Cheng Ye, Chun Ping Liu, Wei Li, Hua Chao Zhu, Liu Lv, Zhen Hong Zhu, Yong Hong Wang, Jie Hu, Xiao Jia Zheng, Jing Ying Fang, Yu Cao Ma, Ming Xuan Liu, Yi Wen Wang, Ying Kai Gao, Zi Yu Zhang, Lu Ming Zhao, Cun Xiang Xie, Min Yee Lim, Hai Long Wang. (2025). Effectiveness of multiple teaching methods in standardized training of internal medicine residents in China: a network meta-analysis. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07020-1
title: Integrate social media platforms (WeChat) into problem-based learning for resident training
description: The article recommends combining PBL with WeChat, finding that "integrating social software into medical education was a very surprising decision" and that WeChat "has built a bridge for communication and discussion between students and teachers". Teachers share materials, provide real-time feedback, and students discuss and upload presentations in WeChat groups, leveraging the platform's immediacy and convenience.
requirements: Requires establishment of a WeChat group consisting of teachers and students where teachers regularly publish learning materials
constraints: The article notes this applies to Chinese residents described as young people with strong acceptance of new things, given WeChat is the most important social software for Chinese students
target_learners: resident physicians in standardized training in China
examples: The NMA found PBL + WeChat ranked first for theoretical scores (SUCRA 88%) and satisfaction (89%) among 13 methods

article_title: Facilitating clinical reasoning for medical students in clinical settings: a scoping review.
citation: Cahyaningrum Yeny Dyah, Suhoyo Yoyo, Rahayu Gandes Retno. (2025). Facilitating clinical reasoning for medical students in clinical settings: a scoping review. Korean Journal of Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.3946/kjme.2025.333
title: Integrate clinical teachers' facilitation role with developing technology for clinical reasoning learning
description: The review recommends that lecturers' role in facilitating clinical reasoning be integrated with currently developing technology. It states that "lecturers' role in facilitating clinical reasoning also needs to be integrated with the currently developing technology." This principle directs clinical educators to leverage technological tools (such as virtual patient simulations) while maintaining attention to the source of information, ensuring students acquire clinical reasoning skills through both human facilitation and technological support.
requirements: Clinical teachers who understand both facilitation principles and available technologies
constraints: The review notes the role of clinical teachers in facilitating virtual simulation learning may be vague
examples: The review cites virtual patient case simulation as a technique where computer-based simulations provide realistic clinical scenarios for practicing clinical reasoning

article_title: Simulation unlocked: transforming thyroid surgery training through high-fidelity and curriculum-based innovation-a systematic review.
citation: Zhang Daqi, Brucchi Francesco, Barbieri Diego, Kim Hoon Yub, Colombo Carla, Donatini Gianluca, Miccoli Paolo, Che-Wei Wu, Dionigi Gianlorenzo, Wan Lanlan (2026). Simulation unlocked: transforming thyroid surgery training through high-fidelity and curriculum-based innovation—a systematic review. Langenbeck's Archives of Surgery. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00423-026-04013-6
title: Integrate multimodal, competency-based education into surgical training
description: The review concludes that structured educational programs—including simulation, supervised learning, and IONM or fellowship curricula—enhance surgical performance and safety in thyroid surgery. It recommends that "findings support integrating multimodal, competency-based education into surgical training" and notes that "Standardized outcome measures and multicenter validation are needed to define optimal learning pathways." This principle directs curriculum designers toward combining multiple training modalities within a competency-based framework rather than relying on any single approach.
requirements: Structured educational programs combining multiple training modalities
Competency-based progression frameworks
constraints: Standardized outcome measures and multicenter validation are needed to define optimal learning pathways
target_learners: Surgical trainees and residents in thyroid surgery
examples: The review synthesized ten primary studies spanning simulation, supervised learning, video modules, IONM education, and fellowship curricula, all showing improvement in at least one performance or safety domain.
