article_title: Video Killed the Radio Star-A Meta-Analysis on Video-Based Coaching to Improve Surgical Skill.
citation: Anderson Steven Mark, Gillanders Sarahlouise, Hickey Anne, Offiah Gozie, Davis Niall. (2025). Video Killed the Radio Star—A Meta‐Analysis on Video‐Based Coaching to Improve Surgical Skill. World Journal of Surgery. https://doi.org/10.1002/wjs.12494
title: Formally integrate video-based coaching into conventional surgical training programs
description: The article concludes that because VBC is an effective and versatile supplement to the apprenticeship model, "Training bodies around the world should now look at how best to formally integrate VBC into conventional surgical training". The recommendation rests on the meta-analytic evidence that VBC outperformed several routinely used forms of feedback, and on its demonstrated effectiveness across session counts, settings and coaching frameworks.
requirements: Access to video footage of trainee performance and capacity to deliver individualized coach feedback sessions
constraints: The article states further research is needed to establish how best VBC can be incorporated into surgical training curricula going forward
examples: The review demonstrated VBC to be effective in both simulated and live surgeries, whether delivered as a single session or over multiple sessions and across a wide range of coaching frameworks

article_title: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis of the Use of High-Fidelity Simulation in Obstetric Ultrasound.
citation: Dromey Brian P. MBChB, MRCOG; Peebles Donald M. MBBS, MD, MRCOG; Stoyanov Danail V. PhD. (2021). A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis of the Use of High-Fidelity Simulation in Obstetric Ultrasound. Simulation in Healthcare. https://doi.org/10.1097/SIH.0000000000000485
title: Integrate simulation training into the clinical curriculum with objective, measurable outcomes rather than case-count logbooks
description: The review recommends that "consideration ought to be given to integrate simulation training into the clinical curriculum," because trainees report clinical commitments as barriers to voluntary engagement and because curricula based on numbers of cases completed do not measure competence. It argues training programs should be "based on objective outcomes, rather than trainer reports and arbitrary numbers of cases recorded in a log book," with audit and revision based on learner feedback.
requirements: Formal guidance and scheduled access so trainees can engage despite clinical workload
Objective, measurable outcome measures for competence assessment
constraints: Even in research settings trainees reported clinical commitments as barriers to engaging with simulation training
target_learners: sonographers and midwives learning obstetric ultrasound
examples: Monsky et al. mandated departmental-level simulator assessment before overnight call, then redesigned the residency program with 8 additional weeks of targeted transvaginal ultrasound training
key_sources: Dromey Brian P. MBChB, MRCOG; Peebles Donald M. MBBS, MD, MRCOG; Stoyanov Danail V. PhD. (2021). A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis of the Use of High-Fidelity Simulation in Obstetric Ultrasound. Simulation in Healthcare. https://doi.org/10.1097/SIH.0000000000000485

article_title: The relationship of non-cognitive factors to academic and clinical performance in graduate rehabilitation science students in the United States: a systematic review.
citation: Reynolds K, Bazemore C, Hanebuth C, Hendren S, Horn M. (2021). The relationship of non-cognitive factors to academic and clinical performance in graduate rehabilitation science students in the United States: a systematic review. Journal of Educational Evaluation for Health Professions. https://doi.org/10.3352/jeehp.2021.18.31
title: Do not use single non-cognitive factors in admissions decisions for rehabilitation science programs
description: The review concludes that no single non-cognitive factor was consistently related to clinical or academic performance across the 21 included studies, so evaluating a specific factor for admissions is not currently supported. It states there is "insufficient evidence currently to recommend the evaluation of a specific non-cognitive factor for admissions decisions." Educators should treat grit, self-efficacy, and stress as promising but unproven indicators.
requirements: More research, including multivariate models and studies spanning both academic and clinical settings, before non-cognitive factors inform major decisions
constraints: All included studies were level 3 observational designs with low certainty, small samples, and few factors studied more than 4 times
target_learners: graduate rehabilitation science students (PT, OT, SLP)
target_learning_goals: admissions selection decisions and identification of students needing additional academic or clinical support
examples: The review synthesized 21 observational studies and found mixed results for all non-cognitive factors examined.
key_sources: Reynolds K, Bazemore C, Hanebuth C, Hendren S, Horn M. (2021). The relationship of non-cognitive factors to academic and clinical performance in graduate rehabilitation science students in the United States: a systematic review. Journal of Educational Evaluation for Health Professions. https://doi.org/10.3352/jeehp.2021.18.31

article_title: Advances in e-learning in undergraduate clinical medicine: a systematic review.
citation: Delungahawatta T., Dunne S. S., Hyde S., Halpenny L., McGrath D., O'Regan A., Dunne C. P. (2022). Advances in e-learning in undergraduate clinical medicine: a systematic review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-022-03773-1
title: Effective e-learning interventions combine interactivity, built-in assessment, asynchronous access and multimedia
description: The review identifies a recurring design pattern in effective undergraduate clinical medicine e-learning: interactive software, active-learning promotion such as built-in quizzes following cases, asynchronous use, multimedia platforms (slideshows, videos, images), ease of use and adaptability. Nineteen interventions had a built-in assessment, mostly multiple-choice questions, to evaluate whether learning improvement had taken place.
requirements: Quality assurance should be considered at the planning stage and built into e-learning interventions
constraints: Justification for the chosen assessment strategy was included in only two of the reviewed studies
target_learners: undergraduate medical students in clinical medicine
target_learning_goals: knowledge acquisition, skills development, and exam preparation in clinical disciplines
examples: Reviewed interventions enabled just-in-time learning through timely access to facts, revision aid use, and flipped-classroom designs where post-e-lecture sessions become interactive
key_sources: Delungahawatta T., Dunne S. S., Hyde S., Halpenny L., McGrath D., O'Regan A., Dunne C. P. (2022). Advances in e-learning in undergraduate clinical medicine: a systematic review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-022-03773-1

article_title: The effects of obstetric emergency team training on patient outcome: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
citation: Brogaard L, Glerup Lauridsen K, Løfgren B, et al. (2022). The effects of obstetric emergency team training on patient outcome: A systematic review and meta‐analysis. Acta Obstet Gynecol Scand. https://doi.org/10.1111/aogs.14263
title: Train entire labor and delivery units locally with in situ multiprofessional simulation-based team training
description: The review concludes that simulation-based team training works best when delivered locally in the actual care environment with all professional groups participating together. The authors state that "Studies with in situ multiprofessional simulation‐based training demonstrated the best effect" and that "local (in situ) multiprofessional training for all staff members is the most beneficial with regards to improving patient outcomes." Most included studies trained staff annually in one-day programs in the Labor and Delivery Unit.
requirements: Training should include all staff members of the Labor and Delivery Unit rather than a partial subset
constraints: None of the two RCTs demonstrated the same effect as cohort studies; only about 50% of studies used pre-defined guidelines or a previously described program; analysis of optimal training frequency was not possible because no studies used interventions more frequently than yearly
target_learners: Multiprofessional obstetric emergency teams in Labor and Delivery Units in high-resource settings
target_learning_goals: Managing obstetric emergencies such as shoulder dystocia, postpartum hemorrhage, umbilical cord prolapse, and emergency cesarean section
examples: The majority of included studies trained delivery ward staff in situ annually with one-day programs, e.g. PROMPT training in England and Australia; only a few trained in simulation centers
key_sources: Brogaard L, Glerup Lauridsen K, Løfgren B, et al. (2022). The effects of obstetric emergency team training on patient outcome: A systematic review and meta‐analysis. Acta Obstet Gynecol Scand. https://doi.org/10.1111/aogs.14263

article_title: The informal curriculum of family medicine - what does it entail and how is it taught to residents? A systematic review.
citation: Rothlind Erica, Fors Uno, Salminen Helena, Wändell Per, Ekblad Solvig. (2020). The informal curriculum of family medicine – what does it entail and how is it taught to residents? A systematic review. BMC Family Practice. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12875-020-01120-1
title: The informal curriculum in Family Medicine comprises three partly interrelated themes: cultural competence, medical professionalism, and dealing with uncertainty
description: A taxonomy developed by the review through narrative synthesis of nine studies addressing what Family Medicine residents learn outside the formal curriculum. The review states that 'Through the process of narrative synthesis three overall, and partly intersecting, elements constituting the informal curriculum of FM were developed: gaining cultural competence, achieving medical professionalism and dealing with uncertainty.' The themes are treated as partly intersecting rather than distinct, and the review treats informal and hidden curriculum terms as interchangeable for its purpose.
requirements: Articles discussing any aspect of the informal curriculum in relation to Family Medicine, identified through iterative literature searches
constraints: The element dealing with uncertainty was derived from only two included articles, which the review acknowledges limits depth
target_learners: postgraduate medical trainees in workplace-based training
examples: The review included 9 studies for question 1 and 11 interventional studies for question 2, published between 2000 and 2019
key_sources: Rothlind Erica, Fors Uno, Salminen Helena, Wändell Per, Ekblad Solvig. (2020). The informal curriculum of family medicine – what does it entail and how is it taught to residents? A systematic review. BMC Family Practice. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12875-020-01120-1

article_title: Exploring gender differences in the Force Concept Inventory using a random effects meta-analysis of international studies
citation: Purwoko Haryadi Santoso, Bayu Setiaji, Wahyudi, Johan Syahbrudin, Syamsul Bahri, Fathurrahman, A. Suci Rizky Ananda, Yusuf Sodhiqin. (2024). Exploring gender differences in the Force Concept Inventory using a random effects meta-analysis of international studies. https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.16988
title: Interpret FCI scores with awareness of the magnitude and direction of gender performance gaps
description: The article recommends that researchers and educators interpret FCI scores while considering the gendered performance gaps the meta-analysis documented. It states that "When interpreting the FCI scores, they should consider the magnitude and direction of the discovered performance gaps", and that studying moderating variables such as students' background preparation can inform learning design to close the gaps. This principle applies the meta-analytic finding of a moderate male-favoring gap to assessment interpretation practice.
requirements: Educators and researchers must know the magnitude and direction of gender gaps documented for the assessment context they use
constraints: The meta-analysis analyzed only pre-instruction FCI data, so findings may be generalized with caution across testing conditions
target_learning_goals: accurate interpretation of Force Concept Inventory results for teaching and learning
examples: The meta-analysis of 38 studies found a moderate significant gap (g = 0.61) favoring male students, wider in NA-based studies
key_sources: Purwoko Haryadi Santoso, Bayu Setiaji, Wahyudi, Johan Syahbrudin, Syamsul Bahri, Fathurrahman, A. Suci Rizky Ananda, Yusuf Sodhiqin. (2024). Exploring gender differences in the Force Concept Inventory using a random effects meta-analysis of international studies. https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.07190

article_title: A Meta-analysis of College Students' Intention to Use Generative Artificial Intelligence
citation: Yifei Diao, Ziyi Li, Jiateng Zhou, Wei Gao and Xin Gong. (2024). A Meta-analysis of College Students' Intention to Use Generative Artificial Intelligence. Preprint submitted to Elsevier. https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.06712
title: Integrated theoretical framework combining TPB, TAM, UTAUT2 and EVT variables for GenAI intention
description: The article builds a comprehensive theoretical framework by integrating core variables from classic technology-acceptance theories: TPB (attitudes, subjective norms, perceived behavioural control), TAM (perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use), UTAUT2 (performance expectancy, effort expectancy, social influence, facilitating conditions, hedonic motivation, price value, habit) and EVT (utility value, intrinsic value, costs). Variables with similar conceptions were merged — for example, "we utilised perceived cost that combines discussions on price value from UTAUT2 and costs from EVT" — and performance expectancy interiorises perceived usefulness and utility value. Nine antecedent variables were defined and meta-analysed against students' behavioural intention to use GenAI.
requirements: Variables with similar conceptions must be merged and those without sufficient empirical evidence eliminated to ensure accuracy and representativeness of meta-analytic results
constraints: Small sample sizes for some variables required merging; variables with effect sizes below 3 were deleted
target_learning_goals: understanding and predicting students' behavioural intention to use generative AI in learning
examples: The framework merged perceived cost (price value from UTAUT2 plus costs from EVT) and performance expectancy (interiorising perceived usefulness from TAM and utility value from EVT) into nine coded antecedent variables
key_sources: Yifei Diao, Ziyi Li, Jiateng Zhou, Wei Gao and Xin Gong. (2024). A Meta-analysis of College Students' Intention to Use Generative Artificial Intelligence. Preprint submitted to Elsevier. https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.06712

article_title: Tools used to assess medical students competence in procedural skills at the end of a primary medical degree: a systematic review.
citation: Morris Marie C., Gallagher Tom K., Ridgway Paul F. (2012). Tools used to assess medical students competence in procedural skills at the end of a primary medical degree: a systematic review. Medical Education Online. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3427596/
title: Establish an international expert consensus on minimum procedural competence required for certification
description: The review calls for an international consensus statement by expert academic clinicians defining the minimum level of competence required in procedural skills at the end point of medical training. It states "Fundamentally an international consensus statement by expert academic clinicians is required depicting the minimum level of competence required in procedural skills at the end point of medical training". Achieving below this expert-agreed level would be a barrier to certification in the interest of public safety.
requirements: Expert academic clinicians must agree the minimum competence level
constraints: The degree of competence could be further honed and improved during residency
target_learners: graduating medical students entering the clinical workforce
target_learning_goals: minimum safe procedural skills competence at certification
examples: The review argues this would ensure the mobile workforce has transferable skill sets irrespective of country of training, making graduates truly fit for practice
key_sources: Morris Marie C., Gallagher Tom K., Ridgway Paul F. (2012). Tools used to assess medical students competence in procedural skills at the end of a primary medical degree: a systematic review. Medical Education Online. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3427596/

article_title: Educational technologies in problem-based learning in health sciences education: a systematic review.
citation: Jun J, Bridges SM. (2014). Educational Technologies in Problem-Based Learning in Health Sciences Education: A Systematic Review. Journal of Medical Internet Research. https://doi.org/10.2196/jmir.3240
title: Interactive whiteboards and plasma screens as PBL interventions
description: Interactive whiteboards (IWBs) and plasma screens were examined in 5 of the 28 reviewed studies, all arising in the 7 years before the review plus one 2005 plasma screen study. IWBs were used to support whole-group engagement in PBL tutorials, enable data sharing and construction of shared understandings about patients, and expand the scaffolding choices available to instructors. The review reports that the integration of face-to-face and virtual modalities through a single PBL group's use of an IWB was seamless and supported whole-group engagement.
requirements: IT support must be provided for all students and facilitators when IWBs are installed in PBL tutorial rooms
constraints: There are limited studies to show the relative advantages or disadvantages of using IWBs in health sciences education
target_learners: undergraduate medical and dental students in PBL tutorials
examples: The review reports that IWBs were installed in all PBL tutorial rooms in a 5-year undergraduate dental PBL curriculum
key_sources: Jun J, Bridges SM. (2014). Educational Technologies in Problem-Based Learning in Health Sciences Education: A Systematic Review. Journal of Medical Internet Research. https://doi.org/10.2196/jmir.3240

article_title: The impact of feedback of intraoperative technical performance in surgery: a systematic review.
citation: Trehan Abhishek, Barnett-Vanes Ashton, Carty Matthew J, McCulloch Peter, Maruthappu Mahiben. (2015). The impact of feedback of intraoperative technical performance in surgery: a systematic review. BMJ Open. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4480038/
title: Intraoperative performance feedback as a means to improve efficiency of surgical training
description: The review defines feedback as "the provision of information pertaining to the operator's surgical performance with the aim of improving subsequent performance". It frames feedback on intraoperative technical performance as a response to declining operating-theatre time for trainees, positioning it as a key component of future surgical training programmes. Across the three included RCTs, feedback was delivered orally after each procedure, with contents covering outcomes, and in one study benchmarking relative to peers.
requirements: Feedback must pertain to the operator's surgical performance with the aim of improving subsequent performance
Delivery after each procedure as in all included studies
constraints: Optimum means and circumstances of feedback delivery are not yet established
May not be effective in some circumstances or when delivered inappropriately
examples: All three included studies delivered oral feedback after each procedure; one used video footage review with a 60 min structured feedback session
key_sources: Trehan Abhishek, Barnett-Vanes Ashton, Carty Matthew J, McCulloch Peter, Maruthappu Mahiben. (2015). The impact of feedback of intraoperative technical performance in surgery: a systematic review. BMJ Open. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4480038/

article_title: Do Interim Assessments Influence Instructional Practice in Year One? Evidence from Indiana Elementary School Teachers
citation: Chojnacki, G., Eno, J., Liu, F., Meyers, C., Konstantopoulos, S., Miller, S., & van der Ploeg, A. (2013). Do Interim Assessments Influence Instructional Practice in Year One? Evidence from Indiana Elementary School Teachers. SREE Fall 2013 Conference Abstract. https://www.sree.org
title: Theory of action: interim assessment effectiveness hinges on teachers changing instructional practice, particularly differentiation of scope and sequence, instructional level, and grouping
description: The article's framework holds that interim assessments improve achievement only through intermediate changes in teacher practice. It states that "The theory of action supporting interim assessments' effectiveness hinges on teachers making changes to their instructional practice," citing Blanc et al. (2010). Drawing on Tomlinson (2000), it identifies "differentiation of content scope and sequence, instructional level and grouping methods" as practices theorized to improve instruction by drawing on improved information about student needs. The study measures these three facets as intermediate outcomes.
requirements: Teachers must use assessment information to make instructional decisions for each student, since the theory of differentiated instruction implies distinct instructional decisions per student
constraints: Impacts on teacher practice may take multiple years to emerge as teachers learn to use the assessment tool, per the article's first-year caveat
target_learners: K-8 students in volunteering Indiana public schools
target_learning_goals: Improved mathematics and ELA achievement through data-informed differentiated instruction
examples: The study operationalized the theory as three facets of practice—scope and sequence of content coverage, instructional level, and instructional grouping—measured with binary variables from 16 teacher checklists per year
key_sources: Chojnacki, G., Eno, J., Liu, F., Meyers, C., Konstantopoulos, S., Miller, S., & van der Ploeg, A. (2013). Do Interim Assessments Influence Instructional Practice in Year One? Evidence from Indiana Elementary School Teachers. SREE Fall 2013 Conference Abstract. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED563059

article_title: A Randomized Controlled Trial of Interleaved Mathematics Practice
citation: Doug Rohrer, Robert F. Dedrick, Marissa K. Hartwig, Chi-Ngai Cheung. (2019). A Randomized Controlled Trial of Interleaved Mathematics Practice. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://osf.io/pfeg4/
title: Interleaved practice works by forcing strategy choice, and inherently guarantees spaced practice and retrieval opportunities
description: The article explains interleaving's benefit through three combined mechanisms. First, a mixture of problem kinds means "interleaved practice requires students to choose a strategy and not merely execute a strategy," mirroring cumulative exams. Second, rearranging problems so no two consecutive problems share a strategy distributes each skill's practice: "interleaved practice guarantees spaced practice." Third, with interleaving the needed formula is not readily available, so "the retrieval opportunity is an artifact of interleaved practice." The authors call spacing and retrieval practice the only strategies receiving the highest rating in a commissioned evaluation of 10 learning strategies.
requirements: Students must receive corrective feedback after attempting problems, which the article suggests may be a necessary ingredient
constraints: The benefit may be smaller at shorter test delays
Students likely need at least some initial blocked practice when encountering a new skill or concept
Interleaved assignments probably take students more time per problem
target_learners: mathematics learners across disciplines encountering superficially similar problems requiring different strategies
target_learning_goals: choosing an appropriate strategy on the basis of the problem itself
delayed retention of mathematics problem-solving skills
examples: Worksheets arranged critical graph, inequality, expression, and circle problems so each kind immediately preceded each other kind equally often for the interleaved group
key_sources: Doug Rohrer, Robert F. Dedrick, Marissa K. Hartwig, Chi-Ngai Cheung. (2019). A Randomized Controlled Trial of Interleaved Mathematics Practice. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://osf.io/pfeg4/

article_title: Think Pair Share: A Teaching Learning Strategy to Enhance Students' Critical Thinking
citation: Mahmoud Kaddoura. (2013). Think Pair Share: A teaching Learning Strategy to Enhance Students' Critical Thinking. Educational Research Quarterly, Vol. 36.4. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Think+Pair+Share+Kaddoura+critical+thinking
title: Educators should incorporate active cooperative strategies such as TPS to foster learners' critical thinking
description: Based on its findings, the article recommends that educators develop curricula incorporating active teaching strategies such as Think-Pair-Share to enhance learners' critical thinking, since the TPS group's CT scores improved significantly more than the Non-TPS group's. The author states that "Educators should continue to develop curricula that incorporate active teaching strategies such as TPS in order to enhance learners' CT."
requirements: Instructors need teaching strategies that give students opportunity to foster CT skills
Individual accountability structures such as having students jot down ideas before pairing
constraints: Evidence base is one quasi-experimental study with a small sample in a single nursing program, which the author states may not generalize to all nursing programs
examples: The study assigned two homogeneous sections of the same course to TPS versus Non-TPS teaching by the same instructor and compared HESI CT gains
key_sources: Mahmoud Kaddoura. (2013). Think Pair Share: A teaching Learning Strategy to Enhance Students' Critical Thinking. Educational Research Quarterly, Vol. 36.4. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1061947

article_title: Efficacy of Multimedia Package in Communicative Skill in English
citation: G. Singaravelu. (2014). Efficacy of Multimedia Package in Communicative Skill in English. i-manager's Journal on English Language Teaching, Vol. 4 No. 4, October - December. https://journals.imanager.com
title: Interactive Multimedia Package for learning communicative skill in English
description: A computer-based interactive multimedia package prepared by the investigator to develop communicative skill in English at upper primary level. It presents content so learners can "learn the content in their own" pace, and it "creates the interest of the learners like video games." Students were first taught to operate the package, then used it independently with on-the-spot problem support, self-monitoring and self-evaluation.
requirements: Students must first be taught the operating system of the package before independent use
An achievement test aligned to a blueprint is needed to assess communicative skill outcomes
constraints: The study administered it only to standard VII students in one school and only for communicative skill
target_learners: standard VII (upper primary) students learning English communicative skills
target_learning_goals: oral and written communicative skill in English
examples: In the study, 38 standard VII students used the package after teacher demonstration, with self-monitoring as the liberated strategy and learner self-evaluation.
key_sources: G. Singaravelu. (2014). Efficacy of Multimedia Package in Communicative Skill in English. i-manager's Journal on English Language Teaching, Vol. 4 No. 4, October - December. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1068384

article_title: Interactive Multimedia Package in Ameliorating Communicative Skill in English
citation: G. Singaravelu. (2011). Interactive Multimedia Package in Ameliorating Communicative Skill in English. i-manager's Journal of English Language Teaching, 1(4), October-December. https://www.imanagerpublications.com
title: Interactive Multimedia Package for standard VI English communicative skill
description: A researcher-prepared computer-based learning package for developing oral and written communicative skill in English at standard VI. It presents "a series of presentation, text about a particular topic and associated illustrations in various information formats", and is designed so learners "practice in their own pace", with self-monitoring and self-evaluation as the liberated strategies. The article reports it creates learner interest "like video games" and was used by the experimental group in the quasi-experiment.
requirements: A teacher first taught the operating system of the package and problems of learners using it were explained at the spot
constraints: The study was administered only for the students of standard VI from Govt Higher Secondary school, Kalveeranpalayam
target_learners: standard VI (upper primary) students in Indian government higher secondary school
examples: Students were given the package to learn the content on their own, with self-monitoring and self-evaluation done by the learners themselves

article_title: Modeling Behavior of Students in E-Learning Courses on the Basis of Use Interactive Animations
citation: Magdin, M., & Turčáni, M. (2016). Modeling the Behavior of Students in E-Learning Courses on the Basis of Use Interactive Animations. TOJET: The Turkish Online Journal of Educational Technology, 15(1). https://tojet.net/
title: Interactive matrix method for modeling student transitions through an e-learning course
description: The interactive matrix is a two-dimensional n x n array whose cells hold the frequency with which activity j follows activity i, built from filtered e-learning access logs using frequency and sequential analysis. The article uses it to model "the real transition through the e-learning course" and to identify behavior patterns, represented by sequence rules, that can guide course modification and improvement.
requirements: Filtering out access-statistics data not connected with knowledge acquisition, such as initial course page view, communication within the course, and profile scanning
constraints: The authors describe the method as an indirect one for determining course effectiveness
target_learners: university students in an e-learning course on computer hardware
target_learning_goals: understanding logical systems of computers, static electricity and electronic circuits
examples: Transition matrices for lessons L1-L9 were constructed for control and experimental groups for each academic year from 2009/2010 to 2013/2014
key_sources: Magdin, M., & Turčáni, M. (2016). Modeling the Behavior of Students in E-Learning Courses on the Basis of Use Interactive Animations. TOJET: The Turkish Online Journal of Educational Technology, 15(1). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1086224

article_title: Assessing Input Enhancement as Positive Factor and Its Impact on L2 Vocabulary Learning
citation: Motlagh, S. F. P., & Nasab, M. S. B. (2015). Assessing Input Enhancement as Positive Factor and Its Impact on L2 Vocabulary Learning. Advances in Language and Literary Studies, 6(1). https://doi.org/10.7575/aiac.alls.v.6n.1p.227
title: Input enhancement as an implicit focus-on-form technique grounded in the noticing hypothesis
description: Input enhancement is a set of techniques for making target linguistic forms visually salient in otherwise meaning-oriented input, so that learners notice them and the forms become intake. The article defines it as "an implicit means of promoting students' noticing", noting it may take the form of input flooding or of modifying text features such as bolding target structures. It rests on Schmidt's noticing hypothesis, that what learners notice in input becomes intake for learning, and on Sharwood Smith's account that enhancing perceptual saliency directs learners' focal attention to targeted forms.
requirements: Learners must actually register and notice the enhanced forms; the article notes externally-created salience does not guarantee internally generated salience
constraints: Whether enhanced input triggers the relevant mental representation is, in Sharwood Smith's words quoted in the article, an empirical question; learners may notice enhanced input fully, partially, or not at all depending on readiness
target_learning_goals: noticing of target linguistic forms in meaning-oriented input
examples: In the study, eight target words each appeared six times in a text, with target words written in bold and underlined for the experimental groups
key_sources: Motlagh, S. F. P., & Nasab, M. S. B. (2015). Assessing Input Enhancement as Positive Factor and Its Impact on L2 Vocabulary Learning. Advances in Language and Literary Studies, 6(1). https://doi.org/10.7575/aiac.alls.v.6n.1p.227

article_title: The Effects of Planned Focus on Form on Iranian EFL Learners' Oral Accuracy
citation: Farahman Farrokhi, Mohammad Hassan Chehrazad. (2012). The Effects of Planned Focus on Form on Iranian EFL Learners' Oral Accuracy. World Journal of Education. https://doi.org/10.5430/wje.v2n1p70
title: Theoretical rationales for focus on form: Interaction, Output, and Noticing hypotheses
description: The article grounds planned focus on form in three SLA hypotheses. Long's Interaction Hypothesis posits that negotiation, feedback, and pushed reformulation facilitate acquisition, including through negative evidence. Swain's Output Hypothesis holds that pushed output pushes learners from semantic to syntactic processing, but output "needs to be supplemented by consistent corrective feedback". Schmidt's Noticing Hypothesis holds that noticing is a conscious process and a necessary condition for second language learning.
requirements: Corrective feedback must be noticed and recognized by learners as corrective for it to facilitate learning
constraints: The article notes that if students receive insufficient or no feedback, output may not serve its hypothesized roles
target_learners: second language learners in classroom settings
target_learning_goals: second language grammatical development through interaction and feedback
examples: The study's recasts and delayed explicit and metalinguistic feedback were designed to draw learners' attention to erroneous simple past tense forms during meaning-focused story retelling
key_sources: Farahman Farrokhi, Mohammad Hassan Chehrazad. (2012). The Effects of Planned Focus on Form on Iranian EFL Learners' Oral Accuracy. World Journal of Education. https://doi.org/10.5430/wje.v2n1p70

article_title: The Effect of Inquiry-Based Learning Method on Students' Academic Achievement in Science Course
citation: Ali Abdi. (2014). The Effect of Inquiry-based Learning Method on Students’ Academic Achievement in Science Course. Universal Journal of Educational Research 2(1): 37-41. https://doi.org/10.13189/ujer.2014.020104
title: Inquiry-based teaching approach in science education
description: The article describes inquiry-based science education as an approach in which "children become engaged in many of the activities and thinking processes that scientists use to produce new knowledge", contrasting with teacher-centered traditional instruction dominated by lectures and textbooks. It rests on research about the learning process and, citing Sandoval & Reiser, requires constructing a classroom community of practice like scientists' work, with students experiencing the process of knowing and the justification of knowledge. Inquiry has forms of varying openness, from structured inquiry to open inquiry.
requirements: Classroom environments in which students are active rather than passive recipients of transmitted information
constraints: The article distinguishes structured inquiry, where the teacher provides problem, procedures and materials, from open inquiry where students formulate their own problems
target_learning_goals: problem solving with logic and evidence
examples: The experimental group's lessons engaged students in observing scientific processes, recording data, isolating variables, designing experiments, creating graphs, interpreting results and developing hypotheses
key_sources: Ali Abdi. (2014). The Effect of Inquiry-based Learning Method on Students’ Academic Achievement in Science Course. Universal Journal of Educational Research 2(1): 37-41. https://doi.org/10.13189/ujer.2014.020104

article_title: The Effect of Inquiry-Based Learning Method on Students' Academic Achievement in Science Course
citation: Ali Abdi. (2014). The Effect of Inquiry-based Learning Method on Students’ Academic Achievement in Science Course. Universal Journal of Educational Research 2(1): 37-41. https://doi.org/10.13189/ujer.2014.020104
title: Inquiry-oriented science instruction design characteristics
description: The article enumerates five characteristics that science educators encourage teachers to use in replacing traditional teacher-centered practices with inquiry-oriented approaches: approaches that "(a) engage student interest in science, (b) provide opportunities for students to use appropriate laboratory techniques to collect evidence, (c) require students to solve problems using logic and evidence, (d) encourage students to conduct further study to develop more elaborate explanations, and (e) emphasize the importance of writing scientific explanations on the basis of evidence". These characteristics define what inquiry lessons should include at lesson level.
requirements: Lessons must move beyond textbooks, lectures and scientific facts toward evidence-based student activity
constraints: The list is attributed to Secker (2002) as reported in the article's background literature
examples: The experimental group's exploration phase had students collect and record data, isolate variables, and design and plan experiments
key_sources: Ali Abdi. (2014). The Effect of Inquiry-based Learning Method on Students’ Academic Achievement in Science Course. Universal Journal of Educational Research 2(1): 37-41. https://doi.org/10.13189/ujer.2014.020104

article_title: Pictures Speak Louder than Words in ESP, Too!
citation: Seyyed Mahdi Erfani. (2012). Pictures Speak Louder than Words in ESP, Too! English Language Teaching, 5(8). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v5n8p164
title: Integrate educationally valid pictures purposefully into ESP reading textbooks
description: The article recommends furnishing ESP textbooks with pictorial context as an alternative to current locally-produced textbooks that lack visual features. Pictures "should make a sense of relevance in the eyes of learners and are integrated purposefully into the text", drawing on the study's finding that pictorial context improved reading comprehension. The author presents this as an innovative alternative for existing ESP materials.
requirements: Pictures must be educationally valid and integrated purposefully into the text
constraints: Recommendation grounded in a single quasi-experimental study with physics majors in Iran
target_learners: Iranian university students majoring physics studying ESP
examples: In the study, the experimental group studied ESP passages furnished with different kinds of pictures while the control group studied the same passages without pictorial context over twenty-two two-hour sessions.
key_sources: Seyyed Mahdi Erfani. (2012). Pictures Speak Louder than Words in ESP, Too! English Language Teaching, 5(8). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v5n8p164

article_title: How a Serious Digital Game Affected Students' Animal Science and Mathematical Competence in Agricultural Education
citation: Bunch, J. C., Robinson, J. S., Edwards, M. C., & Antonenko, P. D. (2014). How a Serious Digital Game Affected Students' Animal Science and Mathematical Competence in Agricultural Education. Journal of Agricultural Education, 55(3), 57-71. https://doi.org/10.5032/jae.2014.03057
title: Teachers can incorporate serious digital games into existing pedagogical practices without fear of decreasing student achievement
description: Because the serious digital game did not diminish student achievement in animal science or mathematics relative to lecture and discussion, the article recommends that "teachers incorporate this teaching method into their existing pedagogical practices without the fear of decreasing student achievement". The principle is framed as permission to adopt DGBL as one of numerous teaching methods, not as a replacement for good teaching.
requirements: Teachers should still employ a variety of instructional strategies rather than relying on only one method
constraints: The finding derives from a 10-day study with a volunteer, conveniently sampled teacher pool, so readers are cautioned against generalizing the results
examples: The quasi-experimental comparison of the game against lecture and discussion over 10 instructional days showed no statistically significant differences on either examination
key_sources: Bunch, J. C., Robinson, J. S., Edwards, M. C., & Antonenko, P. D. (2014). How a Serious Digital Game Affected Students' Animal Science and Mathematical Competence in Agricultural Education. Journal of Agricultural Education, 55(3), 57-71. https://doi.org/10.5032/jae.2014.03057

article_title: The Impact of Quantum Teaching Strategy on Student Academic Achievements and Self-Esteem in Inclusive Schools
citation: Gunarhadi, Mustapa Kassim & Abdull Sukor Shaari. (2014). THE IMPACT OF QUANTUM TEACHING STRATEGY ON STUDENT ACADEMIC ACHIEVEMENTS AND SELF-ESTEEM IN INCLUSIVE SCHOOLS. Malaysian Journal of Learning and Instruction: Vol. 11 (2014): 191-205. http://mjli.uum.edu.my/
title: Use innovative, experiential teaching strategies instead of lecture-based conventional teaching in inclusive classrooms
description: The article argues that conventional teaching—characterized by fixed seating, textbook approach, and teacher dominance—does not develop the experiential, contextual, and collaborative learning expected in constructivist teaching, and leaves children with special needs struggling and psychologically depressed. It recommends introducing innovative strategies such as Quantum Teaching, which develops students' potential through social interaction with the environment, so that learning materials are internalized meaningfully and academic achievement improves.
requirements: A well-arranged learning environment supporting exploration, elaboration, and confirmation
Teachers who orchestrate atmosphere, foundation, environment, and lesson design
constraints: Evidence comes from one quasi-experiment in two Indonesian inclusive elementary schools with 68 sixth graders; the article notes internal threats such as sample selection bias were taken for granted
target_learners: students in inclusive elementary classrooms, including children with special needs and underachievers
target_learning_goals: academic achievement in tested subjects such as Bahasa Indonesia and Science
examples: The experimental treatment replaced lecture method with Quantum Teaching cycles using drama for Bahasa Indonesia and natural environment themes for Science, yielding significant post-test gains over the control group
key_sources: Gunarhadi, Mustapa Kassim & Abdull Sukor Shaari. (2014). THE IMPACT OF QUANTUM TEACHING STRATEGY ON STUDENT ACADEMIC ACHIEVEMENTS AND SELF-ESTEEM IN INCLUSIVE SCHOOLS. Malaysian Journal of Learning and Instruction: Vol. 11 (2014): 191-205. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1137291

article_title: Using the Vocabulary Self-Collection Strategy plus to Develop University EFL Students' Vocabulary Learning
citation: Manal Mohamed Khodary. (2017). Using the Vocabulary Self-Collection Strategy Plus to Develop University EFL Students' Vocabulary Learning. English Language Teaching, 10(8). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v10n8p135
title: Integrate technological tools into vocabulary self-collection so students collaborate to study selected words deeply
description: The article recommends that vocabulary instruction blend the self-collection strategy with technological tools so learners select words that matter to them, collaborate in teams, and use tools to explore meanings, synonyms and definitions. It argues this combination develops vocabulary and motivation, concluding that "the VSSPlus is needed to be implemented by university EFL instructors who teach Vocabulary Building course". The recommendation rests on the study's significant post-test advantage for the VSSPlus group.
requirements: Instructor and student training on the VSSPlus procedures
Availability of technological tools and labs
constraints: Evidence comes from one quasi-experiment with female university EFL students at a single institution; the author calls for replication with larger samples
examples: The experimental group worked in teams of 4, presented words via PPT, and attached audio narrations and podbeans to a class wiki
key_sources: Manal Mohamed Khodary. (2017). Using the Vocabulary Self-Collection Strategy Plus to Develop University EFL Students' Vocabulary Learning. English Language Teaching, 10(8). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v10n8p135

article_title: Formative Assessment as a Tool to Enhance the Development of Inquiry Skills in Science Education
citation: Mária Ganajová, Ivana Sotáková, Stanislav Lukáč, Zuzana Ješková, Veronika Jurková, Renáta Orosová. (2021). Formative Assessment as a Tool to Enhance the Development of Inquiry Skills in Science Education. Journal of Baltic Science Education, Vol. 20, No. 2. https://doi.org/10.33225/jbse/21.20.204
title: 16-item paper-and-pencil test of inquiry skills (Cα=.63)
description: The research instrument is a test of inquiry skills updated from Ješková et al. (2016) and developed from existing tests such as ScInqLiT, TISP, TOSLS and TGSA. As the article states, "The test consisted of 16 items, it was administered in the paper-and-pencil form, and took 45 minutes." Items cover formulating hypotheses, designing experiments, transforming data into tables and graphs, determining relationships between variables, and identifying sources of errors, with at least two items per skill and a maximum of 14 points.
requirements: Requires basic primary-school subject knowledge, but students must apply knowledge and skills in new situations
constraints: Reliability is modest: Cronbach Alpha Cα=.63, which the authors note is acceptable for tests with fewer items
target_learning_goals: transforming data into tables and graphs
examples: Used as pre-test and post-test in the experimental (n=73) and control (n=48) groups; most items were multiple-choice scored 0/1, with four variable-identification items scored up to .5 point
key_sources: Mária Ganajová, Ivana Sotáková, Stanislav Lukáč, Zuzana Ješková, Veronika Jurková, Renáta Orosová. (2021). Formative Assessment as a Tool to Enhance the Development of Inquiry Skills in Science Education. Journal of Baltic Science Education, Vol. 20, No. 2. https://doi.org/10.33225/jbse/21.20.204

article_title: Empirically Examining the Performance of Approaches to Multi-Level Matching to Study the Effect of School-Level Interventions
citation: Hallberg, K., Cook, T. D., & Figlio, D. (2013). Empirically Examining the Performance of Approaches to Multi-Level Matching to Study the Effect of School-Level Interventions. SREE Fall 2013 Conference. https://www.sree.org/conferences/2013f/
title: Applied researchers should match on school-level covariates, not student covariates alone, when estimating school-level intervention effects
description: When selecting non-experimental comparison groups for school-level interventions, researchers should incorporate school-level attributes alongside student characteristics. The paper's two within-study comparisons showed that ignoring school context can bias estimates, and the authors explicitly advise: "go beyond matching only on student level covariates in practice." School-level covariates are readily available from public sources, making this easy to implement.
requirements: School-level covariates must be available for both treatment and comparison units, e.g. from state departments of education or the Common Core of Data.
constraints: Student-only matching still corresponded with the benchmark in the P-SELL dataset, which the authors attribute to the restricted comparison pool rather than general equivalence.
target_learners: K-8 students in statewide assessment studies
elementary school students in LEP-focused efficacy studies
target_learning_goals: unbiased estimation of school-level intervention effects on achievement in mathematics, ELA, and science
examples: In the Indiana WSC, student-only matching would have led to the incorrect conclusion of a significant negative math effect, while multi-level approaches stayed within 0.1 SD of the RCT benchmark.
key_sources: Hallberg, K., Cook, T. D., & Figlio, D. (2013). Empirically Examining the Performance of Approaches to Multi-Level Matching to Study the Effect of School-Level Interventions. SREE Fall 2013 Conference. https://www.sree.org/conferences/2013f/

article_title: Divergence of Scientific Heuristic Method and Direct Algebraic Instruction
citation: Lina S. Calucag. (2016). Divergence of Scientific Heuristic Method and Direct Algebraic Instruction. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.7, No.3. https://www.iiste.org
title: Integrate the scientific heuristic method into mathematics teaching to build effective problem solvers
description: Based on the study's results, the author recommends integrating the scientific heuristic method in mathematics teaching, stating it is "highly recommended that integration of scientific heuristic method in teaching mathematics is essential". The rationale is that effective problem solvers need a repertoire of heuristics useful across varied problem situations, which explicit attention in the curriculum should address. The evidence base is a single quasi-experiment with intact classes, so the recommendation should be applied with that scope in mind.
requirements: Instruction on mathematical problem solving that gives students opportunities to create their own representations, solutions, and heuristics
Curriculum that gives explicit attention to heuristic processes
constraints: Evidence comes from a non-randomized comparison of two intact classes at one institution over four weeks; the author notes a future study should measure more long-range effects on students' success in mathematics
examples: The experimental group was subjected to the scientific heuristic method while the control group received direct instruction on selected algebra topics, and the experimental group out-performed the control group on the post-test
key_sources: Lina S. Calucag. (2016). Divergence of Scientific Heuristic Method and Direct Algebraic Instruction. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.7, No.3. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1089794

article_title: Concept Cartoons Supported Problem Based Learning Method in Middle School Science Classrooms
citation: Balım, A. G., İnel-Ekici, D., & Özcan, E. (2016). Concept Cartoons Supported Problem Based Learning Method in Middle School Science Classrooms. Journal of Education and Learning, 5(2). https://doi.org/10.5539/jel.v5n2p272
title: Inquiry Learning Skills Perception Scale (Taşkoyan, 2008)
description: A three-factor scale developed by Taşkoyan (2008) used to measure students' inquiry learning skills perceptions, with a maximum score of 110 and minimum of 22. Pilot reliabilities of the factors were .67, .73 and .77 with a full-scale coefficient of .94; in this study Cronbach's alpha was recalculated as "0.88 for pre-test and 0.89 for post-test". It was applied pre and post in all three groups.
requirements: administered as pre-test and post-test around the experimental practice
examples: Used as T1 in the symbolic research design (Table 1) across experiment groups 1 and 2 and the control group
key_sources: Balım, A. G., İnel-Ekici, D., & Özcan, E. (2016). Concept Cartoons Supported Problem Based Learning Method in Middle School Science Classrooms. Journal of Education and Learning, 5(2). https://doi.org/10.5539/jel.v5n2p272

article_title: Development and Implementation of an Instructional Design for Effective Teaching of Ecosystem, Biodiversity, and Environmental Issues
citation: Elif Ozata Yucel, Muhlis Ozkan. (2015). Development and Implementation of an Instructional Design for Effective Teaching of Ecosystem, Biodiversity, and Environmental Issues. Educational Sciences: Theory & Practice. https://doi.org/10.12738/estp.2015.4.2579
title: Instructional design model combining need assessment, development, and assessment steps
description: The researchers built a model from the common points of existing instructional design models (including Dick, Carey, and Carey; ASSURE; and ADDIE) to guide development of the design. It comprises three main steps: need assessment, development of the instructional design, and assessment, with sub-steps for each. The article states that "The instructional design was prepared in three main steps: need assessment, development of the instructional design, and assessment. Sub-steps were then set for each main step."
requirements: Need assessment using literature review, teacher experiences, and a readiness test
Technology-supported materials checked before use with a back-up plan prepared
target_learners: Instructional designers and science teachers developing environmental education units
target_learning_goals: Effective teaching of ecosystem, biodiversity, and environmental issues
examples: Need assessment drew on Dick, Carey, and Carey's model; materials checking and back-up planning drew on the ASSURE model
key_sources: Elif Ozata Yucel, Muhlis Ozkan. (2015). Development and Implementation of an Instructional Design for Effective Teaching of Ecosystem, Biodiversity, and Environmental Issues. Educational Sciences: Theory & Practice. https://doi.org/10.12738/estp.2015.4.2579

article_title: Improving Iranian High School Students' Reading Comprehension Using the Tenets of Genre Analysis
citation: Rezvan Adelnia, Hadi Salehi. (2016). Improving Iranian High School Students' Reading Comprehension Using the Tenets of Genre Analysis. Advances in Language and Literary Studies, 7(4). https://doi.org/10.7575/aiac.alls.v.7n.4p.187
title: Incorporate the tenets of genre-based instruction into reading lessons, course books and curricula
description: Based on its findings, the article recommends that stakeholders incorporate genre-based instruction into reading teaching. It states that studies like this one "can help teacher trainers, English teachers, course book writers and curriculum designers to be more aware of the benefits of genre-based instruction and to incorporate the tenets of genre-based into their lessons, course books and curricula". Curriculum developers are also advised to consider students' genre needs during needs analysis and to choose genre-based instructional materials.
requirements: Awareness among teacher trainers, English teachers, course book writers and curriculum designers of genre-based instruction's benefits
constraints: The article cautions its results should not be generalized broadly due to limitations of instruction time, single-site sample, 80 participants, and limited passages
examples: The study itself taught 10 authentic descriptive passages from readworks.org using the genre-based model over five weeks
key_sources: Rezvan Adelnia, Hadi Salehi. (2016). Improving Iranian High School Students' Reading Comprehension Using the Tenets of Genre Analysis. Advances in Language and Literary Studies, 7(4). https://doi.org/10.7575/aiac.alls.v.7n.4p.187

article_title: Comparing the Effectiveness of Processing Instruction and Production-Based Instruction on L2 Grammar Learning: The Role of Explicit Information
citation: Adem Soruç, Jingjing Qin, YouJin Kim. (2017). Comparing the Effectiveness of Processing Instruction and Production-Based Instruction on L2 Grammar Learning: The Role of Explicit Information. TESL Canada Journal/Revue TESL du Canada, 34(2), 49–70. http://dx.doi.org/1018806/tesl.v34i2.1262
title: VanPatten's input processing model and processing instruction as its pedagogical application
description: The article describes input processing as "what learners do to input during comprehension—how intake is derived", a model in which processing mechanisms are strengthened by structured input activities so learners make correct form-meaning connections. Processing instruction is its pedagogical application: a focus-on-form intervention with three components—explicit information, strategy training, and structured input grounded in the primacy of meaning principle, using referential and affective activities where learners never produce the target form. Production-based instruction is presented as its counterpart, using structured output activities in which learners produce the target form.
requirements: Structured input activities must include both referential and affective activity types
Learners' primary attention during processing is on meaning
constraints: The study's findings apply to the targeted structure only, the simple past tense morpheme -ed, at elementary proficiency level
target_learning_goals: Correct processing and production of English regular past simple -ed form-meaning connections
examples: The study's Packet A gave PI groups 10 structured input activities (6 referential, 4 affective) in which students never produced the target form
key_sources: Adem Soruç, Jingjing Qin, YouJin Kim. (2017). Comparing the Effectiveness of Processing Instruction and Production-Based Instruction on L2 Grammar Learning: The Role of Explicit Information. TESL Canada Journal/Revue TESL du Canada, 34(2), 49–70. http://dx.doi.org/1018806/tesl.v34i2.1262

article_title: Interdisciplinary Greek Traditional Dance Course: Impact on Student Satisfaction and Anxiety
citation: Filippou, F., Rokka, S., Pitsi, A., Gargalianos, D., Bebetsos, E., & Filippou, D. A. (2018). Interdisciplinary Greek Traditional Dance Course: Impact on Student Satisfaction and Anxiety. International Journal of Instruction, 11(3), 363-374. https://doi.org/10.12973/iji.2018.11325a
title: Interdisciplinary Greek traditional dance intervention program (music and sociology topics)
description: An eight-lesson, four-week interdisciplinary program teaching Greek traditional dance with "thematic choices from music and sociology", delivered twice weekly in 45-minute physical education classes. Four lessons drew on music concepts (rhythm, tempo, meters) and four on sociology concepts (coexistence, cooperation, bullying), using aids such as metronome marks and collaborative teaching, and was compared against eight typical curriculum folk dance lessons.
requirements: Delivered within the physical education class by the same teacher for both experimental and control groups
Eight 45-minute lessons held twice weekly over four weeks
constraints: The results apply exclusively to 8th grade Middle school students of a certain cultural environment, per the article's limitations section
target_learning_goals: music concepts such as rhythm and tempo
examples: The tempo lesson taught the concept of tempo through the dance Hasapia using music from 120 bpm to 170 bpm with metronome marks; the sociology lesson taught cooperation through Tsamikos with students in four groups led by peers who knew the dance
key_sources: Filippou, F., Rokka, S., Pitsi, A., Gargalianos, D., Bebetsos, E., & Filippou, D. A. (2018). Interdisciplinary Greek Traditional Dance Course: Impact on Student Satisfaction and Anxiety. International Journal of Instruction, 11(3), 363-374. https://doi.org/10.12973/iji.2018.11325a

article_title: Exploring an Appropriate Instructional Design Model for Continuing Medical Education
citation: Omrani, S., Fardanesh, H., Hemmati, N., & Hemmati, N. (2012). Exploring an appropriate instructional design model for continuing medical education. Turkish Online Journal of Distance Education, 13(3). https://tojde.ankara.edu.tr
title: Integrated instructional and motivational design model for eCME (Merrill's CDT + Reigeluth's Elaboration Theory + Keller's ARCS)
description: The study's design framework combines Merrill's Component Display Theory, which separates content from instructional strategy across "four types of content (Facts, Concepts, Procedures and Principles)" and three performance levels, with Reigeluth's Elaboration Theory, a macro strategy sequencing content from simple to complex in elaborating layers, and Keller's ARCS model (Attention, Relevance, Confidence, Satisfaction) for motivational design. The authors selected this combination because the CME program targeted application-level learning of both micro and macro level topics, and used it to build the multimedia courseware on Acute Respiratory Failure.
requirements: Motivation must be considered in all parts of an instructional message, per the Keller assumptions the study is grounded in
constraints: The article notes instruction designed on sound instructional principles oftentimes does not stimulate learners' motivation, motivating the motivational-design layer
target_learners: general physicians and assistants in continuing medical education
target_learning_goals: application-level clinical knowledge of pathogenesis, diagnosis, and clinical management of Acute Respiratory Failure
examples: The multimedia package was developed in Adobe Flash CS3 with Action Script 3.0, burned onto CD-ROM, and delivered on the university server for self-paced individual study
key_sources: Omrani, S., Fardanesh, H., Hemmati, N., & Hemmati, N. (2012). Exploring an appropriate instructional design model for continuing medical education. Turkish Online Journal of Distance Education, 13(3). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ997826

article_title: Exploring an Appropriate Instructional Design Model for Continuing Medical Education
citation: Omrani, S., Fardanesh, H., Hemmati, N., & Hemmati, N. (2012). Exploring an appropriate instructional design model for continuing medical education. Turkish Online Journal of Distance Education, 13(3). https://tojde.ankara.edu.tr
title: Use integrated instructional and motivational design in future electronic continuing medical education programs
description: Because the e-learning program built on the integration of instructional and motivational design models produced significantly higher learning and motivation than lecture-based teaching, the authors recommend that "instructional and motivational design be used in future electronic continuing medical education programs." The principle treats motivation as a designed property of instruction rather than a byproduct, addressing the finding that sound instructional design alone often fails to stimulate motivation to learn.
requirements: Courseware must be designed with attention to all four ARCS components, not merely add color, graphics, or animation
constraints: Evidence comes from one exploratory study at Kermanshah University of Medical Sciences; the authors note generalization is a primary limitation
target_learners: physicians and assistants in continuing medical education, particularly in developing countries
examples: The study's e-learning group studied a CD-ROM course designed with Merrill's, Reigeluth's and Keller's models and outperformed the lecture group on posttest and motivation while studying in about 120±18 minutes versus 6 hours
key_sources: Omrani, S., Fardanesh, H., Hemmati, N., & Hemmati, N. (2012). Exploring an appropriate instructional design model for continuing medical education. Turkish Online Journal of Distance Education, 13(3). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ997826

article_title: Support for Struggling Students in Algebra: Contributions of Incorrect Worked Examples
citation: Barbieri, C. & Booth, J.L. (2016). Support for struggling students in algebra: Contributions of incorrect worked examples. Learning and Individual Differences, 48, 36–44. https://www.google.com/search?q=%22Support+for+struggling+students+in+algebra%22+Barbieri+Booth+incorrect+worked+examples
title: Use incorrect worked examples with highlighted errors to support low-prior-knowledge students in algebra
description: The article recommends having students study and explain incorrect worked examples — fictitious students' errors with the incorrect procedure highlighted — during algebra practice, because this particularly benefits students with low prior knowledge. As the authors conclude, "Findings from the present study support the use of incorrect worked examples by students with low prior knowledge in algebra." Exposure to incorrect methods did not hamper learning.
requirements: Examples must display the incorrect procedure as a student holding the corresponding misconception would solve it, with the error highlighted, and pair with self-explanation prompts targeting concepts students often struggle with
constraints: Overall learning benefit was not found in this classroom study; benefits of incorrect examples have been reported only at a delay in some prior work, and the study did not require students to correct the errors displayed
target_learners: students with low prior knowledge who struggle with learning math
examples: Students in the incorrect examples condition studied four highlighted-error examples per worksheet and responded to self-explanation prompts before solving paired Your Turn problems, over four worksheets during the systems of equations unit
key_sources: Barbieri, C. & Booth, J.L. (2016). Support for struggling students in algebra: Contributions of incorrect worked examples. Learning and Individual Differences, 48, 36–44. https://www.google.com/search?q=%22Support+for+struggling+students+in+algebra%22+Barbieri+Booth+incorrect+worked+examples

article_title: Support for Struggling Students in Algebra: Contributions of Incorrect Worked Examples
citation: Barbieri, C. & Booth, J.L. (2016). Support for struggling students in algebra: Contributions of incorrect worked examples. Learning and Individual Differences, 48, 36–44. https://www.google.com/search?q=%22Support+for+struggling+students+in+algebra%22+Barbieri+Booth+incorrect+worked+examples
title: Incorrect worked examples worksheets with self-explanation prompts for systems of equations
description: Classroom worksheets used in the intervention, covering four methods for solving systems of equations (graphing, substitution, elimination with addition and subtraction, and elimination with multiplication). Each worksheet contained eight problems; example conditions included four example-problem pairs in which "Students were asked to study the examples and then respond to self-explanation prompts designed to direct their attention to important concepts that students often struggle with in algebra" before solving a paired Your Turn problem. Participants attempted M = 13.74 of the 16 Your Turn problems overall.
requirements: Teachers allowed approximately 20 minutes per worksheet and worksheets were aligned with course material
constraints: Control students solved 32 problems while example groups explained 16 examples and solved 16 Your Turn problems, so problem counts differed across conditions
target_learning_goals: understanding of the equal sign as indicating balance of equations
examples: Sample worksheets displayed fictitious students' incorrect work with the incorrect procedure highlighted as a student holding the misconception would solve it
key_sources: Barbieri, C. & Booth, J.L. (2016). Support for struggling students in algebra: Contributions of incorrect worked examples. Learning and Individual Differences, 48, 36–44. https://www.google.com/search?q=%22Support+for+struggling+students+in+algebra%22+Barbieri+Booth+incorrect+worked+examples

article_title: Concept Mapping Strategy: An Effective Tool for Improving Students' Academic Achievement in Biology
citation: Sakiyo, J. & Waziri, K. (2015). Concept mapping strategy: An effective tool for improving students' academic achievement in biology. Journal of Education in Science, Environment and Health (JESEH), 1(1), 56-62. www.jeseh.net
title: Incorporate concept mapping into biology teaching and train teachers in its use
description: Based on its finding that concept mapping outperformed lecture method, the article recommends that "teachers should use this teaching method to teach biology teaching lessons" and that workshops be organized and made compulsory for practicing teachers so they embrace concept mapping skills. It further recommends exposing pre-service teachers to the method and suggesting it for some biology content areas in the curriculum.
requirements: Teachers need training in concept mapping skills, via compulsory workshops for practicing teachers and exposure for pre-service teachers
constraints: The recommendation rests on one quasi-experimental study of selected SSII topics in Adamawa State
target_learning_goals: meaningful learning and academic achievement in biology
examples: In the study, the experimental group was subjected to concept mapping treatment on Nutrition, Habitat and Nutrient cycle topics while the control group was taught by lecture for six weeks
key_sources: Sakiyo, J. & Waziri, K. (2015). Concept mapping strategy: An effective tool for improving students' academic achievement in biology. Journal of Education in Science, Environment and Health (JESEH), 1(1), 56-62. www.jeseh.net. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1105286

article_title: Physics Practical Work and Its Influence on Students' Academic Achievement
citation: Musasia, A. M., Ocholla, A. A., & Sakwa, T. W. (2016). Physics Practical Work and Its Influence on Students' Academic Achievement. Journal of Education and Practice, 7(28). https://www.iiste.org
title: Use intensive practical activities as a central instructional technique in secondary physics to raise achievement
description: The article recommends practical work as a central instructional technique for physics, contrasting it with the lecture method it reports as ineffective. It argues that "something more structured as hands – on, minds – on seems to be required", involving students in data collection, manipulation, analysis, report writing, and class discussion after each practical. The quasi-experiment supports the recommendation for form two physics in average-performing Kenyan schools.
requirements: Learners are fully involved in the practical learning process, as the article states achievement improvement "can be achieved if the learners are fully involved in t he practical learning process".
Each practical is followed by teacher-led class interaction and discussion, with data collection, manipulation and analysis before writing an experimental report.
constraints: Evidence comes from a quasi-experimental non-equivalent group design in average-performing schools in one Kenyan sub-county; the authors recommend repetition with expanded samples and in other subjects and classes.
target_learners: Form two secondary school physics students in average-performing schools
target_learning_goals: Physics achievement on topics such as turning effect of a force, reflection at curved surfaces, and magnetic effect of an electric current
examples: The experimental group was taught by intensive practical activities across term two and three, with tests administered at the end of each of three selected topics, while the control group received theoretical lectures with teacher demonstrations.
key_sources: Musasia, A. M., Ocholla, A. A., & Sakwa, T. W. (2016). Physics Practical Work and Its Influence on Students' Academic Achievement. Journal of Education and Practice, 7(28). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1118591

article_title: The Effect of Teaching Strategies and Curiosity on Students' Achievement in Reading Comprehension
citation: Busmin Gurning & Aguslani Siregar. (2017). The Effect of Teaching Strategies and Curiosity on Students’ Achievement in Reading Comprehension. English Language Teaching, 10(11). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v10n11p191
title: INSERT (Interactive Notation System for Effective Reading and Thinking) strategy
description: INSERT is a reading strategy created by Vaughn and Estes (1986) in which readers mark a text with symbols or notations such as a check mark or a plus sign while reading, responding with decisions like "I knew that," "I don’t understand," and "That’s really important." After reading, students create INSERT summary charts, compare them with one or two peers, and may reorganize their post-notes into a concept map or graphic organizer. In this study it was the experimental teaching strategy for reading comprehension of exposition texts.
requirements: Students record symbols while reading and create their own INSERT summary charts
Peer comparison of charts and optionally a conceptually based map built from the chart
target_learners: Senior high school (grade XI) EFL students
target_learning_goals: Reading comprehension of exposition texts at literal, inferential, and critical levels
examples: In the study, one class of 38 grade XI students was taught with INSERT for six meetings over five weeks and scored higher than the SQ3R class.
key_sources: Busmin Gurning & Aguslani Siregar. (2017). The Effect of Teaching Strategies and Curiosity on Students’ Achievement in Reading Comprehension. English Language Teaching, 10(11). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v10n11p191

article_title: The Role of Independent Activities in Development of Strategic Learning Competences and Increase of School Performance Level, within the Study of High School Pedagogy
citation: Monica-Iuliana Anca & Muşata Bocoş. (2017). The Role of Independent Activities in Development of Strategic Learning Competences and Increase of School Performance Level, within the Study of High School Pedagogy. Educatia 21 Journal, (15). https://doi.org/10.24193/ed21.2017.15.07
title: Use independent activities to develop strategic learning because they require self-organisation, self-monitoring and multi-level reflection
description: The article recommends reconfiguring the role of independent activities in high school pedagogy because they involve cognitive, psycho-motor, affective and emotional involvement, deep inner reflection, and self-organisation of learning. It states that "Independent activities highlight strategic learning because they involve the analysis of tasks, choosing strategies for approaching tasks, evaluation of the tasks` solving manner, monitoring of performances". The experimental results are offered as support for this principle.
requirements: Activities must be based on personal efforts of those who learn, unassisted by teaching staff, per the article's definition of independent activity
examples: The experimental programme organised independent activities valorising individual, collective, cognitive and meta-cognitive reflection in the subject Students' Class Management
key_sources: Monica-Iuliana Anca & Muşata Bocoş. (2017). The Role of Independent Activities in Development of Strategic Learning Competences and Increase of School Performance Level, within the Study of High School Pedagogy. Educatia 21 Journal, (15). https://doi.org/10.24193/ed21.2017.15.07

article_title: Improving First Computer Programming Experiences: The Case of Adapting a Web-Supported and Well-Structured Problem-Solving Method to a Traditional Course
citation: Murat Pasa Uysal. (2014). Improving First Computer Programming Experiences: The Case of Adapting a Web-Supported and Well-Structured Problem-Solving Method to a Traditional Course. Contemporary Educational Technology, 5(3), 198-217. https://www.cedtech.net
title: Instructional root-cause analysis fishbone diagram for diagnosing the CP course
description: Before redesigning the course, the author integrated instructional and root-cause analysis techniques, using a fishbone diagram (Figure 1) with the main problem statement "poor PS sk ills and knowledge transfer". The main branches were Programming Language, Learners, Instructors and Instructional Approach, with sub-branches such as the language paradigm, learner attitudes, instructors' teaching styles and learning goals. The analysis "guided how to assess the current needs, learners, environment, tasks and goals" and informed the choice of C, PS strategies and web support.
requirements: Systematic identification of potential main and sub-causes "before jumping to a conclusion"
constraints: Diagnosis was specific to the faculty's three-decade-old teacher-directed CP course context
target_learning_goals: knowledge transfer from lectures to labs
examples: The analysis identified that transfer of knowledge from lectures to laboratory was a headmost problem of novice learners

article_title: The Effects of Jigsaw Technique Based on Cooperative Learning on Prospective Science Teachers' Science Process Skill

description: Based on the finding that the Jigsaw-based laboratory approach produced higher scientific process skill development than the confirmatory approach, the authors recommend that science teachers embed Jigsaw cooperative learning in laboratory teaching. The article states: "it is suggested that science t eachers and educators can employ Jigsaw technique b uilt on cooperative learning by integrating it into laborat ory practices", so that they "can contribute to the development of learners' cognitive skills".

Groups must be formed to balance academic achievement so responsibility is shared

Some students' failure to complete their tasks properly negatively affected other group members' learning
