citation: Eldy, E.F., Chang, J.H.W., Butai, S.N., Basri, N.F., Awang. H., Din, W.A., & Arshad, S.E. (2019). Inverted classroom improves pre-university students understanding on basic topic of physics: The preliminary study. Journal of Technology and Science Education, 9(3), 420-427. https://doi.org/10.3926/jotse.599
title: Inverted classroom implementation with Padlet-delivered self-paced videos, online quizzes and problem-based learning assessment
description: The experimental intervention offloaded lecture content to self-paced online videos shared via Padlet, with online quizzes and practice problems, while classroom time was used for problem-based learning. The article states that Padlet was used as the medium to share all the materials and that the goals were to provide students with fundamental concepts before class and create opportunities to apply concepts through exercises. Assessment in the inverted classroom was done by problem-based learning (PBL).
requirements: Students must access pre-recorded lecture videos and online materials before class so classroom time can be used for learning activities
constraints: Implemented in a first-semester Foundation of Science mechanics course at University Malaysia Sabah with no laboratory component in the course itself
target_learning_goals: classical mechanics concepts: Work, Energy & Power and Force, Momentum & Impulse
examples: Students in the inverted classroom self-studied at their own pace and time while the traditional group attended lectures; both groups received similar notes and ended with PBL assessment

article_title: Effects of Worksheets Base the Levels of Inquiry in Improving Critical and Creative Thinking
citation: Muskita, M., Subali, B., & Djukri. (2020). Effects of Worksheets Base the Levels of Inquiry in Improving Critical and Creative Thinking. International Journal of Instruction, 13(2), 519-532. https://doi.org/10.29333/iji.2020.13236a
title: Inquiry worksheet syntax graduated by level of learner responsibility
description: The article's worksheets share a common activity syntax — formulate problem, submit hypothesis, do observation/data collection, draw conclusions — but shift responsibility across the three levels. In structured inquiry the lecturer directs students to formulate questions and helps collect and organize data; in guided inquiry the lecturer guides each stage; in open inquiry the lecturer only directs students to formulate questions, form hypotheses, collect and organize data, and draw conclusions independently. This graduated scaffolding is the design pattern the study evaluated.
requirements: Lecturer roles at each level must match the printed syntax table (directing, guiding, or directing-then-independent)
constraints: Evaluated in biology laboratory-related courses; the article notes each subject has characteristics determining which courses suit inquiry-based worksheets
examples: Table 2 details lecturer roles for each level, e.g. guided inquiry: "Guiding students to draw conclusions based on data"

article_title: Improving Teacher Perceptions of Parent Involvement Patterns: Findings from a Group Randomized Trial
citation: Keith C. Herman and Wendy M. Reinke. (2016). Improving Teacher Perceptions of Parent Involvement Patterns: Findings From a Group Randomized Trial. School Psychology Quarterly. http://dx.doi.org/10.1037/spq0000169
title: Incredible Years Teacher Classroom Management (IY TCM) program
description: IY TCM is a 6-day universal teacher training program focused on improving teacher-student and teacher-parent relationships and increasing effective classroom management strategies. Its logic model identifies "positive parent–teacher partnerships" as one of three program goals and targets positive parent-teacher relations as a proximal outcome. Training uses video vignettes of teacher interactions, Socratic questioning, role plays, self-reflection, behavior support plans with parent engagement prompts, take-home communication letters, and coach support between and after workshops.
requirements: Six full-day workshops delivered by doctoral-level group leaders supervised by the program developer
Ongoing coaching after the first workshop through the end of the school year, tailored to teachers' interests and needs
constraints: IY TCM is a multifaceted intervention, so the study could not determine whether changes came from specific components or the package
Fidelity and implementation outcomes are documented in a separate report (Reinke et al., 2013)
target_learners: Elementary school teachers (kindergarten to third grade)
Students in teachers' classrooms, including those with academic and behavior problems
target_learning_goals: Improve teacher classroom management and relationship skills
Examine teacher assumptions and biases about parents
Develop and repair relationships with challenging students and families
examples: In the trial, teachers attended three sets of two full-day trainings in late October, December, and February; workshop attendance was 94%–100%, average coach time was nearly six hours (358 min), and satisfaction ratings ranged 6.44–6.75 on a 1–7 scale.

article_title: A Few Observations and Remarks on Time Effectiveness of Interactive Electronic Testing
citation: Martin MAGDIN, Milan TURČÁNI. (2015). A Few Observations and Remarks on Time Effectiveness of Interactive Electronic Testing. Informatics in Education. http://dx.doi.org/10.15388/infedu.2015.06
title: Interactive question module by Dmitry Pupinin implemented in LMS Moodle
description: A special module implemented into the LMS Moodle environment to enable interactive electronic testing. The article states that "The module allows connection of the data and the database", so that values of variables representing correctly or incorrectly solved parts of an interactive task can be statistically evaluated and partial or overall evaluation allocated to individual students. The experimental group's Moodle course on divai.ukf.sk/moodle contained this module; the control group's equivalent course on edu.ukf.sk lacked it.
requirements: Requires connection of the module to a data source and database so that solved task parts can be statistically evaluated and scored
target_learning_goals: assessing knowledge and psycho-motor skills in Computer Architecture
examples: All tests during the semester for the experimental group were taken using this module type in the Computer Architecture 1 course

article_title: A Few Observations and Remarks on Time Effectiveness of Interactive Electronic Testing
citation: Martin MAGDIN, Milan TURČÁNI. (2015). A Few Observations and Remarks on Time Effectiveness of Interactive Electronic Testing. Informatics in Education. http://dx.doi.org/10.15388/infedu.2015.06
title: Interactive tasks as didactic tests combining animations with conceptual-task assessment
description: The article summarises the use of interactive tasks in three basic points: "Interactive animations can be implemented into these tasks", the interactive type of task equals a didactic test (conceptual task), and they let researchers determine and verify time and didactic effectiveness. Conceptual tasks focus on exploration of understanding of notions and their relations and, per the article citing Haláková, help uncover students' mental models and qualitative perceptions and boost critical thinking.
requirements: Tests must be designed, verified, evaluated and interpreted according to a set of rules formulated in advance, as didactic tests require
constraints: Conceptual tasks are not used very often because of the difficult nature of their execution
target_learning_goals: exploring understanding of notions and their relations
examples: Autotest no. 3 asked students to form a nonlinear transistor level from components defined in advance, in electronic and paper versions of identical content

article_title: Free-Body Diagrams and Problem Solving in Mechanics: An Example of the Effectiveness of Self-Constructed Representations
citation: Vanes Mešić, Sabaheta Mahmutović, Elvedin Hasović, Nataša Erceg. (2017). Free-Body Diagrams and Problem Solving in Mechanics: An Example of The Effectiveness of Self-Constructed Representations. European J of Physics Education, Volume 7 Issue 3. https://portal.issn.org/resource/ISSN/1309-7202
title: Coherence between internal and external representations as a requirement for effective problem solving
description: The article proposes that cognitive processing occurs in a coupled system of internal and external representations, and that the effectiveness of information processing "largely depends on the coherence between internal and external representations". When students construct external representations themselves, the coupled system is more internally coherent, making the representations easier to interpret and use. The study's finding that provided free-body diagrams impeded solving while self-constructed diagrams correlated with success is presented as illustrating this account.
requirements: External representations must be consistent with the learner's internal representations to support effective processing
constraints: The article states the advantage of self-construction applies when students are presented with already completed FBDs without further teacher guidance, and effectiveness depends on students' prior foreknowledge
examples: Control-group students conceptualized problems within the step-by-step construction of their own free-body diagrams, while experimental-group students had to interpret completed diagrams

European J of Physics Education, Volume 7 Issue 3. https://portal.issn.org/resource/ISSN/1309-7202

article_title: Do Effects of Social-Emotional Learning Programs Vary by Level of Parent Participation? Evidence from a Randomized Trial
citation: McCormick, M. P., Cappella, E., O'Connor, E. E., Hill, J., & McClowry, S. G. (2016). Do Effects of Social-Emotional Learning Programs Vary by Level of Parent Participation? Evidence from a Randomized Trial. SREE Spring 2016 Conference Abstract.
title: INSIGHTS into Children's Temperament: comprehensive SEL program with parent, teacher, and classroom components
description: INSIGHTS is a comprehensive social/behavioral SEL intervention with manualized curricula for teachers, students, and parents. It "provides teachers and parents with a temperament framework for supporting the individual differences of children," helping adults recognize a child's temperament and respond with warmth and discipline strategies supporting adaptive social-emotional and behavioral outcomes. Parents and teachers attended 10 weekly 2-hour facilitated sessions while students received 45-minute classroom lessons over the same 10 weeks.
requirements: Facilitators follow scripts, use checklists, document sessions, and receive ongoing training and supervision
constraints: Parent attendance was substantially lower than teacher and classroom dosage, averaging 5.93 sessions (SD = 4.15)
target_learners: low-income urban kindergarten and first grade students
target_learning_goals: social-emotional competencies including behavioral regulation, attentional skills, problem-solving, and social skills to support academic development
examples: In the trial, 93% of the curriculum was adequately covered on average; teacher sessions averaged 9.44 attended and classroom sessions 8.30

article_title: A Quasi-Experimental Study on Using Short Stories: Statistical and Inferential Analyses on the Non-English Major University Students' Speaking and Writing Achievements
citation: Jaya Nur IMAN. (2017). A QUASI-EXPERIMENTAL STUDY ON USING SHORT STORIES: STATISTICAL AND INFERENTIAL ANALYSES ON THE NON-ENGLISH MAJOR UNIVERSITY STUDENTS' SPEAKING AND WRITING ACHIEVEMENTS. International Journal of Languages' Education and Teaching, 5(1). https://doi.org/10.18298/ijlet.1719
title: Integrate literature instruction into the EFL classroom because authentic literary materials can motivate learners to speak and write
description: The article's pedagogical implication is that teachers should consider bringing literature, specifically short stories, into academic EFL classrooms. As printed, "teachers should ponder the integration of literature instruction in the academic classroom as this could develop the EFL learners' motivation to speak and write in terms of the exposure of interesting authentic materials." The recommendation rests on the study's between-group achievement differences and on the authors' motivational interpretation.
requirements: Teachers should be able to select appropriate short stories on the basis of the students' language proficiency level, as the article's suggestions state
constraints: The motivational mechanism is the authors' interpretation; the study measured speaking and writing scores, not motivation
examples: The experimental group worked with short stories from Intermediate Stories for Reproduction 1 across 12 teaching sessions of 90 minutes each

article_title: The Effects of the 3-2-1 Reading Strategy on EFL Reading Comprehension
citation: Hashem Ahmed Alsamadani. (2011). The Effects of the 3-2-1 Reading Strategy on EFL Reading Comprehension. English Language Teaching, 4(3). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v4n3p184
title: The interactive model of reading
description: The article adopts the interactive model as the theoretical basis for strategy instruction. It is described as "a widely accepted model of reading that is based on cognitive psychology and schema theory", in which the reader plays an active role in interpreting the text rather than passively receiving information. The model encompasses both first- and second-language reading, incorporates both bottom-up and top-down processes, and recognizes the contribution of both the reader and the text, including reader variables such as background knowledge and prediction. On this account, the more students engage and interact with the text, the higher the probability of comprehension.
requirements: Readers must actively engage and interact with the text for comprehension probability to rise
examples: The article frames the 3-2-1 strategy as an interactive reading strategy consistent with this model
key_sources: Hashem Ahmed Alsamadani. (2011). The Effects of the 3-2-1 Reading Strategy on EFL Reading Comprehension. English Language Teaching, 4(3). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v4n3p184

article_title: The Effects of the Use of Microsoft Math Tool (Graphical Calculator) Instruction on Students' Performance in Linear Functions
citation: Philip Siaw Kissi, Opoku Gyabaah and Sampson Kwadwo Boateng. (2016). The Effects of the use of Microsoft Math Tool (Graphical Calculator) instruction on students' performance in linear functions. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.7, No.21. http://www.iiste.org
title: Introduce graphical calculators in mathematics teaching to improve students' performance, particularly in linear and quadratic functions
description: Based on the significant post-test advantage of the graphical calculator group, the article recommends that "mathematics teachers and curriculum or textbook developers should introduce the use of the graphical calculator to improve students' performance in mathematics education, particularly linear and quadratic functions", and that high school educators should use the tool in their teaching curriculum.
requirements: Teachers and curriculum or textbook developers adopting the graphical calculator within the teaching curriculum
constraints: The supporting evidence is a single quasi-experiment on linear functions in two Accra senior high schools; the article extends the recommendation to quadratic functions without testing them
target_learning_goals: improved performance in linear and quadratic functions
examples: The quasi-experiment assigned 98 students across two schools to calculator-based or lecture-based instruction by the same instructor and compared WASSCE-based post-test scores

article_title: Investigating the Effectiveness of Audio Input Enhancement on EFL Learners' Retention of Intensifiers
citation: Negari, G. M., Azizi, A., & Arani, D. K. (2018). Investigating the Effectiveness of Audio Input Enhancement on EFL Learners’ Retention of Intensifiers. International Journal of Instruction, 11(1), 123-138. https://doi.org/10.12973/iji.2018.1119a
title: Input enhancement as a focus-on-form technique grounded in the noticing hypothesis
description: The article frames input enhancement within focus on form and Schmidt's noticing hypothesis: learning requires converting input into intake, and enhancement makes selected features of the second language more salient so learners notice them. It defines input enhancement as "techniques and methods which the instructor uses to make selected features of a second language more salient for learners to facilitate language acquisition", replacing Sharwood Smith's earlier consciousness-raising term. The study applies this framework by manipulating audio materials to saliently present English intensifiers.
requirements: Learners must be exposed to input containing the target forms; the article states learning is not possible without exposure to some sort of input
constraints: The article notes researchers are yet to find a positive correlation between language learning and input, and that it is not yet obvious which grammatical forms are more susceptible to input enhancement
target_learners: EFL learners, here male Iranian high school sophomores
target_learning_goals: Noticing and retention of grammatical target forms (English intensifiers)
examples: The experimental group heard listening extracts in which the teacher increased the volume of files containing the target intensifiers before learners saw them in printed form
key_sources: Negari, G. M., Azizi, A., & Arani, D. K. (2018). Investigating the Effectiveness of Audio Input Enhancement on EFL Learners’ Retention of Intensifiers. International Journal of Instruction, 11(1), 123-138. https://doi.org/10.12973/iji.2018.1119a

article_title: The Association of Peer Behavioral Regulation with School Readiness Skills in Preschool
citation: Natalia Rojas. (2016). The Association of Peer Behavioral Regulation with School Readiness Skills in Preschool. SREE Spring 2016 Conference. https://www.sree.org
title: Instructional-time mechanism: classrooms with more children who have difficulty regulating behavior reduce time available for instruction
description: The article proposes a mechanism account for preschool peer effects in behavioral regulation: children with low behavioral regulation exhibit problems such as aggression that interrupt classroom activities and require direct teacher intervention, reducing instructional time. The article states "the time available for instruction may be reduced in classrooms with more children who have difficulties regulating their behaviors" and that "Having peers with higher behavioral regulation skills may allow more time for the teacher to instruct." Low classroom regulation may strain teachers' ability to organize and manage classrooms. This account is offered as an explanation, not a tested result.
requirements: Future research should identify the mechanisms underlying peer effects in preschool; the article calls for experimental or re-analytic tests of whether peer-level behavioral regulation mediates program impacts.
constraints: The article presents this as a possible explanation, not a tested mediation result; most work on peer effects has used correlational methodologies.
target_learners: preschool children in low-income urban public school classrooms
target_learning_goals: school readiness skills (motor, content knowledge, language) and classroom behavioral regulation
examples: The article cites prior work (McCabe et al., 2007; Rimm-Kaufman et al., 2005) that children with low behavioral regulation are more likely to exhibit aggression and interrupt classroom activities.
key_sources: Natalia Rojas. (2016). The Association of Peer Behavioral Regulation with School Readiness Skills in Preschool. SREE Spring 2016 Conference. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED567502

article_title: The Association of Peer Behavioral Regulation with School Readiness Skills in Preschool
citation: Natalia Rojas. (2016). The Association of Peer Behavioral Regulation with School Readiness Skills in Preschool. SREE Spring 2016 Conference. https://www.sree.org
title: Include peer abilities in model specifications of preschool inputs to avoid omitted variable bias
description: The article recommends that estimates of effects of inputs in preschool should include peer abilities in the model specifications. It argues that "the magnitude and strength of the associations between peer behavioral regulation and children's school readiness skills make a compelling case that estimates of effects of inputs in preschool are likely to suffer from omitted variable bias unless peer abilities have been included in the model specifications." This follows from the study's finding that classroom-level peer engagement uniquely predicts readiness growth after adjusting for child, teacher, and program factors.
requirements: Analyses of preschool program effects should measure and model classroom-level peer behavioral regulation alongside other inputs.
constraints: At the moment, most work on peer effects has used correlational methodologies, per the article.
examples: The study itself adjusted for demographic, program-related, and teacher factors as well as fall school readiness skills when estimating classroom-level peer engagement effects.
key_sources: Natalia Rojas. (2016). The Association of Peer Behavioral Regulation with School Readiness Skills in Preschool. SREE Spring 2016 Conference. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED567502

article_title: The Effects of Audio-Visual Recorded and Audio Recorded Listening Tasks on the Accuracy of Iranian EFL Learners' Oral Production
citation: Pooya Drood & Hanieh Davatgari Asl. (2016). The Effects of Audio-visual Recorded and Audio Recorded Listening Tasks on the Accuracy of Iranian EFL Learners' Oral Production. English Language Teaching, 9(9). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v9n9p110
title: Include audio-visual listening tasks in daily listening teaching to support L2 speaking accuracy
description: Based on the finding that the audio-visual group outperformed the audio-only group on post-test accuracy, the article recommends that "Teachers can include audio –visual listening tasks more in their daily teaching of listening tasks" and that providing students the opportunity to watch listening materials is well worthwhile. It frames task type as an important factor in decisions about providing speech input.
requirements: Access to audio-visual materials (videos, movies) and playback equipment during listening sessions
constraints: Findings come from intermediate-level male Iranian EFL learners performing five speaking tasks; the article suggests replication with female learners, other age groups, and other tasks
examples: In the study, one group watched audio-visual materials while the other listened to audio recorded tapes and CDs across five 30-minute sessions

article_title: Emergent Literacy Development and Computer Assisted Instruction
citation: Trotti, J., Hendricks, R., & Bledsoe, C. (2017). Emergent Literacy Development and Computer Assisted Instruction. SRATE Journal, 26(1), 30-39. https://www.sratejournal.org
title: Independent computer practice may not be developmentally appropriate for some pre-K children, who benefit from more interaction with peers and the teacher
description: Based on its findings, the article suggests that "independent practice may not be developmentally appropriate for some children of pre -K age who desire more interaction with peers and the teacher." The control group's greater flexibility in time management and tasks of choice, plus teacher observations of resistance and distraction, support structuring early-literacy technology use around adult and peer interaction rather than solitary computer work.
requirements: Teacher roles remain central; teachers who anchor CAI in developmentally appropriate practices found it more effective
constraints: The article calls for more research across age groups and types of computer software to determine broader findings

target_learning_goals: early literacy development and kindergarten readiness
examples: In the study, experimental groups rotated to computers during time normally allocated for learning centers, while control children experienced greater flexibility in time management and tasks of choice

article_title: The Effect of Lexical Bundles on Iranian EFL Learners Linguistic Production Fluency
citation: Ranjbar, N., Pazhakh, A., & Gorjian, B. (2012). The Effect of Lexical Bundles on Iranian EFL Learners Linguistic Production Fluency. International Education Studies, 5(4). https://doi.org/10.5539/ies.v5n4p243
title: Include lexical bundles teaching methodology in instructional materials and classroom teaching
description: Based on the study's findings, the authors recommend that "content developers should include lexical bundles teaching methodology and their uses in the teaching and learning processes", calling this pedagogically central for materials design and classroom methodology. The principle holds that because bundle use during instruction supports automatic and easy recall during paragraph writing, materials and teaching should deliberately incorporate bundles rather than rely on conventional methods alone.
requirements: Instructional materials that identify and supply the lexical bundles to be taught
Classroom activities giving learners repeated use of bundles across contexts
constraints: The authors note the study was conducted at one institution and that more research in similar situations and state universities is needed to support the findings
The authors state further research is needed to clarify whether improvement was due to bundle instruction or to more paragraph writing practice
target_learners: Iranian EFL university students majoring in TEFL
examples: The experimental group's posttest writing fluency surpassed the control group's after a semester of bundle instruction on the same textbook content

article_title: Development of Knowledge, Awareness, Global Warming Decreasing Behavior and Critical Thinking of Grade 11 Students Using the Four Noble Truths Method with Meta-Cognitive Techniques
citation: Sakkarin Chattuchai, Adisak Singseewo and Paitool Suksringarm. (2015). Development of knowledge, awareness, global warming decreasing behavior and critical thinking of grade 11 students using the Four Noble Truths method with meta-cognitive techniques. Educational Research and Reviews. https://doi.org/10.5897/ERR2015.2360
title: Three metacognitive techniques — intelligibility, plausibility and wide-applicability — as tools for developing critical thinking
description: Adapted from Beeth, the article defines three categories of metacognitive techniques meant to help students use metacognition to develop critical thinking. "Intelligibility" has students reflect on whether an idea makes sense to them; "plausibility" enables students to test their faith in an idea and seek counter-evidence; "wide-applicability" involves applying thinking from one context to another through connection making and transfer. The techniques operate on both intra-personal and interpersonal levels, as shown in the article's Table 1 of characteristic questions.
requirements: Questions embedded at stages of the lesson method so students ask themselves the characteristic questions intra-personally and about others' ideas interpersonally
examples: Intelligibility and plausibility were added to the first FNT stage; intelligibility, plausibility and wide-applicability were added to the fourth stage
key_sources: Sakkarin Chattuchai, Adisak Singseewo and Paitool Suksringarm. (2015). article_title: Pronunciation for the Arab Learners of EFL: Planning for Better Outcomes
citation: Al-Ahdal, A. A. M. H., Al-Hattami, A. A., Al-Awaid, S. A. A., & Al-Mashaqba, N. J. H. (2015). Pronunciation for the Arab Learners of EFL: Planning for Better Outcomes. English Language Teaching, 8(10). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v8n10p100
title: Two main approaches to teaching pronunciation: the intuitive-imitative approach and the analytic-linguistic approach
description: Drawing on Celce Murcia et al. (1996), the article distinguishes two main approaches to pronunciation teaching. The intuitive-imitative approach "depends on the learner's ability to listen to and imitate the rhythms and sounds of the target language without the intervention of any explicit information" and presupposes good models to listen to. The analytic-linguistic approach uses tools such as a phonetic alphabet, articulatory descriptions and contrastive information, and was developed to complement rather than replace the intuitive-imitative approach, which is retained as the practice phase.
requirements: The intuitive-imitative approach presupposes the availability, validity, and reliability of good models to listen to.
constraints: The analytic-linguistic approach was designed to complement, not replace, the intuitive-imitative approach.
target_learners: EFL learners, including Arabic-speaking learners of English
target_learning_goals: English pronunciation, including segmental and suprasegmental features
examples: The article's own intervention used drills in reading aloud focused on speed, pauses, tone and other prosodic features, an analytic supplement to imitation.
key_sources: Al-Ahdal, A. A. M. H., Al-Hattami, A. A., Al-Awaid, S. A. A., & Al-Mashaqba, N. J. H. (2015). Pronunciation for the Arab Learners of EFL: Planning for Better Outcomes. English Language Teaching, 8(10). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v8n10p100

article_title: Effect of Motivational Scaffolding on E-Learning Environments: Self-Efficacy, Learning Achievement, and Cognitive Style
citation: Nilson Valencia-Vallejo, Omar López-Vargas, Luis Sanabria-Rodríguez. (2017). Effect of Motivational Scaffolding on E-Learning Environments: Self-Efficacy, Learning Achievement, and Cognitive Style. Journal of Educators Online. https://www.thejeo.com
title: Introductory Course to Mathematics e-learning environment with embedded four-stage motivational scaffolding
description: A hypermedia e-learning environment built for the study: "The course consists of six learning modules in basic mathematics. Each unit contained text and graphic information, videos, learning activities, evaluation tests, and links to Web pages." Its scaffolding, based on Bandura's self-efficacy theory and Belland et al. and Keller's design postulates, comprises four stages: assessment with reflection and an initial feedback test; goal formulation, self-efficacy judgment, and planning; learning execution and monitoring with a self-evaluation module and motivational messages; and final self-evaluation and reflection.
requirements: The scaffolding is embedded within the structure of the computational environment and requires students to select goals, self-efficacy judgments, and study-time plans
constraints: The control version differed only in the presence or absence of the scaffolding, holding objectives, content, resources, evaluation, and study times the same
target_learners: first-semester higher education students in a Bachelor's in Technological Design
examples: Sixty-five students used the environment for two months; the scaffolding group's environment included reflection questions, goal-selection scales, self-efficacy judgment options, planning tools, and motivational messages
key_sources: Nilson Valencia-Vallejo, Omar López-Vargas, Luis Sanabria-Rodríguez. (2017). Effect of Motivational Scaffolding on E-Learning Environments: Self-Efficacy, Learning Achievement, and Cognitive Style. Journal of Educators Online. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1168944

article_title: On the Role of Media Input in the Learning of Formulaic Sequences by EFL Learners
citation: Didem Koban Koç & Serdar Engin Koç. (2017). On the Role of Media Input in the Learning of Formulaic Sequences by EFL Learners. TESL Canada Journal/Revue TESL du Canada, 34(3), 93–110. https://doi.org/10.18806/tesl.v34i3.1275
title: English teachers and curriculum developers should incorporate teaching of formulaic sequences and raise learners' awareness of the most frequent FSs
description: The article argues that English teaching should move beyond grammatical structures: "English language teachers and curriculum developers should, first of all, incorporate the teaching of FSs into the lessons and help learners become aware of a variety of FSs through appropriate input." It further states it is essential that instructors raise learners' awareness of the most frequently used FSs and involve learners in comprehending and producing them in appropriate contexts. The principle is grounded in the study's retention finding and learners' reports that FSs were neglected in their prior schooling.
requirements: Appropriate input must be provided so learners become aware of a variety of FSs
Learners must be involved in both comprehending and producing FSs in appropriate contexts
constraints: The authors note generalizing their findings to other EFL or ESL learner groups may not be appropriate because participants were advanced first-year ELT students
target_learners: international learners with limited native-speaker interaction
target_learning_goals: knowledge and appropriate use of frequently used formulaic sequences
examples: The study's treatment taught 30 FSs selected for frequency (checked against the British National Corpus and Corpus of Contemporary American English at 30 occurrences per one million words)
key_sources: Didem Koban Koç & Serdar Engin Koç. (2017). On the Role of Media Input in the Learning of Formulaic Sequences by EFL Learners. TESL Canada Journal/Revue TESL du Canada, 34(3), 93–110. https://doi.org/10.18806/tesl.v34i3.1275

article_title: The Impact of Integrated STEM Education on Academic Achievement, Reflective Thinking Skills towards Problem Solving and Permanence in Learning in Science Education
citation: Sarican, G., Akgunduz, D. (2018). The impact of integrated STEM education on academic achievement, reflective thinking skills towards problem solving and permanence in learning in science education. Cypriot Journal of Educational Sciences, 13(1), 94-113. http://www.cjes.eu
title: Integrated STEM education programme with engineering design activities for 6th-grade science units
description: An integrated STEM implementation delivered within the 6th-grade science programme across the units of force and motion, light and sound, electrical conduction, and matter and heat, lasting 22 hours over 5 weeks after a 1-week pilot. The article states that "The students were asked to design proposals for solutions of the problem and to design these solutions, and the designs were transformed into products and the engineering processes of the students were evaluated." A sample activity, 'I design a racing car', followed the engineering design cycle within the velocity topic.
requirements: A teacher trained via a STEM teacher certification programme delivered the whole study
A pilot week prepared students for the engineering design cycle and STEM integration
constraints: This research is limited to the middle school science curriculum and the topics covered
target_learning_goals: reflective thinking skills towards problem solving
examples: In the 'I design a racing car' activity students designed a vehicle, measured distance with a meter and time with a stopwatch, and calculated velocity as the ratio of road covered to passing time
key_sources: Sarican, G., Akgunduz, D. (2018). The impact of integrated STEM education on academic achievement, reflective thinking skills towards problem solving and permanence in learning in science education. Cypriot Journal of Educational Sciences, 13(1), 94-113. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1196043

article_title: Accelerating Vocabulary Development and Reading Comprehension in Grades 3-4-5 through an Inductive Vocabulary Model
citation: Michael R. Vitale & Nancy R. Romance. (2013). Accelerating Vocabulary Development and Reading Comprehension in Grades 3-4-5 through an Inductive Vocabulary Model. SREE Fall 2013 Conference Abstract. https://www.sree.org
title: Multi-part inductive vocabulary model using semantic word families within basal reading stories
description: A four-part instructional pattern built on 4-word semantic word families for 3 key vocabulary words in each basal reading story. Part 1 pre-teaches key words; Part 2 substitutes similar-meaning target words with queries about how the new word changes meaning; Part 3 substitutes untaught target words so students infer meaning in context; Part 4 has students present sentences about their own experience. The article describes it as "a multi-part, semantic word-family-oriented learning strategy to inductively expand vocabulary taught directly".
requirements: Pre-planning identifies 4-word semantic word families for 3 key vocabulary words per story, with project-developed story-specific vocabulary guides for teachers
constraints: Implemented within a district-adopted basal reading series; experimental teachers committed to teaching 8 stories over 18 weeks with follow-up support
target_learners: Grade 3-5 students in diverse elementary schools
examples: Teachers pre-taught key words, queried word meaning in context, substituted similar-meaning and untaught target words in 3-sentence blocks, and had students generate oral sentences from their own experience
key_sources: Michael R. Vitale & Nancy R. Romance. (2013). Accelerating Vocabulary Development and Reading Comprehension in Grades 3-4-5 through an Inductive Vocabulary Model. SREE Fall 2013 Conference Abstract. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED563063

article_title: Interactive Methods of Teaching Physics at Technical Universities
citation: Krišťák, Ľ., Němec, M., Danihelová, Z. (2014). Interactive Methods of Teaching Physics at Technical Universities. Informatics in Education, 13(1), 51–71. https://doi.org/10.15388/infedu.2014.03
title: Interactive P&E method (problem tasks and experiments)
description: The interactive P&E method is the authors' own teaching approach whose "main idea is interactive working with students with the help of experiment and problem tasks analyses". It proceeds in five phases: preparation of 5–10 minute concept blocks, teaching the block, assigning a problem task in one of five ways (text solved theoretically; text solved via real or computer-aided experiment; unfinished experiment solved theoretically then verified; finished experiment reasoned theoretically; finished experiment solved via video-analysis), class discussion with brainstorming and elimination of incorrect solutions, and multi-level feedback. It combines experiments, problem tasks, and elements of Peer Instruction, Interactive Lecture Demonstrations, Just-in-Time Teaching and Interactive Computer Based Tutorials.
requirements: A lecturer prepared with concept blocks and problem tasks, plus students' worksheets and teachers' guidelines for each way of task assignment
constraints: Developed and tested in first-year bachelor physics at technical universities in Slovakia with reduced lesson counts
Exam includes problem tasks as part of the feedback loop
target_learners: first-year bachelor students at technical universities
target_learning_goals: conceptual understanding of Newtonian mechanics and basic physics
examples: In 2010 method C divided lectures into blocks with a problem after each block and used P&E in seminars
In 2012 P&E was combined with new course books and PI was tested in one group
key_sources: Krišťák, Ľ., Němec, M., Danihelová, Z. (2014). Interactive Methods of Teaching Physics at Technical Universities. Informatics in Education, 13(1), 51–71. https://doi.org/10.15388/infedu.2014.03

article_title: Local Potential Integrated Science Video to Improve SPS and Concept Mastery
citation: Wilujeng, I., Suryadarma, I. G. P., Ertika, & Dwandaru, W. S. B. (2020). Local Potential Integrated Science Video to Improve SPS and Concept Mastery. International Journal of Instruction, 13(4), 197-214. https://doi.org/10.29333/iji.2020.13413a
title: Connect science learning to local potentials in the surrounding environment to contextualize concepts
description: The article argues that learning should incorporate activities connecting students to the real world, and that "the integration of local potentials and learning materials can correctly and contextually help students understand concepts." Local potentials include natural resources, human resources, geographical features, culture, and history of a particular location. Integration is expected to give students knowledge to care for, protect, and improve their environment.
requirements: Learning activities should require students to actively participate and perform direct observation of objects, since deeper concept mastery is encouraged only under those conditions
constraints: The article frames this within the Indonesian curriculum principle of diversification adjusted to education units, local potentials, and students' potential
examples: The MHP plant in Wukirsari Village, Singosaren, Imogiri, Bantul, using water from the Opak River, was integrated into the learning video and test indicators
key_sources: Wilujeng, I., Suryadarma, I. G. P., Ertika, & Dwandaru, W. S. B. (2020). Local Potential Integrated Science Video to Improve SPS and Concept Mastery. International Journal of Instruction, 13(4), 197-214. https://doi.org/10.29333/iji.2020.13413a

article_title: Reducing Test Anxiety among Third Grade Students through the Implementation of Relaxation Techniques
citation: Heidi A. Larson, Mera K. El Ramahi, Steven R. Conn, Lincoln A. Estes, and Amanda B. Ghibellini. (2010). Reducing Test Anxiety Among Third Grade Students Through the Implementation of Relaxation Techniques. Eastern Illinois University. https://www.city-data.com
title: Schools should incorporate brief relaxation-training programs into the curriculum to address test anxiety
description: Because high-stakes testing is unlikely to be eliminated in the near future and produces adverse behavioral, cognitive, and physiological effects in children, the article recommends that schools build relaxation training into regular practice. It states that "schools can play a role in addressing test anxiety by incorporating intervention programs such as relaxation training into the curriculum," and that school counselors and teachers can schedule daily time to teach students relaxation responses. The interventions are described as brief and not difficult for children to learn, and generalizable to life skills.
requirements: Scheduled time in the school day for counselors or teachers to lead relaxation training
constraints: If performance anxiety is not addressed in elementary school, the authors note it could continue through the adult years
target_learning_goals: responding to physiological and psychological responses to anxiety and stress
examples: The study's experimental group learned elevator breathing and guided relaxation in ten short sessions across five weeks within the school day
key_sources: Heidi A. Larson, Mera K. El Ramahi, Steven R. Conn, Lincoln A. Estes, and Amanda B. Ghibellini. (2010). Reducing Test Anxiety Among Third Grade Students Through the Implementation of Relaxation Techniques. Eastern Illinois University. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ885222

article_title: The Effect of Internet-Based Education on Student Success in Teaching of 8th Grade Triangles Subject
citation: Deniz KAYA, Cenk KESAN, Dilek IZGIOL. (2013). THE EFFECT OF INTERNET-BASED EDUCATION ON STUDENT SUCCESS IN TEACHING OF 8TH GRADE TRIANGLES SUBJECT. Turkish Online Journal of Distance Education-TOJDE, Volume: 14 Number: 1 Article 17. http://www.vitaminegitim.com
title: Internet-based education as a form of distance education transferring course materials via internet technologies
description: The article defines internet-based education as "one kind of distance education and a teaching system in which the internet technologies are used to transfer course materials to students", stressing that applications furthering education are made via the internet rather than education being carried out entirely online. It lets educators move lesson-necessary work outside the classroom and orient students to reinforcement applications, and it connects to blended learning, which integrates face-to-face interaction, online experiences, guided or self-directed work, digital references and group communications. The article contrasts it with conventional classrooms as discussion-based, flexible, result-oriented and student-independent.
requirements: Internet technologies and connectivity to transfer course materials and run interactive applications
constraints: The article notes internet-based education means applications are made via the internet, not that education is exactly carried out over the internet
target_learners: primary and secondary school students using school-supported online content
target_learning_goals: reinforcement of classroom learning across subject areas
examples: Table 1 contrasts conventional education (lesson based, structural, teacher centered, large classrooms) with internet-based instruction (discussion based, flexible, oriented results, independent student, small classrooms)
key_sources: Deniz KAYA, Cenk KESAN, Dilek IZGIOL. (2013). THE EFFECT OF INTERNET-BASED EDUCATION ON STUDENT SUCCESS IN TEACHING OF 8TH GRADE TRIANGLES SUBJECT. Turkish Online Journal of Distance Education-TOJDE, Volume: 14 Number: 1 Article 17. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1006259

article_title: The Role of Self-Assessment in Promoting Iranian EFL Learners' Motivation
citation: Parviz Birjandi, Nasrin Hadidi Tamjid. (2010). The Role of Self-assessment in Promoting Iranian EFL Learners' Motivation. English Language Teaching, 3(3). https://www.ccsenet.org/elt
title: 39-item intrinsic motivation questionnaire for EFL writing classes
description: A Likert-type questionnaire the researchers developed for this study, targeting situation-specific intrinsic motivation related to a writing course. Items were drawn from reviewed instruments (e.g., Deci and Ryan 1985; Guilloteaux and Dornyei 2008); after factor analysis items with loading below 0.3 were excluded, leaving 39 items. The pilot reliability "came out to be 0.84", and factors were "interest/enjoyment, perceived competence, value/importance, and effort".
requirements: Administered anonymously, as the authors believed anonymity might encourage more accurate and honest responses
constraints: Designed for the students' situation-specific motivational disposition in writing classes; it did not include items tapping general factors such as integrativeness
target_learners: Intermediate EFL university students in writing courses
target_learning_goals: Intrinsic motivation for learning English writing
examples: Piloted on 30 ESL learners (alpha 0.84, Table 1 reports .830/.841 for 50 items) and factor-analysed on 200 total cases; Appendix 2 lists the four factors with subscale alphas of 0.82, 0.83, 0.78 and 0.82
key_sources: Parviz Birjandi, Nasrin Hadidi Tamjid. (2010). The Role of Self-assessment in Promoting Iranian EFL Learners' Motivation. English Language Teaching, 3(3). https://www.ccsenet.org/elt

article_title: Effect of Self Regulated Learning Approach on Junior Secondary School Students' Achievement in Basic Science
citation: Nwafor Chika E, Abigail Chikaodinaka Obodo, Gabriel Okafor. (2015). Effect of Self Regulated Learning Approach on Junior Secondary School Students' Achievement in Basic Science. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.6, No.5. http://www.iiste.org
title: Include self-regulated learning instructional strategy in pre-service teacher curricula and provide regular teacher training on its use
description: Based on the finding that the SRL approach outperformed conventional teaching, the researchers recommend that "self-regulated learning instructional strategy should be included in the curriculum of pre-service teachers". They further recommend that conferences, seminars and workshops be organised regularly to educate basic science teachers on SRL strategies, and that curriculum agencies incorporate and emphasise SRL instruction strategies in the basic science curriculum.
requirements: Government agencies and professional bodies responsible for curriculum design and teacher education to act on the recommendation
constraints: Recommendation rests on a single quasi-experimental study in one education zone of Enugu State, Nigeria
target_learners: Pre-service teachers and practising basic science teachers
target_learning_goals: Capacity to implement self-regulated learning instructional strategies in basic science
examples: The study organised separate pre-experimental trainings for teachers in the treatment and control groups to establish uniform instructional standards
key_sources: Nwafor Chika E, Abigail Chikaodinaka Obodo, Gabriel Okafor. (2015). Effect of Self Regulated Learning Approach on Junior Secondary School Students' Achievement in Basic Science. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.6, No.5. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1083647

article_title: The Effect of Inquiry Training Learning Model Based on Just in Time Teaching for Problem Solving Skill
citation: Betty Turnip, Ida Wahyuni, Yul Ifda Tanjung. (2016). The Effect of Inquiry Training Learning Model Based on Just in Time Teaching for Problem Solving Skill. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.7, No.15. https://www.iiste.org
title: Five-phase Inquiry Training learning model combined with Just In Time Teaching (IT-JITT)
description: The article describes an instructional model that combines the Inquiry Training learning model with the Just In Time Teaching strategy so as "to streamline the learning time in the classroom using intermediate media information and communication technology". It proceeds through five phases: exposing problems via pre-class web assignments, finding problems through hypothesis formulation, reviewing data and conducting experiments in class, organizing and formulating explanations, and analyzing the research process with student presentations. The lecturer acts as facilitator and director during classroom experiments.
requirements: Pre-class assignments and materials delivered via a website so classroom time can start from the experiment phase
Lecturer-developed teaching materials and worksheets tested on students outside the sample
constraints: Evaluated in General Physics II with Physics Department students at State University of Medan
target_learners: undergraduate physics students in General Physics II
target_learning_goals: critical thinking and intellectual skills through inquiry
examples: Table 1 lays out the five phases with implementation activities, including web-delivered review and pre-class tasks, in-class experiments, and PowerPoint presentations assessed by the class
key_sources: Betty Turnip, Ida Wahyuni, Yul Ifda Tanjung. (2016). The Effect of Inquiry Training Learning Model Based on Just in Time Teaching for Problem Solving Skill. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.7, No.15. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1103095

article_title: The Effect of Inquiry Training Learning Model Based on Just in Time Teaching for Problem Solving Skill
citation: Betty Turnip, Ida Wahyuni, Yul Ifda Tanjung. (2016). The Effect of Inquiry Training Learning Model Based on Just in Time Teaching for Problem Solving Skill. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.7, No.15. https://www.iiste.org
title: Design physics lectures around problem solving and investigation using an inquiry approach
description: Based on the preliminary finding that students could not complete Polya's problem-solving stages, the article argues lecturers should "design learning activities based on problem s olving and investigation" using a model "with the inquiry approach", which "emphasizes the active role of students i n doing the learning". The aim is for students to understand physics concepts through scientific study and direct experiments rather than discussion alone.
requirements: Learning tools such as teaching materials, worksheets and a media website prepared in advance
Instruments for problem-solving ability tested before implementation
constraints: The cooperative model, in the authors' view, gives less influence on physics problem-solving ability because it focuses on discussion of subject matter rather than problem-solving results
target_learning_goals: discovering, developing and investigating students' own ideas
examples: The experimental class implemented the five-phase IT-JITT model with website-delivered pre-class work and in-class experiments, while the control class used cooperative learning
key_sources: Betty Turnip, Ida Wahyuni, Yul Ifda Tanjung. (2016). The Effect of Inquiry Training Learning Model Based on Just in Time Teaching for Problem Solving Skill. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.7, No.15. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1103095

article_title: The Effect of Presentation Strategy on Reading Comprehension of Iranian Intermediate EFL Learners
citation: Hooshang Khoshsima & Forouzan Rezaeiantiyar. (2014). The Effect of Presentation Strategy on Reading Comprehension of Iranian Intermediate EFL Learners. Advances in Language and Literary Studies, 5(3). https://doi.org/10.7575/aiac.alls.v.5n.3p.101
title: Interactive model of reading combining bottom-up and top-down processes
description: The article reviews three models of teaching reading — bottom-up, top-down and interactive — and presents the interactive model as the most complete account. As the article describes it, citing Grabe (1991), "this model takes into account different types of L1and L2 reading, considers both bottom-up processing and top-down processing, and recognizes its contribution to both the readers and the texts." The model holds that bottom-up and top-down processes interact and that neither alone can describe the entire reading process, incorporating prior knowledge and guessing processes. The article uses it as background framing for why strategy instruction should address multiple levels of processing.
requirements: Teachers should employ both bottom-up and top-down processes according to students' requirements, skills, abilities, and levels
constraints: Presented in the article as a literature-based theoretical framework attributed to Grabe (1991) and Rumelhart (1977), not tested in the study itself
examples: The article cites Rumelhart's (1977) statement that both sensory and nonsensory sources come together and reading is the joint application of all knowledge sources
key_sources: Hooshang Khoshsima & Forouzan Rezaeiantiyar. (2014). The Effect of Presentation Strategy on Reading Comprehension of Iranian Intermediate EFL Learners. Advances in Language and Literary Studies, 5(3). https://doi.org/10.7575/aiac.alls.v.5n.3p.101

article_title: Impact of the Interactive Story Reading Method on Receptive and Expressive Language Vocabulary of Children
citation: Okyay, O. & Kandir, A. (2017). Impact of the Interactive Story Reading Method on Receptive and Expressive Language Vocabulary of Children. European Journal of Educational Research, 6(3), 395-406. http://www.eu-jer.com/
title: Interactive Story Reading Program: nine researcher-authored stories on scientific concepts with pre- and post-story activities
description: An eight-week classroom program in which experiment group teachers, after three days of training, read nine stories on scientific concepts authored by the researchers using the interactive story reading method, with preparatory and evaluative activities. The article states teachers "had read the nine stories on scientific concepts, authored by the researchers, using the interactive story reading method, and implemented activities to prepare for and to evaluate the stories." Activities ran two days a week for 45-50 minutes a day, with the researcher providing ongoing guidance.
requirements: Teachers received a three-days training on the method's features, communication with children, physical environment, stimulants, and methods and techniques before application
constraints: The program was implemented with 48-72 month old children at nurseries of primary schools in Ankara; the article does not report effects outside this setting
examples: Experiment group teachers read nine stories on scientific concepts over eight weeks, two days a week for 45-50 minutes a day, with activities before and after each story
key_sources: Okyay, O. & Kandir, A. (2017). Impact of the Interactive Story Reading Method on Receptive and Expressive Language Vocabulary of Children. European Journal of Educational Research, 6(3), 395-406. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1149725

article_title: "I Like Computers but My Favourite Is Playing outside with My Friends": Young Children's Beliefs about Computers
citation: Hatzigianni, M. (2014). 'I like computers but my favourite is playing outside with my friends': Young children's beliefs about computers. International Research in Early Childhood Education, 5(1). https://www.education.monash.edu.au/irecejournal/
title: Integrated, playful use of computers as one more classroom centre in early childhood settings
description: The pattern treats computers as classroom 'tools' integrated into the daily program rather than as a separate subject, following NAEYC guidelines. The computer was "'one more centre' in the preschool class and the extension of curriculum areas was attempted", with activities extending current curriculum topics. The study's conclusion identifies "the development of a holistic , integrated and playful approach to children's use of technology" as a prerequisite for computers to contribute to learning, with tasks enjoyable for both teachers and students.
requirements: developmentally appropriate, integrated implementation following NAEYC guidelines
teacher familiarity with the software and planned activities
constraints: the study recommends this approach but its exploratory design does not establish causal effectiveness
target_learners: young children (preschool and early primary, ages four to six)
target_learning_goals: curriculum learning extended through computer activities
examples: The intervention placed the computer as one more centre in the preschool class and extended curriculum areas, e.g. drawing shapes in Paint during a shapes unit
key_sources: Hatzigianni, M. (2014). 'I like computers but my favourite is playing outside with my friends': Young children's beliefs about computers. International Research in Early Childhood Education, 5(1). https://www.education.monash.edu.au/irecejournal/

article_title: On Non-English Majors' Strategy Training in English Reading Comprehension
citation: Xiaoling Yang. (2017). On Non-English Majors' Strategy Training in English Reading Comprehension. English Language Teaching, 10(10). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v10n10p153
title: Interactive model of reading comprehension
description: The article presents the Interactive Model, first proposed by D. Rumelhart in 1977, as the reading theory underpinning the strategy-training study. It posits "a constant interaction between bo ttom-up and top-down processing in reading", in which the reader constructs meaning by integrating text information with information already in memory. The article argues that one corollary is that the use of reading strategies in comprehension is indispensable.
requirements: Readers must draw on multiple knowledge sources simultaneously, including letter-sound correspondences, word meaning, syntactic knowledge and memory of preceding text
constraints: The article notes top-down models tend to emphasize higher-level skills at the expense of lower-level skills such as rapid and accurate identification of lexical and grammatical forms
examples: The article uses the Interactive Model to justify treating reading strategy use as indispensable and to motivate the strategy-training experiment
key_sources: Xiaoling Yang. (2017). On Non-English Majors' Strategy Training in English Reading Comprehension. English Language Teaching, 10(10). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v10n10p153

article_title: Experimental Study of Middle-Term Training in Social Cognition in Preschoolers
citation: Marine Houssa, Nathalie Nader-Grosbois. (2016). Experimental Study of Middle-term Training in Social Cognition in Preschoolers. Journal of Education and Training Studies. https://doi.org/10.11114/jets.v4i1.972
title: Focus preschool social problem solving training on the intersubjective justification level, which matches children's zone of proximal development
description: The article reports that trained children provided fewer wrong/no answers and more intersubjective explanations, and that "the conceptual level of justification generally emerges later in development". It concludes that "focusing training sessions on the intersubjective level is effective because it matches children‟s zone of proximal development". Training should therefore elicit justifications one level above the child's pretest level rather than target conceptual-level reasoning too early.
requirements: Assess each child's justification level at pretest so the experimenter can elicit the next, more complex level
constraints: The conceptual level of justification generally emerges later in development, so trained preschoolers used hardly any conceptual justification
target_learning_goals: social reasoning and justification of judgments about others' social behavior
examples: In pre-test, children tended to justify their answers at a descriptive level or produced a wrong/no answer; in post-test, the trained children provided fewer wrong/no answers and more intersubjective explanations
key_sources: Marine Houssa, Nathalie Nader-Grosbois. (2016). Experimental Study of Middle-term Training in Social Cognition in Preschoolers. Journal of Education and Training Studies. https://doi.org/10.11114/jets.v4i1.972

article_title: Effects of Instruction-Supported Learning with Worked Examples in Quantitative Method Training
citation: Kai Wagner, Martin Klein, Eric Klopp, Thomas Puhl & Robin Stark. (2013). Effects of Instruction-Supported Learning with Worked Examples in Quantitative Method Training. Higher Education Studies, 3(3). https://doi.org/10.5539/hes.v3n3p1
title: Integrated learning environments combining instruction-oriented and problem-oriented design principles
description: The article applies the concept of integrated learning environments (Reinmann & Mandl, 2006), which "combine elem ents from instruction-oriented and problem-oriented learning approaches in an effort to maximize their respective advantages and to minimize their disadvantages". Instruction-oriented principles included elaborative sequencing of increasing complexity and structure-emphasizing example sets; problem-oriented principles included authentic, relevant tasks and multiple perspectives to avoid inert knowledge. The learning environment operationalized this with twelve worked examples based on a real study.
requirements: Worked examples must be contextualized in authentic, relevant tasks when transferred to ill-structured domains
constraints: The article notes results can only be attributed to the combination of the described didactic methods, as the approach was not experimentally varied
target_learners: advanced university students in educational science
target_learning_goals: applicable knowledge for interpreting empirical results
transfer of statistical knowledge to new problems
examples: A 20-page text outlining a real experimental study with twelve worked examples structured as question – empirical evidence – interpretation, sorted by ascending complexity
key_sources: Kai Wagner, Martin Klein, Eric Klopp, Thomas Puhl & Robin Stark. (2013). Effects of Instruction-Supported Learning with Worked Examples in Quantitative Method Training. Higher Education Studies, 3(3). https://doi.org/10.5539/hes.v3n3p1

article_title: Exploring the Classroom: Teaching Science in Early Childhood
citation: Dejonckheere, P. J. N., De Wit, N., Van de Keere, K., & Vervaet, S. (2016). Exploring the classroom: Teaching science in early childhood. International Electronic Journal of Elementary Education, 8(4), 537-558. https://www.iejee.com
title: Inquiry-based preschool science with probe questions and structured phases supports scientific reasoning development
description: The article presents an inquiry-based didactic method for preschool science consisting of 15 activities across 7 weeks, each structured in three phases: an introduction phase, an exploration phase, and a trigger phase. In the trigger phase, "a teacher asked probe questions to direct the child's attention to the phenomenon that occurred and to stimulate the child to manipulate and explore variables, causes and consequences of the observed event". This design aims to develop domain-general process skills such as observing, describing, comparing, questioning, predicting, experimenting, reflecting and cooperating.
requirements: Activities must be connected to classroom themes and children's interests to reach maximal immersion in the environment.
Teachers must receive specific guidelines and probe questions for each activity.
constraints: The study could not determine the exact contribution of particular components such as probe questions, introduction activities, demonstrations, or cooperative learning.
The article notes it is probably not necessary to engage in all 15 activities to gain these results.
target_learning_goals: scientific reasoning and control of variables strategy
domain-general process skills such as observing, predicting and experimenting
examples: Children explored sinking and floating, balance scales, slopes, musical glasses, magnets, gears, shadows and other materials in a science corner during free play initiative.
key_sources: Dejonckheere, P. J. N., De Wit, N., Van de Keere, K., & Vervaet, S. (2016). Exploring the classroom: Teaching science in early childhood. International Electronic Journal of Elementary Education, 8(4), 537-558. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1109852

article_title: Effect of Demonstration Method of Teaching on Students' Achievement in Agricultural Science
citation: Daluba, Noah Ekeyi. (2013). Effect of Demonstration Method of Teaching on Students' Achievement in Agricultural Science. World Journal of Education, 3(6). https://doi.org/10.5430/wje.v3n6p1
title: Teachers should integrate the demonstration method into agricultural science teaching instead of relying on the conventional lecture method
description: The article recommends that teachers thoroughly integrate the demonstration method — in which the teacher shows learners step-by-step how to do a task while learners watch with the intention to act later — into secondary school agricultural science teaching. The recommendation rests on the study's finding that demonstration-taught students significantly outperformed lecture-taught students on the ASAT.
requirements: Teachers need training in demonstration techniques; the study used selected trained agricultural science teachers to deliver both conditions.
constraints: The finding is limited to SSII students in the Kogi East Education Zone of Kogi State, Nigeria, and to the five agricultural science topics covered by the ASAT.
target_learning_goals: Agricultural science knowledge and practical skills
examples: In the study, six schools were assigned to demonstration or lecture teaching for two months, with 240 students in each condition.
key_sources: Daluba, Noah Ekeyi. (2013). Effect of Demonstration Method of Teaching on Students' Achievement in Agricultural Science. World Journal of Education, 3(6). https://doi.org/10.5430/wje.v3n6p1

article_title: Increasing Pupil Motivation: Evaluation Report and Executive Summary
citation: Luke Sibieta, Ellen Greaves, Barbara Sianesi. (2014). Increasing Pupil Motivation: Evaluation Report and Executive Summary. Education Endowment Foundation. https://www.educationendowmentfoundation.org.uk
title: Increasing Pupil Motivation loss-framed incentive schemes (financial and event)
description: Two incentive schemes for Year 11 pupils in deprived English secondary schools, designed by the University of Bristol project team. The financial scheme gave pupils £80 per half-term, deducted at fixed rates for missing thresholds in attendance, behaviour, classwork and homework; the event scheme used tickets lost in the same ratio, with pupils attending a pupil-chosen event if enough tickets were retained. Both were "Framed to pupils as money was 'theirs to lose'", incorporating loss aversion, and were paired with feedback letters detailing performance each half-term.
requirements: Effort must be monitored by schools across the four domains of attendance, behaviour, classwork and homework
Feedback letters to pupils detailing performance and how it determined rewards
constraints: The design does not allow the effects of incentives and feedback to be estimated separately
The design does not allow a direct test of whether loss-framed rewards are more effective
The trial tested one particular level of incentives; effects of higher or lower levels would need further evidence
target_learners: Year 11 pupils (aged 15-16) in relatively deprived secondary schools
target_learning_goals: GCSE attainment in Maths, English and Science
Pupil effort in attendance, behaviour, classwork and homework
examples: Pupils in the financial arm started with £320, losing £10 for missing attendance or behaviour thresholds and £30 for classwork or homework; event-arm pupils needed 12 of a maximum 16 tickets to attend trips such as theme parks, ice skating and the Houses of Parliament
key_sources: Luke Sibieta, Ellen Greaves, Barbara Sianesi. (2014). Increasing Pupil Motivation: Evaluation Report and Executive Summary. Education Endowment Foundation. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED581249

article_title: Understanding the Integrated Learning Course Model: "Academic Transition to Tertiary Education"
citation: David R. Arendale. (2014). Understanding the Integrated Learning Course Model: Academic Transition to Tertiary Education. International Journal of Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.5430/ijhe.v3n4p1
title: Integrated Learning (IL) course model: a linked-course learning community pairing study-strategy instruction with a rigorous content course
description: The IL course model links a learning-strategies and cultural-transition course to an academically-challenging companion course so that "the IL course is customized to use content of its companion class as contex t for mastering learning strategies and orienting students to the rigor of the tertiary learning environment." Its innovations were targeting difficult courses rather than student deficits, immediate application of study skills to real course materials, use of linked courses as a learning community, and explicit attention to cultural transition for historically-underrepresented students. It draws on situated learning, sheltered instruction, constructivism, socio-constructivism and the Zone of Proximal Development, and fits the linked-courses type of learning community.
requirements: A supportive academic department hosting the IL course and offering the paired content course
An IL instructor who knows what happens in the target class by meeting the faculty member weekly
Ongoing professional development for the IL instructor before and during the term
constraints: Reserved for students admitted to the TRIO Student Support Services program; enrollment requires advisor permission
Classes targeted must show 30 percent or more D/F/withdrawal grades before IL introduction
target_learners: First-generation, low-income, and historically-underrepresented first-year tertiary students in TRIO Student Support Services
target_learning_goals: Cultural and academic transition to tertiary education
examples: At UMN, PsTL 1081 is linked to Principles of Psychology and PsTL 1082 sections are linked to Principles of Biological Science and Introduction to Chemistry
key_sources: David R. Arendale. (2014). Understanding the Integrated Learning Course Model: Academic Transition to Tertiary Education. International Journal of Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.5430/ijhe.v3n4p1

article_title: Design and Effects of a Concept Focused Discussion Environment in E-Learning
citation: Yilmaz, E. O., & Yurdugul, H. (2016). Design and effects of a concept focused discussion environment in e-learning. Eurasian Journal of Educational Research, 63, 353-374. https://doi.org/10.14689/ejer.2016.63.20
title: Integrate discussion environments with content in online learning to raise learning perceptions and reduce learning-style-based differences
description: The article recommends that online discussion environments be integrated with the content environment rather than kept as separate hierarchical modules, because physical separation between content and discussion negatively influences the integration and motivation of learning. Its own experiment showed that an integrated, concept-focused design raised cognitive learning and usefulness perceptions and equalized perceptions across learning styles.
requirements: Discussion access must be reachable from within the content without leaving the content screen, e.g. via concept links or sliding discussion frames
constraints: Evidence comes from one six-week course with 90 undergraduates comparing one integrated design against one threaded design; affective perception showed no significant difference
target_learners: university students in blended online courses
target_learning_goals: learner-content and learner-learner interaction around course concepts
examples: The study embedded CFDE in an LMS for the course Teaching Principle and Methods over six weeks and compared it with a traditional threaded discussion environment in a randomized post-test-only design
key_sources: Yilmaz, E. O., & Yurdugul, H. (2016). Design and effects of a concept focused discussion environment in e-learning. Eurasian Journal of Educational Research, 63, 353-374. https://doi.org/10.14689/ejer.2016.63.20

article_title: Effectiveness of an Interactive Multimedia Learning Package in Developing Attitude towards Mathematics
citation: P. Muthulakshmi, A. Veliappan. (2015). Effectiveness of an Interactive Multimedia Learning Package in Developing Attitude Towards Mathematics. i-manager's Journal on School Educational Technology, Vol. 11, No. 3, December 2015 - February 2016.
title: Investigator-developed interactive multimedia learning package and ATMa attitude inventory for standard IX mathematics
description: The article's treatment is an "Interactive Multimedia Learning Package developed by the investigator" used to teach selected standard IX mathematics topics, compared against conventional teaching. Attitude was measured with the Attitude towards Mathematics (ATMa, 2013) tool developed by the investigators, whose "reliability of coefficient of the tool ATMa using the Spearman Prophecy formula was found to be 0.89". Content validity was checked by psychologists, mathematics teacher educators and language experts.
requirements: Administered as a treatment replacing or supplementing traditional teaching over a treatment period, with pre-test and post-test of attitude
constraints: Developed and evaluated only for selected standard IX mathematics topics with 42 high school students
examples: Experimental group taught selected standard IX topics through the package while the control group received the traditional method
key_sources: P. Muthulakshmi, A. Veliappan. (2015). Effectiveness of an Interactive Multimedia Learning Package in Developing Attitude Towards Mathematics. i-manager's Journal on School Educational Technology, Vol. 11, No. 3, December 2015 - February 2016. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1131820

article_title: Effectiveness of an Interactive Multimedia Learning Package in Developing Attitude towards Mathematics
citation: P. Muthulakshmi, A. Veliappan. (2015). Effectiveness of an Interactive Multimedia Learning Package in Developing Attitude Towards Mathematics. i-manager's Journal on School Educational Technology, Vol. 11, No. 3, December 2015 - February 2016.
title: Integrate interactive multimedia learning packages into traditional mathematics teaching at high school level to develop students' attitude towards mathematics
description: Based on the finding that multimedia-taught students showed significantly higher post-test attitude, the authors recommend that "the traditional method of teaching mathematics can be integrated by the interactive multimedia learning package to improve attitude towards mathematics". They further recommend curriculum framers include such packages as a teaching method at high school level, and that school management give teachers sufficient opportunity to use them.
requirements: School administration awareness of techno-pedagogical practices and provision of "sufficient chance to the teachers to use the same at their classroom"
constraints: Recommendation rests on a single small (42-student) study measuring attitude, not achievement
examples: The study itself taught selected standard IX topics with the package while a matched control group received traditional instruction
key_sources: P. Muthulakshmi, A. Veliappan. (2015). Effectiveness of an Interactive Multimedia Learning Package in Developing Attitude Towards Mathematics. i-manager's Journal on School Educational Technology, Vol. 11, No. 3, December 2015 - February 2016. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1131820

article_title: Reusing Comprehensive Charts of Tense Forms to Teach EFL Students in a University of Science and Technology
citation: Tsai, Min-hsiu. (2017). Reusing Comprehensive Charts of Tense Forms to Teach EFL Students in a University of Science and Technology. World Journal of Education, 7(3). https://doi.org/10.5430/wje.v7n3p115
title: Instructional Mode for teaching tense forms with the Comprehensive Charts
description: A circling classroom sequence appended to the article (Appendix 4, Figure 1) consisting of "four classroom teaching activities with three teaching approaches which are the grammar-translation, the cooperative learning (the Tic Tae Toe game), and the communicative approaches, as well as four practices/tests". Teaching of active and passive tenses is divided into two sections to avoid confusing learners, and the mode interchanges teaching with practice/test so users may take a second round. It integrates reading, listening, speaking, and writing practice.
requirements: Sufficient practice opportunities such as form recognition, gap filling, sentence building, and essay writing
A communicative teaching approach added to the presentation process if teachers value communicative grammar learning
constraints: Active and passive tenses are taught in separate sessions due to the complexity and variety of the tenses
target_learning_goals: mastering English tense-aspect forms across the four language skills
examples: The researcher teaches ten of the twelve active tenses then asks students to deduce the future perfect and future perfect continuous tenses, which students very often figure out correctly
key_sources: Tsai, Min-hsiu. (2017). Reusing Comprehensive Charts of Tense Forms to Teach EFL Students in a University of Science and Technology. World Journal of Education, 7(3). https://doi.org/10.5430/wje.v7n3p115
