article_title: Reusing Comprehensive Charts of Tense Forms to Teach EFL Students in a University of Science and Technology
citation: Tsai, Min-hsiu. (2017). Reusing Comprehensive Charts of Tense Forms to Teach EFL Students in a University of Science and Technology. World Journal of Education, 7(3). https://doi.org/10.5430/wje.v7n3p115
title: Instance Theory as an account for storing tense-form knowledge for future retrieval
description: The article proposes storing grammatical knowledge of tense forms in learners' memory for future retrieval based on Instance Theory. It cites Logan's proposal that "as individual solutions to problems accumulated in memory a transition in problem-solving procedures took place", and Truscott's UG-instance theory approach, which the article says could be applied to noisy input, undoing of errors, transfer and fossilization, and the non-discrete character of learning. The theory de-emphasizes abstract principles, focusing on storage and retrieval of specific experiences or instances.
requirements: Accumulation of specific instances in memory through practice and exposure
constraints: The article states whether Instance Theory is totally applicable to tense-form teaching needs more research
target_learning_goals: retaining and retrieving grammatical tense-form knowledge
examples: The article likens the approach to Chinese learners memorizing and reciting content before comprehension, an order of imitation, production, then comprehension
key_sources: Tsai, Min-hsiu. (2017). Reusing Comprehensive Charts of Tense Forms to Teach EFL Students in a University of Science and Technology. World Journal of Education, 7(3). https://doi.org/10.5430/wje.v7n3p115

article_title: Towards a Practical Framework of the Remediation of Cognitive Skills at Primary Level
citation: Outi Kyrö-Ämmälä & Kaarina Määttä. (2011). Towards a Practical Framework of the Remediation of Cognitive Skills at Primary Level. World Journal of Education. https://doi.org/10.5430/wje.v1n1p28
title: Build intrinsic motivation and replace external rewards with task-related rewards
description: Because intrinsic motivation is emphasised in the development of cognitive skills, the article holds that "It is essential that a child wants to learn without any external sanction or reward". Teachers should transmit enthusiasm for tasks, explain their meaning at the lesson's start, and keep assignments neither too easy nor too hard. Since pupils may become addicted to stickers and similar external rewards, the article recommends task-related rewards such as more challenging tasks, more demanding textbooks, added responsibility, or working as an auxiliary teacher, which strengthen sense of competency and self-esteem.
requirements: The teacher's own attitude towards the tasks influences the emergence of intrinsic motivation
constraints: External rewards are described as fairly common at primary level but risk making pupils dependent on them
examples: The article suggests giving a pupil a new and more challenging task, a more demanding textbook, or a teacher's-helper role as rewards
key_sources: Outi Kyrö-Ämmälä & Kaarina Määttä. (2011). Towards a Practical Framework of the Remediation of Cognitive Skills at Primary Level. World Journal of Education. https://doi.org/10.5430/wje.v1n1p28

article_title: Improving Preservice Teachers' Phonemic Awareness, Morphological Awareness and Orthographic Knowledge
citation: McNeill, B. C. (2018). Improving Preservice Teachers' Phonemic Awareness, Morphological Awareness and Orthographic Knowledge. Australian Journal of Teacher Education, 43(1). http://ro.ecu.edu.au/ajte/vol43/iss1/2
title: Integrate phonemic and morphological awareness content into general literacy coursework with sufficient course time for knowledge building
description: The article recommends embedding metalinguistic knowledge for spelling instruction within general literacy courses rather than treating it as a one-off workshop, because one-off sessions may imply the content is an 'add on' and may not allow mastery. The results "signal the importance of integrating phonemic and morphological awareness content into general literacy coursework for students". The authors add that "an appropriate amount of course time must be devoted to the content to enable students more time to build knowledge and integrate that knowledge with other coursework whilst considering what is feasible within teacher education programmes".
requirements: Content must be embedded within an existing literacy education course with enough hours to build and integrate knowledge, as in the evaluated 10-hour (5 x 2-hour lecture) format
constraints: Contact time within teacher preparation programmes is limited, so time allocation must remain feasible; the optimal number of hours is not yet established
target_learners: first-year preservice teachers in undergraduate teacher education
examples: The evaluated course devoted approximately 4 hours to phonological awareness, 2 hours each to orthographic and morphological awareness, and 2 hours to spelling analysis and instructional planning using 17 children's spelling samples, within a blended model with online recordings
key_sources: McNeill, B. C. (2018). Improving Preservice Teachers' Phonemic Awareness, Morphological Awareness and Orthographic Knowledge. Australian Journal of Teacher Education, 43(1). http://ro.ecu.edu.au/ajte/vol43/iss1/2

article_title: Getting a Good Start in School: Differential Effects of "INSIGHTS" on the Behaviors and Engagement of Children with Challenging Temperaments
citation: O'Connor, E. E., McCormick, M. P., Cappella, E., & McClowry, S. G. (2014). Getting a Good Start in School: Differential Effects of INSIGHTS on the Behaviors and Engagement of Children with Challenging Temperaments. SREE Spring 2014 Conference. https://sree.org/
title: INSIGHTS into Children's Temperament: a temperament-based SEL program for early elementary classrooms
description: INSIGHTS is a social-emotional learning program that "provides teachers and caregivers with a framework for supporting the individual differences of children" and teaches temperament-matched behavior management strategies. Children participate in classroom curricula designed to enhance empathy for different temperaments and to use problem-solving techniques for daily dilemmas. A primary goal is improving the goodness-of-fit between children and their classroom environment. It was evaluated in a school-randomized trial against a supplemental reading attention-control condition.
requirements: Delivered as 10-week classroom interventions in kindergarten and first grade with training for teachers and caregivers in temperament-matched behavior management
target_learners: kindergarten and early elementary students in low-income urban schools
examples: Eleven of 22 schools were randomized to INSIGHTS (n = 225 children, 57 teachers); the other eleven hosted a supplemental reading program as attention control.
key_sources: O'Connor, E. E., McCormick, M. P., Cappella, E., & McClowry, S. G. (2014). Getting a Good Start in School: Differential Effects of INSIGHTS on the Behaviors and Engagement of Children with Challenging Temperaments. SREE Spring 2014 Conference. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED562775

article_title: An Efficacy Study of Interleaved Mathematics Practice. Revised
citation: Doug Rohrer, Robert F. Dedrick, Kaleena Burgess. (2013). An Efficacy Study of Interleaved Mathematics Practice. SREE Fall 2013 Conference. https://www.sree.org
title: Interleaved mathematics assignment intervention (rearranged practice problems)
description: An instructional element in which the problems of a typical mathematics course are rearranged so that most problems in each assignment come from previous lessons, arranged in interleaved order. All students received the same practice problems, but "the problems were rearranged to produce two versions of each assignment." In the interleaved condition, "just 4 of the 12 problems appeared together in one assignment, and the remaining 8 were distributed across subsequent assignments." Students received 10 assignments over an 8-week period covering 12 problems on each of four kinds.
requirements: The same set of practice problems must be available for rearrangement into blocked or interleaved versions
Assignments are distributed after solved examples are presented and solutions reviewed the following school day
constraints: Evaluated with seventh grade middle school mathematics content on four focal problem kinds over 8 weeks
target_learners: seventh grade middle school mathematics students
target_learning_goals: retention and test performance on multiple kinds of mathematics problems
examples: After a lesson on ratios, an interleaved assignment included a small block of four ratio problems and one problem from each of eight previous lessons, with the remaining eight ratio problems distributed across future assignments.
key_sources: Doug Rohrer, Robert F. Dedrick, Kaleena Burgess. (2013). An Efficacy Study of Interleaved Mathematics Practice. SREE Fall 2013 Conference. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED563060

article_title: The Effects of Intertextual Reading Approach on the Development of Creative Writing Skills
citation: Akdal, D. & Şahin, A. (2014). The effects of intertextual reading approach on the development of creative writing skills. Eurasian Journal of Educational Research, 54, 171-186. https://dergipark.org.tr/en/pub/ejer
title: Intertextual reading as producing new meanings by setting relationships among texts
description: The article frames intertextuality as texts sharing with and cooperating with other texts, and defines intertextual reading as "producing new meanings by setting up relationships among the thoughts and ideas of the texts" (Akyol, 2010), running two or more texts at the same time to get meaning. On this account, reading involves discussing texts, and intertextual reading and meaning formation allow the reader to think intertextually and develop alternative perspectives. The study operationalizes this framework through four connection categories applied during language instruction.
requirements: Readers make connections across multiple texts rather than reading a single text in isolation
constraints: The article notes there is not a route directing the intertextual reader, who gets rid of limited meaning restrictions of texts (Irwin, 2004, as cited)
examples: The study used intertextual connection categories prepared by Pappas et al. (translated by Ünal, 2007) applied in four categorical operations during instruction.
key_sources: Akdal, D. & Şahin, A. (2014). The effects of intertextual reading approach on the development of creative writing skills. Eurasian Journal of Educational Research, 54, 171-186. https://dergipark.org.tr/en/pub/ejer

article_title: The Role of Cognitive Style in the Collocational Knowledge Development of Iranian EFL Learners through Input Flood Treatment
citation: Elaheh Hamed Mahvelati & Jayakaran Mukundan. (2012). The Role of Cognitive Style in the Collocational Knowledge Development of Iranian EFL Learners through Input Flood Treatment. English Language Teaching, 5(10). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v5n10p105
title: Input flood treatment as an implicit collocation instruction technique
description: Input flood treatment is an input enhancement technique in which the incidence of target items is artificially increased in texts learners read, without explicit instruction or feedback. The article defines it as "the artificially increased incidence of the target items in the audio and visual texts that learners are exposed to without any explicit instruction or feedback", so that learning the target items is a by-product of comprehension activity. In the study, experimental learners read texts containing target collocations and answered comprehension questions, summarized, discussed, or unscrambled sentences, with no mention of the collocations.
requirements: Target items must occur with artificially increased frequency in the input while learners' attention is not directly drawn to them; learners engage in comprehension-focused tasks
constraints: The article reports the treatment was not durable for field-dependent learners and suggests they need more explicit treatment types
target_learning_goals: learning lexical and grammatical collocations implicitly
examples: Experimental materials included reading texts with increased target-collocation frequency, comprehension questions, oral or written summaries, and sentence/paragraph unscrambling tasks.
key_sources: Elaheh Hamed Mahvelati & Jayakaran Mukundan. (2012). The Role of Cognitive Style in the Collocational Knowledge Development of Iranian EFL Learners through Input Flood Treatment. English Language Teaching, 5(10). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v5n10p105

article_title: Digital Literacy and New Technological Perspectives
citation: Elvia Ilaria Feola. (2016). Digital Literacy and New Technological Perspectives. Universal Journal of Educational Research 4(9): 2174-2180. https://doi.org/10.13189/ujer.2016.040929
title: Instant DCA (Digital Competence Assessment) questionnaire
description: The Instant DCA is "a questionnaire easy to apply and verify that analyzes the three dimensions: technological, cognitive and ethical". Its technological items concern the "ability to identify and solve" difficulties arising when working with media and reading typical interfaces; the cognitive dimension measures understanding texts and data organisation, analysis and critical evaluation of the relevance and reliability of information; the ethical dimension covers protection of personal data, respect of netiquette and awareness of the social implications of technology use. It was administered at the start (October) and end (January) of the course to establish learner profiles.
requirements: Administration at both the beginning and the end of the training period to establish pre-post profiles.
target_learners: university students in primary education sciences
target_learning_goals: measuring digital competence across technological, cognitive and ethical dimensions
examples: Used as the pre-test in October and re-administered in January, with T tests applied to the differences between the averages.
key_sources: Elvia Ilaria Feola. (2016). Digital Literacy and New Technological Perspectives. Universal Journal of Educational Research 4(9): 2174-2180. https://doi.org/10.13189/ujer.2016.040929

article_title: The Impact of Authentic Materials and Tasks on Students' Communicative Competence at a Colombian Language School
citation: Castillo Losada, C. A., Insuasty, E. A., & Jaime Osorio, M. F. (2017). The impact of authentic materials and tasks on students’ communicative competence at a Colombian language school. PROFILE Issues in Teachers’ Professional Development, 19(1), 89-104. http://dx.doi.org/10.15446/profile.v19n1.56763
title: Integrate authentic materials with authentic tasks within a pedagogical project framework rather than using materials in isolation
description: The article's central design recommendation: authentic materials should be implemented within a systematic methodological framework of enabling tasks and pedagogical projects, because materials alone do not produce learning. The experimental teacher stated that "it is tasks (what students do with the materials) and not the authentic materials per se that provokes learning", and the discussion warns isolated use "may fall short in the exploitation of the linguistic and cultural richness of the input".
requirements: A well-structured plan or framework preventing teachers from using authentic materials in an isolated way or just as fillers
Detailed lesson planning covering material selection and transitions between pre-activity, activity, and post-activity
A high sense of commitment from the teacher and an in-service training or follow-up plan
constraints: The plan should not be rigid and can be modified according to the teacher's perception and learners' response
Some students seemed confused and overwhelmed by the input and tasks
target_learners: A2 level EFL students in foreign language learning contexts
examples: The nine-week intervention combined enabling tasks (advertisements, Melbourne city tour videos, map reading) with two projects, Tourism in Neiva and Pen-pals, in which learners created touristic stands, brochures, and exchanged letters
key_sources: Castillo Losada, C. A., Insuasty, E. A., & Jaime Osorio, M. F. (2017). The impact of authentic materials and tasks on students’ communicative competence at a Colombian language school. PROFILE Issues in Teachers’ Professional Development, 19(1), 89-104. http://dx.doi.org/10.15446/profile.v19n1.56763

article_title: Exploring Strategies That Influence Children's Physical Activity Self-Efficacy
citation: Merav W. Efrat. (2017). Exploring Strategies That Influence Children's Physical Activity Self-Efficacy. Contemporary Issues in Education Research, 10(2). https://clutejournals.com/index.php/cier
title: Internalization of teacher encouragement into reduced dependence on external prompts for recess activity
description: The article offers an explanatory account for why teacher encouragement raised adult encouragement barrier self-efficacy: children may internalize a teacher's encouragement rather than needing continued external prompting. As the author puts it, "when teachers encourage children to be active, they may internalize the encouragement and become less dependent on external sources of encouragement to motivate them to be active during recess." The account is framed via Bandura's self-efficacy construct and an interaction with children's normal developmental processes by which adults' influence on ability perceptions declines with age.
requirements: Grounded in Bandura's self-efficacy construct as defined in the article: a judgment of one's capability to accomplish a certain level of performance
constraints: Offered as the author's interpretation, not a directly tested mechanism; the study measured self-efficacy, not physical activity amounts
target_learning_goals: self-efficacy for physical activity during recess
examples: The Discussion proposes that a small dose of teacher encouragement may speed developmental processes reducing adults' influence on children's perceptions of their physical abilities
key_sources: Merav W. Efrat. (2017). Exploring Strategies That Influence Children's Physical Activity Self-Efficacy. Contemporary Issues in Education Research, 10(2). https://clutejournals.com/index.php/cier

article_title: The Effect of Teaching Interlanguage Pragmatics on Interpretation Ability of Iranian Translation Students
citation: Mahnaz Mahmoudi Ravesh, Hossein Heidari Tabrizi. (2017). The Effect of Teaching Interlanguage Pragmatics on Interpretation Ability of Iranian Translation Students. Advances in Language and Literary Studies 8(3). https://doi.org/10.7575/aiac.alls.v.8n.3p.44
title: Incorporate interlanguage pragmatic features into university interpretation and translation courses
description: The article recommends that university professors of translation pay attention to the finding that ILP instruction improved interpretation ability and, where required, incorporate ILP features into their courses. It argues that knowledge of ILP features is important in comprehending the situation and then translating it into the mother tongue, and that any educational context concerned with improving pragmatic awareness can incorporate these elements into its curriculum, syllabuses or textbooks.
requirements: Instructors need a set of necessary ILP features to provide to students, as the article states more attention needs to be paid to whether students are provided with them
constraints: The article notes teaching pragmatics can involve a high degree of face threat and that available pedagogical resources are limited, citing Matsuda (1999)
target_learners: BA undergraduate translation students in an Iranian EFL university context
examples: During a two-month period in the semester, the experimental group was presented interlanguage pragmatic features in their interpretation course while the control group received no ILP instruction
key_sources: Mahnaz Mahmoudi Ravesh, Hossein Heidari Tabrizi. (2017). The Effect of Teaching Interlanguage Pragmatics on Interpretation Ability of Iranian Translation Students. Advances in Language and Literary Studies 8(3). https://doi.org/10.7575/aiac.alls.v.8n.3p.44

article_title: Inquiry-Based Integrated Thematic Instruction on Character Education of Primary School Students
citation: Chumdari, Sri Anitah, Budiyono, & Nunuk Suryani. (2018). Inquiry-based Integrated Thematic Instruction On Character Education Of Primary School Students. International Journal of Education & Literacy Studies, 6(2). https://doi.org/10.7575/aiac.ijels.v.6n.2p.69
title: Inquiry-based integrated thematic instructional model
description: The article defines this model, per Regulation of Ministry of Education and Culture No. 57 of 2014, as "a learning model that combines various competencies of various subjects in a variety of themes to provide a meaningful experience to the students", while highlighting students' critical and analytical thinking to seek answers or solve problems. It merges inquiry strategy with thematic learning, with the teacher acting as facilitator and motivator. The article lists eleven characteristics including child-centeredness, direct experiences, flexibility, fun learning while playing, and self-study skill improvement.
requirements: Requires teachers to act as facilitators and motivators with available or enriched facilities, infrastructure, tools/media and resources
constraints: The article states the inquiry-based model complicates activity control and student performance, and lesson-plan preparation is more difficult since it does not match students' learning habits and must fit available time
examples: In the experiment, the theme Animals and Plants with three sub-themes was taught over six meetings, integrating Bahasa Indonesia, Civic education, Mathematics, Cultural arts, and Physical education.
key_sources: Chumdari, Sri Anitah, Budiyono, & Nunuk Suryani. (2018). Inquiry-based Integrated Thematic Instruction On Character Education Of Primary School Students. International Journal of Education & Literacy Studies, 6(2). https://doi.org/10.7575/aiac.ijels.v.6n.2p.69

article_title: Effects of Training and Coaching with Performance Feedback on Teachers' Use of "Pyramid Model" Practices
citation: Mary Louise Hemmeter, Jessica K. Hardy, Alana G. Schnitz, Jessie Morris Adams, and Kiersten A. Kinder. (2015). Effects of Training and Coaching With Performance Feedback on Teachers' Use of Pyramid Model Practices. Topics in Early Childhood Special Education. https://doi.org/10.1177/0271121415594924
title: Plan for intensive coaching dosage when supporting teachers to implement Pyramid Model practices at criterion
description: The article reports that "Intensive coaching was needed for teachers to implement practices at or above criterion," with coaching delivered 2 to 3 times per week in person or via email. Across the three sets of targeted practices, teachers received 16 to 26 live sessions and 8 to 10 emails each. The authors state this intensity should be considered when planning research and allocating professional development resources, and suggest dosage might be reduced in a program-wide model or with group coaching.
requirements: Coaching frequency of roughly 2 to 3 sessions per week combining live debriefing and email feedback
constraints: The article notes it is possible this dosage might be reduced if a program-wide model with other supports were implemented, and that efficient coaching models are needed as resources become more limited
target_learners: preschool teachers implementing tiered social-emotional practices
target_learning_goals: fidelity of implementation of Pyramid Model practices
examples: Bianca had 26 live sessions and 10 emails, Kendra 16 live sessions and 8 emails, and Susan 21 live sessions and 9 emails across all three sets of targeted practices
key_sources: Mary Louise Hemmeter, Jessica K. Hardy, Alana G. Schnitz, Jessie Morris Adams, and Kiersten A. Kinder. (2015). Effects of Training and Coaching With Performance Feedback on Teachers' Use of Pyramid Model Practices. Topics in Early Childhood Special Education. https://doi.org/10.1177/0271121415594924

article_title: Historic and Ethnic Music Found to Increase Geographic Understanding: A Quasi-Experimental Study
citation: Richardson, Ronald; Brouillette, Liane. (2013). Historic and Ethnic Music Found to Increase Geographic Understanding: A Quasi-Experimental Study. Journal for Learning through the Arts, 9(1). http://escholarship.org/uc/item/71g4x3cr
title: Integrate historic and ethnic music into history instruction to deepen geographic and cultural understanding
description: The article recommends using historic and ethnic songs as inquiry materials within the social studies curriculum because music adds "an element of direct, sensory experience that the reading of historic documents lacks," reinforcing conceptual understanding and embedding information more deeply in memory. Songs are treated as evidence — traces of past human activity — that students use, with available facts, to construct inferences about the past, while also building empathy and connection with peers of diverse origins. The recommendation rests on the quasi-experimental gains reported in this study.
requirements: Workshops organized around geography concepts (environment, identity, movement)
Songs paired with geographic representations such as maps and supporting text
constraints: Emotional connection to songs of yearning, struggle and loss "can get in the way of the detachment needed to look at the songs as historical evidence"
target_learners: middle school students in United States history classes
examples: Treatment students traced the migration of musical forms — African Diaspora rhythms, Celtic tunes in Appalachia, German accordion music in Texas — and followed the evolution of African-American music into jazz, gospel, rock and rap
key_sources: Richardson, Ronald; Brouillette, Liane. (2013). Historic and Ethnic Music Found to Increase Geographic Understanding: A Quasi-Experimental Study. Journal for Learning through the Arts, 9(1). http://escholarship.org/uc/item/71g4x3cr

article_title: The Effects of Training in Timing and Rhythm on Reading Achievement
citation: Gordon E. Taub, Philip J. Lazarus. (2012). The Effects Of Training In Timing And Rhythm On Reading Achievement. Contemporary Issues In Education Research, Volume 5, Number 4. http://www.cluteinstitute.com/
title: Interactive Metronome (IM) synchronized metronome tapping intervention
description: A non-academic timing intervention in which participants wear a glove and clap "as close to the point in time when a reoccurring metronome beat is heard through headphones", receiving visual millisecond readouts and auditory feedback. Each participant completed "twelve 45 to 60 minute IM treatment sessions over about four weeks", with eight to twelve tasks per session using four to eight exercises, repetitions increasing from 30 to a maximum of 2000. Performance is scored as a mean millisecond deviation score, with lower scores indicating more accurate timing.
requirements: Headphones, a computer screen showing millisecond deviation, and trigger-activated hand clapping exercises such as toe tapping, heel tapping, and hand clapping
constraints: The intervention is strictly non-academic; participants received no academic instruction during it
examples: In this study the IM intervention was delivered during physical education/health education courses, with post-tests administered by research assistants blind to group assignment
key_sources: Gordon E. Taub, Philip J. Lazarus. (2012). The Effects Of Training In Timing And Rhythm On Reading Achievement. Contemporary Issues In Education Research, Volume 5, Number 4. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1073174

article_title: The Impact of Cooperative Listening Materials Adaptation on Listening Comprehension Performance of Iranian EFL Learners
citation: Mojtaba Ghassemi. (2013). The impact of Cooperative Materials Adaptation on Listening Comprehension Performance of Iranian EFL Learners. English Language Teaching, 6(2). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v6n2p45
title: Involve learners in adapting the listening materials they will use, because adaptation based on their interest and needs raises participation and performance
description: The article's central design recommendation is that syllabus designers, material developers and teachers should involve learners in the process of material adaptation. When learners adapt self-access listening materials cooperatively, the material reflects their interests, their true needs are met, participation increases, and input is enriched culturally. The author states it is "the responsibility of th e syllabus designers and material developers to involve learners in the process of material adaptation".
requirements: Learners should be cooperative and at the same time autonomous
Teacher consultation, assistance and support to supplement what learners do
constraints: The benefit depends on the procedure being employed by material designers and teachers; the article notes grading of materials and tasks remains a professional responsibility
target_learners: EFL learners in university listening classes
examples: Experimental groups selected news and movie materials themselves and adapted them cooperatively over 17 sessions, outperforming a control group exposed to teacher-selected audio programs
key_sources: Mojtaba Ghassemi. (2013). The impact of Cooperative Materials Adaptation on Listening Comprehension Performance of Iranian EFL Learners. English Language Teaching, 6(2). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v6n2p45

article_title: Effect of Inclusion versus Segregation on Reading Comprehension of EFL Learners with Dyslexia: Case of Lebanon
citation: Ghada M. Awada & Mar Gutiérrez-Colón. (2017). Effect of Inclusion Versus Segregation on Reading Comprehension of EFL Learners with Dyslexia: Case of Lebanon. English Language Teaching, 10(9), 49. https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v10n9p49
title: Inclusion theory framing for reading strategy intervention with learners with dyslexia
description: The study frames reading intervention within inclusion theory, in opposition to segregation theory, asking whether learners with dyslexia should be taught in inclusive settings with learners without dyslexia. It draws on the construction-integration (C-I) model and the reader's situation model, in which "text comprehension could be explicated by a collaborative combination of top-down process which is knowledge-guided and bottom-up process which is word-guided." Inclusion "requires full engagement in general education" with support provided "within normalized settings."
requirements: Full inclusion of students with dyslexia alongside those without dyslexia in the same classrooms, as agreed with the participating schools
constraints: The article distinguishes inclusion from integration, where students are placed in regular classes but may be sent out for special instruction
target_learners: Middle school EFL learners with and without dyslexia in inclusive classrooms
target_learning_goals: Reading comprehension of narrative and expository texts
examples: All 298 participants were mixed in groups within the inclusion frame and randomly assigned to experimental and control conditions in both public and private schools
key_sources: Ghada M. Awada & Mar Gutiérrez-Colón. (2017). Effect of Inclusion Versus Segregation on Reading Comprehension of EFL Learners with Dyslexia: Case of Lebanon. English Language Teaching, 10(9), 49. https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v10n9p49

article_title: Early Integration of Tutorial Support in Beginning Algebra
citation: Copus, C., & McKinney, B. (2016). Early Integration of Tutorial Support in Beginning Algebra. Journal of Developmental Education, 40(1). https://www.nade.net
title: Integrated Tutorial Support (ITS) program at Grand Rapids Community College
description: ITS is a short-term developmental education intervention combining supplemental instruction with acceleration "in an accelerated format within the first month of class". Students placing in the lowest third in Beginning Algebra are identified by a first-day arithmetic survey, invited to mandatory twice-weekly tutoring in groups of up to three for the first four weeks, and must pass a Final Quiz at 80%. ALEKS-generated worksheets on whole numbers, fractions, decimals, and signed numbers guide instruction, and tutors tailor instruction to individual needs.
requirements: Attendance is mandatory and students complete worksheets and the Final Quiz within 3 to 4 weeks of the course beginning
Passing the Final Quiz at 80% is required, with retakes allowed after review
Select experienced tutors and a single coordinating instructor deliver the support
constraints: The program has been conducted only in sections of Beginning Algebra taught by a single instructor since Fall 2014
Logistics required relocating tutoring services from near the classroom, with effects of this change under investigation
target_learners: Community college students placing in the lowest third in Beginning Algebra on the ACCUPLACER exam
target_learning_goals: Acquisition of prerequisite arithmetic skills (long division, fractions, signed numbers, order of operations)
Successful completion of Beginning Algebra with a C- or better
examples: Over four semesters, 52 students were invited, 46 accepted, and 39 completed the program; students were exempt from two course projects, with the Final Quiz grade replacing those grades
key_sources: Copus, C., & McKinney, B. (2016). Early Integration of Tutorial Support in Beginning Algebra. Journal of Developmental Education, 40(1). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1152251

article_title: Integration of Histology Lectures and Practical Teaching in China
citation: Xiaoye Lu, Xin Cheng, Ke Li, Kenneth Ka Ho Lee & Xuesong Yang. (2016). Integration of Histology Lectures and Practical Teaching in China. International Journal of Higher Education, 5(4). https://doi.org/10.5430/ijhe.v5n4p157
title: Integrate theory and practice teaching closely in time and space to resolve the disconnect between lecture and laboratory
description: The article proposes that laboratory practice should follow or precede the relevant lecture closely enough that students verify theory with practice immediately, rather than days later. The authors argue this "resolves the disconnect problem between histology theory and practice" and reduces repeated teaching of theory during practical lessons, while increasing teacher-student interaction and letting teachers identify and solve student problems on the spot.
requirements: Laboratory space and staffing sufficient for guided practice during lecture sessions; teacher preparation time
constraints: Teachers reported spending more preparation time than in traditional teaching; the course is inelastic for students and teachers used to the traditional format
target_learning_goals: linking theoretical knowledge of tissue structure with practical microscopic identification
examples: In the pilot, teachers guided slide viewing immediately after explaining epithelial tissue characteristics, and repeated theory during practice was reduced.
key_sources: Xiaoye Lu, Xin Cheng, Ke Li, Kenneth Ka Ho Lee & Xuesong Yang. (2016). Integration of Histology Lectures and Practical Teaching in China. International Journal of Higher Education, 5(4). https://doi.org/10.5430/ijhe.v5n4p157

article_title: Personalizing Post Titles in the Online Classroom: A Best Practice?
citation: Evans, S., Steele, J., Robertson, S., & Dyer, T. (2015). Personalizing Post Titles in the Online Classroom: A Best Practice? Journal of Educators Online. https://www.thejeo.com
title: Instructor discussion-post subject headings as a personalization lever in learning management systems
description: Most learning management systems "offer the ability for the instructor to change the subject heading or title to a post." Instructors can retitle posts using a student's name to signal a class-wide conversation, highlight subtopics, or add humor to entice students to read. The article treats this small, instructor-controlled feature as a valuable personalization of the discussion forum and manipulates it experimentally as personalized versus standard auto-generated reply titles.
requirements: A learning management system that permits instructors to edit post subject headings
target_learning_goals: student participation in weekly discussion forums
examples: Control sections used auto-generated titles such as Re:Re:Topic1 DQ2; experimental sections used personalized titles such as Dr. C to Penelope and Class or Top Ethical Values
key_sources: Evans, S., Steele, J., Robertson, S., & Dyer, T. (2015). Personalizing Post Titles in the Online Classroom: A Best Practice? Journal of Educators Online. https://www.thejeo.com

article_title: The Impact of Modeling Instruction within the Inverted Curriculum on Student Achievement in Science
citation: Dye, J., Cheatham, T., Rowell, G. H., Barlow, A. T., & Carlton, R. (2013). The Impact of Modeling Instruction within the Inverted Curriculum on Student Achievement in Science. Electronic Journal of Science Education, 17(2). https://ejse.southwestern.edu
title: Inverted curriculum: sequencing high school science physics-chemistry-biology to build from simple to complex
description: The inverted curriculum reverses the traditional biology-chemistry-physics sequence so that physics is taken first and biology last. The article states that rather than the traditional sequence, "the inverted curriculum follows a physics–chemistry–biology sequence", resting on the logic that understanding fundamental biology mechanisms depends on previously mastered physical and chemical concepts. Physics lays conceptual groundwork in matter, motion, forces, energy and waves; chemistry constructs an explicit particle model; biology applies these models to molecular interactions at the cellular level.
requirements: An integrated learning continuum with explicit conceptual links across the courses, replacing quantized, unconnected knowledge
target_learners: high school students in grades 9 through 11 science courses
target_learning_goals: deeper, richer integrated understanding of science concepts across physics, chemistry, and biology
examples: CHS phased in the sequence starting fall 2006 with 9th-grade conceptual physics (Physical World Concepts), chemistry in 10th grade, and biology in 11th grade
key_sources: Dye, J., Cheatham, T., Rowell, G. H., Barlow, A. T., & Carlton, R. (2013). The Impact of Modeling Instruction within the Inverted Curriculum on Student Achievement in Science. Electronic Journal of Science Education, 17(2). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1188400

article_title: The Effect of Laboratory Training Model of Teaching and Traditional Method on Knowledge, Comprehension, Application, Skills-Components of Achievement, Total Achievement and Retention Level in Chemistry
citation: Alireza Badeleh. (2011). The Effect of Laboratory Training Model of Teaching and Traditional Method on Knowledge, Comprehension, Application, Skills-Components of Achievement, Total Achievement and Retention Level in Chemistry. i-manager's Journal of School Educational Technology, Vol. 7, No. 1. https://www.imanagerpublications.com
title: Incorporate laboratory-based teaching into chemistry curriculum and materials rather than relying on lecture-only textbooks
description: The article argues that if LTM is to be incorporated into the curriculum, teaching materials must change: "Laboratory equipment must no longer be viewed as a luxury that can occasionally be used in science classes and they must become part of every chemistry course." Materials designed only for lecturing and passive listening cannot be expected to be taught any other way, so materials development should build in LTM.
requirements: Development of teaching materials that incorporate LTM
Laboratory equipment available as a regular part of every chemistry course
constraints: The article notes practical constraints such as needing researcher contacts in a city to run 21 teaching sessions per class
target_learning_goals: Higher-level chemistry learning: application and skills, and retention
examples: The study taught four Karnataka-state-syllabus chemistry chapters through LTM and compared outcomes with traditionally taught parallel classes
key_sources: Alireza Badeleh. (2011). The Effect of Laboratory Training Model of Teaching and Traditional Method on Knowledge, Comprehension, Application, Skills-Components of Achievement, Total Achievement and Retention Level in Chemistry. i-manager's Journal of School Educational Technology, Vol. 7, No. 1. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1102743

article_title: Organizing Educational Activity of a Pupil on the Basis of Learning Technologies
citation: Tatiana V. Sibgatullina and Olga G. Selivanova. (2016). Organizing Educational Activity of a Pupil on the Basis of Learning Technologies. International Journal of Environmental & Science Education, 11(13), 6056-6067. http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/
title: Individual educational program projected by the pupil with teacher support ('I know how to learn' technology)
description: The 'I know how to learn' technology centers on the pupil's individual educational program: "teacher's support of the pupil at projecting his/her individual educational program on the subject (putting an aim, selecting the teaching material (deepening, broadening, systematization), setting the time limits of learning, forms of control and self-control". It proceeds through four stages: diagnostics of educational abilities and needs, putting personally important aims and planning, expertise of the individual learning activity by other teachers, and individual educational activity with summing up. Programs can span a lesson, day, week, term or academic year.
requirements: The content of the individual educational program must include all teaching material required by the state federal educational standard.
constraints: The expertise stage is necessary when teachers and pupils lack experience of projecting individual educational experience.
target_learners: pupils with well-formed learning skills who are aware of their educational needs, including those preparing for olympiads, exams and competitions
target_learning_goals: managing one's own educational activity, achieving personally and socially important learning results
examples: Diagnostics can be done in class via questions, topic review, or pupils choosing tasks and tests of different types; outcomes may be a report, presentation, paper, research, experiment, project or observation.
key_sources: Tatiana V. Sibgatullina and Olga G. Selivanova. (2016). Organizing Educational Activity of a Pupil on the Basis of Learning Technologies. International Journal of Environmental & Science Education, 11(13), 6056-6067. http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

article_title: On the Comparative Impact of Self-Assessment and Teacher-Assessment on Iranian EFL Learners' Academic Motivation
citation: Asghar Salimi, Vahid Nowrozi Larsari. (2015). On the Comparative Impact of Self-assessment and Teacher-assessment on Iranian EFL Learners' Academic Motivation. Advances in Language and Literary Studies 6(6). http://dx.doi.org/10.7575/aiac.alls.v.6n.6p.74
title: Incorporate self-assessment activities into everyday ELT instruction so learners understand outcomes and set improvement goals
description: The article recommends embedding self-assessment routinely in English language teaching rather than treating it as occasional, because it raises awareness of powerful assessment strategies and helps learners locate their own strengths and weaknesses. As printed, "through the incorporation of self- assessment activities into everyday ELT instruction, students can gain a better comprehending of the expected learning outcomes, find their strengths and weaknesses, and set goals for future improvement". The recommendation rests on the study's motivation findings and the authors' cited prior work.
requirements: Teachers and students raise awareness of self-assessment strategies, which the article says are not common in Iranian educational systems
constraints: The supporting evidence comes from one small quasi-experiment with intermediate learners at a single institute
target_learners: intermediate EFL learners in Iranian language institutes
target_learning_goals: learner awareness of strengths and weaknesses
examples: The experimental group self-assessed during five sessions of reading-strategy instruction while the control group received traditional teacher-assessment
key_sources: Asghar Salimi, Vahid Nowrozi Larsari. (2015). On the Comparative Impact of Self-assessment and Teacher-assessment on Iranian EFL Learners' Academic Motivation. Advances in Language and Literary Studies 6(6). http://dx.doi.org/10.7575/aiac.alls.v.6n.6p.74

article_title: The Effects of an Early Motor Skill Intervention on Motor Skills, Levels of Physical Activity, and Socialization in Young Children with Autism Spectrum Disorder: A Pilot Study
citation: Leah Ketcheson, Janet Hauck and Dale Ulrich. (2017). The effects of an early motor skill intervention on motor skills, levels of physical activity, and socialization in young children with autism spectrum disorder: A pilot study. Autism 21(4). https://doi.org/10.1177/1362361316650611
title: Include motor skill programming as part of early intervention services for young children with ASD
description: The article argues that because motor delays emerge early in children with ASD and very few interventions target motor behavior as a primary outcome, motor programming should be part of early intervention services. The authors conclude that "when children with ASD receive direct and intensive instructions on targeted motor skills delivered within an evidence-based framework, the results are positive", and the abstract states the findings "shed light on the importance of including motor programming as part of the early intervention services".
requirements: Direct and intensive instruction on targeted motor skills delivered within an evidence-based framework (here, CPRT strategies with a 1:1 instructor ratio)
constraints: Evidence base is a small non-randomized pilot (n = 20); generalization is difficult per the authors' stated limitations
target_learners: young children with autism spectrum disorder entering preschool or kindergarten
target_learning_goals: gross motor skills, with potential cascading effects on socialization
examples: The study implemented 4 h/day, 5 days/week motor instruction for 8 weeks during summer months with a 1:1 instructor-to-participant ratio
key_sources: Leah Ketcheson, Janet Hauck and Dale Ulrich. (2017). The effects of an early motor skill intervention on motor skills, levels of physical activity, and socialization in young children with autism spectrum disorder: A pilot study. Autism 21(4). https://doi.org/10.1177/1362361316650611

article_title: The Effect of Discourse Markers Instruction on EFL Learners' Writing
citation: Nader Assadi Aidinlou & Hakimeh Shahrokhi mehr. (2012). The Effect of Discourse Markers Instruction on EFL Learners' Writing. World Journal of Education, Vol. 2, No. 2. http://dx.doi.org/10.5430/wje.v2n2p10
title: Include discourse markers in textbooks and writing materials because text markers are a necessary condition for smooth written text
description: Based on the finding that DM instruction raised learners' awareness of where markers belong in written text, the article argues that "the presence of text markers is a necessary condition to have a smooth and enjoyable written text" and that "the syllabus designer should believe that including these elements in texts books and materials is a necessity". It further holds that teachers should treat writing as a skill to be taught explicitly and emphasize frequently used text markers.
requirements: Syllabus designers and materials writers must deliberately incorporate discourse-marker content into textbooks and writing materials
constraints: The article cautions that composing sentences without considering cohesive ties fails to negotiate inter-related events, and that DMs are only one part of grammar
target_learners: EFL learners in institute and school settings
target_learning_goals: Awareness of discourse-marker usage in written text
examples: The study's treatment sessions taught frequently used conjunctive families from authentic reading texts, and the post-test showed instructed learners using DMs in meaningful ways while uninstructed learners misused them
key_sources: Nader Assadi Aidinlou & Hakimeh Shahrokhi mehr. (2012). The Effect of Discourse Markers Instruction on EFL Learners' Writing. World Journal of Education, Vol. 2, No. 2. http://dx.doi.org/10.5430/wje.v2n2p10

article_title: Acquisition of Language and Intercultural Competences in Tourism and Hospitality Studies through Active Experimentation in Second Life
citation: Mercedes Rico García and Paula Ferreira da Silva. (2017). Acquisition of Language and Intercultural Competences in Tourism and Hospitality Studies through Active Experimentation in Second Life. Teaching English with Technology, 18(2), 69-92. http://www.tewtjournal.org
title: Teacher-made intercultural evaluation sheet with Likert-scale indicators validated by expert review and Cronbach's alpha
description: A teacher-made evaluation sheet analysed the language, functions and cultural dimensions of the materials in phase 1. It "included three mai n dimensions, subdivided into a set of indicators, measured on a Likert scale, rang ing from 1 to 5 points, with 1 being totally disagree and 5 totally agree". Indicators covered intercultural awareness (body language, customs, timetable, gestures) and diversity understanding. Validity was checked by two experts in education and cultural studies; reliability testing "concluded with a 0.75 alp ha, that is 0.15 points above the 0.6 standard".
requirements: Expert review of construct validity
Cronbach's alpha check of internal consistency
constraints: Used for in-class phase 1 material analysis, not for scoring the phase 2 SL versus class comparison, which used a 1-10 grading scale
examples: Indicator items included body language, customs/traditions, compliments, habits, timetable punctuality, table manners and gestures, each rated 1-5
key_sources: Mercedes Rico García and Paula Ferreira da Silva. (2017). Acquisition of Language and Intercultural Competences in Tourism and Hospitality Studies through Active Experimentation in Second Life. Teaching English with Technology, 18(2), 69-92. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1177703

article_title: Effect of Blended Learning Educational Model on Secondary School Students' Mathematics Conceptual Understanding
citation: Abdissa, D. G., Duressa, G. F., Olkaba, T. T., & Feyissa, E. G. (2024). Effect of blended learning educational model on secondary school students' mathematics conceptual understanding. Problems of Education in the 21st Century, 82(5), 585–599. https://doi.org/10.33225/pec/24.82.585
title: Integrate blended learning elements into secondary mathematics curricula and support teachers with training
description: Based on the study's findings, the authors recommend that curriculum designers and stakeholders formally incorporate blended learning into mathematics education. They state that "Curriculum designers and stakeholders should acknowledge the effectiveness of BL in improving mathematical understanding and integrate its elements into the curriculum," with emphasis on materials supporting both digital and in-person learning. They also recommend that mathematics teachers use diverse methods such as simulations, visualizations, and interactive exercises within blended settings.
requirements: Teacher training in online teaching and platform use, and instructional materials designed for both digital and in-person learning
constraints: The recommendation rests on a single quasi-experimental study in one Ethiopian region; the authors call for further research in other subjects and on moderators such as sex, socioeconomic background, and learning preferences
examples: The study's experimental group received the blended intervention via Google Classroom with ten days of teacher training before the 20-week intervention
key_sources: Abdissa, D. G., Duressa, G. F., Olkaba, T. T., & Feyissa, E. G. (2024). Effect of blended learning educational model on secondary school students' mathematics conceptual understanding. Problems of Education in the 21st Century, 82(5), 585–599. https://doi.org/10.33225/pec/24.82.585

article_title: Early Number Skills Gains and Mathematics Achievement: Intervening to Establish Successful Early Mathematics Trajectories
citation: Shanley, L., Clarke, B., Doabler, C. T., Kurtz Nelson, E., & Fien, H. (2017). Early number skills gains and mathematics achievement: Intervening to establish successful early mathematics trajectories. Journal of Special Education, 51(3), 177–188. https://doi.org/10.1177/0022466917720455
title: Two-domain framework of early number skills: informal and formal
description: The article organizes early number skills into two general domains. Informal skills are "devoid of numerals, but include relational phrases, counting processes, quantity comparisons, and number words," while "formal early number skills utilize numerals to describe, compare, and combine quantities." The study operationalizes these domains as separate latent gain factors from RAENS items and tests their differential relations with achievement.
requirements: Assessment items must distinguish numeral-free informal tasks from numeral-based formal tasks, as the RAENS informal (n = 7) and formal (n = 25) items do
constraints: All items incorporated some aspect of symbolic and relational understanding, so nonsymbolic skills were not measured
target_learners: kindergarten students at risk for mathematics difficulties
target_learning_goals: whole number concepts and early numeracy
examples: The study modeled informal and formal gain factors with RAENS Items 1 to 7 loading on the informal factor and Items 8 to 32 on the formal factor
key_sources: Shanley, L., Clarke, B., Doabler, C. T., Kurtz Nelson, E., & Fien, H. (2017). Early number skills gains and mathematics achievement: Intervening to establish successful early mathematics trajectories. Journal of Special Education, 51(3), 177–188. https://doi.org/10.1177/0022466917720455

article_title: Differences in Classroom versus Online Exam Performance Due to Asynchronous Discussion
citation: Robert L. Jorczak, Danielle N. Dupuis. (2011). Differences in Classroom Versus Online Exam Performance Due to Asynchronous Discussion. https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=Differences+in+Classroom+Versus+Online+Exam+Performance+Due+to+Asynchronous+Discussion
title: Information internalization-externalization model of learning through discussion
description: The article frames learning via an information-processing model in which students internalize new information into knowledge and externalize knowledge as information, with externalization reinforcing existing knowledge and creating new knowledge by increasing associations among internal representations. Group discussion supports both processes: students "receive divergent information from other students" and "express knowledge relevant to the learning task," promoting divergent thinking and elaborative rehearsal. The model grounds the social constructivist idea of mutual knowledge construction and motivates the prediction that learning activities, especially discussion format, are the key differentiator between environments.
requirements: Learning activities must require students to express knowledge in ways that support elaborative rehearsal and deeper processing
constraints: The article states the study does not address aspects of effective discussion design but compares basic functional differences of discussion (synchronous speech versus asynchronous text)
target_learning_goals: knowledge acquisition and concept formation assessed by multiple-choice exams
examples: The authors use the model to hypothesize that online students using asynchronous discussion would have better exam scores due to the instructional advantages of text-based asynchronous discussion.
key_sources: Robert L. Jorczak, Danielle N. Dupuis. (2011). Differences in Classroom Versus Online Exam Performance Due to Asynchronous Discussion. https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=Differences+in+Classroom+Versus+Online+Exam+Performance+Due+to+Asynchronous+Discussion

article_title: Effects of Infographics on Students Achievement and Attitude towards Geography Lessons
citation: Taner Çifçi. (2016). Effects of Infographics on Students Achievement and Attitude towards Geography Lessons. Journal of Education and Learning, 5(1). https://doi.org/10.5539/jel.v5n1p154
title: Seven design principles for producing infographics as instructional materials
description: The article enumerates seven principles to consider "when producing and designing infographics": setting an aim, determining the topic, keeping it simple and understandable, making visuals, videos, sounds, animations or information attracting, using reliable references, matching students' level, and integrating inscription, figure, graphic and illustrations. It frames infographics as student-centered materials that synthesize information and visualization and encourage multi-dimensional and analytic thinking.
requirements: It must be simple and understandable
It must be appropriate to the students' level
Its inscription, figure, graphic and illustrations are to be integrated
Its references are to be reliable
examples: The researcher developed infographics with online infographic development tools for the 10th-grade topics water, soil and vegetation, used over six weeks (Figure 3).
key_sources: Taner Çifçi. (2016). Effects of Infographics on Students Achievement and Attitude towards Geography Lessons. Journal of Education and Learning, 5(1). https://doi.org/10.5539/jel.v5n1p154

article_title: The Impacts of Presenting New Words in Semantically-Related Sets on Vocabulary Learning
citation: Wang, X. (2015). The Impacts of Presenting New Words in Semantically-Related Sets on Vocabulary Learning. Advances in Language and Literary Studies, 6(6). https://doi.org/10.7575/aiac.alls.v.6n.6p.111
title: Interference theory: words learned at the same time that are too similar interfere with each other and impair retention
description: Interference theory, formulated by McGeoch and McDonald and named by Waring, holds that presenting words that are too similar together harms retention. The article uses it as the explanatory account for the SR group's poorer delayed-test performance, stating the result "adds new testimony" to it. It explains why grouping semantically-related words in the same lesson can impede rather than facilitate vocabulary learning.
requirements: Applies when words are learnt at the same time and share many common elements
constraints: The article applies it to L2 vocabulary presented in semantically-related sets in classroom lessons
examples: The study's SR group, taught synonym, hyponym, homonym, antonym and meronym sets together, scored significantly lower on the delayed translation test than the SU group
key_sources: Wang, X. (2015). The Impacts of Presenting New Words in Semantically-Related Sets on Vocabulary Learning. Advances in Language and Literary Studies, 6(6). https://doi.org/10.7575/aiac.alls.v.6n.6p.111

article_title: Input Providing vs. Output-Prompting Negotiation Strategies in Learning Grammar among Young EFL Learners
citation: Mousavi, K., Alavinia, P., & Gholami, J. (2018). Input Providing vs. Output-Prompting Negotiation Strategies in Learning Grammar among Young EFL Learners. International Journal of Instruction, 11(2), 497-512. https://doi.org/10.12973/iji.2018.11234a
title: Input-providing vs. output-prompting taxonomy of corrective feedback negotiation strategies
description: The article organizes oral corrective feedback into two negotiation-strategy categories drawn from Ellis's classification. Input-providing strategies (recasts and confirmation checks) supply learners with correct input without pushing them to repair: "the learners are provided with some correct forms of input and t he learners are not pushed to modify the incorrect responses". Output-prompting strategies (clarification requests, elicitation, repetition, explicit correction, metalinguistic feedback, labelled prompts) push learners to self-correct by producing modified output. The study operationalized the two categories as treatments in its experimental groups.
requirements: Teachers trained to deliver the assigned feedback type consistently during teacher-learner interaction on target forms
constraints: The study limits analysis to uptake moves on yes/no questions, wh-questions and prepositions in young-learner EFL classes
target_learning_goals: grammar accuracy on target structures (yes/no questions, wh-questions, prepositions)
examples: In the input-providing group the teacher corrected errors via recasts (sometimes with rising intonation) and confirmation checks; in the output-prompting group errors were corrected via clarification requests, repetition, metalinguistic feedback, elicitation and explicit correction
key_sources: Mousavi, K., Alavinia, P., & Gholami, J. (2018). Input Providing vs. Output-Prompting Negotiation Strategies in Learning Grammar among Young EFL Learners. International Journal of Instruction, 11(2), 497-512. https://doi.org/10.12973/iji.2018.11234a

article_title: Investigating the Outcomes and Perceptions of an Inclusive Aquatic Exercise Class for University Students with Physical Disabilities
citation: Dysterheft, J., Chaparro, G., Rice, L., & Rice, I. (2016). Investigating the Outcomes and Perceptions of an Inclusive Aquatic Exercise Class for University Students with Physical Disabilities. Journal of Postsecondary Education and Disability, 31(1), 41-56. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Investigating+the+Outcomes+and+Perceptions+of+an+Inclusive+Aquatic+Exercise+Class
title: Inclusive adapted aquatic exercise class with undergraduate exercise personal assistants
description: A socially-inclusive, university-offered adapted aquatic exercise (AE) class designed from SWD focus-group input. Each participant was paired with two to three kinesiology undergraduate exercise personal assistants who received "two weeks of intensive education and training on AE, care, transfers, etc." and earned three experiential academic credits. "Classes were held twice each week on campus, during the regular spring semester, and lasted 50 minutes," with individualized exercise programs created from initial physical assessments.
requirements: Exercise personal assistants provided by the class, trained in aquatic exercise, transfers, and care
Initial physical assessments to create individualized exercise programs
Instructor supervision allowing assistants to adjust programs to participant needs
constraints: Results may not apply to more diverse campuses, as the intervention took place at a university recognized for its disability services
examples: Six SWD volunteered for the intervention group and completed the five-week class with paired undergraduate assistants
key_sources: Dysterheft, J., Chaparro, G., Rice, L., & Rice, I. (2016). Investigating the Outcomes and Perceptions of an Inclusive Aquatic Exercise Class for University Students with Physical Disabilities. Journal of Postsecondary Education and Disability, 31(1), 41-56. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Investigating+the+Outcomes+and+Perceptions+of+an+Inclusive+Aquatic+Exercise+Class

article_title: Blended Learning and Problem-Based Learning Instructional Strategies as Determinants of Senior Secondary School Students' Achievement in Algebra
citation: Ojaleye, O. & Awofala, A.O.A. (2018). Blended learning and problem-based learning instructional strategies as determinants of senior secondary school students' achievement in algebra. International Journal of Research in Education and Science (IJRES), 4(2), 486-501. https://doi.org/10.21890/ijres.428286
title: Integrate the philosophy of problem-based and blended learning into preservice teacher curricula in Nigeria
description: The article recommends that, because its quasi-experiment showed BL and PBL enhanced algebra achievement relative to traditional lecture method, "efforts should be made to integrate the philosophy of BL and PBL into the  preservice teachers' curriculum at the teacher preparation institutions in Nigeria." The recommendation extends the study's finding about in-service classroom instruction to teacher preparation.
requirements: Teachers need training in the strategy: participating teachers were trained two hours per week for two weeks and assessed through micro teaching before enacting PBL or BL.
constraints: The evidentiary base is a quasi-experimental study without random assignment, in private coeducational Lagos State schools with computer and internet access.
target_learners: Senior secondary school year two students
target_learning_goals: Algebra achievement, including factorisation, quadratic equations, rational fractions, simultaneous equations, and graphing
examples: In the study, PBL teachers led discussions using a five-phase group process (identify the problem, make assumptions, formulate a model, use the model, evaluate the model), and BL teaching alternated pre-computer, computer (algebrator software), and post-computer sessions with email submission of assignments.
key_sources: Ojaleye, O. & Awofala, A.O.A. (2018). Blended learning and problem-based learning instructional strategies as determinants of senior secondary school students' achievement in algebra. International Journal of Research in Education and Science (IJRES), 4(2), 486-501. https://doi.org/10.21890/ijres.428286

article_title: Using Propensity Score Weighting to Reduce Selection Bias in Large-Scale Data Sets
citation: Crystal D. Bishop, Walter L. Leite, and Patricia A. Snyder. (2018). Using Propensity Score Weighting to Reduce Selection Bias in Large-Scale Data Sets. Journal of Early Intervention. https://doi.org/10.1177/1053815118793430
title: Include potential and true confounders as baseline covariates in the propensity score model
description: The article recommends building the propensity score model from baseline covariates related to treatment selection, the outcome, or both, noting "Only true confounders produce selection bias in treatment effect estimates if omitted." It reports that some researchers recommend including all baseline covariates, particularly when the goal is estimating treatment assignment probabilities rather than interpreting covariate effects, and that including potential and true confounders increases precision.
requirements: Covariates must be measured at baseline and hypothesized to relate to selection into treatment, the outcome, or both
constraints: The article notes it is difficult to accurately separate true confounders, potential confounders, and covariates affecting only treatment exposure
target_learners: researchers conducting quasi-experimental secondary analyses of survey data
target_learning_goals: reducing selection bias in treatment effect estimation
examples: The illustration selected 44 variables from a Family Enrollment Interview containing 1,043 variables, covering maternal education, family income, parental self-efficacy, and children's developmental milestones
key_sources: Crystal D. Bishop, Walter L. Leite, and Patricia A. Snyder. (2018). Using Propensity Score Weighting to Reduce Selection Bias in Large-Scale Data Sets. Journal of Early Intervention. https://doi.org/10.1177/1053815118793430

article_title: Wiki Effect on English as a Foreign Language Writing Achievement
citation: Celik, S.S. & Aydin, S. (2016). Wiki effect on English as a foreign language writing achievement. Global Journal of Foreign Language Teaching, 6(4), 218-227. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1112345
title: Integrate wikis into EFL writing instruction to exploit their collaborative and motivational advantages.
description: The article recommends that wikis be deliberately incorporated into EFL writing courses rather than treated as optional add-ons. It states that "wiki existing as an advanced technology tool ought not to be ignored by teachers but benefited from the advantages it serves" and that "curriculum and material developers should include wikis to writing course plans in order to provide learners with power and opportunity to share ideas with others and influence thoughts." The recommendation rests on the finding that wiki-based writing produced higher content scores and supported collaborative knowledge construction.
requirements: Teachers need training in digital media use, as the article recommends that "media literacy and educating teachers to use digital media in the class effectively should be compulsory in teacher training programs."
constraints: The supporting evidence is limited to 42 freshmen at one Turkish university over a four-week administration with TOEFL-format topics.
examples: The experimental group completed writing tasks via wikis while the control group used traditional pen-and-paper, both within a process-based approach over four weeks.
key_sources: Celik, S.S. & Aydin, S. (2016). Wiki effect on English as a foreign language writing achievement. Global Journal of Foreign Language Teaching, 6(4), 218-227. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED573959

article_title: The Effects of Pre- Versus Post-Presentation Input Flooding via Reading on the Young Iranian EFL Learners' Acquisition of Simple Past Tense
citation: Rikhtegar, O., & Gholami, J. (2015). The Effects of Pre- versus Post-Presentation Input Flooding via Reading on the Young Iranian EFL Learners' Acquisition of Simple Past Tense. English Language Teaching, 8(3), 80-88. https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v8n3p80
title: Use input flooding via contextualized reading either before or after grammar presentation to support target grammar acquisition
description: Input flooding supplies learners with "numerous examples of the target form without overtly drawing attention to it", making the form noticeable through frequency alone. This study shows flooding via reading texts, whether before or after explicit grammar presentation, significantly improved simple past tense acquisition in young EFL learners relative to traditional instruction.
requirements: Reading materials containing frequent instances of the target form, such as the Reading Time sections of supplementary exercise books used here
constraints: Benefits were demonstrated for elementary-level young learners acquiring the simple past tense over twelve thirty-minute sessions; delayed retention was not measured
target_learning_goals: acquisition of the simple past tense
examples: Teachers provided reading passages with frequent past tense coverage before (G1) or after (G2) grammar presentation, while the control group followed the school's normal process
key_sources: Rikhtegar, O., & Gholami, J. (2015). The Effects of Pre- versus Post-Presentation Input Flooding via Reading on the Young Iranian EFL Learners' Acquisition of Simple Past Tense. English Language Teaching, 8(3), 80-88. https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v8n3p80

article_title: The Effects of Pre- Versus Post-Presentation Input Flooding via Reading on the Young Iranian EFL Learners' Acquisition of Simple Past Tense
citation: Rikhtegar, O., & Gholami, J. (2015). The Effects of Pre- versus Post-Presentation Input Flooding via Reading on the Young Iranian EFL Learners' Acquisition of Simple Past Tense. English Language Teaching, 8(3), 80-88. https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v8n3p80
title: Input flooding as an implicit form-focused instruction technique
description: Input flooding, a form of input enhancement, is "the enrichment of input by supplying numerous examples of the target form without overtly drawing attention to it". Its assumption is that frequent occurrence of the target form makes it more noticeable and draws learner attention implicitly. Because it avoids overt manipulation or intervention, it is considered an implicit method of focus on form, and this study operationalizes it through contextualized reading passages.
requirements: Sufficient exposure to texts densely containing the target form
constraints: Prior studies (Trahey & White, 1993; Trahey, 1996) found flood effects can be temporary and limited when the input is not contextualized
target_learning_goals: noticing and acquisition of target grammatical forms
examples: The study flooded simple past tense forms through the Reading Time sections of learners' supplementary exercise books
key_sources: Rikhtegar, O., & Gholami, J. (2015). The Effects of Pre- versus Post-Presentation Input Flooding via Reading on the Young Iranian EFL Learners' Acquisition of Simple Past Tense. English Language Teaching, 8(3), 80-88. https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v8n3p80

article_title: The Effect of Incidental Focus on Form on EFL Learners' Grammatical Accuracy
citation: Abdollahzadeh, S. (2015). The Effect of Incidental Focus on Form on EFL Learners’ Grammatical Accuracy. Advances in Language and Literary Studies, 6(5). https://doi.org/10.7575/aiac.alls.v.6n.5p.40
title: Integrate attention to grammatical form within meaning-based communicative activities rather than treating them as separate
description: The study addresses the problem of teachers who separate form-focused activities from communicative activities. It recommends activities that draw attention to form while maintaining meaningful communication, using incidental focus on form techniques like recasting during tasks such as jigsaw retelling.
requirements: Teachers must be willing to provide corrective feedback incidentally during communicative tasks rather than in isolated grammar lessons.
constraints: The study's evidence comes from a specific EFL context with female learners aged 16-18 in Iran.
examples: The experimental group received recast feedback during jigsaw retelling of reading passages, maintaining communication while correcting errors.
key_sources: Abdollahzadeh, S. (2015). The Effect of Incidental Focus on Form on EFL Learners’ Grammatical Accuracy. Advances in Language and Literary Studies, 6(5). https://doi.org/10.7575/aiac.alls.v.6n.5p.40

article_title: Pinch Hitter: The Effectiveness of Content Summaries Delivered by a Guest Lecturer in Online Course Videos
citation: Fanguy, M., Costley, J., & Baldwin, M. (2017). Pinch Hitter: The Effectiveness of Content Summaries Delivered by a Guest Lecturer in Online Course Videos. International Review of Research in Open and Distributed Learning, 18(7). http://www.irrodl.org/index.php/irrodl/article/view/3210
title: Incorporate short lecturer-generated summaries into course videos in MOOCs and flipped and blended classes
description: The authors recommend that instructors embed short summaries delivered by the original lecturer at the middle and end of online course videos, because their data suggest this is a simple way to improve recall. As they state, "inserting short summaries into existing course videos is a simple and facile way to improve student recall of course contents." The recommendation is grounded in the significant quiz advantage of the summaries-only condition.
requirements: Summaries should be delivered by the original lecturer, not a guest lecturer in a different setting
constraints: Summaries may be redundant for shorter videos or straightforward content
Abrupt scene changes accompanying summaries may negate the benefit
examples: In the study, 30-second summaries were spliced into the middle and end of each video, mentioning the main points from the first and second halves respectively.
key_sources: Fanguy, M., Costley, J., & Baldwin, M. (2017). Pinch Hitter: The Effectiveness of Content Summaries Delivered by a Guest Lecturer in Online Course Videos. International Review of Research in Open and Distributed Learning, 18(7). http://www.irrodl.org/index.php/irrodl/article/view/3210

article_title: Enhancing Learners' Problem Solving Performance in Mathematics: A Cognitive Load Perspective
citation: Dhlamini, J. J. (2016). Enhancing learners’ problem solving performance in mathematics: A cognitive load perspective. European Journal of STEM Education, 1(1), 27-36. https://doi.org/10.20897/lectito.201604
title: Design problem solving instruction to minimize extraneous cognitive load by integrating problem elements physically
description: The article recommends that instructional materials for context-based problem solving physically integrate all aspects of a problem — problem statement, formulae, tables, and questions — on the same page to minimize the split-attention effect and reduce unnecessary visual search that heightens cognitive load. In the pilot study, the exchange-rate table, the problem, and the questions were all integrated to minimize split-attention, and no separate sheet for problem formulae was provided.
requirements: All information sources needed to solve a problem should be physically located together rather than separated across pages
constraints: Evidence for this principle in the article comes from a pre-experimental pilot without a control group
examples: The split-attention detector activity compared an integrated A4 task (Example 2) with a split-format task (Example 3); learners in the split condition reported difficulty and the integrated version showed a time-related advantage
key_sources: Dhlamini, J. J. (2016). Enhancing learners’ problem solving performance in mathematics: A cognitive load perspective. European Journal of STEM Education, 1(1), 27-36. https://doi.org/10.20897/lectito.201604

article_title: Using Processing Instruction for the Acquisition of English Present Perfect of Filipinos
citation: Rachelle B. Lintao and Jonathan P. Erfe. (2012). Using Processing Instruction for the Acquisition of English Present Perfect of Filipinos. i-manager's Journal of English Language Teaching, Vol. 2 No. 1, January - March. https://journals.imanagerpublications.com/
title: VanPatten's Input Processing theory and Processing Instruction: altering learners' input-processing strategies to build form-meaning connections
description: Input Processing theory holds that learners process input while comprehending, and that what becomes intake is a filtered subset of the input: "What learners actually wind up with after processing the input is a reduced, sometimes slightly altered set of data that theorists call intake." Processing Instruction is a "psycholinguistically-motivated" grammar intervention designed to "alter[] the processing strategies that learners take to the task of comprehension" so learners make better form-meaning connections, using structured input rather than immediate production. The article applies it to the English present perfect with Filipino college learners.
requirements: Instruction must include explicit information on the structure, information about non-optimal processing strategies, and structured input activities that push learners to attend to form for meaning
