constraints: PI does not require production of the targeted form during the PI segment; output is set aside for later fluency and accuracy work
VanPatten stresses PI need not replace the whole language program and should operate in harmony with other language arts within communicative language teaching
target_learners: young-adult Filipino ESL learners at the tertiary level
target_learning_goals: L2 grammar: accurate interpretation and production of the English present perfect aspect
examples: The experimental treatment taught learners not to rely on time adverbials but to take their cue from the verb form (e.g., "has produced") when interpreting present-perfect sentences, followed by five structured input activities combining referential and affective tasks
key_sources: Rachelle B. Lintao and Jonathan P. Erfe. (2012). Using Processing Instruction for the Acquisition of English Present Perfect of Filipinos. i-manager's Journal of English Language Teaching, Vol. 2 No. 1, January - March. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1070206

article_title: Corrective Feedback (CF) and English-Major EFL Learners' Ability in Grammatical Error Detection and Correction
citation: Sahail M. Asassfeh. (2013). Corrective Feedback (CF) and English-Major EFL Learners' Ability in Grammatical Error Detection and Correction. English Language Teaching, 6(8). http://dx.doi.org/10.5539/elt.v6n8p85
title: Provide informative rather than summative corrective feedback that learners see and act upon
description: The article argues corrective feedback benefits learners when it is informative, giving useable information about the gap between current and desired performance, rather than summative marking. It cites Lee's finding that EFL teachers' feedback was mainly summative and concludes that "CF remains of little use, if any, unless seen and acted upon by learners". Constant, active interaction with their own texts after each submission is proposed as a reason the feedback improved performance.
requirements: Learners must actually see and act upon the feedback for it to be of use
constraints: The article's supporting evidence is its own quasi-experiment plus cited studies, not a direct test of summative versus informative feedback
target_learning_goals: Detecting and correcting grammatical errors in writing
examples: Both study groups received written feedback on their own weekly paragraphs for 12 weeks, with feedback also given on non-target textual aspects so attention was not heightened to target errors
key_sources: Sahail M. Asassfeh. (2013). Corrective Feedback (CF) and English-Major EFL Learners' Ability in Grammatical Error Detection and Correction. English Language Teaching, 6(8). http://dx.doi.org/10.5539/elt.v6n8p85

article_title: Effectiveness of Inductive and Deductive Methods in Teaching Grammar
citation: Mohammad Akram Alzu'bi. (2015). Effectiveness of Inductive and Deductive Methods in Teaching Grammar. Advances in Language and Literary Studies, 6(2). https://doi.org/10.7575/aiac.alls.v.6n.2p.187
title: Inductive and deductive grammar programs as contrasting example-rule-practice sequences
description: The article operationalizes the two teaching models as opposite instructional sequences. The inductive program is represented as "Specific examples → Practice → General rule", so learners work examples and practice before the rule is stated, while the deductive program runs "General rule → Specific examples → Practice". The researcher built one program of each type for each level, based on that level's syllabus, and taught them to the experimental groups.
requirements: Both programs must be based on the syllabus of each level, as the researcher prepared them
target_learning_goals: English grammar achievement (tenses, subject-verb agreement, yes/no and WH questions, negatives)
examples: The researcher designed inductive and deductive instructional programs and taught them to four experimental groups over about one month at each level
key_sources: Mohammad Akram Alzu'bi. (2015). Effectiveness of Inductive and Deductive Methods in Teaching Grammar. Advances in Language and Literary Studies, 6(2). https://doi.org/10.7575/aiac.alls.v.6n.2p.187

article_title: The Impact of Different Instructions on Vietnamese EFL Students' Acquisition of Formulaic Sequences
citation: Do Thi Ha. (2017). The Impact of Different Instructions on Vietnamese EFL Students' Acquisition of Formulaic Sequences. English Language Teaching, 10(8). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v10n8p18
title: Involvement load and depth-of-processing accounts of formulaic-sequence retention
description: The article explains its findings through the involvement load hypothesis (Laufer & Hulstijn, 2001), "which holds that the participants' engagement in a cognitively demanding task will result in better memorization", alongside depth-of-processing and noticing accounts. Translation and contrastive analysis are said to increase "the depth of processing, the degree of elaboration, the quality of attention and the richness of encoding". The article uses this framework to interpret TBI's superiority in two test cases.
requirements: Tasks must engage learners in cognitively demanding processing of form and meaning for retention benefits.
constraints: The article notes it is unpredictable how effective different ways of motivating chunk learning are for particular students.
target_learners: adult L2 learners in formal classroom settings
target_learning_goals: durable retention of formulaic sequences at recognition and recall levels
examples: The article links TBI's delayed-recall advantage over PBI to the involvement load hypothesis and cites Hulstijn's conclusion that the nature of information processing determines retention.
key_sources: Do Thi Ha. (2017). The Impact of Different Instructions on Vietnamese EFL Students' Acquisition of Formulaic Sequences. English Language Teaching, 10(8). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v10n8p18

article_title: Generation of Student Interest in an Inquiry-Based Mobile Learning Environment
citation: Erkka Laine, Marjaana Veermans, Aleksi Lahti, Koen Veermans. (2017). Generation of student interest in an inquiry-based mobile learning environment. Frontline Learning Research Vol.5 No. 4 (2017) 42 - 60. https://doi.org/10.14786/flr.v5i4.306
title: Inquiry-based mobile learning environment with integrated curriculum
description: A one-class pilot learning environment in a Finnish lower secondary school combining inquiry-based learning with an integrated, multidisciplinary curriculum. Students "received personal tablet computers as their primary tool for school work", containing e-books, e-notebooks, and applications for mind mapping, instant messaging, and image and video editing. Learning projects revolved around one overarching theme covered in different subjects, such as a cross-curricular water-themed project in which students collected and analysed water samples and wrote reports. Teachers had opportunities to participate in professional training courses.
requirements: Teachers need sufficient support on how to prepare for the shifted role mobile learning demands, per the article's discussion
constraints: The article states implementation was in many cases far from ideal, with teachers sometimes replicating ordinary classes and hardware and software problems occurring
target_learners: 7th grade students (aged 12–13) in lower secondary school
target_learning_goals: STEM domain interest development; inquiry skills; cross-curricular learning
examples: The water-themed project: field experiments collecting water samples, analysis in biology and chemistry, photography in arts, and report writing in language class
key_sources: Erkka Laine, Marjaana Veermans, Aleksi Lahti, Koen Veermans. (2017). Generation of student interest in an inquiry-based mobile learning environment. Frontline Learning Research Vol.5 No. 4 (2017) 42 - 60. https://doi.org/10.14786/flr.v5i4.306

article_title: The Effectiveness of Intercultural Sensitivity Development Activities Integrated with Scientific Research Methods Course
citation: Tuncel, İ. (2019). The effectiveness of intercultural sensitivity development activities integrated with scientific research methods course. European Journal of Educational Research, 8(1), 301-312. https://doi.org/10.12973/eu-jer.8.1.301
title: Intercultural Sensitivity Scale (Chen & Starosta, 2000; Turkish adaptation by Bulduk, Tosun and Ardıç, 2011)
description: A five-point Likert data collection tool used to measure students' intercultural sensitivity, developed by Chen and Starosta (2000) and adapted into Turkish by Bulduk, Tosun and Ardıç (2011). The article reports that in the adaptation study the Cronbach's Alpha internal consistency coefficient was 0.72, while in this study Cronbach's Alpha was found 0.86. Although the original scale comprises five dimensions, the Turkish adaptation's item distribution was inconsistent with the original, so the scale was used unidimensionally with 24 items scored from 24 to 120 points.
requirements: Used unidimensionally per the adaptation study's approval from Chen, since the Turkish item distribution did not match the original five sub-dimensions
constraints: The article limits its findings to the emotional dimension of intercultural competence measured by this scale and notes it does not show whether students would exhibit intercultural sensitivity in actual circumstances
target_learners: second-year pre-service English teachers in higher education
examples: Administered as pretest at the beginning of the semester and posttest at the end to both the experimental and control groups
key_sources: Tuncel, İ. (2019). The effectiveness of intercultural sensitivity development activities integrated with scientific research methods course. European Journal of Educational Research, 8(1), 301-312. https://doi.org/10.12973/eu-jer.8.1.301

article_title: Practice and Innovations of Inclusive Education at School
citation: Larysa V. Kozibroda, Oksana P. Kruhlyk, Larysa S. Zhuravlova, Svitlana V. Chupakhina & Оlena M. Verzhihovska. (2020). Practice and Innovations of Inclusive Education at School. International Journal of Higher Education, 9(7). https://doi.org/10.5430/ijhe.v9n7p176
title: Integrated and differentiated approaches as two complementary frameworks for implementing inclusive education
description: The article proposes that effective inclusion combines two approaches. The integrated approach introduces innovations across system elements — "the concept (strategy) that defines the model, external preconditions and stages of inclusion; a school that defines the internal prerequisites for inclusion; a community". The differentiated approach is "used in combination with the integrated one in order to identify the internal prerequisites for inclusion: values, beliefs and attitudes of teachers, the competence of educators".
requirements: Inclusion is carried out through socialization of students at the public school while identifying students whose educational needs should be differentiated
constraints: The two approaches complement each other depending on regional differences in inclusive education, determined by the complexity of students' special educational needs and availability of teachers
target_learners: students with special educational needs in general secondary schools
target_learning_goals: equal access to high-quality education through inclusive school organization
key_sources: Larysa V. Kozibroda, Oksana P. Kruhlyk, Larysa S. Zhuravlova, Svitlana V. Chupakhina & Оlena M. Verzhihovska. (2020). Practice and Innovations of Inclusive Education at School. International Journal of Higher Education, 9(7). https://doi.org/10.5430/ijhe.v9n7p176

article_title: Using Videoconferencing Technology to Enhance Classroom Observation Methodology for the Instruction of Preservice Early Childhood Professionals
citation: Pickering, L. E., & Walsh, E. J. (2011). Using Videoconferencing Technology to Enhance Classroom Observation Methodology for the Instruction of Preservice Early Childhood Professionals. Journal of Digital Learning in Teacher Education, 27(3). https://iste.org
title: Use instructor-facilitated, collective live video observation so the whole class can observe, discuss, and be guided in scientific observation methodology
description: The article recommends conducting observation sessions with an entire class collectively viewing a live video feed while the instructor facilitates. The instructor manages what is observed, fields questions, and corrects misconceptions in real time: the instructor can "provide guiding comments as live events occur, and controlling the cameras to hone in on specific actions and behaviors." This creates an open forum for discussion impossible during solo onsite visits, and the authors report it enhanced the observational experience in their course.
requirements: Internet-based cameras and a microphone in the observed classroom, a compatible videoconferencing system, and media consent from parents
Instructor presence during sessions to field questions, guide interpretation, and control the cameras
constraints: Students reported limited camera views and poor sound quality, particularly during open-play periods
The article notes sound quality has no identified technological solution
target_learning_goals: understanding children's developmental behaviors across physical, cognitive, social, and emotional domains
examples: In the child development course, students observed preschoolers at a campus Child Study Center on four assignments, each focused on a different developmental domain, with the instructor prearranging activities with CSC teachers to match the domain being studied
key_sources: Pickering, L. E., & Walsh, E. J. (2011). Using Videoconferencing Technology to Enhance Classroom Observation Methodology for the Instruction of Preservice Early Childhood Professionals. Journal of Digital Learning in Teacher Education, 27(3). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ918901

article_title: Integrative Teaching Techniques and Improvement of German Speaking Learning Skills
citation: Litualy, S. J. (2016). Integrative Teaching Techniques and Improvement of German Speaking Learning Skills. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.7, No.9. https://www.iiste.org
title: Integrative language teaching techniques: the four language skills taught and assessed as interrelated
description: Integrative language teaching techniques are an approach in which the four language skills — listening, speaking, reading and writing — are presented and assessed in an interrelated way rather than in isolation. The article defines it, citing Routman, as "an approach to learning or way of thinking that takes into account the interrelationship between the elements in the process of language including reading, writing, speaking". In the study, a speaking lesson was designed so that listening, reading and writing activities supported the speaking task, on the premise that material presented in one skill proceeds into the others.
requirements: Instruction must deliberately connect the four skills so that material presented in one skill proceeds into the others, as the article's implementation steps show.
constraints: The article's empirical support comes from one single-group quasi-experiment in a German language program, without a comparison group.
target_learners: University students in a German language education program
target_learning_goals: German speaking skills, supported by integrated listening, reading and writing
examples: The lecturer gave questions tied to the theme, students formed hypotheses, determined the title and key words, then discussed with the lecturer.
key_sources: Litualy, S. J. (2016). Integrative Teaching Techniques and Improvement of German Speaking Learning Skills. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.7, No.9. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1095832

article_title: Integrative Teaching Techniques and Improvement of German Speaking Learning Skills
citation: Litualy, S. J. (2016). Integrative Teaching Techniques and Improvement of German Speaking Learning Skills. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.7, No.9. https://www.iiste.org
title: Teach speaking by integrating the other three language skills rather than in isolation
description: The article recommends that speaking instruction be embedded in listening, reading and writing because the four skills are, in its words, "closely intertwined and mutually supportive of each other". It argues that a technique assessing the four skills in an integrated manner is required by the linkage among linguistic elements, and its results showed students became more enthusiastic when the speaking lesson included the three other skills.
requirements: Lessons must include activities from listening, reading and writing connected to the speaking theme, following the article's implementation sequence.
constraints: Evidence is from one small single-group quasi-experiment; the article itself notes teaching without the integrative technique produced very low outcomes in this setting.
target_learners: Foreign-language learners, particularly German language students
target_learning_goals: Speaking proficiency in the target language
examples: Speaking lessons in the study opened with theme-related questions recalling concepts mastered through listening, speaking, reading and writing.

article_title: Understanding Language Learning: Review of the Application of the Interaction Model in Foreign Language Contexts
citation: L. Quentin Dixon & Shuang Wu. (2014). Understanding Language Learning: Review of the Application of the Interaction Model in Foreign Language Contexts. Malaysian Journal of Learning and Instruction, 11, 23-39. http://mjli.uum.edu.my/
title: The interaction model: language learning as an input-output-interaction cycle
description: The interaction model (Long, 1996) synthesizes Krashen's Input Hypothesis and Swain's Output Hypothesis, and posits negotiation of meaning as the bridge between them. As the article states, "the interaction model views language learning as occurring during an input-output-interaction cycle (Gass & Mackey, 2006)". Input is the language the learner encounters, output is the learner's productive language, and interaction lets learners signal (non-)comprehension, request clarification, attempt responses and obtain feedback. Noticing and intake explain why some forms are acquired and others are not.
requirements: All three components — input, interaction and output — must be present and connected for the model to work as described
constraints: The article notes the model should not be accredited as a complete theory of SLA and may not explain political and cultural influences, personality or cognitive factors
target_learners: EFL learners in foreign language contexts

article_title: Building the Oral Language of Young Hispanic Children through Interactive Read Alouds and Vocabulary Games at Preschool and at Home
citation: Baker, D. L., Mogna, V., Rodriguez, S., Farmer, D., & Yovanoff, P. (2016). Building the Oral Language of Young Hispanic Children Through Interactive Read Alouds and Vocabulary Games at Preschool and at Home. Journal of International Special Needs Education, 19(2), 81-94.
title: Cummins's interdependence hypothesis as the bilingual rationale for native-language intervention
description: The article grounds its bilingual home-plus-preschool design in Cummins's (1979) interdependence hypothesis, which holds that second-language learning depends on first-language proficiency. The authors state that "increasing the proﬁciency in the ﬁrst language appears to beneﬁt second language acquisition," so enriching Spanish at home and preschool is expected to support eventual English development. They combine this with evidence on bilingualism's cognitive benefits and the claim that rich interaction requires the adult's most proficient language.
requirements: Rich interactive conversations require that adults can communicate with children in the language they are most proficient in, as the article states
constraints: The article's own English results were weaker than Spanish results, and it cites the threshold level hypothesis as a possible explanation that bilinguals need a native-language threshold before second-language differences appear
target_learners: Spanish-speaking preschool English learners from low-income families
target_learning_goals: Native-language vocabulary and language proficiency supporting later second-language acquisition
examples: The LINK intervention delivered the home component entirely in Spanish and the preschool component in Spanish or English depending on teacher proficiency

Building the Oral Language of Young Hispanic Children Through Interactive Read Alouds and Vocabulary Games at Preschool and at Home. article_title: Effect of Inquiry-Based Learning Approach on Student Resistance in a Science and Technology Course
citation: Demet SEVER, Meral GÜVEN. (2014). Effect of Inquiry-based Learning Approach on Student Resistance in a Science and Technology Course. Educational Sciences: Theory & Practice. https://doi.org/10.12738/estp.2014.4.1919
title: Use inquiry-based learning approaches to reduce student resistance in science courses
description: The article supports constructing science teaching–learning processes based on the inquiry-based learning approach, in which "learners master learning units by obtaining data through asking questions and doing research in the knowledge construction process". In the study, courses for experimental groups used this approach while control groups were taught traditionally, and resistance behaviors changed positively. The recommendation is limited by the non-permanence of the behavioral changes.
requirements: Teaching approaches, methods, and techniques must be applied considering the course structure
constraints: Positive changes in resistance behaviors did not persist as expected in the teaching–learning process
examples: Experimental groups were taught with an inquiry-based learning approach while the control group used the traditional method in a quasi-experimental design
key_sources: Demet SEVER, Meral GÜVEN. (2014). Effect of Inquiry-based Learning Approach on Student Resistance in a Science and Technology Course. Educational Sciences: Theory & Practice. https://doi.org/10.12738/estp.2014.4.1919

article_title: Using Group Discussion with Taiwan's EFL College Students: A Comparison of Comprehension Instruction for Book Club, Literature Circles, and Instructional Conversations
citation: Shen, F.-Y. (2013). Using Group Discussion with Taiwan’s EFL College Students: A Comparison of Comprehension Instruction for Book Club, Literature Circles, and Instructional Conversations. English Language Teaching, 6(12), 58-. https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v6n12p58
title: Instructional Conversations pair direct teaching with teacher-led open-ended group discussion
description: Instructional Conversations is a discussion-centered reading approach combining explicit instruction with teacher-led group discussion. The article states that "The instructional conversation approach included both instructional and conversational elements." The teacher explicitly explains the lesson text, directly teaches reading skills, and then guides discussion with an open-ended initiating question concerning controversial issues in a text segment, offering follow-up uptake questions to prompt further discussion and clarify ambiguities.
requirements: A teacher who provides an initiating open-ended question and follow-up uptake questions to sustain and direct the discussion.
examples: In the study's Instructional Conversations lessons, the teacher explained the text, taught reading skills directly, then led group discussion with open-ended initiating and follow-up questions.

article_title: The Effect of an Intensive English Program on Malaysian Secondary School Students' Language Proficiency
citation: Jayakaran Mukundan, Elaheh Hamed Mahvelati & Vahid Nimehchisalem. (2012). The Effect of an Intensive English Program on Malaysian Secondary School Students’ Language Proficiency. English Language Teaching, 5(11). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v5n11p1
title: Intensive program design combining concentrated instruction with co-curricular and engagement activities
description: The program paired high-intensity language instruction (120 hours of study per month) with co-curricular activities including visits, competitions, sports, motivational talks at universities, weekend workshops by post-graduate students, and a Readerthon combining extensive and intensive reading. The authors state that visits to interesting sites "would provide an escape from the intensive exposure of the students to the materials and help them avoid monotony and boredom" and that workshops and the Readerthon "would add variety and foster learner engagement".
requirements: Collaboration between organizations (school, university, language center, and corporate sponsors) to provide residential facilities, transport, tuition scholarships, and activity resources
target_learners: Low-scoring Malaysian Form 4 secondary school students in a residential intensive program
target_learning_goals: General English proficiency and learner engagement/motivation
examples: Field trips to Melaka, UNITEN, and UPM; weekend workshops by TESL post-graduate students; a Readerthon using ten volumes of the Just English magazine with 20 short-answer questions
key_sources: Jayakaran Mukundan, Elaheh Hamed Mahvelati & Vahid Nimehchisalem. (2012). The Effect of an Intensive English Program on Malaysian Secondary School Students’ Language Proficiency. English Language Teaching, 5(11). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v5n11p1

description: The article concludes that "Collaboration between organizations is important for the success of such programs", citing the contributions of MARA (coordination), the school principal and staff, UPM (residential college, TESL student helpers), ELS Language Centers (tuition scholarships amounting to RM54000, about $18000), UNITEN (motivational talks), and JUST ENGLISH Sdn. Bhd. (300 magazines donated). This multi-party support enabled the residential intensive program to run.
requirements: Coordination from a headquarters-level body, school-level mobilization of staff, university residential facilities, and funded tuition or donated materials

examples: MARA coordinated proceedings from Headquarters; UPM provided residential accommodation; ELS provided scholarships worth RM54000 (about $18000)

article_title: Utilization of Innovations and Techniques of Educational Technology in Delivering of Educational Practicum and Its Impact on Increasing Academic Achievement among Pre-Service Teachers
citation: Ibrahim, H. G. (2017). Utilization of Innovations and Techniques of Educational Technology in Delivering of Educational Practicum and its Impact on Increasing Academic Achievement among Pre-Service Teachers. Journal of Education and Practice, 8(8), 185-194. https://files.eric.ed.gov/fulltext/EJ1142431.pdf
title: Integrate educational technology training into educational practicum programs to bridge academic and practical teacher preparation
description: The article recommends that teacher training must integrate both academic and educational aspects through the educational practicum, which it calls "the bridge between the academic aspect and the educational one." It argues that practicum is where student teachers form attitudes towards teaching and acquire necessary teaching skills, and that training plans should include the scientific aspect that makes teachers master their courses. This principle calls for coordinating practicum program development with colleges of education and providing students with educational methods and strategies through courses, forums and workshops.
requirements: Training of teachers must include both academic and educational aspects
Coordination between colleges of education and practicum schools
constraints: Some supervisors are not originally trainers, which may change training courses into ineffective lectures
target_learning_goals: utilization of educational technology innovations and techniques
examples: The study's experimental group was taught using technological innovations and techniques while the control group was taught the same subject by traditional methods

article_title: Effects of Head Start Hours on Children's Cognitive, Pre-Academic, and Behavioral Outcomes: An Instrumental Variable Analysis
citation: Li, W., Farkas, G., Duncan, G. J., Vandell, D. L., & Burchinal, M. (2013). Effects of Head Start hours on children's cognitive, pre-academic, and behavioral outcomes: An instrumental variable analysis. SREE Spring 2013 Conference.
title: Increase the number of hours children spend in center-based early education to support disadvantaged children's development
description: The article concludes that center-based education serves as a protective factor for the cognitive, language, and academic development of economically disadvantaged children, and that findings support a strategy of increasing hours that children spend in center-based education. This principle is grounded in the IV estimates showing positive effects of additional daily Head Start hours on vocabulary, letter-word, and math outcomes.
requirements: Children must be enrolled in center-based education programs such as Head Start
constraints: Behavioral benefits were found only for the age-3 cohort
examples: The HSIS randomly assigned 4,442 children applying to 383 Head Start centers to treatment or control groups, and IV analysis estimated effects of hours per day attended.

article_title: Integrating Cognitive-Motivational Strategies into Multimedia-Based English Instruction for Low-Achievers
citation: Chang, M. M., & Lin, M.-C. (2012). Integrating cognitive-motivational strategies into multimedia-based English instruction for low-achievers. In L. Bradley & S. title: Integrate cognitive and motivational strategies into multimedia CALL instruction for low-achievers
description: The CMMCALL platform integrates motivational elements (attention, relevance) and cognitive elements (selecting and integrating) to guide instructional materials design for low-achievers. The article states the platform "consists of elements including attention, relevance (motivational aspect) and selecting and integrating (cognitive aspect)" and was developed "according to language learning theories and the findings from the literature review."
requirements: Instructional materials must be designed to embed both motivational strategies (attention, relevance) and cognitive strategies (selecting and integrating)
constraints: The reported benefit was demonstrated with low-achievers in a single class over five weeks
examples: The researchers developed an interactive multimedia environment integrating the cognitive-motivational CALL model and tested it with 44 students over five weeks

article_title: Effects of Blackboard's Discussion Boards, Blogs and Wikis on Effective Integration and Development of Literacy Skills in EFL Students
citation: Alharbi, M. (2015). Effects of Blackboard’s Discussion Boards, Blogs and Wikis on Effective Integration and Development of Literacy Skills in EFL Students. English Language Teaching, 8(6). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v8n6p111
title: Integrated Reading/Writing Test with two parts assessing reading and writing separately
description: A performance reading/writing test used for pre-tests and post-tests to obtain gain scores. Part I asks participants to read two passages and write short answers to comprehension, analysis and synthesis questions; Part II requires an argument essay on a related topic. Part I scores assess reading skills separately while Part II assesses writing skills; the overall score indicates integrated reading/writing performance. Internal consistency was significant at .01 level (reading r = .876, writing r = .861 with total score), and Cronbach's alpha was 0.81.
requirements: Pearson Correlation Coefficient used to measure inter-correlations of test subsets with the entire test for internal consistency
examples: Gain scores were computed for each participant by subtracting the pretest score from the posttest score

article_title: Integrated Reading and Writing: A Case of Korean English Language Learners
citation: Cho, H., & Brutt-Griffler, J. (2015). Integrated reading and writing: A case of Korean English language learners. Reading in a Foreign Language, 27(2), 242-261. http://nflrc.hawaii.edu/rfl
title: Interactive model of reading and writing relationships
description: Shanahan and Lomax (1986) examined three theoretical models of reading and writing relationships: the interactive model (reading influences writing and writing influences reading), the reading-to-writing model, and the writing-to-reading model. They concluded that "the interactive model explained the data better than the reading-to-writing model and the writing-to-reading model." This framework supports the rationale for teaching reading and writing together rather than emphasizing one skill over the other.
requirements: Both reading and writing instruction should be provided, as "reading and writing do not overlap sufficiently to permit complete reading and writing development through an instructional emphasis on one or the other."
constraints: The model was developed from L1 research; L2 studies are relatively few and the transferability of L1 and L2 research findings is complex.
examples: The article cites Grabe (2001) emphasizing that reading and writing should be taught together, and Shanahan (1988) emphasizing instruction of both skills to help students develop a clear understanding of literacy.

citation: Berry, J., Potter, J., & Hollas, V. (2014). Concept Maps and Informational Read-Alouds: Strengthening both Science and Reading for Elementary Students. Texas Journal of Literacy Education, 1(1). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ
title: Informational interactive read-aloud
description: A "multifaceted instructional technique in which a teacher models reading thought processes while engaging students in discussion through sharing and posing questions." Teachers think aloud to reveal strategies proficient readers use, including fix-up strategies when comprehension breaks down. A critical component is dialogic discussion where authority is shared among students and teacher.
requirements: A science trade book selected for content accuracy and aesthetic appeal
Teacher modeling of reading thought processes
Dialogic discussion with shared authority
examples: Science teacher conducted read-alouds with trade books over eight days on soil formation

article_title: Investigation the Relationship among Language Learning Strategies, English Self-Efficacy, and Explicit Strategy Instructions
citation: Yang, P.-L., & Wang, A.-L. (2015). Investigating the relationship among language learning strategies, English self-efficacy, and explicit strategy instructions. Taiwan Journal of TESOL, 12(1), 35-62. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1099307
title: Explicit strategy instruction should be integrated into language learning curricula to promote learner autonomy and strategy application.
description: Based on their findings, the authors recommend that strategy instruction be incorporated into EFL tertiary curricula. They argue it helps learners become more aware of their own learning, apply different strategies, and take more responsibility for learning. They note that "No fixed teaching materials are required; teachers could use the course books they have been using for their own class to show learners how to apply strategies to English learning."
requirements: Strategy instruction can be tailored to meet learners' different needs using existing course books.
constraints: The study's participants were not representative enough of the whole Taiwan English-major student population to make generalizations from this quasi-experimental study.
examples: The experimental group was taught the six kinds of strategies (memory, cognitive, compensation, metacognitive, affective, and social strategies) for six weeks, with handouts uploaded to Moodle after each strategy instruction.

article_title: Teaching Formulaic Sequences in an English-Language Class: The Effects of Explicit Instruction versus Coursebook Instruction
citation: Le-Thi, D., Rodgers, M. P. H., & Pellicer-Sánchez, A. (2017). Teaching Formulaic Sequences in an English-Language Class: The Effects of Explicit Instruction Versus Coursebook Instruction. TESL Canada Journal/Revue TESL du Canada, 34(3), 111–139. http://dx.doi.org/10.18806/tesl.v34i3.1276
title: Integrate systematic explicit teaching of formulaic sequences into language classes rather than relying on coursebook presentation alone.
description: The article recommends that teaching professionals "consider integrating explicit teaching of formulaic sequences into their language classes" because formulaic sequences occurring in coursebook exercises and meaning-focused tasks "are unlikely to be learned if they are not explicitly taught." The study showed that a small amount of systematic explicit teaching (160 minutes, approximately 3.4% of course time) produced large, stable learning gains. Effective explicit teaching was carried out in stand-alone sessions with items selected for usefulness and proficiency fit, ensuring target items were attended to, repeated, and retrieved at weekly intervals.
requirements: Items selected should be useful and befitting to the proficiency level of the learners, co-occurring in both the coursebook and a frequency list targeted to a similar proficiency level
Instruction carried out in stand-alone sessions rather than as part of meaning-focused activities
Procedure ensures target items are attended to, repeated, and retrieved at weekly intervals
constraints: Generalization limited to the study context: a 6-week EFL program with low-proficiency students at a technology university
target_learning_goals: Receptive knowledge of form and meaning of formulaic sequences
examples: In the study, explicit teaching was delivered over four sessions in Weeks 2–5 using PowerPoint slides, paper-based matching exercises, and word cards, with each item encountered twice per session

citation: Snoder, P. (2017). Improving English Learners’ Productive Collocation Knowledge: The Effects of Involvement Load, Spacing, and Intentionality. TESL Canada Journal, 34(3). https://doi.org/10.18806/tesl.v34i3.1277
title: Instructors need not space out collocation exposures; intensive schedules suffice
description: Based on the null spacing result, the authors conclude that "instructors need not consider spacing effects in their classroom practice, as spreading out exposures to target collocations did not significantly outperform an intensive learning schedule". They suggest that multiple retrievals matter for entrenchment but that the intervals at which they occur may not be decisive for L2 collocations.
requirements: Multiple exposures/retrievals of target items are still needed
constraints: Finding limited to classroom collocation learning with an intensive schedule spanning consecutive days; between-subjects design less robust
examples: The intensive schedule held treatments on Day 1, Day 2, and Day 4, emulating typical classroom lesson frequency

article_title: The Relationship between English Language Arts Teachers' Use of Instructional Strategies and Young Adolescents' Reading Motivation, Engagement, and Preference
citation: Varuzza, M., Sinatra, R., Eschenauer, R., & Blake, B. E. (2014). Journal of Education and Learning, 3(2), 108. https://doi.org/10.5539/jel.v3n2p108
title: Successful teachers motivate young adolescents through classroom interaction, challenging literacy activities, and discussion about what was read.
description: The study aligns successful young-adolescent reading motivation with high interaction, challenging literacy activities, and engaging students in discussion about what they read. Teachers who motivated students expressed their own love of reading, engaged students in points-of-view about readings, and used activities such as acting, debates, and games. Students favored group work, fun and challenging activities, interesting topics, positive feedback, clear instructions, and teachers that stressed the importance of reading.
requirements: Teachers must motivate through classroom interaction and challenging literacy activities rather than compliance-based instruction
constraints: Association observed in a convenience sample of downstate New York parochial schools with high minority and subsidized-lunch populations
examples: Four seventh grade and three sixth grade teachers at three locals implemented seven instructional and classroom management strategies associated with positive change in MRQ dimensions

The Water Module required students to "explore controversial social issues and evaluate how these issues can influence the success of an engineered solution," integrating engineering calculations with humanities-based data sources like stakeholder interviews and government documents.

One course alone may not solve limitations in the entire curriculum

Developing holistic approaches to solving complex problems

article_title: The Effect of Oral Interactive Feedback on the Accuracy and Complexity of EFL Learners' Writing Performance: Uptake and Retention
citation: Akbarzadeh, R., Saeidi, M., & Chehreh, M. (2014). The effect of oral interactive feedback on the accuracy and complexity of EFL learners’ writing performance: Uptake and retention. Iranian Journal of Language Teaching Research, 2(2), 105-126. https://www.urmia.ac.ir/ijltr
title: Involve writing students in interactive feedback through elicitation and metalinguistic clues with immediate revision
description: The article recommends that writing teachers treat learners' errors through interaction rather than one-way explicit correction. Specifically, "the students should be involved in the writing process by getting feedback interactively through elicitation and metalinguistic clues and revising their compositions immediately". This rests on the finding that the OIF group outperformed the EF group on accuracy and complexity in both uptake and retention measures.
requirements: A teacher or peer able to prompt learners to self-correct via elicitation and metalinguistic clues during class interaction
constraints: Study conducted with intact groups in an Iranian EFL university context, restricting generalizability
No no-feedback control group was practical because feedback is integral to the writing classes
target_learners: intermediate EFL learners in university writing courses
target_learning_goals: uptake and retention of corrective feedback
examples: In the OIF group, feedback was provided through interaction and discussion among students and teacher using elicitation and metalinguistic clues, while the EF group received explicit correction with no discussion or interaction

article_title: The Effect of Oral Interactive Feedback on the Accuracy and Complexity of EFL Learners' Writing Performance: Uptake and Retention
citation: Akbarzadeh, R., Saeidi, M., & Chehreh, M. (2014). The effect of oral interactive feedback on the accuracy and complexity of EFL learners’ writing performance: Uptake and retention. Iranian Journal of Language Teaching Research, 2(2), 105-126. https://www.urmia.ac.ir/ijltr
title: Interaction Hypothesis: corrective feedback during negotiated interaction promotes L2 development
description: The article frames oral interactive feedback within Long's Interaction Hypothesis, which "highlights the role of negotiated interaction in language development". On this account, corrective feedback that takes place during negotiation for meaning gives learners a chance to attend to linguistic forms, and negotiation supplies feedback on learners' output in the form of conversational adjustments that signal a need to modify production. The study applies this framework by treating written errors through elicitation and metalinguistic clues in classroom interaction.
requirements: Learners must be given enough opportunities to negotiate meaning to avoid communicative breakdown
constraints: The article presents this as a theoretical lens from the SLA literature rather than testing the hypothesis itself
target_learning_goals: attention to linguistic forms during meaning-focused interaction
examples: The OIF treatment sessions involved teacher-student discussion in which students were prompted to locate and repair their own errors
key_sources: Akbarzadeh, R., Saeidi, M., & Chehreh, M. (2014). The effect of oral interactive feedback on the accuracy and complexity of EFL learners’ writing performance: Uptake and retention. Iranian Journal of Language Teaching Research, 2(2), 105-126. https://www.urmia.ac.ir/ijltr

citation: Yufrizal, H., Huzairin, & Hasan, B. (2017). Project Based - Content Language Integrated Learning (Clil) at Mathematics Department Universitas Lampung. English Language Teaching, 10(9). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v10n9p131
title: Integrate language form practice within subject study rather than teaching English separately
description: The article contrasts the traditional integrated English program of reading materials and comprehension questions with its experimental approach where "Language form practice was done integratedly within the subject study." This reflects the CLIL position that merging common subjects with language has a more positive effect than separate language learning, citing Genesee (1994).
requirements: Subject content serves as the vehicle for language use
constraints: Tested in a higher-education English course for non-English majors
examples: Students explored their own field of study using English as the medium of communication

article_title: A Grounded Theory of Inductive Qualitative Research Education: Results of a Meta-Data-Analysis
citation: Robin Cooper, Ronald J. Chenail, and Stephanie Fleming. (2012). A Grounded Theory of Inductive Qualitative Research Education: Results of a Meta-Data-Analysis. The Qualitative Report. http://www.nova.edu/ssss/QR/QR17/cooper52.pdf
title: Grounded theory of inductive qualitative research education: experiential learning early in the learning experience enhances students' learning experiences and outcomes
description: The central theory this meta-data-analysis of 25 published articles developed through constructivist grounded theory proposes that students' learning experiences will be enhanced through the implementation of an inductive approach to qualitative research education that incorporates experiential learning early in the learning experience. The theoretical code chosen was experiential learning/active learning. The authors recommend reversing the typical course structure of philosophy, epistemology, followed by skills, or at least reconsidering it.
requirements: Instructors must incorporate experiential learning early in the learning experience, before philosophical and theoretical instruction, for the theory's predicted enhancement of learning experiences and outcomes.
constraints: The theory was built from 25 published articles reporting students' perspectives only; the authors state the results are not suitable for statistical generalizability and support only analytical generalizability.
examples: The authors propose that the current typical structure of qualitative research courses (i.e., philosophy, epistemology, followed by skills) be reversed or at least reconsidered.
key_sources: Robin Cooper, Ronald J. Chenail, and Stephanie Fleming. (2012). A Grounded Theory of Inductive Qualitative Research Education: Results of a Meta-Data-Analysis. The Qualitative Report. http://www.nova.edu/ssss/QR/QR17/cooper52.pdf

article_title: Integrating Instruction, Curricula, and Assessments in the L2 Classroom
citation: Hill, K. (2015). Integrating Instruction, Curricula, and Assessments in the L2 Classroom. The Electronic Journal for English as a Second Language. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1085906
title: Integrate dynamic and standardized forms of assessment to enhance performance on both
description: The article argues that integrating dynamic assessment approaches with standardized criterion-referenced assessments can significantly enhance performance on both forms of assessment. The study found that "implementing ways to integrate forms of assessment can significantly enhance performance on both and that statistical analyses can be applicable to dynamic assessment results". This principle supports further direction to the social turn in assessment.
requirements: Dynamic assessments based on analogous content from the standardized assessment
constraints: Initial findings and should be approached with caution
examples: The study integrated intervening dynamic speaking assessments using analogous content from a university-wide first-year standardized criterion-referenced pre-/post-assessment.
key_sources: Hill, K. (2015). Integrating Instruction, Curricula, and Assessments in the L2 Classroom. The Electronic Journal for English as a Second Language. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1074705

article_title: Integrating Instruction, Curricula, and Assessments in the L2 Classroom
citation: Hill, K. (2015). Integrating Instruction, Curricula, and Assessments in the L2 Classroom. The Electronic Journal for English as a Second Language. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1085906
title: Integrated assessment sequence alternating curriculum-based instruction, dynamic practice sessions, and CRA-based assessments across a semester
description: The study's treatment followed a 14-week integrated sequence printed in Table 1, moving from a pre-CRA through intervening curriculum-based instruction, dynamic practice sessions, CRA-based DSAs, and a post-CRA revised to include the common-error DRA. This pattern embeds dynamic assessment inside a standard course calendar rather than treating assessment as a separate end-of-course event.
requirements: A pre-/post-CRA with intervening curriculum-based instruction and dynamic practice sessions
constraints: The control group's speaking assessments were non-dynamic and curriculum-based
examples: Week 1 was the pre-CRA; week 7 was CRA-based DSA1 plus analysis of learners' common errors; week 14 was the post-CRA revised to include the common-error DRA.
key_sources: Hill, K. (2015). Integrating Instruction, Curricula, and Assessments in the L2 Classroom. The Electronic Journal for English as a Second Language. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1074705

article_title: Development of Subject Position as a Condition for Forming Communicative Competence of a Future Teacher
citation: Yarullina, A. Sh., & Araslanova, A. T. (2016). Development of Subject Position as a Condition for Forming Communicative Competence of a Future Teacher. International Journal of Environmental & Science Education, 11(9), 2311-2322.
title: Integrative-modular technology with concentric modules
description: The model reflects the usage of integrative-modular technology, which structures the educational material according to the principle of concentric modules. The least module fulfils the function of a fractal: a chain of actions entering the structure of subject pedagogical activity — analysis, purpose, planning, realization, control, estimation — treated as a unit of the educational process. The technology provides "concentrated organization of the educational material" and study of pedagogical knowledge via theoretical schemes of systematic analysis.
requirements: Block-module structure of the educational process with clearly fixed expected results
constraints: The module in question serves as an invariant for structuring competitive modules of educational process in different types of institutions
key_sources: Yarullina, A. Sh., & Araslanova, A. T. (2016). Development of Subject Position as a Condition for Forming Communicative Competence of a Future Teacher. International Journal of Environmental & Science Education, 11(9), 2311-2322. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1114566

article_title: Integrating Simulation Scenarios and Clinical Practices Guided by Concepts of Translational Medicine
citation: Jing Yang, Si-min Huang, Ze-jian Li, Lie Feng & Chun-ting Lu. (2018). Integrating Simulation Scenarios and Clinical Practices Guided by Concepts of Translational Medicine. International Journal of Higher Education, 7(1), 10. https://doi.org/10.5430/ijhe.v7n1p10
title: Integrated clinical skills program alternating lectures, simulator training, bedside practice and case-based integration
description: The article's program arranges each teaching section across four components: classroom lectures, repeated simulator training before patient contact, practice on real patients to strengthen and verify clinical ideas, and "Multidisciplinary integration of clinical information and basic medical science, and clinical skills based on the cases in the ward or the scenarios". Table 1 allocates hours to these components for PE, four internal punctures, diagnostics, internal medicine and internship.
requirements: Identical lecture and practical teaching hours across compared groups
Same teachers and teaching materials
examples: A CML patient with serious splenomegaly could be palpated by only one or two student representatives, so most students returned to the simulation center for scenario-based practice

citation: McCormick, M. P., Neuhaus, R., Horn, E. P., O'Connor, E. E., White, H. S., Harding, S., Cappella, E., & McClowry, S. (2019). Long-Term Effects of Social–Emotional Learning on Receipt of Special Education and Grade Retention: Evidence From a Randomized Trial of INSIGHTS. AERA Open. https://doi.org/10.1177/2332858419867290
title: INSIGHTS into Children's Temperament SEL program
description: INSIGHTS is "a comprehensive SEL program that supports children's ability to self-regulate by enhancing their attention and behavior management". It trains teachers to use information on children's unique temperaments to apply differentiated strategies for responding to individual child behaviors, delivered in kindergarten and first grade. The article describes it as comparatively easier to implement and less intensive than prior SEL interventions, making it potentially more scalable.
requirements: teacher professional development and a classroom-based curriculum delivered during kindergarten and first grade
constraints: the article describes it as less intensive than the interventions studied in prior long-term follow-ups
target_learners: kindergarten and first-grade students in urban elementary schools
examples: In the trial, 11 schools were randomized to INSIGHTS and 11 to an attention-control after-school reading program

citation: Rafey IA, Abdullah A, Saeed Z, Khan UU, Mohyuddin W. (2026). Comparative analysis of university lectures, textbooks, and online video lectures: preferences, engagement, and impact on academic performance among medical students of Nowshera Medical College. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09921-1
title: Integrate digital resources with textbooks and redesign university lectures to be more engaging and effective
description: The article recommends that "OVL should complement, rather than replace, structured teaching" and that UL "need to be redesigned to be more interactive rather than simply giving passive information." Future efforts should adopt qualities of online resources students prefer, including "high-yield content, concise explanations, adding interactive activities, and using multimedia tools such as short videos or animations." This principle arises from the finding that OVL dominate learning habits while TB provide a stable foundation and UL receive the lowest ratings.
requirements: Faculty and institutions must ensure reliable internet access and institutional support for students to make the most of digital resources
constraints: Replacing UL entirely with external platforms is described as not realistic
examples: The article cites a three-step digitization model showing that inclusion of videos, interactivity, and feedback can modernize lectures and improve student performance

article_title: Considering user experience and cognitive load in the design and development of a virtual reality application for embodied anatomy learning.
citation: Gallot Mélanie, Hajj‐Hassan Mira, Chaker Rawad, Collet Christian, Hoyek Nady. (2026). Considering user experience and cognitive load in the design and development of a virtual reality application for embodied anatomy learning. Anatomical Sciences Education. https://doi.org/10.1002/ase.70319
title: inCarne VR functional anatomy tool with real-time body tracking and skeletal mirroring of hip movements
description: The inCarne tool is a VR application for functional anatomy learning that captures the user's body gestures through a high-precision camera and reproduces these movements in real-time within an immersive environment, displaying a dynamic skeletal structure that mirrors the user's actions. Participants completed a 15-min guided VR session involving "real‐time body tracking and skeletal mirroring of hip movements". The tool supports two activities: a handling activity without controllers and an allocentric spatial orientation activity using controllers.
requirements: VR headset and high-precision body-tracking camera
Dynamic skeletal 3D model of anatomical accuracy
constraints: Evaluated only as a first prototype in a pilot study
Limited to hip movements in this evaluation

article_title: Proficiency in Robotic Cardiac Surgery: Toward a Brazilian Training Curriculum.
citation: Poffo R, Curcio SAF, Rosado AR, Senna S, Pope RB, Toschi AP. (2026). Proficiency in Robotic Cardiac Surgery: Toward a Brazilian Training Curriculum. Brazilian Journal of Cardiovascular Surgery. https://doi.org/10.21470/1678-9741-2026-0016
title: Instituto Poffo fellowship in robotic and minimally invasive cardiovascular surgery
description: A one-year, full-time structured fellowship programme launched in 2023 at the Instituto Poffo de Cirurgia Cardiovascular (São Paulo, Brazil), the first of its kind in Latin America. Training encompasses the full continuum of care (preoperative, intraoperative, and postoperative) and is complemented by theoretical instruction, case discussions, and research activities. Technical progression follows a staged model from observation to side-surgeon participation to supervised console experience, with fellows expected to perform at least ten procedures under proctorship. The programme corresponds to approximately 2,880 hours of dedicated training.
requirements: Full-time dedication
Undertaken after residency
constraints: The requirement for full-time dedication and the limited availability of positions restrict its accessibility, particularly for experienced surgeons
target_learners: Early-career surgeons entering directly after residency
target_learning_goals: Technical proficiency in robotic cardiac surgery
Decision-making, complication management, and multidisciplinary coordination
key_sources: Poffo R, Curcio SAF, Rosado AR, Senna S, Pope RB, Toschi AP. (2026). Proficiency in Robotic Cardiac Surgery: Toward a Brazilian Training Curriculum. Brazilian Journal of Cardiovascular Surgery. https://doi.org/10.21470/1678-9741-2026-0016

article_title: The Effect of 3D Printer and Moulage Use on Improving Stoma Care Knowledge and Skills in Nursing Students: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
citation: Avcu Cagla and Yildiz Tülin. (2026). The Effect of 3D Printer and Moulage Use on Improving Stoma Care Knowledge and Skills in Nursing Students: A Randomized Controlled Trial. International Wound Journal. https://doi.org/10.1111/iwj.71068
title: Use high-fidelity simulation with 3D printing and moulage to enhance realism in nursing skills education
description: The article recommends increasing the use of 3D printers, moulage, and high-fidelity simulation applications in nursing education, because augmented physical realism and dynamic learner engagement drive improved knowledge, skills, satisfaction, and self-confidence. Static low-fidelity models "lack the realism of living tissue" and cannot replicate complications, leaving students unprepared for real patients. The authors state it is "recommended to increase the use of 3D printer and moulage and high‐fidelity simulation applications in different nursing care subjects".
requirements: theoretical education on the care topic before simulation practice
a validated scenario and assessment rubric
constraints: the study was conducted in a single centre, which the authors identify as its main limitation
examples: Students in the experimental group performed stoma care on a peer standardized patient wearing the 3D-printed stoma with moulage, practicing cleaning, measuring, and appliance application

article_title: Educational Impact of an Instagram Account on Histology Teaching: Mixed Methods Approach in Medical Education.
citation: Dubois Fatéméh, Ambrosetti Damien, Tosca Lucie. (2026). Educational Impact of an Instagram Account on Histology Teaching: Mixed Methods Approach in Medical Education. JMIR Formative Research. https://doi.org/10.2196/89044
title: Educational social media accounts require intentional pedagogical structure to avoid passive consumption and fragmented attention
description: The article emphasizes that benefits of educational social media depend on intentional pedagogical design. In the absence of a structured framework, Instagram may foster passive content consumption, fragmented attention, or exposure to unverified information. The Histo.Embryo account illustrates how collaborative editorial strategy, standardized templates, institutional endorsement, and curriculum alignment can structure a social media platform for educational purposes.
requirements: Collaborative editorial strategy with peer review
Institutional endorsement and coordination
Alignment with curricular objectives
constraints: Without structured onboarding, students may remain at lower levels of digital engagement, using the platform primarily as a content consumption tool
target_learners: Health sciences students using social media for learning
examples: The Histo.Embryo account used a team of approximately 10 faculty members, posts created in pairs with peer review, and a core coordination team overseeing validation and scheduling
key_sources: Dubois Fatéméh, Ambrosetti Damien, Tosca Lucie. (2026). Educational Impact of an Instagram Account on Histology Teaching: Mixed Methods Approach in Medical Education. JMIR Formative Research. https://doi.org/10.2196/89044

citation: Al‐Rawashdeh, A. B., Shahin, M. A. H., Elgazzar, S. E., Ibrahim, A. M., & Hussien, R. M. (2026). title: Address knowledge, skills and attitudes together through structured mental health education, practical skills training and organizational support in critical care
description: The article recommends that because knowledge, skills and attitudes are strongly associated, these domains should be addressed together rather than in isolation. It states that effective improvement requires structured mental health education, practical skills training and organizational support within the ICU. The recommendation rests on the study's correlational findings and identified training gaps among Jordanian ICU nurses.
requirements: Structured mental health education integrated into critical care nursing curricula and workplace education
constraints: Findings are self‐reported perceptions from a cross‐sectional survey; objective assessment of clinical competence is warranted to complement self‐reported preparedness
target_learning_goals: Mental health care knowledge, clinical assessment skills and non‐stigmatizing attitudes toward patients with mental illness
examples: The survey found only 32% of nurses had received formal mental health training and 79% reported they could be better prepared with additional education

article_title: Competence in the use of a semi-automated external defibrillator among undergraduate dental students: evaluation and proposal for improvement.
citation: Tayebi-Hillali Hoda, Aballe Marta, Santana Denisse, Varela-Aneiros Iván, Diniz-Freitas Márcio, Diz-Dios Pedro. (2026). Competence in the use of a semi-automated external defibrillator among undergraduate dental students: evaluation and proposal for improvement. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-10025-z
title: Integrate specific AED training into the undergraduate dental curriculum
description: The article concludes that dental students demonstrate insufficient preparedness for AED use and that "the provision of clearer verbal instructions markedly improves performance." It explicitly states these findings "support the integration of specific training on the use of the semi-automatic external defibrillator into the dental curriculum," noting that European Degree in Dentistry guidelines already require competence in basic life support and defibrillation devices.
requirements: Structured training in medical emergencies and AED use must be incorporated into dental curricula, consistent with European Union recommendations.
constraints: Optimizing voice instructions should not be regarded as a substitute for comprehensive life-support education.
target_learning_goals: Correct operation of a semi-automated external defibrillator in a cardiac arrest emergency
examples: The study evaluated 81 final-year dental students across two academic years in a simulated cardiac arrest scenario using a Philips HeartStart FRx training AED and a Little Anne QCPR resuscitation manikin.

citation: Kaplan Ceren, Çalışkaner Melis Ünsal. (2026). Self-Perceived Confidence in Pediatric Dental Procedures Among Final-Year Dental Students. International Journal of Paediatric Dentistry. https://doi.org/10.1111/ipd.70142
title: Interpret self-perceived confidence alongside objective measures of clinical performance rather than treating it as competence.
description: The article argues that self-reported confidence is a useful but insufficient indicator in competency-based dental education. It states that "self-perceived confidence should not be considered synonymous with clinical competence" and recommends complementing it with direct clinical observation, workplace-based assessments, and OSCEs when evaluating undergraduate clinical competence.
requirements: Objective assessment methods such as direct clinical observation, workplace-based assessments, and OSCEs must accompany self-reported confidence measures.
constraints: The article notes the absence of standardized performance assessments in this study precluded direct comparison between self-perceived confidence and objectively assessed competence.
examples: The study measured only self-reported confidence via questionnaire and explicitly called for objective performance measures in future evaluations.

Reflective and experiential pedagogical methods as used in the evaluated program

citation: Honegger M., Lindner-Rabl S., Ogliari G., Soraci L., Pertinatsch Ch., Polidori M. C., Roller-Wirnsberger R. (2026). title: Structure geriatric continuing education around interprofessional communication as a cornerstone competency for team-based care
description: The article identifies interprofessional communication as one of the most highly ranked transversal skills among DACH HCPs and argues it underpins geriatric team functioning. It states this capacity "seems the key to work in geriatric teams as it builds the cornerstone for goal-oriented care planning, respectful collaboration and sustainable patient security", and concludes that these findings set the demand for continued education based on the concept of interprofessional education (IPE).

examples: In the survey, communication within a multidisciplinary team received the highest mean knowledge score among DACH respondents (4.23) and was rated comparably to other European countries.

article_title: Psychological predictors of professional readiness: modeling the effects of preservice teachers' 21st-century skills on self-efficacy and professional attitudes.
citation: Serçe Hüseyin, Aydoğmuş Mevlüt, Şentürk Cihad. (2026). Psychological predictors of professional readiness: modeling the effects of preservice teachers' 21st-century skills on self-efficacy and professional attitudes. BMC Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40359-026-05039-7
title: Integrate 21st-century skill development into teacher education curricula to strengthen preservice teachers' psychological readiness
description: The article recommends that teacher education programs treat 21st-century competency development as a pathway to psychological readiness, since the SEM showed these skills significantly predict self-efficacy and professional attitudes. It argues for "the importance of integrating 21st-century skill development into teacher education curricula as a pathway to strengthening preservice teachers' psychological readiness for the teaching profession," and suggests competency-based training models fostering both cognitive and motivational outcomes.
requirements: Curricula that provide mastery experiences, constructive feedback, and opportunities for collaborative practice, which the article says strengthen self-efficacy beliefs
constraints: Evidence is cross-sectional and correlational from a single-region sample, so the recommendation rests on associations rather than demonstrated causal effects
target_learners: preservice teachers in faculties of education
examples: The study tested a structural model in which 21st-century skills predicted teacher self-efficacy and attitudes toward the teaching profession among 401 preservice teachers

citation: Karakaya Suzan Ozge, Gül Uğur, Koyuncu Oğuz, Akdeniz Canberk. (2026). The Mediating and Moderating Roles of Innovation Climate in the Relationship Between Nurses’ Attitudes Toward Artificial Intelligence, Creative Self‐Efficacy, and Clinical Competence. title: Integrated framework assigning innovation climate dual mediating and moderating roles between individual factors and clinical competence
description: The study integrates Social Cognitive Theory, the Componential Theory of Creativity, Organizational Climate Theory, and the Job Demands–Resources Model into one framework in which innovation climate serves two distinct functions. It acts as "an organizational mechanism through which positive attitudes toward AI are reflected in clinical competence" and as "a contextual condition that influences the extent to which nurses’ CSE is translated into competent clinical practice." The framework treats clinical competence as shaped by individual competencies and organizational context jointly rather than by individual factors alone.
requirements: Measures of attitudes toward AI, creative self-efficacy, innovation climate, and perceived clinical competence must be collected to test the dual-role model
constraints: The article states the cross-sectional design supports statistical associations, not causal mechanisms

article_title: Effect of transcranial direct current stimulation on psychomotor skill acquisition during laparoscopic training: a randomized controlled trial.
citation: Lepka Piotr, Szcześniak Dorota, Sikora Zofia, Matkowski Rafał. (2026). Effect of transcranial direct current stimulation on psychomotor skill acquisition during laparoscopic training: a randomized controlled trial. Surgical Endoscopy. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00464-026-12992-2
title: Interhemispheric modulation account of task-specific tDCS effects on laparoscopic skill acquisition
description: The article offers a mechanistic account in which bihemispheric tDCS modulates interhemispheric interactions of the motor system, "reducing transcallosal inhibition from the dominant hemisphere and facilitating the non-dominant effector". It argues this explains why stimulation over bilateral primary motor cortices selectively benefited bimanual coordination, since dual-hemisphere protocols may improve bilateral coordination needed for simultaneous instrument manipulation. The account also holds that tasks dominated by visuospatial transformation (CN/HE) are not helped by M1 modulation, which may be insufficient to overcome perceptual–cognitive bottlenecks.
requirements: Stimulation delivered during active laparoscopic training, not at rest
constraints: The authors note mechanistic claims rest on prior literature; fMRI/MEG studies are proposed as future work to clarify whether benefits arise from reduced interhemispheric inhibition, enhanced bilateral synergy representations, or attentional modulation
target_learners: Medical students without prior laparoscopic experience
target_learning_goals: Laparoscopic psychomotor skills: camera navigation, hand–eye coordination, bimanual coordination
key_sources: Lepka Piotr, Szcześniak Dorota, Sikora Zofia, Matkowski Rafał. (2026). Effect of transcranial direct current stimulation on psychomotor skill acquisition during laparoscopic training: a randomized controlled trial. Surgical Endoscopy. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00464-026-12992-2

title: Intelligent tutoring systems providing adaptive instruction and continuous formative feedback in clinical education
description: AI-based Intelligent Tutoring Systems (ITS) "provide continuous non-summative assessment and instant/permanent feedback" enabling quick error correction, supporting competency-based medical education where progression depends on demonstrated competency rather than time. The review's Table 1 lists ITS as providing adaptive instruction based on learner responses for personalized teaching of clinical concepts and case-based learning, with improved knowledge retention and individualized learning pace.

title: Interpret pretest/posttest competence gains cautiously when no control group is present
description: The article recommends that observed competence improvements in single-group pretest/posttest designs be interpreted with caution because concurrent experiences may also drive change. The authors state that "Due to the absence of a control group in this single‐group pretest–posttest design, it is not possible to attribute the observed changes solely to the intervention", noting that routine ward practice over the approximately 8-week period and the Hawthorne effect may have contributed independently. They call for multicentre studies with controlled designs to confirm validity.
requirements: Future evaluations of simulation training should use controlled designs with randomized groups where feasible
constraints: The principle applies to single-group pretest/posttest designs without a control group, as in this study
target_learning_goals: accurate evaluation of training programme effectiveness
examples: The authors note participants "may have concurrently gained clinical experience through routine ward practice over the approximately 8‐week period"

citation: Wang Sufen, Shen Jun, Qiang Banghong, Xu Honghai, Huang Xiaomei, Wang Lizheng. (2026). An integrated teaching model combining PBL and medical humanities education for pathology laboratory teaching: a randomized controlled study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09701-x
title: Integrated PBL and medical humanities teaching model organized around a single representative clinical case with humanities embedded throughout
description: The experimental intervention organized pathology laboratory teaching around a single representative clinical case of hepatitis B-related liver cirrhosis with complications, serving as "the core instructional context throughout the intervention". Students worked in small groups to identify clinical and pathological problems, formulate diagnostic hypotheses, and define learning objectives, then integrated self-directed learning outside class with microscopic examination during the laboratory session. Medical humanities education was "embedded throughout the PBL process", with humanistic elements such as disease burden, ethical considerations, communication challenges, stigma, and social responsibility incorporated into group discussions and reflections. The session concluded with each group presenting a structured summary of pathological findings, clinicopathological correlations, and humanistic considerations.
requirements: Instructors underwent standardized training to ensure consistency in teaching content, instructional procedures, facilitation strategies, and evaluation criteria
Access to an institutional digital pathology slide repository for self-directed exploration of gross and microscopic morphologic features
constraints: The model places higher demands on instructors' facilitation skills and humanistic competence, requires greater student engagement and preparation, and often necessitates additional instructional time and organizational resources
Inappropriate case selection or insufficient instructional guidance may result in superficial discussions of humanistic issues insufficiently connected to the intended learning objectives
target_learning_goals: pathology laboratory skills including microscopic image interpretation
medical humanities competencies including empathy, ethical awareness, and communication skills
examples: Teaching was organized around a single clinical case of hepatitis B-related liver cirrhosis complicated by upper gastrointestinal bleeding and hepatic encephalopathy; instructors acted as facilitators rather than lecturers during group discussions
key_sources: Wang Sufen, Shen Jun, Qiang Banghong, Xu Honghai, Huang Xiaomei, Wang Lizheng. (2026). citation: Wang Sufen, Shen Jun, Qiang Banghong, Xu Honghai, Huang Xiaomei, Wang Lizheng. (2026). BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09701-x
title: Combine PBL with medical humanities education to foster both cognitive learning and humanistic competencies in medical laboratory teaching
description: The article advocates integrating medical humanities education into PBL-based pathology laboratory teaching, on the grounds that student-centered methods promote active learning, critical thinking, and teamwork, while humanities education fosters empathy, ethical awareness, communication skills, and social responsibility. The integrated model "may encourage students to consider not only the disease itself but also the patient experience and broader social context, thereby facilitating the parallel development of medical knowledge and professional values". The study's empirical support comes from the integrated model's significantly higher questionnaire-based outcomes in learning motivation, self-directed learning ability, and communication and expression skills, and higher teaching satisfaction, compared with LBL.
requirements: Instructors with adequate facilitation skills and humanistic competence
Additional instructional time and organizational resources compared with traditional LBL
constraints: The observed findings likely reflect the overall educational effects of the integrated teaching model rather than the isolated contribution of any single component, since the study compared integrated teaching with LBL rather than PBL alone
target_learning_goals: medical knowledge and professional values developed in parallel
humanistic competencies including empathy, ethical awareness, and communication skills
examples: In the randomized controlled trial, the experimental group received the integrated model while the control group received teacher-centered demonstration-observation teaching (LBL), with the same teaching content, duration, and assessment criteria applied to both groups
