citation: Debelak Rudolf, Ziegler Matthias. (2026). Testing standards for AI-based scores in automated essay scoring. PLOS One. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0354680
title: Assess robustness of AI-based scores by introducing minor construct-irrelevant perturbations and checking score stability
description: This principle recommends making small changes to the input (e.g., inserting typos) that are unrelated to what the model aims to assess, then evaluating whether the score remains stable. The article states this method 'assesses whether the model's score is robust against minor changes to the essay that should be insignificant.' If a few typos cause a drastic score change, the model may focus too strongly on such features, threatening validity.
requirements: Changes must be unrelated to what the model aims to assess
The definition of which changes are minuscule or irrelevant must be informed by a theory of writing
constraints: The outcome is not a universal estimate for reliability but a statement on the behavior of the scores of a specific model, dependent on model architecture and training data
target_learners: students whose essays are scored by AI systems
target_learning_goals: robust automated scoring resistant to construct-irrelevant variance
examples: The article suggests inserting small typos when assessing overall style, or replacing individual words by synonyms when assessing spelling

title: Shanahan and Shanahan's model of increasing literacy specialization
description: The article describes Shanahan and Shanahan's model in which literacy development becomes increasingly specialized. The foundation is basic literacy mastered in primary grades; intermediate literacy is typically mastered by the end of middle school; the top level is disciplinary literacy, the specialized skills needed for specific subjects such as math or science. The article states "This theory highlights the role of language ability as an underlying factor in mastering the literacy of a specific discipline, which is necessary for successful learning and achievement."

constraints: disciplinary literacy skills have fewer parallels to oral language and texts may be abstract or ambiguous

examples: The article links the disciplinary core ideas dimension of the NGSS to Shanahan and Shanahan's disciplinary literacy.

article_title: Punchline with(out) purpose: Integrating research on instructional humour and seductive details.
citation: Bender, L., Renkl, A., & Endres, T. (2026). Punchline with(out) purpose: Integrating research on instructional humour and seductive details. The British Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1111/bjep.70080
title: Instructional humour processing theory: humour benefits learning only when it fulfils both affective-motivational and cognitive functions
description: The instructional humour processing theory (Wanzer et al., 2010) proposes that instructional humour improves learning performance only when two requirements are met: students perceive the humour as appropriate so it evokes amusement (affective-motivational function), and the humorous information helps students process the learning content by clarifying it or demonstrating its relevance (cognitive function). The article tests this framework against seductive details research, predicting that humour lacking a cognitive function acts as a seductive detail. The authors conclude that the presence or absence of a cognitive function may at least partly explain inconsistent findings on teacher humour.
requirements: Humour must be perceived as appropriate to evoke amusement
Humorous information must clarify content or demonstrate its relevance
constraints: The affective-motivational function alone might not suffice for positive effects on learning performance

title: Capture inter‐hand kinematic relationships as key indicators of surgical skill performance
description: Automated skill assessment systems for bimanual surgical tasks should explicitly model the relationships between the two hands rather than processing all kinematic channels uniformly. The study demonstrates that pairing left/right hand channels of the same type (position or rotation) and applying cross‐stream attention yields the best classification performance, with most metrics increasing by 4%–7% compared to processing all channels together. The authors conclude that "the proposed cross‐stream embedding explicitly models hand‐to‐hand interactions across non‐contiguous segments of the surgical task, which constitute key indicators of skill performance."
requirements: Motion sensing equipment capable of capturing kinematic data from both hands simultaneously
Sufficient training data with ground‐truth skill labels
constraints: Benefit demonstrated for Transformer‐based architectures; cross‐attention did not improve BiLSTM‐based models
target_learning_goals: Assessment of bimanual coordination and motion economy in open surgery
examples: The xAtt‐Trans inter‐hand model paired Lp with Rp and Lr with Rr, evaluating interactions between the left and right hands within the same‐type channel embeddings

title: In-situ simulation as a high-fidelity training approach conducted in clinicians' usual working environment
description: The article defines in-situ simulation as "simulated clinical scenarios in participants' usual working environment," offering "a higher level of fidelity compared to other settings." It is described as enhancing knowledge retention, helping learners maintain composure in real encounters, benefiting interdisciplinary teams exposed to ED design and equipment, and identifying systems issues that would otherwise go undiscovered.
requirements: Requires use of the clinical space for the scenario itself, with debriefing possible elsewhere
constraints: A common barrier is the concern that it contributes to a delay in providing patient care
examples: The study surveyed patients about tolerance for delays caused by two in-situ simulation scenarios: a multi-disciplinary trauma case and a pediatric congenital heart disease cardiac arrest scenario
key_sources: Rogan A, Watt E, Murphy S, Wheeler E, Woods L, Galwankar S, Peckler B. (2026). Worth the Wait? Comparison of Emergency Department Patients' Waiting Room Tolerance for Real Patient Care vs Training/Simulation Scenarios. Western Journal of Emergency Medicine. https://doi.org/10.5811/westjem.48916

article_title: Chaplains in Psychedelic Assisted Therapy: Rationale and Competencies.
citation: Lewis Stephen P., Clark-Soles Jaime, Mayorga Oriana, Sawyer Sarah K., Slavet Eliza, Vidt B. Jeffrey, Shanti Saundra, Wiggins Rhiana, Willis Kathleen, Frey Jonathan, Grace R. Mark, Cherniak Aaron D. (2026). Chaplains in Psychedelic Assisted Therapy: Rationale and Competencies. Journal of Religion and Health. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10943-026-02591-9
title: Include chaplains on PAT treatment teams as spiritual care specialists
description: The article argues that chaplains should be included in PAT research trials and clinical practice as subject matter experts in spirituality and health. The presence of qualified chaplains helps ensure participants navigate non-ordinary states of consciousness with safety, sensitivity, and insight. The article states that "the fact that people undergoing psychedelic care are consistently encountering spiritual/mystical experiences calls for the presence of chaplains as trained and skilled clinicians, regardless of whether these mystical experiences are mediators of clinical improvements."
requirements: Chaplains must complete specialized education and supervised experience beyond standard professional requirements
Board certification including at least 1600 hours of Clinical Pastoral Education
constraints: Most psychedelics are not legally accessible, making it difficult for chaplains to gain clinical experience
There are no firm standards by which to evaluate the efficacy of chaplain support in PAT
target_learners: Principal investigators designing PAT research protocols
target_learning_goals: Providing spiritual and emotional support during psychedelic-assisted therapy
Supporting participants making meaning of mystical or spiritual experiences
examples: Studies are underway that utilize chaplains as members of interdisciplinary teams, including phase three clinical trials investigating MDMA-assisted therapy for PTSD and palliative care psilocybin studies at the Dana-Farber Cancer Institute and Emory University.
key_sources: Lewis Stephen P., Clark-Soles Jaime, Mayorga Oriana, Sawyer Sarah K., Slavet Eliza, Vidt B. Jeffrey, Shanti Saundra, Wiggins Rhiana, Willis Kathleen, Frey Jonathan, Grace R. Mark, Cherniak Aaron D. (2026). Chaplains in Psychedelic Assisted Therapy: Rationale and Competencies. Journal of Religion and Health. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10943-026-02591-9

article_title: Reducing parents' vaccination hesitancy: a new educational training model in Turkish sample.
citation: Tümsek Gizem Solmaz and Akmeşe Zehra Baykal. (2026). Reducing parents’ vaccination hesitancy: a new educational training model in Turkish sample. Frontiers in Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpubh.2026.1808239
title: Use structured, interactive, individualized education rather than passive information delivery to address vaccine hesitancy
description: The article argues that addressing vaccine hesitancy requires "moving beyond passive information delivery toward structured, individualized, and interactive educational approaches that foster trust and address parental concerns in a responsive manner". Interactive formats that deconstruct specific misconceptions through one-on-one engagement are reported to be more effective than passive informational materials in influencing deeply rooted cognitive biases related to vaccination. The NETM intervention operationalizes this principle in the NICU setting.
requirements: Trained healthcare professionals (particularly nurses and midwives) to deliver one-on-one, engagement-based counseling
Structured content addressing both informational and cognitive dimensions of hesitancy
constraints: Evidence from a single-group pretest–posttest study without a control group; generalizability limited by small sample (n = 50) and single-center setting
target_learners: Parents of infants in neonatal intensive care
examples: The NETM intervention delivered individual, interactive sessions with question-and-answer format addressing misconceptions
key_sources: Tümsek Gizem Solmaz and Akmeşe Zehra Baykal. (2026). Reducing parents’ vaccination hesitancy: a new educational training model in Turkish sample. Frontiers in Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpubh.2026.1808239

article_title: Virtual reality simulation with eye-tracking feedback versus mannequin-based training for situational awareness in trauma management under simulated emergency department interruptions in Iran: a pilot randomized controlled trial.
citation: Emadi Navaz, Mojtahedzadeh Rita, Allameh Seyyed Farshad, Basiri Kamal, Mohammadi Aeen. (2026). Virtual reality simulation with eye-tracking feedback versus mannequin-based training for situational awareness in trauma management under simulated emergency department interruptions in Iran: a pilot randomized controlled trial. Journal of Educational Evaluation for Health Professions. https://doi.org/10.3352/jeehp.2026.23.8
title: Design trauma training scenarios with realistic emergency department interruptions to approximate real cognitive demands
description: The article embedded realistic interruptions into both training arms: sources were identified through an evidence review and refined by an expert panel using the nominal group technique, adding "ED overcrowding, lack of interprofessional cooperation, and concurrent educational activities". The authors argue the immersive, interruption-rich VR environment may more closely approximate the cognitive demands of real ED settings, supporting interruption-sensitive trauma education design.
requirements: Interruption sources identified through evidence review and expert panel refinement
Interruptions embedded consistently across sessions and groups
constraints: Cognitive load was not formally measured in this pilot study
Modality-related differences in perceived realism and cognitive load may have contributed to performance differences
examples: Interruptions embedded included bystander interference, device alarms, background conversations, staff entry, and abrupt changes in patient condition

article_title: Is all greenspace created equal? Assessing the relationship of public parks and greenness on academic achievement in Washington state.
citation: Fortmann Lea, Rajbhandari Isha. (2026). Is all greenspace created equal? Assessing the relationship of public parks and greenness on academic achievement in Washington state. PLoS One. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0347301
title: Independence-based park-use account for grade-level differences in park effects
description: The article offers an explanatory account for why park proximity benefits only middle schoolers: middle school students "are able to be more independent and thus, could be more likely to spend time in parks in close proximity to their school," while elementary students need parental supervision and use parks near home, and high schoolers have more after-school commitments and driving, reducing park time. This is an untested hypothesis offered to explain the observed grade-level pattern.
requirements: Assumes students are more likely to use parks in close proximity to their school campus
constraints: The study measures only park proximity to schools, not actual student park use; the account applies to the observed middle-school-only effect
target_learners: elementary, middle, and high school students
target_learning_goals: academic achievement on standardized assessment tests
examples: The authors cite Mueller et al. (2023) finding older adolescents (13-15) benefited more from greenspace proximity than younger adolescents, consistent with eighth graders averaging 13-14 years old
key_sources: Fortmann Lea, Rajbhandari Isha. (2026). Is all greenspace created equal? Assessing the relationship of public parks and greenness on academic achievement in Washington state. PLoS One. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0347301

article_title: Interest and effort in learning and performance.
citation: Kehle, L., & Urhahne, D. (2025). Interest and effort in learning. The British Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1111/bjep.70040
title: Three-phase process model of situational interest and subjective effort across the learning process
description: The article extends Thoman et al.'s (2017) process model by pairing three phases of situational interest with three phases of subjective effort across the learning process. Interest phases are triggered interest before engagement, actual interest during engagement, and experienced interest as retrospective evaluation; effort phases are planned effort, actual effort, and experienced effort. The article states that "Within the learning process, three distinct states of situational interest can be identified" and that effort, like interest, "can be classified into distinct subjective phases within the learning process". The model guides the studies' hypotheses about which phase predicts achievement when.
requirements: Measurement of interest and effort prospectively and in real time at each phase (triggered/planned before, actual during, experienced after learning)
constraints: The phases refer to subjective effort and interest, not objectively measurable effort, which the article notes can be dissociated from subjective perceptions
target_learning_goals: learning outcomes in knowledge acquisition and application tasks
examples: Study 1 measured triggered interest and planned effort before two learning tasks, actual interest and effort via semantic differentials between task blocks, and experienced measures after completion
key_sources: Kehle, L., & Urhahne, D. (2025). Interest and effort in learning. The British Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1111/bjep.70040

article_title: An Interprofessional Approach to Teaching About Postpartum Depression.
citation: Howe‐Heyman Abigail CNM, PhD; Schatz Joseph DNP, PMHNP; Siegel Marissa DeCesaris DNP, PMHNP. (2025). An Interprofessional Approach to Teaching About Postpartum Depression. Journal of Midwifery & Women's Health. https://doi.org/10.1111/jmwh.70056
title: Seven-step interprofessional postpartum depression simulation with a standardized patient and warm handoffs
description: A simulation learning experience in which midwifery/WHGRNP and PMHNP students collaboratively diagnose and manage postpartum depression with a standardized patient. The flow includes a postpartum follow-up visit, a "verbal warm handoff to the PMHNP student in front of the patient," a focused depression assessment with behavioral activation, a return handoff, a joint plan including a medication prescription, a debrief, and a collaborative SOAP note submitted for faculty feedback. It was embedded in clinical coursework and aligned with INACSL Sim-IPE standards.
requirements: A trained standardized patient from a standardized patient agency
A patient chart reviewed before the simulation
Faculty from both specialties for prebrief and debrief
constraints: The scenario did not address postpartum anxiety, suicidality, or intimate partner violence, which the patient documents did not endorse
target_learners: Women's health gender-related nurse practitioner students
Psychiatric mental health nurse practitioner students
target_learning_goals: Collaboratively develop a safe plan of care for a patient with postpartum depression
Communicate across disciplines and with patients about PPD diagnosis and management
Describe the benefits of the primary care behavioral health model of care
examples: Students reviewed a chart of a 6-week postpartum patient with an EPDS score of 22 of 30 before the simulation day
key_sources: Howe‐Heyman Abigail CNM, PhD; Schatz Joseph DNP, PMHNP; Siegel Marissa DeCesaris DNP, PMHNP. (2025). An Interprofessional Approach to Teaching About Postpartum Depression. Journal of Midwifery & Women's Health. https://doi.org/10.1111/jmwh.70056

article_title: Effectiveness of a virtual reality simulation based on experiential learning theory for enhancing diabetic ketoacidosis management competencies: a randomized controlled trial.
citation: Baek Gyuli; Lee Eunju. (2026). Effectiveness of a virtual reality simulation based on experiential learning theory for enhancing diabetic ketoacidosis management competencies: a randomized controlled trial. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-08970-w
title: Integrate VR simulation strategically into nursing curricula for high-risk, low-frequency clinical scenarios
description: The authors recommend placing VR simulation where clinical risk or placement scarcity limits real practice: "VR simulation should be integrated strategically within nursing programs, particularly for high-risk, low-frequency clinical scenarios like DKA care." They suggest using it as a capstone activity after core theoretical modules and as a partial substitute for restricted clinical practicum hours.
requirements: Pairing VR with structured pedagogy (lecture, PBL, debriefing) rather than immersion alone, since improving problem-solving "necessitates a structured pedagogical framework"
constraints: Evidence derives from a single institution and self-report outcomes; authors advise caution generalizing to broader nursing contexts
target_learning_goals: clinical readiness and competency in managing complex, high-risk clinical cases
examples: The trial used VR as a capstone-style activity following a 90-minute theoretical lecture on DKA

article_title: Gender differences in causal attributions, self-regulation, achievement motivation, and academic performance following an intervention.
citation: Meshesha Yeshitla Meaza, Weldmeskel Fisseha Mikre. (2026). Gender differences in causal attributions, self-regulation, achievement motivation, and academic performance following an intervention. BMC Psychology, 14, 588. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40359-026-04357-0
title: Integrated framework linking causal attributions, self-regulation, and achievement motivation as dynamically interconnected processes
description: The article integrates Weiner's causal attribution theory, Zimmerman's self-regulated learning theory, and expectancy-value theory into one intervention model. It conceptualizes the constructs as "dynamically interconnected processes in which attributional beliefs shape motivational expectancies, in turn, expectancies guide self-regulatory engagement, and sustained regulation reinforces academic performance". This grounds the study's synergistic intervention targeting all three mechanisms simultaneously rather than in isolation.
requirements: Interventions must target attributional beliefs, motivational expectancies, and self-regulatory engagement simultaneously rather than separately
constraints: The article notes the three constructs are often examined separately in prior literature; the integrated model was tested only in a one-group quasi-experimental design without a control group
target_learning_goals: Adaptive causal attributions for academic success and failure
examples: The eight-session training program devoted sessions 1–3 to causal attributions, sessions 4–6 to self-regulation, and sessions 7–8 to achievement motivation within the expectancy–value framework
key_sources: Meshesha Yeshitla Meaza, Weldmeskel Fisseha Mikre. (2026). Gender differences in causal attributions, self-regulation, achievement motivation, and academic performance following an intervention. BMC Psychology, 14, 588. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40359-026-04357-0

article_title: Implementation of an Integrated Pharmacology Curriculum in a Flipped, Small-Group, Case-Based, Pre-Clerkship Medical Curriculum Improved Student Performance.
citation: Brinda Desai Bradaric, Eric Van Rite, Lalita Prasad‐Reddy, Michael Bradaric. (2026). Implementation of an Integrated Pharmacology Curriculum in a Flipped, Small‐Group, Case‐Based, Pre‐Clerkship Medical Curriculum Improved Student Performance. Pharmacology Research & Perspectives. https://doi.org/10.1002/prp2.70258
title: Offer the integrated flipped case-based pharmacology design as a transferable framework for programs considering curricular change
description: The article presents its curricular redesign as a transferable framework: pharmacology content is distributed across organ-system courses over 15 months, delivered through flipped asynchronous videos, and practiced in collaborative case-based sessions with dedicated pharmacology faculty. The authors state, "We hope the framework presented here will serve as a road map to other medical or pharmacy schools, as well as nursing and physician assistant programs considering curricular changes." The design description is paired with item-statistic and satisfaction evidence from their own implementation.
requirements: A discipline director with expertise in each basic science, plus dedicated pharmacology faculty responsible for all pharmacology content
Team-written cases with answers to all questions provided in script form for facilitating faculty
constraints: Developed and evaluated at a single 4-year allopathic medical school
Classical Test Theory item statistics are sample-dependent, so observed differences may reflect changes in student ability or assessment administration
target_learners: Medical, pharmacy, nursing, and physician assistant programs considering similar curricular changes
target_learning_goals: Integration of pharmacology with other basic and clinical sciences
Preparedness and confidence in pharmacology knowledge and drug-regimen selection
examples: In-person didactic lectures were eliminated and replaced with 45 hours of asynchronous recordings and 72 integrated cases; suggested innovations include case-based approaches, small-group discussion sessions, and flipped content delivery
key_sources: Brinda Desai Bradaric, Eric Van Rite, Lalita Prasad‐Reddy, Michael Bradaric. (2026). Implementation of an Integrated Pharmacology Curriculum in a Flipped, Small‐Group, Case‐Based, Pre‐Clerkship Medical Curriculum Improved Student Performance. article_title: The "Testing Effect" in Undergraduate Endodontic Education: The Impact of Regular Low Stakes Testing on Learning Outcomes and Student Engagement.
citation: Kalyva, M., Kavvadia, K., Louca, L., Televantou, I., & Michaelides, M. P. (2026). The “Testing Effect” in Undergraduate Endodontic Education: The Impact of Regular Low Stakes Testing on Learning Outcomes and Student Engagement. International Endodontic Journal, 59(6), 1227–1235. https://doi.org/10.1111/iej.70022
title: Integrate regular, low-stakes testing into endodontic and dental curricula to enhance learning outcomes
description: The article's central design recommendation is that retrieval practice be built into courses as routine, ungraded post-lecture testing rather than reserved for high-stakes evaluation. The authors conclude that "Integrating regular, low‐stakes testing into endodontic courses can improve long‐term knowledge retention and better prepare students for clinical practice." The intervention was implemented within existing course structure and platform infrastructure, requiring no additional staffing or cost.
requirements: Tests should be framed as learning tools rather than evaluative measures, since perceived high stakes may reduce their learning benefits
Corrective feedback should accompany testing
Participation can be incentivised by grading on submission rather than accuracy
constraints: The study was conducted within a single institution, so the authors note the generalizability of the findings may be limited
The demonstrated effect covers final exam questions targeting the lower levels of Bloom's Taxonomy (knowledge, comprehension, application)
target_learners: undergraduate third-year dental students in preclinical endodontics
target_learning_goals: retention of foundational endodontic knowledge (instruments, root canal treatment procedures, radiographic techniques, obturation materials, pulpal and periapical conditions)
examples: In the study, students were tested immediately after lectures 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, and 12 with five to seven multiple-choice questions on the Blackboard Learn platform, receiving automated corrective feedback 10 min after the lecture ended
key_sources: Kalyva, M., Kavvadia, K., Louca, L., Televantou, I., & Michaelides, M. P. (2026). The “Testing Effect” in Undergraduate Endodontic Education: The Impact of Regular Low Stakes Testing on Learning Outcomes and Student Engagement. article_title: Impact of inpatient volume on residents' In-training examination scores and burnout in Japanese community hospitals: a nationwide cross-sectional study.
citation: Ishizuka K, Nishizaki Y, Kataoka K, Shimizu T, Nojima M, Yamamoto Y, Shikino K, Fukui S, Nagasaki K, Kobayashi H, Ohta M, Tokuda Y. (2026). Impact of inpatient volume on residents' In-training examination scores and burnout in Japanese community hospitals: a nationwide cross-sectional study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-08664-3
title: Assess Very Low-Volume hospitals individually for core training hospital designation rather than relying solely on the inpatient volume threshold
description: The article proposes that hospitals below Japan's 3,000-inpatient regulatory threshold should be evaluated on their educational environment rather than excluded by volume alone, since "residents at Very Low-Volume Hospitals achieve GM-ITE® scores and mental health outcomes comparable to those at larger hospitals." Accreditation decisions should additionally consider supervision quality, rotation availability, and support systems that the study did not fully assess.
requirements: An individual assessment recognizing an educational environment where residents can acquire basic clinical skills
constraints: The study did not assess key accreditation factors such as supervision quality, rotation availability, or resident support systems, so results are evidence on inpatient volume rather than sufficient grounds for accreditation decisions
target_learners: PGY-1 and PGY-2 postgraduate medical residents in Japan
target_learning_goals: acquisition of basic clinical knowledge and skills
examples: The study used the existing regulatory cut-off of 3,000 yearly inpatients to define the Very Low-Volume group so the criterion's educational validity could be evaluated empirically

article_title: Learning gain of an ATLS(®)-based interprofessional and multidisciplinary in-situ simulation training of trauma resuscitation.
citation: Hammer Silke, Lock Johan F., König Sarah, Happel Oliver, Paul Mila M. (2026). Learning gain of an ATLS®-based interprofessional and multidisciplinary in-situ simulation training of trauma resuscitation. European Journal of Trauma and Emergency Surgery. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00068-026-03146-z
title: Include all experience levels in trauma team simulation training and design scenarios that explicitly address communication and reinforce flat hierarchies
description: Because the authors found gains across every subgroup and especially large operational-competence gains among less experienced staff, they conclude "it is reasonable not only to include members at all levels of experience in the training, but also to design scenarios that explicitly address communication-related issues and reinforce flat hierarchies." The principle rests on their own interpretation that team communication and decision making involve using all personnel resources without hierarchical restriction, citing prior work supporting flatter trauma-team structures.
requirements: Structured debriefings within the simulation program
Scenarios that explicitly address communication-related issues
constraints: Based on Kirkpatrick level 2 self-assessment data; behavioral transfer not yet evaluated
target_learners: Early-career staff and all professional levels of ad-hoc trauma teams
target_learning_goals: Team communication, psychological safety, and shared decision making in resuscitation
examples: The iSRST program at Wuerzburg trained mixed groups averaging eight participants from all involved departments twice a year

Learning gain of an ATLS®-based interprofessional and multidisciplinary in-situ simulation training of trauma resuscitation. article_title: Use of a specific set of learner-centered evidence-based teaching practices correlates with higher exam performance across seven STEM departments.
citation: Jackson Mallory A., Liu Hongjiao, Moon Sungmin, Doherty Jennifer H., Wenderoth Mary Pat. (2026). Use of a specific set of learner-centered evidence-based teaching practices correlates with higher exam performance across seven STEM departments. PLOS One. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0327269
title: Learner-centered practice sets shift the responsibility of intellectual work—the learning—to students, aligned with sociocultural constructivism and the ICAP framework
description: The authors propose an explanatory account for why the learner-centered set of PORTAAL practices correlates with higher exam scores: the instructor sets up the problem and interaction format, then "shifts the responsibility of the intellectual work of the problem—the learning—to the students." They link this to sociocultural constructivism, in which learning occurs as learners interact and collaborate to build understanding, and to the ICAP Framework's claim that learning increases as engagement moves from passive toward interactive. Facilitating student answering and explaining, using volunteer and random call to hear varied voices, and giving timely positive feedback are the proposed mechanisms.
requirements: The instructor poses a problem, prompts students to use logic, allows time for answers, and elicits student answers/explanations via volunteer or random call, closing with positive feedback
constraints: The account is the authors' interpretation of correlational data, not an experimentally tested mechanism
target_learners: undergraduate STEM students in large lower- and upper-division courses
target_learning_goals: improved exam performance through student practice of explaining and constructing answers
examples: The article's representative learner-centered scenario: the instructor poses a question, prompts logic, waits, then has volunteers or randomly called students answer and explain, ending with positive feedback
key_sources: Jackson Mallory A., Liu Hongjiao, Moon Sungmin, Doherty Jennifer H., Wenderoth Mary Pat. (2026). Use of a specific set of learner-centered evidence-based teaching practices correlates with higher exam performance across seven STEM departments. PLOS One. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0327269

article_title: Development and evaluation of a literature seminar course based on flipped classroom and team-based learning in the graduate nursing curriculum.
citation: Qi Hong, Ban Jingjing, Wang Nana, Guo Huimin, Yang Yang, Tang Shan. (2026). Development and evaluation of a literature seminar course based on flipped classroom and team-based learning in the graduate nursing curriculum. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-08823-6
title: Integrate flipped classroom pre-class preparation with team-based in-class application and post-class reflection to build research competence and self-efficacy in graduate education
description: The article recommends structuring research-oriented courses so that students complete independent pre-class preparation, engage in team-based collaborative application during class, and consolidate learning through post-class reflection. The authors state that "the flipped classroom component emphasizes students' pre-class knowledge construction, while the TBL component focuses on applying and expressing knowledge through team collaboration." This integration is presented as offering "a replicable framework that promotes inquiry-based, competency-oriented learning" for postgraduate curricula that continue to rely on didactic instruction.
requirements: Instructor roles must shift from lecturer to facilitator, mentor, and evaluator, providing scaffolding, formative feedback, and individualized support rather than information transmission.
The intervention should be standardized and delivered within a short, defined course period with consistent pre- and post-assessment procedures.
constraints: Comparisons with other interventions (EBP programs, journal clubs) should be interpreted cautiously given differences in study design, participant characteristics, and outcome measures.
The single-group pretest-posttest design without a control group limits causal interpretation; future studies should adopt controlled or multi-center designs.
target_learners: graduate students in research-oriented health professions programs
examples: The article's course required each group to select one paper from a Chinese core nursing journal and one from a high-impact SCI journal, present for 30–35 minutes, and submit revised slides after class feedback.
key_sources: Qi Hong, Ban Jingjing, Wang Nana, Guo Huimin, Yang Yang, Tang Shan. (2026). Development and evaluation of a literature seminar course based on flipped classroom and team-based learning in the graduate nursing curriculum. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-08823-6

article_title: Construction and implementation of an AI-enhanced progressive training model for clinical competency development in obstetrics and gynecology residents.
citation: He Lidan, Wu Jianbo, Yang Huijuan, Wang Jinhua, Li Xuemei, Chen Lihong. (2026). Construction and implementation of an AI-enhanced progressive training model for clinical competency development in obstetrics and gynecology residents. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-08751-5
title: Intelligent practice teaching platform with three core modules
description: The intelligent practice teaching platform is the article's central technological artifact, comprising three interconnected modules: a virtual simulation practice platform using LapSim® Haptic System VR/AR simulation for 10 common surgical procedures, an intelligent skills training platform with machine-learning competency assessment and personalized recommendations, and a clinical practice intelligent support platform with decision support and communication simulation. It included "a comprehensive virtual case learning environment containing 60 clinically representative cases stratified by complexity." Residents interacted with rule-based virtual cases in a turn-based format receiving automated feedback.

Machine learning-based competency assessment algorithms fed by individual learning analytics
constraints: Evaluated only within obstetrics and gynecology residency training at a single institution
target_learning_goals: procedural skill proficiency, clinical reasoning, and clinical decision-making
examples: Virtual case studies (n = 30) were generated using rule-based algorithms and expert-validated scenarios, with residents making sequential clinical decisions and receiving automated feedback at each step

article_title: Comparative validation of a cost-effective in-house 3D-printed LLETZ simulator versus a commercial training model.
citation: Scherer-Quenzer AC, Reinhart K, Diessner J, Altides A, Buechel J, Blau-Schneider B, Sauer ST, Deschler-Baier B, Woeckel A, Kiesel M. (2026). Comparative validation of a cost-effective in-house 3D-printed LLETZ simulator versus a commercial training model. Archives of Gynecology and Obstetrics. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00404-026-08413-3
title: In-house 3D-printed LLETZ simulator with agar–agar cervix
description: A low-cost simulator for training large loop excision of the transformation zone, created using "modified algae powder, 3D-printing and casting techniques". It includes an artificial cervical canal, marked precancerous lesions, nulliparous/multiparous cervix variation, and supports a Lugol iodine test. In this study it was compared against the commercial LLETZlearn® simulator with 60 students and 10 residents performing five electrosurgical excisions each.
requirements: Requires an electrosurgical generator and loop electrodes; participants selected from three loop sizes (10 × 10 mm, 15 × 12 mm, and 20 × 15 mm)
constraints: The study assessed short-term performance across five attempts only and did not assess long-term skill retention or transferability to clinical practice
target_learners: medical students without prior LLETZ experience
examples: Produced at an estimated cost of EUR 263.11 with algae-based artificial cervixes at around EUR 0.33 per unit, versus approximately EUR 1300 for the commercial simulator plus about EUR 1 per cervical substitute

article_title: Evaluating medical students' engagement and confidence across three simulation-based education methods: standardized patient, high fidelity simulator, and virtual reality.
citation: Yu Jihye, Lee Sukyung, Kim Mira, Lee Janghoon, Jung Yun Jung. (2026). Evaluating medical students’ engagement and confidence across three simulation-based education methods: standardized patient, high fidelity simulator, and virtual reality. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-08634-9
title: Integrate multiple simulation modalities in clinical curricula, matching each modality's strengths to learning objectives
description: The article recommends designing clinical practice curricula that combine simulation methods according to their distinct educational strengths: SP for patient-facing confidence, HFS and VR for technical detail and complex scenarios. It states "the need to appropriately integrate various simulation methods in medical school clinical practice curricula" and that leveraging SP strengths "while incorporating the technical advantages of HFS and VR, could provide high-quality clinical practice education."
requirements: Educators should consider the unique educational strengths of each simulation modality and select appropriate methods based on students' learning objectives and instructional contexts.
constraints: The SP confidence advantage may partly reflect differences in learning objectives across the three simulation modules.
The evidence comes from a single university sample, potentially restricting generalizability of the findings.
target_learners: Medical students in clinical practice education
target_learning_goals: Clinical performance confidence in history-taking, physical examination, and patient interaction and communication
Comprehensive clinical competencies across diverse clinical situations
examples: In the study, 43 fifth-year medical students completed SP, HFS, and VR modules during a respiratory rotation; SP yielded significantly higher confidence in history-taking, physical examination, and patient communication, while HFS and VR did not differ.

article_title: Could Instructor Talk Drive CURE Effectiveness? A Comparative Study of Instructor Talk in Introductory Lab Courses.
citation: Zajic et al. (2026). Could Instructor Talk Drive CURE Effectiveness? A Comparative Study of Instructor Talk in Introductory Lab Courses. CBE—Life Sciences Education. https://doi.org/10.1187/cbe.24-09-0241
title: Codebook of 14 non-content instructor talk types with definitions and example quotes
description: A qualitative codebook produced from deductive and inductive content analysis of audio recordings of introductory biology lab instruction. The authors state, "We define and describe each talk type and interpret how each relates to the corresponding frame (i.e., our finalized codebook)." It includes immediacy types (sharing personal experiences, engaging in small talk, building trust, emphasizing availability) and self-efficacy types (normalizing struggles, providing encouragement, normalizing iteration, encouraging interdependence, encouraging independence and ownership, scaffolding), each with definitions and verbatim example quotes, plus double-coding of negative examples.
requirements: Transcribed audio recordings of class sessions; iterative pair coding to consensus by at least four team members per transcript
constraints: Quotes too brief to ascribe sufficient meaning (e.g., "Great!") were not coded; course type was masked but often evident from talk content
target_learners: undergraduate students in introductory life science lab courses
target_learning_goals: characterizing instructor talk that may influence student motivation
examples: Immediacy talk comprised 716 quotes or 35% of the corpus; the most prevalent self-efficacy type was normalizing struggles (n = 214; 11%)

title: Integrated simulation with TBL pattern for paediatric CPR training
description: A small-group instructional pattern combining a full-scale paediatric simulator scenario with Team-Based Learning structures. The article states that "TBL was delivered independently through: structured clinical role delineation; pre-session assigned readings; real-time team discussions during crisis management; rotational leadership roles (e.g., team leader, compressor, ventilator); and peer-feedback protocols after each simulation cycle." The simulation supplies a standardized cardiac-arrest scenario whose vital-sign dynamics respond to team performance.

A standardized scenario with defined phases and anticipatory reactions
Defined six-person resuscitation roles with rotation and peer-feedback protocols
constraints: Evaluated only in a single-centre pre-post study of 24 postgraduates without a control group

article_title: Perceptual learning enhances diabetic retinopathy detection skills in novice optometry students.
citation: Choi Kai Yip, Chan Ka Wing, Yau Hiu Ching, Lau Yuet Yan, Leung Tsz Wing. (2026). Perceptual learning enhances diabetic retinopathy detection skills in novice optometry students. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-08691-0
title: Integrate web-based perceptual learning modules into health professions curricula to build foundational pattern-identification skills efficiently
description: The article recommends integrating perceptual learning modules (PLMs) — repetitive classification practice with immediate trial-by-trial correct-answer feedback delivered on a scalable web-based platform — into health professions curricula. Its evidence shows four weeks of self-directed training raised novice diagnostic accuracy to a senior-student benchmark level, with gains retained at three months. As the authors state, these findings "support the integration of PLMs into health professions curricula to efficiently improve pattern identification – a foundation of diagnostic skill."
requirements: Repetitive practice with a high volume of varied examples and immediate, trial-by-trial correct-answer feedback
A curated image set spanning the relevant feature categories, with ground truth established by trained graders
constraints: Perceptual learning is task-specific; transfer to other pathologies or imaging modalities remains unclear
The intervention supplements rather than replaces continued clinical exposure and traditional apprenticeship
Generalisability beyond a single-centre optometry sample requires confirmation
target_learners: novice pre-clinical health professions students (Year 1–2 optometry students in this study)
target_learning_goals: visual pattern identification of pathological signs, a foundation of diagnostic skill
examples: Novice optometry students completed a four-week, self-directed home training program reviewing 200 retinal photographs in random order, identifying the presence or absence of eight DR signs with immediate feedback on a web-based platform compatible with mobile devices
key_sources: Choi Kai Yip, Chan Ka Wing, Yau Hiu Ching, Lau Yuet Yan, Leung Tsz Wing. (2026). Perceptual learning enhances diabetic retinopathy detection skills in novice optometry students. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-08691-0

article_title: Application of project-based and simulation-based approaches in medical curriculum.
citation: Kldiashvili E., Al-Rustum S., Zarnadze M., Goderdzishvili D., Tvildiani M., Mamiseishvili A. (2025). Application of project-based and simulation-based approaches in medical curriculum. BMC Medical Education 25:1707. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-08196-2
title: Integrate research-oriented project-based learning and simulation-based case analysis into the undergraduate medical curriculum to strengthen academic performance and originality
description: The article recommends embedding research-oriented PrBL and simulation technologies such as the Anatomage table into medical training, arguing these active formats support research competence, science communication, and academic integrity. Its exploratory results back this: "The Anatomage table aids in a better understanding of medical problems and helps in formulating research questions," and PrBL groups outperformed comparison groups on rubric scores and Turnitin originality. The authors present this as initial insight for refining competency-based curricula, not as established causal practice.
requirements: Careful integration into medical training with standardized prior academic exposure
Faculty mentorship and common assessment rubrics across comparison groups
constraints: No direct comparison or pedagogical superiority claim between PrBL and SBL is warranted, as the cohorts differed in academic level, curricular exposure, and instructional context
Causal attribution is limited by the non-randomised cross-sectional design and possible novelty (Hawthorne) effects
examples: The study implemented PrBL research projects in one semester cohort and Anatomage-based case reporting in another, evaluating each independently with rubric scores and Turnitin similarity indices

article_title: Medical school grades may predict future clinical competence.
citation: Wu Jr-Wei, Cheng Hao-Min, Huang Shiau-Shian, Liang Jen-Feng, Huang Chia-Chang, Shulruf Boaz, Yang Ying-Ying, Chen Chen-Huan, Hou Ming-Chih, Huey-Herng Sheu Wayne. (2022). Medical school grades may predict future clinical competence. Journal of the Chinese Medical Association. https://doi.org/10.1097/JCMA.0000000000000782
title: Structured interviews as a gatekeeper for noncognitive negative applicant characteristics rather than a linear predictor of clinical competence
description: The article proposes that although structured PGY interview grades did not correlate with OSCE performance, the interview may capture "other noncognitive factors, i.e., interpersonal communication skills, interest in the field, dependability, and honesty". It frames the interview as "an important 'gatekeeper' for certain negative characteristics, which are challenging to analyze by the OSCEs". Some applicant characteristics may require the interviewer's 'gut feeling' or clinical experience.
requirements: Interviewers with clinical experience to identify negative applicant characteristics
constraints: The article states the interview may not linearly reflect clinical competencies; a UK study found multiple mini-interviews associated with subsequent OSCEs, suggesting several mini-interviews may be more helpful

target_learning_goals: Selection of trainees for postgraduate clinical training

article_title: Relationships between cognitive appraisals of threat and challenge, psychophysiological responses, and clinical performance during high-stress simulated osces.
citation: Betson J, Fein EC, Long D, Horrocks P. (2025). Relationships between cognitive appraisals of threat and challenge, psychophysiological responses, and clinical performance during high-stress simulated osces. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-08365-3
title: Integrate stress appraisal and regulation strategies, including practice OSCEs, into paramedicine curricula
description: The article recommends that curricula explicitly address how students appraise high-pressure assessments. It states the results "highlight the need for curricula to explicitly integrate stress appraisal and regulation strategies into paramedicine education", pairing structured reflection on challenge versus threat mindsets and resilience training with practice OSCEs under simulated assessment conditions so students experience authentic stressors in a controlled environment.
requirements: Simulated assessment conditions that replicate authentic examination stressors
Structured reflection activities on challenge versus threat mindsets
constraints: The authors note findings come from a relatively small sample of 26 participants, which may limit generalisability
target_learners: undergraduate paramedicine students facing high-stakes OSCE assessments
target_learning_goals: managing acute stress during clinical performance
examples: Participants completed two simulated OSCE scenarios seven days apart under assessment conditions, and both appraisal groups improved significantly from Scenario 1 to Scenario 2

article_title: Implementing an Interprofessional Simulation Program for Paediatric Patient Safety.
citation: D'Arienzo D., Dandavino M., Matte A.-A., Welsh S., Rich C., Korah N. (2026). Implementing an Interprofessional Simulation Program for Paediatric Patient Safety. The Clinical Teacher. https://doi.org/10.1111/tct.70301
title: Unit-specific interprofessional in situ simulation program for paediatric patient safety
description: A program of eight monthly in situ simulations on a paediatric medical–surgical ward, each scenario built so that a unit-specific safety error was "the critical event in each scenario". Design followed the Healthcare Simulation Instructional Design Framework (analysis, design, development, implementation, evaluation), with structured prebriefing and Gather–Analyse–Summarise debriefing led by consistent facilitator teams. Participants were nurses, nursing assistants, medical students, residents, fellows and pharmacists, achieving an 86% participation rate (n = 125).
requirements: An interdisciplinary planning team with health profession education and patient safety expertise
Leadership support to protect time and make participation mandatory
A physical space on the ward equipped like a patient room
constraints: Scenarios were developed based on unit-specific errors and incidents, limiting generalisability
Logistical challenges such as scheduling and potential disruption to clinical workflows complicate implementation
target_learners: interprofessional hospital ward staff: nurses, physicians, residents, medical students, fellows, pharmacists
target_learning_goals: recognise and respond to unit-specific patient safety errors
examples: An 18-month-old bronchiolitis scenario in which hypoglycaemic seizure followed normal saline instead of D5NS as the IV fluid

description: A simulation laboratory programme in which intervention students "practiced on scenarios created by the researchers on a simulation model (cardiac rhythms, pupil assessment, and lung sounds) besides clinical practice training". Students were taken to the laboratory in groups of 10, and each session ran in three sections: a 5-minute preliminary briefing on the scenario and goals, a 10–15 minute application process, and a 15–20 minute analysis. The design, prebriefing, facilitation and debriefing phases followed the INACSL Healthcare Simulation Standards of Best Practice.
requirements: A simulation laboratory with a simulation model; scenarios prepared by researchers; sessions structured as briefing, application, and analysis phases
constraints: Delivered as an addition to clinical practice for students in one internal medicine nursing course at a single Turkish university

title: Integrate 3D visualization reconstruction technology into PBL clinical teaching to improve performance, critical thinking, and satisfaction
description: The article recommends combining problem-based learning with three-dimensional visualization reconstruction technology in clinical teaching. Its stated implications are that "Incorporating 3D-VRT into clinical teaching enhances anatomical visualization and supports procedural learning" and that "Embedding PBL in trauma orthopaedic education promotes contextualized and collaborative learning". Instructors adopting facilitator roles within a PBL framework

article_title: Clinical simulation and deliberate practice in rapid-cycle deliberate practice: a randomized clinical trial.
citation: da Silva Gisele Cabral, Campanharo Cássia Regina Vancini, Lopes Maria Carolina Barbosa Teixeira, Okuno Meiry Fernanda Pinto, Miura Carla Roberta Monteiro, Batista Ruth Ester Assayag. title: Include all simulation participants, regardless of role, from briefing to debriefing with methodological rigor
description: The article recommends that simulation scenarios be conducted "with methodological rigor, valuing each stage of the process and including all participants, regardless of their role, from briefing to debriefing", calling this essential to ensuring the most effective learning possible. The recommendation rests on the trial's finding that observing students gained as much knowledge as acting students, and on the review literature the authors cite showing observers' outcomes equal to or better than actors'. It treats observers as full learners rather than idle participants.
requirements: Valuing each stage of the simulation process from briefing to debriefing
Deliberate inclusion of observing participants in all stages of the activity
constraints: Supported in this trial only for knowledge acquisition about initial stroke care among nursing students; the authors note the tests were conducted in a single simulation center

target_learning_goals: knowledge of initial care for patients with suspected stroke
examples: In the trial, the 66 SWSP students were redistributed into acting and observing subgroups, and both roles improved knowledge significantly with no statistical difference between them

description: The article recommends that schools implement integrated programs combining motor skill development with fitness and cognitive training, tailored to sex-specific needs. The authors state that "boys may benefit more from cognitively demanding, perceptual–motor activities, while girls may respond better to interventions prioritizing physical fitness enhancement." This recommendation follows from their finding that fitness and executive function partially mediate the relationship between gross motor competence and academic achievement.
requirements: Programs should integrate motor skill development with both fitness and cognitive training
constraints: Cross-sectional design implies association, not causality; longitudinal studies are needed to confirm temporal direction

title: Foreign language teaching should integrate environmental support strategies with cognitive strategies targeting academic emotions
description: Because social support's effect on English achievement operates through foreign language emotions, the article concludes that effective foreign language teaching "should integrate both environmental and cognitive strategies to optimize students' emotional experiences and academic outcomes". Educators are advised to "emphasize strategies that stimulate students' positive emotions and encourage them to discover the enjoyment and value of foreign language learning", while reducing anxiety and boredom and maintaining a safe classroom atmosphere.
requirements: Instruction must address both external social support and students' internal emotional experiences, not support alone
constraints: Grounded in a cross-sectional study, so the causal ordering the recommendation presumes is not established; the article calls for longitudinal tracking to establish directional pathways
target_learning_goals: positive academic emotions in foreign language learning
examples: The study measured support from parents, teachers, classmates, close friends, and the school via the CASSS and linked it to enjoyment, boredom, anxiety, and percentage-converted exam scores

article_title: Exploring the relationship between student-content interaction, student-student interaction, self-efficacy, and learning achievements in a student-centered classroom.
citation: Zhang Lu and Vongurai Rawin. (2025). Exploring the Relationship between Student-Content Interaction, Student-Student Interaction, Self-Efficacy, and Learning Achievements in a Student-Centered Classroom. F1000Research 14:709. https://doi.org/10.12688/f1000research.165290.1
title: Interaction–self-efficacy–achievement model for student-centered classrooms
description: The article proposes and validates a structural model in which student-content interaction and student-student interaction influence learning achievement both directly and through self-efficacy as mediator, grounded in Moore's interaction types and Bandura's self-efficacy theory. The conceptual framework "displays all causal relationships among variables, including student-content interaction, student-student interaction, self-efficacy, and learning achievement". CFA confirmed convergent and discriminant validity of the four latent variables, and SEM fit indices (CMIN/DF=2.270, GFI=0.938, CFI=0.976, RMSEA=0.049) supported the model. The authors present it as a framework for designing educational interventions promoting academic success through interactive learning practices.
requirements: Measurement instruments with demonstrated reliability and validity for the four latent variables (Cronbach's alpha, CR, AVE thresholds met in the study).
constraints: Tested only in a specific sample and population, which the article states limits generalizability to other educational contexts.
Excludes other potentially influential factors such as motivation, emotional intelligence, and learning environment characteristics, per the article's limitations.
examples: Applied to 524 education undergraduates at five Chinese application-oriented universities using online questionnaires analyzed with CFA and SEM in SPSS AMOS version 26.

The authors extend it by proposing "two additional competencies that are highly salient in today's evolving educational and psychological demands: academic competency and coping with stress," and by positioning school engagement as a promotive mechanism mediating effects of both promotive (campus climate) and inhibiting (SLEs) environments on academic and psychological outcomes. constraints: Originally developed with urban, historically marginalized adolescents; the authors state suburban findings suggest additional theoretical refinements for applicability across diverse settings

target_learning_goals: Psychological well-being and coping with stress
examples: Path analyses in a sample of 293 suburban high school students tested school engagement as mediator between campus climate, SLEs, achievement, and distress

examples: The authors cite triad mannequin simulation studies reporting that "triad groups exhibiting high TeamSTEPPS scores demonstrated elevated Shannon entropy of neurodynamic symbols" at the 10-Hz rhythm, consistent with waxing and waning group attention.

article_title: Acute neurology simulation-based training boosts confidence and reduces anxiety in novice neurology residents and nursing staff.
citation: Sela Y, Cassuto M, Capua T, Dadbaeiv L, Molad J, Hallevi H, Gadoth A, Sadan O, Seyman E. (2025). Acute neurology simulation-based training boosts confidence and reduces anxiety in novice neurology residents and nursing staff. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07948-4
title: National multidisciplinary acute-neurology SBME curriculum with five scenarios, mannequins, live actors, and PEARLS debriefing
description: A nationwide simulation-based medical education program for PGY-2 neurology residents and nursing staff, run at the Tel Aviv Sourasky Medical Center simulation center and funded by the Israeli Neurological Association. "The course structure, detailed in Fig. 1, consisted of 5 scenarios, with each scenario individually comprising 20 min of live simulation followed by 25 min of video-assisted debriefing." Scenarios covered acute ischemic stroke, acute coma, meningoencephalitis, status epilepticus, and acute non-traumatic lower limb weakness, using "computer-enhanced mannequin simulators and live actor assistance" aligned with published ENLS protocols.
requirements: Teams of two participants (a resident case manager with a nurse, or two residents) per scenario
Two experienced instructors observing and assessing with standardized scenario-specific checklists
Instructors trained in a 2-hour debriefing session before the course
constraints: Enrollment was determined by neurology department directors at each hospital and was not yet mandatory in the residency curriculum
target_learners: nursing staff in acute neurology care
target_learning_goals: identify and manage acute neurological emergencies
teamwork and communication in emergency care
examples: 79 medical professionals from 11 Israeli medical centers completed the program between January 2020 and April 2024

article_title: Impact of simulation-based learning on the academic performance of medical students during pediatric clerkships.
citation: Elamin Abdelaziz, Ali Maryam Fuad, Almarabheh Amer. (2025). Impact of simulation-based learning on the academic performance of medical students during pediatric clerkships. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07911-3
title: Integrate simulation-based learning as a teaching strategy across clinical specialties, complementing and partially replacing classroom-based instruction
description: The article concludes that its pediatric-clerkship findings justify broader adoption of simulation-based learning: "These findings support the wider integration of SBL as a teaching strategy across various clinical specialties in medicine and nursing worldwide." It frames SBL as able to "progressively complement and, in some cases, partially replace traditional classroom-based instruction." The recommendation rests on the significant pre/post performance gains the study measured.
requirements: Essential elements for effective SBL: clear learning objectives, an appropriate venue, suitable equipment and software, skilled instructors, structured debriefing sessions, constructive feedback, and motivated students actively participating in hands-on practice
constraints: The supporting evidence comes from retrospective cohort comparison across different student cohorts over 12 years, not randomized assignment, which the authors call ethically unacceptable in this context
target_learners: fifth-year undergraduate medical students in clinical clerkships
target_learning_goals: clinical competence in pediatrics, including written knowledge, clinical examination performance, and continuous assessment
examples: At CMHS, AGU, the Medical Skills and Simulation Center was established in 2017, and from 2018–2019 SBL was integrated into Pediatrics, Obstetrics & Gynecology, Internal Medicine, and Surgery curricula using high-fidelity manikins, standardized patients, and realistic equipment.
key_sources: Elamin Abdelaziz, Ali Maryam Fuad, Almarabheh Amer. (2025). Impact of simulation-based learning on the academic performance of medical students during pediatric clerkships. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07911-3

article_title: Evaluation of dental students' tooth preparation skills using conventional phantom labs versus advanced simulation technologies: a comparative study.
citation: Kızılırmak Burcu, Gözen Mehmet, Güntekin Neslihan. (2025). Evaluation of dental students’ tooth preparation skills using conventional phantom labs versus advanced simulation technologies: a comparative study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-08020-x
title: Integrate VR-based haptic simulation into preclinical dental curricula alongside conventional phantom training
description: The article concludes that simulation-based training significantly improved tooth preparation skills and argues for incorporating simulation technologies into conventional dental education because they "facilitate a more individualized and effective learning process". Simulation offers a safe, repeatable, measurable environment that complements the basic foundation conventional training provides, potentially enhancing clinical readiness.
requirements: Instructor training and adaptation time for students transitioning to digital systems
Simulation should be complemented by patient-based training
constraints: The article recommends a student-centered and gradual approach rather than abrupt transitions, noting some students initially experience greater difficulty in simulation environments
examples: In this trial, both groups received 10 h of training from the same instructor, with the simulation group achieving higher post-test scores across all assessed criteria

article_title: Becoming through simulation-based learning: Lived experiences of occupational therapy students from culturally and linguistically diverse backgrounds.
citation: Zhang, L., Forbes, R., Patterson, F., & Penman, A. (2025). Becoming through simulation‐based learning: Lived experiences of occupational therapy students from culturally and linguistically diverse backgrounds. Australian Occupational Therapy Journal, 72(4), e70044. https://doi.org/10.1111/1440-1630.70044
title: Design SBL environments that foster inclusive peer interactions and culturally responsive educator-student relationships
description: The article concludes that supporting CALD students' success in SBL requires environments that foster belonging: culturally diverse group compositions, educators who demonstrate cultural sensitivity and adapt communication, and psychological safety to ask questions without judgement or shame. The authors state it is important to design SBL that helps "students from CALD backgrounds feel a stronger sense of belonging and engagement", recognising both struggles and strengths.
requirements: Educators must carefully evaluate additional sources of stress and thoughtfully structure SBL environments that balance challenge with psychological safety
constraints: Evidence derives from student perspectives only; educator and simulated patient views were not collected
target_learners: Occupational therapy students from CALD backgrounds in Australian entry-level programmes
target_learning_goals: Sense of belonging and engagement in simulation-based learning
examples: A participant described an Iranian tutor who slowed her speaking speed and asked other tutors to give international students more understanding

description: The article argues that because perceiving TBL sessions as systematically organized is linked to active participation, the instructor's role should shift "from a 'knowledge transmitter' traditionally emphasized in lecture-based teaching to a 'course designer' who strategically structures learning activities and the learning environment to achieve educational goals". It states institutional support is essential to help medical education instructors develop these course-design capabilities.
requirements: Adequate institutional support to help instructors develop capabilities as effective TBL course designers
constraints: Derived from correlational moderation findings on self-reported perceptions at one Korean medical school; the article states empirical evidence on optimal TBL frequency and timing remains lacking
target_learning_goals: Sustained active participation in team-based learning
examples: The article recommends ensuring objectives, structure, and evaluation criteria are explicitly aligned with core TBL principles when teaching repeat participants

article_title: A Large-Scale Multispecialty Evaluation of Web-Based Simulation in Medical Microbiology Laboratory Education: Randomized Controlled Trial.
citation: Lei Xu, Xichuan Deng, Tingting Chen, Nan Lu, Yuran Wang, Jia Liu, Yanan Guo, Zeng Tu, Yuxin Nie, Yeganeh Hosseini, Yonglin He. (2025). A Large-Scale Multispecialty Evaluation of Web-Based Simulation in Medical Microbiology Laboratory Education: Randomized Controlled Trial. JMIR Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.2196/72495
title: Integrate virtual simulation with traditional hands-on laboratory practice rather than substituting one for the other
description: The article argues that virtual simulation and real experiments each possess distinct advantages, and that the optimal teaching strategy should involve an organic integration of both approaches. Virtual experiments offer safety, repeatability, standardization, and visualization, while real experiments retain irreplaceable advantages in cultivating practical operational skills and sensory experiences. The combination leverages the safety and flexibility of virtual simulation with the irreplaceable tactile experience of real laboratory practice.
requirements: Access to both a virtual simulation platform and traditional laboratory sessions within the course schedule
constraints: Feedback from 1.1% of students indicated limited assistance from virtual experiments, highlighting persistent limitations in substituting for hands-on operations in real environments
target_learners: medical students in microbiology laboratory education
examples: In the trial, the experimental group received virtual simulation training prior to traditional laboratory practice, and both groups engaged in comprehensive learning activities emphasizing laboratory safety awareness and standardized experimental procedures

article_title: Exploring the integration of OFST and IPE in cross-regional physiology teaching-a novel approach.
citation: Wang Ting-Huai, Xu Xiao-Dan, Long Zhi-Yuan, Cao Ying-Nan, Lai Ning-Yi, Ma Yong-Hong, Tan Xiao-Qiu, Xin Min, Jiang Jin-Yan, Yang Da-Ya. (2025). Exploring the integration of OFST and IPE in cross-regional physiology teaching-a novel approach. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07412-3
title: Interprofessional OFST course structure combining quizzes, case-based team learning, and experience sharing
description: A reusable lesson/unit-level design: teacher guidance with progressively complex checkpoints, an individual quiz baseline after self-regulated learning, interprofessional teams of 5–8 students working a clinical case, a second parallel-form quiz, then group presentations with peer feedback, instructor moderation, and team awards. The article states "Both quizzes covered identical checkpoints to ensure consistency in evaluation", and groups were designed "to maintain a balance of professional diversity, with an effort to include at least two different disciplines in every group".
requirements: Quiz items matched to the guided checkpoints, with parallel forms for Quiz 1 and Quiz 2
An online platform for delivery and quiz administration (Ding Talk; WJX)
A case study chosen for its interdisciplinary relevance across the participating majors
constraints: The reported instance covered one topic (coronary circulation) within a physiology course
target_learners: undergraduate students from ten majors across multiple universities
examples: 31 interprofessional groups of 5–8 students formed freely, selected group leaders, analysed a myocardial infarction case, and presented slides on CHD aetiology, symptoms, examination, diagnosis, and treatment

article_title: Spoilt for Choice in Undergraduate Medical Admission: Selection of Confident and Considerate Students Using Professional Prequalification and Situational Judgement Test.
citation: Mielke I, Hampe W, Ehrhardt M, Knorr M. (2025). Spoilt for Choice in Undergraduate Medical Admission: Selection of Confident and Considerate Students Using Professional Prequalification and Situational Judgement Test. Perspectives on Medical Education 14(1). https://doi.org/10.5334/pme.1571
title: Three observable interpersonal behavior dimensions: agency (assured-dominant), communion (warm-agreeable), and emotional stability
description: The study frames supervisors' ratings of students' actual behavior using three distinct and observable interpersonal dimensions drawn from interpersonal theory. Agency and communion are described as "two fundamental and well-established factors in interpersonal theory" highlighting motives to achieve one's own goals or to establish relationships, with assured-dominant and warm-agreeable behavior as the focused facets; emotional stability describes a tendency to stay calm and stable associated with resilience. The article uses this framework to give admission criteria a behavior-focused validity test rather than relying on broad composite scores.
requirements: Raters must observe students in actual work situations; the article used an adapted short form of the Interpersonal Adjective List rated on a 1–8 scale
constraints: The article reports emotional stability was difficult to assess by observers because the construct includes internally felt emotional states, with lower reliability
target_learning_goals: interpersonal behavior with patients, relatives, and colleagues
examples: Supervisors rated students after a one-week general practice training using four adjectives per dimension from the Interpersonal Adjective List short form

article_title: A novel simulation paradigm for medical ICU cardiopulmonary arrest training: the in situ mirror simulation.
citation: Johnkutty Meenu, Kuperstein Harry, Koroma Fatima, Chen Jessi, Mattson James, Ahmad Sahar. (2025). A novel simulation paradigm for medical ICU cardiopulmonary arrest training: the in situ mirror simulation. Medical Education Online. https://doi.org/10.1080/10872981.2025.2528355
title: In situ mirror simulation program for MICU cardiopulmonary arrest training
description: An adjunct simulation program in which clinical data from a currently admitted MICU patient at high risk of cardiopulmonary arrest is 'mirrored' into a simulation run in a vacant MICU room: "patient data, room configuration and unit equipment are made available in a manner identical to the real patient being simulated." A PGY-3 resident leads up to three PGY-1 residents through an approximately 15-minute scenario using an iSimulate ALSi monitor, mannequin with modeled vascular access, and EMR access, followed by a 15-minute structured debrief and ACLS-instructor checklist scoring.
requirements: A vacant patient room in the unit, which the authors note some planned simulations had to be aborted for lack of
Faculty time, an available simulation technician, and equipment including a simulated telemetry monitor
Close coordination with unit staff to minimize interruption
constraints: Feasibility depended on the institution's MICU keeping a crash bed consistently vacant
No new orders could be physically placed during the event, and patient PHI mentions were confined to the simulation room
target_learners: PGY-3 internal medicine residents as team leaders
target_learning_goals: Cardiac arrest team leadership and management
examples: Twenty-four simulations were completed between July 2022 and October 2024, all during the first 4 months of each academic year

article_title: Medical simulation: an essential tool for training, diagnosis, and treatment in the 21st century.

title: Integrate simulation into medical curricula as a safe complement to conventional patient practice
description: The review argues simulation does not replace conventional training with real patients but should be built into curricula because it offers safe, programmable, adaptable practice. It states simulation is "a technology that has proven to be safe for the training of resident doctors" and that "it is necessary to integrate simulation into medical curricula."
requirements: Institutional integration planning, including recommendations on implementation and standardization of skills assessment measures
constraints: The review states simulation does not replace conventional medical training with real practices
target_learning_goals: safe practice in difficult-to-reproduce clinical scenarios
examples: The review recommends that medical schools and hospitals integrate simulation-based training, noting potential barriers of costs, teacher training requirements, and lack of evidence in certain subject areas.
