article_title: Unveiling team needs: a qualitative study of simulation training for endovascular cerebral thrombectomy.
citation: Fugelli Caroline Guldberg; Hansen Britt Sætre; Ersdal Hege; Kurz Martin. (2025). Unveiling team needs: a qualitative study of simulation training for endovascular cerebral thrombectomy. BMJ Open Quality. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjoq-2024-002981
title: Inclusive simulation design: involving all professional groups from the outset to align NORA simulation training with clinical practice
description: The study's central framework for improving simulation training for non-operating room anaesthesia procedures: "inclusive simulation design, defined as involving input from all professional groups from the outset". It holds that NORA simulations fail to prepare teams unless disciplines such as anaesthesia contribute to scenario design, so that realistic task interactions, haemodynamic challenges and shared understanding can be trained. The authors argue engagement of all disciplines should be an ongoing, iterative improvement process.
requirements: Active input from all professional groups involved in the NORA team, particularly anaesthesia, in designing scenarios and debriefing
constraints: The authors do not present their findings as the definitive solution for optimal NORA simulation scenario design; evidence is single-centre and qualitative
target_learners: multidisciplinary emergency NORA teams (anaesthesia, radiology, neurology, nursing)
target_learning_goals: shared understanding of roles and responsibilities
examples: The findings informed a multidisciplinary expert panel whose modifications included allowing anaesthesia professionals to contribute to both the design and implementation of scenarios

article_title: The relationship and mechanism of screen time and academic performance among adolescents: an empirical study based on CEPS.
citation: Feng Xiaosu, Ren Shuanquan, Shi Peng. (2025). The relationship and mechanism of screen time and academic performance among adolescents: an empirical study based on CEPS. Frontiers in Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpubh.2025.1533327
title: Integrative multi-pathway mechanistic model of screen time effects on academic performance
description: The article constructs a hypothetical mechanistic model (H2, Figure 1) in which screen time affects adolescent academic performance through three levels: cognitive performance as the proximal predictor, physical and mental health (BMI, subjective health perception, sleep duration, mental health), and social constructs (peer and parent–child relationships). It extends prior pathway models that tested only cognition, adopting "an integrative perspective, examining the role of cognitive, health, and social relationship factors more broadly". Path analysis on the CEPS sample tested the model's 21 paths.
requirements: Requires measures of cognitive performance, physical and mental health indicators, and social relationship variables alongside academic scores, as provided by the CEPS cognitive test and questionnaire items
constraints: Confirmed with cross-sectional data, so causal ordering is not established; the BMI and subjective health perception paths and the mental health path were not supported in this sample
target_learners: Chinese junior middle school students (grades 7 and 9)
target_learning_goals: Academic performance in Chinese, mathematics and English; cognitive performance
examples: The model was tested with structural equation modeling on 17,150 CEPS students, with fit indices CMIN/DF = 4.127, RMSEA = 0.013 and CFI = 0.999
key_sources: Feng Xiaosu, Ren Shuanquan, Shi Peng. (2025). The relationship and mechanism of screen time and academic performance among adolescents: an empirical study based on CEPS. Frontiers in Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpubh.2025.1533327

article_title: Mindfulness and sustainability competencies in physical education teachers: Demographic factors as moderators.
citation: Işıkgöz Mustafa Enes. (2025). Mindfulness and sustainability competencies in physical education teachers: Demographic factors as moderators. BMC Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40359-025-02885-9
title: Two-dimensional model of mindfulness in teaching: intrapersonal and interpersonal mindfulness
description: The study's organizing model distinguishes two dimensions of teacher mindfulness. Intrapersonal mindfulness is "the ability to understand and manage one's own feelings, thoughts, and behaviors while establishing a deep connection with oneself", while interpersonal mindfulness is "the ability to understand and respond appropriately to the emotions, cognitions and needs of others". The model positions both dimensions as predictors of PE teachers' sustainability competencies, with gender, school level and education level as hypothesized moderators (hypotheses H1–H5b), tested via structural equation modeling and moderator analysis.
requirements: Measurement of both dimensions, operationalized by the 14-item Mindfulness in Teaching scale (Intra_MF 9 items, Inter_MF 5 items)
constraints: The article frames the model for PE teachers in middle and high schools in Turkey, tested with a cross-sectional design
target_learners: Physical education teachers in middle and high schools
target_learning_goals: Understand how teacher mindfulness relates to sustainability competencies in teaching
examples: The research model (Fig. 1) specifies Intra_MF and Inter_MF as predictors and demographic variables as moderators

title: Brief in situ multidisciplinary first-responder code simulation with simple objectives for generalizability across disciplines and settings

article_title: Nursing students' experiences and perceptions regarding in-class flipped classroom: a mixed-methods study.
citation: Zhang Dongmei, Huang Anle, Lei Yunxiao, Liu Haiyang, Yang Liu, Wang Congzhi, Yuan Ting, Li Xiaoping, Zhang Lin, Shang Wenyuan. (2025). Nursing students’ experiences and perceptions regarding in-class flipped classroom: a mixed-methods study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07248-x
title: In-class flipped classroom model for nursing practice teaching
description: The in-class flipped classroom is a localized variant of the flipped classroom in which, unlike the traditional flipped classroom approach, the in-class flipped model relocates self-directed pre-class learning activities from outside to within the classroom setting. The article grounds it in Community of Inquiry theory (teaching, social, and cognitive presence) and situated learning theory, and implemented it in pediatric nursing skills lab courses to alleviate workload, time constraints, and lack of familiarity associated with pre-class activity.
requirements: Instructors must possess "extensive professional expertise and contingency ability" to guide students' self-directed problem-solving.
constraints: The approach was implemented within pediatric nursing skills courses; when applied in other courses, appropriate adjustments may be needed, such as modifications to the time allocation of the instructional procedures.

target_learning_goals: practical nursing skills and clinical competence
self-directed learning and higher-order cognitive skills
examples: Implemented across four pediatric nursing skill modules in 160-minute skills lab courses at Wannan Medical College, with students engaging in self-directed learning during the initial segment of the class.

title: Interprofessional education should be incorporated into all health and social service education programs
description: The article asserts that interprofessional competencies are essential for managing chronic non-communicable diseases and should be broadly integrated into professional education. The authors state that "Interprofessional competencies should therefore be incorporated into all health and social service education programs." They argue that interprofessional education strengthens collaborative work, reduces duplication of professional acts, improves communication, and increases user satisfaction.
requirements: Training programs that integrate multiple health professional categories
constraints: The article notes that the effectiveness of interprofessional approaches depends on socioeconomic and cultural aspects of the context
target_learners: Health and social work students and professionals across all professional categories
examples: The UFSC specialization course integrated several health professions and served as a practical example of applying experiential learning to develop interprofessional skills
key_sources: Ramos Saulo Fabio; Amadigi Felipa Rafaela; Gonçalves Natália; de Souza Thaise Honorato; Backes Vânia Marli Schubert; Tourinho Francis Solange Vieira; Meirelles Betina Hörner Schlindwein; Lino Monica Motta. (2025). Experiential learning in interprofessional health training on chronic non-communicable diseases: an ex-post-facto evaluation. Revista da Escola de Enfermagem da USP. https://doi.org/10.1590/1980-220X-REEUSP-2024-0300en

article_title: The role of video and direct laryngoscopy in medical student intubation training: a comparative study on success rates and learning curves.
citation: Öcal Mustafa. (2025). The role of video and direct laryngoscopy in medical student intubation training: a comparative study on success rates and learning curves. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07239-y
title: Integrate both video laryngoscopy and direct laryngoscopy into intubation training programs
description: The article recommends that intubation training programs combine VL and DL rather than teaching either method alone. VL "can enhance motivation by providing novice learners with rapid learning and higher initial success rates", while "DL supports long-term skill development, and training programs should allocate significant focus to this method as well". The combination lets learners achieve quick initial results while progressively developing proficiency for complex scenarios.
requirements: Training programs must include both VL and DL practice opportunities, with significant focus allocated to DL for long-term skill development
constraints: Evidence comes from a mannequin-based study with a normal airway configuration; simulated scenarios may not fully replicate real clinical conditions
target_learners: inexperienced medical students without prior endotracheal intubation training
target_learning_goals: preparation for complex and difficult airway scenarios
examples: 130 medical students practiced with both the McGrath video laryngoscope and the Macintosh laryngoscope across two randomized scenarios with up to three attempts each
key_sources: Öcal Mustafa. (2025). The role of video and direct laryngoscopy in medical student intubation training: a comparative study on success rates and learning curves. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07239-y

article_title: Institutional proficiency and learning curves in robotic-assisted thoracoscopic surgery: a single-center retrospective analysis using the cumulative sum method.
citation: Uchida Tsuyoshi, Matsubara Hirochika, Tando Chihiro, Mobara Koshi, Muto Mamoru, Sugimura Aya, Nakajima Hiroyuki (2025). Institutional proficiency and learning curves in robotic-assisted thoracoscopic surgery: a single-center retrospective analysis using the cumulative sum method. Journal of Robotic Surgery. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11701-025-02387-1
title: Intuitive Surgical certification pathway for adopting RATS surgeons
description: Before performing robot-assisted surgeries, all four surgeons in the study "received Intuitive Surgical certification, including online Da Vinci technology modules, simulator exercises (> 20 h), and console surgeon training (a 1-day course with hands-on practice)." The pathway combines didactic online modules, simulator practice exceeding 20 hours, and a one-day hands-on console course. Each surgeon also brought substantial prior VATS experience, ranging from over 300 to 150 anatomical lung resections, so the pathway supplemented rather than replaced open surgical experience.
requirements: Prior VATS experience in anatomical lung resections characterized the adopters in this program
Completion of online modules, over 20 hours of simulator exercises, and the 1-day console course
constraints: The article does not evaluate the pathway in isolation; proficiency outcomes reflect the whole program
target_learners: experienced thoracic surgeons adopting robotic-assisted thoracoscopic surgery
examples: Surgeon A had 13 years of VATS experience with over 300 anatomical lung resections before starting RATS
key_sources: Uchida Tsuyoshi, Matsubara Hirochika, Tando Chihiro, Mobara Koshi, Muto Mamoru, Sugimura Aya, Nakajima Hiroyuki (2025). Institutional proficiency and learning curves in robotic-assisted thoracoscopic surgery: a single-center retrospective analysis using the cumulative sum method. article_title: Perceived vs. experienced care: a comparison between nursing students' self-assessed competence and patients' reported care.
citation: Ulupınar Fadime, Karasu Şeyda. (2025). Perceived vs. experienced care: a comparison between nursing students’ self-assessed competence and patients’ reported care. BMC Health Services Research. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12913-025-12880-w
title: Integrate relational competencies (communication, empathy, emotional support) into clinical training alongside technical skills
description: The article recommends that while "technical skills remain foundational", nursing education may benefit from more explicit inclusion of training modules focused on communication, empathy, and emotional support to help bridge the perceptual gap between what students intend to provide and what patients experience. It further suggests that "simulation-based exercises or role-playing scenarios that blend technical proficiency with empathetic engagement" could better equip students, and that educators should emphasize interpersonal aspects of care during practical placements.
requirements: Clinical training programs with practical placements in which students provide direct care to patients, so relational behaviors can be practiced and observed.
constraints: The supporting evidence is cross-sectional and correlational from a single hospital region, so the recommendation rests on associations rather than tested causal effects.
target_learners: undergraduate nursing students in clinical placements (years 2–4)
examples: The authors propose integrating simulation-based exercises or role-playing scenarios that blend technical proficiency with empathetic engagement, and emphasizing interpersonal aspects of care during practical placements.
key_sources: Ulupınar Fadime, Karasu Şeyda. (2025). Perceived vs. experienced care: a comparison between nursing students’ self-assessed competence and patients’ reported care. BMC Health Services Research. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12913-025-12880-w

article_title: General practitioners' scanning competence following tailored ultrasound training: a hybrid effectiveness-implementation study.
citation: Andersen Camilla Aakjær, Lundbye-Christensen Søren, Riis Allan, Mehnert Ulrike, Løkkegaard Thomas, Mengel-Jørgensen Troels, Rasmussen Liv Dyre, Soll Nicolai, Stork Bo, Andersen Søren Kæseler, Pil Louise, Stjernebjerg Christian, Graumann Ole, Jensen Martin Bach. (2025). General practitioners’ scanning competence following tailored ultrasound training: a hybrid effectiveness-implementation study. BMC Medical Education 25:733. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07356-8
title: Assess individual scanning competence rather than requiring a fixed number of performed examinations
description: The article argues that certification goals based on a fixed number of performed ultrasound examinations are being replaced by individual competence assessment, and its own finding of no clear relationship between the number of performed examinations and OSAUS sum score supports this shift. The authors note that "simply requiring an arbitrary number of examinations has been found insufficient" and state that their findings support individual competence assessment, while cautioning that the missing relationship should be interpreted with caution owing to lack of statistical power.
requirements: A standardized competence assessment tool such as the OSAUS instrument rated by trained assessors
constraints: The missing relationship between educational elements, including number of scans, and OSAUS sum scores should be interpreted with caution owing to the lack of statistical power and interaction between elements
target_learners: Office-based general practitioners learning point-of-care ultrasound
target_learning_goals: Certification and quality assurance of POCUS training
examples: In this study, scanning competence was assessed as observed overall scanning competence on a scale from 7–35, calculated competence using a predefined cut-off, and self-perceived competence, rather than by scan counts
key_sources: Andersen Camilla Aakjær, Lundbye-Christensen Søren, Riis Allan, Mehnert Ulrike, Løkkegaard Thomas, Mengel-Jørgensen Troels, Rasmussen Liv Dyre, Soll Nicolai, Stork Bo, Andersen Søren Kæseler, Pil Louise, Stjernebjerg Christian, Graumann Ole, Jensen Martin Bach. (2025). General practitioners’ scanning competence following tailored ultrasound training: a hybrid effectiveness-implementation study. BMC Medical Education 25:733. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07356-8

article_title: The use of 360-videos to bridge the gap between pre-clinical and clinical dental teaching.
citation: Nabeela C, Shykhon M, Milward M, Yonel Z. (2025). The use of 360-videos to bridge the gap between pre-clinical and clinical dental teaching. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-06946-w
title: Interactive annotated 360-video of the periodontology clinic with linked learning-resource buttons
description: A 360-degree video of the clinical environment, captured with an Insta360 Pro 2 camera and annotated in ThingLink, embedded in the Canvas learning platform and usable with a mobile-phone-based VR headset. Interactive "buttons" were placed on key structures such as the dental chair; clicking them linked out to additional resources including text, audio, videos, documents and standard operating procedures. Access was limited to the 13-student intervention group two weeks before standard induction.
requirements: A 360-degree camera capture of the clinical environment and an annotation platform (ThingLink) to add interactive buttons
Hosting on an online learning platform with access restricted to the intended student group
constraints: 360-video interactivity is limited to views captured by the camera and scenes are pre-recorded and fixed, unlike fully immersive VR
The supplied headset had no controllers, limiting interactivity
target_learners: undergraduate dental students in the pre-clinical to clinical transition
target_learning_goals: clinic orientation and familiarity with the clinical environment
examples: Buttons were added to key structures such as the dental chair, linking to videos, podcasts, documents and standard operating procedures
key_sources: Nabeela C, Shykhon M, Milward M, Yonel Z. (2025). The use of 360-videos to bridge the gap between pre-clinical and clinical dental teaching. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-06946-w

article_title: Design of an interactive brain model for neuroanatomy education and MRI training.
citation: McNaughton EP, Bilbie L, Zuljevic M, Allen LK, Pur D‐R, Eagleson R, de Ribaupierre S. (2025). Design of an interactive brain model for neuroanatomy education and MRI training. Anatomical Sciences Education. https://doi.org/10.1002/ase.70009
title: Dual-platform interactive 3D brain model with MRI superimposition for neuroanatomy education
description: A virtual application offering an interactive 3D brain model deployable on desktop and mobile devices, with the mobile app presenting the model in augmented reality. Users can highlight, isolate, and read functional descriptions of neural structures, complete a 10-question quiz, and view MRI slices: "With 75 images accessible across the three spatial planes, users gain comprehensive exposure to MRI data in the sagittal, coronal, and axial views." The model was built from Visible Human Project data segmented in FMRIB Software Library and rendered in Amira, with the mobile app developed in Unity 3D using AR Foundation.
requirements: Deployable on both Android and iOS devices via a model-driven software development approach
Users scan their local environment for horizontal plane detection before deploying the AR model
constraints: Open access on app stores awaits prospective results of a comprehensive study on the app's utility
target_learning_goals: identifying neural structures on MRI slices
examples: The mobile app was developed with Unity 3D (2020.3.33f1) and edited using Unity's AR Foundation (5.0.7), with plane detection used for model deployment and raycast translation
key_sources: McNaughton EP, Bilbie L, Zuljevic M, Allen LK, Pur D‐R, Eagleson R, de Ribaupierre S. (2025). Design of an interactive brain model for neuroanatomy education and MRI training. Anatomical Sciences Education. https://doi.org/10.1002/ase.70009

article_title: Interactional competencies in medical student admission- what makes a "good medical doctor"?
citation: Fleck, L., Amelung, D., Fuchs, A., Mayer, B., Escher, M., Listunova, L., Schultz, J.-H., Möltner, A., Schütte, C., Wittenberg, T., Schneider, I., & Herpertz, S. C. (2024). Interactional competencies in medical student admission– what makes a “good medical doctor”?. Advances in Health Sciences Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10459-024-10348-w
title: Use theory-based, construct-driven measures of interactional competencies to complement cognitive criteria in medical student selection
description: The article advocates grounding simulation-based admission assessments in an established, observably measurable psychological construct rather than expert-consensus competency lists, to avoid construct validity ambiguities. It concludes that "Measures of interactional competencies should be used as selection tools to complement traditional (cognitive) selection criteria, reflecting the ideal profile of a medical school candidate", since selection should identify candidates suited to both cognitive and interactional demands.
requirements: A measurement construct that is readily observable under quasi-realistic conditions, conceptually clear, empirically well-founded, and reflects basic competencies in human communication beyond specific medical competencies
constraints: The article states no claims can yet be made about the procedure's incremental prognostic validity; predictive validity for study success and clinical performance remains to be addressed in future studies
target_learning_goals: interactional competencies relevant to the medical setting
examples: The IC-MD MMI circuit used five four-minute simulation patient scenarios, each posing a clear challenge to discriminate between performance levels, with scenarios such as discussing lifestyle changes or resolving waiting-room conflicts
key_sources: Fleck, L., Amelung, D., Fuchs, A., Mayer, B., Escher, M., Listunova, L., Schultz, J.-H., Möltner, A., Schütte, C., Wittenberg, T., Schneider, I., & Herpertz, S. C. (2024). Interactional competencies in medical student admission– what makes a “good medical doctor”?. Advances in Health Sciences Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10459-024-10348-w

article_title: Undergraduate STEM Students' Perceptions of Grading Practices Reveal that Quiz Retakes Positively Impact Drivers of Self-determination.
citation: Tripp Brie, Ravi Akshaya, Pang Ethan, Furrow Robert E. (2025). Undergraduate STEM Students’ Perceptions of Grading Practices Reveal that Quiz Retakes Positively Impact Drivers of Self-determination. CBE—Life Sciences Education 24(1). https://doi.org/10.1187/cbe.24-06-0167
title: In-class quiz retakes integrated into a two-part final exam
description: A low-effort alternative grading practice in which several evenly distributed low-stakes quizzes during the term can be retaken during a scheduled final exam period. "The instructors integrated retakes into scheduled course time through a two-part final exam; one part contained a cumulative final exam (mandatory) and the second part an opportunity to take new versions of earlier quizzes (optional)." Retake quizzes assessed the same learning outcomes with novel questions, and a student's highest score for each quiz counted. Quizzes carried 28–30% of the course grade across a statistics and a neurobiology course.
requirements: Retake quizzes must assess the same learning outcomes as the initial versions
The highest score for each quiz (initial or retake) becomes the final score for that assessment
constraints: In one course students could retake any of 6–7 quizzes; in the other students chose two of five quizzes to retake
target_learners: undergraduate STEM students in statistics and neurobiology courses
target_learning_goals: demonstrating proficiency with course learning outcomes
examples: R.E.F. embedded 6–7 quizzes per term in statistics for biologists; B.T. embedded 5 quizzes in neurobiology, delivered in class for 15 minutes or online for 60 minutes
key_sources: Tripp Brie, Ravi Akshaya, Pang Ethan, Furrow Robert E. (2025). Undergraduate STEM Students’ Perceptions of Grading Practices Reveal that Quiz Retakes Positively Impact Drivers of Self-determination. CBE—Life Sciences Education 24(1). https://doi.org/10.1187/cbe.24-06-0167

article_title: Undergraduate STEM Students' Perceptions of Grading Practices Reveal that Quiz Retakes Positively Impact Drivers of Self-determination.
citation: Tripp Brie, Ravi Akshaya, Pang Ethan, Furrow Robert E. (2025). Undergraduate STEM Students’ Perceptions of Grading Practices Reveal that Quiz Retakes Positively Impact Drivers of Self-determination. CBE—Life Sciences Education 24(1). https://doi.org/10.1187/cbe.24-06-0167
title: Integrate retake opportunities into scheduled course time rather than optional outside-of-class work to avoid participation inequities
description: The article recommends embedding retakes into course meeting times because optional, outside-of-class retake systems risk unequal uptake. The authors state that "systems that require optional, outside-of-class work risk lower participation rates by students with lower initial performance (Walck-Shannon et al., 2019) and can perpetuate inequities by preferentially advantaging students with more flexible schedules (Supriya et al., 2024)." They therefore favored retakes integrated into class sessions in their own courses.
requirements: Retakes must occur during scheduled course time, such as a two-part final exam
constraints: The article frames this as avoiding biases in task completion that perpetuate inequities; it does not claim in-class integration maximizes learning
target_learners: undergraduate students, including those with less flexible schedules or work obligations
examples: The authors implemented retakes during a scheduled two-part final exam period in three statistics offerings and two neurobiology offerings rather than as optional out-of-class work
key_sources: Tripp Brie, Ravi Akshaya, Pang Ethan, Furrow Robert E. (2025). Undergraduate STEM Students’ Perceptions of Grading Practices Reveal that Quiz Retakes Positively Impact Drivers of Self-determination. CBE—Life Sciences Education 24(1). https://doi.org/10.1187/cbe.24-06-0167

article_title: Application of ultrasound simulation training in intensive care nursing teaching.
citation: Cheng G, Yanling S, Jing W, Ping Z, Zhen L. (2025). Application of ultrasound simulation training in intensive care nursing teaching. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-06968-4
title: Introduce ultrasound simulation training into the ultrasound training of ICU nurses
description: Based on the randomized comparison showing significantly higher theoretical scores, practical scores, and satisfaction for simulation training, the article recommends adoption: "it is recommended to introduce ultrasound simulation training into the ultrasound training of ICU nurses." The authors add that "if the case database in the background of the training system can be improved regularly, graded training will be even more helpful for improving the skills of trainees." Simulation offers standardized, repeatable practice free from patient-availability and ethical constraints.
requirements: Access to an ultrasound simulator platform; instructors able to give professional guidance; regular improvement of the training system's case database to support graded training
constraints: The article states simulation training has the characteristic of high cost, citing an estimated average cost of $638 to train one trainee in an ultrasound simulator; the limited case base may not help trainees at an advanced stage; further research is needed to directly evaluate the impact of ultrasound simulation training on trainee skill development
target_learners: ICU nurses receiving advanced ultrasound training
target_learning_goals: Ultrasound theoretical knowledge and practical operation skills in intensive care
examples: In this study, 20 nurses trained on the Vimedix simulator for 30 days outperformed 20 traditionally taught nurses on theoretical, practical, and satisfaction measures
key_sources: Cheng G, Yanling S, Jing W, Ping Z, Zhen L. (2025). Application of ultrasound simulation training in intensive care nursing teaching. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-06968-4

article_title: Improving Tanzanian student nurse-midwives' knowledge, skills and attitude in postpartum hemorrhage prevention through simulation-based education: a pre-post quasi experimental study.
citation: Faustine Rose, Tjoflåt Ingrid, Risa Eva Christina Furskog, Rogathi Jane, Mahande Michael Johnson. (2025). Improving Tanzanian student nurse-midwives’ knowledge, skills and attitude in postpartum hemorrhage prevention through simulation-based education: a pre-post quasi experimental study. BMC Pregnancy and Childbirth. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12884-025-07590-4
title: Integrate standardized simulation scenarios and educator training into nurse-midwifery curricula
description: Based on the demonstrated gains in knowledge, skills, self-confidence, and satisfaction, the article recommends that "the Ministry of Health and Nurse and Midwifery Council in Tanzania should support nurse training institutions by integrating standardized postpartum hemorrhage scenarios into the ordinary diploma curriculum and by training nurse educators in simulation-based teaching methods." This responds to reported underutilization of simulation, with only 53% of Tanzanian educators incorporating it.
requirements: Institutional and regulatory support from health and nursing-midwifery authorities
Trained nurse educators in simulation-based teaching
constraints: How simulation-based education fits into an already tight curriculum needs further exploration with the Tanzanian nursing and midwifery council
target_learners: Student nurse-midwives in ordinary diploma programs in Tanzania
target_learning_goals: Competence in preventing and managing postpartum hemorrhage; quality of maternal care
examples: The study delivered simulation two hours daily for eight days as an extra teaching activity alongside existing theory and skills practice.

Improving Tanzanian student nurse-midwives’ knowledge, skills and attitude in postpartum hemorrhage prevention through simulation-based education: a pre-post quasi experimental study. BMC Pregnancy and Childbirth. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12884-025-07590-4

article_title: Evaluation of acquisition and retention of non-technical skills of residents submitted to interprofessional simulation-based training in pediatric cardiopulmonary resuscitation.
citation: Friedlaender Rafaella Fadel, Gubert Eduardo Maranhão, Fernandes Cláudia Maria Baroni, Mello Rosiane Guetter, Coelho Izabel Cristina Meister Martins. (2025). Evaluation of acquisition and retention of non-technical skills of residents submitted to interprofessional simulation-based training in pediatric cardiopulmonary resuscitation. Jornal de Pediatria. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jped.2024.12.003
title: Interprofessional team simulation with fixed roles and deliberately high-complexity scenarios for non-technical skill training
description: This session-level design organizes residents into stable interprofessional teams (four to seven members, at least one resident from each year of pediatrics and nursing) who repeat the same simulated scenario with roles fixed across repetitions. The scenario was deliberately demanding: ventricular fibrillation was "purposefully chosen to increase the degree of technical and non-technical skill difficulty", since a high-complexity, low-frequency situation demanded more from the team in leadership, communication, task management, and teamwork. Before each simulation, residents decided who would be leader and other roles; the leader was the higher-degree medical resident and roles were maintained through all scenarios.
requirements: Stable team composition across repeated scenarios
Simulator orientation on operation and limitations before each simulation
Trained instructors delivering structured debriefing
constraints: The article notes residents were not used to frequent simulation training and some worked together clinically but not regularly on the same team
target_learners: Pediatric medicine and nursing residents in interprofessional teams
target_learning_goals: Leadership, communication, task management, and effective teamwork in emergency care
examples: 16 teams of four to seven residents completed a 10-minute scenario of a 6-year-old male patient developing cardiopulmonary arrest in ventricular fibrillation, repeated at three moments.
key_sources: Friedlaender Rafaella Fadel, Gubert Eduardo Maranhão, Fernandes Cláudia Maria Baroni, Mello Rosiane Guetter, Coelho Izabel Cristina Meister Martins. (2025). Evaluation of acquisition and retention of non-technical skills of residents submitted to interprofessional simulation-based training in pediatric cardiopulmonary resuscitation. Jornal de Pediatria. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jped.2024.12.003

article_title: Comfortable knowing little about lymphoedema? A qualitative study of medical interns in Australia.
citation: Kruger N, Plinsinga M, Window P, Hayes S, Bunzli S. (2025). Comfortable knowing little about lymphoedema? A qualitative study of medical interns in Australia. BMJ Open. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjopen-2024-089789
title: Integrate lymphatic system research and clinical exposure into medical curricula so graduates can assess, diagnose and refer people with lymphoedema
description: The article recommends that current lymphatic research and its clinical implications be built into medical curricula, with sufficient learning opportunities and clinical exposure. It argues this is needed because interns showed knowledge gaps and ambivalent attitudes, and because "lymphoedema is absent from published curricula frameworks". The recommendation is grounded in the study's finding of a discord between recalled teaching and expected graduate capabilities.
requirements: Curricula review and alignment of learning objectives with current evidence and expert consensus
constraints: Findings are of limited transferability to interns in other countries; the sample was a convenience sample concentrated in Queensland
target_learning_goals: assessing, diagnosing and managing or referring lymphoedema
understanding the lymphatic system's role in health and disease
examples: Participants suggested lectures on lymphoedema and greater exposure to real-life patients to appreciate its importance
key_sources: Kruger N, Plinsinga M, Window P, Hayes S, Bunzli S. (2025). Comfortable knowing little about lymphoedema? A qualitative study of medical interns in Australia. BMJ Open. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjopen-2024-089789

article_title: Comfortable knowing little about lymphoedema? A qualitative study of medical interns in Australia.
citation: Kruger N, Plinsinga M, Window P, Hayes S, Bunzli S. (2025). Comfortable knowing little about lymphoedema? A qualitative study of medical interns in Australia. BMJ Open. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjopen-2024-089789
title: Four-theme ambivalence framework for intern attitudes towards lymphoedema
description: The article organises its qualitative findings into an overarching theme of ambivalence captured in four themes: 'gaps in knowledge', 'low expectation to know about lymphoedema', 'unclear relevance to the intern role' and 'low sense of responsibility towards lymphoedema care'. This framework, derived inductively through reflexive thematic analysis, explains how interns reconcile knowledge gaps with comfort: they do not expect to know about lymphoedema, see little role relevance, and assign responsibility to others.
requirements: Semistructured interviews with first-postgraduate-year medical graduates analysed via reflexive thematic analysis
constraints: Derived from a homogeneous convenience sample of 12 interns, mostly Queensland-based; limited transferability to interns in other countries
target_learning_goals: understanding attitudes towards chronic condition care
identifying curricular gaps in medical education
examples: Figure 1 presents the thematic structure; table 2 provides codes and supporting quotes for themes 1–4
key_sources: Kruger N, Plinsinga M, Window P, Hayes S, Bunzli S. (2025). Comfortable knowing little about lymphoedema? A qualitative study of medical interns in Australia. BMJ Open. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjopen-2024-089789

article_title: Effectiveness of a scenario-based simulation course on improving the clinical communication skills of dietetic students.
citation: Liu Mei-Yuan, Liao Li-Ling, Huang Yu-Ting, Lee Yi-Chen, Lai I-Ju. (2025). Effectiveness of a scenario-based simulation course on improving the clinical communication skills of dietetic students. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-06684-z
title: Integrate structured, simulation-based communication courses with OSCE assessment into undergraduate dietetics curricula
description: The article concludes that dietetics programs should combine theoretical learning with simulated practical application and use OSCE with standardized patients to assess and reinforce clinical communication skills. Its evidence is the significant post-test advantages in confidence, self-efficacy, competence, and OSCE performance after a 12-week scenario-based course. The authors note OSCE is "resource-intensive" but valuable where dietitian licensing exams lack clinical skill components.
requirements: Structured scenarios with clearly defined learning objectives and gradual increase in complexity
Trained standardized patients providing consistent, repeatable scenarios and immediate feedback
Validated assessing materials and examiner/SP scoring training
constraints: OSCE application is resource-intensive
The two-station design may have restricted the scope of skill evaluation; more stations could give a more comprehensive assessment
target_learning_goals: clinical readiness for nutrition counseling practice
examples: The study's 12-week course paired weekly simulation practice with pre- and post-intervention two-station OSCEs using registered-dietitian examiners and certified standardized patients
key_sources: Liu Mei-Yuan, Liao Li-Ling, Huang Yu-Ting, Lee Yi-Chen, Lai I-Ju. (2025). Effectiveness of a scenario-based simulation course on improving the clinical communication skills of dietetic students. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-06684-z

article_title: Effects of intra-class peer mentorship intervention programme on the academic performances of academically underperforming medical students in Nigeria.
citation: Eleje George Uchenna, Ikwuka David Chibuike, Nwosu Kingsley Chinaza, et al. (2025). Effects of intra-class peer mentorship intervention programme on the academic performances of academically underperforming medical students in Nigeria. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-06728-4
title: Structured intra-class peer mentorship programme for underperforming medical students
description: A structured same-class peer mentorship intervention in which academically underperforming students (mentees scoring below 45% on a continuous assessment test) were paired with high-performing same-class mentors (scoring 70% or above). "The mentorship programme lasted for six months, with regular weekly meetings between mentors and mentees" addressing academic challenges, goal-setting, and emotional support, plus group activities fostering community and shared learning. It was led by an experienced educationist and evaluated with the SVS, USEI, and CAT scores.
requirements: Mentors receive prior training covering mentoring techniques, communication skills, confidentiality, etiquette in conversations, roles of mentors and mentees, instructional procedures, and limits of the mentor and mentee
constraints: The article notes the small mentee group size (n = 7) and short six-month duration may have limited detection of changes in SVS and overall USEI scores
target_learners: Preclinical medical students scoring below 45% on continuous assessment
target_learning_goals: Behavioural, cognitive, and emotional school engagement
examples: At Nnamdi Azikiwe University, 7 mentees, 12 mentors, and 30 controls participated; mentees' median CAT score rose from 40.0 to 70.0 over the programme
key_sources: Eleje George Uchenna, Ikwuka David Chibuike, Nwosu Kingsley Chinaza, et al. (2025). Effects of intra-class peer mentorship intervention programme on the academic performances of academically underperforming medical students in Nigeria. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-06728-4

article_title: An integrated communication and technical skills educational intervention in critical healthcare situations: A qualitative method.
citation: Juliá‐Sanchis, R., Escribano, S., Sánchez‐Marco, M., García‐Aracil, N., Perpiñá‐Galvañ, J., & Cabañero‐Martínez, M. J. (2025). An integrated communication and technical skills educational intervention in critical healthcare situations: A qualitative method. Nursing Open, 12, e70002. https://doi.org/10.1002/nop2.70002
title: Train technical and communication skills together in integrated scenarios rather than as separate components
description: The article argues that clinical and communication skills are inextricably linked in real-world practice, so curricula that teach them separately are reductionist. Lecturers valued that the intervention "enables training technical and communicative skills in a session using a learning approach without separate components because these two skills are integrated and not treated separately in care delivery". The conclusion recommends prioritizing communication skills during training in interprofessional teams, with nurses leading communication techniques.
requirements: Scenarios must include hybrid patients and realistic equipment so both skill types can be exercised simultaneously; at least one integrated training session to familiarize trainees with the methodology
constraints: High-fidelity integrated scenarios can cause inexperienced students to disengage and feel dissatisfied; balancing interprofessional groups with varying professional experience levels is challenging
target_learners: postgraduate interprofessional teams of nurses and physicians
examples: The intervention's single integrated session trained both skill types simultaneously in a 1-hour team simulation with a hybrid patient adapting to team actions
key_sources: Juliá‐Sanchis, R., Escribano, S., Sánchez‐Marco, M., García‐Aracil, N., Perpiñá‐Galvañ, J., & Cabañero‐Martínez, M. J. (2025). An integrated communication and technical skills educational intervention in critical healthcare situations: A qualitative method. Nursing Open, 12, e70002. https://doi.org/10.1002/nop2.70002

article_title: Analysis of Oncology and Radiation Therapy Representation on the National Board of Medical Examiners Official Practice Material for the United States National Standardized Medical Board Examinations.
citation: Mahoney Mary T., Linkowski Lauren C., Wu Trudy C., Chen Jie Jane, Neilsen Beth K., Thompson Petria S., Mix Michael D., Sura Karna T., Mattes Malcolm D. (2024). Analysis of Oncology and Radiation Therapy Representation on the National Board of Medical Examiners Official Practice Material for the United States National Standardized Medical Board Examinations. Journal of Cancer Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s13187-024-02475-0
title: Involve radiation oncology topic experts in the writing and review of medical licensing examination content to portray multidisciplinary cancer care accurately
description: The article advocates that radiation oncologists participate in writing and reviewing USMLE and NBME examination content, because exam material shapes what students learn and currently under-represents and negatively portrays radiation therapy. It argues that "a multidisciplinary expert approach for topic coverage, as was done for the construction of nutrition and obesity MCQ on NBME examinations, is indicated," citing precedent where exam content drove curricular reform.
requirements: Examination content-creation processes must be open to involvement from topic experts in each treatment modality, as the article notes only one board-certified radiation oncologist was involved per 2021 USMLE and NBME taskforce documents.
constraints: The study assessed published practice materials as a surrogate for actual tested content, and its reviewers were not explicitly trained in MCQ construction or review, which the article states is standard practice for NBME test writers.
target_learners: US medical students preparing for USMLE Step 1–3 and NBME shelf examinations
target_learning_goals: Accurate understanding of the role of radiation therapy and multidisciplinary cancer care
examples: The article cites 1980s–1990s nutrition education initiatives that recommended increasing nutrition questions on National Board exams to encourage medical schools to include nutrition in their curriculum, and similar advocacy by the Society of Critical Care Medicine and the American Board of Obesity.
key_sources: Mahoney Mary T., Linkowski Lauren C., Wu Trudy C., Chen Jie Jane, Neilsen Beth K., Thompson Petria S., Mix Michael D., Sura Karna T., Mattes Malcolm D. (2024). Analysis of Oncology and Radiation Therapy Representation on the National Board of Medical Examiners Official Practice Material for the United States National Standardized Medical Board Examinations. article_title: Student evaluations of teaching do not reflect student learning: an observational study.
citation: Gilbert R. O., Gilbert D. R. (2025). Student evaluations of teaching do not reflect student learning: an observational study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-06896-3
title: Interpret student evaluations of teaching with caution and prefer external, objective measures of learning when evaluating teaching effectiveness
description: The article recommends that SET be treated as unreliable indicators of teaching effectiveness because favorable evaluations tracked grades but not independent learning measures. It states "SET should be interpreted with caution" and that it "may be desirable to use objective measures of learning as a proxy for determining effectiveness of teaching, such as pre- and post-course testing", while noting an external instrument like the VEA is even more desirable because pre-post testing is susceptible to teaching to the assessment.
requirements: An external, standardized measure of learning that instructors and the institution cannot manipulate, such as the VEA, must be available to benchmark teaching against actual learning.
constraints: Pre- and post-course testing is susceptible to instructors teaching specifically to the assessment; the article's evidence is from one veterinary curriculum with a single survey instrument of unknown origin.
target_learning_goals: accurate institutional evaluation of teaching effectiveness and curricular efficacy
examples: The study related SET, grades, and VEA sectional scores for 160 courses across 12 cohorts, and modeled how modified Hofstee cut points would change grade-evaluation relationships.
key_sources: Gilbert R. O., Gilbert D. R. (2025). Student evaluations of teaching do not reflect student learning: an observational study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-06896-3

article_title: Youth experiences in gender-sexuality alliances predict academic engagement but not disaffection through social-emotional wellbeing.
citation: Poteat, V. P., Calzo, J. P., Yoshikawa, H., Kellogg, D., Marx, R. A., Richburg, A., & Lipkin, A. (2025). Youth experiences in gender–sexuality alliances predict academic engagement but not disaffection through social–emotional wellbeing. Child Development, 96, 847–864. https://doi.org/10.1111/cdev.14209
title: Integrative model (Development-in-Sociocultural-Context Model for Children's Engagement in Learning) linking social and emotional factors to academic engagement
description: The article draws on the integrative model, "also known as the Development-in-Sociocultural-Context Model for Children's Engagement in Learning" (Wang et al., 2019), which speaks directly to academic engagement. In this model, "academic engagement is indicated by cognitive, emotional, and behavioral elements such as a student's involvement, enthusiasm, interest, and persistence in learning and class activities." The model highlights the dynamic interplay between individual and social factors—such as feelings, self-appraisals, relationships with peers and teachers, and school climate—that shape engagement or disaffection. The article uses this model to hypothesize that GSA experiences predict academic outcomes indirectly through social–emotional wellbeing rather than directly.
requirements: The model presupposes that academic engagement and disaffection can be shaped by social and emotional factors, which the article identifies as relevant to the efforts of GSAs.
constraints: The article notes that GSAs are not expressly academically oriented clubs, so associations with academic outcomes are expected to be indirect through wellbeing rather than direct.
target_learners: Secondary school students, including LGBTQ+ youth
key_sources: Poteat, V. P., Calzo, J. P., Yoshikawa, H., Kellogg, D., Marx, R. A., Richburg, A., & Lipkin, A. (2025). Youth experiences in gender–sexuality alliances predict academic engagement but not disaffection through social–emotional wellbeing. Child Development, 96, 847–864. https://doi.org/10.1111/cdev.14209

article_title: Third-year medical students' perceptions of confidence and readiness to perform EFAST after training.
citation: Rocic Petra, Garrison Ryan, Stitle Kyle, Reynolds Austin, Andrews-Dickert Rebecca. (2024). Third-year medical students’ perceptions of confidence and readiness to perform EFAST after training. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-06513-9
title: Two-week Introduction to EFAST curriculum with didactics, standardized-patient skills practice, and OSCE assessment
description: A required pre-clerkship curriculum for OMS III students in the Clinical Clerkship Preparation course, built from EFAST competencies mapped to institutional and AACOM core competencies. It comprised two 50-minute didactic sessions, a 2-hour hands-on skills session with standardized patients, checkout handheld probes, and an OSCE with faculty and standardized-patient rubrics plus MCQs. Respondents rated quality items highly, with "mean values of 4.41–4.76 on a 5 point Likert scale".
requirements: Requires handheld portable ultrasound machines, standardized patients, and knowledgeable faculty to design and teach the sessions
constraints: Implementation without these resources may require increased reliance on online learning materials and simulation of cases
target_learners: Third-year osteopathic medical students entering clinical clerkships
target_learning_goals: Performing and interpreting the EFAST exam, communicating with patients and teams about the exam, and recognizing indications and limitations of POCUS
examples: Delivered July 2022 to incoming OMS III students; assessed via an OSCE in a trauma scenario with standardized patients and one-on-one faculty observers
key_sources: Rocic Petra, Garrison Ryan, Stitle Kyle, Reynolds Austin, Andrews-Dickert Rebecca. (2024). Third-year medical students’ perceptions of confidence and readiness to perform EFAST after training. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-06513-9

article_title: Effect of two teaching methods on nursing students' acquisition of patient-centered communication competence in older people care: a cluster randomized trial.
citation: Cortés-Rodríguez, López-Rodríguez, Roman, Granero-Molina, Fernández-Sola and Hernández-Padilla. (2024). Effect of two teaching methods on nursing students' acquisition of patient-centered communication competence in older people care: a cluster randomized trial. Frontiers in Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpubh.2024.1510620
title: Incorporate both standardized patient simulation and role-play into nursing curricula for patient-centered communication in older people care
description: Because both methods produced equivalent, significant gains in knowledge, skills, and self-efficacy, the article concludes that "it advocates for the incorporation of these methods into nursing curricula, equipping students with vital communication skills for older people care." Educators can choose either method based on resources, since neither was superior; role-play requires less time and financial investment while standardized patient simulation offers higher realism at higher resource cost.
requirements: Experiential sessions with observation, practice, and feedback or debriefing components
A facilitator trained in the chosen method
constraints: Generalization is limited: the sample came from a local university with specific inclusion criteria
It is not possible to determine the effect of each individual activity within the multi-component interventions
target_learning_goals: Patient-centered communication competence in older people care
examples: The trial assigned eight teaching groups of 16-18 students to either method and found equivalent benchmark attainment across pre-test, post-test, and 6-week follow-up
key_sources: Cortés-Rodríguez, López-Rodríguez, Roman, Granero-Molina, Fernández-Sola and Hernández-Padilla. (2024). Effect of two teaching methods on nursing students' acquisition of patient-centered communication competence in older people care: a cluster randomized trial. Frontiers in Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpubh.2024.1510620

article_title: Effect of integrated case-based and problem-based learning on clinical thinking skills of assistant general practitioner trainees: a randomized controlled trial.
citation: Jiang Dingyuan, Huang Danpei, Wan Hua, Fu Wuliang, Shi Weidong, Li Jin, Zou Huan, Hou Niannan, Li Qing, Li Nan. (2025). Effect of integrated case-based and problem-based learning on clinical thinking skills of assistant general practitioner trainees: a randomized controlled trial. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-06634-9
title: Integrate case-based and problem-based learning to combine the strengths of both pedagogies
description: The article argues that "the integration of CBL and PBL optimises the benefits of the two pedagogical approaches": CBL engages trainees through case analysis while PBL fosters a problem-oriented approach that enhances critical thinking. It recommends a student-centered, teacher-guided implementation with in-depth case discussion and clinical reasoning practice. The RCT supports this integration over lecture-based learning for AGP trainees.
requirements: Cases closely related to trainees' daily work and instructors able to guide discussion and provide expert review
constraints: PBL alone may pose challenges for novice learners with limited self-study skills; CBL may depend heavily on case quality and instructor expertise
target_learners: medical trainees in primary care programs
examples: The trial compared a seven-module integrated CBL-PBL curriculum against traditional lecture-based learning in 70 AGP trainees
key_sources: Jiang Dingyuan, Huang Danpei, Wan Hua, Fu Wuliang, Shi Weidong, Li Jin, Zou Huan, Hou Niannan, Li Qing, Li Nan. (2025). Effect of integrated case-based and problem-based learning on clinical thinking skills of assistant general practitioner trainees: a randomized controlled trial. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-06634-9

article_title: Using a flipped teaching strategy in undergraduate nursing education: students' perceptions and performance.
citation: Andargeery Shaherah Yousef, Bahri Hibah Abdulrahim, Alhalwani Rania Ali, Alahmedi Shorok Hamed, Ali Waad Hasan. (2024). Using a flipped teaching strategy in undergraduate nursing education: students’ perceptions and performance. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-05749-9
title: Integrate flipped teaching into nursing curricula to improve education quality and student performance
description: Based on its finding of significantly higher course scores and positive student perceptions, the article recommends that flipped teaching pedagogy be integrated in the nursing curriculum to improve the quality of the education process and outcomes. It argues flipped teaching provides an interactive learning environment that enhances development of essential nursing competencies such as communication, teamwork, collaboration, life-long learning, clinical reasoning, and critical thinking, and suggests the strategy could also be applied in clinical and practice settings.
requirements: Students must independently prepare before class using provided pre-class materials
Class time must be reserved for discussion, group activities, and feedback
constraints: The study was conducted in a theoretical course (therapeutic communication); the article states causal association cannot be investigated due to lack of randomization
examples: The article implemented flipped teaching in the therapeutic communication course across randomly assigned course sections and measured cumulative assessment scores
key_sources: Andargeery Shaherah Yousef, Bahri Hibah Abdulrahim, Alhalwani Rania Ali, Alahmedi Shorok Hamed, Ali Waad Hasan. (2024). Using a flipped teaching strategy in undergraduate nursing education: students’ perceptions and performance. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-05749-9

article_title: Simulation-based echocardiography learning contribution on training of medical residents.
citation: Maatouk Iyed, Maatouk Amani, Gafsi Besma, Mili Emna, Chaouch Mohamed Ali, Toumi Samir, Ouanes Islem, Ben Salem Faouzi, Ouanes Besbes Lamia. (2023). Contribution de l'apprentissage de l'échocardiographie par simulation à la formation des résidents en médecine. La Tunisie Médicale. https://doi.org/10.62438/tunismed.v102i7.4793
title: Integrate simulator-based echocardiography training into residency curricula because simulators offer a safe, low-stress environment for skill acquisition
description: The article recommends incorporating simulator-based echocardiography training into residents' learning curricula, arguing that simulators "can offer a safe environment for skill acquisition, thereby reducing patient risk" and provide a low-stress environment for learning and practising clinical problem-solving using various scenarios. All 28 participants endorsed ultrasound teaching as necessary for physicians in cardiopulmonary-emergency specialties, and 75% strongly agreed mandatory diploma training should be included during residency.
requirements: Access to an ultrasound simulator and experienced mentors; the intervention used three experienced mentors and combined three hours of theoretical training with three hours of simulator-based practical training
constraints: "More studies are needed to evaluate the effective clinical practice and to assess the durability of the training"
"Transferring knowledge between simulation and real-world settings can be challenging to evaluate"
target_learners: Medical residents in specialties that deal with cardiopulmonary emergencies
target_learning_goals: Echocardiography mastery for managing critically ill patients
examples: The study itself delivered the recommended training at the Simulation Center of the Faculty of Medicine of Monastir and measured significant pre-to-post gains in theoretical and practical scores
key_sources: Maatouk Iyed, Maatouk Amani, Gafsi Besma, Mili Emna, Chaouch Mohamed Ali, Toumi Samir, Ouanes Islem, Ben Salem Faouzi, Ouanes Besbes Lamia. (2023). Contribution de l'apprentissage de l'échocardiographie par simulation à la formation des résidents en médecine. La Tunisie Médicale. https://doi.org/10.62438/tunismed.v102i7.4793

article_title: Comparison of education using the flipped class, gamification and gamification in the flipped learning environment on the performance of nursing students in a client health assessment: a randomized clinical trial.
citation: Ghafouri Raziyeh, Zamanzadeh Vahid, Nasiri Malihe. (2024). Comparison of education using the flipped class, gamification and gamification in the flipped learning environment on the performance of nursing students in a client health assessment: a randomized clinical trial. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-05966-2
title: Integrate complementary teaching methods according to situation, time, cost and available resources
description: The article recommends that teachers improve educational effectiveness by combining methods rather than choosing one: "Teachers can improve the effectiveness of education with their creativity, depending on situation, time, cost, and available resources, by using and integrating educational methods." It argues combining flipped class with gamification yields both more study time and more attractiveness, and that the flipped class is more cost-effective while gamification demands more resources.
requirements: Instructor mastery of the chosen methods; the article states the professor's ability to teach with gamification in a flipped learning environment and mastery of the application are necessary
constraints: The gamification method requires more resources, equipment, and skilled personnel; the application was not available on iOS in this study
target_learners: undergraduate nursing students in health assessment courses
target_learning_goals: learning, satisfaction and self-efficacy in clinical assessment skills
examples: The trial combined a flipped structure with a gamified mobile application, with students reading content before class and solving scenario games as in-class assignments
key_sources: Ghafouri Raziyeh, Zamanzadeh Vahid, Nasiri Malihe. (2024). Comparison of education using the flipped class, gamification and gamification in the flipped learning environment on the performance of nursing students in a client health assessment: a randomized clinical trial. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-05966-2

article_title: Augmented reality visualization for ultrasound-guided interventions: a pilot randomized crossover trial to assess trainee performance and cognitive load.
citation: Liao Shu-Chen, Shao Shih-Chieh, Gao Shi-Ying, Lai Edward Chia-Cheng. (2024). Augmented reality visualization for ultrasound-guided interventions: a pilot randomized crossover trial to assess trainee performance and cognitive load. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-05998-8
title: Introduce AR-assisted ultrasound training early in medical education, such as during clerkship
description: The article recommends introducing AR-US at an early stage of medical education because junior learners are more receptive to new technologies: "introducing AR-US to medical education at an early stage, such as during clerkship, could be beneficial". In the trial, junior trainees reported significantly lower effort and frustration with AR-US than with S-US, and the authors argue novice physicians are less vulnerable to pre-existing biases or habits that may hinder learning.
requirements: Trainees without prior AR experience need an acclimation period; before the trial "the trainees were given a ten-minute acclimation period with the AR-HMDs in the simulation lab"
constraints: Findings come from simulator-based CVC placement; the article states "further research involving real patients instead of simulators is needed to validate the effectiveness of AR in clinical settings"
target_learners: junior medical trainees such as clerkship students and postgraduate year 1-4 physicians
target_learning_goals: acquiring ultrasound-guided central venous catheter placement skills with reduced effort and frustration
examples: The trial randomized trainees to start with either AR-US or S-US in a crossover design, gave a ten-minute AR-HMD acclimation period, and found junior trainees' effort and frustration scores significantly lower with AR-US.
key_sources: Liao Shu-Chen, Shao Shih-Chieh, Gao Shi-Ying, Lai Edward Chia-Cheng. (2024). Augmented reality visualization for ultrasound-guided interventions: a pilot randomized crossover trial to assess trainee performance and cognitive load. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-05998-8

article_title: Optimizing modern surgical simulation through instructor feedback - insights from a retrospective observational study in a tertiary hospital.
citation: Tee Yu-San, Cheng Chi-Tung, Li Pei-Hua, Hsieh Ming-Ju, Liao Chien-Hung, Fu Chih-Yuan. (2024). Optimizing modern surgical simulation through instructor feedback – insights from a retrospective observational study in a tertiary hospital. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-06090-x
title: Pair step-by-step simulation-based training with instructor feedback in later, complex stages; allow self-directed practice in early basic-skill stages
description: The article recommends tailoring simulation-based training to training stage: a self-directed SBT can work for junior residents learning basic laparoscopic techniques, while instructor feedback remains a key component for complex laparoscopic surgeries. Instructors also design step-by-step curricula and convey surgical concepts and experience simulators cannot replicate, such as managing emotions and handling complications. The article states, "we believe a self-directed SBT can be effective for junior residents who are learning basic laparoscopic techniques such as depth perception and bimanual dexterity. However, instructor feedback remained a key component in more complex laparoscopic surgeries."
requirements: Individualized one-to-one feedback from qualified instructors (surgeons with at least 200 laparoscopic surgeries each, as in the study) after observed simulator performance.
constraints: The article's evidence is retrospective, small (32 residents), without a control group lacking instructor feedback, and the effect of feedback timing and frequency was not evaluated; the recommendation rests on improvement patterns across different tasks rather than a controlled comparison.
target_learning_goals: laparoscopic surgical skills, from basic tasks such as pattern cutting to complex procedures such as laparoscopic appendectomy
examples: In the study program, each resident completed a 1-hour orientation and 4-hour simulator session, then repeated the procedure after individualized feedback from one of three qualified surgeons; seniors performed appendectomy and juniors pattern cutting.
key_sources: Tee Yu-San, Cheng Chi-Tung, Li Pei-Hua, Hsieh Ming-Ju, Liao Chien-Hung, Fu Chih-Yuan. (2024). Optimizing modern surgical simulation through instructor feedback – insights from a retrospective observational study in a tertiary hospital. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-06090-x

article_title: Virtual reality simulation training in laparoscopic surgery - does it really matter, what simulator to use? Results of a cross-sectional study.
citation: Sparn Moritz B., Teixeira Hugo, Chatziisaak Dimitrios, Schmied Bruno, Hahnloser Dieter, Bischofberger Stephan. (2024). Virtual reality simulation training in laparoscopic surgery – does it really matter, what simulator to use? Results of a cross-sectional study. BMC Medical Education 24, 589. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-05574-0
title: Incorporate virtual reality simulation training, regardless of simulator used, into all surgical training programs
description: The article recommends that virtual reality simulation training be adopted as an integral, universal component of basic surgical skills training, independent of which commercial simulator is available. It argues VRST "should be incorporated in all surgical training programs" because all three tested simulators trained the same basic skills efficiently even in short, loosely structured sessions. This rests on the study's finding of significant entry-to-exit improvement across all sequences and simulators.
requirements: Access to at least one virtual reality simulator with basic laparoscopic skill exercises; the study's two-hour time slots on three consecutive days illustrate a workable format
constraints: Implementing and maintaining mandatory VRST with structured feedback and expert guidance involves significant costs that may be prohibitive, especially for smaller, non-academic institutions; the authors suggest centralized training centers open to trainees from different institutions as one way of addressing this
target_learners: surgical trainees, especially early-career trainees beginning laparoscopic skills acquisition
target_learning_goals: basic laparoscopic surgical skills: bimanual coordination, eye-hand coordination, safe application of technical devices, tissue dissection
examples: At the 38th annual Davos Course 2021, trainees were randomly assigned to groups rotating across LaparoS, LapSim, and LAP Mentor III with entry exams, two hours of free training per simulator, and a repeated exit exam
key_sources: Sparn Moritz B., Teixeira Hugo, Chatziisaak Dimitrios, Schmied Bruno, Hahnloser Dieter, Bischofberger Stephan. (2024). Virtual reality simulation training in laparoscopic surgery – does it really matter, what simulator to use? Results of a cross-sectional study. BMC Medical Education 24, 589. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-05574-0

article_title: Comparison of blended learning and traditional lecture method on learning outcomes in the evidence-based medicine course: a comparative study.
citation: Liu Kui, Liu Shuang, Ma Yifei, Jiang Jun, Liu Zhenhua, Wan Yi. (2024). Comparison of blended learning and traditional lecture method on learning outcomes in the evidence-based medicine course: a comparative study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-05659-w
title: Blended learning design for evidence-based medicine: pre-class materials and subgroup debriefing plus instructor summary
description: The article's blended learning intervention combines 'internet plus' resources with a flipped classroom: one week before class students receive "a learning material including short videos, handouts, and knowledge maps" plus advance questions; students self-form into subgroups and create debriefing slides of learning outcomes. In class, subgroups debrief, the instructor comments and scores reports on "content integrity, response to questions, production of slides, and fluency of presentation," then gives a detailed summary targeting common problems and distributes multimedia resources for review. Figure 1 depicts this design.
requirements: Teachers must invest time in transition to the learning pattern and pre-class preparation of resources such as videos and handouts
Classroom equipment including projectors, screen, and appropriate lighting
constraints: Effectiveness was affected by the time, energy, and experience invested by the teachers
target_learning_goals: mastering evidence-based medicine basic theory (question-finding, evidence grading, evidence retrieval)
examples: 37 postgraduates studied the same three EBM chapters with this design while 39 peers took lecture-based teaching
key_sources: Liu Kui, Liu Shuang, Ma Yifei, Jiang Jun, Liu Zhenhua, Wan Yi. (2024). Comparison of blended learning and traditional lecture method on learning outcomes in the evidence-based medicine course: a comparative study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-05659-w

article_title: High-Quality Contact With Fellow Majority Group Students Is Associated With Better Academic Performance of Minority Group Students.
citation: Kahalon, R., Shnabel, N., Sharvit, K., Halabi, S., & Wright, S. C. (2023). High-Quality Contact With Fellow Majority Group Students Is Associated With Better Academic Performance of Minority Group Students. Personality & Social Psychology Bulletin, 49(12), 1723–1736. https://doi.org/10.1177/01461672221115943
title: Create opportunities for high-quality intergroup contact to reduce minority-majority achievement gaps in higher education, even in highly segregated societies
description: The article's practical implication is that universities in segregated, high-hostility societies should create opportunities for meaningful, high-quality contact between minority and majority students, because such contact was associated with better minority academic performance. The authors state that "our findings point to the potential benefits of creating opportunities for intergroup contact to reduce achievement gaps between minority and majority students even in highly segregated societies." Quality of contact mattered more than frequency, and effects were strongest for minority students.
requirements: Contact must be high in quality (positivity, intimacy, equality, friendship), not merely frequent
constraints: Evidence is correlational and non-randomized; the literature is criticized as non-policy ready because much of it does not meet randomized controlled trial standards
Mandatory contact programs could produce negative contact or reactance, leading to fundamentally different outcomes
Findings are limited to minority psychology students who chose to study in majority-dominated institutions
target_learners: Minority students in majority-dominated higher education institutions
examples: Study 1 used experiential group dynamics courses with weekly facilitated sessions as a structured opportunity for sustained, intimate Arab-Jewish contact
Study 2 measured naturally occurring spontaneous contact with Jewish students during students' first academic year
key_sources: Kahalon, R., Shnabel, N., Sharvit, K., Halabi, S., & Wright, S. C. (2023). High-Quality Contact With Fellow Majority Group Students Is Associated With Better Academic Performance of Minority Group Students. Personality & Social Psychology Bulletin, 49(12), 1723–1736. https://doi.org/10.1177/01461672221115943

article_title: Clinical simulation scenarios for the planning and management of infusion therapy by nurses.
citation: Meszaros Mariana de Jesus; de Almeida Angélica Olivetto; da Silva Ruana Luiz Ferreira; Eduardo Aline Helena Appoloni; Lima Maria Helena de Melo; Oliveira-Kumakura Ana Railka de Souza. (2023). Clinical simulation scenarios for the planning and management of infusion therapy by nurses. Revista Brasileira de Enfermagem. https://doi.org/10.1590/0034-7167-2023-0019
title: Two 15-minute high-fidelity clinical simulation scenarios for infusion therapy planning and management
description: The article built two high-fidelity clinical simulation scenarios structured on the Vessel Health and Preservation model: "Scenario 1 - Patient assessment and vascular device selection and Scenario 2 - Identification and management of deep vein thrombosis (DVT), with a time of 15 minutes for each scenario." Each scenario specifies objectives, high fidelity, problem-solving demands, cues (e.g., medical prescriptions, patient records, patient complaints), and cognitive, non-technical skill and attitude learning outcomes, plus verification checklists used to examine performance and guide debriefing.
requirements: Expert judge evaluation and pilot testing with the target audience, as carried out in the study's stages 2 and 3
constraints: Designed for nurses working in care of adult patients in infusion therapy; the article notes the theme must be previously adjusted for the undergraduate audience
target_learners: Practicing nurses in adult care and infusion therapy units
target_learning_goals: Patient assessment and vascular device selection
Identification and management of PICC-related deep vein thrombosis
Clinical judgment and decision-making in infusion therapy planning
examples: Scenario 1 cues included irritant and vesicant medications, norepinephrine infusion indication, left mastectomy and hemodynamic instability; Scenario 2 cues included patient pain report, upper arm circumference records and previous thrombosis
key_sources: Meszaros Mariana de Jesus; de Almeida Angélica Olivetto; da Silva Ruana Luiz Ferreira; Eduardo Aline Helena Appoloni; Lima Maria Helena de Melo; Oliveira-Kumakura Ana Railka de Souza. (2023). Clinical simulation scenarios for the planning and management of infusion therapy by nurses. Revista Brasileira de Enfermagem. https://doi.org/10.1590/0034-7167-2023-0019

article_title: Towards improving online learning in physical education: Gender differences and determinants of motivation, psychological needs satisfaction, and academic achievement in Saudi students.
citation: Frikha Mohamed et al. (2024). Towards improving online learning in physical education: Gender differences and determinants of motivation, psychological needs satisfaction, and academic achievement in Saudi students. PLOS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0297822
title: Individualize teachers' didactic-pedagogical behaviors in online PE according to students' motivation, autonomy, and online skills
description: The article recommends that teachers "adapt their didactic-pedagogical behaviors during PE online learning according to students' motivation and autonomy perceptions", structuring teaching activities with more individualized support for autonomy, competence, intrinsic motivation, and students' online skills and competencies. This rests on the study's findings that these variables predict PNS, motivation, and GPA. The authors state this "ensures better learning efficiency and academic achievements" and emphasize a personalized approach accounting for gender differences.
requirements: Teachers able to adjust didactic-pedagogical behaviors during online PE delivery
Activities supporting autonomy, competence, and intrinsic motivation
Attention to students' online skills and competencies
