article_title: Exploring the relationships between first impressions and MMI ratings: a pilot study.
citation: Klusmann Dietrich, Knorr Mirjana, Hampe Wolfgang. (2023). Exploring the relationships between first impressions and MMI ratings: a pilot study. Advances in Health Sciences Education, 28(2), 519-536. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10459-022-10151-5
title: In-group casting: MMI ratings partly reflect a tacit professional role-fit criterion blended with the instructed rating task
description: The article proposes that MMI ratings partly reflect an "unintended and unadvertised in-group-casting-aspect": raters blend the specific rating task outlined in the instructions with the general question of "could this candidate become a good medical doctor?", superposing the psychometric logic of measuring a trait with a tacit criterion of expected role-fit. On this account, first impression and MMI ratings correlate and their predictive contributions overlap because both capture the same tacit role-fit variance. The authors suggest it may be more fruitful to cultivate this view than to suppress it, making the sampling of raters from the clinic's staff important.
requirements: Raters drawn from the clinic's medical and psychological staff, since this sampling "determines the mix of tacit criteria for expected role-fit" and should be controlled carefully.
constraints: The account is offered as an interpretation of correlational overlap, not a tested mechanism; the authors list many unknowns, including whether narcissistic charm at first sight predicts long-term exploitative behavior.
target_learning_goals: assessment of social competence in medical student selection
examples: The first impression rating asked "Does this applicant appear to be qualified for studying medicine?" rather than matching the MMI performance wording, yet still correlated moderately with MMI ratings.

description: The article organizes the performance metrics affected by the AI-enhanced curriculum into three categories. constraints: Derived from one simulated neurosurgical task (subpial tumor resection) in a cohort of medical students; the authors note the mechanism behind some extrinsic changes is not clearly understood

target_learning_goals: technical surgical competencies in safety, movement, and efficiency domains
examples: Instrument divergence and changes in bipolar force are given as implicit metrics; rate of healthy tissue removal is given as an extrinsic metric

article_title: Effect of active learning and online discussions on the academic performances of dental students.
citation: Lim Jaeseo, Ko Hyunwoong, Park Jooyong, Ihm Jungjoon. (2022). Effect of active learning and online discussions on the academic performances of dental students. BMC Medical Education, 22, 312. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-022-03377-9
title: Match instructor intervention during discussion to the preceding learning activity: intervene after lectures, favor free discussion after self-study
description: The article draws a design principle from its interaction finding: the value of instructor intervention with a worksheet during discussion depends on what students did beforehand. It concludes that "the instructors need to employ different types of intervention depending on the student learning environments or conditions", because free discussion after self-study lets students answer each other's questions and discuss in depth, while intervention after lecture supports deeper learning.
requirements: A pre-discussion learning phase (lecture or self-study) whose type is known before deciding on intervention format
constraints: The supporting pattern is partly descriptive; several constituent pairwise contrasts were not statistically significant, and the experimental group was limited to dental students
target_learning_goals: deeper comprehension of learning material through discussion
examples: The LW group (lecture plus worksheet) scored higher than the LD group, while the SW group (self-study plus worksheet) scored lower than the SSD group without intervention
key_sources: Lim Jaeseo, Ko Hyunwoong, Park Jooyong, Ihm Jungjoon. (2022). Effect of active learning and online discussions on the academic performances of dental students. BMC Medical Education, 22, 312. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-022-03377-9

article_title: A Study on the Role of Intelligent Medical Simulation Systems in Teaching First Aid Competence in Anesthesiology.
citation: He Wei, Lu Jiayu, Zheng Wei, Zhang Xingyu, Yu Zhaoxiang, Shen Lin, Zhang Duo. (2022). A Study on the Role of Intelligent Medical Simulation Systems in Teaching First Aid Competence in Anesthesiology. Journal of Healthcare Engineering. https://doi.org/10.1155/2022/8163546
title: Intelligent medical comprehensive simulation system for anesthesia and first aid training
description: An integrated simulator-based system used to replace real patients in clinical teaching. The anesthesia simulation software "includes 80 patients, covering various anesthesia scenes", with "more than 100 kinds of drug reactions" built in, and can simulate pathophysiological processes and critical events. It records diagnostic and treatment inputs, allows case management without instructors, and automatically summarizes evaluation. In this study it supplemented traditional respiratory-medicine teaching for 50 interns.
requirements: Arranged during normal working hours so learning time is comparable to traditional teaching
constraints: The authors state there is still a gap between the system and the actual clinical environment, and that simulated patients cannot completely replace real people as clinical training objects
target_learners: clinical postgraduate students in anesthesiology and respiratory medicine
examples: The experimental group used the system during clinical internship alongside the traditional respiratory-medicine teaching plan
key_sources: He Wei, Lu Jiayu, Zheng Wei, Zhang Xingyu, Yu Zhaoxiang, Shen Lin, Zhang Duo. (2022). A Study on the Role of Intelligent Medical Simulation Systems in Teaching First Aid Competence in Anesthesiology. Journal of Healthcare Engineering. https://doi.org/10.1155/2022/8163546

article_title: Problem based learning approach increases the academic satisfaction of health science students in Ethiopian universities: a comparative cross sectional study.
citation: Tadesse Selamawit Girma, Tadesse Dereje Girma, Dagnaw Eyaya Habtie. (2022). Problem based learning approach increases the academic satisfaction of health science students in Ethiopian universities: a comparative cross sectional study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-022-03397-5
title: Incorporate problem-based learning as a formal instructional method across higher education curricula to enhance health science students' academic satisfaction
description: The article recommends that Ethiopian higher education institutions formally adopt PBL, arguing that its constructivist nature makes students owners of their learning. It states that "Incorporating PBL as a formal instructional method in the curriculum across higher education institutions of Ethiopia" should enhance academic satisfaction and maintain education quality, and that PBL will help students use appropriate energy and effort because students "involve in the construction of their own understanding".
requirements: PBL requires well-constructed clinical problems as a learning context and small groups of five to ten students analyzing problem or case scenarios
constraints: The supporting evidence is a cross-sectional comparison with a modest adjusted association (AOR = 1.50) and similar overall satisfaction magnitudes, not a causal trial
The study covered only regular undergraduate health science students at two universities, which the authors state might affect generalizability
target_learners: regular undergraduate health science students in universities
target_learning_goals: lifelong learning and responsibility for one's own learning process
examples: Debretabor University implemented a hybrid PBL curriculum since 2014 for health science students, supported by lecture and skill training sessions, and was compared with Mekelle University's lecture-based method in this survey
key_sources: Tadesse Selamawit Girma, Tadesse Dereje Girma, Dagnaw Eyaya Habtie. (2022). Problem based learning approach increases the academic satisfaction of health science students in Ethiopian universities: a comparative cross sectional study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-022-03397-5

article_title: A Short Intervention and an Interactive e-Learning Module to Motivate Medical and Dental Students to Enlist as First Responders: Implementation Study.
citation: Taramarcaz V, Herren T, Golay E, Regard S, Martin-Achard S, Mach F, Schnetzler N, Ricci G, Zamberg I, Larribau R, Niquille M, Suppan M, Schiffer E, Suppan L. (2022). A Short Intervention and an Interactive e-Learning Module to Motivate Medical and Dental Students to Enlist as First Responders: Implementation Study. Journal of Medical Internet Research. https://doi.org/10.2196/38508
title: Interactive BLS-AED e-learning module aligned with Swiss Resuscitation Council guidelines
description: A 30-minute interactive e-learning module developed under Storyline 3 and hosted on a Joomla-based study platform, adapted from a module used with second-year students and designed according to Swiss Resuscitation Council BLS-AED provider guidelines with COVID-19 adaptations. Its goal was to enable students to "(1) identify a cardiorespiratory arrest" through "(5) use an AED", with all subjects "presented in an interactive way". No time limit was set for completion, and 124 participants completed it.
requirements: Completion of the precourse questionnaire before access.
Registration on the study platform; access to the follow-up 1-hour practice session for certification.
constraints: The article states the module was designed to last 30 minutes with no time limit, and that interactive e-learning modules cannot replace hands-on practice.
examples: The module was followed by a web-based booking form for a 1-hour practice session, after which a course completion certificate allowed registration on the Save a Life platform.
key_sources: Taramarcaz V, Herren T, Golay E, Regard S, Martin-Achard S, Mach F, Schnetzler N, Ricci G, Zamberg I, Larribau R, Niquille M, Suppan M, Schiffer E, Suppan L. (2022). A Short Intervention and an Interactive e-Learning Module to Motivate Medical and Dental Students to Enlist as First Responders: Implementation Study. Journal of Medical Internet Research. https://doi.org/10.2196/38508

article_title: Putting self-regulated learning in context: Integrating self-, co-, and socially shared regulation of learning.
citation: Bransen D, Govaerts MJB, Panadero E, Sluijsmans DMA, Driessen EW. (2022). Putting self‐regulated learning in context: Integrating self‐, co‐, and socially shared regulation of learning. Med Educ. 2022;56(1):29–36. https://doi.org/10.1111/medu.14566
title: Integrated framework of self-, co-, and socially shared regulation of learning as embedded levels
description: The article proposes that regulation of learning in healthcare occurs at three levels: individual SRL, co-regulation (CRL), and socially shared regulation (SSRL). CRL is an 'unevenly distributed' form of social regulation in which one or more group members guide another's regulation, whereas SSRL is an 'evenly distributed' form shaped through reciprocal group interaction. The authors argue the three levels 'may therefore best be considered as embedded in one another during collaborative learning situations', with the balance shifting across individuals and over time depending on team composition, relationships, and task and context features.
requirements: Collaborative learning situations in which team members share collective goals
constraints: The conceptualisations refer to an idealised and theoretical situation, which may differ from actual work settings
target_learning_goals: regulation of individual and collaborative learning
examples: Box 3 illustrates a surgical team concurrently engaging in SRL, CRL aimed at another's SRL, and CRL aimed at the team's SSRL while adopting new technology
key_sources: Bransen D, Govaerts MJB, Panadero E, Sluijsmans DMA, Driessen EW. (2022). Putting self‐regulated learning in context: Integrating self‐, co‐, and socially shared regulation of learning. Med Educ. 2022;56(1):29–36. https://doi.org/10.1111/medu.14566

article_title: A novel retraining strategy of chest compression skills for infant CPR results in high skill retention for longer.
citation: Gugelmin-Almeida Debora, Jones Michael, Clark Carol, Rolfe Ursula, Williams Jonathan. (2022). A novel retraining strategy of chest compression skills for infant CPR results in high skill retention for longer. European Journal of Pediatrics 181(12):4101-4109. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00431-022-04625-2
title: Instrumented mannequin assessment system with four chest-compression quality metrics and real-time feedback
description: The study's assessment system comprises an ALS Baby mannequin modified for a 56 mm physiological compression depth, instrumented with two accelerometers, connected to a PC running a bespoke MATLAB algorithm that generates four metrics: 'chest-compression-depth (CCD), chest compression-rate (CCR), residual leaning (RL) and duty-cycle.' Target ranges are guideline-based (e.g., rate 100-120 min-1, depth > 35-45 mm, residual leaning < 2.5 kg, duty cycle 30-50%). A Labview component 'provided real-time feedback if needed during practice between assessments,' while assessments themselves gave no feedback.
requirements: All four performance metrics must be achieved concurrently for a PASS; the mannequin must be placed on a hard surface to eliminate mattress damping
constraints: Chest compliance of mannequins may not be entirely biofidelic; ventilation and hands-off time were not assessed in this system's use here
target_learners: university healthcare students training in pediatric basic life support
target_learning_goals: quantitative assessment and feedback on infant chest compression quality
examples: A two-minute assessment after training determined PASS/FAIL against the four target ranges, with the algorithm computing metrics from acceleration data converted to displacement
key_sources: Gugelmin-Almeida Debora, Jones Michael, Clark Carol, Rolfe Ursula, Williams Jonathan. (2022). A novel retraining strategy of chest compression skills for infant CPR results in high skill retention for longer. European Journal of Pediatrics 181(12):4101-4109. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00431-022-04625-2

article_title: The impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on the mental health and academic performance of medical postgraduates.
citation: Yu Yibo, Tang Qiaomei, Shi Haifei, Chen Ting, Wang Yaping, Hu Hanguang, Yao Ke. (2022). The impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on the mental health and academic performance of medical postgraduates. Frontiers in Public Health. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC9521680/
title: Take appropriate interventions to lighten medical postgraduates' psychological burdens and improve their academic performance during prolonged disruptions
description: The article concludes that it is "necessary and important to pay special attention to the psychological status of medical students and take appropriate interventions to improve their mental health" during the COVID-19 crisis. It recommends monitoring postgraduates' psychological status and intervening to lighten psychological burdens and improve academic performance when normal clinical learning and research supervision are disrupted. The recommendation rests on the survey's findings that most postgraduates had mild symptoms, females reported more anxiety, and doctoral students worried more about graduation standards.
requirements: Attention to the psychological status of medical students as part of institutional support during prolonged disruption of clinical learning
constraints: The article states the sample size was relatively small and that a few related factors affecting mental health and academic performance were covered in the questionnaire, so influencing factors need stronger investigation
target_learners: medical postgraduate students (master's and doctoral) in clinical medicine programs
target_learning_goals: maintaining mental health during disrupted clinical education
maintaining and improving academic performance and progress toward graduation standards
examples: The survey found 78.4% of postgraduates believed the pandemic had varying degrees of impact on their academics, and 85.0% were not seeking psychological counseling, motivating the call for interventions
key_sources: Yu Yibo, Tang Qiaomei, Shi Haifei, Chen Ting, Wang Yaping, Hu Hanguang, Yao Ke. (2022). The impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on the mental health and academic performance of medical postgraduates. Frontiers in Public Health. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC9521680/

article_title: Improving neuromuscular monitoring and reducing residual neuromuscular blockade via e-learning: A multicentre interrupted time-series study (INVERT study).
citation: Thomsen JLD, Mathiesen O, Hägi‐Pedersen D, Skovgaard LT, Østergaard D, Gätke MR; the INVERT collaborator group. (2022). Improving neuromuscular monitoring and reducing residual neuromuscular blockade via e‐learning: A multicentre interrupted time‐series study (INVERT study). Acta Anaesthesiol Scand. https://doi.org/10.1111/aas.14038
title: INVERT e-learning module on neuromuscular monitoring for anaesthetists
description: A roughly 30-minute online module developed with a regional learning-technology unit to teach anaesthetists neuromuscular monitoring. It covered "theory of NMBA, residual neuromuscular block and reversal, as well as practical tips on neuromuscular monitoring and troubleshooting equipment malfunction," with interactive synaptic-cleft animations split into smaller sections "to reduce cognitive load," optional clickable content adapting to learners' needs, real monitor-output examples, and patient cases about butyrylcholinesterase deficiency aimed at changing attitudes. It included a ten-question pre- and post-course test.
requirements: Requires internet access and equipment integrated in anaesthesia machines so learning can transfer to practice; designed for clinically active anaesthesiologists and nurse anaesthetists
constraints: The article reports it did not by itself change monitoring behaviour in a setting where use was already high
target_learners: clinically active anaesthesiologists and nurse anaesthetists
target_learning_goals: knowledge of neuromuscular blocking agents, residual block and reversal
practical use and troubleshooting of acceleromyography monitoring
examples: 429 anaesthetists completed the module during a 2-week intervention window; median post-course score rose from 7 to 9
key_sources: Thomsen JLD, Mathiesen O, Hägi‐Pedersen D, Skovgaard LT, Østergaard D, Gätke MR; the INVERT collaborator group. (2022). Improving neuromuscular monitoring and reducing residual neuromuscular blockade via e‐learning: A multicentre interrupted time‐series study (INVERT study). Acta Anaesthesiol Scand. https://doi.org/10.1111/aas.14038

article_title: Academic outcome and moderator of flipped classroom learning program "Teaching on the Run".
citation: Chen Kuo-Su, Hsieh Ming-Ju, Huang Min-Ping, Chen Chih-Ken, Hung Ming-Jui. (2021). Academic outcome and moderator of flipped classroom learning program “Teaching on the Run”. Biomedical Journal, 44(5), 636–643. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bj.2020.05.009
title: Include a brief mini-lecture in flipped classroom class time to reinforce pre-class knowledge
description: The article reports that its FC format included a mini-lecture in class time to briefly review background knowledge, aiming to "enhance the knowledge retention of well-prepared learners and make up the knowledge gap for unprepared students". Interpreting the significant mid-to-post score gain, the authors state that "the addition of mini-lecture in class time is highly warranted when using FC style learning", citing consistency with pre-class exercise plus in-class reinforcement findings.
requirements: A brief in-class mini-lecture reviewing key concepts of the pre-class learning material
constraints: The mid-to-post gain explanation is the authors' interpretation, not a tested comparison against a no-mini-lecture condition
target_learners: clinical teachers in flipped classroom programs
examples: In TOTR classroom time, a mini-lecture briefly reviewed key concepts of the pre-class learning material after active learning activities
key_sources: Chen Kuo-Su, Hsieh Ming-Ju, Huang Min-Ping, Chen Chih-Ken, Hung Ming-Jui. (2021). Academic outcome and moderator of flipped classroom learning program “Teaching on the Run”. Biomedical Journal, 44(5), 636–643. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bj.2020.05.009

article_title: Physical Activity in High School Classrooms: A Promising Avenue for Future Research.
citation: Fenesi B., Graham J.D., Crichton M., Ogrodnik M., Skinner J. (2022). Physical Activity in High School Classrooms: A Promising Avenue for Future Research. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph19020688
title: The inverted-U hypothesis of age-related responsiveness to physical activity interventions
description: The essay describes the inverted-U shape hypothesis as an account of why behavioural interventions such as physical activity are assumed to benefit the youngest and oldest learners most. Under this hypothesis, "children and older adults are on the tail ends of the inverted-U spectrum and, thus, have the most room for upwards mobility", making them the most likely to gain neurocognitive benefits. The essay presents this hypothesis as a lingering misconception that has discouraged high-school research, and counters it with evidence that the adolescent brain, especially the prefrontal cortex, continues dramatic myelination and synaptic pruning, making adolescence a sensitive period amenable to lifestyle factors such as physical activity.
requirements: Interpreting intervention responsiveness requires considering the developmental state of the brain regions supporting the targeted cognitive functions.
constraints: The essay argues this hypothesis is a misconception when applied to adolescents, whose prefrontal cortex continues developing well into adolescence.
target_learning_goals: higher-order cognitive functions including attention regulation, inhibitory control, working memory and problem solving
key_sources: Fenesi B., Graham J.D., Crichton M., Ogrodnik M., Skinner J. (2022). Physical Activity in High School Classrooms: A Promising Avenue for Future Research. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph19020688

article_title: Latent Safety Threats and Countermeasures in the Operating Theater: A National In Situ Simulation-Based Observational Study.
citation: Long Jennifer A., Webster Craig S., Holliday Timothy, Torrie Jane, Weller Jennifer M. (2022). Latent Safety Threats and Countermeasures in the Operating Theater: A National In Situ Simulation-Based Observational Study. Simulation in Healthcare 17(1). https://doi.org/10.1097/SIH.0000000000000547
title: Use in situ simulation in real clinical environments as a mechanism for identifying latent safety threats and prompting quality improvement initiatives
description: In situ simulation runs simulated clinical scenarios in the actual work environment using the site's own equipment, drugs, and procedures, making it possible to proactively identify latent safety threats before they cause patient harm. The article concludes that "In situ simulation is an effective mechanism both for identifying threats to patient safety and to prompt initiatives for improvement, supporting the use of in situ simulation in the quality improvement cycle in healthcare." The national NetworkZ program embedded this principle by encouraging hospitals to nominate a course instructor liaison to bring identified issues to local quality groups.
requirements: Structured debrief after each scenario with generic prompts about opportunities for improvement
Postcourse report template for recording identified threats, protective factors, and countermeasures
Trained local instructors (in this program, a 2-day training program supplemented by online modules)
constraints: Data from postcourse reports may underreport the true rate of LSTs, as some threats may not have been identified or recorded
Delays or failure to address threats identified during simulation is common
target_learners: Multidisciplinary hospital teams in operating theaters and other high-acuity clinical settings
target_learning_goals: Identifying latent safety threats in the local work system and initiating corrective countermeasures
examples: NetworkZ delivered surgical simulations lasting 15 to 45 minutes in 21 New Zealand hospitals; identified threats prompted actions such as replacing emergency bells, correcting written information, and meting with the local blood bank to clarify emergency ordering processes
key_sources: Long Jennifer A., Webster Craig S., Holliday Timothy, Torrie Jane, Weller Jennifer M. (2022). Latent Safety Threats and Countermeasures in the Operating Theater: A National In Situ Simulation-Based Observational Study. Simulation in Healthcare 17(1). https://doi.org/10.1097/SIH.0000000000000547

article_title: Using Patient Simulation to Promote Best Practices in Fall Prevention and Postfall Assessment in Nursing Homes.
citation: Acosta DJ, Rinfret A, Plant J, Hsu AT. (2021). Using Patient Simulation to Promote Best Practices in Fall Prevention and Postfall Assessment in Nursing Homes. Journal of Nursing Care Quality. https://doi.org/10.1097/NCQ.0000000000000599
title: In situ hybrid fall simulation pattern: standardized patient actor, brief prebrief, 7–10 minute scenario, and three-phase debrief
description: This lesson-level pattern embeds a scripted resident-fall scenario, enacted by a trained nurse actor as a standardized patient, directly on a living unit. Each activity combines a prebrief to establish psychological safety, a 7–10 minute simulation observed by a lead nurse, and a debrief with reaction, description, and analysis phases. The article describes it as "a lower-cost hybrid approach, using a trained actor representing a standardized patient—enacting a scripted scenario—and available technology" suited to resource-constrained nursing homes.
requirements: A lead nurse trained in simulation design and facilitation to observe and debrief
Nurse actors prepared with scenario objectives and a script, with training sessions before the first simulation
constraints: High-fidelity manikin simulation may be less feasible in resource-constrained nursing home settings
Participation was expected of all staff within the vicinity; some participants found being observed intimidating
target_learners: Frontline nursing home staff: RNs, registered practical nurses, and nurse aides/personal support workers
target_learning_goals: Postfall assessment and postfall huddle procedures
examples: 27 simulations on 13 units over 5 months across day, evening, and night shifts, each with a 5-minute prebrief, 7–10 minute simulation, and 7–10 minute debrief
key_sources: Acosta DJ, Rinfret A, Plant J, Hsu AT. (2021). Using Patient Simulation to Promote Best Practices in Fall Prevention and Postfall Assessment in Nursing Homes. Journal of Nursing Care Quality. https://doi.org/10.1097/NCQ.0000000000000599

article_title: Comparison of Interactive Teaching in Online and Offline Platforms among Dental Undergraduates.
citation: Veeraiyan Deepak Nallaswamy, Varghese Sheeja S., Rajasekar Arvina, Karobari Mohmed Isaqali, Thangavelu Lakshmi, Marya Anand, Messina Pietro, Scardina Giuseppe Alessandro. (2022). Comparison of Interactive Teaching in Online and Offline Platforms among Dental Undergraduates. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph19063170
title: Offer interactive teaching in either online or offline platforms, since both supported equivalent performance
description: The article concludes that interactive teaching methods, whether delivered online or offline, give students a beneficial learning environment: "interactive teaching methods in both offline and online platforms in Periodontics resulted in equivalent performance by the undergraduate dental students." The principle recommends that institutions may deliver interactive lecture-plus-activity sessions on either platform without expecting a difference in assessed performance. It rests on a single non-randomized study at one center.
requirements: Interactive method with lectures followed by activities must be implemented identically on the chosen platform
Assessments and time limits held constant across platforms
constraints: Study was not randomized; students self-selected platform
Small sample size and a single study center restrict generalizability, per the authors
examples: Students were given the option to choose either an online class through Zoom or an offline class, with identical topics, teaching methods, lectures and activities across groups
key_sources: Veeraiyan Deepak Nallaswamy, Varghese Sheeja S., Rajasekar Arvina, Karobari Mohmed Isaqali, Thangavelu Lakshmi, Marya Anand, Messina Pietro, Scardina Giuseppe Alessandro. (2022). Comparison of Interactive Teaching in Online and Offline Platforms among Dental Undergraduates. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph19063170

article_title: Surgical cognitive simulation improves real-world surgical performance: randomized study.
citation: Cragg J, Mushtaq F, Lal N, Garnham A, Hallissey M, Graham T, Shiralkar U. (2021). Surgical cognitive simulation improves real-world surgical performance: randomized study. BJS Open. https://doi.org/10.1093/bjsopen/zrab003
title: Incorporate SCS training as an essential, low-resource part of surgical training programmes
description: The authors recommend that surgical training bodies adopt SCS because it is free, accessible and less resource-intensive than physical simulators: after initial facilitator-led training, trainees can practise it anywhere and in their own time, potentially shortening the learning curve by using what the article calls the "simulation centre in the brain". They state that "Those responsible for surgical training need to acknowledge the benefit of such training and incorporate it as an essential part of surgical training", positioning SCS as an adjunct to, not a replacement for, technical simulation.
requirements: Initial training with a facilitator before independent unsupervised practice
constraints: The supporting evidence comes from a small randomized trial with data lost for seven of 21 recruited trainees; the article notes a Hawthorne effect cannot be discounted
target_learning_goals: Improvement of real-world surgical performance and skill acquisition efficiency
examples: In the trial, SCS-trained trainees improved procedure times and global performance scores more than controls over 4 months while continuing routine theatre work
key_sources: Cragg J, Mushtaq F, Lal N, Garnham A, Hallissey M, Graham T, Shiralkar U. (2021). Surgical cognitive simulation improves real-world surgical performance: randomized study. BJS Open. https://doi.org/10.1093/bjsopen/zrab003

article_title: Front-loading of anatomy content has no effect on long-term anatomy knowledge retention among physical therapy students: a prospective cohort study.
citation: Amabile Amy H., Nixon-Cave Kim, Georgetti Larry J., Sims Ashley C. (2021). Front-loading of anatomy content has no effect on long-term anatomy knowledge retention among physical therapy students: a prospective cohort study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-021-02925-z
title: Intermediate effect: clinical experience can interfere with retention of basic science facts
description: The intermediate effect is the account the article invokes to explain why clinical experience did not boost, and may have attenuated, factual recall. It holds that "clinical experience can actually interfere with knowledge retention", because developing clinical reasoning "requires a certain amount of forgetting of the details of underlying basic science and medical knowledge". The authors use it to explain why the LONG cohort, which had completed clinical affiliations before the post-test, did not show better retention than the less clinically experienced SHORT cohort.
requirements: Applies to learners transitioning from didactic basic science study toward clinical expertise, as described for medical students, residents, and physicians
constraints: The article presents the intermediate effect as an explanatory account drawn from prior research, not as a result tested within this study
target_learning_goals: long-term retention of basic science knowledge
examples: The authors propose that the LONG cohort's completed clinical affiliations before the post-test may have given it relative expert status, attenuating factual recall relative to the intermediate-expertise SHORT cohort
key_sources: Amabile Amy H., Nixon-Cave Kim, Georgetti Larry J., Sims Ashley C. (2021). Front-loading of anatomy content has no effect on long-term anatomy knowledge retention among physical therapy students: a prospective cohort study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-021-02925-z

article_title: Asynchronous Distance Learning of the National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale During the COVID-19 Pandemic (E-Learning vs Video): Randomized Controlled Trial.
citation: Suppan M, Stuby L, Carrera E, Cottet P, Koka A, Assal F, Savoldelli GL, Suppan L. (2021). Asynchronous Distance Learning of the National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale During the COVID-19 Pandemic (E-Learning vs Video): Randomized Controlled Trial. Journal of Medical Internet Research. https://doi.org/10.2196/23594
title: Highly interactive e-learning pattern combining content-skipping prevention, video-based scoring questions, and tailored feedback
description: The article's module uses several learning mechanics per chapter: users are "prevented from skipping content, as they must click on each numbered button to discover the score"; they must "correctly score the NIHSS item" from subtitled video extracts; and "Feedback is provided for each question," with a clue on incorrect answers and reinforcement on correct answers. Branching logic generates the tailored feedback, and chapters may be taken in any order.
requirements: A platform supporting branching logic and gamified interactivity (the module was built in Articulate Storyline 3)
Sufficient authentic video material to cover each scored item
constraints: 13 content chapters plus introduction, coma-score chapter, and gated summary; the summary unlocks only after all chapters are completed
Developed and validated for NIHSS-scale learning in medical and paramedic populations
target_learning_goals: reliable application and scoring of the NIHSS
examples: Figures 1–10 illustrate the mechanics: gated continue buttons, lightboxed content, a video-based scoring question, wrong-answer clue feedback, and interactive explanations of visual field deficits and extinction/inattention.
key_sources: Suppan M, Stuby L, Carrera E, Cottet P, Koka A, Assal F, Savoldelli GL, Suppan L. (2021). Asynchronous Distance Learning of the National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale During the COVID-19 Pandemic (E-Learning vs Video): Randomized Controlled Trial. Journal of Medical Internet Research. https://doi.org/10.2196/23594

article_title: An integrative process model of resilience in an academic context: Resilience resources, coping strategies, and positive adaptation.
citation: Fullerton Dayna J., Zhang Lisa M., Kleitman Sabina. (2021). An integrative process model of resilience in an academic context: Resilience resources, coping strategies, and positive adaptation. PLoS ONE 16(2): e0246000. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0246000
title: Integrative process model of resilience in an academic context (trait–process–outcome synergy)
description: An explanatory framework integrating prior resilience theories (Richardson's metatheory, Mancini and Bonanno's individual differences model, Fletcher and Sarkar's grounded theory) and adapting them to tertiary study: personal resilience resources influence how students appraise and respond to stressors via coping strategies, producing positive adaptation outcomes (well-being, adjustment, somatic health). The article argues "we propose resilience may be best examined with a view of synergy between traits, process, and outcomes", and the path analysis provided empirical support for the proposed mechanisms in the academic context.
requirements: A contextually relevant set of resilience resource measures, coping strategy measures, and positive adaptation outcome measures, with covariates controlled
constraints: The model was tested cross-sectionally in a homogeneous undergraduate sample, so causal direction cannot be inferred; stress or adversity was assumed rather than quantified
target_learning_goals: student well-being and positive adaptation to academic stressors
examples: The authors tested a path model with coping factors as mediators and well-being, adjustment, and somatic symptoms as outcomes in 306 undergraduates
key_sources: Fullerton Dayna J., Zhang Lisa M., Kleitman Sabina. (2021). An integrative process model of resilience in an academic context: Resilience resources, coping strategies, and positive adaptation. PLoS ONE 16(2): e0246000. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0246000

article_title: Switching from a traditional undergraduate programme in (clinical) pharmacology and therapeutics to a problem-based learning programme.
citation: Brinkman David J., Monteiro Teresa, Monteiro Emilia C., Richir Milan C., van Agtmael Michiel A., Tichelaar Jelle. (2021). Switching from a traditional undergraduate programme in (clinical) pharmacology and therapeutics to a problem-based learning programme. European Journal of Clinical Pharmacology. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00228-020-03027-3
title: Integrated longitudinal PBL curriculum design for pharmacology and CPT education
description: The article describes a curriculum redesign in which pharmacology is integrated with pathophysiology, microbiology and neurosciences across the second and third years, with a new fifth-year CPT course, all "based on the principles of PBL" and focusing "on solving written patient cases in working groups under the supervision of clinical pharmacologists". It replaced a discipline-based lecture programme and used 10% fewer teaching hours (129 vs 144 h), yet was associated with better prescribing competencies. The design integrates content and context across the whole curriculum rather than concentrating CPT in one or two courses.
requirements: Integration of PBL modules throughout the medical curriculum starting as early as possible; content and context of teaching matter more than teaching hours
constraints: The integration of training sessions throughout the medical curriculum can be challenging for medical schools with few CPT teachers; evidence comes from one medical school with a historic control, limiting generalizability
target_learning_goals: rational prescribing knowledge, skills and attitudes (effective, safe and low-cost prescribing)
examples: NOVA Medical School replaced discipline-based pharmacology and CPT courses with integrated PBL courses totalling 129 teaching hours instead of 144, supervised by clinical pharmacologists
key_sources: Brinkman David J., Monteiro Teresa, Monteiro Emilia C., Richir Milan C., van Agtmael Michiel A., Tichelaar Jelle. (2021). Switching from a traditional undergraduate programme in (clinical) pharmacology and therapeutics to a problem-based learning programme. European Journal of Clinical Pharmacology. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00228-020-03027-3

article_title: Assessing communication skills during OSCE: need for integrated psychometric approaches.
citation: Piumatti Giovanni, Cerutti Bernard, Perron Noëlle Junod. (2021). Assessing communication skills during OSCE: need for integrated psychometric approaches. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-021-02552-8
title: Integrated psychometric evaluation of OSCE rating scales combining measurement invariance testing and item response theory
description: The article advocates a dual analytical framework for evaluating communication-skill instruments in performance-based assessment: multi-group confirmatory factor analysis to test whether a scale measures the same latent construct across stations (configural, metric, scalar and strict invariance), and IRT to assess each item's difficulty and discrimination and to reveal where along the trait spectrum items provide information. The authors state that "IRT can prove to be very useful for the continuous evaluation of CS measurement instruments in performance-based assessments" and that the joint use of these techniques provides knowledge to improve instrument adoption. The framework treats instrument evaluation as continuous rather than one-off validation.
requirements: Adequate sample sizes for Rasch modeling and factor analysis; the article notes future studies should estimate item performances in single OSCE stations provided they have adequate sample sizes
constraints: The article notes, citing De Champlain, that IRT might not be particularly well suited to OSCEs since students' performances on the same skills may vary across different stations' domains; averaging item scores across stations threatens unidimensionality and local independence assumptions
target_learners: undergraduate medical students assessed in OSCEs
target_learning_goals: valid and reliable measurement of communication skills in performance-based assessment
examples: The study applied this dual approach to the Hodges and McIlroy four-item scale, which no prior study had tested for invariance across stations or analyzed with IRT
key_sources: Piumatti Giovanni, Cerutti Bernard, Perron Noëlle Junod. (2021). Assessing communication skills during OSCE: need for integrated psychometric approaches. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-021-02552-8

article_title: A Faculty Development Workshop for Planning and Implementing Interactive Virtual Case-Based Teaching.
citation: Spicer J. O., Nguyen T. T., Arnold M. W., Anderson T., Khalife R. (2021). A Faculty Development Workshop for Planning and Implementing Interactive Virtual Case-Based Teaching. MedEdPORTAL. https://doi.org/10.15766/mep_2374-8265.11126
title: 90-minute faculty development workshop on interactive virtual tools for case-based teaching
description: A 90-minute virtual workshop, delivered twice, that demonstrates interactive teaching tools (Zoom chat, whiteboard and annotations, polling, breakout rooms; Backchannel Chat; Padlet; PollEverywhere) within videoconferencing platforms for case-based teaching. Participants experience each tool as learners, then work in small breakout groups to plan how to integrate tools into case-based sessions of different sizes, considering anonymity and learner level. Materials include six peer-reviewed appendices (readings, worksheets, presentation, facilitator guide, evaluation).
requirements: Participants need basic videoconferencing knowledge (e.g., logging on, muting/unmuting)
Facilitators need familiarity with the interactive tools and should test software and rehearse beforehand
Computer with reliable internet, microphone, speakers; Zoom link; word-processing program
constraints: Technology changes rapidly, so specific tools may change or become unavailable; the workshop mitigates this by teaching broad tool categories and general features
Small audience sample sizes and self-report evaluation limited robust effectiveness evaluation
target_learners: Graduate students in health professions education
target_learning_goals: Explain learning theories underpinning a multimodal model of online learning
Identify features and limitations of interactive virtual tools
Integrate online tools into interactive case-based virtual teaching sessions
examples: Workshop 1 was a final seminar for 26 MHPE candidates; Workshop 2 was a faculty development session for 30 Emory faculty small-group facilitators with an 86% participation rate.
key_sources: Spicer J. O., Nguyen T. T., Arnold M. W., Anderson T., Khalife R. (2021). A Faculty Development Workshop for Planning and Implementing Interactive Virtual Case-Based Teaching. MedEdPORTAL. https://doi.org/10.15766/mep_2374-8265.11126

article_title: Simulation-based education for selected communication skills: exploring the perception of post-graduate dental students.
citation: Mascarenhas Sharon, Al-Halabi Manal, Otaki Farah, Nasaif Mohamed, Davis Dave. (2021). Simulation-based education for selected communication skills: exploring the perception of post-graduate dental students. Korean J Med Educ 33(1):11-25. https://doi.org/10.3946/kjme.2021.183
title: In-situ SBE session pattern: three 35-minute scripted scenarios each with pre-brief, simulated consultation, and debrief
description: Each group of six to eight post-graduate dental students went through three 35-minute scenarios conducted at the dental clinic in-situ, with simulated patients working from a detailed a priori script. Per the sample schedule, each scenario comprised "Pre-briefing (5 min)", a 15-minute consultation with the simulated patient, and "Debriefing (15 min)", with sessions opening with introductions, a safe container discussion, and confidentiality forms, and the final 15 minutes allocated to summarizing. Skills targeted were communication during consent, breaking bad news, and communication during an unexpected outcome.
requirements: Simulated patients given a priori a detailed script including possible responses and questions
Human resources including simulation educator technologist, dental faculty, and simulated patients
Complementary resources such as pre-reading materials and Dubai Dental Hospital policies
constraints: Sessions were conducted in-situ at the dental clinic within one institution's postgraduate programs

examples: Table 1 prints the sample schedule: 10-minute introduction, three 35-minute scenarios, 15-minute feedback and reflection, and a 45-minute focus group discussion

article_title: Framework for interprofessional case conferences - empirically sound and competence-oriented communication concept for interprofessional teaching.
citation: Posenau André, Handgraaf Marietta. (2021). Framework for interprofessional case conferences – empirically sound and competence-oriented communication concept for interprofessional teaching. GMS Journal for Medical Education. https://www.egms.de/en/journals/zma/2021-38/zma001461.shtml
title: Framework for interprofessional case conferences combining conversation-phase structure with ICF-based action tasks
description: The article develops a framework for interprofessional case conferences from literature analysis, empirical conversation research, and the ICF. It distinguishes verbal tasks present in every conversation (organising, formulating, coordinating, maintaining relationships, constituting modality, generating reciprocity) from extra-linguistic tasks specific to the case conference type. Conversations consist of "opening, core, and termination phases, which must be actively established by the parties involved". The framework serves as orientation for teaching content and for describing and evaluating communication processes.
requirements: Participants must process both the verbal micro-level tasks and the extra-linguistic case-based tasks for the conversation to count as a case conference
constraints: Developed for the conversation type of the interprofessional case conference in health professions education
target_learners: health professions students in nursing, physiotherapy, occupational therapy, speech therapy and midwifery
examples: Used as orientation for the module 'Interprofessional Case Conferences' at the Hochschule für Gesundheit

article_title: Framework for interprofessional case conferences - empirically sound and competence-oriented communication concept for interprofessional teaching.
citation: Posenau André, Handgraaf Marietta. (2021). Framework for interprofessional case conferences – empirically sound and competence-oriented communication concept for interprofessional teaching. GMS Journal for Medical Education. https://www.egms.de/en/journals/zma/2021-38/zma001461.shtml
title: Interprofessional case conference as an educational format for role knowledge and communication strategies
description: An interprofessional case conference is a multidisciplinary meeting of two or more health professionals to plan care for a person with chronic and complex care needs. The article positions it as an educational measure "to increase knowledge and awareness of the role of other healthcare professionals in patient care" and "to promote specific communication strategies for negotiating objectives and decisions". Success requires that participants assess other professions' expertise, understand their roles, and access an organising framework.
requirements: Participants assess the expertise of other professions and have a clear understanding of their roles
Targeted, planned communication rather than chance encounters
constraints: Existing German training structures provide few structural opportunities for interprofessional communication
examples: Conducted weekly with groups of 20 interprofessional students over ten weeks at the Hochschule für Gesundheit

article_title: Consistency and variability in human performance during simulate infant CPR: a reliability study.
citation: Almeida Debora, Clark Carol, Jones Michael, McConnell Phillip, Williams Jonathan. (2020). Consistency and variability in human performance during simulate infant CPR: a reliability study. Scandinavian Journal of Trauma, Resuscitation and Emergency Medicine. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC7488154/
title: Modified instrumented infant manikin with accelerometer-based capture of four chest compression metrics
description: A Laerdal ALS Baby manikin representing a three-month-old, 5 kg infant, modified so maximum compression depth varies between 40 mm and 56 mm, paired with two accelerometers, a data acquisition unit, a flow sensor and LabView/MATLAB processing. A bespoke algorithm converts double-integrated acceleration into "average compression depth, average compression rate, average residual leaning and average duty cycle", which are then converted into guideline-based quality indices.
requirements: Validated displacement data and known manikin stiffness to convert residual leaning from mm to kg
constraints: The article recognizes manikins "may not exactly replicate the characteristics and chest compliance of human beings"
Simulated individual performance lacked background noise, other rescuers, distractions and stress of real cardiac arrest, limiting transferability
target_learners: university healthcare students with no previous paediatric life support training
target_learning_goals: measurement of infant chest compression skill quality and consistency
examples: Used to capture three 2-min iCPR trials per participant at two time points with 1-min intervals between trials and no feedback during data collection.

article_title: Blended learning: ten tips on how to implement it into a curriculum in healthcare education.
citation: Hege I, Tolks D, Adler M, Härtl A. (2020). Blended learning: ten tips on how to implement it into a curriculum in healthcare education. GMS Journal for Medical Education 37(5): Doc45. https://www.egms.de/en/journals/zma/2020-37/zma001338.shtml
title: Redesign the whole course with an instructional framework rather than adding technology to traditional courses, emphasizing application and integration online
description: The article warns that a common approach — converting traditional courses by simply adding technology-based activities — often results in extra workload for teachers and especially students, and recommends instead re-designing the entire curriculum or course with an instructional framework, citing Merrill's five principles of instruction: problem-centeredness, learner activation, demonstration, application, and integration with synthesis and reflection. Because "online activities do not include the application and integration level" in many cases despite being technically possible, the authors recommend "putting a special emphasis on these steps", for example having learners collaboratively develop their own examples or cases online that are then presented and discussed in a seminar.
requirements: Application of an instructional framework to both the online and the face-to-face phases
Deliberate design of online activities that reach application and integration levels
constraints: Simply adding technology-based activities to unchanged traditional courses risks extra workload for teachers and students
target_learning_goals: Active engagement and higher-level learning objectives in online phases
examples: Engaging learners in collaboratively developing their own examples or cases in an online environment which then can be presented and discussed in a seminar
key_sources: Hege I, Tolks D, Adler M, Härtl A. (2020). Blended learning: ten tips on how to implement it into a curriculum in healthcare education. GMS Journal for Medical Education 37(5): Doc45. https://www.egms.de/en/journals/zma/2020-37/zma001338.shtml

article_title: Blended learning: ten tips on how to implement it into a curriculum in healthcare education.
citation: Hege I, Tolks D, Adler M, Härtl A. (2020). Blended learning: ten tips on how to implement it into a curriculum in healthcare education. GMS Journal for Medical Education 37(5): Doc45. https://www.egms.de/en/journals/zma/2020-37/zma001338.shtml
title: Involve the target group — learners and educators — in all steps of blended learning curriculum development
description: The article recommends involving the target group — the learners at a specific stage in their education and the educators who will teach in the setting — "in all steps of the curriculum development process", including pilot testing activities and learning scenarios and obtaining their feedback as a basis for refinement. In interprofessional contexts all relevant target groups should be included. Involvement can also serve to assess learners' digital competency early, and a more challenging variant is involving learners as content creators whose material can be re-used. The authors state that involving the target group in multiple ways makes it more likely that learners' needs are met and that they accept the implemented formats.
requirements: Involving learners and educators in pilot testing and obtaining their feedback for refinement
Including all relevant target groups in interprofessional settings
target_learners: Healthcare profession students, including interprofessional groups such as medical, nursing and physiotherapy students
target_learning_goals: Meeting learner needs and acceptance of blended learning formats
examples: Involving the target group as content creators by designing learning scenarios in which they create content, e.g. a video clip, that can be re-used for the next group of learners

article_title: Interdisciplinary clinical debriefing in the emergency department: an observational study of learning topics and outcomes.
citation: Coggins Andrew, Santos Aaron De Los, Zaklama Ramez, Murphy Margaret. (2020). Interdisciplinary clinical debriefing in the emergency department: an observational study of learning topics and outcomes. BMC Emergency Medicine. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12873-020-00370-7
title: Blended I.N.F.O. and S.T.O.P. facilitation model for interdisciplinary clinical debriefing
description: The study assembled a locally appropriate blended approach to clinical debriefing facilitation that combined two published debriefing models: the psychological safety focus of "I.N.F.O." ("Immediate, Not for personal assessment, Fast facilitated feedback, and Opportunity to ask questions") and the structure of "S.T.O.P." ("Summarise the case; Things that went well; Opportunities for improvement; Points of action"). A debriefing cognitive aid with suggested scripting supported facilitators, and the model was used to train 13 ED specialists, 1 social worker, 5 senior nurses and 18 ED registrars in 40 min of faculty training. Debriefers standardised the opening of CDs but were not instructed on what to discuss.
requirements: Faculty development in the blended approach (40 min training) plus a debriefing cognitive aid with suggested scripting
Debriefings of clinical events with at least 3 persons, occurring within 1 h of the event in an acute care setting
constraints: The authors state there is no universally applicable clinical debriefing method; all methods have pros and cons and should be applied with consideration of local historical, clinical and cultural context
target_learners: Emergency department healthcare providers and students, including physicians, nurses, social workers and registrars
target_learning_goals: Identification of improvement opportunities and latent patient safety threats
examples: The blended model was used for faculty development with 13 ED specialists, 1 social worker, 5 senior nurses and 18 ED registrars trained in CD

article_title: In-situ Simulation Use for Rapid Implementation and Process Improvement of COVID-19 Airway Management.
citation: Munzer Brendan W. MD, Bassin Benjamin S. MD, Peterson William J. MD, Tucker Ryan V. MD, Doan Jessica MD, Harvey Carrie MD, Sefa Nana MD, Hsu Cindy H. MD, PhD. (2020). In-situ Simulation Use for Rapid Implementation and Process Improvement of COVID-19 Airway Management. Western Journal of Emergency Medicine. https://doi.org/10.5811/westjem.2020.7.48159
title: In-situ COVID-19 airway management simulation scenario with deliberate practice and critical action checklist
description: An in-situ simulation scenario featuring a decompensating patient with COVID-19 requiring intubation, run three times daily before clinical shifts and limited to six participants in their typical roles. Following a pre-brief reviewing the algorithm, "the participants engaged in the simulation scenario as a team, using a deliberate practice framework to correct errors in real time, noted by a critical action checklist," followed by debriefing. The scenario is publicly available through the Association of American Medical Colleges iCollaborative.
requirements: Sessions limited to providers working the oncoming resuscitation-area shift to comply with social distancing guidelines
Teachers recruited on a volunteer basis and trained via a train-the-trainers framework with observation of a session
constraints: Due to national shortages of PPE, simulated equipment such as Styrofoam masks replicating N95s were used to practice donning and doffing techniques

target_learning_goals: PPE donning and doffing for high-risk aerosol-generating procedures
Role understanding and closed-loop communication in interprofessional airway teams
Intubation and post-intubation management under infection control precautions
examples: Between March 16–April 1, 2020, 93 physicians completed the training through 37 simulation sessions, reaching 86.7% of residents and 83.6% of faculty working ED shifts

article_title: Interactive Clinical Avatar Use in Pharmacist Preregistration Training: Design and Review.
citation: Jessica Thompson, Simon White, Stephen Chapman. (2020). Interactive Clinical Avatar Use in Pharmacist Preregistration Training: Design and Review. Journal of Medical Internet Research. https://doi.org/10.2196/17146
title: Three interactive clinical avatar simulations for pharmacist preregistration training
description: Three high-fidelity virtual patient simulations were built at Keele University on emergency hormonal contraception, calculation of renal function, and childhood illness (measles), chosen because "Due to training variations, trainees may find it difficult to demonstrate competence in these areas." Each case has an ideal pathway with decisions categorized as more or less favorable, and users receive spoken and textual feedback plus the ability to repeat the simulation. The EHC case uses a mix of multiple-choice and free-text inputs with a built-in consultation form; the renal case has users calculate renal function from hospital notes and a drug chart; the measles case uses two avatars with enlarged rash and Koplik spots images.
requirements: Case scripts must meet predefined learning objectives and be aligned via constructive alignment with the intended learning outcomes
Clinical content must be based on guidelines and resources pharmacists use in everyday practice
constraints: Free-text input was associated with software recognition problems, with users rewording phrases until recognized
target_learning_goals: renal function calculation and dose adjustment
diagnosis and triage of childhood illness
examples: A YouTube demonstration video of the EHC avatar simulation was created (Multimedia Appendix 1)

It replaces classroom-based lecturing alone and is designed to shift students "from passive to active participants" during clinical training. Access to electronic resources for the e-learning components

article_title: Models to predict injury, physical fitness failure and attrition in recruit training: a retrospective cohort study.
citation: Orr Robin M., Cohen Bruce S., Allison Stephen C., Bulathsinhala Lakmini, Zambraski Edward J., Jaffrey Mark. (2020). Models to predict injury, physical fitness failure and attrition in recruit training: a retrospective cohort study. Military Medical Research. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40779-020-00260-w
title: Designers of short training courses should treat entrants' initial fitness level as a critically important factor in curriculum design
description: The article concludes that entry fitness should drive curriculum design decisions, especially for short courses. Its conclusion states that "fitness level at the commencement of training is a critically important factor to consider when designing the course curriculum, particularly short courses", because the 28-day course showed much higher fitness-test failure (30.0% vs 12.1%) despite similar attrition. Initial fitness test scores (push-ups, sit-ups, shuttle run) were among the retained predictors in the models.
requirements: Requires entry screening of cardiovascular fitness (the 20-m MSFT) and other fitness components before course commencement, as the study's Pre-enlistment Fitness Assessment provided.
constraints: The authors caution that the identified predictors of failure and attrition "should be viewed with caution" given model AUCs of only failing-to-fair accuracy.
target_learners: Army recruits entering basic training with varying fitness levels
target_learning_goals: Physical preparedness to pass final fitness assessment and complete training without injury
examples: The 28-day reservist course produced a 30.0% final fitness assessment failure rate versus 12.1% in the 80-day course; the authors suggest the shorter course may not adequately physically prepare some recruits for subsequent training such as infantry or artillery training.

article_title: Teaching the National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale to Paramedics (E-Learning vs Video): Randomized Controlled Trial.
citation: Koka A, Suppan L, Cottet P, Carrera E, Stuby L, Suppan M. (2020). Teaching the National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale to Paramedics (E-Learning vs Video): Randomized Controlled Trial. Journal of Medical Internet Research. https://doi.org/10.2196/18358
title: Prefer highly interactive e-learning over non-interactive video when teaching structured assessment scales to paramedics, provided completion time is acceptable
description: The article's results support recommending highly interactive self-paced e-learning modules over passive video for teaching the NIHSS to paramedics: the e-learning group scored better, was more satisfied, and was more likely to recommend the course. The trade-off the article states is time — the module took longer to complete (93 vs 59 minutes) — though most e-learning participants judged the duration adequate. The authors conclude the module "should be improved according to the study results and user feedback" and tested in the field.
requirements: Interactive module design with per-item chapters, embedded clinical video extracts for every assessed item, and feedback on wrong answers
constraints: Results from a single small trial in one prehospital system; the study assessed learning material only and might not predict field performance
target_learning_goals: Accurate prehospital use of the NIHSS for stroke identification and triage
examples: The Geneva RCT assigned 39 paramedics 1:1 to the interactive module or the subtitled Lyden video and compared quiz performance and satisfaction

article_title: Impact of a national basic skills in colonoscopy course on trainee performance: An interrupted time series analysis.
citation: Siau K, Hodson J, Anderson JT, Valori R, Smith G, Hagan P, Iacucci M, Dunckley P. (2020). Impact of a national basic skills in colonoscopy course on trainee performance: An interrupted time series analysis. World Journal of Gastroenterology. https://doi.org/10.3748/wjg.v26.i23.3283
title: Interrupted time series analysis as a method for measuring the impact of training courses on trainee outcomes
description: The article applies interrupted time series regression to evaluate a training intervention against trainees' natural learning curves. A linear regression models the outcome with three covariates: procedure number relative to the course, a variable capturing how the gradient changed post-course, and a dichotomous course-attendance variable that "looked for any step-change improvement immediately after the course". The authors argue this method enables estimation of post-course performance while accounting for pre-course trajectories, and propose it "may be used across different training courses for research and quality assurance purposes".
requirements: Sufficient pre- and post-course outcome data per trainee (the study required at least 25 procedures pre-course)
constraints: The authors note a limitation of the models: a continuing linear trend would not be feasible as outcome rates approach a ceiling effect, which may explain the significant gradient changes in the intermediate group
target_learners: Researchers and quality-assurance bodies evaluating training interventions
target_learning_goals: Measuring the impact of training courses on trainee performance outcomes
examples: Applied to CIR and PICI outcomes over 50 procedures pre and post course in three experience strata

citation: Rauch A, Hahnel SF, Schierz O. (2020). Development of an instructional movie illustrating a standardized clinical examination on patients with TMD symptoms. GMS Journal for Medical Education 37(4), Doc39. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC7346288/
title: Use instructional video as a supplement to, not a replacement for, instructor-based practical training
description: The article recommends video-based learning as an adjunct for learning clinical examination skills: "video-based learning should not be used as the sole method to learn the examination technique, but rather as a supplementary tool alongside classical instructor-based practical training." For inexperienced learners, supervisor feedback is described as integral; for experienced users, video can serve as just-in-time refresher training.
requirements: Access to classical instructor-based practical training alongside the video
Supervisor feedback for inexperienced learners
constraints: The article cites Swedish evidence that manual-plus-video preparation achieved diagnoses of similar accuracy to practical-course training, but positions video as supplementary
examples: The authors note a Swedish research group found individual preparation with manual and instructional video achieved diagnoses with similar accuracy to examiners who attended a practical training course
key_sources: Rauch A, Hahnel SF, Schierz O. (2020). Development of an instructional movie illustrating a standardized clinical examination on patients with TMD symptoms. GMS Journal for Medical Education 37(4), Doc39. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC7346288/

article_title: Relationship between Emotional Intelligence, Cybervictimization, and Academic Performance in Secondary School Students.
citation: Martínez-Martínez, A.M.; López-Liria, R.; Aguilar-Parra, J.M.; Trigueros, R.; Morales-Gázquez, M.J.; Rocamora-Pérez, P. (2020). Relationship between Emotional Intelligence, Cybervictimization, and Academic Performance in Secondary School Students. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health 17, 7717. https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph17217717
title: Integrate emotional education and EI training into bullying and cyberbullying prevention in schools
description: The article recommends that schools promote socio-emotional development programs, stating that "training or education in EI issues should be integrated into bullying and cyberbullying education in schools". Emotional education is presented as a prevention mechanism: promoting it in the classroom helps students understand their emotions and learn alternative skills to violence. The authors link this to school climate, classroom management, and discipline.
requirements: Schools must take responsibility for prevention and early detection of incidents
Programs should place emphasis on observers, raising awareness of their role
constraints: Findings rest on self-reported data and one region/educational stage; the authors state generalization should be with some caution
examples: The study measured EI with the TMMS-24 and cybervictimization with a 26-item risk-factor questionnaire, then modeled their relations with grades
key_sources: Martínez-Martínez, A.M.; López-Liria, R.; Aguilar-Parra, J.M.; Trigueros, R.; Morales-Gázquez, M.J.; Rocamora-Pérez, P. (2020). Relationship between Emotional Intelligence, Cybervictimization, and Academic Performance in Secondary School Students. article_title: Effects of a mixed media education intervention program on increasing knowledge, attitude, and compliance with standard precautions among nursing students: A randomized controlled trial.
citation: Xiong Peng, Zhang Jun, Wang Xiaohui, Wu Tat Leong, Hall Brian J. (2017). Effects of a mixed media education intervention program on increasing knowledge, attitude, and compliance with standard precautions among nursing students: A randomized controlled trial. American Journal of Infection Control. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ajic.2016.11.006
title: Pair group-based mixed media instruction with individual follow-up supervision and feedback to reinforce standard precautions learning
description: Beyond the group sessions, each intervention participant received "15-20 minutes of individual online supervision and feedback sessions following each class," during which the researcher asked about difficulties, reviewed uploaded materials, and encouraged continued practice. This individualized follow-up is presented as an integral component of the effective intervention, complementing lectures, videos, and role-play with personalized support. The article reports the intervention was effective in improving knowledge, attitude, and compliance with standard precautions.
requirements: A researcher available to conduct one-on-one telephone or online calls after each session
An online communication platform for uploading materials and answering questions between sessions
constraints: The article does not isolate the individual supervision component's effect from the group sessions, so its separate contribution is not established
examples: After each session the researcher asked each student: "How do you feel about implementing SPs during these 2 weeks?" and "Did you perform your nursing procedures using standard precautions?"
key_sources: Xiong Peng, Zhang Jun, Wang Xiaohui, Wu Tat Leong, Hall Brian J. (2017). Effects of a mixed media education intervention program on increasing knowledge, attitude, and compliance with standard precautions among nursing students: A randomized controlled trial. American Journal of Infection Control. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ajic.2016.11.006

article_title: Interprofessional team-based learning (TBL): how do students engage?
citation: Burgess A, Kalman E, Haq I, Leaver A, Roberts C, Bleasel J. (2020). Interprofessional team-based learning (TBL): how do students engage? BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-020-02024-5
title: Interprofessional 'back pain' TBL module for medical and physiotherapy students
description: A 2.5-hour interprofessional TBL session on back pain piloted within the Musculoskeletal Sciences block, joining Year 1 medical students with Year 2 physiotherapy students (311 participants). The article states: "Key principles of our TBL design included: prescribed out-of-class preparation, pre-class individual tests, and in-class team tests, immediate feedback, and clinical problem-solving activities." Physiotherapy students were randomly allocated two or three per established medical team of four to six, and each class had an interprofessional facilitator team.
requirements: compulsory pre-class readings and pre-recorded lectures
an online 10-MCQ IRAT before class
facilitators trained in TBL facilitation
shared learning outcomes aligned with both curricula
constraints: the mismatch in student cohort numbers compromised the TBL format
physiotherapy students had no prior TBL experience
held outside regular weekly schedules due to timetabling
target_learning_goals: describe vertebral column anatomy and function
apply spinal cord and nerve anatomy and physiology
examples: Two or three physiotherapy students were randomly allocated to existing medical TBL teams; four TBL classes ran simultaneously with 11 or 12 teams each
key_sources: Burgess A, Kalman E, Haq I, Leaver A, Roberts C, Bleasel J. (2020). Interprofessional team-based learning (TBL): how do students engage? BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-020-02024-5

article_title: Preparing undergraduate students for clinical work in a complex environment: evaluation of an e-learning module on physiotherapy in the intensive care unit.
citation: Major ME, Ramaekers SPJ, Engelbert RHH, Van der Schaaf M. (2020). Preparing undergraduate students for clinical work in a complex environment: evaluation of an e-learning module on physiotherapy in the intensive care unit. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-020-02035-2
title: Integrate e-learning with, or closely connect it to, students' clinical placement when preparing for complex clinical environments
description: The article's central design recommendation: e-learning can sufficiently prepare students for complex clinical work only when its timing and content are tied to the clinical experience that follows. The authors conclude it works "as long as it is integrated with, or closely connected to, the students' clinical placement", and that "Timing in which the educational tool is offered in relation to the clinical experience is essential". Reasoning-provoking material completed during the rotation could support higher competence levels.
requirements: The e-learning module must be completed prior to the clinical rotation and paired with supervised clinical practice
constraints: E-learning alone could not achieve higher-level reasoning, equipment handling and emergency preparedness
target_learners: Final-year undergraduate health-professions students preparing for complex clinical rotations
target_learning_goals: Preparedness for clinical tasks in complex environments
examples: The module was implemented as a compulsory course completed before ICU placements, with a case report about an ICU patient observed during the placement determining the final course grade
key_sources: Major ME, Ramaekers SPJ, Engelbert RHH, Van der Schaaf M. (2020). Preparing undergraduate students for clinical work in a complex environment: evaluation of an e-learning module on physiotherapy in the intensive care unit. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-020-02035-2

article_title: Adding to the debate on the numbers of options for MCQs: the case for not being limited to MCQs with three, four or five options.
citation: Tweed Mike. (2019). Adding to the debate on the numbers of options for MCQs: the case for not being limited to MCQs with three, four or five options. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-019-1801-x
title: MCQ option lists should include both psychometrically and clinically important distractors
description: The article argues option lists should be "sufficient to include both psychometrically important distractors and clinically important distractors". Because the numbers of each differ across content areas, their inclusion likely requires more than three or four options and is best supported by variable option numbers.
requirements: A policy of variable option numbers
examples: Panels of clinicians can stratify incorrect options for potential (un)safeness

article_title: Development of an empathy and clarity rating scale to measure the effect of medical improv on end-of-first-year OCSE performance: a pilot study.
citation: Terregino Carol A., Copeland H. Liesel, Sarfaty Suzanne C., Lantz-Gefroh Valeri, Hoffmann-Longtin Krista. (2019). Development of an empathy and clarity rating scale to measure the effect of medical improv on end-of-first-year OCSE performance: a pilot study. Medical Education Online. https://doi.org/10.1080/10872981.2019.1666537
title: Sequence communication ratings inductively: write behavioral comments first, then rate
description: The ECRS instructs raters to first record narrative observations of a learner's behaviors and only then assign a numeric rating using the behavioral anchors. Expert raters found "it more helpful to write down specific behaviors of the learner, and then give a rating for the behavior," so that the rater attends to the context of the interaction before evaluating. The final instructions specify ratings from 5 = desired behaviors to 1 = ineffective communication, with intermediate points based on the adjustment needed to reach desired performance.
requirements: Raters must be willing to write narrative comments for each behavior before assigning a numeric rating
constraints: The narrative-comments step may challenge current electronic scoring systems for an OSCE
target_learning_goals: empathetic and clear communication with patients
examples: During reviews with 12 clinician educators, the expert faculty proposed the inductive sequence, and the scale instructions were revised accordingly
key_sources: Terregino Carol A., Copeland H. Liesel, Sarfaty Suzanne C., Lantz-Gefroh Valeri, Hoffmann-Longtin Krista. (2019).
