Medical Education Online. https://doi.org/10.1080/10872981.2019.1666537

article_title: Measuring the impact of an interdisciplinary learning project on nursing, architecture and landscape design students' empathy.
citation: Donnelly S, Dean S, Razavy S, Levett-Jones T. (2019). Measuring the impact of an interdisciplinary learning project on nursing, architecture and landscape design students’ empathy. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0215795
title: Interdisciplinary refuge design project: three collaborative meetings, fieldwork and stakeholder panel over a 12-week semester
description: A 12-week authentic interdisciplinary learning experience in which nursing, architecture and landscape students enrolled in concurrent separate subjects collaborated on designing women’s refuges. "The students from all disciplines met on three formal occasions of three-hour sessions throughout the 12-week semester as well as negotiated out of class meetings." The first meeting formed mixed-discipline teams working on refuge-user case studies, the second involved fieldwork with service providers at a local council, and the third was a presentation of design guides containing ten best-practice principles to a stakeholder panel. Nursing students shared knowledge from four-week placements in women’s health services to support the design students’ understanding of user needs.
requirements: Participation of all three disciplines as a simulation of a disciplinary consultation team, with stakeholder access for fieldwork and panel presentation
constraints: Nursing and architecture subjects were electives while landscape was core, so the cohorts differed in motivation and prior exposure
target_learning_goals: understanding the needs and perspectives of refuge service users
examples: Mixed-discipline teams of two nursing, one architecture and one landscape student each worked on a case study describing a refuge user’s background, situation and needs
Designs addressed safety, access to sunlight, cross-ventilation and flexible room layouts, including external play areas with specific planting for children experiencing anxiety and depression
key_sources: Donnelly S, Dean S, Razavy S, Levett-Jones T. (2019). Measuring the impact of an interdisciplinary learning project on nursing, architecture and landscape design students’ empathy. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0215795

article_title: Institutional differences in USMLE Step 1 and 2 CK performance: Cross-sectional study of 89 US allopathic medical schools.
citation: Burk-Rafel J, Pulido RW, Elfanagely Y, Kolars JC. (2019). Institutional differences in USMLE Step 1 and 2 CK performance: Cross-sectional study of 89 US allopathic medical schools. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0224675
title: Institutional dataset of self-reported GPA, MCAT, and USMLE scores for 89 US allopathic medical schools (2012–2014)
description: A tabulated dataset of institution-level aggregate means and percentages for 131 US allopathic medical schools, drawn from US News and World Report "Best Graduate Schools" (2008–2016 editions) and AAMC Medical School Admission Requirements (2008–2012 editions). Complete USMLE data were available for 89 schools (54 public, 35 private), representing 39,615 Step 1 and 39,252 Step 2 CK examinees. The article states "All relevant data are within the paper and its Supporting Information files," including S1 Table listing per-institution means.
requirements: Data were self-reported by institutions via third-party publications; the NBME does not publish institutional score performance
constraints: Only 89 of 131 schools (68%) reported complete data; non-reporters may differ in important ways
It is unclear how institutions formulated their institutional MCAT averages, which can introduce bias
target_learners: medical students in US allopathic medical schools
target_learning_goals: assessing institutional medical knowledge outcomes on USMLE Step 1 and Step 2 CK
examples: Table 1 reports 3-year combined institutional means: Step 1 229.7 (SD 5.5) and Step 2 CK 238.3 (SD 4.7) for the 89 reporting schools
key_sources: Burk-Rafel J, Pulido RW, Elfanagely Y, Kolars JC. (2019). Institutional differences in USMLE Step 1 and 2 CK performance: Cross-sectional study of 89 US allopathic medical schools. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0224675

article_title: Guidelines: The dos, don'ts and don't knows of remediation in medical education.
citation: Chou Calvin L., Kalet Adina, Costa Manuel Joao, Cleland Jennifer, Winston Kalman. (2019). Guidelines: The dos, don’ts and don’t knows of remediation in medical education. Perspectives on Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40037-019-00544-5
title: Intensive, longitudinal tutoring with study skills, collaboratively designed plans, frequent high-quality feedback, and individualized assessment as the design of effective remediation
description: The guidelines specify the design of effective remediation as trainees undergoing "intensive, longitudinal tutoring with emphasis on study skills, collaboratively designed plans, frequent high-quality feedback, and individualized assessment". A common hallmark of successful programs is regular pre-arranged meetings to assess progress and achievement of goals, with high-quality feedback and assessments determining mid-course corrections or consequences. For medical knowledge remediation, ongoing facilitated small-group work uses evidence-based strategies such as retrieval rehearsal, interleaved practice, generating explanations, and writing multiple-choice questions.
requirements: Regular pre-arranged meetings to assess progress and achievement of goals, with high-quality feedback and assessments determining the need for mid-course corrections
Remediation plans collaboratively designed with the learner, targeting both cognitive and affective domains and using relevant academic content as exemplars for study skills
constraints: A dose effect for clinical skills remediation is unclear, although the approach is quite similar to that of pre-clerkship remediation
It is unknown exactly how many interventions are necessary for optimal performance, and too many interventions may decrease self-efficacy or independence
target_learners: Struggling medical trainees from beginning medical school through specialty training
target_learning_goals: Medical knowledge and clinical skills competence
Study skills and self-regulated learning strategies
examples: The guidelines describe pre-clerkship remediation in which fifteen or more sessions doubled long-term pass rates over ten or fewer sessions
Successful programs combine content development with improving self-regulated learning strategies, using relevant academic content as exemplars for study skills
key_sources: Chou Calvin L., Kalet Adina, Costa Manuel Joao, Cleland Jennifer, Winston Kalman. (2019). Guidelines: The dos, don’ts and don’t knows of remediation in medical education. Perspectives on Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40037-019-00544-5

article_title: Operating room technician trainees teach medical students - an inter-professional peer teaching approach for infection prevention strategies in the operation room.
citation: Breckwoldt Jan, Knecht Monika, Massée Ralph, Flach Barbara, Hofmann-Huber Caroline, Kaap-Fröhlich Sylvia, Witt Claudia M., Aeberhard Ruth, Sax Hugo. (2019). Operating room technician trainees teach medical students - an inter-professional peer teaching approach for infection prevention strategies in the operation room. Antimicrobial Resistance and Infection Control. https://doi.org/10.1186/s13756-019-0526-2
title: Three combined educational strategies for inter-professional peer teaching of infection prevention
description: The article grounds its module in three named educational strategies: establishing a meaningful overarching learning objective, using an inter-professional setting for early professional identity formation, and using near-peer teaching to strengthen the self-confidence of teaching peers. The authors state they "drew on three specific well-founded educational strategies" and connected patient safety to inter-professional collaboration, arguing this combination explains the module's success in complex OR team settings.
requirements: Requires an emotionally engaging overarching goal (patient safety) that legitimizes the module within both curricula
constraints: Evidence for actual learning gain was not demonstrated; outcomes were limited to reaction-level evaluation
target_learning_goals: infection prevention behavior in the operating room
inter-professional collaboration and patient safety culture
examples: Patient safety was set as the overarching learning outcome linking the abstract theme of infection prevention to a collaborative OR team goal; the module was placed early in both curricula at comparable training stages
key_sources: Breckwoldt Jan, Knecht Monika, Massée Ralph, Flach Barbara, Hofmann-Huber Caroline, Kaap-Fröhlich Sylvia, Witt Claudia M., Aeberhard Ruth, Sax Hugo. (2019). Operating room technician trainees teach medical students - an inter-professional peer teaching approach for infection prevention strategies in the operation room. Antimicrobial Resistance and Infection Control. https://doi.org/10.1186/s13756-019-0526-2

article_title: A brief interactive training with medical students improves their diabetes knowledge about hypoglycemia.
citation: Beverly Elizabeth A., Ritholz Marilyn D., Rennie Rochelle G., Mort Sophia C. (2019). A brief interactive training with medical students improves their diabetes knowledge about hypoglycemia. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-019-1615-x
title: Two-hour interactive hypoglycemia and glucagon training session
description: A two-hour interactive lecture developed as an alternative to a standard 10-minute didactic PowerPoint, covering diabetes self-management education and support topics including "hypoglycemia treatment". It used rhetorical and straightforward questions, a group training exercise, a hypoglycemia treatment kit (glucose tablets, gel, juice boxes, meter), and demonstration of an emergency glucagon administration kit followed by group practice, delivered on three campuses by an experienced behavioral diabetes researcher.
requirements: An experienced lecturer trained in interactive lecturing
Glucagon administration kits available on all campuses for group practice
A hypoglycemia treatment kit with glucose products and a blood glucose meter
constraints: Evaluated only with second-year medical students in an Endocrine and Metabolism course at one medical school
examples: Delivered January 9, 2019 in lecture rooms across three campuses; 217 students completed pre- and post-assessments
key_sources: Beverly Elizabeth A., Ritholz Marilyn D., Rennie Rochelle G., Mort Sophia C. (2019). A brief interactive training with medical students improves their diabetes knowledge about hypoglycemia. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-019-1615-x

article_title: Simulation-based interdisciplinary education improves intern attitudes and outlook toward colleagues in other disciplines.
citation: Bullard Mark J., Fox Sean M., Wares Catherine M., Heffner Alan C., Stephens Casey, Rossi Laura. (2019). Simulation-based interdisciplinary education improves intern attitudes and outlook toward colleagues in other disciplines. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-019-1700-1
title: Interprofessionality and Intergroup Contact Theory as explanatory frameworks for why interdisciplinary simulation affects attitudes
description: The article interprets its findings through two paradigms. D'Armour's interprofessionality is defined as "the development of a cohesive practice between professionals from different disciplines", and Allport's Intergroup Contact Theory proposes that attitude change requires conditions beyond simply assembling a mixed group. The authors argue the 4Cs curriculum inadvertently met these conditions: all interns were of equal training level, shared common goals, had cooperative non-competitive discussions, and had institutional support.
requirements: Learning environments need conditions beyond mere contact: learners of equal status, commonality in goals, support from authorities, and a cooperative forum
constraints: Having different disciplines learn together in the simulation environment is not sufficient to produce improved interprofessionality
target_learning_goals: interdisciplinary attitudes, collegiality, and collaborative practice
examples: The 4Cs curriculum placed interns from seven disciplines in small mixed groups with shared debriefings, though attitudes were never an explicit curricular objective
key_sources: Bullard Mark J., Fox Sean M., Wares Catherine M., Heffner Alan C., Stephens Casey, Rossi Laura. (2019). Simulation-based interdisciplinary education improves intern attitudes and outlook toward colleagues in other disciplines. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-019-1700-1

article_title: Using in situ simulation to improve care of the acutely ill patient by enhancing interprofessional working: a qualitative proof of concept study in primary care in England.
citation: Halls Amy, Kanagasundaram Mohan, Lau-Walker Margaret, Diack Hilary, Bettles Simon. (2019). Using in situ simulation to improve care of the acutely ill patient by enhancing interprofessional working: a qualitative proof of concept study in primary care in England. BMJ Open. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjopen-2018-028572
title: In situ cardiac arrest simulation scenario with actors, high-fidelity mannequin swap, and filmed debrief for whole primary care teams
description: A research-team-designed in situ simulation of a cardiac arrest occurring in a GP waiting room. An actor collapses and is swapped for a high-fidelity mannequin behind a dividing screen so staff can use chest compressions and their own defibrillator; a second actor plays a distressed relative and a third an annoyed patient. The scenario ran for approximately 20 minutes followed by a roughly 45-minute debrief using 'the diamond' debriefing method, with filming tagged for the debrief. All consenting staff had an active role with no observers.
requirements: Actors and rehearsals to elaborate the clinical outline and pre-empt participant questions
The centre's own emergency equipment and space appropriate for the simulation
A separate private room for the postsimulation debrief and signage to shield the public from distress
constraints: Space constraints in each centre provided an additional challenge, though viewed as beneficial
Filming increased participant stress levels for some
target_learners: Clinical and non-clinical primary care staff (GPs, nurses, healthcare assistants, managers, receptionists, administration)
target_learning_goals: Managing acute medical emergencies as a team
examples: Three general practices in south east England ran the scenario between May and August 2018 with nine staff per centre, followed by interviews within a fortnight
key_sources: Halls Amy, Kanagasundaram Mohan, Lau-Walker Margaret, Diack Hilary, Bettles Simon. (2019). article_title: Does academic interest play a more important role in medical sciences than in other disciplines? A nationwide cross-sectional study in China.
citation: Wu Hongbin, Zheng Juan, Li Shan, Guo Jianru. (2019). Does academic interest play a more important role in medical sciences than in other disciplines? A nationwide cross-sectional study in China. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-019-1737-1
title: Interest-effort-perseverance mechanism account of the interest-achievement relationship
description: The article adopts, from prior studies, a mechanism account in which academic interest raises achievement indirectly through learning behaviour rather than through cognitive capacity alone. As the authors put it, "academic interest affects achievement through higher effort and perseverance in learning, demonstrating an add-on effect in addition to cognitive ability, which affects achievement through quicker and deep-level understanding". The article also offers discipline-specific explanations, such as interest helping natural-sciences students cope with negative affect, but presents these as interpretations rather than tested results.
requirements: The account presumes that interest produces sustained engagement behaviours (effort, perseverance) that translate into performance
constraints: The article presents this mechanism as suggested by previous studies, not as a mechanism tested in this study
examples: The authors' proposed explanation that natural sciences are demanding subjects where students experience more anxiety and less enjoyment, making interest particularly important
key_sources: Wu Hongbin, Zheng Juan, Li Shan, Guo Jianru. (2019). Does academic interest play a more important role in medical sciences than in other disciplines? A nationwide cross-sectional study in China. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-019-1737-1

article_title: Evaluating Academic Mentorship Programs in Low- and Middle-Income Country Institutions: Proposed Framework and Metrics.
citation: Chi BH, Belizan JM, Blas MM, Chuang A, Wilson MD, Chibwesha CJ, Farquhar C, Cohen CR, Raj T. (2019). Evaluating Academic Mentorship Programs in Low- and Middle-Income Country Institutions: Proposed Framework and Metrics. Am J Trop Med Hyg 100(1 Suppl): 36-41. https://doi.org/10.4269/ajtmh.18-0561
title: Evaluate mentorship programs at the institutional level, not only the individual pair
description: The article argues that mentorship evaluation should emphasize measurement at the program, department, or school level rather than only the individual mentor–mentee pair. It states: "we emphasize the role of measurement and evaluation at the institutional level. This perspective has been largely overlooked in the mentorship literature." Institutional-level data can identify gaps in support, direct resources, demonstrate return on investment, and help LMIC institutions optimize management of their mentoring resources.
requirements: Evaluation plans must clearly articulate institutional priorities so expectations between mentors, mentees, and institutions are aligned
constraints: Downstream metrics such as career advancement and academic productivity have inherent attribution problems, which the authors acknowledge
target_learners: Program administrators, department chairs, and institutional leaders in LMIC institutions
target_learning_goals: Building and sustaining institutional mentoring capacity
examples: The framework's Table 1 pairs each domain's individual-level metrics with institutional-level counterparts, e.g., aggregate scholarship assessments at the program, department, or school level
key_sources: Chi BH, Belizan JM, Blas MM, Chuang A, Wilson MD, Chibwesha CJ, Farquhar C, Cohen CR, Raj T. (2019). Evaluating Academic Mentorship Programs in Low- and Middle-Income Country Institutions: Proposed Framework and Metrics. Am J Trop Med Hyg 100(1 Suppl): 36-41. https://doi.org/10.4269/ajtmh.18-0561

article_title: The podiatric surgery theatre environment in the UK; is it conducive to learning? A quantitative study using the surgical theatre educational environment measure (STEEM).
citation: Austen Thomas, Otter Simon. (2019). The podiatric surgery theatre environment in the UK; is it conducive to learning? A quantitative study using the surgical theatre educational environment measure (STEEM). Journal of Foot and Ankle Research. https://doi.org/10.1186/s13047-018-0312-z
title: Informal workplace learning as the framing account of podiatric surgical theatre training
description: The article frames the podiatric surgery theatre as a workplace, not classroom, environment in which learning is informal: "a naturally occurring form of learning based in and around personal experience of situations". Drawing on Manuti et al., Eraut and Ajjawi and Higgs, it holds that learning occurs through problem solving, mentoring, coaching and job shadowing, activated by anticipated or actual problems, with individual characteristics such as intellectual curiosity, self-directedness and self-efficacy affecting its quality. Eraut's factors — challenge and value of work, feedback, support, confidence and commitment — and context factors are presented as shaping workplace learning, supporting the value of evaluating the theatre environment itself.
requirements: A workplace environment where the principal objective is not learning but where problems activate learning; a mentor (the consultant) to guide the trainee
constraints: Factors' importance will differ in different situations with different people; learning is situated and enriched in practice itself, so it is best done in the workplace
target_learners: Podiatric surgical trainees and registrars in UK podiatric surgery departments
target_learning_goals: Surgical skills and clinical reasoning developed through experiential workplace learning
examples: The article situates the podiatric surgery route within this framework, with the consultant acting as a mentor through an otherwise formal route whose experiential learning makes the environment informal
key_sources: Austen Thomas, Otter Simon. (2019). The podiatric surgery theatre environment in the UK; is it conducive to learning? A quantitative study using the surgical theatre educational environment measure (STEEM). Journal of Foot and Ankle Research. https://doi.org/10.1186/s13047-018-0312-z

article_title: The subject-dependent, cumulative, and recency association of aerobic fitness with academic performance in Taiwanese junior high school students.
citation: Hsieh Shu-Shih, Tsai Jia-Ren, Chang Shao-Hsi, Ho Jen-Yu, Chen Jui-Fu, Chen Po-Hsi, Sung Yao-Ting, Hung Tsung-Min. (2019). The subject-dependent, cumulative, and recency association of aerobic fitness with academic performance in Taiwanese junior high school students. BMC Pediatrics. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12887-018-1384-4
title: Increase time allocated to aerobic exercise in the school curriculum as part of a strategy to enhance academic performance
description: Based on observed positive associations between aerobic fitness and exam performance across subjects, the article recommends that "educators and/or policy makers might consider increasing time allocated to aerobic exercise in the school curriculum". It notes schools are cutting physical education to expand academic instruction, and that Taiwanese junior high PE (90 min per week) falls far short of ACSM guideline levels of 60-min or more daily exercise.
requirements: Students must have opportunities to reach and maintain high aerobic fitness levels (top 25% of age- and sex-adjusted norms) sustained across school years for the largest observed benefits.
constraints: The evidence is associational; the article states the design does not allow a definitive causal conclusion.
target_learning_goals: Academic achievement across math, science, social science and language subjects
examples: The study compared five fitness-pattern groups across three years and found students highly fit in all years outperformed two- and one-year groups by about 2 and 4 exam points respectively.
key_sources: Hsieh Shu-Shih, Tsai Jia-Ren, Chang Shao-Hsi, Ho Jen-Yu, Chen Jui-Fu, Chen Po-Hsi, Sung Yao-Ting, Hung Tsung-Min. (2019). The subject-dependent, cumulative, and recency association of aerobic fitness with academic performance in Taiwanese junior high school students. BMC Pediatrics. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12887-018-1384-4

article_title: The effect of an empathy role-play program for operating room nursing students.
citation: Larti N, Ashouri E, Aarabi A. (2018). The effects of an empathy role-playing program for operating room nursing students in Iran. J Educ Eval Health Prof. https://doi.org/10.3352/jeehp.2018.15.29
title: Integrate theoretical empathy instruction with role-playing practice rather than relying on either component alone
description: The article argues that improved empathy scores were not produced by theoretical training or role-playing by itself: "integrating theoretical issues with the role-playing technique could affect empathy scores in participants after the intervention." Teaching students who had received no prior empathy education requires learning techniques and theory, then consolidating skills through practice. Because the operating room can be a stressful learning environment, engaging techniques such as role-playing are described as helpful.
requirements: Prior theoretical instruction on empathy concepts and techniques, followed by practice consolidating skills
constraints: The claim concerns operating room nursing students who had previously received no education about empathy
target_learners: Health profession students without prior empathy education
examples: The experimental program paired two theory/discussion sessions with a role-playing scenario session before post-testing.
key_sources: Larti N, Ashouri E, Aarabi A. (2018). The effects of an empathy role-playing program for operating room nursing students in Iran. J Educ Eval Health Prof. https://doi.org/10.3352/jeehp.2018.15.29

article_title: Investigating the self-study phase of an inverted biochemistry classroom - collaborative dyadic learning makes the difference.
citation: Kühl Susanne J., Schneider Achim, Kestler Hans A., Toberer Matthias, Kühl Michael, Fischer Martin R. (2019). Investigating the self-study phase of an inverted biochemistry classroom – collaborative dyadic learning makes the difference. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-019-1497-y
title: In inverted-classroom designs, instruct learners to prepare in collaborative dyads during the self-study phase
description: The article's central design recommendation is that the instructions given for the self-study phase, more than the material, determine learning success in an e-learning-based inverted classroom. Students "were told to deal with the tasks from the self-study phases in cooperation with a learning partner of their own choice". Dyadic preparation produced higher test scores, motivation, interest and time on task than individual preparation. The authors state "Instructed collaborative dyadic learning had the highest success rate in the learning outcome".
requirements: Students must actually prepare before the on-site phase; the method "can only be implemented successfully if the students prepare for the on-site phase".
constraints: Only 64% (self-study phase 1) and 58.7% (self-study phase 2) of the collaborative group actually prepared in a learning dyad as instructed; the study is mono-institutional with two lecturers who are also investigators.
examples: In the study, the collaborative group was told to solve the self-study tasks with a learning partner of their own choice, with dyads formed during on-site phase 0.
key_sources: Kühl Susanne J., Schneider Achim, Kestler Hans A., Toberer Matthias, Kühl Michael, Fischer Martin R. (2019). Investigating the self-study phase of an inverted biochemistry classroom – collaborative dyadic learning makes the difference. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-019-1497-y

article_title: Inappropriately Firing Defibrillator: A Simulation Case for Emergency Medicine Residents.
citation: Thorpe Rachel Lauren, Rohant Namit, Cryer Michael, Gainey Christopher. (2019). Inappropriately Firing Defibrillator: A Simulation Case for Emergency Medicine Residents. MedEdPORTAL. https://doi.org/10.15766/mep_2374-8265.10808
title: Inappropriately firing defibrillator simulation case with lecture, high-fidelity simulator, and debriefing materials
description: A published simulation case in which learners first attend an informational lecture on normal defibrillator function, then manage a simulated 63-year-old male with supraventricular tachycardia and an inappropriately firing defibrillator in groups of four. Learners "needed to recognize the inappropriately firing defibrillator, inactivate it with a magnet, and treat the arrhythmia." The package includes surveys, a PowerPoint lecture, case template, laboratory results and images, a critical actions checklist, and debriefing materials as appendices.
requirements: A simulation room equipped with a high-fidelity simulator, patient monitor, code cart, defibrillator, and pacemaker magnet
A simulation specialist and an emergency medicine or cardiology content expert to administer the case and debriefing
constraints: The authors note it may be difficult for some educators to engage cardiology experts, so PowerPoint and debriefing materials are provided to allow implementation without additional assistance
target_learners: Emergency medicine residents of all levels of training
target_learning_goals: Identify an inappropriately firing ICD in the setting of a tachyarrhythmia
Manage an inappropriately firing ICD, including magnet use and transcutaneous pads
Develop a differential diagnosis for inappropriate ICD firing including SVT
Manage stable SVT with vagal maneuvers and synchronized cardioversion
examples: Implemented with 16 emergency medicine residents in four groups of four during a routine educational conference day
key_sources: Thorpe Rachel Lauren, Rohant Namit, Cryer Michael, Gainey Christopher. (2019). Inappropriately Firing Defibrillator: A Simulation Case for Emergency Medicine Residents. MedEdPORTAL. https://doi.org/10.15766/mep_2374-8265.10808

article_title: Clinical Virtual Simulation in Nursing Education: Randomized Controlled Trial.
citation: José Miguel Padilha, Paulo Puga Machado, Ana Ribeiro, José Ramos, Patrício Costa. (2019). Clinical Virtual Simulation in Nursing Education: Randomized Controlled Trial. Journal of Medical Internet Research. https://doi.org/10.2196/11529
title: Integrate clinical virtual simulation with other pedagogical strategies and simulator resources rather than using it in isolation
description: The authors recommend that clinical virtual simulation act as a complementary strategy: "The use of clinical virtual simulation as a pedagogical strategy should be integrated and coordinated with other pedagogical strategies in classes and with other resources, such as high-, medium-, and low-tech simulators" to maximize development of cognitive, affective, and psychomotor skills. In the trial it was itself combined with briefing, simulation, and debriefing within a case-based learning approach.
requirements: Coordination with other pedagogical strategies and simulation resources in the curriculum
constraints: Evidence comes from a single context, second-year nursing students, one course on the respiratory process
examples: The experimental lesson combined the Body Interact virtual scenario with a case-based learning approach and a briefing–simulation–debriefing structure led by the regular subject teacher
key_sources: José Miguel Padilha, Paulo Puga Machado, Ana Ribeiro, José Ramos, Patrício Costa. (2019). Clinical Virtual Simulation in Nursing Education: Randomized Controlled Trial. Journal of Medical Internet Research. https://doi.org/10.2196/11529
